questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman reports fatigue, constipation and cold intolerance. Thyroid function tests show a markedly raised TSH and a low free T4. Which diagnosis best explains this pattern?

options.B: Secondary hypothyroidism

questions.correct_answer: A. Primary hypothyroidism
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Primary hypothyroidism Explanation: In primary thyroid failure, the thyroid gland produces insufficient hormone, so free T4 falls and pituitary TSH rises in response. Subclinical hypothyroidism has a raised TSH with free T4 still within the reference range. Central hypothyroidism generally produces a low free T4 with a TSH that is low or inappropriately normal. Assessment: R2 — Explain. Straightforward but appropriate for core endocrine interpretation. NICE NG145. <Cite refs={["turn174335search0"]}/> MRCP1-057 | STRUCTURED — EDITORIAL REVIEW Source: 304_Advise_On_MRCP_Gate.m

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance and a diffuse goitre. Her TSH is suppressed, and both free T4 and free T3 are raised. Which investigation is recommended to help confirm Graves’ disease?

options.B: TSH-receptor antibodies
options.E: A serum TSH measurement repeated the following day

questions.correct_answer: B. TSH-receptor antibodies

TSH-receptor antibodies Explanation: NICE recommends measuring TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAbs) in adults with confirmed thyrotoxicosis to help confirm Graves’ disease. If TRAbs are negative, a technetium thyroid scan may be considered. Thyroid ultrasound is not routinely indicated for thyrotoxicosis unless there is a palpable thyroid nodule. Assessment: R3 — Discriminate. The question tests the investigation that distinguishes Graves’ disease rather than simply recognising thyrotoxicosis. questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with established type 1 diabetes develops vomiting and abdominal pain during a febrile illness. His capillary glucose is elevated and he appears dehydrated. Which additional bedside test is most directly useful when assessing for diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.B: Urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio

questions.correct_answer: A. Capillary blood ketones
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Capillary blood ketones Explanation: In a person with type 1 diabetes who is acutely unwell and may have DKA, blood ketone measurement helps identify ketosis and guide urgent assessment. Glucose or HbA1c alone cannot establish or exclude DKA; assessment also requires acid–base and electrolyte evaluation. Assessment: R4 — Interpret/apply. questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman develops progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and wide violaceous abdominal striae. She has no history of glucocorticoid treatment. Which is an appropriate initial test for endogenous Cushing syndrome?

options.B: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
options.D: Serum growth hormone after a meal
options.E: A single morning ACTH measurement as the sole screening test

questions.correct_answer: B. Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test Explanation: The clinical features raise suspicion of cortisol excess. The overnight dexamethasone suppression test is an accepted initial screening test; late-night salivary cortisol and urinary free cortisol are other established approaches. A random cortisol or ACTH measurement alone is not an appropriate screening test for Cushing syndrome. Assessment: R3 — Discriminate. The item tests the distinction between a screening test for hypercortisolism and tests used later to investigate its cause. MRCP1-062 | STRUCTURED — EDITORIA

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Pregnancy testing is negative. Her serum prolactin is substantially elevated on repeat measurement. She takes no medicines known to raise prolactin, and thyroid function and renal function are normal. Which investigation is most appropriate to identify a likely structural cause?

options.B: CT pulmonary angiography

questions.correct_answer: A. MRI of the pituitary
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. MRI of the pituitary Explanation: Persistent, substantial hyperprolactinaemia without an evident physiological, medication-related or systemic cause warrants assessment for a pituitary lesion. MRI is the principal imaging investigation. The prolactin result, symptoms, potential assay interference and possibility of a large lesion with a disproportionately modest prolactin result should be considered together. Assessment: R4 — Apply/interpret. This tests investigation after common alternative causes have been addressed, rather than simply recognising galactorrhoea. MRCP1-063

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has repeated measurements showing raised adjusted serum calcium. Her parathyroid hormone concentration is also raised, rather than suppressed. Which mechanism best explains this biochemical pattern?

options.A: PTH secretion is appropriately suppressed by hypercalcaemia
options.B: PTH secretion is inappropriate for the raised serum calcium
options.C: Excess calcitonin is stimulating osteoclast activity
options.D: Reduced PTH secretion is causing renal calcium retention
options.E: Increased insulin secretion is driving calcium release from bone

questions.correct_answer: B. PTH secretion is inappropriate for the raised serum calcium
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. PTH secretion is inappropriate for the raised serum calcium Explanation: When serum calcium is elevated, normal parathyroid glands should suppress PTH secretion. A raised or inappropriately normal PTH therefore suggests a PTH-dependent cause of hypercalcaemia, such as primary hyperparathyroidism. This differs from many malignancy-related causes, in which endogenous PTH is usually suppressed. Assessment: R3 — Discriminate. options.B: Serum aldosterone alone

questions.correct_answer: A. Plasma free metanephrines

options.B: Vitamin B12

questions.correct_answer: B. Vitamin B12
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Vitamin B12 Explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause megaloblastic anaemia and neurological dysfunction, including peripheral neuropathy and impaired proprioception. Neurological manifestations can occur without prominent anaemia, so a normal haemoglobin does not reliably exclude deficiency. Assessment: R3 — Discriminate. The neurological signs make B12 deficiency more likely than isolated folate deficiency. questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops jaundice and fatigue. Her haemoglobin has fallen, reticulocytes are raised, unconjugated bilirubin is elevated, and haptoglobin is low. Which process best explains this combination?

options.B: Increased red-cell destruction
options.C: Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
options.D: Suppressed bone-marrow activity without red-cell destruction
options.E: Reduced intestinal folate absorption as the sole mechanism

questions.correct_answer: B. Increased red-cell destruction
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Increased red-cell destruction Explanation: Reticulocytosis reflects a marrow response to red-cell loss or destruction. Increased unconjugated bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin support haemolysis. These findings establish a haemolytic pattern but do not, by themselves, identify its cause; the blood film, direct antiglobulin test and other investigations help distinguish the possibilities. Assessment: R2 — Explain. This tests interpretation of a coherent biochemical pattern rather than recognition of a specific haemolytic disorder. MRCP1-068 | STRUCTURED — EDITORIAL REVIEW So

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is found to have marked leukocytosis on a routine blood test. The blood film shows granulocytes at different stages of maturation, and examination reveals splenomegaly. Which molecular abnormality is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia?

options.B: PML::RARA fusion
options.E: MYC rearrangement as the defining abnormality

questions.correct_answer: A. BCR::ABL1 fusion
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. BCR::ABL1 fusion Explanation: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is characterised by the BCR::ABL1 fusion, usually resulting from the Philadelphia chromosome translocation t(9;22). The fusion encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Molecular or cytogenetic testing is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Assessment: R2 — Explain. The distractors are other genuine molecular abnormalities, but they are not the defining lesion of CML. questions.presentation: Suspected deep-vein thrombosis: choosing the next investigation
questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. After clinical assessment, her two-level DVT Wells score is 3. A proximal leg-vein ultrasound scan can be obtained promptly. According to NICE guidance, what is the appropriate next investigation?

options.A: D-dimer as the only initial test, irrespective of clinical probability
options.B: Proximal leg-vein ultrasound
options.E: No investigation unless the D-dimer is elevated

questions.correct_answer: B. Proximal leg-vein ultrasound
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Proximal leg-vein ultrasound Explanation: A two-level DVT Wells score of 2 or more makes DVT likely. NICE recommends proximal leg-vein ultrasound, with the result available within 4 hours if possible. If it cannot be obtained within that time, the recommended pathway includes D-dimer testing, interim therapeutic anticoagulation when appropriate, and ultrasound within 24 hours. Assessment: R5 — Apply. This is a current pathway question, not a general question about the causes of thrombosis. questions.source_heading: MRCP and PACES > QUESTIONS 0001-0150
questions.presentation: Sickle cell disease: acute painful episode
questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with established sickle cell disease presents to hospital with severe limb pain typical of his previous painful episodes. He is haemodynamically stable and has no features suggesting an alternative diagnosis. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Delay analgesia until the full blood count and haemoglobin electrophoresis are available
options.B: Treat as an acute medical emergency and provide prompt, appropriate analgesia
options.C: Give corticosteroids routinely to shorten the episode
options.D: Withhold analgesia until imaging confirms bone infarction
options.E: Arrange an outpatient haematology appointment before treating the pain

questions.correct_answer: B. Treat as an acute medical emergency and provide prompt, appropriate analgesia

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-116 — Acute confusion in an older adult An 82-year-old woman is admitted with a urinary tract infection. Her daughter reports that, over the past 24 hours, the patient has become unusually inattentive and intermittently disorientated. She was managing independently before this illness. Her attention and alertness fluctuate during the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Delirium

questions.correct_answer: B. Delirium
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Delirium Explanation: The acute onset, fluctuating course and impaired attention strongly suggest delirium, precipitated here by an acute illness. Dementia usually develops more gradually. Delirium can coexist with dementia, and uncertainty between the diagnoses should prompt management of possible delirium first. <Cite refs={["turn329791search0","turn329791search2"]}/> - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-117 — Falls and comprehensive assessment A 79-year-old man has fallen three times in the past six months. He reports feeling unsteady when turning and has difficulty rising from a chair. He takes several regular medicines and lives alone. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe a walking frame without further assessment
options.B: Arrange a comprehensive falls assessment and individualised management
options.C: Reassure him that falls are an inevitable consequence of ageing
options.D: Request a CT head scan as the sole investigation
options.E: Advise him to avoid walking outdoors

questions.correct_answer: B. Arrange a comprehensive falls assessment and individualised management
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Arrange a comprehensive falls assessment and individualised management Explanation: Recurrent falls warrant a comprehensive assessment rather than a single intervention. Assessment should consider gait and balance, muscle strength, medicines, cardiovascular factors, vision, functional ability and environmental hazards. Management should address the factors identified. NICE advises against using falls prediction tools to estimate an individual's future risk. <Cite refs={["turn329791search3"]}/> - Assessment: R5 — Apply - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-118 — Recognising frailty An 86-year-old woman has gradually lost weight, walks slowly, feels exhausted with everyday activities and has become less physically active. She needs increasing help with shopping and housework. There is no acute illness. Which concept best describes this clinical picture?

options.B: Frailty
options.D: Sarcopenia as the only possible diagnosis

questions.correct_answer: B. Frailty
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Frailty Explanation: Frailty describes reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to adverse outcomes when exposed to stressors. Weight loss, exhaustion, slow walking and reduced activity are characteristic features. Sarcopenia may contribute, but it does not fully explain the broader functional vulnerability described. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination - Release note: The stem supports frailty clinically; avoid implying that these features alone establish a formal frailty category or score.

Orthostatic hypotension Explanation: The substantial fall in blood pressure after standing, associated with postural symptoms, supports orthostatic hypotension. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-123 — Capacity and a specific decision A 79-year-old inpatient with mild dementia refuses a recommended blood test. He can explain that the test involves taking blood but cannot retain the information about why it is needed long enough to weigh the risks and benefits. His ability to make decisions varies with the time of day. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A diagnosis of dementia automatically means he lacks capacity
options.B: Refusal of treatment establishes incapacity
options.C: Capacity must be assessed for the particular decision at the relevant time, after appropriate support is offered
options.D: His family can automatically make the decision for him

questions.correct_answer: C. Capacity must be assessed for the particular decision at the relevant time, after appropriate support is offered
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Capacity must be assessed for the particular decision at the relevant time, after appropriate support is offered Explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A diagnosis of dementia or an apparently unwise decision does not, by itself, establish incapacity. The person should be supported to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information and communicate a decision. If the person lacks capacity for that decision, the applicable legal framework for decision-making must be followed. - Assessment: R5 — Apply - Difficulty: D3 — Integration - Release note: T

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-124 — Malignant spinal cord compression A 68-year-old man with known prostate cancer develops severe progressive back pain, worse at night. He now reports leg weakness and difficulty walking. Examination reveals bilateral lower-limb weakness. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.B: Peripheral neuropathy caused by diabetes

questions.correct_answer: C. Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression Explanation: Cancer with progressive back pain and new neurological deficits is a red-flag presentation for metastatic spinal cord compression. This is an oncological emergency requiring immediate escalation for urgent assessment and investigation; routine outpatient review is inappropriate. - Assessment: R5 — Apply - Difficulty: D3 — Integration - Release note: The final version should specify the current UK emergency pathway and source the precise timing of imaging or treatment if any timing threshold is included.

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-125 — Neutropenic sepsis A 59-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy presents with fever, rigors and marked lethargy. Her neutrophil count is severely reduced. Her blood pressure is falling, and she appears acutely unwell. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Wait for blood culture results before starting treatment
options.B: Treat as a medical emergency and initiate the local neutropenic sepsis pathway promptly
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and arrange routine review in 48 hours
options.D: Give an antipyretic and discharge if the fever falls
options.E: Assume the fever is caused by the malignancy and avoid antibiotics

questions.correct_answer: B. Treat as a medical emergency and initiate the local neutropenic sepsis pathway promptly
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Treat as a medical emergency and initiate the local neutropenic sepsis pathway promptly Explanation: Neutropenic sepsis can deteriorate rapidly and may present with few localising signs. Urgent assessment, cultures and other indicated investigations, and prompt empiric antimicrobial treatment according to the current local protocol are required. Investigations must not cause an unsafe delay in treatment. - Assessment: R5 — Apply - Difficulty: D3 — Integration - Release note: Any antibiotic regimen, dose or timing threshold must be verified against current authoritative UK gu

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-126 — Tumour lysis syndrome A 54-year-old man is admitted with newly diagnosed high-grade lymphoma and a large tumour burden. Shortly after starting chemotherapy, he develops nausea, muscle cramps and reduced urine output. Blood tests show raised potassium, phosphate and urate, with reduced calcium and worsening renal function. Which process best explains these findings?

options.A: Increased renal calcium excretion as the sole abnormality
options.B: Rapid release of intracellular contents from lysed tumour cells
options.E: Inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone alone

questions.correct_answer: B. Rapid release of intracellular contents from lysed tumour cells
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Rapid release of intracellular contents from lysed tumour cells Explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome results from rapid tumour-cell breakdown, releasing potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids, which are metabolised to uric acid. Hyperphosphataemia can lower serum calcium, while urate and calcium-phosphate deposition and other mechanisms can contribute to acute kidney injury. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-127 — Paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia A 65-year-old man with a heavy smoking history presents with weight loss, thirst, constipation and confusion. Investigations confirm hypercalcaemia. His parathyroid hormone concentration is suppressed, and imaging identifies a lung mass. Which mechanism is most characteristic of hypercalcaemia associated with squamous cell lung carcinoma?

options.A: Ectopic production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide
options.B: Increased secretion of calcitonin
options.D: Increased renal activation of vitamin D caused by PTH

questions.correct_answer: A. Ectopic production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Ectopic production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide Explanation: Squamous cell lung carcinoma can cause humoral hypercalcaemia through secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). Suppressed circulating PTH supports a non-parathyroid cause. Malignancy can cause hypercalcaemia through other mechanisms too, including osteolytic bone metastases. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-128 — Cancer-associated thrombosis A 61-year-old woman with newly diagnosed pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops unilateral calf swelling and pain. Compression ultrasonography confirms a proximal deep vein thrombosis. She has no active bleeding. Which statement best explains her increased risk of venous thromboembolism?

options.A: Most solid tumours cause a generalised deficiency of clotting factors
options.B: Malignancy can activate coagulation through tumour-related and host inflammatory mechanisms
options.C: Cancer reliably increases fibrinolysis enough to prevent thrombosis
options.D: Venous thromboembolism in cancer is usually caused by thrombocytopenia alone
options.E: Pancreatic cancer protects against venous thrombosis unless chemotherapy has begun

questions.correct_answer: B. Malignancy can activate coagulation through tumour-related and host inflammatory mechanisms
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Malignancy can activate coagulation through tumour-related and host inflammatory mechanisms Explanation: Cancer can promote thrombosis through procoagulant activity, inflammatory pathways, platelet activation and other changes in haemostasis. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is particularly associated with venous thromboembolism. Treatment choices depend on factors such as bleeding risk, renal function, interactions and the patient's overall circumstances. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

options.B: Central retinal artery occlusion

questions.correct_answer: C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma Explanation: Sudden painful red eye, reduced vision, halos, nausea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil are characteristic of acute angle-closure glaucoma. She reports a brief episode of visual loss in one eye earlier that day. Which is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Arrange routine optometry review before further action
options.B: Start treatment for suspected giant cell arteritis urgently and arrange immediate specialist assessment
options.C: Wait for temporal artery biopsy results before starting treatment
options.D: Reassure her because transient visual loss is not associated with giant cell arteritis
options.E: Prescribe migraine treatment and review in one month

questions.correct_answer: B. Start treatment for suspected giant cell arteritis urgently and arrange immediate specialist assessment
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Start treatment for suspected giant cell arteritis urgently and arrange immediate specialist assessment Explanation: The combination of new headache, jaw claudication and transient visual loss strongly suggests giant cell arteritis, with a risk of irreversible blindness. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting confirmatory tests. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-132 — Optic neuritis A 32-year-old woman develops blurred vision in her right eye over three days. She describes pain that worsens when moving the eye and says colours appear less vivid in that eye. Examination reveals reduced visual acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect. The optic disc appears normal. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.B: Central retinal vein occlusion

questions.correct_answer: C. Optic neuritis
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Optic neuritis Explanation: Subacute visual loss, pain on eye movement, impaired colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect are characteristic of optic neuritis. The optic disc can appear normal in retrobulbar optic neuritis because the inflammation affects the optic nerve behind the visible disc. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D3 — Integration ---

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-133 — Major depressive episode A 46-year-old man reports six weeks of persistent low mood, loss of interest, early-morning waking, reduced appetite, poor concentration and feelings of worthlessness. These symptoms have impaired his ability to work. He has no history of mania or hypomania. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

options.B: Major depressive episode

questions.correct_answer: B. Major depressive episode
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Major depressive episode Explanation: Persistent low mood or loss of interest, accompanied by other depressive symptoms and significant functional impairment, supports a depressive episode. The duration, symptom pattern and absence of a history of mania or hypomania make this more likely than the alternatives. Assessment should also include suicide risk, possible bipolar disorder and relevant physical or substance-related causes. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-134 — Generalised anxiety disorder A 38-year-old woman describes excessive, difficult-to-control worry about work, finances, family and health. She feels tense, sleeps poorly and struggles to concentrate. The symptoms have persisted for many months and interfere with daily functioning. She does not experience discrete episodes of intense fear. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Generalised anxiety disorder

questions.correct_answer: B. Generalised anxiety disorder
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Generalised anxiety disorder Explanation: Generalised anxiety disorder is characterised by persistent, excessive and difficult-to-control anxiety across multiple areas of life, often accompanied by tension, sleep disturbance and impaired concentration. He is unusually talkative, has racing thoughts, believes he has exceptional business abilities and has spent most of his savings on an implausible venture. His behaviour has caused major disruption at work. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Mania

questions.correct_answer: B. Mania
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Mania Explanation: A sustained period of elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity and markedly impaired functioning supports mania. The severity and substantial disruption distinguish it from hypomania. She recognises that the checking is excessive but feels intense anxiety if she tries to resist it. The ritual takes more than an hour each day and makes her late for work. Which feature most strongly supports obsessive-compulsive disorder?

options.A: A fixed false belief that cannot be questioned
options.B: Recurrent intrusive thoughts or urges and repetitive behaviours intended to reduce distress
options.C: Recurrent unexpected episodes of intense fear alone
options.D: Persistent worry across several everyday domains without rituals
options.E: Progressive loss of memory and executive function

questions.correct_answer: B. Recurrent intrusive thoughts or urges and repetitive behaviours intended to reduce distress
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Recurrent intrusive thoughts or urges and repetitive behaviours intended to reduce distress Explanation: OCD involves obsessions, compulsions or both. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed in response to obsessions or according to rigid rules, often to reduce distress. Insight can vary, and the symptoms cause significant distress or functional impairment. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-137 — Schizophrenia: positive symptoms A 23-year-old man has become socially withdrawn and increasingly suspicious over four months. He hears voices discussing him when nobody is present and believes that strangers are transmitting messages specifically for him through the television. His drug screen is negative. Which finding is a positive symptom of schizophrenia?

options.B: Poverty of speech

questions.correct_answer: C. Auditory hallucinations
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Auditory hallucinations Explanation: Positive symptoms include hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thought or behaviour. Reduced emotional expression, poverty of speech and reduced motivation are negative symptoms. Social withdrawal can occur in several conditions and is not specific to schizophrenia. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-138 — Lithium toxicity A 67-year-old man with bipolar disorder has been stable on lithium for several years. He develops vomiting and diarrhoea and continues taking his usual medicines despite poor oral intake. He subsequently develops coarse tremor, unsteady gait and confusion. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Increase the lithium dose because the mood disorder may be relapsing
options.B: Continue lithium and arrange a routine outpatient review
options.C: Withhold lithium and arrange urgent medical assessment for possible toxicity
options.D: Prescribe an additional antipsychotic and discharge him
options.E: Reassure him that these are expected effects of long-term treatment

questions.correct_answer: C. Withhold lithium and arrange urgent medical assessment for possible toxicity
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Withhold lithium and arrange urgent medical assessment for possible toxicity Explanation: Gastrointestinal illness and dehydration can increase the risk of lithium toxicity. Coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion are concerning neurological features. Lithium should be withheld and urgent assessment arranged, including lithium concentration, renal function, electrolytes and evaluation of fluid status. Severe toxicity may require specialist management. - Assessment: R5 — Apply - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

Blood tests show a markedly elevated creatine kinase concentration. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

questions.correct_answer: B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a potentially fatal reaction associated with dopamine antagonism, typically involving hyperthermia, severe rigidity, altered mental state and autonomic instability. Creatine kinase is often markedly elevated due to muscle injury. The causative drug should be stopped and emergency supportive medical care initiated. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

Within hours, she develops agitation, sweating, diarrhoea, tremor, hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus. Which diagnosis best explains the findings?

options.B: Serotonin syndrome

questions.correct_answer: B. Serotonin syndrome
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Serotonin syndrome Explanation: Serotonin syndrome follows excessive serotonergic activity and may develop rapidly after a medicine is started, increased or combined with another serotonergic agent. Clonus and hyperreflexia are particularly useful clues. The suspected causative medicines should be stopped and urgent assessment and supportive treatment provided according to severity. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

Approximately 24 hours after his last drink, he develops tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea and tachycardia. He remains orientated and has no hallucinations. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Wernicke encephalopathy

questions.correct_answer: A. Alcohol withdrawal
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Alcohol withdrawal Explanation: Tremor, sweating, anxiety, nausea and autonomic activation after reducing or stopping prolonged heavy alcohol consumption are consistent with alcohol withdrawal. Delirium tremens involves a more severe syndrome with delirium and usually marked autonomic disturbance. Withdrawal can progress, so the patient requires appropriate clinical assessment and monitoring. - Assessment: R3 — Discriminate - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-142 — Wernicke encephalopathy A 58-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence is admitted with poor nutrition and persistent vomiting. He develops confusion, an unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.B: Urgent parenteral thiamine

questions.correct_answer: B. Urgent parenteral thiamine
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Urgent parenteral thiamine Explanation: The combination of nutritional deficiency, confusion, gait ataxia and ocular abnormalities raises strong suspicion of Wernicke encephalopathy. This is a medical emergency: give parenteral thiamine promptly and correct associated nutritional and metabolic problems. Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for confirmatory investigations. If hypoglycaemia is present, glucose must also be treated promptly; thiamine should be given before or alongside it where feasible, without delaying emergency glucose treatment. - Assessment: R5 —

Investigations show heavy proteinuria, low serum albumin and hyperlipidaemia. He subsequently develops a painful, swollen leg. Which mechanism contributes to the increased risk of venous thrombosis in nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Increased urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, including antithrombin
options.B: Universal severe thrombocytopenia
options.C: Increased urinary loss of red blood cells
options.D: Reduced hepatic synthesis of all clotting factors

questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Increased urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, including antithrombin Explanation: Nephrotic syndrome creates a prothrombotic state through several mechanisms, including urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, increased hepatic synthesis of procoagulant proteins and altered platelet activity. options.B: Reduced angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure
options.C: Direct immune-mediated destruction of glomerular basement membranes

questions.correct_answer: B. Reduced angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure

Reduced angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure Explanation: When renal perfusion is compromised, angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction helps maintain glomerular filtration pressure. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-146 — Chronic kidney disease and anaemia A 68-year-old woman with established chronic kidney disease develops fatigue and exertional breathlessness. Her haemoglobin is low, mean corpuscular volume is normal, ferritin is not reduced and there is no evidence of haemolysis or active bleeding. Which mechanism is a major contributor to her anaemia?

options.B: Reduced renal erythropoietin production

questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Reduced renal erythropoietin production Explanation: Healthy kidneys produce erythropoietin, which stimulates red-cell production in the bone marrow. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-147 — Diagnostic test interpretation A diagnostic test is evaluated in 200 people who have a disease and 800 people who do not. It gives a positive result in 180 people with the disease and 160 people without it. What is the specificity of the test?
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. 80% Explanation: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. - True negatives = \(800-160=640\) - Specificity = \(640/800=0.80=80\%\) - Assessment: R4 — Interpret - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination Overlap check: This differs from MRCP1-013, which tests the interpretation of sensitivity and false-positive counts. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-148 — Confidence intervals A clinical trial reports that a treatment reduces the relative risk of an outcome to 0.75 compared with control. The 95% confidence interval is 0.60–0.94. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The treatment reduces risk by exactly 25% in every patient
options.B: The result is statistically compatible with no treatment effect
options.C: The result is statistically significant at the conventional 5% level, assuming this is the prespecified relevant analysis
options.D: The treatment has been proved to be safe
options.E: The confidence interval means that 95% of patients benefit

questions.correct_answer: C. The result is statistically significant at the conventional 5% level, assuming this is the prespecified relevant analysis
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. The result is statistically significant at the conventional 5% level, assuming this is the prespecified relevant analysis Explanation: For a relative risk, the null value is 1. A confidence interval of 0.60–0.94 excludes 1, supporting a statistically significant reduction in risk at the conventional 5% level. It does not prove safety, guarantee benefit for an individual, or remove the need to consider bias, study design and clinical importance. - Assessment: R4 — Interpret - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-150 — Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of a recessive disease allele is \(q=0.1\). Assume the disease is fully penetrant and occurs only in homozygotes for that allele. What proportion of the population is expected to have the disease?
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. 1% Explanation: Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the expected frequency of homozygous recessive individuals is \(q^2\). \[ q^2=0.1^2=0.01=1\% \] This calculation assumes the stated genetic model and population equilibrium. - Assessment: R4 — Interpret - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

options.B: Respiratory alkalosis

questions.correct_answer: D. Metabolic alkalosis

Its half-life is six hours, and the patient has stable drug distribution and clearance. Approximately what proportion of the original drug amount remains after 18 hours?
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. 12.5% Explanation: Eighteen hours represents three half-lives. options.A: A leftward shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
options.B: A rightward shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
options.D: A reduction in hydrogen ion concentration
options.E: A reduction in carbon dioxide concentration

questions.correct_answer: B. A rightward shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. A rightward shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve Explanation: Increased temperature shifts the dissociation curve to the right, reducing haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and facilitating oxygen unloading in tissues. questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-154 — Starling forces and oedema A 67-year-old man with severe hypoalbuminaemia develops bilateral ankle oedema. His cardiac function is normal, and there is no evidence of venous obstruction. Which mechanism most directly contributes to the oedema?

options.B: Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure
options.E: Increased intracellular oncotic pressure in red blood cells

questions.correct_answer: B. Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Reduced plasma colloid osmotic pressure Explanation: Albumin contributes substantially to plasma colloid osmotic pressure. A marked reduction in plasma albumin decreases the force retaining fluid within the vascular compartment and can promote movement of fluid into the interstitial space. Renal sodium retention and other mechanisms may also contribute to oedema in clinical disease. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-155 — Immunoglobulin class switching A patient with a B-cell immune response initially produces IgM antibodies against a newly encountered antigen. Following an appropriate immune response, the same B-cell lineage begins producing antigen-specific IgG. Which process allows this change?

options.B: Class-switch recombination

questions.correct_answer: B. Class-switch recombination
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Class-switch recombination Explanation: Class-switch recombination changes the immunoglobulin heavy-chain constant region, allowing a B cell to produce a different antibody class while retaining antigen specificity. Somatic hypermutation instead introduces mutations into variable-region genes and contributes to affinity maturation. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-156 — Mitochondrial inheritance A woman carries a pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variant associated with a mitochondrial disorder. She has children with a man who does not carry the variant. The clinical severity varies among affected members of her family. Which phenomenon best explains variation in disease severity between individuals carrying the mitochondrial variant?

options.A: Anticipation caused by expansion of nuclear DNA repeats
options.B: Heteroplasmy, with different proportions of mutant and normal mitochondrial DNA
options.C: Genomic imprinting of the paternal mitochondrial genome
options.E: Independent assortment of homologous nuclear chromosomes alone

questions.correct_answer: B. Heteroplasmy, with different proportions of mutant and normal mitochondrial DNA
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Heteroplasmy, with different proportions of mutant and normal mitochondrial DNA Explanation: Heteroplasmy refers to the coexistence of different mitochondrial DNA populations within a cell or individual. The proportion and distribution of mutant mitochondrial DNA can influence whether a tissue reaches the threshold at which dysfunction becomes apparent. Mitochondrial DNA is generally maternally inherited. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-157 — Sensitivity and negative predictive value A screening test is evaluated in a population with a relatively low prevalence of a disease. The test's sensitivity and specificity remain unchanged, but the disease prevalence falls further in a comparable population. What is the expected effect on the negative predictive value (NPV)?

options.B: It increases
options.E: It becomes equal to the false-positive rate

questions.correct_answer: B. It increases
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. It increases Explanation: When disease prevalence falls, a negative result is more likely to come from someone who does not have the disease. Assuming sensitivity and specificity remain constant, NPV therefore increases. Predictive values depend on prevalence, unlike sensitivity and specificity as conventionally defined. - Assessment: R4 — Interpret - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-158 — Autonomic physiology A healthy volunteer stands rapidly from a supine position. Venous return and stroke volume initially decrease, causing a transient fall in arterial blood pressure. Which response is expected from the arterial baroreceptor reflex?

options.A: Increased baroreceptor firing with reduced sympathetic output
options.B: Reduced baroreceptor firing with increased sympathetic output
options.C: Increased vagal output to the ventricles with reduced heart rate

questions.correct_answer: B. Reduced baroreceptor firing with increased sympathetic output
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Reduced baroreceptor firing with increased sympathetic output Explanation: Reduced arterial stretch decreases firing from carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors. The reflex increases sympathetic activity and reduces parasympathetic activity, promoting tachycardia, increased contractility and peripheral vasoconstriction to help restore blood pressure. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-159 — Inheritance patterns A genetic disorder affects males and females. An affected father transmits the disorder to all his daughters but none of his sons. An affected mother can transmit the disorder to children of either sex. Which inheritance pattern best fits this pedigree?

options.B: Autosomal recessive

questions.correct_answer: C. X-linked dominant
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. X-linked dominant Explanation: A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. In an X-linked dominant condition, an affected father therefore transmits the variant to all daughters and no sons. An affected heterozygous mother may transmit the variant to children of either sex. - Assessment: R4 — Interpret - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-160 — Randomised controlled trials A randomised controlled trial allocates participants to treatment or control using a concealed randomisation process. At baseline, measured and unmeasured prognostic factors are expected to be distributed comparably between the groups on average. What is the principal methodological advantage of randomisation?

options.A: It guarantees that every participant receives the allocated intervention
options.B: It eliminates all loss to follow-up
options.C: It reduces confounding by balancing prognostic factors between groups on average
options.D: It guarantees that the results apply to every patient population
options.E: It removes the need for blinding or appropriate outcome measurement

questions.correct_answer: C. It reduces confounding by balancing prognostic factors between groups on average
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. It reduces confounding by balancing prognostic factors between groups on average Explanation: Randomisation reduces the risk that treatment allocation is systematically associated with prognostic factors, including unmeasured factors. It does not guarantee perfect balance in a particular trial, prevent attrition, eliminate measurement bias or ensure generalisability. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-161 — Type I and type II errors A clinical trial fails to demonstrate a statistically significant difference between a new treatment and placebo. The treatment actually has a genuine effect in the population, but the trial fails to detect it. What type of error has occurred?

options.B: Type II error

questions.correct_answer: B. Type II error
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Type II error Explanation: A type II error occurs when a study fails to reject the null hypothesis despite a genuine effect. The probability of a type II error is denoted by \(\beta\); statistical power is \(1-\beta\). A non-significant result does not, by itself, establish that the treatments are equivalent. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-162 — Membrane transport A laboratory experiment measures glucose uptake into intestinal epithelial cells. Uptake across the apical membrane occurs against the glucose concentration gradient and depends on the sodium concentration gradient maintained by the basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase. Which transport mechanism accounts for apical glucose uptake?

options.B: Primary active transport directly powered by ATP hydrolysis at the glucose transporter
options.C: Secondary active transport coupled to sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient
options.D: Facilitated diffusion independent of ion gradients

questions.correct_answer: C. Secondary active transport coupled to sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Secondary active transport coupled to sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient Explanation: The sodium–glucose cotransporter uses the energy stored in the sodium electrochemical gradient to move glucose against its gradient. The basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase maintains that sodium gradient using ATP. The cotransporter itself does not directly hydrolyse ATP. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration ---

options.B: Respiratory compensation through increased alveolar ventilation
options.E: Increased carbon dioxide production without a change in ventilation

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-164 — Bilirubin metabolism A 24-year-old man develops mild jaundice during a febrile illness after several days of reduced food intake. His unconjugated bilirubin is raised, but liver enzymes, haemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal. The jaundice resolves as he recovers. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?

options.B: Complete obstruction of the common bile duct

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-165 — Enzyme kinetics An enzyme-catalysed reaction is studied at different substrate concentrations. In the presence of a reversible competitive inhibitor, the maximum reaction velocity can still be achieved by increasing the substrate concentration sufficiently. Which change is expected?

options.B: Increased apparent \(K_m\) with unchanged \(V_{\max}\)
options.E: Complete irreversible loss of enzyme activity

questions.correct_answer: B. Increased apparent \(K_m\) with unchanged \(V_{\max}\)
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Increased apparent \(K_m\) with unchanged \(V_{\max}\) Explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for enzyme binding. More substrate is required to reach half of \(V_{\max}\), so the apparent \(K_m\) increases. At sufficiently high substrate concentration, the same \(V_{\max}\) can be achieved. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-168 — Genomic imprinting A child develops a characteristic neurodevelopmental disorder because a gene that is normally expressed from the paternal chromosome is absent or inactive. The corresponding maternal copy is present but normally silenced in the relevant tissue. Which genetic mechanism best explains this pattern?

options.B: Genomic imprinting

questions.correct_answer: B. Genomic imprinting
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Genomic imprinting Explanation: Genomic imprinting causes gene expression to depend on the parent of origin, usually through epigenetic regulation. If the normally active paternal copy is absent or inactive in the relevant tissue, the maternally inherited copy may not compensate because it is silenced. The clinical consequences depend on the specific gene and tissue. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-169 — Type I hypersensitivity A patient develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension within minutes of exposure to a known allergen. Previous exposure has sensitised the patient to that allergen. Which mechanism is primarily responsible for this immediate reaction?

options.A: IgG-mediated activation of complement against cell-surface antigens
options.B: Allergen-mediated cross-linking of IgE bound to mast cells
options.C: Immune-complex deposition in small blood vessels
options.E: Direct activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes against infected cells

questions.correct_answer: B. Allergen-mediated cross-linking of IgE bound to mast cells
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Allergen-mediated cross-linking of IgE bound to mast cells Explanation: In type I hypersensitivity, allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcεRI receptors on sensitised mast cells triggers mediator release. Histamine and other mediators contribute to urticaria, bronchoconstriction and vascular leakage. The clinical presentation is consistent with anaphylaxis, which requires immediate emergency treatment. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-170 — Intention-to-treat analysis A randomised trial compares a new treatment with standard care. Some participants assigned to the new treatment stop taking it, while some participants in the control group obtain the new treatment outside the trial. The investigators analyse participants according to their original randomised allocation. What is the principal rationale for this intention-to-treat approach?

options.A: It guarantees complete adherence to the assigned treatment
options.B: It preserves the benefits of randomisation and reduces bias associated with excluding participants after allocation
options.C: It removes all effects of missing outcome data
options.D: It always produces a larger treatment effect than a per-protocol analysis
options.E: It proves that the treatment is effective in every subgroup

questions.correct_answer: B. It preserves the benefits of randomisation and reduces bias associated with excluding participants after allocation
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. It preserves the benefits of randomisation and reduces bias associated with excluding participants after allocation Explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis retains participants in their originally assigned groups, helping preserve comparability created by randomisation. It does not automatically solve missing data, eliminate all bias or guarantee a particular effect estimate. The handling of missing outcomes must still be appropriate and transparently reported. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-171 — Oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes A tumour is found to contain a mutation that constitutively activates a growth-signalling protein. The mutation increases signalling even when the normal extracellular growth stimulus is absent. Which description best fits this genetic change?

options.A: Inactivation of a tumour suppressor gene through loss of function
options.B: Activation of a proto-oncogene to form an oncogene
options.C: Loss of a DNA mismatch-repair gene as the only possible mechanism
options.D: Increased expression of a normal cell-cycle inhibitor
options.E: Silencing of every gene on one chromosome

questions.correct_answer: B. Activation of a proto-oncogene to form an oncogene
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Activation of a proto-oncogene to form an oncogene Explanation: Proto-oncogenes encode proteins involved in normal growth and survival signalling. Activating mutations can make these proteins constitutively active, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation. Tumour suppressor genes generally restrain growth or maintain genomic integrity and contribute to cancer when their function is lost. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-173 — Volume of distribution A medicine is highly lipid-soluble and extensively partitions into tissues. After administration, its measured plasma concentration is low relative to the total amount of drug in the body. Which pharmacokinetic property best explains this finding?

options.B: High apparent volume of distribution

questions.correct_answer: B. High apparent volume of distribution
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. High apparent volume of distribution Explanation: The apparent volume of distribution relates the total amount of drug in the body to its measured plasma concentration. Extensive tissue distribution can produce a high apparent volume of distribution, even though this value does not represent a literal anatomical fluid volume. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-174 — Cytochrome P450 inhibition A patient who is stable on a medicine metabolised by a particular cytochrome P450 enzyme starts a second medicine that strongly inhibits that enzyme. Assume the original medicine is active and that its metabolism is an important route of elimination. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: Reduced plasma concentration of the original medicine
options.B: Increased clearance of the original medicine
options.C: Increased plasma concentration of the original medicine
options.D: Complete prevention of absorption of the original medicine

questions.correct_answer: C. Increased plasma concentration of the original medicine
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. Increased plasma concentration of the original medicine Explanation: Inhibition of a major metabolic pathway can reduce the clearance of an active parent drug and increase its plasma concentration, raising the risk of adverse effects. The effect depends on the fraction metabolised by that pathway and other routes of elimination. This relationship may differ for prodrugs, whose activation depends on metabolism. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-176 — Partial agonism A drug binds to the same receptor as a full agonist but produces a smaller maximal response, even when it occupies all available receptors. When given alongside the full agonist, it reduces the overall response. Which description best fits this drug?

options.B: Partial agonist
options.E: Physiological antagonist acting at a different receptor

questions.correct_answer: B. Partial agonist
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Partial agonist Explanation: A partial agonist activates a receptor but has lower intrinsic efficacy than a full agonist. In the presence of a full agonist, it can compete for receptor occupancy and reduce the overall response. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-177 — Zero-order elimination A drug is eliminated at a constant amount per unit time over the concentration range relevant to a patient. Its elimination pathways are saturated. Which statement best describes this process?

options.A: A constant proportion of the drug is eliminated per unit time
options.B: The elimination half-life is necessarily constant at all concentrations
options.C: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time
options.D: Elimination rate increases proportionally with concentration
options.E: The drug cannot accumulate with repeated dosing

questions.correct_answer: C. A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C. A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time Explanation: In zero-order elimination, the elimination rate is approximately constant because the relevant pathways are saturated. Unlike first-order elimination, the proportion eliminated per unit time is not constant, and the half-life can vary with concentration. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-178 — Loading dose A medicine has a long elimination half-life. A clinician wants to achieve a therapeutic plasma concentration rapidly rather than waiting for repeated maintenance doses to accumulate. Which pharmacokinetic principle primarily determines the loading dose?

options.B: Apparent volume of distribution and the target change in plasma concentration
options.E: The percentage of the drug excreted unchanged, regardless of other factors

questions.correct_answer: B. Apparent volume of distribution and the target change in plasma concentration
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Apparent volume of distribution and the target change in plasma concentration Explanation: The loading dose is determined primarily by the apparent volume of distribution and the desired change in plasma concentration, with adjustment for bioavailability when the drug is not administered intravenously. Clearance is a key determinant of maintenance dosing, while half-life influences how quickly steady state is approached. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D3 — Integration

questions.stem: Text: ### MRCP1-179 — Herd immunity A communicable infection spreads through a population. A vaccine reduces the probability that vaccinated individuals become infected and transmit the pathogen. Vaccination coverage increases substantially. Which mechanism best explains how this may indirectly protect some people who remain unvaccinated?

options.A: Vaccination makes every infected individual non-infectious
options.B: Reduced transmission decreases the probability that susceptible people encounter an infectious person
options.C: Vaccination changes the pathogen's genome in every transmission event
options.D: Unvaccinated people acquire vaccine-induced antibodies through ordinary social contact
options.E: The pathogen is immediately eradicated once a majority is vaccinated

questions.correct_answer: B. Reduced transmission decreases the probability that susceptible people encounter an infectious person
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Reduced transmission decreases the probability that susceptible people encounter an infectious person Explanation: Herd protection occurs when immunity in a population reduces transmission, indirectly lowering exposure risk for susceptible individuals. The extent of protection depends on factors such as vaccine effectiveness against infection and transmission, coverage, contact patterns and pathogen characteristics. High coverage does not guarantee eradication. - Assessment: R2 — Explain - Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with headache, nausea and confusion after using a petrol-powered generator in an enclosed garage. His conventional pulse oximeter reads 99%. Which statement best explains why this reading does not exclude significant carbon monoxide poisoning?

options.A: Carbon monoxide causes a right shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve
options.B: Conventional pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin
options.C: Carbon monoxide causes falsely low arterial oxygen tension
options.D: Carbon monoxide increases dissolved oxygen in plasma
options.E: Conventional pulse oximetry measures only deoxygenated haemoglobin

questions.correct_answer: B. Conventional pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin
questions.explanation_raw: Answer: B. Conventional pulse oximetry cannot reliably distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. Explanation: Standard pulse oximeters can give reassuringly high readings in carbon monoxide poisoning because their light-absorption method does not reliably separate carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin. Diagnosis requires appropriate assessment, including co-oximetry. A normal arterial oxygen tension also does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning. Assessment: R4 — Interpret; D2 — Discrimination. questions.stem: A drug binds to a cell-surface receptor and activates a G protein, resulting in increased intracellular cyclic AMP. Which enzyme directly synthesises cyclic AMP from ATP?

options.B: Adenylyl cyclase

questions.correct_answer: B. Adenylyl cyclase
questions.explanation_raw: Answer: B. Adenylyl cyclase. Explanation: Activated G proteins can regulate adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP into cyclic AMP. questions.correct_answer: C. No general tumour-marker panel can reliably screen for all common cancers; testing should be guided by the specific clinical context
questions.explanation_raw: Answer: C. No general tumour-marker panel can reliably screen for all common cancers; testing should be guided by the specific clinical context. Explanation: Tumour markers vary in sensitivity and specificity. Some are useful in selected diagnostic pathways, monitoring treatment response or detecting recurrence, but they are not a universal cancer-screening solution. A normal result does not exclude malignancy, and an abnormal result does not necessarily prove it. Assessment: R3 — Discriminate; D2 — Discrimination. questions.stem: A patient with advanced pancreatic cancer has progressive weight loss, reduced muscle mass and weakness despite attempts to increase caloric intake. Which statement best describes cancer cachexia?

options.A: It is always caused solely by inadequate food intake
options.B: It is a multifactorial syndrome involving altered metabolism and loss of skeletal muscle
options.D: It can always be reversed by increasing calories alone
options.E: It occurs only during the final 24 hours of life

questions.correct_answer: B. It is a multifactorial syndrome involving altered metabolism and loss of skeletal muscle
questions.explanation_raw: Answer: B. It is a multifactorial syndrome involving altered metabolism and loss of skeletal muscle. Explanation: Cancer cachexia involves ongoing loss of skeletal muscle, often with loss of fat, and is associated with metabolic and inflammatory changes. Reduced intake can contribute, but nutritional supplementation alone may not fully reverse the syndrome. Management should be individualised and may include symptom control, nutritional support and functional goals. Assessment: R2 — Explain; D2 — Discrimination. questions.correct_answer: C. Stop the infusion immediately and follow the drug-specific extravasation protocol

questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Familial Mediterranean fever Explanation of options - A. Correct. Adult-onset Still’s disease typically causes a systemic inflammatory illness with quotidian fever, an evanescent rash and often prominent arthritis. The measured carbon dioxide tension is also lower than expected for a patient with uncomplicated metabolic acidosis. Which is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.B: A concurrent respiratory alkalosis may be present
options.C: The reduced carbon dioxide tension proves primary respiratory acidosis
options.D: The acidemia excludes a mixed acid–base disorder

questions.correct_answer: B. A concurrent respiratory alkalosis may be present

Explanation of options - A — Incorrect: A second acid–base process must be considered when the respiratory response is inconsistent with the expected compensation. - B — Correct: Diarrhoea can cause metabolic acidosis through bicarbonate loss. If carbon dioxide is lower than expected for appropriate compensation, a concurrent respiratory alkalosis may be present. - C — Incorrect: Respiratory acidosis is associated with increased carbon dioxide tension, not a reduced value. - D — Incorrect: Mixed acid–base disorders can occur

questions.stem: A screening programme reports that the number of people diagnosed with a disease has increased substantially since screening was introduced. However, mortality from the disease has not fallen. The programme also identifies cases that might otherwise have remained clinically silent throughout the individuals’ lifetimes. Which phenomenon may partly explain the increase in diagnosed cases without a corresponding mortality reduction?

options.B: Overdiagnosis

questions.correct_answer: B. Overdiagnosis
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B. Overdiagnosis. Explanation of options - A — Incorrect: Lead-time bias makes survival measured from diagnosis appear longer when diagnosis occurs earlier, even if the time of death is unchanged. It may affect survival statistics but does not, by itself, explain the detection of disease that would never have become clinically apparent. - B — Correct: Overdiagnosis occurs when screening identifies disease that would not have caused symptoms or harm during the person’s lifetime. questions.stem: A 37-year-old man develops recurrent abdominal pain, constipation and distal weakness. During an episode, his blood pressure is elevated, and investigations show anaemia with a microcytic pattern. He works in an industry involving the handling of old paint and metal-containing materials. Which additional finding would most strongly support lead toxicity as the unifying diagnosis?

options.B: A raised serum vitamin B12 concentration
options.D: A reduced serum thyroxine concentration with raised TSH

questions.correct_answer: A. An elevated venous blood lead concentration
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: A. Explanation - A — Correct: A venous blood lead concentration is the appropriate test to investigate suspected lead exposure. Lead can cause abdominal colic, constipation, anaemia, peripheral neuropathy and hypertension. - B — Incorrect: A raised B12 concentration does not establish lead exposure or explain the overall presentation. - C — Incorrect: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cholangitis. - D — Incorrect: Primary hypothyroidism can cause constipation and fatigue but does not explain the occupational exposure pattern and motor neuropathy.

questions.stem: Text: ## 2. Repair MRCP1-172 — Number needed to harm (NNH) Defect: The original answer options omitted the correct rounded answer. The calculation is: \[ \text{NNH}=\frac{1}{0.05-0.02} =\frac{1}{0.03}=33.33 \] Conventionally, round up to the next whole number: 34. <WritingBlock id="63082" variant="document">### MRCP1-172R — Number needed to harm In a clinical study, an adverse effect occurs in 5% of patients receiving a new medicine and 2% of patients receiving placebo over the study period. Assuming the difference is attributable to treatment, what is the number needed to harm (NNH)?
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: D. 34 Explanation: The absolute increase in risk is 5% − 2% = 3%, or 0.03. NNH is the reciprocal of this difference: \(1/0.03 = 33.33\). Rounding up gives 34 patients treated for one additional adverse event, on average, over the study period. Assessment level: R5 — Apply Difficulty: D2 — Discrimination</WritingBlock> Audit: The answer is now present in the options, and the calculation is internally consistent. The interpretation depends on the specified study period and the assumption that the risk difference is attributable to treatment.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman reports increasing glare when driving at night and difficulty reading despite appropriate spectacles. Examination confirms bilateral cataracts. questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with rapid weight loss, restrictive eating and recurrent self-induced vomiting. She is bradycardic and has a significant electrolyte disturbance. She says she is willing to attend outpatient appointments but does not want to be admitted. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange routine outpatient psychological treatment without further medical assessment
options.B: Use BMI alone to determine whether treatment is necessary
options.C: Provide acute medical assessment and treatment, including emergency admission if indicated by her physical compromise
options.D: Delay referral until she acknowledges having an eating disorder
options.E: Arrange psychological treatment first and investigate the electrolyte disturbance later

questions.correct_answer: C. Provide acute medical assessment and treatment, including emergency admission if indicated by her physical compromise
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C Explanation: Significant physical compromise, including severe electrolyte disturbance, can require acute medical care and emergency admission. Assessment must consider physical health and immediate risk; BMI or duration of illness must not be used alone to determine whether treatment is needed. <Cite refs={["turn526885search2","turn526885search4"]}/> Audit note: Distinct from the existing depression, anxiety and OCD items. questions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer is thought to be in the last days of life. They have distressing thirst and possible dehydration-related delirium, but oral hydration is inadequate. There is no clear advance decision refusing clinically assisted hydration. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Withhold hydration because the patient is dying
options.B: Start clinically assisted hydration automatically and continue regardless of response
options.C: Discuss the potential benefits and harms and consider an individualised therapeutic trial, monitoring for benefit and harm
options.D: Give fluids solely to prolong life, irrespective of the patient's goals
options.E: Encourage unrestricted oral fluids even if swallowing is unsafe

questions.correct_answer: C. Discuss the potential benefits and harms and consider an individualised therapeutic trial, monitoring for benefit and harm
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C Explanation: NICE recommends an individualised decision. A therapeutic trial of clinically assisted hydration can be considered when distressing symptoms may be related to dehydration and oral hydration is inadequate. The patient's wishes, swallowing, consciousness and risk of fluid overload matter; treatment should be reviewed and reduced or stopped if harm occurs or benefit is absent. <Cite refs={["turn526885search1","turn526885search6"]}/> Audit note: This is distinct from the existing palliative breathlessness and advance-care-planning items. questions.presentation: Palliative medicine: medication review in the last days of life
questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with advanced malignancy is recognised as being in the last days of life. He is increasingly unable to swallow tablets. His regular medicines include a statin for long-term cardiovascular prevention and medicines prescribed for symptom relief. What is the most appropriate general approach to his medication regimen?

options.A: Continue every medicine unchanged until death
options.B: Stop every prescribed medicine immediately, without discussion
options.C: Review each medicine with the patient or appropriate decision-makers, stopping medicines that offer no symptomatic benefit or may cause harm, while preserving appropriate symptom relief
options.D: Replace all oral medicines with intravenous equivalents
options.E: Continue preventive medicines in preference to medicines for comfort

questions.correct_answer: C. Review each medicine with the patient or appropriate decision-makers, stopping medicines that offer no symptomatic benefit or may cause harm, while preserving appropriate symptom relief
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: C Explanation: NICE recommends reviewing current medicines when a person may be entering the last days of life and, following appropriate discussion, stopping those that do not provide symptomatic benefit or may cause harm. Decisions should be individualised; this is not a blanket instruction to stop every medicine. <Cite refs={["turn526885search1"]}/> Audit note: Distinct from the existing palliative-care items on delirium and breakthrough cancer pain. questions.stem: An 82-year-old man is recovering from an uncomplicated myocardial infarction. He is clinically stable, mobilising independently and has no contraindication to an appropriately adapted exercise programme. A team member suggests that cardiac rehabilitation is unnecessary because of his age. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Cardiac rehabilitation is indicated only for patients younger than 70 years
options.B: Offer cardiac rehabilitation with an exercise component, adapting it to his clinical needs

questions.correct_answer: B. Offer cardiac rehabilitation with an exercise component, adapting it to his clinical needs

questions.stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has several risk factors for fragility fracture but no previous DXA scan. She has not sustained a fragility fracture, and the clinician wants to estimate her fracture risk before deciding whether bone-density measurement is needed. Which is the recommended initial approach?

options.A: Arrange DXA before undertaking any fracture-risk assessment
options.B: Use FRAX or QFracture, within the tool's applicable age range, to estimate absolute fracture risk
options.C: Measure serum calcium and use it as the sole estimate of fracture risk
options.D: Use BMI alone to determine whether osteoporosis is present
options.E: Reassure her because a previous fragility fracture is required before risk assessment

questions.correct_answer: B. Use FRAX or QFracture, within the tool's applicable age range, to estimate absolute fracture risk
questions.explanation_raw: Correct answer: B Explanation: NICE recommends using FRAX or QFracture to estimate absolute fracture risk. DXA can then be considered when the estimated risk is around the intervention threshold, with risk recalculated using the bone mineral density result where appropriate. Risk tools have limitations and must be interpreted in clinical context. <Cite refs={["turn884218search1"]}/> Audit note: Distinct from the existing frailty and falls questions. questions.explanation_raw: Answer: B. The confidence interval excludes the null value for an odds ratio Explanation: For ratios such as OR, RR and HR, the null value is 1. questions.explanation_raw: Clinical Pearl A low MCV in a thalassaemia carrier does not by itself justify iron supplementation. options.B: Coronary atherosclerosis

questions.correct_answer: B. Coronary atherosclerosis
questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ B. Coronary atherosclerosis Why It Is Correct Stable angina is most commonly caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries. During exertion, myocardial oxygen demand increases and exceeds the blood supply available through the narrowed vessels. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Coronary artery vasospasm Typically causes Prinzmetal angina occurring at rest. C. Pulmonary embolism Causes acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. D. Acute myocarditis Usually follows a viral illness and does not cause predictable exertional symptoms. E. Pericardial inflammation

questions.stem: Which vessel is most likely to have been the original source of the embolus?

options.B: Femoral vein

questions.correct_answer: B. Femoral vein
questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ B. Femoral vein Why It Is Correct Most pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thromboses in the lower limbs, particularly the femoral and popliteal veins. The embolus travels through the venous system to the pulmonary arteries. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Pulmonary vein Does not cause pulmonary embolism. C. Coronary artery Supplies the myocardium. D. Subclavian artery An arterial vessel and not a common source of PE. E. Carotid artery Supplies the brain.

options.B: Diltiazem

questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ D. Propranolol Why It Is Correct The patient has Prinzmetal (vasospastic) angina. Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol may worsen coronary vasospasm by allowing unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Amlodipine Effective treatment for coronary vasospasm. B. Diltiazem Commonly used for vasospastic angina. C. Verapamil Also effective. E. Glyceryl trinitrate Relieves acute vasospasm.

options.B: Glyceryl trinitrate

questions.correct_answer: C. Aspirin
questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ C. Aspirin Why It Is Correct Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing thromboxane A₂ production and platelet aggregation. This reduces the risk of future myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular events. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Bisoprolol Provides symptom control but is not primarily an antiplatelet drug. B. Glyceryl trinitrate Provides symptomatic relief only. D. Amlodipine Improves symptoms through vasodilation. E.
