options.B: Atrioventricular node

questions.correct_answer: B. Atrioventricular node
questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ B. Atrioventricular node Why It Is Correct The atrioventricular (AV) node is supplied by the right coronary artery in most individuals. Inferior STEMI due to RCA occlusion can therefore cause complete heart block through AV nodal ischaemia. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Sinoatrial node May be affected but does not classically cause complete heart block. C. Bundle of His Less commonly affected in inferior MI. D. Left bundle branch Would produce bundle branch block rather than complete AV block. E. Purkinje fibres Not the classic structure responsible.

questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ B. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Right coronary artery Usually supplies the inferior wall. C. Left circumflex artery Usually supplies the lateral wall. D. questions.stem: Which physiological abnormality most commonly causes hypoxaemia in pulmonary embolism?

options.B: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch

questions.correct_answer: B. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
questions.explanation_raw: Correct Answer ✅ B. Ventilation-perfusion mismatch Why It Is Correct Pulmonary emboli obstruct pulmonary arterial blood flow. Affected alveoli remain ventilated but are not adequately perfused, producing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia. Why The Other Options Are Wrong A. Right-to-left intracardiac shunt Not the usual mechanism. C. Reduced haemoglobin concentration Causes anaemia rather than PE-related hypoxaemia. D. Alveolar hypoventilation Not the primary abnormality. E. Carbon monoxide poisoning Unrelated to PE.

stations.title: Metallic Click and Irregular Pulse / Warfarin, Never a Direct Oral Anticoagulant
stations.source_heading: stations/R2-13 Mechanical mitral valve with AF

sections.preamble: R2-13 Cardiovascular exam - Mechanical mitral valve with AF
sections.1. Title: Metallic Click and Irregular Pulse / Warfarin, Never a Direct Oral Anticoagulant
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Physical examination PACES encounter Station 3, cardiovascular examination Skills marked A, B, D, E, G Setting Cardiology outpatient clinic Time 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) Guidelines British Committee for Standards in Haematology: Guidelines on oral anticoagulation with warfarin, fourth edition (2011; last updated 2012); ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease (2025) Related AMaC stations AMaC mechanical aortic valve and mitral stenosis examination stations; this one tests the mitral position and the anticoagulation rules
sections.3. Candidate brief: Mrs Judith Marchbanks is 59 and works as a bookkeeper. She attends for a routine review after heart surgery. Please examine her cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A loud metallic click at the apex with an irregular pulse means a mechanical mitral valve with atrial fibrillation: warfarin to a higher INR target, and never a direct oral anticoagulant. The Examiner Trap. Candidates hear the click, say "aortic", and call a direct oral anticoagulant the modern choice. Pass: mitral position from the click at the apex, an INR target of 3.0, warfarin only. Fail: the wrong valve, or a direct oral anticoagulant.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Look for the scar and the click before you touch her: they name the operation. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; hands, bruising, face, pulse, then JVP and the chest wall. Time the click against the apex beat and the carotid pulse, and listen for a murmur beside it. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the heart, then ask you to roll onto your left side." Apex beat; thrill; heart sounds at four areas; carotid; lung bases; ankles; cover her; clean hands. Say the valve, the rhythm and the drug rule together, because the anticoagulation is the point. "She has a mechanical mitral valve with atrial fibrillation. She needs warfarin; a direct oral anticoagulant is not safe." Present in order; diagnosis; INR target; complications; urgent signs; thank her.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; presses on the scar; leaves her exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards. Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and pauses if she tires. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the pulse, JVP, apex or one auscultation area. Hands, pulse, face, JVP, chest wall, apex, four auscultation areas, carotids, lung bases and ankles. Also turns her onto her left side, listens at the apex in held expiration, and checks the dentition. R3 B Identifying signs Misses the scar or the irregular pulse, or reports a murmur that is not present. Finds the sternotomy scar, irregularly irregular pulse, a loud metallic click at the apex with the apex beat, and no murmur. Also finds the soft diastolic opening sound, forearm bruising, and no failure or endocarditis signs. R4 D Differen
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: slim, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 14; pulse 86, irregularly irregular; blood pressure 126/74; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hands: warm, no splinter haemorrhages, no pallor; bruising on both forearms. Face: no jaundice. JVP not raised. Healed median sternotomy scar. Apex beat in the fifth space, mid-clavicular line, not displaced; palpable click; no thrill. Heart sounds: loud crisp metallic closing click at the apex with the apex beat, just before the carotid pulse; soft early diastolic opening sound; no murmur; normal second sound. Lungs clear. No oedema. Dentition good. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) Told: bileaflet valve. 3. What anticoagulant, and what INR target? (E) 4. Complications? (E) 5. She becomes breathless and the click is muffled: what now? (E) Curveballs: A friend says a newer tablet is easier than warfarin: not for a mechanical valve. Her INR is 2.0: below target, adjust warfarin with the anticoagulation clinic. Can she have dental work? Yes, with the INR checked.

Header: Field Detail Station type Consultation PACES station and encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation encounter Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) Setting Rheumatology outpatient clinic Time 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min Guidelines British Society for Rheumatology, The 2024 guideline for management of systemic sclerosis, Rheumatology 2024;keae394 (2024; published September 2024) Related AMaC stations Cardiovascular examination: tricuspid regurgitation with pulmonary hypertension (R2-15)
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Ruth Haverford, 43, piano teacher. Years of cold white then blue fingers, now tight skin on her hands and face, breathlessness on stairs and aching joints. Her GP has started a short course of prednisolone. Please assess and advise. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Haverford.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Raynaud's with tight skin is systemic sclerosis: screen the lungs at baseline and the pulmonary circulation every year, and minimise glucocorticoid, which raises the risk of scleroderma renal crisis (BSR 2024). The Examiner Trap. She asks for something for her aching joints and her GP has started prednisolone. Candidates continue it. Pass: stop to review the steroid, check blood pressure and kidney function, arrange lung and heart screening. Fail: continue or raise the steroid without recognising the renal-crisis risk.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Raynaud's alone or systemic disease? Get the story. "Tell me about the fingers, the skin and your breathing. Any swallowing trouble or heartburn?" Introduce, consent, ask about pain; Raynaud's, ulcers, skin, dyspnoea, reflux, drugs, steroid. Look for sclerosis and organ involvement. "May I examine your hands, face, chest and heart, and check your blood pressure?" Hands, mouth opening, skin, telangiectasia, ulcers, lungs, JVP, P2, BP. Screen the lungs and heart; protect the kidneys. "This looks like scleroderma. I'd like to check your lungs and heart every year and review the steroid." Lung tests, CT, echo, NT-proBNP; blood pressure and kidney function; steroid review. Share the plan; find her worry. "What worries you most?" Explain tests, treatment, alternatives; safety net; check understanding.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Handles painful, ulcerated fingertips roughly; no consent Introduces, consents, asks about pain, handles the hands gently, covers her Offers a chaperone, warms the room and asks about her playing R2 C History No lung, swallowing or steroid history Asks Raynaud's, ulcers, breathlessness, reflux, swallowing, joint pain and drugs Also asks about headaches, new blood pressure readings, family history and how her work is affected R3 F Her concern Ignores her worry Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her Finds the fear of losing her hands and her teaching, and answers honestly R4 A, B Examination Reports ulcers or oedema that are absent Sclerodactyly, digital pitting scars, tight facial skin, telangiectasia, fine basal crackles, BP 148/92 Adds mouth opening, calcinosis, JVP, loud P2 and states negatives: no oedema, no digital ulcers now R5 D Differential Primary Raynaud's Systemic sclerosis Limited versus diffuse disease, with overlap syndromes and drug causes considered R6 E Screening and safety Continues or raises prednisolone (Critical fail) Reviews and minimises steroid; baseline CT and lung function; annual echo and NT-proBN
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are. Ruth Haverford, 43, piano teacher. Thoughtful, worried about your hands. Married with a teenage son. Opening line. "My hands are stiff and sore and the prednisolone helps. Can I stay on it?" Volunteered. Fingers turn white and blue in the cold for years; skin on the hands and face tightening for a year; aching joints. Only if asked. Breathless on stairs for six months, dry cough. Heartburn most nights. Occasional trouble swallowing dry food. Tender sores at the fingertips last winter. Prednisolone 20 mg daily for a week from your GP (scenario). No headaches. No blood pressure readings at home. Non-smoker. Alcohol: a glass of wine at weekends. No allergies. No recent travel abroad. Other medicines: antacid tablets for the heartburn, nothing else. Mother has an underactive thyroid; no other family illness. Works from home teaching piano; no driving problems. Hidden concern. You fear that you will lose the use of your hands and your teaching. Reveal only if asked what worries you most. Your questions. "Is it scleroderma?" "Will I lose my fingers?" "Can I stay on the steroid?" "Will it affect my lungs?" How you react. Good handling: you agree to stop and have tests. Poor h
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings (released as each step is done). Sclerodactyly with tight shiny skin to the knuckles, digital pitting scars and calcinosis; tight facial skin with reduced mouth opening; telangiectasia on the face and palms. No digital ulcers today. Fine basal crackles. JVP not raised; loud P2. No oedema. BP 148/92, pulse 82 (scenario values). Lung function: gas transfer low; chest film shows basal shadowing (scenario). Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): systemic sclerosis, limited or diffuse. Q2 Lung screening (R6): baseline high-resolution CT and lung function including gas transfer (BSR 2024). Q3 Pulmonary hypertension (R6): annual screening with lung function, echocardiography and NT-proBNP, using the DETECT tool where appropriate (BSR 2024). Q4 Kidney (R6): glucocorticoid should be minimised, with caution above 10 mg prednisolone equivalent; scleroderma renal crisis presents with new hypertension and kidney injury; check BP, kidney function and urine; ACE inhibitor started if it occurs (BSR 2024). Q5 Advice (R7): warmth, stop smoking, reflux treatment, return with headache or high pressure. Curveball 1. "She has headaches and a BP of 190/110." (R6) Safe: suspect renal crisis; same-da

sections.preamble: R2-56 Blurred vision in diabetes Station ID:
sections.1. Title: Blurred Vision in a Taxi Driver with Diabetes / Grade the Eye, Check He Can Drive
sections.2. Header: Field Detail Station type Consultation PACES station and encounter Station 5, consultation encounter Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) Setting Diabetes outpatient clinic Time 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min Guidelines NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (2015; last updated February 2026); gov.uk, Eye conditions and driving (page accessed October 2026); gov.uk, Diabetic eye screening: retinal image grading criteria (2012; last updated December 2025) Related AMaC stations Consultation: hypoglycaemia and driving
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Ravinder Dosanjh, 56, taxi driver. Type 2 diabetes for 12 years on metformin and gliclazide. Blurred vision in the right eye for three weeks. HbA1c 84 mmol/mol, BP 156/94. Missed his last eye screening. Please assess and advise. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination, including looking at the fundi, and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Dosanjh.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Blurred vision in poorly controlled diabetes with a missed screening visit is diabetic eye disease until the eye specialists show otherwise; describe what you see, refer urgently, and ask whether he can still meet the driving standard. The Examiner Trap. He wants new glasses and says he is fine to drive. Candidates agree. Pass: examine the fundi, name the retinopathy and maculopathy, refer urgently, advise on driving. Fail: say he can keep driving the taxi.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Eye disease or a glucose swing? Get the story. "Tell me about the vision. Does it come and go, and is it painful? Any floaters or flashes?" Introduce, consent, ask about pain; vision, floaters, glucose, driving, last screening. Look at the eye and the whole picture. "May I check your vision, look into your eyes and take your blood pressure?" Acuity, fields, pupils, fundi, BP, feet, urine. Grade, refer and tighten control. "I can see bleeds and fatty deposits near the centre of the retina. You need an urgent eye clinic review." Name grade; refer; agree HbA1c and BP plan; driving advice. Share the plan; find his worry. "What worries you most?" Explain risks, options, safety net; check understanding.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Shines a bright light without warning; no consent Introduces, consents, warns before the light, asks about comfort Offers a chaperone, dims lights, thanks him R2 C History No vision, glucose or driving history Asks onset, floaters, flashes, pain, glucose control, screening and driving Also asks about hypoglycaemia, smoking, kidney disease and how work is affected R3 F His concern Ignores his worry Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns him Finds the fear of losing his taxi licence and his sight, and answers honestly R4 A, B Examination Reports new vessels that are absent Acuity reduced right eye; dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates near the macula; no new vessels Adds cotton wool spots, venous beading, fields, pupils and BP, and states negatives: no new vessels, no vitreous bleed R5 D Grade Cataract or glasses Diabetic retinopathy with maculopathy Describes features of pre-proliferative retinopathy with maculopathy, names proliferative disease and cataract as alternatives, and says formal grading needs retinal imaging by the eye service R6 E Referral and control No referral; just glasses Refers urgently to eye services; agree
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are. Ravinder Dosanjh, 56, taxi driver. Practical, defensive about work, anxious. Married, two children. Opening line. "My right eye is blurry. I just need new glasses. I'm fine to drive." Volunteered. Blurred vision in the right eye for three weeks. Only if asked. A dark shadow floating at times. No flashes or pain. Last eye screening three years ago. Tablets irregularly. Smoker. No hypoglycaemia. No kidney problems known. No blood pressure tablets or statin. You drink about two pints at weekends. Your father had diabetes. No recent travel. Married with two children; you are the main earner. You drive about nine hours a day and struggled to read a sign this week. No allergies. Hidden concern. You fear losing your taxi licence and your sight. Reveal only if asked what worries you most. Your questions. "Can I keep driving?" "Will I go blind?" "Do I need laser?" "Is it my sugar?" How you react. Good handling: you agree to stop driving until assessed. Poor handling: if told you cannot work you say you will drive anyway.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings (released as each step is done). Visual acuity right eye 6/18, left 6/9 (scenario values). Pupils equal and reactive. Right fundus: dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates close to the macula, two cotton wool spots, venous beading in two quadrants; no new vessels. Left fundus: scattered dot haemorrhages. BP 156/94. HbA1c 84 mmol/mol. Feet: reduced sensation. Urine: protein 1+. Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis and grade (R4, R5): diabetic retinopathy with maculopathy in the right eye, with features of pre-proliferative change (cotton wool spots, venous beading); the exact grade needs retinal imaging and assessment by the eye service. Q2 Management (R6): urgent referral to hospital eye services; HbA1c target agreed individually (NICE NG28: 53 mmol/mol is the usual aim on a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia, such as gliclazide, relaxed case by case); BP treatment. Q3 Risk (R5): proliferative change, vitreous bleed. Q4 Driving (R7): must read a number plate from 20 metres; tell DVLA if the condition affects both eyes, if retinopathy is treated with laser, or if a doctor, optician or eye specialist says he should not drive or may not meet the standard (gov.uk). sections.preamble: Consultation - Cough, tender shins and hilar lymph nodes Tender Shins and Hilar Nodes / Think Sarcoidosis, Then Check Calcium, Eyes and Heart Station ID:
sections.2. Header: Field Detail Station type Consultation PACES station and encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min Guidelines ERS clinical practice guidelines on treatment of sarcoidosis, Eur Respir J 2021;58(6):2004079 (published June 2021); BTS Clinical Statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis, Thorax 2021;76:4-84 Related AMaC stations Respiratory examination: interstitial lung disease; upper lobe fibrosis and TB
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Tamsin Orrell, 29, primary school teacher. Three weeks of dry cough, painful red lumps on both shins and sore ankles. Her GP arranged a chest film, which reports enlarged lymph nodes at both lung roots. Please assess and advise. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Orrell.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Tender shin lumps, ankle pain and bilateral hilar nodes in a young adult is most likely Löfgren-type sarcoidosis; the lesson is to consider TB and lymphoma, check calcium and the heart, and ask about the eyes. The Examiner Trap. Candidates stop at the label "sarcoidosis" or start steroid at once. Pass: say it is likely, consider TB and lymphoma, check calcium and heart, ask about the eyes, and explain that it often settles. Fail: no screening, or steroid before the work-up.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Cough with shin lumps: infection, sarcoidosis or lymphoma? Get the story. "Tell me about the cough, the shins and your ankles. Any fever, weight loss, night sweats or contacts with TB?" Introduce, consent, ask about pain; cough, skin, joints, eyes, palpitations, fainting, TB risk, drugs. Look for the skin, joint and chest signs. "May I look at your shins and ankles, feel your neck and armpits, and listen to your chest?" Shins, ankles, nodes, eyes, chest, pulse, blood pressure, saturation. Exclude mimics; screen the organs. "This looks like sarcoidosis. I'd like blood tests and a heart tracing, to ask about your eyes, and to consider TB according to your risk." Calcium, kidney, liver, TB risk assessment (blood TB test if indicated), ECG, lung function, eye review if symptoms or specialist advice, specialist plan. Share the plan; find her worry. "What worries you most?" Explain it often settles; options; safety net; check understanding.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Presses on tender shins without asking Introduces, consents, asks about pain, handles the shins and ankles gently, covers her Offers a chaperone, explains each step and asks how the pain affects teaching R2 C History No TB, eye or heart symptom questions Asks cough, fever, weight, joints, rash, eye symptoms, palpitations, TB contact and drugs Also asks about fainting, family history, travel, occupation and the timing of the rash R3 F Her concern Ignores her worry Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her Finds the fear of cancer like her father's and the worry about infecting pupils, and answers honestly R4 A, B Examination Reports nodes or eye signs that are absent Tender red nodules on both shins, ankle swelling, clear chest, pulse 78, BP 118/74, saturation 98% (scenario) Checks nodes, eyes, joints and heart sounds, and states negatives: no peripheral nodes, no red eye, no lupus pernio R5 D Differential Cellulitis or DVT only Löfgren-type sarcoidosis Also TB, lymphoma and drug causes considered, with why each is less likely R6 E Screening No calcium or heart check Calcium, kidney and liver tests, ECG, lung function; asks ab
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are. Tamsin Orrell, 29, primary school teacher. Practical, anxious, tired. Lives with a partner. Opening line. "I've got a cough and sore red shins. The GP says my chest X-ray isn't normal." Volunteered. Dry cough for three weeks; painful red lumps on both shins; sore ankles. Only if asked. Mild fever and tiredness. Drinks little alcohol; not pregnant and no hormonal contraception. No weight loss, no night sweats. No TB contact; no travel. No eye symptoms. No palpitations, no fainting. No new drugs; no allergies. Non-smoker. You drive to work. Hidden concern. Your father died of cancer, and you fear this is cancer; you also fear passing something to your pupils. Reveal only if asked what worries you most. Your questions. "Is it cancer?" "Am I infectious?" "Can I go to work?" "Will it come back?" How you react. Good handling: you agree to tests and a review. Poor handling: if steroid is given with no explanation you ask why and hesitate.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings (released as each step is done). Tender raised red-purple nodules over both shins; ankles swollen and tender with warmth. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. Eyes not red; no lupus pernio. Chest clear. Pulse 78 regular; BP 118/74; saturation 98% on air; temperature 37.6 C (scenario values). Chest film: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, clear lung fields. Corrected calcium within the laboratory range; ECG sinus rhythm, normal PR interval (scenario). Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): Löfgren-type sarcoidosis; TB and lymphoma to consider; biopsy is not usually needed when the picture is typical. Q2 Screening (R6): calcium, kidney and liver tests, ECG, lung function, eye review if symptomatic or advised. Q3 Heart (R6): palpitations, fainting, heart block or arrhythmia suggest cardiac sarcoid; specialist review. Q4 Treatment (R7): symptomatic care (many patients improve with supportive treatment); ERS 2021 covers glucocorticoid for pulmonary disease that needs treatment. Q5 Eyes (R6): uveitis can be silent, so ask about symptoms and arrange review according to symptoms and specialist advice. Curveball 1. "Her calcium is raised." (R6) Safe: repeat, check kidney function, hydrate, sp
sections.9. Mark Triggers: Introduces, consents and asks about pain (G) Asks cough, fever, weight and TB contact (C) Asks eye symptoms, palpitations and fainting (C) Acknowledges her view and asks what worries her (F) Examines shins, ankles and nodes (A) Examines eyes, chest and takes pulse and pressure (A) Reports shin nodules, ankle swelling and clear chest (B) Names Löfgren-type sarcoidosis and the mimics (D) Plans calcium, ECG, eye symptom check and TB risk assessment (E) Explains the plan and checks understanding (E)

sections.preamble: R2-63 — Thirst and passing a lot of urine Thirst and Litres of Urine on Lithium / Find the Cause, Keep Fluids Flowing, Check the Lithium Station ID:
sections.2. Header: Field Detail Station type Consultation PACES station and encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min Guidelines Nandoshvili et al, Partial nephrogenic diabetes insipidus associated with lithium therapy, Drug Ther Bull 2020;58(3):45 (case report); Specialist Pharmacy Service, Lithium monitoring (last updated 6 December 2024) Related AMaC stations Consultation: hyponatraemia; hypercalcaemia
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Naomi Brereton, 47, library assistant. Three months of intense thirst, drinking several litres a day and passing large volumes of urine, including at night. Her GP found no sugar in her urine. She takes lithium for bipolar disorder. Please assess and advise. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Brereton.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Thirst and polyuria is diabetes mellitus, high calcium, diabetes insipidus or excess drinking; the lesson is to find the cause, and in a woman on lithium never to restrict fluids, and to urgently assess whether lithium must be withheld for toxicity or AKI. The Examiner Trap. She is on lithium and the thirst is blamed on the drink habit. Candidates say cut fluids or stop lithium. Pass: confirm the cause, maintain access to fluids and urgently review lithium safety, arrange supervised tests and liaise with psychiatry. Fail: restrict fluids or stop lithium.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Polyuria: sugar, calcium, kidney, pituitary or drug? Get the story. "Tell me about the thirst, how much you drink and how often you pass urine, including at night." Introduce, consent, ask about pain; volume, nocturia, drugs, lithium history, mood, headaches, vision. Look for dehydration and clues. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, and your vision fields?" Hydration, orthostatic pressure, fields, fundi, thyroid, tremor, urine dipstick. Sort the causes; protect the patient. "This looks like lithium affecting the kidney's ability to concentrate urine. I'd confirm it with a supervised test." Glucose, calcium, sodium, urine osmolality; lithium level and kidney function today; supervised testing in a specialist unit; keep drinking. Share the plan; find her worry. "What worries you most?" Explain tests, options, amiloride; psychiatry liaison; safety net; check understanding.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Ignores the effect of nocturia on sleep and work Introduces, consents, asks about discomfort, offers water, gives privacy Acknowledges the tiredness and thanks her for being open about her illness R2 C History No lithium, drug or mood history Asks volumes, nocturia, onset, lithium duration, other drugs, headaches, vision and weight Also asks about lithium levels, kidney tests, dehydration risks, family history and fluid habits R3 F Her concern Ignores her worry Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her Finds the fear that lithium will be stopped and her illness will return, and answers honestly R4 A, B Examination Reports dehydration or field loss that is absent BP 122/76 lying and 118/72 standing, pulse 80, full fields, no tremor, urine dipstick negative for glucose (scenario) Adds fundi, thyroid, hydration and states negatives: no postural drop, no goitre, no visual field defect R5 D Differential Primary diabetes mellitus without a test Lithium-related nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Also diabetes mellitus, hypercalcaemia, cranial diabetes insipidus and primary polydipsia, with reasons R6 E Investigation and safety Critical
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are. Naomi Brereton, 47, library assistant. Quiet, tired, a little guarded. Lives alone with a cat. Opening line. "I'm so thirsty all the time and up all night passing water. Can you just make it stop?" Volunteered. Thirst for three months; drinks about five litres a day (scenario); passes urine every hour and four times at night. Only if asked. Taking lithium for bipolar disorder for twelve years; mood stable. No other regular drugs. No headaches; vision normal. No weight loss. Not drinking alcohol. No allergies. You drive to work. You have never smoked. No family history of kidney disease or diabetes. No recent travel. Your last lithium blood test was a few months ago and you were told it was fine. Hidden concern. You fear the doctor will stop your lithium and that you will become unwell again, as in the hospital stay years ago. Reveal only if asked what worries you most. Your questions. "Is it diabetes?" "Is the lithium damaging my kidneys?" "Should I drink less?" "Do I have to stop lithium?" How you react. Good handling: you agree to tests and seek medication advice urgently if unwell. Poor handling: if told to stop lithium you say you will stop it today.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings (released as each step is done). Well, not dehydrated. Pulse 80 regular; BP 122/76 lying and 118/72 standing (scenario values). No tremor, no goitre; full visual fields; fundi normal. Urine dipstick negative for glucose. Plasma glucose and HbA1c within range; corrected calcium within range; sodium at the upper end of range; kidney function mildly reduced; lithium level in her usual range; urine osmolality low for plasma osmolality (scenario). Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): likely lithium-related nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; diabetes mellitus and hypercalcaemia excluded by the tests. Q2 Confirmation (R6): supervised water deprivation test with copeptin, under a specialist protocol. Q3 Management (R6): keep drinking to thirst; amiloride is a specialist decision if fluids do not control symptoms (Drug Ther Bull case report). Q4 Safety (R6): fluid restriction risks hypernatraemia; dehydration raises lithium level. Check the lithium level and kidney function today; if toxicity, dehydration or AKI is suspected, arrange urgent assessment and agree withholding lithium with the treating team. Q5 Psychiatry (R7): review lithium with the psychiatrist; do not stop it on the sp
sections.9. Mark Triggers: Introduces, consents and offers water (G) Asks volumes, nocturia and onset (C) Asks lithium duration, other drugs and mood (C) Acknowledges her view and asks what worries her (F) Checks lying and standing blood pressure (A) Examines fields, thyroid and tests urine (A) Reports no dehydration and negative urine glucose (B) Names lithium-related nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and the alternatives (D) Plans glucose, calcium, sodium, osmolality and supervised test (E) Explains the plan and checks understanding (E)

stations.title: Blue, Clubbed, Loud P2, No Murmur / The Defect Has Gone Quiet

sections.preamble: R3-09 Cardiovascular exam - Eisenmenger syndrome
sections.1. Title: Blue, Clubbed, Loud P2, No Murmur / The Defect Has Gone Quiet
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Physical examination PACES encounter Station 3, cardiovascular examination Skills marked A, B, D, E, G Setting Adult congenital heart disease clinic Time 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) Guidelines ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (2020) Related AMaC stations AMaC atrial septal defect station; this one tests a shunt that has reversed
sections.3. Candidate brief: Ms Lorna Trewin is 31 and works in a library. She has been breathless on gentle exertion for years and is always tired. Please examine her cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A blue, clubbed patient with a loud palpable P2 and no shunt murmur has Eisenmenger syndrome. The murmur of her original defect has disappeared because the shunt has reversed. The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for the murmur, hear none and call the heart normal, or advise closing the defect. Pass: cyanosis, clubbing, loud P2 and no shunt murmur, so Eisenmenger. Fail: normal heart, or closure.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do She is blue at rest: look at the lips, hands and face before you touch her. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; look at lips, hands, face, eyes; pulse; JVP. Feel for a heave and a palpable second sound, then listen for what is missing. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the heart, then lean you forward." Heave; thrill; P2; four areas; Graham Steell murmur; lung bases; ankles; cover her; clean hands. Say the diagnosis, why the murmur is missing, and what pregnancy means for her. "She has Eisenmenger syndrome, probably from an unrepaired ventricular septal defect. Pregnancy is contraindicated." Present in order; diagnosis; complications; pregnancy and contraception; specialist care; thank her.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; asks her to lie flat despite breathlessness; leaves her exposed. sections.preamble: 13 | R3-10 Cardiovascular exam - Mitral valve prolapse
sections.1. Title: A Click Then a Murmur / Common, Usually Benign, But Know Who Needs Follow-up
sections.2. sections.3. Candidate brief: Ms Annika Lindqvist is 28 and works as a physiotherapist. She has occasional palpitations and an abnormal sound heard at a routine check. Please examine her cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex is mitral valve prolapse. It is common and usually benign; the marks come from knowing which patients need closer follow-up. The Examiner Trap. Candidates hear a murmur and call it mitral regurgitation or aortic stenosis, then either alarm her or discharge her. Pass: click then late murmur, standing makes it more obvious, and follow-up by risk. Fail: wrong valve, or no follow-up plan.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do She is well. Look carefully: the click is the diagnosis, and her build may point to a connective tissue cause. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; hands, face, build, pulse, JVP; chest wall. Time the click against the apex beat, then listen after she stands. "I'm going to listen over the heart lying down, then standing, and ask you to breathe out." Apex; thrill; four areas; axilla; click timing; stand and re-listen; carotids; lung bases; ankles; cover her. Name the lesion, grade the leak by what you find, and say who needs follow-up. "She has mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. I'd confirm it with echocardiography and arrange follow-up by risk." Present in order; diagnosis; complications; echo; follow-up interval; red flags; thank her.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; presses hard on the chest; leaves her exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards. Also offers a chaperone, keeps exposure to the minimum, and checks she is comfortable standing. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the pulse, apex or axilla, or does not re-listen standing. Hands, pulse, JVP, apex, four auscultation areas, axilla, then re-listens standing, then carotids and lung bases. Also leans her forward in held expiration and checks the build and arm span. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a diastolic murmur, a thrill or heart failure that is not present. Finds a mid-systolic click and a late systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, more obvious standing. Also states occasional ectopic beats, no thrill or failure, and no Marfan features. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it aortic stenosis or a ventricular septal defect. Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. Also separates it from rheumatic
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: slim, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 14; pulse 74, regular apart from occasional ectopic beats; blood pressure 112/68; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Hands: normal; arm span equal to height. Palate normal. JVP not raised. Apex beat in the fifth space, mid-clavicular line, not displaced; no thrill. Mid-systolic click at the apex, followed by a late systolic murmur radiating to the axilla; the click comes earlier and the murmur is longer and louder standing. Second sound normal. Lungs clear. No oedema. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B, R3) Mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur at the apex, more obvious standing; occasional ectopics; no thrill or failure. 2. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Mitral valve prolapse with a mild leak. 3. Complications? (E, R6) Regurgitation, arrhythmia, stroke, rarely sudden death. 4. Investigation and follow-up? (E, R5) Echocardiography; ECG and Holter for palpitations; echo every 3 to 5 years if asymptomatic with a mild leak (BSE 2024). 5. Who needs closer follow-up? (E, R5) Moderate or severe regurgitation, symptoms, LV dilatation, LVEF below 60%, raised pulmonary pressure, new atrial fibrillation.

sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Lionel Hargreaves is 71 and a retired surveyor. He had heart surgery four months ago and attends for review. Please examine his cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A sternotomy scar, a leg vein-harvest scar and a quiet soft murmur with no metallic click mean bypass grafts and a tissue valve. The anticoagulation is not the lifelong warfarin of a mechanical valve. The Examiner Trap. Candidates see the sternotomy, call it a mechanical valve and advise lifelong warfarin to a high INR. Pass: no click, so tissue valve; an early course of warfarin or aspirin, then aspirin. Fail: lifelong warfarin at the mechanical target.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do He has two kinds of scar. Look for both, and for a click, before you decide what is inside. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; hands, face, pulse, JVP; chest wall and both legs. Listen for what is absent: no metallic click. Then grade the flow murmur. "I'm going to feel your chest, listen over the heart, and lean you forward." Apex; thrill; four areas; carotids; lean forward in held expiration; lung bases; ankles; leg scar; cover him; clean hands. Say the operations, say it is a tissue valve, and give the anticoagulation plan. "He has had bypass grafts and a tissue aortic valve replacement. His anticoagulation differs from a mechanical valve." Present in order; diagnosis; why not mechanical; antithrombotic plan; endocarditis advice; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the legs, pulse or one auscultation area. Hands, pulse, JVP, chest wall, apex, four auscultation areas, carotids, lung bases, ankles and the leg scar. Also leans him forward in held expiration and checks the teeth. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a metallic click, or misses a scar. Finds a sternotomy scar, a left leg vein-harvest scar, a soft ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area and no click. Also finds normal heart sounds, no diastolic murmur, no failure, and no endocarditis signs. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it a mechanical valve, or aortic stenosis that was never treated. Coronary artery bypass grafting and a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. Also says why not mechanical: no metalli

sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 138/76; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. First sound normal; soft ejection systolic murmur at the right second space, not radiating; second sound soft; no click; no diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No oedema. Teeth good. Question ladder: 1. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A tall young man with long fingers and an early diastolic murmur is most likely Marfan syndrome. The station turns on seeing the body as well as the heart. The Examiner Trap. Candidates go straight to the chest and call it aortic regurgitation. Pass: body signs first, then the murmur, then the aortic root and the dissection warning. Fail: murmur only.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Look at the whole person first: height, limbs, fingers, chest wall, palate, spine and feet. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs, palate, pulse. Pulse and pulse pressure first, then listen with him leaning forward in held expiration. "I'm going to listen over the heart, then lean you forward and ask you to breathe out." Collapsing pulse; apex; thrill; four areas; leaning forward; lung bases; sacrum; spine; ankles; cover him. Name the syndrome, the valve lesion and the danger, and say where he needs follow-up. "He has features of Marfan syndrome with aortic regurgitation. The aortic root needs measuring." Present in order; diagnosis; echo; root size; family testing; thank him.

Looks at build, arm span, hands, thumb and wrist signs and palate, then pulse, apex, four auscultation areas leaning forward, bases, spine and ankles. Also checks feet, skin stretch marks and the eyes for lens dislocation. R3 B Identifying signs Reports signs that are not present, or finds only the murmur. Finds tall build, long fingers, positive thumb and wrist signs, pectus excavatum, high palate, scoliosis, collapsing pulse and an early diastolic murmur. Apex beat displaced to the sixth space, anterior axillary line; no thrill. Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder leaning forward in held expiration. Lungs clear. No oedema. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A trachea pulled towards the side with reduced expansion and a dull base suggests collapse of the lung on that side, probably the right lower lobe on these findings; the lesson is to tell it from an effusion and to say a bronchial tumour must be excluded, without telling him cancer is established. The Examiner Trap. Candidates call any dull base an effusion, or forget the trachea. Pass: find the trachea pulled towards the dull side, say collapse, and name cancer as the cause to exclude. Fail: effusion, or no cause given.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Look at the whole man. "Mr Redfern, may I examine your chest? Tell me if you get breathless and we'll pause." Introduce, consent, sit at 45 degrees, expose; tar staining, clubbing, cyanosis, rate, nodes. Where is the trachea, and what does the chest do? "I'm going to feel your windpipe and your chest, then tap and listen." Trachea; expansion; percussion; tactile or vocal resonance; breath sounds; back. Look for cause and complications. "May I check your neck glands, face and the rest of your chest?" Supraclavicular nodes, Horner's, hoarse voice, SVC signs, liver. Say what it is and the plan. "These findings suggest right-sided volume loss or collapse; the likely cause is a blockage, so I'd arrange urgent imaging." Cover him, thank him; present findings, causes, tests, plan.

stations.title: Tired, Cold and Slow, with Angina / Start Low, Go Slow
stations.source_heading: stations/R3-30 Hypothyroidism in an older woman with angina

sections.preamble: R3-30 — Hypothyroidism in an older woman with angina
sections.1. Title: Tired, Cold and Slow, with Angina / Start Low, Go Slow Station ID:
sections.2. Header: Field Detail Station type Consultation PACES station and encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min Guidelines NICE NG145 Thyroid disease: assessment and management (2019; last updated October 2023) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Winifred Gaunt, 74, retired seamstress. Six months of tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain and constipation. Her GP found a high TSH and a low free T4 on two occasions. She has stable angina. Please assess and advise. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Gaunt.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Tiredness and cold intolerance with a high TSH and low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism; the lesson is to start levothyroxine low and slow in an older woman with angina, and to monitor TSH. The Examiner Trap. Candidates give the standard full dose by weight. Pass: start 25 to 50 micrograms with titration, check an ECG, and warn about chest pain. Fail: a full replacement dose in a woman with angina.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Hypothyroid, and why? Get the story. "Tell me about the tiredness, the cold, your weight and bowels. Any chest pain on effort?" Introduce, consent, ask about pain; symptoms, angina, drugs, family, past thyroid treatment. Look for signs and heart disease. "May I feel your neck and pulse, check your reflexes and blood pressure?" Pulse, BP, skin, hair, voice, goitre, ankle reflexes, oedema. Treat safely in the older heart. "I'd start a low dose of levothyroxine and build up slowly." Dose, ECG, titration, TSH at set intervals, chest-pain warning. Share the plan; find her worry. "What worries you most?" Explain tablets, timing, monitoring, options; safety net; check understanding.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Rushes her or ignores that she is tired and cold Introduces, consents, asks about discomfort, keeps her warm and covered Offers a chaperone, a seat and a blanket, and thanks her for coming R2 C History Does not ask about chest pain or drugs Asks symptoms, angina pattern, drugs, past thyroid problems, family history and mood Also asks about amiodarone, lithium, previous radioiodine, biotin and calcium or iron tablets R3 F Her concern Ignores her worry Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her Finds the fear that her forgetfulness is dementia, and answers honestly R4 A, B Examination Reports a goitre or exophthalmos that is absent Pulse 54 regular, BP 148/88, dry skin, slow-relaxing ankle reflexes, no goitre (scenario) Adds hair, voice and periorbital puffiness, carpal tunnel signs, and states negatives: no oedema, no heart failure R5 D Diagnosis Depression or normal ageing Primary hypothyroidism Primary hypothyroidism, likely autoimmune, with other causes and drug causes considered R6 E Treatment and monitoring Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): starts a full replacement dose Starts 25 to
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are. Winifred Gaunt, 74, retired seamstress. Gentle, a bit slow, worried. Widowed, lives alone, daughter nearby. Opening line. "I'm always cold and tired. The doctor says my thyroid is underactive." Volunteered. Tired and cold for six months; weight gain; constipation. Only if asked. Dry skin and hair. Chest tightness on walking uphill, relieved by rest and a GTN spray; no rest pain. Forgetfulness. No thyroid surgery or radioiodine. No lithium or amiodarone. Takes aspirin, a statin and a calcium tablet daily, and uses GTN spray when needed. No allergies. Never smoked. A sherry at Christmas. No recent travel. Your mother had an underactive thyroid and your sister has dementia. You do not drive. Hidden concern. You fear your forgetfulness means dementia like your sister. Reveal only if asked what worries you most. Your questions. "Will the tablets cure it?" "Is it safe for my heart?" "How long will I take them?" "Will I stop feeling forgetful?" How you react. Good handling: you agree to start low and have the tests. Poor handling: if told to start the full dose you say you will take it and ask no questions.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings (released as each step is done). Slow, dry skin, thin hair. Pulse 54 regular; BP 148/88 (scenario values). No goitre. Ankle reflexes slow to relax. No oedema. Chest clear; heart sounds normal. Weight 68 kg (scenario). TSH raised and free T4 low on two samples; ECG sinus bradycardia, no ischaemic change (scenario). Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): primary hypothyroidism. Q2 Dose (R6): NICE NG145 advises considering 25 to 50 micrograms daily with titration for adults aged 65 and over or with cardiovascular disease; 1.6 micrograms per kilogram for others. Q3 Monitoring (R6): TSH every 3 months until stable, then yearly; it may take up to 6 months to settle. Q4 Risk (R6): levothyroxine can provoke angina. Q5 Advice (R7): timing and spacing of tablets. Curveball 1. "She has chest pain at rest after the first dose." (R6) Safe: stop the dose rise; urgent assessment; ECG. Curveball 2. "The TSH is raised but free T4 is normal." (R5) Safe: subclinical hypothyroidism; repeat and discuss. Curveball 3. "She is drowsy, hypothermic and confused." (R5) Safe: myxoedema coma; emergency care. Curveball 4. "Her daughter wants her to take the full dose." (R7) Safe: explain why slow titratio

sections.preamble: R3-31 Consultation - Headaches and loss of libido in a lorry driver
sections.1. Title: Headaches, Low Libido and a Lorry Licence / Test Fields, Check Hormones, Tell DVLA
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia (2011); DVLA: Visual disorders, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 26 September 2025); GMC: Confidentiality, reporting concerns about patients to the DVLA or DVA (2017) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Gareth Halloran, 41, lorry driver. Six months of headaches, tiredness and loss of sex drive, and he thinks he has been bumping into things. Blood pressure 128/80. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Halloran.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Headache, low libido and a visual field loss together point to a pituitary tumour pressing on the optic chiasm. The most likely cause of the raised prolactin is a prolactinoma, which usually responds to a tablet rather than an operation. The Examiner Trap. Mr Halloran drives a lorry for a living and fears an operation. Candidates treat the hormones and forget his licence, or send him straight to surgery. Pass: fields, hormones, cabergoline, DVLA. Fail: no driving advice.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the headache and vision, then about the sex drive, and then ask what he drives. "Where is the headache? Have you noticed losing sight at the sides? What do you drive?" Headache; vision; erections; libido; fatigue; breast changes; medicines; weight; drive; partner. Test the visual fields and look for lost hormones. "May I test your sight at the edges, look at your eyes and check your blood pressure lying and standing? Tell me if anything hurts." Fields to confrontation; acuity; fundi; eye movements; hair; testes; lying and standing pressure; cover him. Name the diagnosis, say what blood tests and scans you need, explain the tablet, and give clear driving advice. "I think a growth on the pituitary gland is pressing on the nerves for your sight. You must stop driving until the DVLA advise." Prolactin; other hormones; MRI; fields; cabergoline; DVLA; red flags; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before sensitive questions about sexual function. R2 C History Asks about headache only; omits vision, libido, medicines or his job. Asks headache, vision, erections, libido, tiredness, breast changes, medicines, and what he drives. Also asks about a partner, fertility, thirst, and whether he has had a recent fall or crash. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits visual fields or fundi; reports defects that are absent. Finds a bitemporal field loss to confrontation, normal fundi, reduced facial hair, small soft testes and normal eye movements. Also finds no galactorrhoea, normal acuity and no postural fall, and reports acromegalic features as absent. R4 D Diff
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Gareth Halloran, 41, a lorry driver for a haulage firm. You are practical, a little embarrassed about sexual problems, and anxious about money. Opening line: "Doc, my head's been banging for months, I'm knackered, and the wife says I'm not interested any more. I keep catching the wing mirror on things." Volunteered: six months. A dull headache across the forehead. Tired all day. Libido gone. Only if asked: your erections are poor and you shave less. No breast changes. No thirst or passing a lot of urine. You do not smoke; a couple of pints at weekends; no allergies; no family history of pituitary or hormone problems; married with two children. You have not noticed a clear loss of sight but you miss things on both sides. You take no regular tablets. Only if asked what you drive: a heavy lorry, long distance, about five days a week. You have not told your firm. You nearly clipped a van last week. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are terrified of an operation on your brain and of losing your licence and your job. Say: "If I can't drive, we lose the house." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it a brain tumour?" "Will I need an operation?" "Can I car
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 64 regular; blood pressure lying 128/80, standing 126/78; temperature 36.6 °C. Visual acuity normal in both eyes. Visual fields to confrontation: bitemporal loss. Fundi normal. Eye movements normal. Reduced facial hair; testes small and soft; no breast tissue or galactorrhoea; no acromegalic features. Results, only when requested: prolactin 1,200 micrograms/litre; testosterone low with low LH and FSH; 9 am cortisol borderline low; TSH low-normal with low free T4; IGF-1 normal. MRI: a pituitary macroadenoma touching the optic chiasm. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. What do you make of the hormone results? (D) 3. What is first-line treatment? (E) Cabergoline. 4. Which hormone do you replace first? (E) Cortisol, before thyroid hormone. 5. What are the driving rules? (E) Curveballs: He says he will carry on driving: no; he must stop and tell DVLA, the Group 2 field standard is not met and a bitemporal defect is usually unacceptable for a car, and if he refuses the doctor may tell DVLA (GMC). Sudden severe headache with vomiting and falling vision: pituitary apoplexy, call 999. He asks about children: fertility may return with t

stations.title: Headache, Sweating and a Racing Heart / Alpha Blocker First, Never Beta Blocker Alone

sections.preamble: R3-32 Less acute consultation - Attacks of headache sweating and palpitations
sections.1. Title: Headache, Sweating and a Racing Heart / Alpha Blocker First, Never Beta Blocker Alone
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (2014; J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014;99:1915) Related AMaC stations AMaC secondary hypertension station; this one tests a catecholamine-secreting tumour
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Beatrice Oyelaran, 34, dental hygienist. Four months of attacks of headache, sweating and a racing heart. Blood pressure 190/112 during an attack. Her GP started bisoprolol three weeks ago and she feels worse. Sertraline for low mood. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Oyelaran.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. The triad of headache, sweating and palpitations with severe episodic hypertension points to a catecholamine-secreting tumour. The danger is in the treatment: a beta blocker given before an alpha blocker can make a crisis worse. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Oyelaran is anxious, her GP thought of panic attacks, and she takes sertraline. Candidates order imaging first, or add a beta blocker. Pass: metanephrines, alpha blocker first, genetics. Fail: beta blocker alone.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask what an attack is like, what brings it on and what she takes, including the new tablet. "Tell me about an attack. What brings it on? What do you take, and did the new tablet change anything?" Headache; sweating; palpitations; pallor; triggers; weight; blood pressure readings; medicines; family history of tumours. Check lying and standing blood pressure and look for the signs of a tumour. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your pulse, your hands, skin and neck? Tell me if anything hurts." Both arms; lying and standing; tremor; sweating; skin lesions; neck; abdomen; fundi; cover her. Explain what you suspect, the blood tests, the safe order of tablets and the warning signs. "I think a small gland tumour releases hormones that cause the attacks. Please stop the bisoprolol while we arrange tests and the right tablet." Tests; stop beta blocker; alpha blocker; fluids and salt; scan; genetics; red flags; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and checks she is comfortable being examined during a possible attack. R2 C History Asks about headache only; omits the other symptoms, medicines or family history. Asks the triad, triggers, weight, home blood pressures, medicines including bisoprolol and sertraline, and family history. Also asks about other drugs and supplements, pregnancy plans, and relatives with thyroid cancer or tumours. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure or the postural fall; reports signs that are absent. Finds blood pressure 168/100 lying and 150/90 standing, pulse 96, tremor, sweating, and no goitre. Also finds no neurofibromas or café-au-lait spots, normal fundi and a non-tender abdo
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Beatrice Oyelaran, 34, a dental hygienist. You are quick to worry and have been told by several people that it is anxiety. Opening line: "I get terrible attacks: a pounding headache, drenching sweats and my heart goes crazy. The new tablet has made them worse, not better." Volunteered: four months of attacks, about three a week, lasting twenty minutes. You look pale and feel dread. Only if asked: attacks can come on when you bend over or lift. You have lost some weight. Home blood pressure during an attack 190/112. You take bisoprolol since three weeks and sertraline for low mood since last year. No other medicines or supplements. You do not smoke and drink little alcohol. No allergies. No recent travel. You are not pregnant. You have two young children. Only if asked about family: your mother had a thyroid cancer and died at 52. A cousin had "a kidney tumour". Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are frightened it is cancer like your mother, and you feel nobody believes you. Say: "Everyone just tells me to relax." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it cancer?" "Why did the tablet make it worse?" "Do I need an operation?" "Is it in the family?" How
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: pale and sweating; pulse 96 regular; blood pressure lying 168/100, standing 150/90; temperature 36.8 °C. Fine tremor. No goitre. No neurofibromas or café-au-lait spots. Fundi normal. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Results, only when requested: plasma free metanephrines more than three times the upper limit of normal; TSH normal; glucose, calcium and kidney function normal. CT abdomen: a 4 cm right adrenal mass. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why did the tablet make it worse? (D) Unopposed alpha stimulation. 3. Tests and imaging order? (E) 4. Safe tablet order? (E) 5. Genetic testing? (E) Curveballs: She asks to stay on bisoprolol: no, alpha blocker first. She develops a severe headache, chest pain and confusion: emergency. She asks about her children: genetic testing and counselling.

sections.preamble: 19 | R3-33 Less acute consultation - Painful breast enlargement in a young man
sections.1. Title: Painful Breast Enlargement in a Young Man / Examine the Testes Before Blaming Steroids
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines American Society of Andrology and European Academy of Andrology: Gynecomastia evaluation and management clinical practice guidelines (Andrology 2019, doi 10.1111/andr.12636); NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015; last reviewed April 2026) Related AMaC stations None identified (gynaecomastia is not covered by an earlier AMaC station)
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Dylan Fairbairn, 33, gym instructor. Four months of painful enlargement of both breasts, the left more than the right. He has been embarrassed to come. No regular prescribed medicines. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Fairbairn.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Painful bilateral breast enlargement in a young man has a long list of causes, and drugs are one of them. The marks come from examining the testes anyway, because a testicular tumour can cause it too. The Examiner Trap. Mr Fairbairn is embarrassed and only admits to anabolic steroids when asked directly. Candidates blame the steroids and stop. Pass: full history, breast and testicular examination, scrotal ultrasound, hCG. Fail: steroids blamed, testes not examined.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the breasts, then ask kindly and directly about steroids, supplements and sexual function. "When did it start? Are you taking anything to build muscle, or any supplements? Any change in sex drive or erections?" Pain; discharge; lumps; steroids; supplements; alcohol; libido; fertility; weight; family history of cancer. Examine both breasts, then the testes with a chaperone, and look for other signs. "May I examine your chest and then your testicles? You can have a chaperone. Tell me if anything hurts." Breast tissue; lump; nipple; axillae; testes; thyroid; liver stigmata; visual fields; cover him. Name the likely causes, including the one you must exclude, and explain the tests and the plan. "The steroids may be causing this, but I found a lump in the right testicle, so I want an urgent scan." Tests; scrotal ultrasound; stop steroids; hormones; breast imaging; referral; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines the testes without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, offers a chaperone before the testicular examination, asks about discomfort, covers him and thanks him. Also acknowledges how embarrassing this is, and keeps exposure to the minimum. R2 C History Asks about the breasts only; omits drugs, supplements or sexual function. Asks onset, pain, discharge, drugs including steroids and supplements, alcohol, libido, erections and fertility. Also asks about weight, liver disease, family history of cancer and use of hCG or tamoxifen to cover steroids. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the testes; reports a breast lump or nipple discharge that is absent. Finds bilateral tender glandular tissue, left more than right, no hard lump or discharge, no nodes, and a firm right testicular nodule. Also finds a small soft left
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Dylan Fairbairn, 33, a gym instructor. You are muscular, polite and visibly embarrassed. You do not want to seem weak. Opening line: "I'm a bit embarrassed, doc. My chest has been getting bigger and it's sore, especially on the left." Volunteered: four months of enlarged, tender breasts. No nipple discharge. You have not noticed a lump in the breast. Only if asked directly about steroids or supplements: you have injected a testosterone-type steroid for eight months for a competition, and you take a "testosterone booster" supplement. You are afraid of being judged. Only if asked: libido a bit lower. No weight loss. No liver problems. A friend told you hCG helps recovery and you have taken some for a month. Only if asked about your testicles: you noticed the right felt a little firm a few weeks ago but ignored it. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid it is cancer, and that people will find out about the steroids. Say: "Please don't tell my gym." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it the steroids?" "Will it go away?" "Is it cancer?" How you react: if judged or lectured, you refuse the scan. If told confidentiality is kept and he is not judge
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: muscular; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 124/74; temperature 36.6 °C. Breasts: bilateral firm, mobile, tender glandular tissue under the nipples, left more than right; no hard lump, no discharge, no axillary nodes. Testes: right firm 2 cm nodule, non-tender; left small and soft. Thyroid normal. No liver stigmata. Results, only when requested: hCG markedly raised; AFP normal; testosterone low with low LH and FSH; estradiol raised; prolactin and TSH normal; liver and kidney function normal. Scrotal ultrasound: a 2 cm hypoechoic lesion in the right testis. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Steroid-related gynaecomastia with a right testicular mass, suspected hCG-secreting tumour. 2. Why might hCG be raised? (D, R4) A germ cell tumour, or the hCG he has injected himself, so the ultrasound decides. 3. Which tests? (E, R5) Scrotal ultrasound, hCG, AFP, testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH, SHBG, TSH, prolactin, liver and kidney function. 4. Is tamoxifen appropriate? (E, R6) No; SERMs are not recommended. 5.
