sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines National Osteoporosis Guideline Group (NOGG): UK clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis, summary of main recommendations (2024; updated December 2024) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Dorothea Kingsley, 69, retired librarian. Sudden mid-back pain after a sneeze two weeks ago. X-ray shows a wedge fracture of a thoracic vertebra. Prednisolone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for five months. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Kingsley.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A vertebral fracture after minimal trauma on long-term prednisolone is osteoporosis until another cause is found. The danger is in the advice: stopping the steroid suddenly can cause an adrenal crisis, and some fractures have other causes. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Kingsley blames the prednisolone and wants to stop it today. Candidates agree, or give a bisphosphonate and forget the other causes. Pass: keep the steroid, exclude myeloma and cord compression, treat the bones. Fail: stop prednisolone.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the pain and its red flags, then ask about the steroid, falls and her bone risk factors. "Tell me about the pain. Any weakness, numbness or trouble passing urine? How long on prednisolone? Any falls?" Pain; red flags; steroid dose and duration; falls; height loss; diet; smoking; alcohol; family history; fractures. Check the spine and the legs, and look for height loss and other causes. "May I look at your back and test the strength and feeling in your legs? Tell me if anything hurts." Height; kyphosis; spinal tenderness; leg power; sensation; reflexes; gait; cushingoid signs; cover her. Explain the diagnosis, the safe steroid advice, the tests and the bone treatment, and give warning signs. "Your bones have thinned. Please keep taking prednisolone, we'll check your blood and start a bone-protecting tablet." Tests; steroid unchanged; calcium and vitamin D; bisphosphonate; falls; red flags; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and helps her to move without pain. R2 C History Asks about pain only; omits red flags, steroid duration or falls. Asks red flags, steroid dose and duration, falls, height loss, diet, smoking, alcohol and family history of fracture. Also asks about weight loss, night pain, previous fractures, menopause, reflux and dental work. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the neurology; reports cord signs that are absent. Finds height loss, a thoracic kyphosis, tenderness over one vertebra, normal leg power and sensation, and normal gait. Also finds normal reflexes, no cushingoid signs and no bladder or bowel changes. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it a muscle strain. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with a vertebral fragility fracture. Also excludes myeloma, metastases, hypercalcaemia, vitamin D deficiency,
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Dorothea Kingsley, 69, a retired librarian. You are quietly stoic, health-conscious and suspicious of long-term tablets. Opening line: "I sneezed and heard something crack. I've read the steroids thin the bones, so I'd like to stop them today." Volunteered: two weeks of mid-back pain, worse on standing. Prednisolone 10 mg for five months for polymyalgia rheumatica; the stiffness is much better. Only if asked about red flags: no leg weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel change. No weight loss. Some night pain. Only if asked: you have lost about 3 cm in height. No previous fractures. A glass of wine most evenings. Your mother broke her hip at 78. You take no calcium or vitamin D. You have mild reflux. You have never smoked. You take no other regular medicines and have no allergies. No recent travel. You live alone in a bungalow. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are frightened of falling and ending up in a care home like your mother. A friend told you bone tablets rot the jaw. Say: "I don't want any tablet that wrecks my teeth." Your questions, in your own words: "Can I stop the steroids?" "Why did my bones go?" "Are the bone tablets safe?" How you re
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable sitting; pulse 76 regular; blood pressure 136/82; temperature 36.7 °C. Height 3 cm below her recorded height. Mild thoracic kyphosis; tenderness over one thoracic vertebra. Leg power, sensation and reflexes normal; gait normal. No cushingoid features. Results, only when requested: calcium normal; vitamin D low; kidney function normal; blood count normal; myeloma screen negative; ESR consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica. DXA: osteoporosis at the spine. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. What else must you exclude? (D) 3. Which tests first? (E) 4. Which treatment? (E) 5. Why is stopping prednisolone dangerous? (E) Curveballs: She asks to stop prednisolone: no, adrenal crisis risk; the rheumatology team reduces it. She has new leg weakness and urinary retention: emergency. She declines tablets: discuss infusion.

stations.title: Tired, Dizzy, Craving Salt / Name Addison's Disease and Teach the Emergency Rules

sections.preamble: X-01 Tired, dizzy and dark-skinned
sections.1. Title: Tired, Dizzy, Craving Salt / Name Addison's Disease and Teach the Emergency Rules
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Society for Endocrinology: Adrenal crisis, clinical guidance (supporting guidance dated 10 March 2021); NHS England patient safety alert on the NHS Steroid Emergency Card (August 2020) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Harriet Lowndes, 29, trainee solicitor. Four months of tiredness, weight loss and feeling dizzy on standing. Her skin has darkened. Sodium 128 mmol/litre, potassium 5.6 mmol/litre. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Lowndes.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Tiredness, weight loss, postural dizziness, pigmentation and low sodium with high potassium is primary adrenal insufficiency. The danger is a crisis: she has been vomiting and her pressure falls on standing, so the marks come from treating her today and teaching her how to avoid one. The Examiner Trap. Ms Lowndes wants to hear it is stress. She also has a stomach bug and exams next week, which hides how unwell she is. Candidates diagnose but wait for tests or give no emergency advice. Pass: diagnosis, hydrocortisone without waiting for the synacthen test, admission, sick day rules, emergency card. Fail: waiting for tests, or no crisis plan.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the tiredness, weight, dizziness and salt craving, then about illness, infections and other autoimmune disease. "When do you feel dizzy? Have you lost weight? Do you crave salt? Any vomiting or diarrhoea?" Tiredness; weight; dizziness; salt craving; nausea; abdominal pain; periods; mood; other autoimmune disease; family history. Check lying and standing blood pressure, the skin and the mouth. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your skin, your mouth and your thyroid? Tell me if anything hurts." Postural drop; pigmented creases and scars; vitiligo; buccal pigmentation; thyroid; abdomen; cover her. Name the diagnosis, say how you will confirm it, explain the daily tablets and the emergency rules. "I think your adrenal glands are not making cortisol. I'll take blood tests now, but start treatment today without waiting for them, and keep you in for fluids." Blood for cortisol and ACTH; hydrocortisone and fluids; admit; sick days; card; injection; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before looking at the skin and mouth. R2 C History Asks about tiredness only; omits weight, dizziness, salt craving or other autoimmune disease. Asks weight loss, postural dizziness, salt craving, nausea, abdominal pain, current illness, and thyroid or diabetes history. Also asks about periods, vitiligo, coeliac symptoms, steroid use and family autoimmune disease. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits standing blood pressure or the skin; reports signs that are absent. Finds a postural fall, pigmentation of the palmar creases, scars and the buccal mucosa, and vitiligo. Also finds a normal thyroid and a non-tender abdomen, and notes she is thin. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it depression or chronic fatigue. Primary adrenal insufficiency, probably autoimmune. Also names tuberculosis, a
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Harriet Lowndes, 29, a trainee solicitor. You are driven, a little anxious and sure it is stress. Opening line: "I'm exhausted and dizzy when I stand. I think it's overwork, but my GP said my bloods were odd." Volunteered: four months. You have lost 5 kg. You crave crisps and salty food. Only if asked: nausea most mornings and some abdominal aches. Your periods are lighter. You had vitiligo patches as a teenager. You have an underactive thyroid on levothyroxine. Non-smoker; alcohol at weekends; no allergies; no recent travel and no TB contact. Your mother has an underactive thyroid. You live with a flatmate. Only if asked about illness: you had diarrhoea and vomiting yesterday and are not keeping fluids down well. Exams start next week. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of lifelong tablets and of failing your exams. Say: "I can't be ill now." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it stress?" "Will I need tablets forever?" "Can I still sit my exams?" How you react: if told it is stress, you carry on. If told you must be admitted with no reason given, you refuse. If given the reason and a letter for your exams, you agree to stay.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: thin; pulse 98 regular; blood pressure lying 102/64, standing 84/54; temperature 36.9 °C. Pigmentation of palmar creases, scars and buccal mucosa. Vitiligo on the hands. Thyroid not enlarged. Abdomen soft and non-tender. Results, only when requested: 9 am cortisol low; ACTH high; renin high; short synacthen test: inadequate cortisol response; adrenal antibodies positive; TSH normal on levothyroxine; glucose normal. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why is the skin dark? (D) High ACTH stimulates melanocytes. 3. Treatment? (E) 4. What are sick day rules? (E) 5. What is the emergency treatment? (E) 100 mg hydrocortisone injected, then fluids. 6. Should treatment wait for the synacthen test? (E) No: take blood for cortisol and ACTH, then treat; the test follows. Curveballs: She is vomiting now: urgent injection and admission. She asks to stop the tablets when well: no, lifelong. She asks about pregnancy: specialist advice.

stations.title: High Calcium, Stones and a Broken Wrist / Name Hyperparathyroidism, Refer to Surgery
stations.source_heading: stations/X-02 High calcium stones and a broken wrist

sections.preamble: 22 | X-02 Less acute consultation - High calcium stones and a broken wrist
sections.1. Title: High Calcium, Stones and a Broken Wrist / Name Hyperparathyroidism, Refer to Surgery
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines NICE NG132 Hyperparathyroidism (primary): diagnosis, assessment and initial management (2019) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Winifred Abernethy, 63, retired school cook. Tiredness, low mood and constipation for a year. A kidney stone last year and a wrist fracture after a trip two years ago. Repeated adjusted calcium 2.92 mmol/litre, parathyroid hormone raised. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Abernethy.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A raised adjusted calcium with a raised parathyroid hormone, stones, a fragility fracture and low mood is primary hyperparathyroidism. The decision that matters is referral for surgery. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Abernethy has been told it is her age. She fears an operation on her neck and plans to cut down fluids because of her stone. Candidates diagnose and watch. Pass: confirm, assess for end-organ disease, refer to surgery. Fail: wait and see, or restrict fluids.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about stones, bones, abdominal pain and moods, then about medicines and family history. "Have you had stones, fractures or abdominal pain? Any thirst or constipation? What do you take, including calcium tablets?" Stones; fractures; pain; constipation; thirst; mood; medicines; calcium and vitamin D; family history of tumours. Check hydration and look at the neck, then the bones and abdomen. "May I check your blood pressure, your neck, your abdomen and your spine? Tell me if anything hurts." Pulse; blood pressure; hydration; neck; abdomen; spine; band keratopathy; cover her. Explain the diagnosis, the tests, why she needs a surgeon, and the safe fluid advice. "I think a gland in your neck makes too much hormone and has raised your calcium. You should see a surgeon. Please keep drinking." Confirm; assess; refer; fluids; DXA; stones; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and checks she is comfortable being examined on the neck. R2 C History Asks about tiredness only; omits stones, fractures, medicines or family history. Asks stones, fractures, abdominal pain, constipation, thirst, mood, medicines including calcium tablets, and family history. Also asks about thiazides, lithium, kidney problems, previous neck surgery and relatives with tumours. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure or the neck; reports a lump that is absent. Finds mild dehydration, no neck mass, a tender spine and a healed wrist fracture. Also finds no band keratopathy, no proximal weakness and a normal abdomen. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it age or depression. Primary hyperparathyroidism. Also names familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, malignancy, vitamin D excess and thiazides, and s
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Winifred Abernethy, 63, a retired school cook. You are practical and resigned to "getting old". Opening line: "I'm worn out and low, and my tummy's bunged up. The doctor says it's my age but I don't think so." Volunteered: one year. A kidney stone passed last year. A wrist fracture after a trip two years ago. Only if asked: you are thirsty and pass a lot of urine. You take calcium tablets (no vitamin D) from the chemist, two a day, more than the box says, because of your fracture. No other tablets. No relatives with tumours, stones or high calcium. Only if asked about fluids: you are drinking less because you think it makes the stone pain worse. Never smoked. A glass of wine at weekends. No allergies. No recent travel. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you fear an operation on your neck and your voice. Say: "I'd rather not be cut." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it my age?" "Will I need an operation?" "Is it cancer?" How you react: if told to wait and see, you accept. If listened to and given a clear plan, you accept referral. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: tired; pulse 80 regular; blood pressure 132/78; temperature 36.7 °C. Mildly dehydrated. No neck mass. Tender lumbar spine. Healed wrist fracture. No proximal weakness. Abdomen soft. Results, only when requested: adjusted calcium 2.92 mmol/litre; PTH raised; vitamin D low; urinary calcium excretion raised; kidney function normal. DXA: osteoporosis at the spine. Renal ultrasound: a small stone. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why is urinary calcium raised? (D) Excludes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. 3. Who needs surgery? (E) 4. What imaging? (E) 5. What if she declines? (E) Curveballs: She asks to carry on cutting her fluids: no. Calcium rises and she is vomiting and confused: emergency. She asks about stopping calcium tablets: review them with the team.

sections.preamble: X-03 Dilated cardiomyopathy with an ICD
sections.1. Title: Displaced Apex, Third Sound, a Box Under the Collarbone / Failure, an ICD, a Licence
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Physical examination PACES encounter Station 3, cardiovascular examination Skills marked A, B, D, E, G Setting Heart failure clinic Time 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) Guidelines ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (2021); NICE NG106 Chronic heart failure in adults (2018; reviewed September 2025); NICE TA314 Implantable cardioverter defibrillators and cardiac resynchronisation therapy (2014); DVLA, Cardiovascular disorders: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025) Related AMaC stations Cardiovascular examination: pacemaker or ICD with heart failure (R2-17); this one centres on dilated cardiomyopathy, the third sound and a coach driver's licence
sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Rupert Aldous is 54 and drives a coach. He has become short of breath on stairs over the past year. Please examine his cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A displaced diffuse apex, a third heart sound, a raised JVP and a box under the left collarbone is heart failure with a defibrillator. The marks come from finding the device and knowing what it means for his licence. The Examiner Trap. Candidates see the scar, name the box wrongly or miss it, and forget his job. Pass: heart failure, an ICD, a cause, drugs and driving advice. Fail: no device or no licence advice.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Look for a scar, a bulge, a device and signs of failure before touching him. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; breathing, device, hands, pulse, JVP; chest wall. Feel the apex, listen for the third sound and murmur, then check for fluid. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the heart, then lean you forward and check your back and legs." Apex; heave; four areas; third sound; murmur; lung bases; sacrum; liver; ankles; cover him. Name the failure, the cause you must look for, the device and the licence advice. "He has heart failure with an ICD, probably from a dilated cardiomyopathy. He must stop driving his coach." Present in order; diagnosis; causes; drugs; device; DVLA; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; lays him flat despite breathlessness; presses on the device; leaves him exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone, pauses if he is breathless, and avoids pressing on the device. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the device, apex, third sound or ankles. Looks at the chest wall, hands, pulse, JVP, apex, four auscultation areas, bases, liver and ankles. Also listens for a third sound with the bell at the apex in left lateral position. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a murmur or a valve lesion that is not present, or misses the device. Finds a left infraclavicular ICD, a displaced diffuse apex, a third heart sound, a raised JVP and ankle oedema. Also finds a soft pansystolic murmur of functional mitral regurgitation, bibasal crackles and a tender liver edge. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it a valve lesion or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Heart failure with reduced ejection fract
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: thin and mildly breathless; respiratory rate 20; pulse 92 regular; blood pressure 104/70; SpO2 95% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Left infraclavicular scar over a firm box. JVP raised 6 cm above the sternal angle. Apex beat displaced to the anterior axillary line, diffuse; no thrill. First and second sounds normal; a third sound; soft pansystolic murmur at the apex. Bibasal crackles. Tender liver edge. Pitting ankle oedema to mid-shin. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Possible causes? (E) 4. Treatment? (E) 5. What does the box do, and what are his driving rules? (E) Curveballs: He asks if he can keep driving his coach: no; any ICD is a permanent bar to Group 2 and he is NYHA III. He asks about his car: the rules depend on the reason for the ICD. He has just been shocked: urgent same-day device check, and 999 if he is unwell; DVLA rules for his car depend on whether the shock was appropriate.

sections.preamble: 24 | X-04 Respiratory exam - Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale
sections.1. Title: Obese, Plethoric, Raised JVP, Clear Chest / Hypoventilation, Not the Lungs
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Physical examination PACES encounter Station 1, respiratory examination Skills marked A, B, D, E, G Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) Guidelines ATS Clinical practice guideline: Evaluation and management of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (2019); BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults in healthcare and emergency settings (2017); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated November 2025) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Desmond Pettifer is 52 and drives a delivery van. He is always sleepy, wakes with morning headaches and has swollen legs. Please examine his respiratory system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. An obese, plethoric, sleepy man with a clear chest, a raised JVP and swollen legs has hypoventilation with right heart failure. The lungs are not the problem, and the diagnosis comes from saying so. The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for lung disease, hear a clear chest and call him normal, or give high-flow oxygen. Pass: obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, probably with sleep apnoea, and driving advice. Fail: a normal chest, or high-flow oxygen and sedatives.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Look at his build, colour and breathing before you touch him. "May I examine your chest? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; build, colour, neck, hands, flap, pulse, JVP. Check the chest, then the right heart and the legs. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen over the lungs and heart, then check your neck, tummy and legs." Expansion; percussion; breath sounds; heave; P2; murmur; liver; ankles; sacrum; cover him. Name the syndrome, the cause of the swelling, and what needs doing urgently and safely. "He has obesity hypoventilation with right heart failure. I'd check blood gases urgently and give only controlled oxygen, aiming for 88 to 92%." Present in order; diagnosis; gases; sleep study; CPAP or NIV; weight; driving; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; lays him flat despite breathlessness; leaves him exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone, pauses if he is breathless, and checks he is comfortable leaning forward. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the neck, JVP, heave or ankles. Looks at build, colour, hands, flap, pulse, neck, JVP, chest, heave, liver and ankles. Also checks neck circumference by eye, the sacrum and the fundi. R3 B Identifying signs Reports crackles, wheeze or clubbing that are not present. Finds central obesity, plethora, mild cyanosis, a flapping tremor, a raised JVP, a loud P2, hepatomegaly and pitting oedema, with a clear chest. Also finds a bounding pulse, a right ventricular heave and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it heart failure from the left side only, or COPD. Obesity hypoventilation with cor pulmonale, probably with obstructive sleep apnoea. Also separates i
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: obese, drowsy but rousable; respiratory rate 22; pulse 100 and bounding; blood pressure 148/92; SpO2 88% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. Plethoric face; mild central cyanosis; flapping tremor. JVP raised with a prominent v wave. Chest expansion symmetrical; percussion resonant; vesicular breath sounds; no crackles or wheeze. Right ventricular heave; loud P2; pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder in inspiration. Hepatomegaly. Pitting oedema to the thighs. Results, only when requested: arterial blood gas on air: respiratory acidosis with raised carbon dioxide; bicarbonate raised; TSH normal. Echo: dilated right ventricle, raised pulmonary pressure. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. What investigations? (E) 4. How do you treat? (E) 5. What advice do you give about driving? (E) Curveballs: He is admitted drowsy with a respiratory rate of 10: urgent gases, controlled oxygen and NIV. He asks for sleeping tablets: no. He asks if he can drive his van: no, until sleepiness is controlled; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe OSA is confirmed.

stations.title: Weight Gain, Bruising, Purple Striae / Ask About Every Capsule Before You Test
stations.source_heading: stations/X-05 Weight gain, bruising and purple stretch marks

sections.preamble: X-05 Weight gain, bruising and purple stretch marks
sections.1. Title: Weight Gain, Bruising, Purple Striae / Ask About Every Capsule Before You Test
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2008;93:1526-40) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Naomi Fairweather, 38, hairdresser. Eight months of weight gain, easy bruising, purple stretch marks and weak legs. Newly raised blood pressure and HbA1c. Combined oral contraceptive pill. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Fairweather.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A round face, purple striae, bruising and proximal weakness is Cushing's syndrome until the cause is found. The first step is not a test: it is to ask about every steroid she takes, because a drug is a recognised cause. The Examiner Trap. Ms Fairweather is embarrassed and has been taking herbal capsules for her joints. Candidates order a pituitary scan before asking. Pass: ask about all products, exclude exogenous steroid, then test. Fail: scan first, or stop the capsules abruptly.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the changes, then ask about every pill, capsule, cream and injection, including herbal and online products. "What do you take for your joints or skin? Anything from a market, shop or website? Are you on the pill?" Weight; bruising; striae; weakness; mood; sleep; periods; hair; steroids; contraceptive pill; infections; fractures. Look for the discriminating features and check blood pressure and strength. "May I look at your face and skin, check your blood pressure, and see how strong your thighs are? Tell me if anything hurts." Face; fat pads; striae; bruises; thin skin; proximal myopathy; blood pressure; fundi; cover her. Explain what you suspect, why you will ask about the capsules first, and the safe plan. "I think a steroid is raising your cortisol. Don't stop the capsules suddenly; we'll plan that safely and test your own hormones." Exclude exogenous; stop safely; steroid card; tests; bone, sugar, pressure; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before looking at the abdomen and thighs. R2 C History Asks about weight only; omits steroids, herbal products or the contraceptive pill. Asks weight, bruising, striae, weakness, mood, periods, every tablet, capsule, cream and injection, and online products. Also asks about fractures, infections, sleep, previous prednisolone courses and who supplied the capsules. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure or proximal strength; reports pigmentation that is absent. Finds moon face, central fat, thin skin with bruises and purple striae, proximal myopathy and blood pressure 156/96. Also finds supraclavicular fat pads, no pigmentation and normal fundi. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it simple obesity or polycystic ovary syndrome. Exogenous glucocorticoid Cushing's syndrome from t
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Naomi Fairweather, 38, a hairdresser. You are self-conscious about your appearance and polite, and you do not want to be told off. Opening line: "I've put on loads of weight, I bruise at the slightest bump and I've got these purple lines on my tummy. I can't climb the stairs at work without holding on." Volunteered: eight months. Mood low and tearful. Periods irregular. Only if asked what you take: the combined contraceptive pill. Nothing else prescribed. Never smoked; alcohol a few glasses at weekends; no allergies; no recent travel. Your mother has type 2 diabetes. You live with your partner. Only if asked specifically about herbal products or anything from shops or websites: eight months ago you started "joint relief" capsules from a market stall, two daily, for aching hands. They helped at once and you do not want to stop. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you have a brain tumour, and ashamed that you took capsules you could not name. Say: "I'm scared you'll take them away and the pain will come back." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it a brain tumour?" "Do I have to stop the capsules?" "Will my body go back?" How you react: if
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 84 regular; blood pressure 156/96; temperature 36.7 °C. Round face; plethora; central obesity; supraclavicular fat pads; thin skin with bruises; purple striae on the abdomen and thighs. Proximal myopathy: cannot rise from a chair without arms. No pigmentation. Fundi normal. Results, only when requested: HbA1c in the diabetic range; potassium low-normal; ACTH suppressed; late-night salivary cortisol low; DXA: low bone density. Capsule analysis (if sent): prednisolone. Question ladder: 1. What is your first step? (E) Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid. 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Which tests for endogenous Cushing's syndrome? (E) 4. How could the pill mislead you? (E) 5. How do you stop it safely? (E) Curveballs: She asks to stop the capsules today: no, adrenal crisis risk. She is vomiting and faint: urgent hydrocortisone. She asks whether she needs brain surgery: no, not for an exogenous cause.

stations.title: Bigger Hands, Snoring and Sweats / Measure IGF-1, Not a Random Growth Hormone
stations.source_heading: stations/X-06 Bigger hands snoring and sweating

sections.preamble: 26 | X-06 Less acute consultation - Bigger hands snoring and sweating
sections.1. Title: Bigger Hands, Snoring and Sweats / Measure IGF-1, Not a Random Growth Hormone
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society: Acromegaly clinical practice guideline (2014); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated November 2025) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Emrys Pritchard, 49, joiner. A year of bigger hands and feet, sweating, loud snoring and aching joints. He fell asleep at the wheel of his van last month. Blood pressure 150/94. A random growth hormone was reported as normal. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Pritchard.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Enlarging hands and feet, sweating, snoring and joint pain points to acromegaly. A normal random growth hormone does not exclude it, and a sleepy van driver is a danger today. The Examiner Trap. Mr Pritchard is reassured by the normal growth hormone and does not want to stop work. Candidates agree it is normal, or forget his driving. Pass: IGF-1, glucose tolerance test, MRI, no driving while sleepy. Fail: random GH accepted, or driving allowed.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the changes, then ask about sleep, sweating, vision and driving. "What has changed in your hands, feet or face? How do you sleep? Do you fall asleep driving?" Rings and shoes; sweating; headaches; vision; snoring; sleepiness; driving; joints; carpal tunnel; sexual function. Look at the hands, face and jaw, test the fields, and check the blood pressure. "May I look at your hands, face and mouth, test your sight at the edges and check your blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts." Hands; spade shape; face; jaw; tongue; fields; fundi; Tinel; blood pressure; goitre; cover him. Explain what you suspect, the right test, why it matters, and the safe advice about driving. "I think a gland in your head is making too much growth hormone. A random level can miss it. Please don't drive while sleepy." IGF-1; glucose test; MRI; sleep; driving; treatment; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before examining the mouth and neck. R2 C History Asks about hands only; omits sleep, sweating, vision or driving. Asks ring and shoe size, sweating, headache, vision, snoring, sleepiness, driving, joint pain, carpal tunnel and sexual function. Also asks about weight change, old photographs, family history and previous colon problems. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the visual fields or the hands; reports field loss that is absent. Finds large spade-like hands, coarse features, prominent jaw, large tongue, positive Tinel sign, normal fields and blood pressure 150/94. Also finds oily skin, skin tags, a normal thyroid and normal fundi. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it obesity or ageing. Acromegaly from a pituitary adenoma, with sleep apnoea. Also names Paget disease, hypothyroidi
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Emrys Pritchard, 49, a self-employed joiner. You are cheerful, stubborn and worried about money. Opening line: "My hands have got huge, my wedding ring won't come off, I sweat like a pig and my wife says I snore like a train." Volunteered: one year. Shoe size up two sizes. Aching knees and hands. Only if asked: tingling in both hands at night. A dull headache most days. No change in vision. Libido is a bit lower. No regular tablets. No allergies. Never smoked. Two pints at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of pituitary problems. Only if asked about driving: you fell asleep at the wheel last month and woke on the verge. You drive your van every day. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will lose your job and the house if you cannot drive. Say: "If I can't drive, I can't work." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it serious?" "Is it a tumour?" "Can I carry on driving?" How you react: if told to stop driving with no help, you refuse. If listened to and offered a letter and a plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 78 regular; blood pressure 150/94; temperature 36.7 °C. Large spade-like hands; coarse features; prominent jaw; large tongue; oily skin; skin tags. Positive Tinel sign. Visual fields normal. Fundi normal. Thyroid normal. Results, only when requested: IGF-1 markedly raised; growth hormone not suppressed after a glucose load; HbA1c in the diabetic range; prolactin normal. MRI: a pituitary macroadenoma not touching the chiasm. Sleep study: moderate obstructive sleep apnoea. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why is a random growth hormone not enough? (D) 3. Which tests? (E) 4. What is first-line treatment? (E) 5. What do you tell him about driving? (E) Curveballs: He says he will carry on driving: no; he must tell DVLA if moderate or severe sleep apnoea is confirmed. He asks about tablets rather than surgery: medical therapy if disease persists. Sudden severe headache and visual loss: emergency.

sections.preamble: X-07 No periods, hot flushes and a wish for a baby
sections.1. Title: No Periods at 31, Hot Flushes, Wanting a Baby / Premature Ovarian Insufficiency, Handled Kindly
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines ESHRE, ASRM, CRE-WHiRL and IMS: Evidence-based guideline on premature ovarian insufficiency (2024; Fertil Steril 2024, doi 10.1016/j.fertnstert.2024.11.007) Related AMaC stations AMaC Addison's disease consultation; this one tests the ovarian failure that can accompany it
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Philippa Dunmore, 31, graphic designer. No periods for eight months, hot flushes, night sweats and low mood. Negative pregnancy test. FSH raised on two occasions five weeks apart. She is hoping to have a baby. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Dunmore.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Loss of periods with menopausal symptoms and a raised FSH before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency. The marks come from the cause you look for, the replacement you offer and the way you tell her. The Examiner Trap. Ms Dunmore is devastated and feels it is her fault. She also feels dizzy on standing. Candidates give the label and stop, or miss the adrenal clue. Pass: confirm, look for causes including adrenal antibodies, offer HRT, discuss fertility. Fail: label only.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the periods and symptoms, then about other illnesses and what she hopes for. "When did your periods stop? Any hot flushes, dryness or low mood? Do you feel dizzy? What are you hoping for?" Periods; flushes; dryness; mood; dizziness; salt craving; autoimmune disease; family history; treatment; fertility wish. Look for causes and for signs of low oestrogen, and check lying and standing blood pressure. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your skin and your thyroid? Tell me if anything hurts." Lying and standing pressure; pigmentation; vitiligo; thyroid; height; breasts if agreed; cover her. Explain what you found, the tests for cause, what replacement offers, and what her fertility options are. "Your ovaries have stopped working early. We'll look for a cause, replace the hormones you've lost and talk about having a baby." Tests; HRT; bones; heart; contraception; fertility; support; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before any intimate questions. R2 C History Asks about periods only; omits symptoms, other illness or her wishes. Asks periods, flushes, dryness, mood, dizziness, salt craving, autoimmune disease, family history and her fertility wishes. Also asks about chemotherapy, pelvic surgery, smoking and a family history of early menopause. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure, skin or thyroid; reports signs that are absent. Finds blood pressure 106/68 lying and 92/58 standing, vitiligo on the hands and a normal thyroid. Also finds normal height, no webbing or short stature, and no pigmentation of the palmar creases. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it stress or early menopause and nothing else. Premature ovarian insufficiency, possibly autoimmune, with adrenal insufficiency to ex
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Philippa Dunmore, 31, a graphic designer. You are tearful, articulate and ashamed. You think it is your fault for working too hard. Opening line: "My periods stopped in February, I'm having hot flushes, and my doctor says I'm in the menopause. I'm 31. I want a baby." Volunteered: eight months. Sex is painful because of dryness. You feel low and flat. Only if asked: you feel dizzy when you stand and you crave salty snacks. You have vitiligo patches on your hands. No chemotherapy or surgery. Your mother went through the menopause at 44. Never smoked; alcohol a glass of wine at weekends; no regular medicines and no allergies; no recent travel. You live with your partner, and you work from home. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will never have a child and that your partner will leave. Say: "Is it my fault?" Your questions, in your own words: "Can I still have a baby?" "Is it my fault?" "Do I need hormones?" How you react: if told bluntly that you will never have children, you cry and shut down. If listened to with kindness and a clear plan, you engage. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 80 regular; blood pressure lying 106/68, standing 92/58; temperature 36.7 °C. Vitiligo on the hands. Thyroid normal. Normal height. No webbing. No palmar crease pigmentation. Results, only when requested: FSH raised on two occasions more than 4 weeks apart; oestradiol low; karyotype 46,XX; fragile X premutation not found; 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive; thyroid antibodies positive with normal TSH. Short synacthen test: inadequate cortisol response. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why test 21-hydroxylase antibodies? (D) Adrenal autoimmunity. 3. What replacement? (E) 4. For how long? (E) 5. What are her fertility options? (E) 6. What does the short synacthen result mean, and what comes first? (E) Adrenal insufficiency; glucocorticoid replacement before oestrogen, with admission if she is unwell. Curveballs: She asks if the pill is the same as HRT: discuss; the specialist decides. She asks about natural pregnancy: uncommon but possible, so contraception if she does not want it. Dizzy and vomiting: urgent hydrocortisone.

stations.title: Third Ketoacidosis in a Year / Ask Why Without Blame, Never Say Stop Insulin
stations.source_heading: stations/X-08 Third ketoacidosis admission in a year

sections.preamble: 28 | X-08 Less acute consultation - Third ketoacidosis admission in a year
sections.1. Title: Third Ketoacidosis in a Year / Ask Why Without Blame, Never Say Stop Insulin
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Diabetes clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Joint British Diabetes Societies: Management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults, single-page pathway (March 2023); NHS Scotland: Sick day guidance for type 1 diabetes (last updated April 2025) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Ms Tamsin Ridgeway, 24, student physiotherapist. Type 1 diabetes for eleven years. Her third admission with diabetic ketoacidosis in twelve months, discharged yesterday after two days. She has lost weight. HbA1c 98 mmol/mol. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Ms Ridgeway.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Repeated ketoacidosis in a young woman with type 1 diabetes needs one question asked kindly: is she leaving out insulin? The task is to find the reason without blame and keep her safe. The Examiner Trap. Ms Ridgeway is ashamed and has been told off by every team. Candidates lecture about adherence or switch to a pump. Pass: ask openly, find the reason, never advise stopping insulin, offer joint support. Fail: blame, or no sick-day plan.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask what happened before each admission, then ask kindly about insulin doses, mood and food. "What was happening before each admission? Do you ever miss or reduce insulin? How are you feeling in yourself?" Admissions; insulin doses; missed doses; weight worries; mood; food; infection; alcohol; support; ketone testing. Check her hydration and fundi, her injection sites and her meter. "May I check your blood pressure and pulse, your eyes, your injection sites and your meter? Tell me if anything hurts." Pulse; blood pressure; hydration; fundi; injection sites; feet; meter download; weight; cover her. Explain the cause in plain words, the sick-day safety rules, and the support you will arrange. "Missing insulin can cause these admissions, and many people struggle. Never stop your insulin; I'd like a team to help." Reason; sick-day rules; ketone testing; urgent signs; joint support; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; weighs her without asking; comments on her body. Introduces self, asks consent, asks before weighing or examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and lets her decline being weighed in front of others. R2 C History Asks about adherence only; omits triggers, mood, food or her own view. Asks events before each admission, doses and missed doses, infections, alcohol, mood including any thoughts of self-harm, weight worries and support. Also asks about previous eating problems and whether anyone has asked her openly before. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits fundi, injection sites or hydration; reports signs that are absent. Finds a thin young woman, dry mucous membranes, normal injection sites and early background retinopathy. Also finds normal feet, no ketotic breath and a meter download showing few readings, mostly high. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it poor control and nothing else. Recurrent ketoacidosis from omitted insulin, with a possible eat
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Tamsin Ridgeway, 24, a student physiotherapist. You are polite, guarded and exhausted. Every team has told you to try harder. Opening line: "I know, I know. I've ended up in hospital again. Everyone just tells me I'm not looking after myself." Volunteered: each time you felt sick, thirsty and very tired for a few days before you went in. Only if asked kindly and directly about insulin: you often skip or cut your doses, especially the long-acting one, because you are afraid of gaining weight. You have done this for over a year. Only if asked: you restrict food some days. Your mood is low. You have had thoughts of not wanting to be here but no plan. You have not told anyone. You take insulin glargine once a day and insulin aspart with meals (when you take them). No allergies. You do not smoke. A few drinks at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of note. You do not drive. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are terrified of gaining weight and ashamed that you are lying to your team. Say: "If I take it all, I'll get fat." Your questions, in your own words: "Will I keep ending up in hospital?" "Will you tell my course?" "Am I going to go blind?" H
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: thin; pulse 88 regular; blood pressure 104/66; temperature 36.6 °C. Mucous membranes slightly dry. Fundi: early background retinopathy. Injection sites normal. Feet normal. Capillary ketones today 0.3 mmol/litre. Meter download: few readings, mostly high. Results, only when requested: HbA1c 98 mmol/mol; kidney function normal; TSH normal; coeliac screen negative. Question ladder: 1. What is the likely cause of her admissions? (D) 2. What are the criteria for ketoacidosis? (E) 3. What are the sick-day rules? (E) 4. When must she go to A&E? (E) 5. Who should be involved? (E) Curveballs: She says she will skip insulin on days she does not eat: no; never stop basal insulin. She says she has thoughts of not wanting to be here: assess risk the same day with the mental health team and do not leave her alone while the risk is current. She asks if you will tell her university: no, without her consent unless there is a safety concern.

stations.title: A Neck Lump and a Hoarse Voice / Hard Nodule and Node: Cancer Until Excluded
stations.source_heading: stations/X-09 A neck lump and a hoarse voice

sections.preamble: X-09 A neck lump and a hoarse voice
sections.1. Title: A Neck Lump and a Hoarse Voice / Hard Nodule and Node: Cancer Until Excluded
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management (2022) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Lorraine Beecham, 47, bank clerk. A lump in the front of her neck for four months and a hoarse voice for three weeks. Thyroid function normal. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Beecham.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A firm, irregular thyroid nodule with a neck node and a new hoarse voice is suspected thyroid cancer until the work-up says otherwise. A normal thyroid function test does not make a lump benign. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Beecham has been told a normal blood test means it is nothing. Candidates reassure, or start thyroid tablets. Pass: examine the neck and nodes, request ultrasound, FNAC and a vocal cord check, and refer urgently. Fail: reassurance.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the lump and voice, then about swallowing, breathing, past radiation and family history. "When did you notice it? Has your voice changed? Any trouble swallowing or breathing? Any neck radiation or family thyroid problems?" Lump; speed of growth; voice; swallowing; breathing; weight; radiation; family history; palpitations. Examine the thyroid from behind, feel the neck nodes, and check the voice and breathing. "May I feel your neck from behind? I'll ask you to swallow some water. Tell me if anything hurts." Inspect; swallow; palpate; nodes; trachea; retrosternal extension; stridor; voice; eyes; cover her. Name what you suspect, say which tests she needs, and explain the plan and urgent signs. "I'm concerned this could be thyroid cancer, though it isn't certain. You need a scan, a needle test and a voice box check." Ultrasound; needle test; vocal cords; MDT; surgery; follow-up; urgent signs.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines the neck without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and a glass of water before the swallowing test. R2 C History Asks about the lump only; omits voice, swallowing, breathing or family history. Asks onset and growth, voice change, swallowing, breathing, weight, past radiation and family history. Also asks about palpitations, sweating, heat intolerance and relatives with thyroid cancer or endocrine tumours. R3 A, B Focused examination Examines from the front only; omits the nodes or the swallow; reports a goitre or eye signs that are absent. Finds a firm irregular right-lobe nodule moving on swallowing, a firm level III node, a central trachea and a hoarse voice. Also finds no stridor, no retrosternal extension, no tremor and no eye signs. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it a simple goitre or a cyst. Suspected thyroid cancer, probably papillary
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Lorraine Beecham, 47, a bank clerk. You are organised and anxious. Your aunt died of cancer and you are afraid. Opening line: "I found a lump in my neck and my voice has gone croaky. My doctor says my thyroid blood test is fine, so I should relax." Volunteered: four months. The lump has grown. A scratchy, hoarse voice for three weeks. Only if asked: some difficulty swallowing large mouthfuls. No trouble breathing. No weight loss. Palpitations: none. Never smoked; alcohol a glass of wine at weekends; no regular medicines and no allergies; no recent travel. Married with two children. Only if asked about radiation: you had radiotherapy to your neck as a teenager for a lymph problem. Your aunt had thyroid cancer. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are terrified it is cancer and that you will not see your children grow up. Say: "Please be honest with me." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it cancer?" "Will I need an operation?" "Will I lose my voice?" How you react: if falsely reassured, you leave and say you will relax. If listened to and told honestly, you accept the tests. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 76 regular; blood pressure 126/78; temperature 36.6 °C. Hoarse voice. A 3 cm firm irregular nodule in the right lobe, moving on swallowing. A firm 1 cm node at level III on the right. Trachea central. No stridor. No retrosternal extension. No tremor or eye signs. Results, only when requested: TSH normal; calcium normal. Ultrasound: a suspicious solid nodule on an established grading system with an abnormal node. Cytology: Thy4. Laryngoscopy: right vocal cord paresis. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Which tests? (E) 4. What does Thy4 mean? (E) 5. What is the treatment? (E) Curveballs: She asks if the thyroid blood test excludes cancer: no. She asks whether she needs radioiodine: depends on the final histology and risk; the multidisciplinary team decides. She becomes breathless and noisy: emergency airway assessment.

stations.title: Unsteady, Nauseous and Low Sodium / Find the Drug, Correct Slowly, Never Push Water
stations.source_heading: stations/X-10 Unsteady and low sodium on a new water tablet

sections.preamble: 30 | X-10 Less acute consultation - Unsteady and low sodium on a new water tablet
sections.1. Title: Unsteady, Nauseous and Low Sodium / Find the Drug, Correct Slowly, Never Push Water
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines European clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (ESE, ESICM, ERA-EDTA; 2014); Society for Endocrinology: Emergency management of severe and moderately severely symptomatic hyponatraemia in adult patients (2022) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Dilys Penhallow, 73, retired shop owner. Three weeks of feeling unsteady and nauseated, with two falls and a dull headache. Indapamide was started for blood pressure a month ago. Sertraline for low mood. Serum sodium 127 mmol/litre. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Penhallow.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A low sodium in an older woman on a thiazide-like diuretic and an SSRI is most likely drug-induced hyponatraemia. The danger is in the treatment: forcing water, or correcting too fast. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Penhallow has read that she should drink more water and has started drinking four litres a day. Candidates agree, or plan rapid correction. Pass: stop the diuretic, assess volume, test properly, arrange same-day hospital assessment, correct slowly. Fail: more water, or fast correction.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the symptoms and falls, then about every drug and how much she drinks. "What symptoms do you have? What do you take, and when did you start the new tablet? How much do you drink?" Nausea; headache; falls; confusion; drugs; fluid intake; vomiting; diarrhoea; smoking; weight loss; alcohol. Assess her volume status carefully, then her neurology and gait. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your neck veins, your legs and your walking? Tell me if anything hurts." Lying and standing pressure; JVP; oedema; mucous membranes; orientation; gait; chest; cover her. Explain the likely cause, the safe plan to correct the sodium slowly, and when to seek urgent help. "I think your water tablet and perhaps your sertraline have lowered your sodium. Please stop drinking extra water, and we'll correct it slowly." Stop thiazide; fluids; tests; same-day hospital assessment; slow correction; urgent signs; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and a chair for the walking test. R2 C History Asks about nausea only; omits drugs, drinking or falls. Asks symptoms, falls and any head injury, confusion, every drug and its start date, fluid intake, vomiting, diarrhoea and alcohol. Also asks about smoking, weight loss, cough and previous low sodium. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits volume assessment or gait; reports oedema or dehydration that is absent. Finds blood pressure 138/82 with no postural fall, JVP not raised, no oedema, moist membranes and mild unsteadiness. Also finds normal orientation, clear chest, no goitre and no focal neurology. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it dehydration or stroke. Euvolaemic hyponatraemia from indapamide, possibly with sertraline, with SIADH to exclude. Also names hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, lung dis
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Dilys Penhallow, 73, a retired shop owner. You are sensible, a little deaf and keen to be independent. Opening line: "I feel sick and wobbly, and I've fallen twice. The doctor says my sodium is low. Should I drink more water?" Volunteered: three weeks. A dull headache. You have been drinking about four litres of water a day because you read that it helps. Only if asked about tablets: indapamide for blood pressure since a month ago. Sertraline for low mood for a year. Nothing else. Only if asked: no vomiting or diarrhoea. You stopped smoking ten years ago. No cough or weight loss. A glass of sherry at weekends. No allergies. No travel. Both falls were at home on level ground: you did not hit your head or black out, and the headache is dull and the same each day. Nothing relevant in the family. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid your falls mean dementia and that you will lose your independence. Say: "I don't want to end up in a home." Your questions, in your own words: "Should I drink more?" "Is my brain affected?" "Do I have to stop my tablets?" How you react: if told to drink more, you carry on. If listened to and given a clear plan, you ag
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 78 regular; blood pressure lying 138/82, standing 134/80; temperature 36.6 °C. JVP not raised. Mucous membranes moist. No oedema. Chest clear. Orientated. Mild unsteadiness on walking; no focal neurology. Results, only when requested: serum sodium 127 mmol/litre; serum osmolality low; urine osmolality 340 mOsm/kg; urine sodium raised; TSH normal; 9 am cortisol normal; glucose normal. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why can you not diagnose SIADH now? (D) 3. What do you stop? (E) 4. How fast may you correct? (E) 5. Why does she need hospital assessment today? (E) Curveballs: She asks for salt tablets: not routinely; address the cause. She becomes confused and vomits: emergency, senior review and treatment of symptomatic hyponatraemia. Overcorrection is feared: the team is called. She refuses to come into hospital: assess capacity (MCA 2005), explain the risks, offer a same-day review and a written safety net, and document.

stations.title: A Hot, Red, Painless Foot in Diabetes / Think Charcot, Offload, Refer Within a Day
stations.source_heading: stations/X-11 Consultation - A hot red swollen foot that does not hurt

sections.preamble: Consultation - A hot red swollen foot that does not hurt
sections.1. Title: A Hot, Red, Painless Foot in Diabetes / Think Charcot, Offload, Refer Within a Day
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Diabetes clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (2015; last updated October 2019) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Reginald Hollis, 58, retired postman. Type 2 diabetes for fifteen years with numb feet. A hot, red, swollen right foot for three weeks after a stumble. Two courses of antibiotics from his GP made no difference. HbA1c 70 mmol/mol. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Hollis.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A hot, red, swollen foot in a person with diabetic neuropathy and no wound is most likely acute Charcot arthropathy. The station turns on not calling it cellulitis, and on stopping him walking on it. The Examiner Trap. Mr Hollis feels no pain and wants to keep walking his dog. Candidates give more antibiotics and let him walk. Pass: suspect Charcot, X-ray, non-weight-bearing, a non-removable device, referral within one working day. Fail: antibiotics and walking.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the stumble, the swelling and any pain, then about the antibiotics, his feet and his walking. "When did it start? Does it hurt? Did the antibiotics help? How much do you walk?" Onset; injury; pain; fever; antibiotics; ulcers; numbness; walking; footwear; previous foot problems. Compare both feet by touch, check the pulses and sensation, and look for a wound. "May I look at and feel both feet, check the pulses and test your sensation? Tell me if anything hurts." Temperature; swelling; deformity; pulses; monofilament; skin between toes; cover him. Name the likely diagnosis, explain why walking is dangerous, and give the plan and urgent signs. "The nerve damage is injuring the bones of your foot. Please don't walk on it; the foot team will see you within a day." Non-weight-bearing; X-ray; cast; foot team; return signs.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; handles the foot roughly; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and checks he is comfortable with his foot raised. R2 C History Asks about swelling only; omits injury, antibiotics, neuropathy or walking. Asks onset, injury, pain, fever, antibiotics, numbness, ulcers, walking and footwear. Also asks about kidney disease, previous ulcers, smoking and who checks his feet. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits comparing feet, pulses or sensation; reports a wound or pus that is absent. Finds a warm, red, swollen right foot, bounding pulses, absent monofilament sensation, no ulcer and no fever. Also finds early midfoot flattening, normal skin between the toes and a cool, normal left foot. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it cellulitis, gout or a deep vein thrombosis. Acute Charcot arthropathy. Also names osteomyelitis, gout, cellulitis and deep vein thrombosis, and says a p
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Reginald Hollis, 58, a retired postman. You are cheerful, stubborn and proud of your daily walks with your dog. Opening line: "My right foot's swollen and red, but it doesn't hurt. I've had two lots of antibiotics and nothing has changed." Volunteered: three weeks. You stumbled off a kerb and thought nothing of it. You have carried on walking. Only if asked: no fever. No wound that you know of. Your feet have been numb for years. No history of ulcers. Your kidneys are a bit weak, you have been told. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): your brother lost his leg to diabetes and you fear the same. You also cannot bear to stop walking your dog. Say: "I'm not giving up my walks." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it infected?" "Will I lose my foot?" "Can I carry on walking?" How you react: if told to stop walking with no help, you refuse. If listened to and offered help with the dog, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 80 regular; blood pressure 140/84; temperature 36.8 °C. Right foot: warm, red and swollen, with early midfoot flattening and bounding pedal pulses; no ulcer, no pus. Monofilament sensation absent in both feet. Left foot normal. Results, only when requested: CRP mildly raised; HbA1c 70 mmol/mol; kidney function reduced. Weight-bearing X-ray: early midfoot changes. MRI: bone marrow oedema without osteomyelitis. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. Why not cellulitis? (D) 3. What imaging? (E) 4. What is the treatment? (E) 5. Would you give a bisphosphonate? (E) No. Curveballs: He insists on walking: explain the risk of collapse and offer help. He develops fever and a spreading ulcer: immediate acute care and inform the foot team. He asks about surgery: later, by the specialist team.

The marks come from feeling both the radial and femoral pulses at the same time. The Examiner Trap. Candidates treat the blood pressure as primary hypertension, and never feel the femorals. Pass: radiofemoral delay, arm and leg pressure difference, back murmur, bicuspid valve. Fail: essential hypertension.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do He is well. Take the blood pressure in both arms and feel the pulses before the chest. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; both arms' pressure; radials; brachials; femorals; face; fundi. Feel radial and femoral together, then listen at the front and the back. "I'm going to feel your wrist and groin pulses together, then listen over the heart and your back." Radiofemoral delay; apex; heave; click; murmur; back; scapular bruits; carotids; lung bases; cover him. Name the lesion, the likely valve, the complications and what treatment is used. "He has coarctation of the aorta, probably with a bicuspid aortic valve. He needs imaging and treatment, usually a stent." Present in order; diagnosis; complications; imaging; stent; follow-up; thank him.

Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone before palpating the femoral pulses, and keeps exposure to the minimum. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the femoral pulses, both arms' blood pressure or the back. Measures pressure in both arms, feels radial and femoral pulses together, listens at the front and the back, then checks fundi. Also checks the brachial pulses, listens for scapular bruits and takes a leg pressure. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a diastolic murmur or heart failure that is not present. Finds raised blood pressure in the arms, radiofemoral delay, weak femorals, an ejection click and a systolic murmur at the back. Also finds a heaving apex, collateral vessels at the scapulae and hypertensive f

sections.8. Radial pulses full; femoral pulses weak and delayed. Collateral vessels palpable around the shoulder blades. Fundi: arteriolar narrowing. Apex beat heaving, not displaced. Ejection click at the apex. Systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder at the back between the shoulder blades. No diastolic murmur. Lungs clear. No oedema. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Complications? (E) 4. Which tests? (E) 5. How do you treat it? (E) Curveballs: He asks if he needs a brain scan: not routinely if there are no symptoms; sudden severe headache is an emergency. sections.preamble: Consultation - Sweats, confusion and low sugars without diabetes
sections.1. Title: Low Sugars Without Diabetes in a Bus Driver / Catch the Episode, Stop the Driving
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycemic disorders (2009), as summarised in Endotext (last updated November 2025); DVLA: Diabetes mellitus, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025); GMC Confidentiality (2017) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Hugh Blackwood, 44, bus driver. Six months of episodes of sweating, shaking and confusion, usually before breakfast. A paramedic recorded a glucose of 2.3 mmol/litre last month, and it rose after a sugary drink. He does not have diabetes. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Blackwood.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Episodes of low glucose that settle with sugar, in a man without diabetes, are hypoglycaemia until a cause is found. The station turns on proving it with a sample taken during an episode, and on stopping a bus driver driving. The Examiner Trap. Mr Blackwood still drives his bus and treats the episodes with sweets. Candidates organise tests and say nothing about driving, or send him home to fast. Pass: Whipple's triad, a supervised critical sample, no driving, DVLA. Fail: driving allowed.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the episodes, then about food, drugs, alcohol, family history and his job. "What happens during an episode, and when? Does sugar fix it? Do you take any tablets, injections or alcohol? What do you drive?" Timing; symptoms; relief; weight; drugs; insulin in the household; alcohol; surgery; family history; driving. Look for causes and for signs of other endocrine disease, and check the abdomen. "May I check your blood pressure, your hands and face, your neck and your abdomen? Tell me if anything hurts." Weight; acromegaly; adrenal signs; liver stigmata; abdomen scars; lymph nodes; fundi; cover him. Explain that the sample during an episode is the key test, say what you suspect, and give clear driving advice. "Your sugar drops too low and I need to catch it in hospital. Please don't drive your bus. You must tell the DVLA yourself, and I'll help you." Supervised fast; hormone tests; imaging; treatment; driving; glucose; return signs.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before questions about alcohol and sexual function. R2 C History Asks about sweating only; omits timing, relief, drugs, insulin access or his job. Asks timing, symptoms, relief with sugar, drugs, insulin or tablets at home, alcohol and driving. Also asks about family history of tumours, kidney stones and calcium problems, and whether others have seen an episode. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the abdomen or the neck; reports tumour signs that are absent. Finds weight gain, a normal abdomen with no scar, no hepatomegaly, no acromegalic features and no lymph nodes. Also finds normal blood pressure, no adrenal signs and normal fundi. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it panic attacks or reactive hypoglycaemia alone. Hypoglycaemia from endogenous hyperinsulinism, most likely insulinom
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Hugh Blackwood, 44, a bus driver. You are friendly, a little sheepish and worried about your job. Opening line: "I keep getting these funny turns, sweaty and shaky and fuzzy in the head. A biscuit sorts it out. I've put on weight because I'm always eating." Volunteered: six months. The turns come before breakfast or when you skip lunch. Only if asked: once you were so confused a colleague thought you were drunk and had to give you a sugary drink. Non-smoker. You do not drink much. You take no tablets. No diabetes in the family that you know of. Only if asked about driving: you drive a bus most days. You have never had an incident, but you felt woozy at the wheel last week and ate chocolate at the lights. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of crashing with passengers on board, and of losing your job. Say: "If I can't drive, I'm finished." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it diabetes?" "Can I carry on driving?" "Is it a tumour?" How you react: if told to stop driving with no support, you refuse. If listened to and offered a letter for work, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 132/82; temperature 36.6 °C. Weight up over the past year. Abdomen soft, no scars, no mass. No hepatomegaly. No acromegalic features. No lymphadenopathy. Fundi normal. Results, only when requested: critical sample during a supervised fast and a symptomatic episode: plasma glucose below 3.0 mmol/litre; insulin raised; C-peptide raised; proinsulin raised; beta-hydroxybutyrate low; sulfonylurea screen negative. Calcium and prolactin normal. MRI: a small pancreatic lesion. Question ladder: 1. What is Whipple's triad? (D) 2. What do you suspect? (D) 3. What do the results show? (D) 4. How do you treat the episode? (E) 5. What are the driving rules? (E) Curveballs: He asks to fast at home: no; a supervised fast is safer. He asks if he can drive his car: stop driving and notify DVLA for severe hypoglycaemia (needing another person's help, as here) not caused by diabetes treatment, whichever licence he holds. 4. He says he will not tell DVLA: the duty is his; tell him you will have to inform the DVLA medical adviser if he does not, and document it (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). He becomes confused in clinic: urge
