sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Eamon Brightwell is 63 and a retired shipwright. He has had pain in his right shoulder and arm for four months and has noticed his right hand getting weak. Please examine his respiratory system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Shoulder and arm pain, a small droopy eyelid and a wasted hand in a smoker point to a tumour at the top of the lung. The marks come from looking at the face and hand, not just the chest. The Examiner Trap. Candidates stop at the shoulder and call it a rotator cuff or neck problem, or find nothing in the lungs. Pass: Horner syndrome, hand wasting, apical signs, then lung cancer. Fail: musculoskeletal diagnosis.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Start with the face and hands: look for tar staining, clubbing, a small pupil and a droopy lid. "May I examine your chest and arms? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; hands, nails, tar staining, face, eyes, neck nodes, trachea. Examine the chest, then the arm: power, muscle bulk and sensation on the inner side. "I'm going to feel and listen to your chest, then check the strength and feeling in your arm." Expansion; percussion; apex; breath sounds; back; nodes; hand muscles; ulnar sensation; reflexes; cover him. Name the tumour, its effects on the nerves and the tests that decide treatment. "He has a right apical lung tumour with Horner syndrome and a lower brachial plexus lesion. He needs urgent imaging." Present in order; diagnosis; why Horner; CT; MRI; PET-CT; MDT; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; moves the painful arm roughly; leaves him exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone, supports the painful arm, and stops if the pain worsens. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the eyes, the hand muscles or the apex. Looks at hands and nails, face and eyes, then neck nodes, trachea, chest front and back, and the arm. Also tests the supraclavicular fossae, hand grip and sensation over the inner arm. R3 B Identifying signs Reports crackles, a pleural rub or a rash that are not present. Finds tar staining, a right Horner syndrome, wasting of the small hand muscles, reduced right apical air entry and a dull apex. Also finds weak finger abduction, reduced sensation over the inner forearm, and a supraclavicular node. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: thin; respiratory rate 16; pulse 84 regular; blood pressure 134/80; SpO2 95% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. Tar staining; no clubbing. Right ptosis and a small right pupil; reduced sweating on the right side of the face. Trachea central. Right supraclavicular fossa: a firm node. Right apex: dull percussion and reduced breath sounds. Right hand: wasting of the small muscles and weak finger abduction; reduced sensation over the inner forearm. Left side normal. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Explain the Horner syndrome and the hand wasting. (D) 4. Which investigations? (E) 5. How is it treated? (E) Curveballs: He asks if it could be arthritis: it does not fit. He asks if he will need a biopsy: yes, after staging imaging. He becomes breathless with a swollen face: superior vena cava obstruction, emergency.

sections.preamble: Consultation - Snoring and sleepiness in a lorry driver
sections.1. Title: Snoring and Sleepiness in a Lorry Driver / Test Him Quickly, Stop the Driving

Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines NICE NG202 Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome in over 16s (2021); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025); GMC Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) Related AMaC stations AMaC obesity hypoventilation station; this one tests obstructive sleep apnoea and driving
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Desmond Harlow, 52, long-distance lorry driver. His wife says he snores loudly and stops breathing at night. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Loud snoring, witnessed pauses, daytime sleepiness and a near miss at the wheel in a heavy man is most likely obstructive sleep apnoea. The station turns on the right test, the right treatment and stopping a lorry driver driving. The Examiner Trap. Mr Harlow still drives his lorry and fears losing his job. Candidates book a sleep study and send him home driving. Pass: Epworth is not enough, home polygraphy, CPAP, no driving, DVLA. Fail: driving allowed.

Have you nodded off while driving? Do you drink or take sleeping tablets?" Snoring; witnessed apnoeas; unrefreshing sleep; near misses; hours driven; alcohol; sedatives; mood; morning headache. Check weight, neck, airway, blood pressure and the signs of heart or lung disease. "May I measure your weight and neck, look in your mouth, and check your pulse and blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts." BMI; neck; jaw; tonsils; blood pressure; heart; chest; ankles; thyroid; cover him. Explain what you suspect, the home sleep test, the treatment, and that he must stop driving today. "Your breathing stops in your sleep, which makes you dangerously sleepy. Please don't drive from today. If the test confirms it, you must tell the DVLA, and I'll help you." Home test; CPAP; weight; alcohol; driving; DVLA; letter; review.

Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before questions about alcohol and sexual function. R2 C History Asks about snoring only; omits near misses, the job, alcohol or sedatives. Asks snoring, witnessed pauses, unrefreshing sleep, near misses at the wheel, hours driven, alcohol, sedatives and mood. Also asks about morning headache, nocturia, hypertension, thyroid disease and whether he has fallen asleep in a conversation. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits weight, neck or airway; reports signs of heart failure that are absent. Finds raised BMI, a thick neck, crowded airway, raised blood pressure and no signs of heart failure. Also finds a small jaw, large tonsils, and checks the thyroid. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it laziness, or sleepiness from shift work alone. Obstructive sleep apnoea, with obesity and hypertensi
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Desmond Harlow, 52, a long-distance lorry driver. You are tired, a little defensive and worried about your job. Opening line: "My wife made me come. She says I snore like a tractor. I'm just a bit tired, that's all." Volunteered: the tiredness has been getting worse for a year. You feel worse after a long drive. Only if asked: your wife says you stop breathing and then gasp. You wake with a headache. You drink about a pint most evenings. You take no sleeping tablets. Only if asked about driving: twice in the last month you drifted onto the hard shoulder and woke with a jolt. You have not told your employer. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of a crash and of losing your job. Say: "If I lose my licence, I can't pay the mortgage." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it serious?" "Can I keep driving?" "Will I need a machine on my face?" How you react: if told to stop driving with no support, you argue. If listened to and offered a letter for work, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: BMI 38; neck thick; small jaw; large tonsils; blood pressure 152/94; pulse 78 regular; SpO2 96% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. What do you suspect? (D) 2. Does a normal Epworth score exclude it? (D) 3. Which test first? (E) 4. How do you treat it? (E) 5. What are the driving rules? (E) Curveballs: He asks to keep driving his car: no, the same rule applies to cars and lorries. He asks about a splint: considered if he cannot tolerate or declines CPAP. He falls asleep in clinic: record it, stress the safety message.

sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Gwendoline Ashby, 76. An irregular pulse was found at her flu vaccination. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes, and she buys aspirin to protect her heart. She feels tired. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Ashby.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A new irregular pulse in an older woman means atrial fibrillation and a stroke-prevention decision. The marks come from scoring the stroke risk, and from asking about bleeding before any anticoagulant is started. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Ashby has had dark stools for a week on aspirin, and mentions it only when asked. Candidates prescribe an anticoagulant or keep the aspirin. Feel the pulse, check the heart, the chest, the abdomen and for pallor. "May I feel your pulse, check your blood pressure, listen to your heart and chest, and press your tummy? Tell me if anything hurts." Pulse; rate; blood pressure; pallor; murmurs; failure; abdomen; rectal findings; cover her. Explain the diagnosis, the stroke risk, and why the bleeding must be dealt with first. "Your heart rhythm is irregular, which raises your stroke risk. Your dark stools may be bleeding, so I need to treat that first." ECG; blood count; stop aspirin; same-day assessment; anticoagulant later; rate control; driving.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before the abdominal and rectal examination. R2 C History Asks about palpitations only; omits bleeding, aspirin, falls or stroke symptoms. Asks symptoms, black stools, aspirin use, other tablets, falls, alcohol and any weakness or speech trouble. Also asks about indigestion, weight loss, hypertension control, thyroid disease and her driving. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the pulse or abdomen; reports a murmur that is absent. Apex; thrill; heave; heart sounds; murmur; axilla; lung bases; liver; ankles; cover him. Name the lesion, what the shunt does, and the tests that decide closure. sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Tobias Ormerod, 47, type 2 diabetes. Three days of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and tiredness after a stomach bug. He takes metformin and dapagliflozin and has kept taking them. A finger-prick glucose today was 11 mmol/litre. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Ormerod.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Vomiting, abdominal pain and deep breathing on an SGLT2 inhibitor can be ketoacidosis even when the glucose is only modestly raised. The marks come from asking about the tablets and the sick days, and from refusing to be reassured by the glucose. The Examiner Trap. The glucose looks reassuring, so Mr Ormerod expects a stomach-bug reply. Candidates reassure and send him home on his tablets. Pass: ketoacidosis suspected, blood ketones, stop the tablet, urgent admission. Fail: sent home.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the illness, the tablets he kept taking, what he has eaten and drunk, and any recent surgery. "What has happened since the bug? Did you stop any tablets? Are you eating or drinking? Have you changed your diet?" Vomiting; pain; drinking; tablets; diet; alcohol; surgery; infection; urine symptoms; foot problems. Check breathing, hydration, abdomen, temperature and the feet and look for an infection source. "May I check your pulse, blood pressure, breathing and tummy, and look at your feet? Tell me if anything hurts." Pulse; blood pressure; respiratory rate; breath smell; dry mouth; abdomen; feet; chest; cover him. Explain that this may be ketoacidosis, why the glucose misleads, and that he needs the hospital now. "Your sugar is only a little high, but your tablet can still make you acidic. I'd like a blood ketone test and to admit you." Blood ketones; stop tablet; admission; fluids; insulin; restart decision; sick-day rules.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and acknowledges how unwell he looks. R2 C History Asks about vomiting only; omits the tablets, his diet or the recent illness. Asks onset, vomiting, pain, intake, whether he kept taking dapagliflozin and metformin, alcohol and diet. Also asks about a recent low-carbohydrate diet, urinary symptoms, foot problems and any recent procedure. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits breathing or the abdomen; reports signs of a surgical abdomen that are absent. Finds fast deep breathing, dry mouth, a fast pulse, mild abdominal tenderness and a ketone smell. Also checks the feet and chest for a trigger and records a low blood pressure. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it gastroenteritis
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Tobias Ormerod, 47, a delivery manager. You are tired, a little irritable and want to go home. Opening line: "I've had a stomach bug for three days and I just can't shake it. My sugar is fine, so I don't see why I'm here." Volunteered: you have been sick on and off and have barely eaten. You have kept on taking all your tablets. Only if asked: you started a very low carbohydrate diet a month ago to lose weight. You have had abdominal pain. You feel short of breath. You have not been drinking much. Only if asked about alcohol: two glasses of wine most nights. No surgery. No fever. You have never smoked; no allergies; you live with your wife; your father had type 2 diabetes; no recent travel. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): your father went onto insulin and then died of kidney failure. Say: "Please don't put me on insulin, like my dad." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it my diabetes?" "Why am I breathing like this?" "Do I really have to stay in?" How you react: if told to go to hospital with no explanation, you resist. If listened to and told it is treatable, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: drowsy but orientated; respiratory rate 28 and deep; pulse 112 regular; blood pressure 98/60; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.9 °C. Question ladder: 1. What do you suspect? (D) 2. Why is the glucose misleading? (D) 3. Which tests do you need? (E) 4. What do you do with the tablets? (E) 5. How do you prevent it in future? (E) Curveballs: He asks to take dapagliflozin as usual: no, stop it. He asks about insulin: he is not on insulin now; in hospital the ketoacidosis pathway uses insulin with glucose-containing fluid even though his glucose is only modestly raised (JBDS, per local protocol), and his future treatment is decided with the diabetes team. He says his sick-day rules were never explained: reasonable, give them in writing.

Do you smoke? What exactly do you fly, and when do you want to return?" Onset; treatment; breathlessness; pain; smoking; vaping; drugs; family history; flying; diving. Examine the chest, check for a recurrence and look at the build and any signs of lung disease. "May I look at your chest, feel it and listen? Tell me if anything hurts." Height; hands; trachea; expansion; percussion; breath sounds; scars; cover him. Explain what happened, the chance of it returning, and why surgery is worth discussing for a pilot. "The lung has re-expanded, but it can collapse again. In your job I'd like you to see the chest surgeons." X-ray result; recurrence; smoking; surgery; return signs; work; plan.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before questions about drug use. R2 C History Asks about the pain only; omits smoking, his job or breathlessness now. Asks onset, treatment, current breathlessness, smoking, his work and any previous episode. Also asks about vaping and cannabis, family history of collapsed lung, diving and flying plans. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits percussion or breath sounds; reports a pneumothorax that is not present. Finds a tall slim man, a central trachea, equal expansion, resonant percussion and equal breath sounds, with no recurrence. Also finds a healed aspiration site and no signs of underlying lung disease. R4 D Diagnosis Calls it a chest infection or a muscle strain. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax, resolved after aspiration. Also separates it from a secondary pneumothorax from lung
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Lachlan Fairbrother, 29, an airline pilot. You are fit, confident and keen to get back. Opening line: "I feel completely normal now. I just need a note so I can get back to flying." Volunteered: you were breathless with a sharp right chest pain three weeks ago. They put a needle in and sent you home. Only if asked: you smoke ten a day, and vape. No lung disease. No previous collapse. No family history that you know of. No regular medicines or allergies; a few drinks a week. Only if asked about diving: you dive on holiday. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are terrified it will happen at altitude and end your career. Say: "If I lose my licence, I've got nothing." Your questions, in your own words: "Will it come back?" "Can I fly next week?" "Do I need an operation?" How you react: if told you are grounded with no help, you argue. If listened to and offered a letter for work, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: tall and slim; respiratory rate 14; pulse 68 regular; blood pressure 122/74; SpO2 99% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Trachea central. Expansion equal. Percussion resonant. Breath sounds equal. No added sounds. Small healed puncture mark at the right chest. Results, only when requested: chest X-ray today: lung fully expanded, no pneumothorax. CT chest, if requested: small apical blebs; no other lung disease. Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. When is a chest X-ray repeated? (E) 3. Which advice reduces recurrence? (E) 4. Why consider surgery now? (E) 5. When can he fly as a passenger? (E) Curveballs: He asks about diving: permanently discouraged unless definitive prevention has been done. He asks to fly this weekend: as a passenger, not until full resolution on X-ray, then 7 days; as a pilot, not without a decision from the aviation medical authority. sections.preamble: X-22 Less acute consultation - Sore throat on a thyroid tablet
sections.1. Title: Sore Throat and Fever on Carbimazole / Stop the Drug and Count the White Cells
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic, seen as a same-day add-on Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines American Thyroid Association guidelines for hyperthyroidism and other causes of thyrotoxicosis (2016); Carbimazole summary of product characteristics (electronic medicines compendium, updated May 2025) Related AMaC stations AMaC Graves' disease station; this one tests the main danger of the tablets
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Beatrix Pendrell, 41, school cook. Hyperthyroidism with a nodular goitre was diagnosed five weeks ago, and she started carbimazole. She has had a sore throat and fever for two days and rang for advice. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Pendrell.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A sore throat and fever in the first weeks of an antithyroid drug are agranulocytosis until a white cell count excludes it. The station turns on stopping the drug at once, getting a differential count the same day and treating fever with a very low neutrophil count as neutropenic sepsis. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Pendrell is still taking the tablets and thought a sore throat was minor. Candidates treat the throat and let her carry on. Pass: stop the drug, same-day differential count, no other antithyroid drug, urgent care. Fail: continue the tablet.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the throat and the fever, when she started the tablet, whether she still takes it and any rash or jaundice. "When did the throat start? Have you taken the tablet today? Any rash, itching, dark urine or yellow eyes?" Onset; fever; drug start; last dose; rash; jaundice; palpitations; weight; eyes; pregnancy. Look at the throat, check the temperature and pulse, and examine the neck and for signs of thyrotoxicosis. "May I look at your throat, feel your neck and check your pulse and temperature? Tell me if anything hurts." Temperature; pulse; throat; mouth ulcers; goitre; tremor; eyes; skin; liver; cover her. Explain that the tablet may have lowered her white cells, that she must stop it, and what happens next. "I'm worried the tablet has lowered your infection-fighting cells. Please stop it today; I need a blood test now." Stop drug; differential count; admission; no other drug; beta-blocker; definitive treatment; return.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and acknowledges that she did the right thing by ringing. R2 C History Asks about the throat only; omits the drug dates, her last dose, rash or jaundice. Asks onset, fever, when the drug started, last dose, rash, itching, dark urine, yellow eyes and palpitations. Also asks about pregnancy, other drugs and whether she was told to report a sore throat. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the throat or temperature; reports a tonsillar abscess that is absent. Finds a fever, a fast pulse, a red throat, a nodular goitre and a fine tremor. Also finds no mouth ulcers, no jaundice and no lid lag. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it a viral throat infection and stops there. Suspected
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Beatrix Pendrell, 41, a school cook. You are hot, tired and apologetic about taking up time. Opening line: "I've had a bad throat and I feel shivery. I didn't want to make a fuss, but the nurse said to come in." Volunteered: you started the thyroid tablet five weeks ago. You took it this morning as usual. Only if asked: the throat is very sore and swallowing hurts. You feel feverish. No rash. No yellow eyes. Your heart feels fast. You are not pregnant and use condoms. No other medicines, no allergies, no recent travel. You do not smoke and drink very little. Nobody in the family has had a blood problem. Only if asked about warnings: the leaflet mentions a sore throat, but you thought it was a normal cold. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will need an operation or lose the tablet that is helping. Say: "My heart has settled since I started it." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it a cold?" "Do I stop the tablet?" "Will my thyroid get worse?" How you react: if told to stop with no plan, you worry. If listened to and told another treatment will control the thyroid, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: flushed; respiratory rate 18; pulse 104 regular; blood pressure 118/70; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 38.2 °C. Red inflamed throat, no exudate, no mouth ulcers. Nodular goitre. Fine tremor. No jaundice. No lid lag. Results, only when requested: full blood count: neutrophils 0.2 x 10^9/L (scenario value). Liver panel normal. Thyroid function: still thyrotoxic. Question ladder: 1. What do you suspect? (D) 2. What do you do with the tablet? (E) 3. Which test and when? (E) 4. Can she switch to the other antithyroid drug? (E) 5. What else controls her symptoms? (E) 6. Her neutrophils are very low and she is febrile: what now? (E) Treat as neutropenic sepsis: admit, cultures, intravenous antibiotics per the local protocol, senior and haematology advice. Curveballs: She asks to take one more tablet today: no, stop now. She asks to swap to the other drug: no, serious reactions cross-react. She becomes drowsy and hypotensive: sepsis, emergency care.

Oxygen; pulse; blood pressure; neck veins; loud second sound; murmur; oedema; liver; cover her. Explain that she may be pregnant, that one tablet is unsafe in pregnancy, and what happens today. "I need a pregnancy test now. One tablet can harm a baby, so it must stop today, and a specialist team will help." Pregnancy test; stop drug; sildenafil; specialist team; admission; options; support.

I had to stop twice on the stairs this week." Volunteered: you take bosentan and sildenafil every day. You faint if you rush. Only if asked: your period is two weeks late. You use no contraception. You did not plan this but you did not tell the clinic. Only if asked about fainting: once last week when you stood up quickly. No chest pain. Your ankles are swollen. Background, only if asked: no other medicines. No allergies. Never smoked. You drink rarely. No recent travel. No family history of heart disease. You live with your partner, who knows nothing yet. (E, R6) Sildenafil, calcium channel blockers and prostacyclin analogues, with limited evidence. 4. Where should she be looked after? (E, R6) A pulmonary hypertension centre with a multidisciplinary pregnancy team. 5. How is pulmonary hypertension defined? (D, R4) Mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg at rest. sections.3. Candidate brief: Mrs Cordelia Brackenbury is 58 and a retired postmistress. She had a pulmonary embolus two years ago and has been more breathless since. She nearly fainted climbing stairs last week. Please examine her cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Breathlessness after a pulmonary embolus, a raised venous pressure, a right ventricular heave and a loud second sound mean pulmonary hypertension. The station turns on reading the neck and the right heart before the left. The Examiner Trap. Candidates look for left heart failure and listen at the apex only. Pass: venous pressure, right ventricular heave, loud pulmonary second sound, tricuspid murmur, then the cause. Fail: left heart failure.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do She is breathless but comfortable. Look at her colour, hands and neck veins before the chest. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; pulse; blood pressure; neck veins. Palpate for a right ventricular heave, then listen over the pulmonary and tricuspid areas. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs, liver and ankles." Venous pressure; heave; second sound; tricuspid murmur; bases; liver; ankles; calves; cover her. Name the signs and the cause, and say how the diagnosis is confirmed and treated. "She has pulmonary hypertension with right heart strain, possibly from chronic clots. She needs echo and specialist assessment." Present in order; diagnosis; cause; echo; catheter; anticoagulation; centre; thank her.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; ignores her breathlessness; leaves her exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits her at 45 degrees, covers her afterwards. Also offers a chaperone and pauses if she is breathless. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the neck veins, the heave or the liver. Looks at hands, colour and neck veins, palpates for a heave, listens at the pulmonary and tricuspid areas, then bases, liver and ankles. Also checks the calves and for the v wave in the neck. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a left-sided third sound or crackles that are absent. Finds a raised venous pressure, a right ventricular heave, a loud second sound, a tricuspid murmur, ankle oedema and a palpable liver edge. Also finds large v waves, a palpable second sound and oxygen saturation of 93%. R4 D Diagnosis and cause Calls it left heart failure or mitral stenosis.
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: breathless on exertion; respiratory rate 20; pulse 94 regular; blood pressure 104/66; SpO2 93% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. No clubbing. Jugular venous pressure raised with large v waves. Right ventricular heave. Loud second heart sound at the left sternal edge. Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration. Chest clear. Ankle oedema. Liver edge palpable. Calves soft. If asked: she takes a long-term anticoagulant. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. What is the likely cause? (D) 4. How do you confirm it? (E) 5. How is it treated? (E) Curveballs: She asks if she can stop her blood thinner: no, lifelong anticoagulation for chronic thromboembolic disease. She nearly faints in the room: lie her flat, urgent review. She asks about holidays: advice from the specialist team.

stations.title: Red Shins, Sore Ankles and Palpitations / Do Not Skip the Heart in Sarcoidosis

sections.preamble: X-25 Consultation - Red shins sore ankles and palpitations
sections.1. Title: Red Shins, Sore Ankles and Palpitations / Do Not Skip the Heart in Sarcoidosis
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines BTS clinical statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis (Thillai et al., Thorax, published online 2 December 2020) Related AMaC stations R2-57 Cough, tender shins and hilar lymph nodes (sarcoidosis, same disease from the lung side); this station tests Löfgren syndrome with cardiac involvement
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Miss Tamsin Greaves, 27, teaching assistant. Three weeks of painful ankles and red lumps on her shins. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymph nodes. She wants to know what it is. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Miss Greaves.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Red tender shin lumps, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar nodes in a young woman is Löfgren syndrome, a form of sarcoidosis that often needs no biopsy. Ask about palpitations and do not skip the heart. The Examiner Trap. Miss Greaves mentions palpitations and a near-faint only if asked. Candidates explain the benign pattern and discharge her on anti-inflammatories. Pass: Löfgren syndrome, ECG, echo, Holter, urgent cardiology review. Fail: reassured with no heart check.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the ankles and shins, then fever, cough, palpitations, fainting, eyes and her calcium or vitamin D tablets. "Tell me about the ankles and the lumps. Any palpitations or fainting? Any cough, fever, or red eyes?" Joints; skin; fever; cough; palpitations; syncope; eyes; fatigue; tablets; family history; pregnancy. Examine the shins, the ankles, the chest and the heart, and look for other skin or eye signs. "May I look at your shins and ankles and listen to your chest and heart? Tell me if anything hurts." Shins; ankles; nodes; eyes; skin; pulse; heart sounds; chest; liver; cover her. Explain what it is, why a biopsy may not be needed, what treats the joints and why the heart is checked. "This looks like a type of sarcoidosis that often settles by itself. I also want to check your heart rhythm." Löfgren syndrome; NSAIDs; steroids if needed; ECG; echo; Holter; follow-up; remission.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before pregnancy questions. R2 C History Asks about the ankles only; omits palpitations, fainting, cough or eye symptoms. Asks joints, skin, fever, cough, palpitations, fainting, eye symptoms, tablets and pregnancy. Also asks about fatigue, family history and breathlessness out of proportion to the chest X-ray. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the shins or heart; reports a rash or murmur that is absent. Finds tender red shin nodules, swollen tender ankles, a normal chest and a regular pulse at a normal rate. Also finds no lymphadenopathy, red eyes or lupus pernio, and records the pulse rhythm. R4 D Diagnosis Calls it a viral arthritis or tuberculosis with no reasoning. Löfgren syndrome: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with erythema nodosum and ankle arthritis. Also names tuberculosi
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Tamsin Greaves, 27, a teaching assistant. You are fit, anxious and a little tearful. Opening line: "I've got these red lumps on my shins, and my ankles hurt so much I can hardly walk. Is it serious?" Volunteered: three weeks. You felt tired and slightly feverish before it started. Only if asked: your heart sometimes flutters at night. Last week you felt faint on the stairs and had to sit down. No cough. No red eyes. Background, only if asked: no allergies; you do not smoke; you drink a little at weekends; no recent travel; no family history apart from your uncle; you live with two flatmates. Only if asked about tablets: none; you take the contraceptive pill. You are not pregnant. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of a lung illness like your uncle had. Say: "My uncle died of a lung disease." Your questions, in your own words: "What is it?" "Will it go away?" "Do I need steroids?" How you react: if reassured with no heart check, you leave worried. If listened to and offered the tests, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 116/68; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 37.4 °C. Tender red nodules on both shins. Both ankles swollen and tender. Chest clear. Heart sounds normal. No lymph nodes, red eyes or skin lesions on the face. Results, only when requested: blood count, kidney and liver tests normal; calcium normal (recent GP bloods). ECG in clinic: first-degree atrioventricular block. Chest X-ray: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Echo and Holter are requested for after the consultation, so no results are available in the room. Question ladder: 1. What is the diagnosis? (D, R4) Löfgren syndrome, a form of sarcoidosis. 2. Do you need a biopsy? (D, R4) Not if the picture is typical and nothing points elsewhere. 3. How do you treat the joints? (E, R6) An NSAID; a short tapered steroid course only for significant symptoms. 4. Why check the heart? (E, R6) Palpitations, a near-faint and first-degree AV block may mean cardiac sarcoidosis; arrange echo, Holter, cardiology review and cardiac MRI. 5. How long does it last and how is she followed? (E, R8) Most remit within 2 years; review every 6 months for 2 years. Curv

Hydration; pulse; blood pressure; abdomen; nodes; skin; eyes; chest; reflexes; cover him. Explain that the sarcoidosis raises the calcium, that the supplements and sun make it worse and how it is checked. "Your sarcoidosis makes your body over-activate vitamin D. sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Barnaby Whitlock, 52, a gardener. You are practical and a bit confused about why tablets that were meant to help have made you unwell. Opening line: "I've been so thirsty and bunged up, and I'm exhausted. My GP gave me vitamin D and calcium and I thought they'd help." Volunteered: you have worked outdoors in the sun all summer, mostly without a hat. Only if asked: you are passing a lot of urine. You have had abdominal pain and nausea. You had a kidney stone ten years ago. No steroids at present. You take no other medicines. You do not smoke and drink two pints at weekends. No allergies. No recent travel. Only if asked about thinking: you have felt a bit foggy. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will lose your kidneys and your business. Say: "My dad ended up on dialysis." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it the tablets?" "Do I need an operation?" "Can I carry on gardening?" How you react: if told to stop everything with no explanation, you worry. If listened to and told the plan protects your kidneys, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

He asks to garden: with sun protection, and calcium checks. He declines admission: explore why, check capacity, and agree the safest alternative with a calcium recheck within 24 hours and clear return advice.

Feel the apex and listen for the first sound, then check the lungs and ankles. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles." Apex; first sound variation; murmur; cannon waves; bases; ankles; nodes; eyes; cover him. Name the rhythm and its dangers, find the likely cause and say what he needs today. "He has complete heart block, probably from cardiac sarcoidosis. He needs admission, monitoring and a pacemaker assessment." Present in order; diagnosis; cause; ECG; echo; MRI; admission; pacing; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welfare Starts without consent; ignores his pallor; leaves him exposed. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone and stops if he feels faint. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the pulse rhythm, the neck or the face. Looks at face, hands and skin, counts the pulse, checks the neck veins, palpates the apex, listens, then bases and ankles. Also checks the eyes and the neck and groin nodes. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a regular sinus rhythm or a murmur that is absent. Finds a slow regular pulse, cannon waves, a variable first sound, a systolic flow murmur and a purple lesion on the nose. Also finds normal blood pressure, clear lungs and no oedema. R4 D Diagnosis and cause Calls it sinus bradycardia or an athlete's heart. Complete heart block, probably from cardiac sarcoidosis, given the skin lesion. Also names drugs, ischaemia, infection and congenital block as other causes. R5 E Tests Asks for a chest X-ray only. As
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: pale, comfortable; respiratory rate 16; pulse 38 regular; blood pressure 138/72; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 36.7 °C. A purple plaque on the nose. Jugular venous pressure with intermittent large cannon waves. Variable intensity first heart sound. Soft systolic flow murmur. Lungs clear. No oedema. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B, R3) Slow regular pulse of 38, cannon waves, variable first sound, purple nasal plaque, soft flow murmur. 2. Diagnosis? (D, R4) Complete heart block. 3. What could be the cause? (D, R4) Cardiac sarcoidosis given the nasal plaque; also drugs, ischaemia, infection, congenital block. 4. Which tests? (E, R5) ECG with continuous monitoring, echo, calcium and blood tests, cardiac MRI or PET. 5. What does he need today? (E, R6) A monitored bed, pacing assessment and the cardiac sarcoidosis team; he must not drive. Curveballs: He asks if he can drive home: no. He faints in the room: lie him flat, call for help. He asks about steroids: decided with the sarcoidosis team.

stations.title: Low Libido, No Pregnancy, Tall Young Man / Testosterone Would Switch Off His Sperm
stations.source_heading: stations/X-28 Low libido and no pregnancy in a tall young man

sections.preamble: X-28 Less acute consultation - Low libido and no pregnancy in a tall young man
sections.1. Title: Low Libido, No Pregnancy, Tall Young Man / Testosterone Would Switch Off His Sperm
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715) Related AMaC stations AMaC gynaecomastia and premature ovarian insufficiency stations; this one tests primary testicular failure
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Ewan Kettering, 31, joiner. He and his partner have tried for a baby for 18 months without success. He has low libido and tiredness. He is tall with sparse facial hair. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Kettering.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Low libido, tiredness and infertility in a tall man with small testes is hypogonadism, and the pattern of the pituitary hormones tells you where it comes from. The station turns on not giving testosterone to a man who wants children. The Examiner Trap. Mr Kettering asks for testosterone to feel better. Candidates agree, which would suppress sperm production. Pass: two morning testosterone levels, LH and FSH, karyotype, fertility first. Fail: testosterone started.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about libido, erections, energy, the baby attempts, puberty, headaches, vision, drugs and infections. "How are your libido and erections? How long have you tried for a baby? Any headaches or vision problems? Any drugs?" Libido; erections; puberty; testicular history; headaches; vision; opioids; mumps; family history; fertility. Examine the build, hair, breasts and testes, and test the visual fields. "May I check your height, hair and chest, examine your testes and test your vision? Tell me if anything hurts." Height; arm span; hair; breasts; testes size; penis; visual fields; cover him. Explain what the tests will show, why testosterone could harm his fertility, and what happens next. "I need blood tests on two mornings and a chromosome test. Testosterone would lower your sperm count, so I'd rather not start it now." Testosterone twice; LH and FSH; karyotype; semen; fertility team; sperm banking; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines the testes without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, offers a chaperone before the genital examination, covers him and thanks him. Also acknowledges how hard it is to talk about libido and fertility. R2 C History Asks about libido only; omits fertility, puberty, headaches or drugs. Asks libido, erections, the baby attempts, puberty, testicular history, headaches, vision and opioids. Also asks about mumps, undescended testes, family history and alcohol. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the testes or visual fields; reports signs that are absent. Finds a tall man with sparse hair, small firm testes and normal visual fields. Also records testis size by orchidometer and looks for breast enlargement. R4 D Diagnosis Calls it stress or low mood. Hypogonadism, probably testicular (primary) in cause, with inferti
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Ewan Kettering, 31, a joiner. You are embarrassed, practical and desperate to be a father. Opening line: "We've been trying for a baby for a year and a half and nothing's happening. I've also got no interest in sex and I'm knackered all the time." Volunteered: your partner is 29 and has had tests that were fine. You were always the tallest at school. Only if asked: you shave about twice a week. Erections are weak. No headaches or vision trouble. No drugs. No mumps that you know of. You do not smoke and drink a few pints at weekends. No other medicines and no allergies. No recent travel. No family history of infertility or hormone problems. Only if asked about puberty: it was a bit late, and your voice broke late. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you are not a real man and will lose your partner. Say: "She deserves someone who can give her a family." Your questions, in your own words: "Can you give me testosterone?" "Will I be able to have children?" "Why is it me?" How you react: if told no with no reason, you are hurt. If listened to and given a plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: tall; respiratory rate 14; pulse 70 regular; blood pressure 124/76; temperature 36.6 °C. Sparse facial and body hair. Mild breast enlargement. Both testes small and firm. Visual fields normal. Results, only when requested: fasting morning total testosterone low on two mornings; LH and FSH raised; prolactin normal. Testes about 3 mL each. Semen: no sperm. Karyotype: 47,XXY. Question ladder: 1. How do you diagnose hypogonadism? (D) 2. What do high LH and FSH tell you? (D) 3. Why check the karyotype? (E) 4. Should he have testosterone now? (E) 5. How do you monitor testosterone later? (E) Curveballs: He asks to start it anyway: no, it would suppress sperm; the fertility team first. He asks about sperm banking: banking ejaculate will not help if the semen has no sperm; the fertility team can discuss surgical sperm retrieval. He reports new headaches and blurred vision: urgent pituitary imaging and visual fields.

sections.preamble: X-29 Consultation - A request for testosterone
sections.1. Title: A Request for Testosterone / Treat the Sleep Apnoea and the Driving First
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society: Testosterone therapy in men with hypogonadism (Bhasin et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:1715-1744); DVLA: Miscellaneous conditions, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 7 November 2025); GMC: Confidentiality, patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) Related AMaC stations AMaC obstructive sleep apnoea station; this one tests testosterone requests with contraindications
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Gareth Ainsworth, 58, company director. A private clinic found a low testosterone on one morning sample and advised testosterone. He is tired, has low libido and a BMI of 36. His GP notes severe obstructive sleep apnoea, for which he does not use his CPAP. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Ainsworth.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Tiredness and low libido in an obese man with untreated sleep apnoea has several treatable causes before testosterone. Check the contraindications, repeat the levels and deal with the risk of him falling asleep at the wheel. The Examiner Trap. Mr Ainsworth wants testosterone, drives 90 minutes to work and dozes in traffic. Candidates write the prescription. Pass: repeat levels, contraindications, treat sleep apnoea, stop driving. Fail: testosterone prescribed, driving allowed.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the symptoms, his sleep, his driving, his weight, drugs and any prostate or heart problems. "What symptoms bother you most? Do you use your CPAP? Do you doze while driving? Any urinary symptoms or heart trouble?" Libido; energy; sleep; CPAP; driving; weight; opioids; prostate symptoms; heart; fertility. Check weight, blood pressure, the chest, breasts, testes and a rectal examination if appropriate. "May I check your weight, blood pressure, chest and testes? Tell me if anything hurts." BMI; blood pressure; neck; breasts; testes; prostate; ankles; cover him. Explain why testosterone is not safe to start now, what tests come first and why he must not drive. "Your sleep apnoea and a thick blood count make testosterone unsafe for now. Please don't drive, and you must tell the DVLA." Repeat levels; LH, FSH; blood count; PSA; sleep apnoea; weight; DVLA; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines the testes without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, offers a chaperone before the genital examination, covers him and thanks him. Also acknowledges how personal these symptoms are. R2 C History Asks about libido only; omits CPAP use, driving, prostate symptoms or heart disease. Asks symptoms, CPAP use, dozing while driving, urinary symptoms, heart disease, opioids and fertility plans. Also asks about stroke, clots, alcohol and what the private clinic told him. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure, weight or the testes. Finds a raised BMI, a thick neck, normal-sized testes and mild breast enlargement. Also finds a smooth prostate on rectal examination, and no oedema. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it testosterone deficiency and nothing else. Low testosterone with obesity and sleep apnoea as reversible causes, not yet confirmed. Also names opioids, systemic illness and pituitary disease, and says a single level is not e
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Gareth Ainsworth, 58, a company director. You are brisk, tired and used to getting what you ask for. Opening line: "The clinic says my testosterone is low. I've got no energy and no drive. I just need the prescription." Volunteered: the clinic took one blood test. They quoted a monthly price. Only if asked: you stopped CPAP a year ago because the mask annoyed you. You doze in traffic jams on your 90-minute commute. You have not told anyone. Only if asked about urination: you get up twice a night and the stream is weaker. No heart problems. No opioids. Background, only if asked: no regular medicines and no allergies. You do not smoke. You drink a few glasses of wine at weekends. No recent travel. No family history of note. You live with your wife. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of losing your edge and your business. Say: "If I can't drive, how do I get to work?" Your questions, in your own words: "Why can't I have it?" "Is it dangerous?" "What about driving?" How you react: if told no with no reason, you argue. If listened to and given a clear plan, you agree. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: BMI 36; thick neck; blood pressure 146/90; pulse 78 regular; temperature 36.6 °C. Mild breast enlargement. Testes normal in size. Prostate smooth, mildly enlarged. No oedema. Results, only when requested: repeat fasting morning testosterone: low-normal. LH and FSH inappropriately normal. Haematocrit 56%. PSA 4.6 ng/mL. Prolactin normal. Question ladder: 1. Why not start testosterone now? (E, R5) One low level is not diagnostic, and a haematocrit of 56%, a PSA of 4.6 ng/mL and untreated severe sleep apnoea are contraindications. 2. Which results are contraindications? (E, R5) Raised haematocrit and PSA above 4 ng/mL without urology review. 3. How many testosterone levels are needed? (E, R5) Two fasting morning levels. 4. What are the driving rules? (E, R6) Moderate or severe sleep apnoea: he must not drive and must notify DVLA until controlled. 5. How would you monitor treatment later? (E, R6) Testosterone and haematocrit at 3 to 6 months, then annually. Curveballs: He asks to carry on driving: no, moderate or severe sleep apnoea means he must not drive until it is controlled, and he must notify DVLA. He says the clinic can monitor him: monitoring n

stations.title: A Growing Aortic Root and a Brother Who Died / Growth Rate and Family Screening
stations.source_heading: stations/X-30 A growing aortic root and a brother who died

sections.preamble: X-30 Less acute consultation - A growing aortic root and a brother who died
sections.1. Title: A Growing Aortic Root and a Brother Who Died / Growth Rate and Family Screening
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Cardiology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (Circulation 2022;146:e334); 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases (Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538) Related AMaC stations AMaC Marfan syndrome and coarctation stations; this one tests a bicuspid valve with an enlarging aortic root
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Alasdair Whitcombe, 46, secondary school teacher. A bicuspid aortic valve was found years ago. His aortic root measured 4.6 cm last year and is 4.9 cm on this year's echo. His brother died suddenly at 41. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Whitcombe.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A bicuspid valve with a root that grew 0.3 cm in a year is a rapid-growth aorta, and a brother's sudden death raises an inherited cause. The station turns on the growth rule, the aortic team and screening relatives. The Examiner Trap. The root is under 5.0 cm, so he expects to hear all is fine. Candidates quote one size threshold and book a routine scan. Pass: growth rate, aortic team, family screening. Fail: routine scan only.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about chest or back pain, breathlessness and fainting, then his brother's death and other family history. "Any chest or back pain, breathlessness or faints? How did your brother die? Anyone else with heart or aorta problems?" Pain; breathlessness; syncope; palpitations; brother; relatives; blood pressure; smoking; drugs; activity. Check the pulses, the blood pressure in both arms, the heart for the valve and look for features of connective tissue disease. "May I check the pulses and blood pressure in both arms, listen to your heart and look at your build? Tell me if anything hurts." Both-arm blood pressure; pulses; click; murmur; aortic regurgitation; build; joints; skin; cover him. Explain the growth rate, why the aortic team matters, why the relatives are screened and what pain to act on. "Your aorta has grown a little faster than we'd like. I'd like the aortic team to review you, and your relatives to be scanned." Growth; CT or MRI; aortic team; relatives; blood pressure; warning pain; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also acknowledges his loss and offers a chaperone. R2 C History Asks about the valve only; omits the brother, pain or relatives. Asks chest and back pain, breathlessness, fainting, how his brother died and other relatives with aorta or heart disease. Also asks about blood pressure, smoking, drugs and his activity and sport. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure in both arms or the heart; reports a murmur that is absent. Finds equal pulses and arm pressures, an ejection click, a soft systolic murmur and no diastolic murmur. Also finds no features of a connective tissue disorder. R4 D Assessment Calls the aorta safe because it is under 5.0 cm. Rapid growth of 0.3 cm in a year in a bicuspid valve is an indication for intervention to be considered, not only the size. Also names a possible heritable aortic condition give
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Alasdair Whitcombe, 46, a secondary school teacher. You are thoughtful, quiet and haunted by your brother's death. Opening line: "They said my aorta was fine last year, and now it's bigger. I thought under five centimetres was safe." Volunteered: your brother died suddenly at 41. Nobody told you why. Only if asked: no chest or back pain, no faints. You get a little breathless on hills. Your sister is 49 and your daughter is 17. Neither has been scanned. Only if asked about blood pressure: it has been a little high. You do not smoke. You drink a little alcohol. You take no regular medicines and have no allergies. No recent travel. Your only relative with heart or aorta problems is your brother. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid your daughter could die the way your brother did. Say: "If it's in the family, I need to know about my daughter." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it dangerous?" "Do I need surgery?" "Should my daughter be tested?" How you react: if falsely reassured, you leave worried. If listened to and given a plan for the family, you engage. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 68 regular; blood pressure 142/84 right arm and 140/84 left arm; temperature 36.6 °C. Pulses equal. Ejection click and a soft systolic murmur at the right sternal edge. No diastolic murmur. No features of a connective tissue disorder. Results, only when requested: echo: bicuspid valve with mild stenosis, aortic root 4.9 cm, previously 4.6 cm a year ago. CT or MRI: root 4.9 cm, no dissection. Question ladder: 1. Is the growth rate significant? (D) 2. What is the size threshold for surgery? (E) 3. Who should be screened? (E) 4. Which warning symptoms matter? (E) 5. Where should he be managed? (E) Curveballs: He asks whether he can wait for the next scan: not without the aortic team's view. He asks about his daughter: first-degree relatives are screened. He develops sudden severe back pain in clinic: emergency, suspect dissection.

sections.preamble: X-31 Consultation - A lump on the adrenal gland found by chance
sections.1. Title: An Adrenal Lump Found by Chance / Check the Hormones Before Anyone Takes a Needle
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines European Society of Endocrinology and ENSAT clinical practice guidelines on the management of adrenal incidentalomas (2023; Eur J Endocrinol 2023;189(1):G1-G42) Related AMaC stations AMaC phaeochromocytoma and Cushing's stations; this one tests an incidental adrenal mass
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Winifred Haldane, 61, retired seamstress. A CT scan for abdominal pain showed a 3.1 cm left adrenal mass and no other cause. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. The radiologist suggests a biopsy. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Haldane.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. An adrenal mass found by chance needs two answers: is it dangerous, and is it making hormones. The station turns on the unenhanced CT density, the dexamethasone test and metanephrines before any biopsy. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Haldane's mass is indeterminate and a biopsy is on offer. Candidates agree to the biopsy, or call the mass harmless. Pass: CT density, dexamethasone test, metanephrines, no biopsy. Fail: biopsy before excluding phaeochromocytoma.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the pain, then about sweating, palpitations, headaches, weight, bruising, fractures and cancer history. "What brought you for the scan? Any sweats, palpitations or headaches? Any easy bruising, fractures or past cancer?" Pain; episodes; headaches; weight; bruising; fractures; cancer history; drugs; blood pressure; diabetes. Look for Cushing's features, check the blood pressure and examine the abdomen. "May I check your blood pressure, your face and skin and your tummy? Tell me if anything hurts." Blood pressure; face; skin; bruising; proximal strength; spine; abdomen; cover her. Explain that most such lumps are harmless, but hormones and imaging details decide, and that a biopsy is not the first step. "I want to check whether the lump makes hormones and how it looks on CT. A biopsy is not routine and could be risky." Dexamethasone test; metanephrines; aldosterone; imaging; surgery; follow-up.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also acknowledges her worry about the word mass. R2 C History Asks about the pain only; omits episodes, bruising, fractures or cancer history. Asks sweats, palpitations, headaches, weight, bruising, fractures, cancer history, drugs and blood pressure control. Also asks about steroid tablets, potassium problems and family history. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure or skin; reports Cushing's signs that are absent. Finds raised blood pressure and central obesity; no thin skin, striae or proximal weakness; a soft abdomen and no mass. Also tests proximal power (normal) and records mild thoracic spinal tenderness. R4 D Assessment Calls the mass cancer or harmless without reasoning. An incidenta
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Winifred Haldane, 61, a retired seamstress. You are polite, anxious and frightened of the word mass. Opening line: "They found a lump on my adrenal gland by accident. The doctor said it could be cancer and wanted to put a needle in it." Volunteered: your blood pressure has been hard to control, and your sugars are creeping up. Only if asked: you do not bruise more than most people. You broke a bone in your back last year after a minor fall. No sweats, headaches or palpitations. No cancer before. Only if asked about drugs: three blood pressure tablets and metformin. No steroids. No allergies. You live with your husband, who is anxious too. You have never smoked, drink little alcohol and have not travelled recently. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of cancer, like your sister. Say: "My sister died of it at 58." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it cancer?" "Do I need the needle test?" "Do I need an operation?" How you react: if rushed to a biopsy, you agree out of fear. If listened to and given a clear plan, you engage. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 76 regular; blood pressure 168/96; temperature 36.6 °C. Central obesity (BMI 31). No striae, skin not thin, no bruising. Proximal power normal. Mild tenderness over the mid-thoracic spine. Abdomen soft, no mass. Results, only when requested: unenhanced CT: homogeneous mass 3.1 cm, 18 HU. Cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone: 118 nmol/litre. Plasma metanephrines normal. Aldosterone and renin: no excess. Spinal X-ray: a vertebral compression fracture. Question ladder: 1. What does the CT density tell you? (D) 2. What does the cortisol result mean? (D) 3. Which further tests? (E) 4. Is a biopsy indicated? (E) 5. When is surgery considered? (E) Curveballs: She asks to have the biopsy to be sure: not routinely, and not before phaeochromocytoma is excluded. She asks about surgery: considered for mild autonomous cortisol secretion with relevant comorbidities. She has a severe headache and a very high blood pressure: emergency.

sections.1. Title: Breathless, Dizzy on Standing, Numb Hands / Think of Amyloid Before More Heart Failure Drugs

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in an older man who cannot tolerate standard drugs and had both carpal tunnels released should raise cardiac amyloidosis. The marks come from the right tests to find which type. The Examiner Trap. He fell on standing and his pressure is low. Candidates add heart failure drugs, or call it age. Pass: amyloid suspected, no pressure-lowering drugs, plasma cell tests, pyrophosphate scan, amyloid centre. Fail: more tablets.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about breathlessness, swelling, dizziness on standing and falls, then carpal tunnel surgery, numbness, bowels and tablets. "What stops you walking? Check the lying and standing blood pressure, the neck veins, the heart, the abdomen and the tongue and skin. "May I check your blood pressure lying and standing, your neck, heart, tummy, tongue and skin? Tell me if anything hurts." Postural blood pressure; neck veins; heart sounds; lungs; liver; oedema; tongue; periorbital bruising; cover him. Explain that a protein may be stiffening his heart, why more tablets could make him worse and what tests come next. "I think a protein is building up in your heart. I'd rather not add tablets that drop your pressure while we find out." Blood and urine tests; scan; biopsy if needed; amyloid centre; diuretic care; falls; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chair, a chaperone and help standing safely. R2 C History Asks about breathlessness only; omits carpal tunnel surgery, falls or neuropathy. Asks breathlessness, swelling, postural symptoms, falls, carpal tunnel surgery, numbness, bowels and tablets. Also asks about weight loss, family history and a past blood disorder. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits postural blood pressure or the neck veins; reports a murmur that is absent. Finds a postural drop in blood pressure, a raised venous pressure, quiet heart sounds, ankle oedema and a firm liver edge. sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Cyril Hartnoll, 77, a retired surveyor. You are courteous, worn out and frightened of becoming a burden. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of ending up in a home. Say: "My wife can't lift me if I fall." Your questions, in your own words: "What's wrong with my heart?" sections.preamble: X-33 Consultation - Early emphysema and a brother with cirrhosis
sections.1. Title: Early Emphysema and a Brother With Cirrhosis / Test the Family, Stop the Smoking First
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines European Respiratory Society statement: diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary disease in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Eur Respir J 2017;50:1700610); NICE technology appraisal TA965 Human alpha1-proteinase inhibitor for treating emphysema (terminated appraisal, 28 March 2024) Related AMaC stations AMaC COPD station; this one tests the genetic cause of early emphysema
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Declan Mulligan, 44, electrician. He is breathless on hills and has a morning cough. A CT scan shows emphysema at the lung bases. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His brother has cirrhosis. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Mulligan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Emphysema at the bases at 44, with a brother who has cirrhosis, is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency until tested. The station turns on the right test, the family testing and the fact that smoking must stop first. The Examiner Trap. Mr Mulligan hopes a drug will fix his lungs so that he can carry on smoking. Candidates promise an infusion, or label him as COPD. Pass: level then genotype, smoking cessation first, liver check, family testing. Fail: treat as ordinary COPD.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about breathlessness, cough, smoking, alcohol, liver problems and his family's lung and liver history. "How far can you walk? How much do you smoke and drink? Has anyone in the family had lung or liver disease?" Breathlessness; cough; smoking; alcohol; jaundice; brother; parents; children; work; vaccines. Examine the chest, look for liver disease and check his oxygen levels. "May I listen to your chest, check your oxygen and examine your tummy? Tell me if anything hurts." Oxygen; chest shape; breath sounds; clubbing; jaundice; spider naevi; liver; spleen; cover him. Explain what you suspect, the blood test and what it means for his family, and why smoking must stop. "I think an inherited protein shortage is damaging your lungs. A blood test will tell us. Your family may need testing." Level; genotype; liver tests; smoking; alcohol; vaccines; family; follow-up; augmentation is not an NHS option.

R3 A, B Focused examination Omits oxygen saturation or the abdomen; reports signs that are absent. Finds a hyperinflated chest, quiet breath sounds at the bases and a normal abdomen. Your brother has cirrhosis and your father died of lung disease at 55. You have two children, 14 and 11. Only if asked about jaundice or swelling: none. You have had chest infections most winters. You use a blue inhaler now and then and take no other regular medicines; no allergies. As an electrician you have worked around some dust and fumes but no asbestos that you know of. No recent travel. sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Miss Clementine Whitworth, 24, dental nurse. Periods every three to four months since she was 15, facial hair and acne. BMI is 31. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Irregular cycles with signs of excess androgens in a young woman is polycystic ovary syndrome, a metabolic and mental health condition as well as a reproductive one. The marks come from the criteria, the screening and listening to her fears. The Examiner Trap. Miss Whitworth expects a scan and a contraceptive pill. Candidates diagnose from the scan and treat only the periods. Pass: two criteria, exclusions, metabolic and mood screening, treatment by goal. Fail: pill and discharge.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the cycle, the hair and acne, then her weight, mood, sleep, fertility wishes and family history of diabetes. "How often do you bleed? Tell me about the hair and skin. How is your mood? Do you want children? Any family diabetes?" Cycle; hair; acne; weight; mood; sleep; snoring; fertility; family history; drugs; eating. Check the blood pressure, the weight and waist, the skin and hair, and look for other causes. "May I check your blood pressure, your weight, your skin and the hair on your face and tummy? Tell me if anything hurts." BMI; waist; blood pressure; hirsutism; acne; acanthosis; striae; galactorrhoea; thyroid; cover her. Explain the diagnosis, the long-term risks, and the options for periods, hair and fertility. "You have polycystic ovary syndrome. It affects periods, hair, sugar and mood, and it is treatable." Criteria; tests; lifestyle; pill; metformin; hair treatment; fertility; mood; review.

sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Respiratory outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines British Thoracic Society guidelines for the investigation and management of pulmonary nodules (Thorax 2015;70 Suppl 2:ii1-ii54) Related AMaC stations AMaC R4-32 (incidental lung nodule, same topic); lobar collapse examination station
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Alun Tregarth, 67, retired bus mechanic. A CT scan of his chest and abdomen for back pain showed a 9 mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe. He smoked for 40 years and stopped ten years ago. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an older ex-smoker is a risk calculation, not a reassurance. The station turns on the size rule, the risk score and the growth rate, and on giving him the red flags. The Examiner Trap. Mr Tregarth hopes it is nothing. Candidates reassure and discharge, or rush to biopsy. Pass: size of 8 mm or more so Brock risk model; risk above 10% means PET-CT and a chest team; growth tells you more. Fail: discharged with no plan.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about cough, blood, weight loss and breathlessness, then smoking, asbestos, past cancer and family history. "Any cough, blood, weight loss or breathlessness? When did you stop smoking? Any asbestos or past cancer?" Cough; haemoptysis; weight loss; breathlessness; smoking; asbestos; cancer; family history; back pain. Examine the chest and neck, the hands and the spine, and look for signs of spread. "May I look at your hands, neck and chest, and press along your back? Tell me if anything hurts." Clubbing; nodes; chest; spine tenderness; liver; weight; cover him. Explain what the nodule is, why size and risk matter, what happens next and which symptoms are urgent. "The nodule is bigger than the size we watch, so I'd like the lung team to see it. Come back quickly if you cough blood." Risk score; repeat CT; PET; biopsy; growth rate; red flags; review.
