Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him. Also offers a chaperone and acknowledges how frightening a lung finding is. R2 C History Asks about smoking only; omits haemoptysis, weight loss, asbestos or past cancer. Asks cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, breathlessness, smoking history, asbestos and past cancer. Also asks about family history, previous chest imaging and why the CT was done. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits the nodes or spine; reports signs of lung cancer that are absent. Finds no clubbing, no neck nodes, a clear chest, no spinal tenderness and no hepatomegaly. Also records the weight loss he describes and the otherwise unremarkable examination. R4 D Assessment Calls it harmless, or calls it cancer with no reasoning. A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an ex-smoker: indeterminate, with a malignant risk that must be calculated. Also names infection, a benign
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Alun Tregarth, 67, a retired bus mechanic. You are practical, a little anxious and hoping for good news. Opening line: "They said they found a spot on my lung while looking at my back. I feel fine, so I'm sure it's nothing." Volunteered: you smoked about 20 a day for 40 years and stopped ten years ago. Only if asked: a slight morning cough for a year. No blood. You have lost a little weight without trying. You worked near asbestos lagging years ago. You take amlodipine for blood pressure; no allergies; you drink little alcohol; no recent travel; you live with your wife. Only if asked about family: your brother died of lung cancer at 70. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you have the same cancer as your brother. Say: "He went downhill in months." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it cancer?" "Do I need a biopsy?" "How long will it take?" How you react: if falsely reassured, you leave worried. If listened to and given a clear plan, you engage. If offered options, you choose.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 132/78; SpO2 96% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Thin; weight 4 kg lower than a year ago. No clubbing. No neck nodes. Chest clear. No spinal tenderness. No hepatomegaly. Results, only when requested: CT (dedicated chest): solid 9 mm nodule right upper lobe, spiculated edge; no other nodules. Risk model: above 10%. Repeat CT at 3 months, if done: volume increase of 40%. Question ladder: 1. What do you do with a nodule of 8 mm or more? (E) 2. What does a risk above 10% mean? (E) 3. What does a volume doubling time under 400 days mean? (E) 4. When can a nodule be discharged? (E) 5. Which symptoms are red flags? (E) Curveballs: He asks for a quick biopsy: not before the team has planned it. He asks why not just repeat the scan in a year: the size and risk need earlier assessment. He coughs up blood: urgent review.

sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A continuous machinery murmur below the left collarbone with a collapsing pulse in a young adult is a patent ductus arteriosus. The marks come from timing the murmur through both heart sounds, and from asking about the shunt and the pulmonary pressure. The Examiner Trap. Candidates call it aortic regurgitation and listen at the apex only. Pass: left infraclavicular, continuous, collapsing pulse, shunt, pulmonary pressure. Fail: aortic regurgitation, with no check of the toes.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do She is well. Look at her colour, hands, fingers and toes, then feel the pulse and the neck before the chest. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit her at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; pulse character; blood pressure; neck veins. Palpate the apex and the left upper chest, then listen below the left collarbone and over the back. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles." Apex; thrill; murmur timing; second sound; lung bases; feet and toes; ankles; cover her. Name the lesion, what the shunt does, and the tests that decide closure. "She has a patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt. She needs echo and pulmonary pressure assessment." Present in order; diagnosis; complications; echo; catheter; closure; follow-up; thank her.

Also compares fingers with toes and checks the blood pressure for a wide pulse pressure. R3 B Identifying signs Reports a diastolic murmur or cyanosis that are absent. Finds a collapsing pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced apex and a continuous murmur with a thrill below the left collarbone; pink fingers and toes. Also finds a loud second sound that would suggest rising pulmonary pressure. R4 D Differential diagnosis Calls it aortic regurgitation or a venous hum. Patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt. Also separates it

No oedema. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? sections.preamble: X-37 Consultation - Chest pain again after a heart attack at 46
sections.1. Title: Chest Pain Again After a Heart Attack at 46 / Avoid Routine Angiography
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Consultation (Station 5) Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Cardiology outpatient clinic Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and Acute Cardiovascular Care Association position paper on spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Adlam D et al, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3353-3368); American Heart Association scientific statement on spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Hayes SN et al, Circulation 2018;137:e523-e557) Related AMaC stations None identified
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mrs Henrietta Blackthorn, 46, school receptionist. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection was diagnosed at angiography three weeks ago after a heart attack, and she was treated with tablets alone. She has had two further episodes of chest tightness this week. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mrs Blackthorn.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A heart attack from a coronary artery tear in a woman in her forties is a different disease from ordinary coronary disease. The station turns on careful assessment of new chest pain, avoiding unnecessary angiography, and the long-term plan. The Examiner Trap. Mrs Blackthorn is anxious and wants another angiogram, or her pain is dismissed as anxiety. Candidates either rush her back for angiography or reassure with no ECG. Pass: ECG and troponin, conservative approach, plan. Fail: no tests or routine repeat angiography.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the pain, its pattern and triggers, then her tablets, her pregnancy plans, her mood and her exercise. "Describe the tightness. What brings it on? Are you taking your tablets? Do you plan more children? How is your mood?" Pain; triggers; duration; breathlessness; drugs; contraception; pregnancy plans; mood; exercise; migraine. Check the blood pressure, pulse and heart, look for signs of heart failure and for fibromuscular dysplasia clues. "May I check your blood pressure in both arms, your pulse, heart, chest and neck? Tell me if anything hurts." Blood pressure both arms; pulse; heart sounds; chest; neck bruits; ankles; cover her. Explain the diagnosis and the plan: tests for the new pain, long-term tablets, a scan of other arteries and rehabilitation. "Your artery tore rather than blocked, so treatment is different. I'd like an ECG and blood test today." ECG; troponin; admission; aspirin; beta-blocker; blood pressure; scan; rehabilitation; pregnancy; mood.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves her exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers her and thanks her. Also offers a chaperone and acknowledges how frightening this has been. R2 C History Asks about the pain only; omits tablets, pregnancy plans, mood or exercise. Asks pain pattern and triggers, breathlessness, tablets, contraception, pregnancy plans, mood and exercise. Also asks about migraine, headaches and any history of high blood pressure. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure in both arms or the heart; reports signs of heart failure that are absent. Finds normal blood pressure, a regular pulse, normal heart sounds, a clear chest and no oedema. Also finds no neck bruits and notes the arm pressures are equal. R4 D Assessment Calls it anxiety or ordinary angina with no reasoning. Recurrent c
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Henrietta Blackthorn, 46, a school receptionist. You are tearful, exhausted and frightened of another attack. Opening line: "I've had the tight chest again twice this week. I'm terrified it's another one. Do I need another angiogram?" Volunteered: you are on aspirin, a beta-blocker and a tablet for blood pressure (ramipril). No allergies. You have never smoked and drink little alcohol. Only if asked: each episode lasted about ten minutes and came on when you were stressed, not exercising. No breathlessness. You get migraines. Only if asked about children: you have two children, and you would like another baby; your husband agrees. Contraception: condoms only; you stopped the pill when you were admitted. No recent travel. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will die in front of your children. Say: "I can't stop checking my pulse." Your questions, in your own words: "Is it happening again?" "Will I have another one?" "Can I have another baby?" How you react: if brushed off, you leave frightened. If listened to and told the tests, you engage. If offered options, you choose.

Examiner material: Findings, released when examined: anxious, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 16; pulse 64 regular; blood pressure 126/76 right arm and 124/76 left arm; temperature 36.6 °C. CT of the head to the pelvis, if requested: changes of fibromuscular dysplasia in the renal arteries. Question ladder: 1. Why was she managed conservatively? (E) 2. Why is repeat angiography avoided? (E) 3. Which tests for the new pain? (E) 4. Which tablets? (E) 5. What about another pregnancy? (E) Curveballs: She asks for angiography to be sure: only with hard evidence of ischaemia. She asks about running a marathon: avoid high-intensity and competitive contact sport. She develops ongoing pain with ST changes: emergency pathway.

sections.1. Title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia, Vomiting and No Tablets / Cover the Crisis Before the Fertility
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Consultation PACES encounter Station 5 (less acute), consultation Skills marked A, B, C, D, E, F, G Setting Endocrinology outpatient clinic, seen as a same-day add-on Time 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) Guidelines Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2018;103:4043-4088; slide set dated March 2019); Society for Endocrinology, Emergency management of acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) in adult patients (Clin Med 2016) Related AMaC stations Addison's disease consultation (R2-55) and any Klinefelter station; this one tests classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia in an adult man
sections.3. Candidate brief: Dear Doctor, Mr Jasper Wetherby, 29, warehouse supervisor. Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia since birth, on prednisolone and fludrocortisone. He and his partner have tried for a baby for 18 months. He has been vomiting for two days and has not taken his tablets. Please assess and advise. The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to Mr Wetherby.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A man with classic adrenal enzyme deficiency who has been vomiting and has stopped his steroid is heading for an adrenal crisis, whatever his reason for coming. The marks come from treating the emergency first, then the fertility problem. The Examiner Trap. Mr Wetherby came to talk about fertility and mentions the vomiting only when asked. Candidates discuss semen tests and send him home. Pass: assess for adrenal crisis, urgent hydrocortisone and fluids, then fertility. Fail: fertility only.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Ask about the vomiting, the missed tablets and how he feels, then about his fertility and his usual control. "When did you last take your steroid? Are you keeping fluids down? Do you feel dizzy or weak? Tell me about the baby attempts." Vomiting; last dose; dizziness; abdominal pain; steroid card; sick-day plan; fertility; libido; testicular pain. Check for dehydration and shock, then examine the abdomen and the testes. "May I check your pulse, blood pressure and tummy, and feel your testes? Tell me if anything hurts." Pulse; blood pressure; hydration; pigmentation; abdomen; testes; lumps; cover him. Explain that he may be in danger from the missed steroid, what you will give him now and how you will return to fertility. "You need an injection of steroid and fluids now. Once you are well, we'll look at your fertility properly." Injection; fluids; tests; admission; sick-day rules; ultrasound; hormones; semen; review.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and dignity No introduction or consent; examines the testes without asking; leaves him exposed. Introduces self, asks consent, offers a chaperone before the genital examination, covers him and thanks him. Also acknowledges how hard it is to discuss fertility when feeling ill. R2 C History Asks about fertility only; omits the vomiting, the last steroid dose or his sick-day plan. Asks vomiting, last dose, dizziness, pain, steroid card, sick-day rules and fertility. Also asks about adherence, testicular pain and previous crises. R3 A, B Focused examination Omits blood pressure or hydration; reports signs that are absent. Finds a fast pulse, low blood pressure, a dry mouth, pigmentation, mild abdominal tenderness and small firm testicular masses. Also finds the testicular masses are bilateral and non-tender. R4 D Assessment Calls it gastroenteritis, or calls the problem fertility

Opening line: "We've been trying for a baby for a year and a half and it's not working. I wanted to ask about my sperm. I've had a bug, but I'll be fine." You have an emergency card but left it at home. Medicines: prednisolone 5 mg twice daily and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily (scenario values); no other medicines; no allergies. Non-smoker; alcohol a few units at weekends; no recent travel. Your brother has the same condition. You live with your partner. Only if asked about adherence: you often skip evening doses. No testicular pain, but you have noticed lumps. Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you are the reason your partner cannot get pregnant. Say: "She deserves a family." Mild abdominal tenderness. Both testes contain firm non-tender masses. Results, only when requested: sodium low; potassium raised; glucose low; urea raised. 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androstenedione markedly raised; renin raised. Testicular ultrasound: bilateral hypoechoic lesions consistent with adrenal rest tumours. Semen: very few sperm. Question ladder: 1. What is your immediate concern? sections.preamble: X-39 Communication - Request to switch off a defibrillator at the end of life
sections.1. Title: Request to Switch Off a Defibrillator in Advanced Heart Failure / Shocks Off, Pacing On, Resuscitation Separate
sections.2. Header: Station ID Station type Communication PACES encounter Station 1 or 4, communication encounter Skills marked C, E, F, G Setting Cardiology ward, side room Time 10 minutes (warning at 8 minutes; no examiner questions) Guidelines Cardiovascular implanted electronic devices in people towards the end of life, during cardiopulmonary resuscitation and after death (Resuscitation Council UK, British Cardiovascular Society and National Council for Palliative Care; 2015); Clinical Guideline for Deactivation of Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators towards the end of life (SPAGG; version 2.1, July 2026); Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) Related AMaC stations AMaC DNACPR station; this one tests a patient with capacity who asks for his defibrillator shocks to be stopped
sections.3. Candidate brief: You are the cardiology registrar. Mr Gethin Maddox, 71, a retired bus driver, has ischaemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 20 percent and a combined pacemaker and defibrillator (CRT-D) fitted five years ago. This is his third admission with heart failure this year. The team has agreed his outlook is months at most. He has asked a nurse, "Can you switch the shocking thing off?" Please speak to Mr Maddox about his request.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A patient with capacity asks for the shocks to be stopped. The task is to find out why, explain exactly what switching off does and does not do, and link it, without merging it, to resuscitation wishes. The Examiner Trap. Candidates either refuse because it feels like giving up, or promise "the whole thing will be turned off". Pass: shock therapy only, pacing stays, not immediate death, reversible, planned by the device team. Fail: refusing, or switching off everything.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Find out what he knows, what he has experienced and what has made him ask now. "I hear you asked about the device. Can you tell me what has made you think about that?" Introduce yourself, sit, open questions; ask about shocks, fears, his wife and what he understands of his heart. Explain what switching off shocks means, in plain words, and check he understands. "Switching off stops the shocks. It will not stop your heart or make you feel different. The pacing carries on." Shocks off, pacing on, not immediate death, can be turned back on, done by the device team, magnet only in an emergency. Link, but separate, his resuscitation wishes, then agree a plan and who is told. "Switching off the shocks and not being resuscitated are separate choices. Shall we talk about both?" DNACPR discussion, written consent, record, ReSPECT, tell the team and his wife, palliative care, date.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Welcome and privacy Starts without introducing self; stands by the door; checks a phone. Introduces self and role, sits down, closes the door and asks if he wants anyone with him. Also asks how he prefers to be addressed and whether he is comfortable and not in pain. R2 C His story and reasons Argues about the device before asking why he wants it off. Asks what has made him ask, about shocks he has had, and what he understands about his heart. Also asks what he fears most about the end of life, and what matters to him. R3 F Acknowledging fear Dismisses his fear of being shocked, or changes the subject. Acknowledges the fear of the shock he had and of a shock at the end, in his words. Also names his wish not to frighten his wife. R4 E Explaining what switching off does Says the whole device will be switched off, or that he will die if it is. Says shocks stop, pacing continues, he will feel no different, death is not immediate, and it can be reversed. Also says this suits the last weeks or months, and that shocks ca
sections.7. Role-player brief: Who you are: Gethin Maddox, 71, a retired bus driver, living with your wife, Marian. You are breathless at rest, tired and thin. You speak plainly and are not afraid of dying, but you are afraid of being shocked. Opening line: "I want the shocking thing turned off. I had one in the garden two years ago and it was like being kicked by a horse. I'm not having another." Volunteered: you have had one shock. You take furosemide, bisoprolol, ramipril and spironolactone; no allergies. You gave up smoking 20 years ago and drink almost no alcohol. You are sick of hospital. You have stopped driving and told the DVLA when the device was fitted. Only if asked: you understand your heart is very weak and you will not get better. You do not want to die in a shock with Marian watching. You have not discussed resuscitation with anyone. Marian is your only close family; you have two grown-up children who live away. You live in a ground-floor flat. Hidden concern (only if asked what you fear most): you are afraid that turning it off means you will be left to die suddenly. Say: "Will it just stop my heart?" Your questions, in your own words: "Will it kill me?" "Will I feel anything?" "Does the pacing
sections.8. Examiner material: No examiner questions in this encounter. No findings are released. Surrogate prompts, if not raised naturally: at about 3 minutes, "Will it kill me?"; at about 5 minutes, "Does the pacing go too?"; after the 8-minute warning, accept a plan if one is offered. Observe: whether the reason is explored before facts are given; whether shocks and pacing are separated; whether the decision is respected and recorded; whether resuscitation is raised as a separate matter. Curveballs and safe answers: 1. "Can you do it now with a magnet?" No; planned deactivation by the device team, a magnet only in an emergency. 2. "Does Marian have to agree?" No; it is his decision, and we will tell her with his consent. 3. "If I get better?" It can be switched on again.

sections.1. Title: Scars, a Parasternal Heave and a Quiet Diastolic Murmur After Childhood Surgery

sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Emlyn Fairclough is 36 and a joiner. He had heart surgery as a child and attends for review. Please examine his cardiovascular system. You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A man with two chest scars, a right ventricular heave and a soft diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge has repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation. The marks come from separating it from aortic regurgitation, and from acting on a report of near-fainting. The Examiner Trap. Candidates call a quiet low-pitched diastolic murmur aortic regurgitation and look for a collapsing pulse. Pass: heave, single second sound, no collapsing pulse, scars. Fail: aortic regurgitation, and routine review after near-fainting.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do He looks well. Check colour and hands, both radial pulses and both arm blood pressures, then the neck and the scars. "May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?" Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; both pulses; blood pressure; neck veins; scars. Feel for the apex and a heave, then listen at the left sternal edge in held expiry and inspiration. "I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles." Apex; heave; thrill; second sound; murmurs in inspiration; lung bases; liver edge; ankles; cover him. Name the lesion, the late problem and what decides intervention, and say what to do about near-fainting. "This is repaired tetralogy of Fallot with pulmonary regurgitation and right ventricular dilatation. He needs urgent review for the near-fainting." Present in order; diagnosis; complications; tests; urgent rhythm assessment; follow-up; thank him.
sections.6. Scoring grid: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards. Also offers a chaperone and stops if he is breathless. R2 A Systematic technique Disorganised; omits the scars, the second radial pulse or the left sternal edge. Also checks blood pressure in both arms and the liver edge. R3 B Identifying signs Reports cyanosis, clubbing or a collapsing pulse that are absent. Finds a sternotomy scar, a left thoracotomy scar, a weak left radial pulse, a heave, a single second sound and a diastolic murmur. Also finds the murmur louder in inspiration and a soft systolic murmur, with blood pressure lower in the left arm. R4 D Differe
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not used for this station type.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings, released as each step is done: well; respiratory rate 14; pulse 76 regular, left radial weaker than right; blood pressure 124/74 right arm, 104/66 left arm; SpO2 97% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. No cyanosis, no clubbing. Midline sternotomy scar and a left thoracotomy scar. JVP not raised. Apex not displaced; sustained left parasternal heave. Second sound single. Soft ejection systolic murmur and an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, louder in inspiration. No collapsing pulse. Lung bases clear. No oedema. Question ladder: 1. What do you find? sections.preamble: R5-166 — Thyroid eye disease — sight-threatening context
sections.1. Title: Thyroid eye disease — sight-threatening context: examine, localise and make the safe next decision
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · Station 3: Neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10-minute encounter (up to 6 minutes examining, remaining time for examiner questions) · Station ID: R5-166 · Educational draft, 14 October 2026 · Not an official PACES mark scheme.
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 43-year-old with a history of thyroid disease reports eye prominence and recent difficulty seeing clearly. Perform a focused examination of the eyes and relevant cranial nerve functions. Please obtain consent and adapt to the patient's comfort. Present key findings and your immediate clinical priorities.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK: Checks acuity, colour desaturation, pupils and corneal exposure in addition to proptosis and ocular motility. TRAP: Reduced acuity or colour vision, an afferent defect or corneal breakdown is sight-threatening: escalate immediately, not routine thyroid follow-up. Advise smoking cessation.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Localise before naming “I’ll compare both sides and explain the tests.” Check comfort and clinically relevant symmetry. Make signs reproducible “Please tell me if this becomes uncomfortable.” Checks acuity, colour desaturation, pupils and corneal exposure in addition to proptosis and ocular motility. Identify the competing lesion “I also want to check what is preserved.” Test relevant spared functions; do not invent negatives. Turn findings into action “I will explain which signs affect urgency.” Urgent same-day ophthalmology/orbital assessment for suspected optic neuropathy, threatened cornea or rapidly deteriorating vision; thyroid status, ocular imaging and joint endocrine care as indicated.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Criterion Fail Pass High-performance R1 A/G Consent and welfare Moves or exposes patient without explanation. Introduces, obtains consent, positions comfortably. Checks fatigue or functional limitations; adapts and preserves dignity. R2 A Targeted technique Incomplete or unfocused neurological tests. Performs essential side-by-side examination. Selects the most discriminating manoeuvre for this case. R3 B Positive findings Misses or misstates characteristic signs. Accurately states observed abnormal signs. Explains significance of the specific pattern, without overclaim. R4 B Relevant negatives Assumes features absent without examining. Checks important preserved functions. Uses verified negatives to reject a close mimic. R5 D Diagnosis and localisation Labels a condition without justified localisation. Names leading syndrome and anatomical level. Compares competing diagnosis using a specific sign. R6 E Next decision Vague or inappropriate investigation/referral. Names key confirmatory action or referral. Prioritises sequence and proportionate use of tests. R7 E/G Safety and welfare Ignores major scenario-specific harm. Identifies escalation trigger and safe action. Couns
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable — physical examination. Release only findings elicited by examination; provide no unasked-for diagnosis or extra history.
sections.8. Examiner material: Release on relevant testing: Upper lid retraction, bilateral proptosis and restricted upgaze; assess visual acuity, colour vision, pupils, fields and ocular surface. Do not assume optic neuropathy without objective evidence. 1. EXAMINER: “What pattern have you demonstrated?” EXPECTED: Upper lid retraction, bilateral proptosis and restricted upgaze; assess visual acuity, colour vision, pupils, fields and ocular surface. stations.title: Painful Ischaemic Fingers / Tobacco Abstinence Is the Decisive Intervention

sections.1. Title: Painful Ischaemic Fingers / Tobacco Abstinence Is the Decisive Intervention
sections.2. Header: R5-101 | Physical examination | PACES23 Station 3, cardiovascular examination | 10 min (up to 6 examination, at least 4 examiner questions) | Skills A, B, D, E, G | Medical assessment unit | Station ID: __________ Sources and versions: CDC: Smoking and Buerger’s Disease, 2022, accessed 13 Oct 2026; Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine: Nonatherosclerotic limb ischemia, 2016. Related AMaC stations: cross-register duplication confirmation required.
sections.3. Candidate brief: You are the medical registrar. Please examine the cardiovascular system of Mr Kieran Mallory, aged 34, to assess the cause of painful discoloured fingertips. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions. You may ask the patient to change position during the examination.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger’s disease), provisionally is the unifying possibility, but findings must be described accurately before naming a cause. The Examiner Trap. Do not call all digital ischaemia Buerger disease, and do not tell the patient that reducing smoking is enough. Pass behaviour: identify the signs, articulate uncertainty, and give a safe next step.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Orient “I will explain the examination and ask if anything is uncomfortable.” Introduce, consent, assess comfort and position. Find the pattern “I will examine the peripheral signs, pulses and heart.” Follow targeted examination sequence; describe positive and absent findings. Synthesise “The findings suggest thromboangiitis obliterans (buerger’s disease), provisionally.” Offer alternative(s); avoid overclaiming confirmation. Prioritise “I would investigate the key risk and plan specialist follow-up.” Check safety red flags, choose tests and escalation appropriate to this case.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Pain and dignity Does not check consent or discomfort; proceeds despite objection. Checks finger pain before touching, gains consent and avoids unnecessary manipulation Checks finger pain before touching, gains consent and avoids unnecessary manipulation; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. R2 A Peripheral vascular survey Omits the focused examination or uses disorganised, unreliable technique. Examines colour, temperature, ulceration and pulses in all four limbs, then heart Examines colour, temperature, ulceration and pulses in all four limbs, then heart; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. R3 B Ischaemic signs Misses supplied signs or invents absent signs. Identifies distal ischaemic ulcer and weak/absent distal pulses without claiming embolic stigmata Identifies distal ischaemic ulcer and weak/absent distal pulses without claiming embolic stigmata; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. R4 D Differential Names one unrelated diagnosis without evidence. Proposes Buerger disease provisionally while explicitly excluding embolic/autoimmune causes Proposes Buerger disease provisionall
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable to this physical-examination encounter. The patient answers routine comfort and positioning requests; there is no scripted surrogate negotiation.
sections.8. Examiner material: Release only when the candidate examines the relevant area: Hands/skin and peripheral circulation: Right index fingertip cool with a small dry ulcer; right ulnar and radial pulses reduced distally; brachial pulses palpable; left foot dorsalis pedis absent, femoral pulses present; normal cardiac auscultation. Other examination and normal findings: No fever, no proximal limb oedema, no major systemic inflammatory features. Examiner question ladder (answers are teaching models, not an official mark scheme): Q1 (B/D; grid R3): Your working diagnosis? Answer: Buerger disease is strongly linked to tobacco in a younger person with distal limb ischaemia; confirm by excluding alternatives. Q2 (B/D; grid R4): What other diagnoses must you exclude? Answer: Cardiac emboli, atherosclerosis, autoimmune vasculitis, thrombophilia and other causes of digital ischaemia. Q3 (E; grid R5): What tests help? Answer: Vascular duplex and specialist arterial imaging, selected inflammatory/autoimmune and metabolic tests according to presentation. Q4 (E; grid R6): What changes prognosis most? Answer: Complete cessation of tobacco and nicotine exposure with specialist cessation support; cutting down is not a s
sections.9. Mark Triggers: • Checks finger pain before touching, gains consent and avoids unnecessary manipulation (G; R1) • Examines colour, temperature, ulceration and pulses in all four limbs, then heart (A; R2) • Identifies distal ischaemic ulcer and weak/absent distal pulses without claiming embolic stigmata (B; R3) • Proposes Buerger disease provisionally while explicitly excluding embolic/autoimmune causes (D; R4) • Explains complete tobacco/nicotine cessation with support, without promising a cure (E; R5) • Clinical interpretation: In suspected thromboangiitis obliterans, check pulses and distal perfusion; rapidly progressive pain, pallor, coldness or sensory/motor deficit raises concern for acute limb ischaemia and needs emergency vascular assessment. • Safety / escalation: Smoking cessation is the essential disease-modifying intervention. Do not offer revascularisation or vasodilators as a guaranteed cure.

stations.title: Severe Aortic Stenosis in a Frail Older Adult / Treat the Person, Not the Murmur

sections.1. Title: Severe Aortic Stenosis in a Frail Older Adult / Treat the Person, Not the Murmur
sections.2. Header: Code R5-105 | Physical examination | PACES Station 3, cardiovascular encounter | Skills A, B, D, E, G | Older adult cardiology clinic | 10 min: up to 6 min examination, at least 4 min examiner questions | Date: 13 October 2026 | Principal guidance: 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines (29 August 2025). Related AMaC stations: check live station register before allocation.
sections.3. Candidate brief: Please examine this patient’s cardiovascular system to assess the cause of worsening exertional breathlessness and discuss your findings with the examiners.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK — An elderly patient with a slow-rising pulse and late-peaking systolic murmur may have severe aortic stenosis. The decision is not “too old for TAVI”: assess symptoms, echo severity, function, frailty and goals. EXAMINER TRAP — Declaring that a 90-year-old must have TAVI—or must be denied treatment—without asking about frailty, expected benefit and preference. A safe candidate requests Heart Team assessment and offers an informed choice.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Avoid premature labels. “I am going to examine your heart and circulation, if that is all right.” Consent; hand hygiene; ask about pain; position and drape. Look for the discriminating signs. “Please tell me if you are uncomfortable while I check your pulse and listen.” Pulse, BP, JVP, apex, auscultation, relevant peripheral signs. Name an appropriately qualified diagnosis. “I would like to put the findings together before discussing tests.” Present positive and pertinent normal findings; offer differential. Plan against the actual clinical risk. “I would confirm the severity with an echocardiogram and arrange specialist review.” Select relevant echo, ECG and management; address patient safety.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row / skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and welfare Starts without consent or exposes patient unnecessarily. Introduces self, asks consent and discomfort, covers patient. Checks positioning and adapts examination for comfort. R2 A Examination sequence Omits focused pulse, precordium or auscultation. Checks pulse, BP, JVP, apex and valve areas systematically. Uses manoeuvres relevant to the suspected lesion without distress. R3 B Specific physical signs Reports normal auscultation or invents unrelated signs. Identifies: Harsh ejection systolic murmur loudest at right upper sternal edge radiating to carotids; soft second sound. Also relates: Small-volume, slow-rising carotid pulse; pulse 76 regular. No resting pulmonary crackles or ankle oedema. No syncope during the encounter. R4 D Specific differential Misses the principal valve lesion or fails to link it to clinical signs. States: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is likely; severity must be confirmed by echocardiography. Contrasts: Aortic sclerosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, coexistent coronary artery disease or anaemia. R5 E Decision-changing tests Offers definitive surgery or discharge without imaging. Sel
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable: physical examination encounter; no patient role-player dialogue required. Patient prompt if asked: “I have to stop halfway across my sitting room. I am worried an operation would finish me off.”
sections.8. Examiner material: Release findings only when examined. Candidate must elicit, not be handed, physical signs: 1. Small-volume, slow-rising carotid pulse; pulse 76 regular. 2. Harsh ejection systolic murmur loudest at right upper sternal edge radiating to carotids; soft second sound. 3. No resting pulmonary crackles or ankle oedema. No syncope during the encounter. 4. Mobilises slowly with a stick; no chest pain at rest. Examiner question ladder (ask after examination): What is your leading diagnosis? [R4] — Symptomatic aortic stenosis, potentially severe; echo confirms severity. Which investigations matter? [R5] — Echo, ECG, functional and frailty assessment, and procedure-planning imaging if appropriate. Would you recommend TAVI because she is 90? [R6] — No age-only decision; discuss candidacy, prognosis and her wishes through the Heart Team. What if intervention offers little benefit? [R6] — Discuss symptom management, multidisciplinary support and advance care preferences. Curveball: “Does this mean the diagnosis and treatment are certain?” Safe answer: No; correlate examination with echo and personalised specialist assessment.
sections.9. Mark Triggers: • Introduces self, obtains consent and checks comfort (G/R1). • Examines pulse, blood pressure, apex and auscultation appropriately (A/R2). • Finds and presents the case-specific signs without inventing findings (B/R3). • Names the leading lesion and a plausible differential (D/R4). • Selects echo and appropriate complementary testing (E/R5). • Clinical interpretation: Echocardiography, symptom burden, LV function and valve haemodynamics establish aortic-stenosis severity; physical signs alone do not choose TAVI or surgery. • Safety / escalation: Frailty, anatomy, life expectancy, values and likely benefit belong in the Heart Team discussion. New syncope, angina or pulmonary oedema requires urgent reassessment.

sections.3. Candidate brief: Please examine this patient’s cardiovascular system to identify a possible cause of increasing exertional breathlessness and outline what information you would need before recommending intervention.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK — An apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla points towards mitral regurgitation; quantify severity and ventricular consequences rather than guessing surgery timing from murmur loudness. EXAMINER TRAP — Saying “watch and wait because the patient is coping” or treating a loud murmur as proof of severe regurgitation. The correct next step is expert echo-based grading and Heart Valve Team evaluation.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Avoid premature labels. “I am going to examine your heart and circulation, if that is all right.” Consent; hand hygiene; ask about pain; position and drape. Look for the discriminating signs. “Please tell me if you are uncomfortable while I check your pulse and listen.” Pulse, BP, JVP, apex, auscultation, relevant peripheral signs. Name an appropriately qualified diagnosis. “I would like to put the findings together before discussing tests.” Present positive and pertinent normal findings; offer differential. Plan against the actual clinical risk. “I would confirm the severity with an echocardiogram and arrange specialist review.” Select relevant echo, ECG and management; address patient safety.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row / skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Consent and welfare Starts without consent or exposes patient unnecessarily. Introduces self, asks consent and discomfort, covers patient. Checks positioning and adapts examination for comfort. R2 A Examination sequence Omits focused pulse, precordium or auscultation. Checks pulse, BP, JVP, apex and valve areas systematically. Uses manoeuvres relevant to the suspected lesion without distress. R3 B Specific physical signs Reports normal auscultation or invents unrelated signs. Identifies: Displaced, hyperdynamic apex; blowing pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to left axilla. Also relates: Pulse 84 regular, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg (scenario values). Soft first heart sound; no pulmonary crackles or peripheral oedema today. R4 D Specific differential Misses the principal valve lesion or fails to link it to clinical signs. States: Probable primary mitral regurgitation with possible haemodynamic significance. Contrasts: Secondary functional MR, tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defect; differentiate by site/radiation and echo. R5 E Decision-changing tests Offers definitive surgery or discharge without imaging. Selects: Com
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable: physical examination encounter; no patient role-player dialogue required. Patient prompt if asked: “I can still manage everyday tasks, but the stairs have become much harder over the last few months.”
sections.8. Examiner material: Release findings only when examined. Candidate must elicit, not be handed, physical signs: 1. Pulse 84 regular, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg (scenario values). 2. Displaced, hyperdynamic apex; blowing pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to left axilla. 3. Soft first heart sound; no pulmonary crackles or peripheral oedema today. 4. No mechanical valve click or sternotomy scar. Examiner question ladder (ask after examination): What lesion do you suspect? [R4] — Mitral regurgitation, probably primary; examination alone cannot determine severity. How would echo influence timing? [R5] — Combine severity, symptoms, LV dimensions/EF, left atrial and pulmonary pressure findings per contemporary valve guidance. Repair or replace? [R6] — Prefer durable repair where feasible; replacement if repair is unlikely to succeed or last. What would you tell him today? [R6] — An echo and specialist valve review are needed; discuss risks, benefits and alternatives without promising surgery. EXAMINER TRAP — Calling an annuloplasty ring a mechanical prosthesis and prescribing lifelong warfarin automatically—or saying anticoagulation is never needed after repair. The indication and postoperative timing matter.

Contrasts: Mitral replacement with tissue prosthesis, prior CABG or other surgery; confirm using operation records and echocardiography. Pulse 78, regular; normal prosthetic click absent. 3. A very soft apical pansystolic murmur may indicate mild residual MR; no congestion. 4. Patient comfortable supine and haemodynamically stable. Name an appropriately qualified diagnosis. “I would like to put the findings together before discussing tests.” Present positive and pertinent normal findings; offer differential. Plan against the actual clinical risk. “I would confirm the severity with an echocardiogram and arrange specialist review.” Select relevant echo, ECG and management; address patient safety.

Communicate a provisional conclusion The pattern suggests a problem affecting a particular nerve region. Present positive and normal findings, differentials and safety plan.

[R5/R6] — Orthostatic symptoms, urinary retention/urgency, erectile dysfunction, constipation. 4. What is a dangerous respiratory feature? [R5/R6] — Nocturnal or daytime stridor. 5. Identifies: Marked asymmetric left arm rigidity and bradykinesia. Also identifies: Unable to mime brushing teeth with the left hand despite understanding and adequate elementary movement: limb apraxia. R4 B Negative physical findings Invents signs absent from the scenario. Notes: No prominent rest tremor; basic sensation relatively preserved. Explains why the absence changes differential. R5 D Localisation and differential Offers a diagnosis inconsistent with the observed signs. Corticobasal syndrome (CBS): asymmetric parkinsonism with cortical signs, especially limb apraxia. Idiopathic Parkinson disease, stroke, progressive supranuclear palsy, focal structural lesion; pathology causing CBS is not uniquely corticobasa
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable: physical examination encounter. Standardised patient: Mr Daniel Okoro, 69. Progressive clumsiness of the left hand, which sometimes seems to move without intention.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings released on examination: • Marked asymmetric left arm rigidity and bradykinesia. • Unable to mime brushing teeth with the left hand despite understanding and adequate elementary movement: limb apraxia. • Intermittent purposeless left arm posturing; patient calls it “not my hand”. • No prominent rest tremor; basic sensation relatively preserved. Normal-findings variant: An early focused cranial nerve examination may be normal; do not infer Parkinson disease simply from rigidity. Question ladder (examiner questions, with concise model answers): 1. What is the key cortical sign? [R5/R6] — Limb apraxia despite sufficient motor strength and comprehension. 2. How does it differ from Parkinson disease? [R5/R6] — Marked asymmetry and cortical signs such as apraxia and alien-limb phenomena. 3. Does CBS prove a single pathology? [R5/R6] — No. Several pathologies can produce the syndrome. 4. Which test would help exclude mimics? [R5/R6] — Brain MRI. 5. What supportive care matters? [R5/R6] — OT, physiotherapy, falls assessment and speech/swallow input as disease progresses. Curveball: Over one hour the patient develops new facial droop and aphasia. Treat this as possible acute stroke
sections.9. Mark Triggers: • [R1] Obtains consent and explains tasks clearly while accommodating apraxia and limited movement. • [R2] Examines asymmetry, rigidity, bradykinesia, cortical sensory loss, praxis and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. • [R3] Identifies asymmetric limb apraxia or cortical features beyond simple extrapyramidal rigidity. • [R4] Distinguishes corticobasal syndrome from a single definitive pathology and screens for PSP, stroke and other mimics. • [R5] Describes corticobasal syndrome as a clinical phenotype, not proof of corticobasal degeneration. • [R6] Requests specialist movement-disorder/cognitive evaluation, relevant brain imaging and functional/occupational support. • [R7] Protects against falls, aspiration and new focal neurological deficits; abrupt change triggers urgent stroke assessment.

sections.3. Candidate brief: Please examine this patient’s head, neck and relevant neurological system to explain abnormal head posture.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK: Cervical dystonia with a sensory trick and task-modifiable abnormal posture. TRAP: Treating the sensory trick as evidence of fabrication, or manipulating the painful neck forcefully.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Consent, comfort, localisation “I will explain each step; tell me if it hurts.” Introduce, seek consent, position safely; offer assistance. Seek characteristic pattern “I would like to check the affected movements.” Examine relevant cranial nerves or limbs systematically. Check for mimics and danger “I will check other nerve functions as well.” Seek associated motor, sensory, gait and urgent signs. Formulate safely “The findings point to a particular neurological pattern.” Present positive and negative findings; state differential and next action.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 A Consent and technique Omits consent or performs unsafe painful manoeuvres. Introduces, obtains consent and examines safely. Adapts positioning and pauses for discomfort. R2 A Structured examination Unfocused movements without an anatomical sequence. Completes focused system examination. Targets additional examination to localise the lesion. R3 B Positive physical findings Does not identify the characteristic abnormality. Identifies: Head intermittently rotates right with hypertrophy and overactivity of selected cervical muscles. Also identifies: Lightly touching the cheek temporarily improves the posture (sensory trick). R4 B Negative physical findings Invents signs absent from the scenario. Notes: No focal limb weakness, pyramidal signs or sensory loss. Explains why the absence changes differential. R5 D Localisation and differential Offers a diagnosis inconsistent with the observed signs. Cervical dystonia with a sensory trick and task-modifiable abnormal posture. Drug-induced dystonia (antipsychotics/antiemetics), structural neck disorder, functional movement disorder, parkinsonian dystonia. R6 E Investigation and management Fails
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable: physical examination encounter. Standardised patient: Ms Sophie Bennett, 43. Involuntary turning of the head to the right with painful neck tightness; no recent injury.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings released on examination: • Head intermittently rotates right with hypertrophy and overactivity of selected cervical muscles. • Lightly touching the cheek temporarily improves the posture (sensory trick). • Neck range and pain are assessed gently, without forcing rotation. • No focal limb weakness, pyramidal signs or sensory loss. Normal-findings variant: Examination outside a spasm may show near-normal posture; do not force abnormal positioning. Question ladder (examiner questions, with concise model answers): 1. What is the phenomenon when touch improves posture? [R5/R6] — Geste antagoniste, or sensory trick. 2. Which medicines can provoke dystonia? [R5/R6] — Antipsychotics and dopamine-blocking antiemetics. 3. What is usual specialist focal treatment? [R5/R6] — Botulinum toxin injected into selected overactive muscles. 4. How would you investigate? [R5/R6] — Clinical diagnosis with medication review; investigate atypical neurological signs or structural suspicion. 5. What other support helps? [R5/R6] — Pain control, targeted physiotherapy and psychosocial support. Curveball: After a new antipsychotic, the patient develops tongue spasm and stridor. Escalate to emergency a
sections.9. Mark Triggers: • [R1] Obtains consent, asks about pain and stops manoeuvres that worsen neck discomfort. • [R2] Observes resting posture, patterned rotation/tilt, tremor, range of motion and a possible sensory trick without forcing the neck. • [R3] Identifies patterned involuntary cervical muscle contraction and geste antagoniste when present. • [R4] Distinguishes cervical dystonia from fixed torticollis, focal weakness and potentially secondary medication-related dystonia. • [R5] Suggests cervical dystonia and checks for offending dopamine-blocking drugs and other neurological abnormalities. • [R6] Offers specialist assessment; discusses botulinum toxin and supportive treatment rather than indiscriminate sedatives. • [R7] Recognises acute laryngeal dystonia, stridor or swallowing obstruction after a drug exposure as an airway emergency.

sections.1. Title: Eyes That Barely Move / Consider Mitochondrial Disease Beyond the Orbit
sections.2. Header: Station ID: R5-138 | R5-138 | Physical examination | PACES Station 3 · Neurological encounter | Skills A, B, D, E, G | Neurology clinic | 10 minutes (6 examining + 4 questions). sections.3. Candidate brief: Mr Daniel Iqbal, aged 43, has been referred because of slow progressive drooping eyelids. Please examine the eye movements and relevant neurological system to explain this patient’s symptoms.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook: Symmetrical ptosis with marked global limitation of ocular movements and little diplopia suggests chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia; look beyond the eyes.The Examiner Trap: Assuming that absence of diplopia excludes ophthalmoplegia loses the localisation. Pass: assess full movements, pupils and systemic complications, especially conduction disease.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Risk and task “Is it safe for you to stand or walk?” Introduce yourself; gain consent and assess discomfort/fall risk. Localise “I will test movements, strength and reflexes.” Perform focused neurological examination and identify positive and normal signs. Synthesis “I will summarise the pattern, not guess from one sign.” Present coherent localisation and reasoned differential. Next step “I would check the most important complication.” State investigations, timely specialist referral and patient-safety action.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row/skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 (G) Consent and safety Starts examination without consent or checking risk Obtains permission, explains examination and protects the patient Adapts examination to the individual, checks fall or airway risks and obtains consent R2 (A) Focused sequence Omits relevant focused examination and function Performs a safe relevant system examination Efficiently demonstrates positive and negative findings relevant to alternatives R3 (B) Positive signs Fails to identify the key observed positive finding Correctly describes: Bilateral ptosis and slowly progressive symmetric limitation of extraocular movements Links observed pattern to anatomical and functional implications R4 (B) Discriminating signs Mistakes a non-specific feature for a discriminator Distinguishes: Marked ophthalmoplegia without prominent diplopia or fatigability, with preserved pupillary light responses Explains why marked ophthalmoplegia without prominent diplopia or fatigability, with preserved pupillary light responses matters and its limitations R5 (D) Clinical synthesis States definitive diagnosis without considering differentials Proposes Chronic progressive external ophtha
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable: examination encounter (no role-player dialogue). The simulated patient gives consent and reports discomfort if asked; examiner supplies findings only after the corresponding examination action.
sections.8. Examiner material: Findings released after the relevant manoeuvre: Bilateral symmetrical ptosis and compensatory chin-up posture. Markedly limited eye movements in all directions, including pursuit; pupils reactive. No marked fatigable fluctuation, no nystagmus and no facial sensory loss. Limb tone, power and reflexes largely normal; no cerebellar signs. Normal-findings variant: State normal pupils and limb function: not all CPEO patients show systemic signs on bedside examination. Q1 [R5–R7; D/E]: What is the pattern? Answer: Chronic bilateral external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis. Q2 [R5–R7; D/E]: Why little diplopia? Answer: Slow, often symmetrical restriction may produce less perceived diplopia than acute nerve palsy. Q3 [R5–R7; D/E]: Which systemic diagnosis? Answer: Mitochondrial myopathy; assess for syndromic features. Q4 [R5–R7; D/E]: Which screening can be lifesaving? Answer: ECG and specialist assessment for cardiac conduction disease. Q5 [R5–R7; D/E]: How would you confirm? Answer: Specialist-directed mitochondrial DNA or nuclear gene testing, depending on phenotype. Curveball: The patient reports fainting yesterday. Prioritise same-day ECG and urgent cardiac assessment for possible conduct

Offers a provisional diagnosis of Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO), potentially part of mitochondrial disease, and considers myasthenia gravis, thyroid eye disease, orbital restriction and supranuclear gaze disorders (D; R5). Proposes focused investigations: Neuro-ophthalmology/neuromuscular and mitochondrial genetics input; ECG and urgent rhythm assessment if syncope; targeted systemic screening (E; R6). States immediate safety priorities and disposition: Ask specifically about syncope or palpitations: conduction block can cause sudden deterioration; assess ocular exposure (E/G; R7).

Subacute painful asymmetric proximal wasting in an older person with diabetes suggests diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy, not simply distal diabetic neuropathy. The Examiner Trap. Source status: Historical nerve/plexus review and NICE NG127 cited as background; specific long-thoracic management claims not independently guideline-verified.
sections.3. Candidate brief: Ms Nisha Vale, 39, is attending for a neurological assessment. Please examine this patient’s upper-limb neurological system to investigate difficulty lifting the right arm. You may ask for relevant findings as you examine. Please present your findings and discuss your assessment with the examiners.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK: Right serratus anterior weakness compatible with long thoracic nerve palsy. The pattern of deficits, rather than a single weak movement, determines localisation. EXAMINER TRAP: Diagnosing FSHD from one winged scapula without checking facial strength, bilateral involvement or family history. Pass behaviour: demonstrate discriminating findings and state a safe next step. Fail behaviour: anchor on an incomplete pattern and miss the red flag.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Respect and prepare May I examine you? Tell me if anything hurts. Introduce, consent, position, expose minimally. Localise the lesion I will compare movements, sensation and reflexes on both sides. Inspect, test key motor groups, sensory territories and reflexes. Look for the missing discriminators I will check nearby nerves and additional warning signs. Test the specific distinguishing findings; seek fundoscopy or vascular status where relevant. Communicate a provisional conclusion The pattern suggests a problem affecting a particular nerve region. Present positive and normal findings, differentials and safety plan.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row / Skill Label Fail Pass High-performance R1 / G Consent and comfort Examines without consent or ignores discomfort. Introduces self; obtains consent; asks about pain and preserves dignity. Positions safely, explains potentially uncomfortable steps and responds to fatigue. R2 / A Systematic technique Tests only the most obvious weak muscle. Examines relevant power, reflexes and sensation on both sides. Sequences tests to distinguish nerve, root and central patterns efficiently. R3 / B Identifies key sign States a sign not present or misses the defining deficit. Correctly describes: Right scapula rotates poorly on active forward flexion; shoulder abduction is limited by weakness, not joint pain. Identifies key abnormal and preserved findings, avoiding invented signs. R4 / B Discriminating examination Misses adjacent cranial nerves or segmental testing. Checks the nearby structures needed to localise the lesion. Demonstrates why the pattern supports or refutes a competing localisation. R5 / D Differential and localisation Labels the syndrome without anatomically localising it. Names Right serratus anterior weakness compatible with long thoracic nerve palsy. Contrasts with Neuralgi
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable to this physical examination encounter; clinical findings are supplied in Section 8.
sections.8. Examiner material: Case setup: Right shoulder discomfort followed by difficulty pushing against doors, without major trauma. Release findings only when the corresponding examination step is performed: 1. Right medial scapular border protrudes when she pushes both palms against a wall. 2. Right scapula rotates poorly on active forward flexion; shoulder abduction is limited by weakness, not joint pain. 3. Deltoid, biceps, triceps and intrinsic hand power preserved; reflexes and sensation normal. 4. Left scapula does not wing; facial strength and hip flexion normal; no longstanding family history given. 5. Skin and shoulder joint examination normal. Examiner: What is the leading diagnosis and localisation? Answer: Right serratus anterior weakness compatible with long thoracic nerve palsy. [R5] Examiner: What alternative diagnoses would you consider? Answer: Neuralgic amyotrophy; direct long thoracic nerve traction injury; spinal accessory nerve palsy; facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy. [R5] Examiner: Which examination feature most helps here? Answer: Differentiate medial winging on forward pushing from trapezius-related lateral winging; seek pain-onset and family-history clues. [R3–R4] Examiner: Wh
sections.9. Mark Triggers: • Seeks consent, checks shoulder pain and compares both shoulders without forcing painful movement. • Inspects both scapulae at rest and during active forward elevation. • Demonstrates medial scapular winging on pushing against a wall, consistent with serratus anterior weakness. • Tests trapezius shrug, rhomboid retraction, deltoid and proximal/distal limb strength; screens sensation and reflexes. • Localises likely long thoracic nerve dysfunction while considering spinal accessory palsy, neuralgic amyotrophy and FSHD. • Plans physiotherapy and appropriate specialist evaluation; considers neurophysiology or imaging if course is atypical or progressive. • Explains expected functional impact, follow-up of recovery, and red flags of progressive or generalised weakness. • Explains risk, next steps and restores patient comfort (E, G)

sections.3. Candidate brief: Mrs Naila Mercer, aged 76, has been referred because of repeated falls and slower walking. Please examine this patient’s neurological system to establish the cause of her difficulty walking.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook: A broad-based, short-stepped gait with difficulty initiating and turning points to a frontal gait disorder; do not diagnose Parkinson disease from small steps alone.The Examiner Trap: The patient reports poor memory. A candidate who performs only a cognitive screen misses the dominant gait abnormality. Pass: demonstrate and describe the gait safely, then consider treatable hydrocephalus.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Risk and task “Is it safe for you to stand or walk?” Introduce yourself; gain consent and assess discomfort/fall risk. Localise “I will test movements, strength and reflexes.” Perform focused neurological examination and identify positive and normal signs. Synthesis “I will summarise the pattern, not guess from one sign.” Present coherent localisation and reasoned differential. Next step “I would check the most important complication.” State investigations, timely specialist referral and patient-safety action.

sections.8. Examiner material: Findings released after the relevant manoeuvre: Alert, conversational, mildly slowed responses; seated cranial nerve examination normal. Normal limb bulk and power; no resting tremor or lead-pipe rigidity. Gait: broad base, short shuffling steps, start hesitation and many small turning steps; needs assistance. No clear cerebellar limb ataxia; plantar responses flexor. Normal-findings variant: If the gait is normal on the day, state this explicitly, ask about variable function and witnessed falls, and do not invent magnetic gait. Proposes focused investigations: MRI brain to assess ventriculomegaly and alternative pathology; quantify gait and cognition; discuss CSF tap testing with specialist team (E; R6). States immediate safety priorities and disposition: Protect the patient from falls; assess cognition and bladder function; do not promise that a tap test or shunt confirms or cures iNPH (E/G; R7). Pass: retest after muscle activation and connect the diagnosis to small-cell lung cancer screening.

sections.1. Title: Charcot neuroarthropathy of the foot — A hot insensate foot needs offloading, not reassurance
sections.2. Header: R5-141 | Station ID: R5-141 | MRCP(UK) PACES Station 3: Neurological examination | Assessed skills A, B, D, E, G | Diabetes foot service | 10 minutes: up to 6 minutes examination plus examiner questions | AMaC educational station, not official PACES mark scheme | Reviewed sources listed in §15 | Related station links: confirm against live register.
sections.3. Candidate brief: Please examine the lower limbs, with particular attention to this patient’s swollen foot. Explain your findings and immediate priorities.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK — An intact, warm, swollen, relatively painless foot in a person with neuropathy may have acute Charcot arthropathy. EXAMINER TRAP — Labelling the foot as simple cellulitis or permitting weight-bearing while awaiting X-rays.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Patient first “May I examine you? Please tell me if any movement hurts.” Consent, exposure, comfort; adapt examination. Define pattern “I will check strength, sensation and reflexes to localise the problem.” Inspect, test power, tone, reflexes and sensation. Interpret without overclaim “I will explain the pattern and what tests could confirm it.” Name positive findings and meaningful negatives. Safety before labels “My next step depends on whether anything needs urgent attention.” Prioritise the case-specific red flag and investigations.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row / skill Observable skill Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Comfort and consent Examines without permission; disregards pain. Obtains consent, adapts exposure and checks comfort. Anticipates task-specific discomfort and preserves dignity. R2 A Targeted examination Skips key neurological domains or laterality. Examines named nerves, strength, reflexes and sensation as relevant. Selects discriminating tests and compares sides efficiently. R3 B Specific signs Misreports the positive neurological pattern. Identifies: One foot is red, markedly warm and swollen; the skin is intact without a visible ulcer. Integrates: Protective sensation is reduced to monofilament testing bilaterally; vibration perception is reduced. R4 D Recognition and differential Fails to recognise a hot swollen neuropathic foot or dismisses it because pain is limited. States: Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy versus infection, fracture, gout and deep-vein thrombosis. Explains why neuropathy with warmth and swelling warrants immediate protection while excluding infection and fracture. R5 E Investigation choice Offers reassurance without adequate assessment. Requests: Arrange foot and ankle radiographs as recommended by
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable — physical examination. Patient should respond only to respectful examination instructions; findings below are examiner-controlled simulated signs.
sections.8. Examiner material: Release these clinical findings only after the relevant component is examined: • One foot is red, markedly warm and swollen; the skin is intact without a visible ulcer. • Protective sensation is reduced to monofilament testing bilaterally; vibration perception is reduced. • Foot pulses are palpable; an early arch-shape change is visible. There is no systemic instability in this scenario. EXAMINER (R4): Where do you localise the abnormalities?MODEL: Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy versus infection, fracture, gout and deep-vein thrombosis. EXAMINER (R3): Which positive sign matters most?MODEL: One foot is red, markedly warm and swollen; the skin is intact without a visible ulcer. EXAMINER (R5): What is your investigation strategy?MODEL: Arrange foot and ankle radiographs as recommended by the specialist pathway; consider MRI if films are normal but Charcot remains suspected. Evaluate for infection and vascular disease as appropriate. EXAMINER (R6): What would you do next?MODEL: Immediately advise non-weight-bearing pending definitive care; refer within one working day to the multidisciplinary foot-care service for triage within one further working day. sections.9. Mark Triggers: • G/R1 — Gains consent and inspects both feet safely without requiring unnecessary walking. • A/R2 — Compares warmth, swelling, erythema, deformity, skin breaks and pulses. • B/R3 — Checks protective sensation and neuropathy while assessing infection signs. • D/R4 — Suspects acute Charcot arthropathy despite little pain or a normal initial radiograph. • E/R5 — Arranges prompt foot-and-ankle imaging and specialist diabetic-foot assessment. • E/R6 — Starts non-weight-bearing offloading pending definitive multidisciplinary care. • G/R1 — Explains urgent protection of the foot without blaming the patient.

Header: Code R5-153 | Station 3: Neurological examination | Skills A, B, D, E, G | 10 minutes total (up to 6 minutes examination) | Station ID: __________ | Related station: R5-150 | Guideline(s): NICE NG127, updated 2 October 2023; Femoral nerve palsy from anticoagulant-induced retroperitoneal haematoma, 2014
sections.3. Candidate brief: Examine this patient’s lower limbs to localise weakness and sensory loss. You have six minutes, followed by examiner questions on likely causes and next steps.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Weak right knee extension and hip flexion, reduced right patellar reflex, numbness over anterior thigh and medial leg; ankle power and reflex preserved. Trap: Do not label this a routine compressive femoral neuropathy or delay acute bleed evaluation for outpatient EMG.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Femoral neuropathy; consider L2–L4 radiculopathy, lumbar plexopathy and iliopsoas/retroperitoneal haematoma. "I will compare the pattern on both sides." Examine hip flexion and quadriceps power carefully against gravity and resistance. Do not label this a routine compressive femoral neuropathy or delay acute bleed evaluation for outpatient EMG. "I will check strength, reflexes and sensation together." Compare knee jerks, including intact ankle jerks, and define anterior-thigh/medial-leg sensory loss. Anticoagulated patient with acute groin/flank pain, falling haemoglobin or haemodynamic instability may have major retroperitoneal haemorrhage. "I must check for urgent red flags." Screen abdomen, back pain and vital-sign concerns; urgently ask about anticoagulation and bleeding symptoms. Urgent physiological assessment, haemoglobin/coagulation and renal function, and appropriate urgent CT abdomen/pelvis if bleeding suspected; involve acute care and relevant procedural specialists. "I will select tests based on progression and risk." Present localisation and an appropriate safe plan. 6. Scoring grid — AMaC practice descriptors (not official RCPE marks) Row / skill Fail Pas

What positive and negative findings support it? Model answer: Weak right knee extension and hip flexion, reduced right patellar reflex, numbness over anterior thigh and medial leg; ankle power and reflex preserved. Q3. Model answer: Urgent physiological assessment, haemoglobin/coagulation and renal function, and appropriate urgent CT abdomen/pelvis if bleeding suspected; involve acute care and relevant procedural specialists. sections.9. Mark Triggers: R1 [G] Introduces self, gains consent and accommodates pain or balance before lower-limb assessment. R2 [A] Assess knee extension, hip flexion, knee reflex and medial-leg/anterior-thigh sensation; record pulse, BP and abdominal/groin symptoms. R3 [A] Femoral nerve dysfunction can reflect iliopsoas/retroperitoneal haematoma, especially with anticoagulation; a stable isolated neuropathy assumption is unsafe. R4 [B] Screen abdomen, back pain and vital-sign concerns; urgently ask about anticoagulation and bleeding symptoms. R5 [D] Femoral neuropathy; consider L2–L4 radiculopathy, lumbar plexopathy and iliopsoas/retroperitoneal haematoma. R6 [E] Urgent physiological assessment, haemoglobin/coagulation and renal function, and appropriate urgent CT abdomen/pelvis if bleeding suspected; involve acute care and relevant procedural specialists. R7 [E/G] Acute flank/groin pain plus weakness, anticoagulant use or instability requires emergency haemorrhage assessment and appropriate imaging/resuscitation.

sections.1. Title: Deltoid weakness after dislocation — recognising axillary nerve palsy
sections.2. Header: Code R5-154 | Station 3: Neurological examination | Skills A, B, D, E, G | 10 minutes total (up to 6 minutes examination) | Station ID: __________ | Related station: R5-150 | Guideline(s): Axillary nerve injury review and algorithm, 2018
sections.3. Candidate brief: Examine the upper limb of this patient following a recent shoulder dislocation. You have six minutes. Explain your localisation and follow-up plan to the examiner.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Reduced deltoid contraction and abduction, mild reduced sensation over lateral upper arm (“regimental badge”); distal hand strength, pulses and sensation normal. Trap: Normal lateral-shoulder sensation does not exclude axillary motor injury; palpate deltoid contraction.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Axillary nerve palsy following dislocation; consider rotator cuff tear, pain-limited effort, upper trunk plexopathy or C5 root lesion. "I will compare the pattern on both sides." Ask permission to expose shoulder; inspect contour and deltoid wasting without forcing movement. Normal lateral-shoulder sensation does not exclude axillary motor injury; palpate deltoid contraction. "I will check strength, reflexes and sensation together." Palpate deltoid contraction and assess active abduction within comfort, comparing both sides. Check and document radial pulse, limb perfusion, distal neurology and new severe pain; do not miss arterial or wider plexus injury. "I must check for urgent red flags." Map lateral-shoulder sensation and document distal nerve function plus radial pulse. Document serial deltoid strength and sensory findings; specialist shoulder/nerve review, with nerve conduction/EMG if deficits persist or severe. "I will select tests based on progression and risk." Present localisation and an appropriate safe plan. 6. sections.9. Mark Triggers: R1 [G] Introduces self, gains consent and accommodates pain or balance before upper-limb assessment. R2 [A] Check deltoid contraction and safe abduction, lateral-shoulder sensation, distal nerves and circulation after shoulder dislocation. sections.3. Candidate brief: A 34-year-old reports occipital headaches on coughing and progressive hand clumsiness. Examine the cranial nerves, coordination and relevant upper-limb sensation. Obtain consent, avoid unnecessary discomfort, and present your examination findings to the examiner.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK — Cough headache, downbeat nystagmus and a syrinx pattern. TRAP — Do not force a diagnosis from one sign or imply that an unperformed investigation is positive. Progressive dysphagia, new weakness, breathing difficulty or rapidly worsening ataxia warrants urgent assessment.

Look for mimics and danger “I will check related functions too.” Test relevant adjacent pathways and red flags. Summarise proportionately “My findings suggest a syndrome; I would confirm its cause.” Give positive/negative signs, localisation, differential and next step.
