sections.preamble: R5-165 — Myotonia congenita
sections.1. Title: Myotonia congenita: examine, localise and make the safe next decision
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · Station 3: Neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10-minute encounter (up to 6 minutes examining, remaining time for examiner questions) · Station ID: R5-165 · Educational draft, 14 October 2026 · Not an official PACES mark scheme.
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 26-year-old reports that their hands sometimes remain clenched after gripping objects, particularly in the cold. Examine the upper limbs and relevant neuromuscular signs. Please obtain consent and adapt to the patient's comfort. Present key findings and your immediate clinical priorities.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK: Demonstrates grip myotonia and warm-up, testing power rather than assuming muscular appearance proves normal function. TRAP: Flag the diagnosis to anaesthetics before surgery; suxamethonium can precipitate severe myotonic contraction and should be avoided.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Localise before naming “I’ll compare both sides and explain the tests.” Check comfort and clinically relevant symmetry. Make signs reproducible “Please tell me if this becomes uncomfortable.” Demonstrates grip myotonia and warm-up, testing power rather than assuming muscular appearance proves normal function. Identify the competing lesion “I also want to check what is preserved.” Test relevant spared functions; do not invent negatives. Turn findings into action “I will explain which signs affect urgency.” Neuromuscular referral, electrodiagnostic myotonic discharges where appropriate and CLCN1 genetic testing. Discuss treatment if functionally troublesome, through a specialist.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Criterion Fail Pass High-performance R1 A/G Consent and welfare Moves or exposes patient without explanation. Introduces, obtains consent, positions comfortably. Checks fatigue or functional limitations; adapts and preserves dignity. R2 A Targeted technique Incomplete or unfocused neurological tests. Performs essential side-by-side examination. Selects the most discriminating manoeuvre for this case. R3 B Positive findings Misses or misstates characteristic signs. Accurately states observed abnormal signs. Explains significance of the specific pattern, without overclaim. R4 B Relevant negatives Assumes features absent without examining. Checks important preserved functions. Uses verified negatives to reject a close mimic. R5 D Diagnosis and localisation Labels a condition without justified localisation. Names leading syndrome and anatomical level. Compares competing diagnosis using a specific sign. R6 E Next decision Vague or inappropriate investigation/referral. Names key confirmatory action or referral. Prioritises sequence and proportionate use of tests. R7 E/G Safety and welfare Ignores major scenario-specific harm. Identifies escalation trigger and safe action. Couns
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable — physical examination. Release only findings elicited by examination; provide no unasked-for diagnosis or extra history.
sections.8. Examiner material: Release on relevant testing: Well-developed limb muscles; delayed finger extension after forceful grip which improves on repetition (warm-up). Percussion myotonia may be present. Power, tendon reflexes and sensation are otherwise preserved. 1. EXAMINER: “What pattern have you demonstrated?” EXPECTED: Well-developed limb muscles; delayed finger extension after forceful grip which improves on repetition (warm-up). Percussion myotonia may be present. Power, tendon reflexes and sensation are otherwise preserved. 2. sections.3. Candidate brief: A 64-year-old taking lithium develops two days of diarrhoea, coarse tremor and increasing confusion. Their partner reports recent ibuprofen use. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: HOOK — Suspected lithium toxicity, potentially chronic or acute-on-chronic; neurological features and renal function may be more informative than a single level. TRAP — EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for severe toxicity with reduced consciousness, seizures or dangerous dysrhythmia irrespective of level; severe renal impairment with high levels is another indication. Do not make dialysis depend on a single arbitrary level.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Is the patient unstable? “I need to check how unwell you are first.” ABCDE, observations, immediate escalation as needed. What changes risk? “I will tell you what we are monitoring closely.” EXTRIP recommends extracorporeal treatment for severe toxicity with reduced consciousness, seizures or dangerous dysrhythmia irrespective of level; severe renal impairment with high levels is another indication. Assesses gait, reflexes, consciousness, arrhythmia risk, volume status and urine output while maintaining safe monitoring. Suspects lithium toxicity clinically; considers dehydration, renal impairment and other causes of confusion. Explains co

sections.9. Mark Triggers: • [R1 C/G] Recognises confusion with coarse tremor on lithium as a potential emergency; checks consciousness, ABCDE and vital signs promptly. • [R2 A/C] Elicits lithium dose and last dose, recent diarrhoea/vomiting, fluid intake, NSAID use, renal disease and other interacting medicines. • [R3 A/B] Requests ECG, bedside glucose, renal function/electrolytes, timed lithium level and repeated neurological observations; arranges serial lithium concentrations. • [R4 D/E] Identifies likely lithium toxicity worsened by dehydration and ibuprofen; recognises that a single lithium concentration may underestimate clinical neurotoxicity. • [R5 E] Stops lithium and NSAIDs immediately, arranges emergency hospital management, provides clinically appropriate IV isotonic fluids with monitoring, and seeks toxicology advice. • [R6 F/G] Explains to patient/partner why urgent treatment and monitoring are required, checks understanding, and avoids blaming the patient for over-the-counter NSAID use. • [R7 E/G] Escalates reduced consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmia for urgent dialysis assessment regardless of concentration; distinguishes recommended from suggested EXTRIP criteria.

Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · R5-214 · Station 2 acute consultation · 10 minutes · Assessed skills: A clinical assessment, B physical signs where appropriate, C communication, D differential diagnosis, E clinical judgement, F patient concerns, G welfare · Station ID: editorial assignment pending · Educational draft dated 14 October 2026 · Not an official PACES mark scheme.
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 29-year-old with longstanding atopic eczema reports a sudden painful blistering facial eruption, fever and lesions near the eyelid. Assess and explain your management. You are the medical registrar in the acute assessment unit (or appropriately designated acute clinician). Explore concerns, assess risk and explain the immediate plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Suspected eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous HSV on eczema); distinguish bacterial impetigo and other viral eruptions without withholding antiviral treatment. Examiner trap: Potential herpetic keratitis and vision loss: do not use topical steroid eye drops without ophthalmological advice, and do not delay antivirals for swab results.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Stability “First I need to check you are safe.” ABCDE and observations. Diagnostic discriminators “I will ask a few focused questions.” Rapid painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions on eczema, sometimes with fever or malaise; assess periocular skin, red eye, pain, light sensitivity and visual disturbance. Immediate decision “I will explain the likely problem and alternatives.” Suspected eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous HSV on eczema); distinguish bacterial impetigo and other viral eruptions without withholding antiviral treatment. Safety “This is the priority for today.” Start systemic aciclovir today; urgent same-day dermatology assessment and same-day ophthalmology if periocular involvement or eye symptoms; consider admission/IV treatment if severe, widespread or unable to take oral therapy.
sections.6. Scoring grid: ID Skill Criterion Fail Pass High-performance R1 G/C Recognition Treats painful monomorphic blisters as routine eczema Recognises suspected eczema herpeticum from rapid painful vesicles, fever and erosions Notes risks of disseminated HSV and ocular involvement R2 A Ocular danger Does not ask about eye symptoms Checks vision, eye pain, redness, photophobia and eyelid lesions Urgently arranges ophthalmology review with periocular involvement R3 A/B Assessment Focuses only on cosmetic rash Assesses temperature, hydration, immune status, lesions and systemic illness Checks for secondary bacterial infection without making it the sole diagnosis R4 D Time-critical treatment Offers topical steroid alone and routine review Starts prompt systemic aciclovir under urgent clinician/specialist assessment Uses IV route if severe/unwell or unable to take oral treatment as clinically indicated R5 E Escalation Defers specialist contact for a week Same-day dermatology and ophthalmology assessment given eyelid involvement Arranges admission if systemically ill or widespread severe disease R6 E Infection prevention Assures patient there is no contagious risk Explains HSV precautions and local infection
sections.7. Role-player brief: Patient is anxious but cooperative. Open with: “I am worried something serious is happening.” Answer history questions using these facts only: Rapid painful monomorphic vesicles or punched-out erosions on eczema, sometimes with fever or malaise; assess periocular skin, red eye, pain, light sensitivity and visual disturbance. Ask “Will I need to stay in hospital?” and accept calm, specific explanations. No unscripted extra examination findings.
sections.8. Examiner material: Q1. What is the urgent differential?Model: Eczema herpeticum is high priority; impetigo and other blistering conditions remain differential diagnoses. Q2. Why ask about visual symptoms?Model: Periocular disease risks herpetic eye involvement and sight-threatening complications. Q3. What treatment cannot wait?Model: Prompt systemic aciclovir and urgent specialist management; do not wait for confirmatory virology. Q4. Is topical corticosteroid alone sufficient?Model: No; topical steroid alone misses the potentially serious HSV infection. Q5. Who should review this patient?Model: Same-day dermatology and ophthalmology, with admission assessment for systemic illness.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 58-year-old has one swollen painful calf after a recent admission. They ask if it is an infection or blood clot. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Suspected deep vein thrombosis; cellulitis is an alternative. The physical examination alone cannot confirm or exclude DVT.Trap: A swollen red calf must not be labelled cellulitis without VTE assessment.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Immediate harm “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety. Diagnostic discriminator “I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.” Ask about onset, immobility, cancer, prior VTE, pulmonary embolism symptoms, skin injury and systemic infection. Inspect swelling, erythema and skin breaches; compare calf circumference and examine pulses. Working diagnosis “There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.” Suspected deep vein thrombosis; cellulitis is an alternative. The physical examination alone cannot confirm or exclude DVT. Explain next steps “I’ll explain what happens next and why.” Use the 2-level DVT Wells score. If likely, arrange proximal ultrasound within 4 hours if possible; if unavailable, follow NICE's D-dimer, interim anticoagulation and scan-within-24-hours pathway after bleeding-risk review.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 32-year-old develops a painful swollen knee and heel pain two weeks after gastroenteritis. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Reactive arthritis may follow enteric or genitourinary infection; a septic joint remains the immediate dangerous alternative.Trap: A history of infection does not safely rule out current septic arthritis.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Immediate harm “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety. Diagnostic discriminator “I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.” Clarify number and pattern of involved joints, fever, inability to bear weight, diarrhoeal resolution, conjunctival symptoms, urethritis, sexual history and immunosuppression. Examine for effusion, enthesitis, dactylitis and eye inflammation. Working diagnosis “There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.” Reactive arthritis may follow enteric or genitourinary infection; a septic joint remains the immediate dangerous alternative. Explain next steps “I’ll explain what happens next and why.” If a hot, severely painful joint or systemic illness is present, seek urgent hospital assessment and joint aspiration for infection. Otherwise consider inflammatory tests, relevant stool/STI testing, NSAID suitability, rheumatology follow-up and physiotherapy.

sections.1. Title: Back pain and fever in a person who injects drugs — urgent recognition and next decision
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-217 | Station 2 consultation | Skills C, E, F, G (and clinical assessment/judgement as applicable) | 10 minutes | Station ID: to assign | Working draft 14 October 2026 | AMaC educational criteria, not official PACES marks
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 37-year-old with a history of injecting drugs presents with worsening back pain, fever and difficulty walking. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Spinal epidural abscess with possible cord or cauda equina compression; vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and metastatic compression are alternatives.Trap: No stigma: ask about substance use sensitively and offer harm-reduction support.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Immediate harm “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety. Diagnostic discriminator “I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.” Explore onset, constitutional symptoms, current injecting, neurological weakness, saddle sensation, bladder/bowel change, spinal procedures and endocarditis symptoms. Examine neurological level, gait if safe, spine tenderness and vital signs. Working diagnosis “There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.” Spinal epidural abscess with possible cord or cauda equina compression; vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis and metastatic compression are alternatives. Explain next steps “I’ll explain what happens next and why.” Immediate admission; blood cultures promptly, inflammatory markers, sepsis assessment and urgent MRI of the spine with contrast when appropriate. Liaise urgently with spinal surgery, infectious diseases and microbiology; give empiric antibiotics promptly when septic or neurologically impaired, after cultures if feasible without delay.
sections.6. sections.7. Role-player brief: Patient worries about long-term consequences and asks ‘What is this? Do I need to go to hospital?’ Answer naturally; provide the scenario details when elicited. If the candidate minimises severe symptoms, ask whether going home is safe.
sections.8. Examiner material: Q1: What is the dangerous diagnosis?Expected answer: Spinal epidural abscess or vertebral infection with possible cord/cauda equina compromise. Q2: What findings change urgency?Expected answer: New leg weakness, sensory loss, retention or incontinence, hypotension and altered consciousness. Q3: What imaging?Expected answer: Urgent MRI of affected spine with contrast if suitable, directed by radiology/spine service. Q4: Do blood cultures delay antibiotics?Expected answer: No. In high-risk sepsis start IV antibiotics promptly, following local pathway. Q5: What specialist input?Expected answer: Urgent spinal surgery/neurosurgery and microbiology/infection advice.

sections.1. Title: Headache, vomiting and a red eye — urgent recognition and next decision
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-218 | Station 2 consultation | Skills C, E, F, G (and clinical assessment/judgement as applicable) | 10 minutes | Station ID: to assign | Working draft 14 October 2026 | AMaC educational criteria, not official PACES marks
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 65-year-old reports severe unilateral eye pain, blurred vision and vomiting over several hours. Take a focused history, assess urgency and explain your initial plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms.Trap: Headache with vomiting may be ocular rather than purely neurological.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Immediate harm “First I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE when indicated; observations and immediate safety. Diagnostic discriminator “I’ll ask a few questions to narrow down the cause.” Ask about onset, halos, previous attacks, recent pupil-dilating medicines, cataract surgery and other visual symptoms. Check visual acuity, pupil size/reactivity, corneal clarity, conjunctival injection and overall condition; avoid pressing on the painful globe. Working diagnosis “There is a serious possibility that we should check promptly.” Suspected acute angle-closure glaucoma: red painful eye, reduced vision, hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil; migraine or uveitis can resemble some symptoms. Explain next steps “I’ll explain what happens next and why.” Immediate emergency ophthalmology assessment, measure intraocular pressure where competent, initiate pressure-lowering therapy under specialist/local protocol and prepare for definitive laser peripheral iridotomy when indicated.
sections.6. sections.7. Role-player brief: Patient worries about long-term consequences and asks ‘What is this? Do I need to go to hospital?’ Answer naturally; provide the scenario details when elicited. If the candidate minimises severe symptoms, ask whether going home is safe.
sections.8. Examiner material: Q1: Why immediate referral?Expected answer: Acute angle closure can cause rapid irreversible sight loss. Q2: Which symptom cluster?Expected answer: Severe eye pain/redness, blurred vision/halos, headache and nausea or vomiting. Q3: Which examination?Expected answer: Visual acuity, pupil and anterior eye assessment; tonometry if skilled and available. Q4: Do you wait for formal tonometry?Expected answer: No, refer urgently on clinical suspicion. Q5: Who directs pressure lowering?Expected answer: The emergency ophthalmology service using its local pathway.

sections.1. Title: Fever in a kidney transplant recipient — focused assessment and safe immediate decisions
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 • R5-220 • Station 2 acute consultation • Skills C, E, F, G plus relevant assessment • 10 minutes • Station ID: editor to assign • 14 October 2026 • Educational assessment, not official PACES marking
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 44-year-old kidney-transplant recipient taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisolone develops fever and malaise. Take a focused history, explain your differential and initiate a safe management plan.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Infection in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient, including bacterial urinary infection and CMV disease; consider rejection if graft dysfunction, but fever alone does not diagnose rejection.Trap: Hypotension, rigors, organ dysfunction or falling urine output requires immediate admission and senior review. Do not independently stop baseline immunosuppression or prescribe a macrolide without checking tacrolimus interactions.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Assess risk “First I want to check how unwell you are.” ABCDE and vital signs as indicated. Look for the discriminator “May I ask about these symptoms and exposures?” Ask when transplanted, immunosuppression and adherence, urinary and respiratory symptoms, graft pain, sick contacts and recent antimicrobials; check sepsis observations and graft tenderness. Explain concern “There are several causes, including one requiring prompt treatment.” Infection in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient, including bacterial urinary infection and CMV disease; consider rejection if graft dysfunction, but fever alone does not diagnose rejection. Decide and act “I will arrange urgent tests and care.” Obtain cultures, FBC, CRP, kidney function, urinalysis/culture, tacrolimus trough and CMV PCR as clinically appropriate; involve transplant team immediately; follow sepsis guidance and assess drug interactions.

sections.1. Title: Headaches in several family members in winter — focused assessment, critical decision and communication
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | R5-227 | Station 2: Acute consultation | Skills C, E, F, G; appropriate clinical assessment | 10 minutes | Station ID: editor to assign | Draft dated 14 October 2026 | AMaC educational mark grid, not official MRCP(UK) marks.
sections.3. Candidate brief: Two adults and a child in one household have morning headaches, nausea and dizziness that improve when they leave home. Take a focused history and explain your immediate plan. A nurse can provide observations or blood results on request.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Suspected carbon monoxide exposure. Trap: Multiple co-located headaches suggest an environmental toxin: ordinary pulse oximetry cannot exclude carbon monoxide.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Stabilise “Before anything else, I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE and urgent observations. Elicit discriminator “I have a few specific questions to help work out the cause.” Ask about gas boilers, heaters, fires, other affected people or pets and temporal relation to being indoors. Assess airway, neurological status, pregnancy and chest pain; do not rely on a normal pulse oximeter. Name uncertainty “I am concerned about a potentially serious condition.” Suspected carbon monoxide exposure Prioritise “I will explain the tests and what happens next.” Immediately move everyone into fresh air; contact emergency services, provide high-concentration oxygen and urgent assessment. Send carboxyhaemoglobin via blood co-oximetry without delaying oxygen; consider ECG and troponin, and specialist advice for severe poisoning or pregnancy.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 C/G Exposure recognition Diagnoses migraine without asking about others at home Suspects CO when household members have headaches improving outdoors Asks about heating, fires, generators, gas appliances and pets affected R2 C/E Immediate safety Advises returning to home to open windows Directs everyone to leave building immediately and not re-enter until declared safe Calls emergency services/gas emergency service and arranges safe alternative accommodation R3 E Urgent clinical assessment Uses routine GP appointment in confused or breathless patient Checks symptoms, consciousness, chest pain, pregnancy and organ risk; arranges ED assessment Escalates urgently for collapse, confusion, chest pain or breathlessness R4 E Testing Excludes CO on normal fingertip pulse oximetry Requests blood COHb measurement with appropriate co-oximetry and considers ECG if relevant Explains that elapsed time and oxygen treatment reduce measured COHb R5 E/G Treatment States opening a window cures established poisoning Initiates high-concentration oxygen while urgent hospital assessment proceeds Seeks toxicology/hyperbaric advice in severe illness or pregnancy
sections.7. Role-player brief: You are frightened and ask “Can I go home?” Give the opening complaint spontaneously; answer focused questions consistently with examiner findings. Ask one question about long-term consequences or family safety as appropriate.
sections.8. Examiner material: Q1: What finding is diagnostic clue?Expected answer: Several cohabitants symptomatic in winter, especially with improvement outside. Q2: What immediate instruction?Expected answer: Leave exposure site, call emergency help, do not re-enter until safe. Q3: Will pulse oximetry exclude CO toxicity?Expected answer: No, standard SpO2 readings may be normal despite significant CO poisoning. sections.3. Candidate brief: A malnourished 55-year-old with prolonged heavy alcohol use becomes confused, unsteady and appears to have abnormal eye movements. Take a focused history and explain your immediate plan. A nurse can provide observations or blood results on request.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. Trap: A confused malnourished patient needs presumptive treatment without waiting for an unreliable diagnostic test.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Stabilise “Before anything else, I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.” ABCDE and urgent observations. Elicit discriminator “I have a few specific questions to help work out the cause.” Assess confusion, nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia, gait and truncal ataxia, malnutrition, blood glucose, falls, infection and risk of alcohol withdrawal. The complete classic triad is often absent. Name uncertainty “I am concerned about a potentially serious condition.” Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy Prioritise “I will explain the tests and what happens next.” Admit and administer parenteral thiamine promptly at the treatment dose under local guidance; provide magnesium and nutritional support as needed. If hypoglycaemic, give glucose immediately alongside thiamine—do not withhold life-saving glucose. Monitor and treat withdrawal separately.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 C/G Recognition Attributes confusion and ataxia only to intoxication Suspects Wernicke encephalopathy in malnutrition with confusion, gait and eye signs Understands full classic triad is not required R2 C/E Immediate stabilisation Discharges confused patient Checks ABCDE, glucose, consciousness, falls and acute medical causes Assesses infection, head injury and metabolic disorders in parallel R3 E Thiamine therapy Gives oral vitamin only for likely Wernicke disease Arranges immediate high-dose parenteral thiamine per local/BNF protocol Continues appropriate parenteral course then oral treatment as recommended R4 E Glucose and nutrition Withholds emergency glucose to await vitamins Treats hypoglycaemia immediately while giving thiamine urgently; does not delay lifesaving glucose Addresses magnesium, electrolytes, refeeding risks and nutrition support R5 E/G Investigation Waits for MRI or thiamine level before treatment Orders glucose, U&E, Mg, LFT, FBC and relevant tests without delay Considers imaging if alternative intracranial diagnosis suspected R6 F/G Disposition Sends patient home alone Admits for acute medical care and supervised
sections.7. Role-player brief: You are frightened and ask “Can I go home?” Give the opening complaint spontaneously; answer focused questions consistently with examiner findings. Ask one question about long-term consequences or family safety as appropriate.
sections.8. Examiner material: Q1. Must all three classic features be present?Model: No. A low threshold for presumptive diagnosis is needed in an at-risk malnourished patient. Q2. What is the immediate treatment?Model: Urgent parenteral thiamine, not oral-only treatment, under an established clinical protocol. Q3. Should hypoglycaemia treatment wait for thiamine?Model: No. Treat dangerous hypoglycaemia promptly while giving thiamine as soon as possible. Q4. Why consider magnesium?Model: Deficiency may undermine response and broader electrolyte or nutritional problems must be addressed. Q5. What is a safe disposition?Model: Urgent hospital admission for clinical assessment, monitoring and treatment.
sections.9. sections.3. Candidate brief: A 34-year-old has recurrent spiking fevers, an evanescent pink rash during fevers and painful wrists and knees. Take a focused history, determine urgency and explain your plan to the patient.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Adult-onset Still disease is possible, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion: infection, haematological malignancy and other autoinflammatory conditions require evaluation. Elevated ferritin is supportive but not diagnostic. Trap: Do not prescribe immunosuppression before appropriately assessing infection and malignancy, especially in an acutely unwell patient.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Immediate threat “First, I want to check how unwell you are.” Assess stability and the specific emergency signs. Discriminator “I’ll ask questions that help us distinguish the causes.” Ask duration of fever, sore throat, rash timing, joint swelling, weight loss, infection exposures, travel and lymphadenopathy; assess observations, joints, rash and hepatosplenomegaly. Next action “I will arrange tests and support appropriate to the risk.” Arrange urgent physician/rheumatology assessment, FBC with differential, inflammatory markers, ferritin, liver tests and targeted infection/haematology investigations. Specialist treatment may involve IL-1/IL-6 inhibition with short-course glucocorticoids. Anticipatory safety “I will explain when we must act urgently.” New cytopenias, coagulopathy, rapidly rising ferritin, liver dysfunction, neurological change or shock raise concern for macrophage activation syndrome and require emergency escalation.

stations.title: Twisting neck and eyes after metoclopramide — acute decision and patient-centred explanation

sections.1. Title: Twisting neck and eyes after metoclopramide — acute decision and patient-centred explanation
sections.2. Header: AMaC · MRCP PACES23 · R5-243 · Station 2 acute consultation · 10 minutes · Skills C, E, F, G (A/B/D if applicable to scenario) · Station ID: to assign · Reviewed references: 14 October 2026 · AMaC educational rubric, not an official PACES mark scheme.
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 19-year-old has painful neck twisting and involuntary upward deviation of the eyes shortly after taking metoclopramide for nausea. Assess the event and respond. Take a focused history and explain your diagnosis, investigation priorities, immediate management and safety-net.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook — Acute drug-induced dystonia with oculogyric crisis; distinguish from seizure, tetany, tetanus, structural neurological disease and airway-threatening laryngeal dystonia.Examiner trap — Stridor, dysphonia, swallowing difficulty or breathing compromise is an airway emergency. Do not diagnose epilepsy solely on the dramatic posture, nor assume all such symptoms are psychological. MHRA limits metoclopramide to short-term use (up to 5 days), with more restricted paediatric indications.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Is the patient stable? “First, I need to check for immediate danger.” ABCDE and vital signs appropriate to the encounter. Which clues matter? “Can I ask about the symptoms and key risks?” Ask the exact drug, dose and timing, other dopamine-blocking medicines, previous reactions, seizure markers, consciousness, neck pain, swallowing, stridor and dyspnoea. Observe ocular deviation, involuntary contraction and stable awareness; check airway. What working problem? “I am concerned about an illness that needs assessment.” Acute drug-induced dystonia with oculogyric crisis; distinguish from seizure, tetany, tetanus, structural neurological disease and airway-threatening laryngeal dystonia. What now? “I will explain what the tests and treatment are for.” Stop metoclopramide, assess ABCDE and treat promptly with an available injectable antimuscarinic per local emergency pathway (e.g. benzatropine where stocked) with monitoring; discuss prevention, document adverse reaction and select a safer antiemetic. UK injectable procyclidine was discontinued in 2026; verify stock and protocol.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 46-year-old recovering from pancreatitis reports sudden itchy yellow-red bumps over the buttocks and elbows. Diabetes control has deteriorated. Take a focused history, explain your impression and agree a safe plan.

Context and impact “How has this affected your life, sleep or work?” Ask about treatment history, work, mood and patient priorities. Next steps “There are useful treatments; some depend on tests or specialist assessment.” Arrange urgent fasting/non-fasting lipid profile as locally appropriate, triglycerides, glucose/HbA1c, renal, liver and thyroid tests and review medications. Urgent hospital review if current severe abdominal pain or systemic illness. sections.1. Title: Family history of medullary thyroid cancer

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 28-year-old says their parent was diagnosed with medullary thyroid cancer and asks whether they need a blood test or preventive surgery. Take a focused history, discuss the clinical implications and negotiate a safe plan.
sections.4. The hook and examiner trap: Hook: Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma may indicate MEN2 due to a pathogenic germline RET variant. Cascade testing is variant-directed with specialist counselling.Trap: Screen for a phaeochromocytoma before thyroid surgery in established MEN2, and treat it first if present; unrecognised catecholamine secretion can cause perioperative catastrophe.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Patient perspective “What is most worrying you?” Elicit concern and desired outcome. sections.3. Candidate brief: You are reviewing a patient with unprovoked dvt: what next. Take a focused history, explain your differential and agree an investigation, treatment and safety-netting plan.
sections.4. The Hook and Examiner Trap: Hook: Unprovoked venous thrombosis: treatment duration, cancer and thrombophilia assessment. After an unprovoked DVT, review at three months whether to continue anticoagulation beyond the minimum three months. NICE NG158 advises against routine thrombophilia testing while continuing anticoagulation, and against indiscriminate occult-cancer investigations absent symptoms or signs.Trap: Do not order blanket CT scans, tumour markers or routine thrombophilia panels in all cases. New chest pain, dyspnoea or syncope warrants urgent pulmonary embolism evaluation.

Diagnostic pattern “Can we explore how this started?” Clarify provoking factors, confirmed proximal/distal DVT, prior events, anticoagulant adherence, bleeding risk, family history, cancer red flags, symptoms of pulmonary embolism and patient values. Reasoning “There are several possible explanations.” After an unprovoked DVT, review at three months whether to continue anticoagulation beyond the minimum three months. NICE NG158 advises against routine thrombophilia testing while continuing anticoagulation, and against indiscriminate occult-cancer investigations absent symptoms or signs. Next steps “I will explain what we should do now.” Check history, baseline bloods and focused examination; arrange investigations only for relevant symptoms or signs, plus routine age-appropriate screening. Discuss recurrence versus bleeding risk, medication safety and long-term anticoagulation choice. sections.3. Candidate brief: A 39-year-old has passed a third kidney stone in four years and asks how to stop future attacks. Please assess the concern and discuss a safe management plan with the patient.
sections.4. The Hook and Examiner Trap: Hook: Recurrent nephrolithiasis warrants stone composition, renal assessment and investigation for metabolic risks; hypercalcaemia raises concern about hyperparathyroidism.Trap: Fever with obstruction, anuria, solitary kidney or deteriorating renal function warrants emergency urological assessment; do not simply advise more water during an infected obstructed system.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Listen “How is this affecting your life?” Ask worries, function and desired outcome. Discriminate “I need to ask some focused questions.” Ask episodes and stone composition, infection or obstruction, medications/supplements, family history, bowel disease, fluids, salt intake, occupation and impact on life. sections.preamble: R5-314 | Long-standing reflux and Barrett’s oesophagus
sections.1. Title: Long-standing reflux and Barrett’s oesophagus
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | Station 5 consultation | 10 minutes | 14 October 2026 | Provisional | Core skills communication, clinical judgement and patient safety; AMaC educational grid, not official PACES criteria
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 57-year-old with long-term reflux has biopsy-confirmed nondysplastic Barrett’s oesophagus and asks whether it will become cancer and how often scopes are needed. Please assess the concern and discuss a safe management plan with the patient.
sections.4. The Hook and Examiner Trap: Hook: Barrett’s metaplasia raises oesophageal cancer risk but most people do not progress. Surveillance frequency depends on length, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, fitness and preferences.Trap: Progressive dysphagia, food impaction, weight loss or GI bleeding requires urgent assessment; do not wait for scheduled surveillance. Explain that surveillance does not eliminate cancer risk.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Listen “How is this affecting your life?” Ask worries, function and desired outcome. Discriminate “I need to ask some focused questions.” Ask symptom control and adherence, dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, smoking, family history and previous endoscopy findings: Prague length, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia. Reason “I can explain the likely cause and what else matters.” Barrett’s metaplasia raises oesophageal cancer risk but most people do not progress. Surveillance frequency depends on length, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, fitness and preferences. Plan “Let us make a practical plan together.” Confirm histology and segment length; optimise symptom-directed PPI and discuss weight and smoking. NICE NG231 offers surveillance every 2–3 years for segments ≥3 cm and every 3–5 years for segments <3 cm with intestinal metaplasia; no surveillance for confirmed short segment without intestinal metaplasia after two endoscopies. Any dysplasia needs expert histological review and specialist endoscopic therapy planning.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 24-year-old describes repeated self-limiting episodes of high fever and severe abdominal pain since childhood and asks why repeated infection tests are negative. Please assess the concern and discuss a safe management plan with the patient.
sections.4. The Hook and Examiner Trap: Hook: Familial Mediterranean fever is an autoinflammatory clinical diagnosis supported by typical recurrent attacks, inflammatory markers and sometimes MEFV genetic variants; genetic testing cannot always confirm or exclude it.Trap: Severe persistent abdominal pain still requires exclusion of surgical causes, sepsis or peritonitis; proteinuria may signal AA amyloidosis needing urgent renal assessment. Do not assume all future fever is FMF.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Listen “How is this affecting your life?” Ask worries, function and desired outcome. Discriminate “I need to ask some focused questions.” Ask duration and periodicity of attacks, chest pain/pleuritis, swollen monoarthritis, erysipelas-like rash, ancestry, family history, interval wellness, prior appendectomy and proteinuria/oedema. Reason “I can explain the likely cause and what else matters.” Familial Mediterranean fever is an autoinflammatory clinical diagnosis supported by typical recurrent attacks, inflammatory markers and sometimes MEFV genetic variants; genetic testing cannot always confirm or exclude it. Plan “Let us make a practical plan together.” Arrange rheumatology/autoinflammatory specialist referral; check CRP/ESR during and between attacks, renal function and urinary protein/albumin for AA amyloidosis risk. Discuss regular colchicine to suppress attacks and prevent amyloidosis, with adherence, interactions and monitoring. Consider IL-1 pathway treatment under specialists if appropriately treated disease remains uncontrolled.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 31-year-old describes episodic non-itchy facial swelling and severe unexplained abdominal pain; antihistamines have not helped. Please assess the concern and discuss a safe management plan with the patient.

Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency and ACE-inhibitor angioedema are differentials.Trap: Tongue, laryngeal or throat swelling is a medical emergency: airway team and immediate HAE-specific on-demand treatment such as C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant under protocol. sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Hook: the current clinical decision must support the patient’s circumstances. Trap: Do not abruptly stop a working antipsychotic. Symptoms of marked hyperglycaemia or ketoacidosis require prompt assessment. NICE monitors weight weekly first six weeks, then at 12 weeks, 1 year and annually; HbA1c/lipids at 12 weeks, year one and annually.

Explain choices “There are options that we can plan safely.” Assess weight, BMI, waist, BP, HbA1c, lipids and physical health. Offer practical diet/activity and diabetes prevention or treatment; arrange joint psychiatry-primary care review of antipsychotic options, possible metformin and monitoring with shared decisions. sections.preamble: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | R5-330

sections.2. Header: Round 5 | R5-330 | Station 5 Consultation | 10 minutes | Draft 14 October 2026 | Not an official PACES mark scheme | AMEND — not approved
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 27-year-old with persistent microscopic haematuria and progressive hearing loss asks whether the two problems are linked. His uncle developed kidney failure in his forties. Explain the issues, respond to concerns and agree safe next steps.
sections.4. The hook and examiner trap: Hook: Alport spectrum disease: collagen IV-related inherited kidney disease with variable hearing and ocular features.Trap: Progressive proteinuria, impaired eGFR, hypertension or sudden hearing change requires prompt specialist assessment.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Start with the person “Before I explain, what matters most to you?” Check permission, emotional concerns and preferred people in the room. Clarify the decision “Can I ask what you understand so far?” Onset and pattern of deafness; visible versus microscopic haematuria; urine protein, hypertension, kidney function; family kidney failure, hearing loss and inheritance; eye symptoms and reproductive plans. Safety and rights “There is one important point we must handle carefully.” Progressive proteinuria, impaired eGFR, hypertension or sudden hearing change requires prompt specialist assessment. Practical next step “Here is what I suggest, and why.” Check BP, urine ACR, urinalysis and renal profile. Arrange nephrology, audiology and appropriate ophthalmic assessment; discuss COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5 panel with genetic counselling, cascade testing and renoprotective ACE inhibition according to risk and specialist guidance.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 73-year-old attends a memory clinic with his wife. Cognitive assessment supports Alzheimer disease. Before the consultation, his wife asks you to tell her first and not tell him. Explain the issues, respond to concerns and agree safe next steps.
sections.4. The hook and examiner trap: Hook: Patient autonomy, consent to share information, sensitive disclosure, practical aftercare.Trap: Do not disclose the diagnosis to the spouse against the patient’s wishes or treat an Alzheimer diagnosis as proof of incapacity.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Start with the person “Before I explain, what matters most to you?” Check permission, emotional concerns and preferred people in the room. Clarify the decision “Can I ask what you understand so far?” Ask the patient whom he wishes involved, what he understands, whether he wants results today and what worries him most. Capacity is assumed unless evidence to the contrary; speak directly to him. Safety and rights “There is one important point we must handle carefully.” Do not disclose the diagnosis to the spouse against the patient’s wishes or treat an Alzheimer diagnosis as proof of incapacity. Practical next step “Here is what I suggest, and why.” Deliver the diagnosis in plain language with pauses; explain uncertainty and available treatment/support, driving and DVLA/insurer notifications where relevant, memory-service contact, LPA and future planning; document consent for sharing and arrange follow-up.

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCP PACES23 | R5-334
sections.1. Title: Switching off ICD shocks near end of life
sections.2. Header: Round 5 | R5-334 | Station 4 Communication and ethics | 10 minutes | Draft 14 October 2026 | Not an official PACES mark scheme | AMEND — not approved
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 68-year-old in a hospice has end-stage heart failure and an implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD). The device has delivered two painful shocks this week. Discuss turning off shock therapy with him. Explain the issues, respond to concerns and agree safe next steps.
sections.4. The hook and examiner trap: Hook: Prevent distressing shocks at end of life while preserving treatments the patient still values; shock deactivation is not necessarily pacemaker deactivation.Trap: Do not promise that deactivation stops the heart or that a pacing function will necessarily stop. Do not attempt untrained device reprogramming.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Start with the person “Before I explain, what matters most to you?” Check permission, emotional concerns and preferred people in the room. Clarify the decision “Can I ask what you understand so far?” Ask what the patient understands about the device, recent shocks, fears, desired goals, understanding of prognosis, possible pacing dependence and preference for family participation. Safety and rights “There is one important point we must handle carefully.” Do not promise that deactivation stops the heart or that a pacing function will necessarily stop. Do not attempt untrained device reprogramming. Practical next step “Here is what I suggest, and why.” Explain ICD shock therapy may treat dangerous fast rhythms but cause painful shocks; deactivating shocks can allow natural progression of illness and ordinarily leaves bradycardia pacing intact. Obtain informed preference, check capacity, involve electrophysiology/device team and palliative team, arrange reprogramming, document and plan for urgent recurrent shocks.

sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · Station 4 communication/ethics · 10 minutes · Code R5-335 · 14 October 2026 · Educational scheme (not official MRCP scoring)
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 67-year-old with advanced cancer asks, “Can you help me die? I cannot bear this any longer.” Their partner is outside. Conduct a patient-centred discussion, explain the relevant choices and agree a safe next step.
sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Hook: the candidate must integrate empathy, autonomy and clinical safety. Trap: Do not promise an assisted death, threaten abandonment, mislabel a capacity-valid refusal as assisted dying, or leave an acutely suicidal patient unsupported.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Explore meaning “I am sorry things feel unbearable. Can you tell me what has been hardest and what you are hoping for?” Clarify symptom burden, depression, coercion, immediate self-harm risk and whether they seek information, symptom relief or an act to end life. Ask permission before involving family. Assess urgent risk “Before deciding what happens next, I want to be sure you are safe.” Check pain, breathlessness, isolation and access to palliative care; assess immediate safety and capacity for any actual care decision. Explain choices “Here are the options and what each would mean.” Explain without judgement that assistance to end life is not currently lawful in England; the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill remains a proposal, not enacted law. Distinguish this from lawful symptom relief, refusing treatment and appropriate palliative sedation. Offer same-day palliative review and mental-health input where indicated.

sections.1. Title: Request for predictive Huntington’s testing
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 · Round 5 · Station 4 communication/ethics · 10 minutes · Code R5-337 · 14 October 2026 · Educational scheme (not official MRCP scoring)
sections.3. Candidate brief: A healthy 29-year-old whose mother has Huntington’s disease asks for genetic testing immediately before getting married. Conduct a patient-centred discussion, explain the relevant choices and agree a safe next step.
sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Hook: the candidate must integrate empathy, autonomy and clinical safety. Trap: Do not pressure testing before marriage, disclose results to relatives without lawful basis or confuse predictive testing with a definitive symptom prognosis.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Explore meaning “What would knowing or not knowing mean for your future and your family?” Explore family diagnosis and age of onset, the patient’s understanding of autosomal dominant inheritance, motivations, mood, social support, reproductive plans and potential pressure. Assess urgent risk “Before deciding what happens next, I want to be sure you are safe.” Explain that with an affected parent the prior probability is approximately 50%, but test results have profound implications; the person has a right not to know and usually engages in specialist pre-test genetic counselling. Explain choices “Here are the options and what each would mean.” Arrange clinical genetics referral for a voluntary predictive-testing protocol, including psychological support, confidentiality, implications for relatives and carefully framed insurance considerations. Do not order a stand-alone genetic test in a routine consultation.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 43-year-old admitted with pneumonia and schizophrenia refuses intravenous antibiotics, saying “The medicine is poisoned.” They are hypoxic but awake and conversing. Conduct a patient-centred discussion, explain the relevant choices and agree a safe next step.
sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Hook: the candidate must integrate empathy, autonomy and clinical safety. Trap: Do not equate psychosis with incapacity, treat a capable adult against refusal, or use mental-health detention as a shortcut for physical-treatment consent.

Examine whether delusional beliefs prevent using/weighing information, and support communication. Assess urgent risk “Before deciding what happens next, I want to be sure you are safe.” Offer explanation and choices, including an oral or different IV antibiotic if clinically suitable; involve a senior clinician and liaison psychiatry. Document the capacity assessment for this specific decision at this time. Explain choices “Here are the options and what each would mean.” If patient retains capacity, respect refusal despite disagreement. If they lack capacity and treatment is necessary, make a proportionate, least-restrictive MCA best-interests decision with appropriate consultation and safeguards. The MHA does not by itself provide authority to treat unrelated pneumonia without consent.

sections.3. Candidate brief: An 81-year-old man is admitted with dehydration, poor hygiene and pressure damage. His son provides most care and says, 'He refuses everything.' Speak to the patient. Conduct a patient-centred conversation, establish the relevant ethical or clinical issues and agree safe next steps.
sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Possible neglect in an adult with care and support needs; assess immediate harm, wishes, capacity and whether the Care Act section 42 threshold may be met. TRAP: Do not assume capacity is absent because the patient is frail, or label the son abusive without investigating. Do not send the patient back into imminent danger.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Rapport Can we talk about what matters most to you? Are you comfortable talking alone? Do you feel safe at home? Explore I want to understand your situation before recommending anything. Who helps with food, washing, medicines and mobility? Clarify What have you understood and what worries you? Has anyone prevented you from obtaining help or money? Plan I will explain your options and check you are comfortable with the next step. Escalate to the hospital safeguarding lead and local authority for consideration of a section 42 enquiry. Invite adult's preferences and consider advocacy, care assessment, and safe discharge; share without consent only with a justified legal/public-interest basis.

sections.7. Role-player brief: Older patient: “My son takes my pension and sometimes leaves me without food. Please do not get him into trouble.” If asked privately, explain you are afraid of losing your home.

sections.1. Title: Sibling feels pressured to be a kidney donor

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 36-year-old is being considered to donate a kidney to a sibling. Alone in clinic they say, 'Everyone expects me to do it. I can't say no.' Conduct a patient-centred conversation, establish the relevant ethical or clinical issues and agree safe next steps.
sections.4. Hook and examiner trap: Voluntary informed consent is essential. Explore coercion confidentially and separate donor welfare from family expectations. TRAP: Do not pressure the donor or disclose their reasons to the recipient without permission. No living donor procedure may proceed without valid voluntary consent and regulatory approval.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Rapport Can we talk about what matters most to you? When did you first feel pressured? Explore I want to understand your situation before recommending anything. Have there been threats, money offers or consequences if you say no? Clarify What have you understood and what worries you? What do you understand about donation risks and recovery? Plan I will explain your options and check you are comfortable with the next step. Pause donor work-up; inform the living donor coordinator privately, offer separate counselling and explain HTA independent assessor assessment. Respect confidentiality; work with the transplant team on a neutral explanation of withdrawal without disclosing the donor's private concerns.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Domain Fail Pass High-performance R1 C Respect Discusses donor doubts in front of recipient Invites donor to speak privately without recipient or family Explicitly confirms donor can stop assessment at any point R2 C Open exploration Fails to ask whether decision is freely made Asks about pressure, threats, incentives and voluntary wish Checks how donor expects family to react to refusal R3 E Case-specific facts States donor must continue once tests started Explains independent donor assessment and confidentiality Offers independent advocate/donor coordinator R4 E Interpretation Persuades donor to proceed for recipient benefit Offers time to decide with no coercion Provides acceptable opt-out without revealing private reasons R5 F Collaborative plan Shares donor hesitation with recipient without permission Pauses donor work-up and escalates coercion concerns Arranges independent safeguarding and transplant-team review R6 G Safety, law and professionalism Creates a record accessible to coercive family without safeguards Documents voluntariness concerns and next steps privately Checks safe follow-up contact details
sections.7. Role-player brief: Potential donor: “My family says I owe my brother a kidney. I am unsure.” If asked confidentially, explain that parents threaten to withdraw support.
sections.8. Examiner material: Question 1. How can you check that organ donation is voluntary?Expected answer 1. Establish whether the potential donor is making a free decision without family coercion.Question 2. What independent support should be offered?Expected answer 2. Offer a private conversation, independent donor assessment and discussion of consequences.Question 3. Can a potential living donor withdraw?Expected answer 3. Explain that donation is voluntary and the donor may withdraw at any stage.Question 4. How should confidentiality be handled?Expected answer 4. Protect confidentiality and arrange transplant-team/independent assessor follow-up without giving misleading assurances.Question 5. How would you manage pressure from the recipient?Expected answer 5. Curveball: The recipient insists on attending; request separate assessments and avoid implying donation is obligatory.

Assess safety promptly and involve senior mental-health/crisis services as needed. Act “Here is what I can do next, with your involvement.” For imminent danger arrange emergency assessment and safeguarding of access to firearms, with police involvement when justified. In England, instruct an IMCA for proposed serious NHS medical treatment when the person lacks capacity and has no appropriate non-paid consultee, subject to emergency exceptions. Agree the next step Which option feels most consistent with your values? Plan: Convene a best-interests process involving the clinical team and IMCA, ensure least restrictive approach; urgent life-saving treatment must not be delayed solely to complete a non-emergency advocacy process.

sections.preamble: R5-377 | Prisoner patient in handcuffs
sections.1. Title: Prisoner patient in handcuffs
sections.2. Header: AMaC MRCP PACES23 • R5-377 • Station 4: Communication and ethics • 10-minute encounter • Draft 14 October 2026 • AMEND — provisional educational descriptors, not official PACES marking rules
sections.3. Candidate brief: A man attending hospital from prison is in handcuffs attached to an escort officer. He asks to discuss his HIV results without officers listening. Conduct a sensitive consultation, address immediate safety and reach a clear, defensible plan.
sections.4. The hook and examiner trap: Explain that prisoners are entitled to the same clinical respect and confidentiality as other patients; custody does not authorise officers to hear sensitive information routinely. Balance privacy against proportionate security needs through a specific risk assessment.Must not miss: Do not unilaterally remove restraints or promise total privacy regardless of safety; equally do not discuss HIV results in front of officers purely for convenience.
sections.5. Think–Say–Do: THINK SAY DO Hear the concern “Thank you for telling me. What matters most to you about this?” Listen without interruption; clarify the request. Assess risks “May I ask a few questions about safety and what has happened?” Check whether the prisoner is medically stable; ask for a private consultation; identify any specific, documented escape or violence risks with officers and whether security restraints can be modified safely. Explain “I will explain the relevant rules and options clearly.” Explain that prisoners are entitled to the same clinical respect and confidentiality as other patients; custody does not authorise officers to hear sensitive information routinely. Balance privacy against proportionate security needs through a specific risk assessment. Act “Here is what I can do next, with your involvement.” Arrange a confidential discussion out of hearing, negotiating positioning and restraints with the escort officers and senior staff if needed. Relationship alone does not confer a general right to information. Offer to speak to the patient directly and ask whom they wish involved. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Marked obesity, sleepiness and peripheral oedema despite clear lung fields should prompt consideration of obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS); daytime hypercapnia must be demonstrated, not assumed. Pass: examine for hypoventilation and cardiopulmonary consequences; fail: label symptoms simple deconditioning without checking blood gases or sleep-disordered breathing.

Look for consequences “May I check your neck veins and ankles?” Check JVP, oedema, cyanosis and signs of pulmonary hypertension or heart failure. Make a diagnostic plan “Your examination suggests a breathing problem that needs further tests.” Propose awake blood gas and sleep respiratory assessment; discuss CPAP versus NIV context.

Suggests obesity hypoventilation and possible sleep-disordered breathing. Distinguishes OHS from isolated OSA, COPD and cardiac failure; seeks daytime CO₂ evidence. There is a left subcostal scar, consistent with previous splenic surgery; I would confirm the operation from records. I would check vaccination, antibiotic and emergency fever plans before discharge. State signs, not assumptions. I will summarise what I have found. Complete targeted signs and offer appropriate additional examination. Turn findings into a plan. My main concern is…; I would investigate promptly. Confirm splenectomy from history and records, review vaccination status and blood film when relevant, assess indications for prior surgery.

sections.3. Candidate brief: A 70-year-old has had several painless neck and armpit swellings noticed during a routine review. Please examine the relevant lymph node groups and abdomen to establish a cause.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: Generalised painless lymphadenopathy suggests a lymphoproliferative process, but examination cannot confirm CLL without blood testing. Examiner Trap: Equating any lymphadenopathy with a need for immediate chemotherapy or assuming CLL without demonstrating a circulating clonal B-cell population.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Establish safety, consent and relevant exposure. May I examine you? Tell me if anything hurts. Introduce, confirm consent, position comfortably and expose only what is needed. Examine cervical, supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal nodes and the abdomen with consent. There are multiple non-tender enlarged node groups without palpable organomegaly. CLL is one possibility; full blood count, film and flow cytometry will help establish the diagnosis. State signs, not assumptions. I will summarise what I have found. Complete targeted signs and offer appropriate additional examination. Turn findings into a plan. My main concern is…; I would investigate promptly. Full blood count, film, peripheral-blood immunophenotyping; look for anaemia/thrombocytopenia and symptoms or progressive bulky nodes; haematology staging.

sections.3. Candidate brief: Please examine this patient’s abdomen to establish the cause of a swelling noticed during routine review.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook: A painless expansile central mass suggests abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), but a normal abdominal examination cannot exclude one. The Examiner Trap: Do not repeatedly palpate a suspected aneurysm or confuse a transmitted aortic pulsation with expansile pulsation. If new pain, collapse or hypotension appears, switch from elective imaging to emergency vascular assessment.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do Find the problem, not only the scar. “I will examine your abdomen. Is anything painful?” Introduce yourself, confirm comfort and obtain consent; avoid causing pain. Locate the relevant signs. “I will examine gently and tell you what I find.” Inspect for scars, distension and visible pulsation; assess peripheral perfusion. Make the clinical distinction. “I want to check the significance of these findings.” Palpate gently once to assess expansile pulsation without deep repeated pressure. Synthesize and plan. “I would confirm this with appropriate tests.” Request aortic ultrasound and vascular assessment; urgent emergency action for pain or shock.

History on request: Smokes cigarettes; no abdominal pain, collapse or back pain; father had an AAA. Inspection and palpation findings: Comfortable and stable; an expansile, non-tender pulsatile mass centred above the umbilicus; no abdominal tenderness or peritonism; femoral pulses palpable. Link signs to diagnosis “I have finished examining; I will explain what I found.” There is firm hepatomegaly with macroglossia and purpura; together these suggest an infiltrative systemic disorder such as AL amyloidosis. sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A smooth, midline, dull suprapubic mass that cannot be palpated below suggests a distended bladder; protect kidney function.The Examiner Trap. Link signs to diagnosis “I have finished examining; I will explain what I found.” The midline, dull, non-tender fullness is most consistent with chronic bladder distension; I would confirm retained urine and renal effects. Identify risk and next step “I would also check for related problems and arrange appropriate tests.” Bladder scan/post-void residual, urinalysis, renal function and upper tract imaging; review prostate symptoms, medications and neurologic red flags; arrange urology.

sections.3. Candidate brief: You are asked to examine this patient’s cardiovascular system to assess the cause of a persistently fast pulse.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. A resting tachycardia can be physiological after cardiac denervation. It does not rule out rejection, allograft vasculopathy or infection.The Examiner Trap. Calling this sinus tachycardia an arrhythmia and offering rate-limiting treatment without assessing the transplant history. Safe: identify denervation and seek transplant-team input for new symptoms.

sections.8. Examiner material: Findings released on appropriate examination: A 52-year-old stable recipient of a heart transplant 4 years ago. Midline sternotomy, regular pulse 104/min at rest, normal blood pressure, no oedema, no pathological murmur. No fever or breathlessness. Q1 [R3, D/E]: Why is the pulse fast? | Denervation usually raises resting sinus rate; obtain ECG. Q2 [R4, D/E]: What long-term graft problems matter? | Rejection, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, infection and immunosuppression harms. Q3 [R5, D/E]: How is graft vasculopathy sought? | Structured transplant surveillance, with coronary imaging as advised by the transplant centre. Q5 [R7, D/E]: What if a new fever appears? | Urgent infection assessment and contact with transplant team. Curveball: Do not change immunosuppression without the transplant service. sections.preamble: AMaC MRCP PACES — R5-090
sections.1. Title: Breathlessness With Oedema / Preserved Ejection Fraction Is Not Normal Filling
sections.2. Header: Station ID: [AMaC to assign] | Physical examination | PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination | 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examination, at least 4 minutes examiner questions) | Skills A, B, D, E, G | Setting: Cardiology clinic | Source checked: 13 October 2026: NICE NG106, recommendations, updated 2025 | Related AMaC stations: check register before release. AMaC examiner-style practice; not an official mark scheme.
sections.3. Candidate brief: A 76-year-old woman with progressive exertional breathlessness and ankle swelling has been referred after an echocardiogram reported preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. Please examine her cardiovascular system and explain your principal findings to the examiners.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: Hook: HFpEF with atrial fibrillation and congestion. The clue is the combination of signs rather than any one isolated finding. Examiner trap: Assuming preserved EF excludes heart failure or giving an SGLT2 inhibitor without reviewing kidney function. Pass behaviour is to examine systematically, state the positive and absent signs accurately, and propose safe next steps.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: Think Say Do What does the referral ask me to establish? “May I check your pulse, blood pressure and examine your heart?” Introduce, gain consent, assess comfort and expose respectfully. Find the discriminating signs. “I will examine the circulation and listen to the heart.” Irregularly irregular pulse at 88/min. sections.3. Candidate brief: You are the medical registrar. Please examine the cardiovascular system of Ms Lara Whitcombe, aged 42, to assess the cause of leg pain when walking. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions. You may ask the patient to change position during the examination.
sections.4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap: The Hook. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) with peripheral arterial involvement is the unifying possibility, but findings must be described accurately before naming a cause. The Examiner Trap. Do not treat weak foot pulses as isolated atherosclerosis or omit the retinal complication. Pass behaviour: identify the signs, articulate uncertainty, and give a safe next step.
sections.5. Think – Say – Do: THINK SAY DO Orient “I will explain the examination and ask if anything is uncomfortable.” Introduce, consent, assess comfort and position. Find the pattern “I will examine the peripheral signs, pulses and heart.” Follow targeted examination sequence; describe positive and absent findings. Synthesise “The findings suggest pseudoxanthoma elasticum (pxe) with peripheral arterial involvement.” Offer alternative(s); avoid overclaiming confirmation. Prioritise “I would investigate the key risk and plan specialist follow-up.” Check safety red flags, choose tests and escalation appropriate to this case.
sections.6. Scoring grid: Row Skill Focus Fail Pass High-performance R1 G Permission and comfort Does not check consent or discomfort; proceeds despite objection. Offers explanation, consent and comfortable positioning before exposing legs and neck Offers explanation, consent and comfortable positioning before exposing legs and neck; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. R2 A Cardiovascular and limb examination Omits the focused examination or uses disorganised, unreliable technique. Examines neck skin, radial/femoral/foot pulses, temperature, capillary refill, cardiac auscultation Examines neck skin, radial/femoral/foot pulses, temperature, capillary refill, cardiac auscultation; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. Describes neck papules and reduced pedal pulses without inventing a murmur Describes neck papules and reduced pedal pulses without inventing a murmur; explains why it matters and what would change urgency. R4 D Diagnostic synthesis Names one unrelated diagnosis without evidence. Suggests PXE with peripheral vascular disease and a reasoned alternative Suggests PXE with peripheral vascular diseas
sections.7. Role-player brief: Not applicable to this physical-examination encounter. The patient answers routine comfort and positioning requests; there is no scripted surrogate negotiation.
sections.8. Examiner material: Release only when the candidate examines the relevant area: Hands/skin and peripheral circulation: Fine yellow papules coalescing into lax, cobblestoned folds on both sides of the neck; cool feet; dorsalis pedis pulses absent bilaterally, posterior tibial pulses weak; femoral pulses palpable; regular pulse, normal heart sounds, no bruits. Other examination and normal findings: No cardiac murmur, no heart failure, no acute limb threat. Examiner question ladder (answers are teaching models, not an official mark scheme): Q1 (B/D; grid R3): What unifies the findings? Answer: PXE causes abnormal mineralisation of elastic fibres affecting skin, retina and arteries. Q2 (B/D; grid R4): What eye complication matters? Answer: Angioid streaks can be complicated by choroidal neovascularisation and central visual loss; arrange retinal assessment. Q3 (E; grid R5): How investigate the limb symptoms? Answer: Document pulses and perfusion, assess with ABPI and vascular duplex as appropriate; urgent review if rest pain or tissue loss. Q4 (E; grid R6): How confirm the inherited disorder? Answer: Clinical skin/retinal findings and specialist genetic assessment for biallelic ABCC6 variants; skin biopsy
