stations.title: Jaundice After Cholecystectomy

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B • B2-100 Jaundice After Cholecystectomy Type: Data interpretation / postoperative complication | Station time: 9 minutes | Development draft — not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A 48-year-old woman is jaundiced with right upper quadrant discomfort five days after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Review the observations and written investigation reports, explain the likely causes, prioritise investigations, and state an immediate management plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Initial disclosures: temperature 37.9°C, HR 104, BP 112/70, oxygen saturation 97% air. Bilirubin 92 µmol/L, ALP 370 U/L, ALT 190 U/L, WCC 13 ×10⁹/L, CRP 115 mg/L; bilirubin was normal preoperatively. Ultrasound: CBD 10 mm, mild intrahepatic dilatation, 4-cm fluid collection in gallbladder bed; no clearly seen stone. Operation report: difficult dissection near Calot’s triangle; no intraoperative cholangiogram. If asked: oral intake reduced; no documented bilious drain. The candidate must not assume that a CBD stone is the only possible diagnosis. Provide a written MRCP report on request: distal CBD filling defect approximately 5 mm, with fluid collection communicating uncertainly with biliary tree; anatomy of proximal ducts incompletely characterised. Worsening pain or sepsis changes urgency and demands source-control planning.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are anxious and ask, “Does this mean something went wrong in my operation?” If the candidate gives a definitive answer before investigations, ask whether there could be injury to the bile duct. If they explain uncertainty compassionately and offer a senior-led investigation plan, you are reassured.
sections.1. Recognises urgency: Labels mild jaundice routine without checking systemic condition. Identifies a potentially serious postoperative biliary complication; evaluates stability promptly. Explicitly seeks cholangitis, leak/peritonitis and duct injury while reprioritising with physiological change.
sections.2. Structured assessment: Omits observations, abdominal examination or hydration status. Uses ABCDE if unwell; examines abdomen, wounds and any drain; checks fluid balance and sepsis features. Connects fever, guarding, bilious output or shock to escalating biliary sepsis or peritonitis.
sections.3. Analyses blood tests: Calls isolated ALT rise hepatitis and ignores bilirubin/ALP. Recognises predominantly cholestatic pattern with inflammatory response and requests trend of LFTs. Relates patterns to obstruction versus leak/injury but stresses that blood tests alone cannot distinguish them.
sections.4. Differential diagnosis: Mentions only retained CBD stone. Includes retained CBD stone, bile leak/biloma and bile duct injury or stricture. Prioritises retained stone and postoperative duct injury; recognises associated infected collection/cholangitis.

stations.title: Dislodged Gastrostomy Tube

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B • B2-101 Dislodged Gastrostomy Tube Type: Procedural decision / patient safety | Station time: 9 minutes | Development draft — not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar receiving an urgent ward call: a patient’s gastrostomy tube has fallen out. Take a focused history, decide if and how tract patency can be maintained, explain what must happen before the tube is used and describe your escalation plan. You are not required to perform tube insertion.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Patient is a 72-year-old man on enteral feeds after head and neck cancer treatment. At baseline has limited oral intake. Tube placed endoscopically 12 days ago, accidentally pulled out 45 minutes ago. No abdominal pain or fever; HR 94, BP 126/76, afebrile, abdomen soft and not tender. Nursing staff have a similar replacement balloon tube and suggest putting it back now. If candidate asks, original PEG type and size are documented. No competent specialist operator currently at bedside. Actor asks whether feeds and medications can continue immediately. Examiner reveals if prompted: local pathway mandates urgent gastroenterology/enteral feeding review and radiological verification of any early replacement.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are frightened of not receiving medicines or nutrition. You ask: “The hole is still open; can’t you just put the new tube in and feed me?” If unsafe blind insertion is proposed, ask whether the tube could go into the abdomen rather than the stomach.
sections.1. Tract age and mechanism: Does not ask when gastrostomy was first placed. Establishes original insertion date, method and elapsed time since displacement. States that this 12-day tract is immature, so blind replacement risks intraperitoneal placement.
sections.2. Immediate patient check: Assumes well appearance excludes an internal injury. Checks observations, abdominal pain, peritonism, leak, bleeding and vital medication needs. Identifies peritonitis/sepsis indicators needing emergency surgical assessment and resuscitation.
sections.3. Immediate safety: Directs nurse to blindly insert and flush a replacement tube. Stops feeds, water and medicines via the absent/uncertain tube; covers site and protects patient. Explicitly prohibits feeding or flushing via unverified placement and records the reason.
sections.4. Tract preservation: Leaves patient without a prompt plan because appearance is stable. Contacts experienced enteral-feeding/GI team urgently; recognises tract may close rapidly. Balances urgent specialist assessment with avoiding forced, unsupervised manipulation of a recent tract.

stations.title: Reflux and Hiatus Hernia — When to Operate
stations.source_heading: B2-102 Reflux and Hiatus Hernia — When to Operate

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-102 — Reflux and Hiatus Hernia — When to Operate Status: PROVISIONAL • editorial and clinical sign-off required • no MB identifier allocated Format: Applied knowledge / counselling | 9-minute practice encounter | UK surgical exam preparation; not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are a surgical registrar in upper-GI clinic. A 46-year-old with troublesome reflux despite treatment asks if a hiatus-hernia operation would cure it. Explain when surgery is appropriate, what tests are needed beforehand and the trade-offs. No image is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Patient is otherwise stable. Symptoms: three years of heartburn and regurgitation; currently taking omeprazole inconsistently, often after meals. BMI 31. No dysphagia, bleeding, unintentional weight loss or persistent vomiting. Endoscopy: 3-cm sliding hiatus hernia, mild oesophagitis, no Barrett’s; biopsies benign. The candidate must distinguish anatomical hernia from proven pathological reflux and must not promise an operation solely for hernia size. Reveal test results if requested: following optimised PPI, persistent troublesome regurgitation; ambulatory reflux study confirms pathological acid exposure; high-resolution manometry shows no major motility disorder.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You dislike taking medicines for the rest of your life and worry about cancer. If reassured carefully, ask: “Will I be able to burp or vomit normally afterwards?” If candidate claims the surgery is a permanent cure, press: “So it can never come back?”
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: What makes surgery reasonable? Troublesome objectively confirmed reflux with persistent symptoms or preference to avoid prolonged medication, after optimisation and shared decision-making; assess suitability and expectations. What should be checked? Adequate PPI trial and adherence; upper-GI endoscopy, high-resolution oesophageal manometry, ambulatory pH testing (or impedance-pH according to prior PPI response); consider anatomy and other diagnoses. What operation? Laparoscopic hiatus repair with antireflux fundoplication in suitable patients; type of wrap selected with specialist assessment. Main disadvantages? Dysphagia, gas-bloat, difficulty belching/vomiting, recurrence or ongoing PPI need, and operative/anaesthetic complications.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Award the band by observable action; a critical fail overrides an otherwise competent performance. Do not award credit for an unsaid plan. Domain Fail Pass High-performance History and red flags Asks about heartburn only and overlooks dysphagia or weight loss. Asks reflux pattern, regurgitation, swallowing, bleeding, weight loss and alarm symptoms. Clarifies reflux versus dyspepsia, nocturnal aspiration, atypical symptoms and their effect on quality of life. Treatment optimisation Recommends immediate fundoplication without reviewing PPI use. Checks adherence, timing, dose, response and lifestyle measures before referral. Explains correct PPI timing, weight management and realistic medical alternatives without blaming the patient. Endoscopy appraisal Treats 3-cm sliding hernia as automatic operative indication. Interprets mild oesophagitis and sliding hernia in clinical context; checks relevant histology. Explains that hernia size alone does not demonstrate symptom causation and reviews Barrett’s/alarm features. Reflux confirmation Offers surgery without objective reflux assessment. Requests ambulatory reflux monitoring to document reflux before elective surgery. Distinguishes pH f
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Proceeding directly to antireflux surgery without assessing for significant motility disorder, creating avoidable postoperative obstruction risk. 2. Dismissal of progressive dysphagia or weight loss without urgent evaluation for serious pathology. 3. Assuring the patient that a sliding hiatus hernia alone mandates surgery, without confirming reflux or considering other causes of symptoms. 4. Deliberately misleading consent by promising permanent cure and denying dysphagia or gas-bloat risk.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Patient adds: “My friend had the same operation and now cannot swallow properly. Can that happen to me?” Expected response: acknowledge postoperative dysphagia, explain that it may be temporary but sometimes persistent, and connect motility testing and informed choice to minimising risk. Do not trivialise the concern.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I said the hernia proves I need surgery; I should correct that. The decision depends on the symptom pattern and objective reflux testing.” • “I omitted manometry. We should check oesophageal motility before committing to a wrap.” • “I implied surgery always stops the need for medication; recurrence or residual symptoms mean some people still need PPIs.”

stations.title: Endoscopy Report — Gastric Ulcer

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-103 — Endoscopy Report — Gastric Ulcer Status: PROVISIONAL • editorial and clinical sign-off required • no MB identifier allocated Format: Data interpretation / management | 9-minute practice encounter | UK surgical exam preparation; not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are the surgical registrar reviewing an upper-GI endoscopy report for a 64-year-old patient investigated for iron-deficiency anaemia and epigastric discomfort. Interpret the findings, identify missing information, and set out treatment and follow-up.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Written endoscopy report: “OGD reached D2. A 15-mm ulcer on the lesser curve of the gastric body with slightly irregular raised edge; clean base, no active bleeding. Photographs taken. Four biopsies from ulcer edge for histology. Antral rapid urease test negative. Patient takes omeprazole and naproxen.” Hb 101 g/L, haemodynamically stable. Histology is awaited. On asking about H. pylori: urease testing was performed while on PPI. If examiner asks for more: no known family history of gastric cancer and no weight loss. Candidate must not call this benign before histology; irregular margins require sufficient targeted sampling and active follow-up. A repeat OGD is booked within 12 weeks after diagnosis; if original biopsies had been omitted entirely, arrange early repeat within 2 weeks.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient asks if it is cancer, whether naproxen is responsible and whether the ulcer can simply be treated with tablets. If told it is definitely benign, ask how they can be certain before histology.
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: Primary concern? Potential gastric malignancy until adequate targeted biopsy and histology exclude it; assess ulcer location, size, margins and photographs. What to do about histology? Track the pathology result; ensure enough targeted biopsies of ulcer edge and base according to current BSG guidance, particularly when irregular. How to manage? Review/stop NSAID where possible, use PPI, test and treat H. pylori when positive, consider PPI effect on testing. Follow-up timing? Repeat upper-GI endoscopy to assess healing, with BSG/JAG guidance recommending within 12 weeks; NICE specifically advises 6–8 weeks for gastric ulcer with H. pylori. If ulcer was not biopsied at index OGD, repeat within 2 weeks.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Award the band by observable action; a critical fail overrides an otherwise competent performance. Do not award credit for an unsaid plan. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Systematic report reading Says “gastric ulcer” without assessing detail. Identifies ulcer size, location, morphology, haemostasis and biopsy status. Highlights irregular raised edge and missing base sampling as factors needing endoscopist review. Cancer recognition Calls ulcer benign because clean based. States gastric cancer must be excluded and awaits histology. Explains false reassurance from appearance alone and plans follow-up even if initial biopsy benign when appropriate. Biopsy adequacy Accepts four biopsies uncritically for suspicious ulcer. Seeks adequate targeted ulcer biopsies and histology review. Notes current BSG recommendation for ≥6 targeted edge/base samples, 8 for suspicious features, adapting to safety. H. pylori interpretation Assumes negative urease test excludes infection while on PPI. Recognises false-negative testing on PPI and arranges reliable reassessment. Discusses PPI washout when clinically appropriate and subsequent eradication confirmation. Drug review Continues naproxen with no
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Declaring an irregular gastric ulcer definitively benign before adequate histology and no surveillance plan. 2. Failing to arrange timely reassessment when an ulcer was not biopsied at index OGD. 3. Leaving a suspicious histology report untracked, delaying cancer diagnosis. 4. Ignoring signs of active major upper GI haemorrhage or perforation requiring emergency escalation.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner states: “Histology comes back as nonspecific inflammation, no malignancy; patient still takes naproxen.” Expected response: reassure cautiously only, review whether original sampling was adequate, withdraw NSAID if practicable, treat with PPI and ensure documented healing / repeat endoscopy. Histology alone does not cancel appropriate follow-up.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I called this benign on appearance; that was unsafe. We must wait for histology and ensure adequate targeted samples.” • “I accepted the negative urease test without noticing the PPI; I will organise appropriate repeat testing.” • “I forgot ownership of the pathology result. I will assign a named clinician and book a dated healing endoscopy.”

stations.title: Examination of the Peripheral Arterial System

near_match.title: Peripheral arterial examination of the lower limb

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-104 — Examination of the Peripheral Arterial System Status: PROVISIONAL • editorial and clinical sign-off required • no MB identifier allocated Format: Physical examination | 9-minute practice encounter | UK surgical exam preparation; not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are the vascular registrar examining a 69-year-old person with exertional right calf discomfort. Perform a focused examination of the lower limb arterial system on a consenting simulated patient. Talk through any manoeuvres that cannot be demonstrated; conclude with findings, differential, investigation and escalation.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Patient stable, pain-free at rest. Right calf pain after 100 metres resolves within 3 minutes of stopping. Smokes 15 cigarettes daily, diabetes and hypertension. Right foot cooler than left, reduced right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses; no ulceration, gangrene, sensory loss or rest pain. Femoral pulses palpable bilaterally; right popliteal diminished. Right handheld Doppler ABPI 0.68 and left 0.96 if requested. Ask the candidate to distinguish stable claudication from limb-threatening ischaemia. No imaging supplied.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient agrees to examination; answers symptoms only if asked: “It happens when I walk and settles when I stop.” Denies nocturnal rest pain, wounds, sudden onset, fever or limb weakness. Ask at the end: “Could I lose my leg?” The candidate should explain without guaranteeing outcomes.
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: Initial actions? Introduce, consent, pain assessment, hand hygiene, adequate exposure, patient supine, compare both legs; offer chaperone where appropriate. What findings? Colour, temperature, capillary refill, skin thinning/hair loss, nails, dependent rubor, pallor on elevation, ulcers/gangrene and prior scars. Which pulses? Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis on both sides; abdominal aorta and femoral bruits as relevant. Special test? Buerger elevation/dependency manoeuvre may support severe ischaemia but must not replace pulse/ABPI assessment. What confirms PAD? Resting supine Doppler ABPI with pressures in both arms and ankle arteries; document Doppler waveforms; diabetes can falsely elevate values. Red flags? New severe limb pain, cold or pale limb, new motor or sensory deficit, absent pulses -> urgent acute limb ischaemia assessment; rest pain and wounds -> urgent vascular service.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Award bands for observable actions, not intentions. A critical safety omission may override the overall mark. Each row has a distinct task-specific descriptor. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Weight E1 Introduction/consent Examines without consent or dignity. Explains purpose, obtains consent, checks discomfort. Tailors position, exposure and symptom limitation before starting. Standard E2 Inspection Looks only at calf, overlooks toes and wounds. Compares feet and legs, colour, trophic changes, ulcers. Identifies limb-threatening skin signs and previous vascular scars. Critical E3 Temperature/perfusion Does not examine foot warmth or perfusion. Compares temperature and capillary refill. Interprets asymmetry alongside pulses; avoids relying on refill alone. Standard E4 Pulse sequence Checks only one pedal pulse. Checks bilateral femoral, popliteal, DP and PT pulses. Uses consistent anatomical landmarks, recognises asymmetric level of disease. Critical E5 Additional signs Omits vascular bruits/aorta entirely. Assesses femoral bruits and abdominal aorta when appropriate. States limited diagnostic value of bruit absence; prioritises core limb assessment. Standard E6 Buerger manoeu
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Missing evidence of tissue loss or new neurological deficit and discharging a potentially threatened limb without escalation. 2. Failing to assess femoral and both pedal pulses then falsely asserting normal arterial examination. 3. Declaring PAD excluded solely because the ABPI is normal/high in a patient with diabetes. 4. Recommending compression for an ulcerated, potentially ischaemic limb without arterial evaluation.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner says: “The right foot has become suddenly painful and the patient can no longer move the toes.” Candidate must stop routine examination, seek immediate senior vascular assessment and recognise possible acute limb ischaemia; urgent neurovascular documentation and emergency pathway.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I have not checked the toes for ulceration or gangrene; I need to inspect them before concluding.” • “I missed the posterior tibial pulse; I will reassess both ankles, and request Doppler assessment if uncertain.” • “A normal ABPI in diabetes does not safely rule out PAD; I would consider waveforms and specialist testing.”

stations.title: Intermittent Claudication — First Management

near_match.title: History: intermittent claudication

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-105 — Intermittent Claudication — First Management Status: PROVISIONAL • editorial and clinical sign-off required • no MB identifier allocated Format: Communication / applied management | 9-minute practice encounter | UK surgical exam preparation; not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are seeing a 67-year-old patient with gradually progressive exertional calf pain and a recent ABPI of 0.70. Explain the working diagnosis and agree a first-line management plan, including the role of exercise, vascular risk reduction, follow-up and when procedures are considered.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Claudication after 150 metres, settles within 2–3 minutes of rest. No rest pain, wounds, cold foot, rapid deterioration or focal neurological deficit. Smokes 10/day; blood pressure 148/86 mmHg; LDL elevated; not taking lipid lowering or antiplatelet medication. ABPI 0.70 on affected side, 1.0 contralaterally. No heart failure or contraindication to exercise given. If asked about medication, no known antiplatelet allergy, bleeding history or active anticoagulation. Candidate must offer supervised exercise rather than immediate angioplasty.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You fear losing the leg and want “a stent straightaway.” When asked, you are keen to walk but the pain discourages you. You ask “Does pushing through the pain make the artery burst?” and “Can I just take a tablet instead?” The candidate should acknowledge priorities, check understanding and explain a realistic stepwise pathway.
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: Diagnosis and red flags? Reproducible exertional calf discomfort relieved by rest with low ABPI supports PAD; differentiate rest pain, tissue loss, acute ischaemia. Initial treatment? Offer a supervised exercise programme to all people with intermittent claudication; NICE considers 2 hours weekly for 3 months with exercise towards maximal pain under supervision. Cardiovascular prevention? Smoking cessation support, exercise, diet, blood pressure and diabetes control, high-intensity/statin therapy as appropriate, antiplatelet therapy according to PAD/CV risk and contraindications. Revascularisation? Only consider angioplasty when risk-factor advice and supervised exercise have not provided satisfactory symptom relief and imaging supports a suitable lesion; vascular MDT/shared decision. Investigations? Doppler ABPI and review of cardiovascular risk; duplex when evaluating revascularisation, not automatic CT angiography for every stable patient. Follow-up? Review walking distance, function, smoking and medication tolerance; urgent review for new rest pain, wounds, suddenly cold/pale weak foot.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Award bands for observable actions, not intentions. A critical safety omission may override the overall mark. Each row has a distinct task-specific descriptor. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Weight M1 Elicit impact Never asks walking distance or goals. Asks onset, distance, limitation and impact. Establishes patient priorities and records baseline walking capacity. Standard M2 Threat screen Treats rest pain/wound as routine claudication. Asks about rest pain, tissue loss, sudden worsening. States appropriate urgent vascular action for limb-threatening features. Critical M3 Explain diagnosis Says leg pain is only age-related and ABPI irrelevant. Explains PAD, reduced blood flow on exertion and ABPI result. Uses plain language and addresses systemic cardiovascular disease risk. Standard M4 Supervised exercise Recommends rest and avoidance of walking. Offers structured supervised exercise as first-line. Explains exercise towards maximal tolerable pain with supervised progression and accessibility planning. Critical M5 Smoking cessation Omits tobacco despite current smoking. Offers stop-smoking intervention/support. Agrees practical referral and pharmacotherapy discussion where s
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Advising the patient to avoid walking altogether and denying the benefit of first-line supervised exercise. 2. Ignoring new rest pain, ischaemic wounds or acute limb ischaemia symptoms and offering only routine follow-up. 3. Recommending angioplasty as automatic first-line therapy for uncomplicated claudication without discussing supervised exercise and cardiovascular prevention. 4. Dismissing cardiovascular risk reduction entirely despite established symptomatic peripheral arterial disease.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Patient says: “I woke last night with pain in my foot, and hanging it over the bed helped.” Candidate should recognise possible ischaemic rest pain, reassess tissue viability and arrange urgent vascular assessment rather than proceed with a routine claudication exercise-only plan.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I suggested a stent immediately; for stable claudication first offer supervised exercise and cardiovascular prevention, then reassess need for intervention.” • “I failed to ask about night pain or wounds; I need those answers before calling it uncomplicated claudication.” • “I said aspirin is mandatory for everybody; the antiplatelet choice requires assessing indications, contraindications and bleeding risk.”

stations.title: Diabetic Foot Infection with Osteomyelitis
stations.source_heading: B2-106 Diabetic Foot Infection with Osteomyelitis

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-106 — Diabetic Foot Infection with Osteomyelitis PROVISIONAL DRAFT • Clinical review and duplicate-register clearance required • No MB identifier assigned Format: Management / critical care | 9-minute practice station | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A 64-year-old person with type 2 diabetes is admitted with a worsening plantar foot ulcer, redness and possible bone infection. Assess the information supplied, explain your immediate plan and answer the examiner’s questions. No image is needed.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Observations: T 38.3°C, HR 112/min, BP 102/64, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 97% air. A 3-cm plantar ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head with purulent discharge, surrounding erythema and a deep tract; dorsalis pedis pulse weak. Foot X-ray report: soft-tissue swelling, no definite bone destruction. CRP 42 mg/L, glucose 17 mmol/L, creatinine 145 µmol/L (usual 90). Wound duration 5 weeks. If asked: reduced sensation; no crepitus; capillary refill 4 seconds; no exposed bone. No antibiotic allergies.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: “Will I lose my foot?” Has progressive discharge and fevers; has missed recent podiatry appointments due to transport problems. Wishes to understand the purpose of tests and whether admission is necessary. If asked about pain: surprisingly little because of neuropathy.
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: First priority? ABCDE and sepsis assessment; IV access, observations, blood cultures when indicated, lactate, renal profile and glucose; begin appropriate treatment promptly. Examine what? Expose entire foot, depth and extent, cellulitis, fluctuance, necrosis, deformity, perfusion, pulses, sensation; assess contralateral foot. Does a negative X-ray rule out bone infection? No. Consider osteomyelitis with a deep or chronic ulcer even if initial X-ray, inflammatory markers or probe-to-bone are normal. Next imaging? Initial plain radiograph; MRI if osteomyelitis suspected but not confirmed on plain radiograph; coordinate with specialist foot team. Microbiology? Obtain tissue/bone sample when feasible after debridement or deep wound sampling near antibiotic start; avoid reliance on superficial swabs when deeper sampling possible. Treatment and team? Prompt antibiotics selected by severity, renal function and local policy; urgent multidisciplinary foot care, vascular assessment, offloading, drainage/debridement where needed and glycaemic support.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Score observable actions. Critical safety omissions override aggregate performance. Each cell describes actual candidate behaviour. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Weight Recognition / stability Calls this a simple chronic ulcer and ignores fever/tachycardia. Recognises infected diabetic ulcer, records observations and screens for sepsis. Identifies systemic illness plus AKI and acts urgently while arranging definitive limb assessment. 3 History and risk Does not ask ulcer duration, neuropathy or preceding antibiotics. Asks duration, worsening symptoms, diabetes control, vascular symptoms and prior infection. Adds prior resistance/cultures, prior ulcers, footwear/offloading and barriers to follow-up. 1 Focused foot examination Looks only at the surface wound. Checks whole foot for spread, depth, necrosis, pulses, sensation and perfusion. Maps tissue loss, infection extent and ischaemia, and examines contralateral foot. 2 Osteomyelitis reasoning Excludes osteomyelitis because X-ray is normal. Suspects osteomyelitis given chronic deep wound and requests MRI if uncertain. Explains limits of negative early films, markers and probe-to-bone and seeks specialist diagnostic sampling.
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Treating systemic illness as a trivial ulcer and not escalating sepsis or organ dysfunction. 2. Ruling out osteomyelitis solely from a normal X-ray or normal inflammatory markers. 3. Withholding indicated antibiotics while waiting for MRI or culture results in an unwell patient. 4. Failing to escalate suspected deep infection or limb ischaemia for urgent specialist review.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: The examiner reports spreading erythema, BP 86/54 and new confusion. Stop routine discussion: call emergency help, repeat ABCDE, urgent sepsis resuscitation and cultures where feasible without delaying antibiotics; alert senior/critical care and surgical source-control teams.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I have not yet assessed perfusion; I would check both pedal pulses, capillary refill and request vascular input if compromised.” • “A normal radiograph does not rule out early osteomyelitis; I would ask the diabetic foot MDT about MRI and deep sampling.” • “This patient is now hypotensive and confused; I must prioritise ABCDE, sepsis care and urgent senior review.”

stations.title: Swollen Leg After Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-107 — Swollen Leg After Surgery PROVISIONAL DRAFT • Clinical review and duplicate-register clearance required • No MB identifier assigned Format: Data interpretation / clinical management | 9-minute practice station | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible durin: You are the surgical registrar asked to review a 59-year-old patient with a newly swollen and painful left calf on day 6 after elective bowel resection. Take a focused history from the patient, interpret the written data, and outline investigation and safe management.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Left calf 4 cm greater circumference than right measured 10 cm below tibial tuberosity, unilateral pitting oedema and deep venous tenderness. Patient had major abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia six days ago; mobile with support. HR 96, BP 122/76, SpO₂ 98% air, RR 17. No chest pain or dyspnoea initially. Wound dry, Hb 106 g/L and stable, platelets 225, eGFR 74. Receiving prophylactic LMWH. No active bleeding. The alternative diagnoses are less likely. The two-level DVT Wells score is 4: major surgery +1, tenderness +1, calf swelling ≥3 cm +1, unilateral pitting oedema +1.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: “Could this be a clot? Will blood thinners make me bleed after the operation?” Pain began yesterday. No haemoptysis, chest pain or shortness of breath unless asked in the curveball. No known prior DVT, no current bleeding. Wishes a plain explanation of ultrasound and treatment.
sections.4. Directed questions and expected answe: How do you stratify? Two-level DVT Wells score; in this case 4 means DVT likely (≥2), using postoperative status plus findings. Next test? Proximal leg vein compression ultrasound within 4 hours if possible. If ultrasound unavailable promptly? For likely DVT, request D-dimer and consider interim therapeutic anticoagulation with ultrasound within 24 hours, after individual bleeding-risk assessment and senior discussion following recent surgery. Is a positive D-dimer diagnostic? No; postoperative D-dimer is often raised, so interpret with the NICE pathway and ultrasound. If proximal scan negative? Follow NICE pathway: D-dimer if not already done; if D-dimer positive, repeat proximal scan in 6–8 days; consider alternatives. If DVT confirmed? Treat with therapeutic anticoagulation after checking haemostasis, bleeding risk, interactions, renal function and the operative plan; discuss choice with surgical team.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Score observable actions. Critical safety omissions override aggregate performance. Each cell describes actual candidate behaviour. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Weight Safety assessment / PE Assesses calf only, omitting respiratory symptoms and observations. Checks observations, chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis and instability. Identifies potential PE or bleeding emergencies and adapts pathway immediately. 3 Focused history Does not establish onset, procedure or anticoagulant status. Asks onset, unilateral symptoms, surgery, mobility, previous VTE and prophylaxis. Includes cancer, provoking factors, bleeding, drug history and evolving PE symptoms. 1 Leg examination Uses calf swelling alone without comparing both limbs. Examines bilateral swelling, calf circumference, tenderness, pitting oedema and perfusion. Checks skin, wounds and alternative diagnoses while avoiding misleading physical signs. 2 Wells interpretation Calls probability low despite the four documented points. Calculates DVT Wells 4 correctly and classifies likely (≥2). Explains which items contribute and avoids substituting an isolated D-dimer for structured probability. 2 Diagnostic ultrasound Requests D-di
sections.6. Critical fails (safety overrides): 1. Failing to assess for symptoms or signs of pulmonary embolism or haemodynamic instability. 2. Treating a likely DVT as excluded by a positive/negative D-dimer alone without the indicated ultrasound pathway. 3. Giving full-dose anticoagulation after recent major surgery without assessing current bleeding and discussing the plan with the surgical team. 4. Missing a required ultrasound or repeat-imaging arrangement and discharging without a safety-net.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Before ultrasound the patient develops sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain with SpO₂ 90% and HR 125. Stop the isolated DVT pathway. ABCDE, call for urgent help, oxygen according to saturation, haemodynamic assessment and urgent PE work-up/management with senior surgical and acute medical teams; weigh anticoagulation against recent operative bleeding risk.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: • “I have not asked about chest pain or breathlessness; I need to screen for PE immediately.” • “With a Wells score of four, I must arrange a proximal ultrasound rather than rely on a postoperative D-dimer.” • “I should not prescribe therapeutic anticoagulation automatically after recent bowel surgery; I will assess haemostasis and agree the plan with the surgical registrar/consultant.”

stations.title: AAA Screening - A 4.8 cm Aneurysm
stations.source_heading: B2-108 AAA Screening - A 4.8 cm Aneurysm

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | B2-108 AAA Screening - A 4.8 cm Aneurysm Communication / vascular • 9-minute practice station • Draft: 12 October 2026 • Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the vascular clinic doctor seeing a 67-year-old man following an NHS AAA screening ultrasound showing an infrarenal aortic diameter of 4.8 cm. He feels well and fears an imminent rupture. Explain the result, surveillance, specialist care, risk reduction and what to do if symptoms develop. Check his understanding and concerns. You have 9 minutes. Speak to the person as you would in an outpatient or ward consultation; ask for findings or investigation results when relevant.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Age 67, asymptomatic, scan shows 4.8 cm maximum anteroposterior diameter on ultrasound. BP 146/86 mmHg, ex-smoker with hypertension; no abdominal or back pain. No previous AAA assessment. Provide other findings only if asked. Key examiner distinction: the NHS screening pathway schedules 4.5–5.4 cm AAA surveillance scans every 3 months; NICE NG156 recommends regional vascular-service assessment within 12 weeks for AAAs 3.0–5.4 cm. If the candidate asks about surgery: asymptomatic 4.8 cm aneurysm is generally managed with surveillance, not automatically repaired. Symptomatic AAA, rapid growth (>1 cm/year), or ≥5.5 cm call for vascular assessment of repair suitability; individual risk and anatomy matter.
sections.3. Simulated patient / actor brief: You are Mr David Hughes, aged 67. You are worried because a friend died of a “burst aneurysm”. Ask: “Does 4.8 cm mean I need an operation now?” If reassured with surveillance, ask: “Why would I see a specialist if I am just having scans?” If asked about symptoms, you have no abdominal/back pain, collapse or new tenderness. You stopped smoking 2 years ago. Curveball only when prompted: “Could I wait until the next scan if I suddenly got severe back pain?” Be worried, not hostile.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Assess each domain using the specific behavioural descriptors. Safety-critical domains are flagged ★. Overall judgements are Fail / Pass / High-performance, not a mathematical substitute for examiner judgement. Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Explanation and empathy: Dismisses anxiety or incorrectly calls 4.8 cm normal. Explains abdominal aorta and aneurysm clearly; acknowledges fear. Checks prior understanding, gives a clear personalised explanation without alarmism.
sections.2. Size classification: Calls 4.8 cm “large” or gives a 12-month scan interval. Identifies 4.8 cm as medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm). Connects size category to why monitoring rather than immediate operation is usual. 3. ★ Surveillance No follow-up or annual scan only. Specifies ultrasound every 3 months in NHS AAA screening surveillance. Adds reliability of attendance, growth comparison and how results are reviewed. 4. ★ Specialist referral States vascular referral is unnecessary unless ≥5.5 cm. Arranges/ confirms regional vascular assessment for 3.0–5.4 cm AAA within 12 weeks of diagnosis. Separates specialist assessment from operation threshold and confirms communication with screening/GP teams.
sections.5. Repair decisions: Promotes prophylactic repair immediately for an asymptomatic 4.8 cm AAA or promises no future surgery. Explains repair is typically considered if ≥5.5 cm, symptomatic or growth >1 cm/year; vascular specialist weighs risks. Explains individual anatomy, fitness and patient preference may change recommendation.
sections.6. Risk-factor action: Offers reassurance without preventive care. Reviews smoking, BP and cardiovascular risks; advises GP-led medical optimisation. Includes lipid management, activity, adherence and secondary prevention where indicated without claiming drugs shrink AAA. 7. ★ Rupture safety net Suggests awaiting appointment with new severe pain or collapse. Instructs immediate emergency help/999 for sudden severe abdominal or back pain, collapse or fainting. Confirms exact action, emergency urgency and not driving oneself.

stations.title: Consent for Below-Knee Amputation

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | B2-109 Consent for Below-Knee Amputation Communication / vascular • 9-minute practice station • Draft: 12 October 2026 • Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a vascular surgical registrar speaking to a 74-year-old patient with severe chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, painful gangrene of the left forefoot and a non-healing wound. The vascular MDT has assessed imaging and considers further revascularisation unsuitable. A left below-knee amputation is proposed. Explain the indication, options, expected benefits and important risks; explore the patient’s wishes and support informed decision-making. Do not assume consent simply because an operation is recommended. You have 9 minutes. Speak to the person as you would in an outpatient or ward consultation; ask for findings or investigation results when relevant.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: The patient is haemodynamically stable and has decision-making capacity. Limb perfusion is severely impaired; extensive vascular assessment found no durable revascularisation option. There is no uncontrolled sepsis at present. No operation has been scheduled until patient discussion. Current medication includes antiplatelet and statin; comorbidities: diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, chronic kidney disease stage 3. No need for exact numerical risk prediction; refer to anaesthetic/MDT personalised estimates. For questions about prostheses: rehabilitation and prosthetic suitability must be assessed individually; walking independently is not guaranteed.
sections.3. Simulated patient / actor brief: You are Mrs Margaret Lewis, aged 74. The pain is intolerable but you fear loss of independence. Start: “Are you saying I’ll never walk again?” Ask: “Why can’t you just remove my toes, or try another bypass?” and “What if I say no?” If the candidate does not mention phantom pain, ask whether you will still feel your missing foot. If rushed into signing: become withdrawn and say you want your daughter present and more time.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Assess each domain using the specific behavioural descriptors. Safety-critical domains are flagged ★. Overall judgements are Fail / Pass / High-performance, not a mathematical substitute for examiner judgement. Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Rapport and values: Uses coercive or euphemistic language and ignores fear. Acknowledges shock and asks what independence and mobility mean to patient. Checks emotional response and preferences before tailoring the explanation. 2. ★ Indication Calls amputation routine for any ulcer; never mentions salvage review. Explains ongoing pain, gangrene and non-healing due to poor blood flow; MDT judged salvage unsuitable. Connects proposed treatment to relief of pain, removal of nonviable tissue and prevention of deterioration without guaranteeing cure.
sections.3. Procedure and level: Misdescribes below-knee as removing the knee joint. Explains removal of diseased lower leg below knee with knee preservation where viable. Explains final level balances healing potential, function and possible revision. 4. ★ Alternatives / refusal Conceals alternatives or claims the patient must agree. Explains MDT considered revascularisation; discusses limited wound/pain approaches, palliation and option to decline. Outlines consequences of no operation, offers second discussion, respects an informed decision. 5. ★ Major procedural risks Omits major harm or promises uncomplicated healing. Names bleeding, infection, delayed/non-healing stump, revision/higher amputation, DVT/PE, anaesthetic/cardiovascular complications and death. Discusses relevance of diabetes, heart and kidney disease and offers individualised perioperative risk assessment.
sections.6. Pain and phantom sensations: Says pain disappears permanently or dismisses phantom pain as psychological. Explains stump pain and phantom limb sensations/pain; plans analgesia. Explains that phantom pain is real and managed through specialist rehabilitation and pain teams.
sections.7. Rehabilitation and function: Promises walking with prosthesis or omits rehabilitation. Describes wound healing, physiotherapy, mobility aids and prosthetic assessment; outcomes vary. Addresses home layout, falls, transfer ability, mental health and early multidisciplinary planning. 8. ★ Capacity and consent Seeks immediate signature despite uncertainty or withholds decision time. Checks capacity and understanding; supports questions, time and patient’s right to refuse. Uses teach-back, offers family involvement with permission and records material individual risks.

stations.title: Examination of an Arteriovenous Fistula
stations.source_heading: B2-110 Examination of an Arteriovenous Fistula

near_match.title: Hip examination

sections.preamble: B2-110 — Examination of an Arteriovenous Fistula AMaC | MRCS Part B | Development draft | 12 October 2026 Station format: Examination • 9 minutes • No image required Purpose: Assess an established haemodialysis fistula systematically, identify dysfunction and hand ischaemia, and protect the access.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are in a vascular clinic. Examine the arteriovenous fistula in the left arm of a patient on haemodialysis. Explain your findings and next steps to the examiner. You do not need to insert needles or perform ultrasound.
sections.2. Examiner briefing: The left radiocephalic fistula is 3 years old. Supply requested findings below. Observe consent, protection of the access arm, actual examination sequence, and appropriate urgency if the thrill is absent.
sections.3. Actor / patient briefing: Age 57, dialysis three times weekly. Initially well and cooperative. If asked: dialysis needles have been more difficult to position over 2 weeks; the hand occasionally feels cold on dialysis; no current pain at rest. Ask: “Will you need to take my blood pressure on this arm?”
sections.4. Examiner disclosure — only if request: Inspection: healed forearm scar, enlarged superficial vein, two old needling sites; no erythema, skin breakdown or active bleeding. Palpation: continuous thrill felt at anastomosis; more pulsatile segment proximally. Skin warm, no focal tenderness. Auscultation: continuous bruit over fistula, with change in pitch toward a short narrowed segment; may suggest stenosis, not diagnostic alone. Hand: warm fingers at rest, capillary refill around 2 seconds, palpable radial pulse, normal sensation and motor function; no tissue loss. If asked what investigations follow the abnormal access findings: discuss with dialysis access team and arrange duplex/further access imaging as clinically indicated.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score each row at the level actually demonstrated. Critical fails are judged separately; do not infer competence from fluent but incomplete speech. Domain / action Fail Pass High-performance Consent, positioning, exposure Touches fistula without explanation or adequate exposure. Introduces self, confirms permission, compares arms, exposes safely. Checks comfort, dialysis hand dominance and baseline access history while maintaining dignity. History and urgent symptoms Does not ask about access function or alarm symptoms. Asks about dialysis flow, difficult needling, bleeding, fever, pain and hand coldness. Characterises changes over time, prolonged post-needle bleeding, digital rest pain or tissue change. Inspection Misses skin damage and aneurysmal changes. Inspects scar, course, needling sites, dilatation, redness and ulceration. Identifies thin shiny skin over enlargement as rupture risk and avoids trauma. Thrill and pulse Does not palpate the access or declares patency from appearance. Palpates anastomosis, thrill and character of pulse along its length. Explains absent thrill means possible thrombosis; increasing pulsatility can suggest outflow stenosis. Bruit Omits auscultatio
sections.6. Critical fails — unsafe acts or omiss: Fails to act urgently on suddenly absent thrill or suspected access thrombosis. Attempts routine IV cannulation or BP cuff on fistula arm despite knowing it is dialysis access. Dismisses finger rest pain, ulceration or severe ischaemic changes as harmless. Fails to initiate firm direct pressure and emergency escalation for uncontrolled fistula haemorrhage.
sections.7. Curveball: Examiner: “The thrill has suddenly disappeared since yesterday.” Candidate should stop routine reassurance and arrange urgent same-day renal/dialysis access service assessment for suspected thrombosis.
sections.8. Recovery opportunities: If the BP cuff is placed on the fistula arm, remove it, apologise and use the other arm. If hand perfusion was omitted, return to assess colour, refill, sensation, motor function and pain at rest. If the candidate wrongly reassures after absent thrill, explicitly reverse the conclusion and contact the dialysis access team urgently.

stations.title: Varicose Veins — Duplex Result and Treatment
stations.source_heading: B2-111 Varicose Veins — Duplex Result and Treatment

sections.preamble: B2-111 — Varicose Veins — Duplex Result and Treatment AMaC | MRCS Part B | Development draft | 12 October 2026 Station format: Data interpretation / communication • 9 minutes • No image required Purpose: Interpret a written venous duplex, explain symptomatic truncal reflux, and offer treatment options in the sequence recommended by NICE.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the vascular registrar in clinic. A 48-year-old patient has painful right-leg varicose veins and an ultrasound report. Explain the scan findings and discuss management in understandable language.
sections.2. Examiner briefing: Patient has aching and heaviness after work despite lifestyle changes. Duplex findings below are supplied in written form. Assess accurate superficial versus deep venous interpretation, management sequencing, and meaningful consent.
sections.3. Actor / patient briefing: Age 48, supermarket worker, veins worsening over three years, troublesome aching and itching at end of long shifts. No ulcer, previous DVT or pregnancy. Wants to avoid a general anaesthetic and asks whether stockings will cure the problem.
sections.4. Examiner disclosure — only if request: Written duplex: right great saphenous vein reflux from saphenofemoral junction to below knee; incompetent tributaries at medial calf. Deep femoral and popliteal veins patent and compressible; no DVT and no reported deep venous reflux. No history of previous venous intervention; skin shows mild ankle eczema without ulceration. If asked: patient is suitable for endovenous thermal ablation after clinical and anatomical assessment.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score each row at the level actually demonstrated. Critical fails are judged separately; do not infer competence from fluent but incomplete speech. Domain / action Fail Pass High-performance Symptoms and impact Only discusses cosmetic appearance. Explores aching, swelling, itching, daily impact and patient priorities. Recognises skin eczema as chronic venous disease and addresses expectations. Report interpretation Calls superficial reflux a DVT or deep obstruction. Identifies great saphenous truncal reflux and incompetent tributaries. Distinguishes superficial reflux from patent deep venous system and relates anatomy to symptoms. Clinical eligibility Offers intervention without symptoms or vascular assessment. Links troublesome symptomatic veins and skin change to vascular treatment eligibility. Checks prior DVT, ulceration, pregnancy, mobility and procedural suitability. First-line intervention Offers stripping first with no explanation. Offers endothermal ablation for suitable truncal reflux. Explains vein closure with laser/radiofrequency under local anaesthetic and expected recovery. When unsuitable Calls foam and open surgery equally first line without reasoning. Offers ultra
sections.6. Critical fails — unsafe acts or omiss: Misreads duplex reflux as acute DVT and commences anticoagulation without indication. Recommends surgery as obligatory first-line treatment despite suitable endothermal ablation, without explaining alternatives. Ignores active bleeding from a varicose vein or fails to advise immediate pressure and urgent assessment. Promises a permanent cure and refuses to discuss material treatment risks or alternatives.
sections.7. Curveball: Actor: “I have a friend who wore stockings for years. Can’t I just do that?” Candidate should distinguish symptom control from treatment of reflux, support informed preference, and explain why intervention is generally offered when suitable.
sections.8. Recovery opportunities: If the deep-vein report was misread, re-state that deep veins are patent and the problem is superficial truncal reflux. If the hierarchy was reversed, correct it explicitly: endothermal → foam if unsuitable → surgery if foam unsuitable. If an unrealistic cure was promised, acknowledge recurrence/retreatment possibility and apologise for misleading certainty.

stations.title: Groin Swelling After Angioplasty

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B B2-112 — Groin Swelling After Angioplasty Critical care / vascular • 9-minute practice station • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • 12 October 2026 AMaC educational marking framework; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Draft pending clinical sign-off and live station-register check.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar asked to review a 73-year-old man six hours after femoral-access angioplasty. He has a painful enlarging right groin swelling and feels faint. Assess the situation, explain your differential and immediate actions to the examiner. You may request observations, examination findings and investigation results verbally.
sections.2. Examiner brief and setting: At start: BP 94/58 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 97% room air; pale, tender tense right groin swelling, dressing blood-stained. Examination on request: swelling not clearly pulsatile; right foot warm with palpable Doppler signals; pain extends toward right flank. Bloods if requested: Hb 102 g/L (was 128 g/L pre-procedure), platelets 214 ×10⁹/L, INR 1.0; repeat Hb may fall further. If appropriate urgent imaging requested: bedside duplex shows a femoral pseudoaneurysm with flow through a neck; clinical shock means also consider active bleeding and retroperitoneal haemorrhage, which duplex of the groin alone cannot exclude. For deterioration curveball: BP falls to 78/42 and HR rises to 132/min.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Conscious and anxious: “The lump keeps getting bigger. Am I bleeding inside?” If asked: takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a recently placed peripheral stent; no known anticoagulant. Pain began 40 minutes ago. If reassured without action: “But I am more dizzy now.”
sections.4. Structured marking grid: Assessed domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate recognition Calls it a routine bruise and leaves patient unattended. Recognises possible access-site bleeding/pseudoaneurysm and treats the patient as potentially unstable. States expanding haematoma plus shock may indicate ongoing arterial or retroperitoneal haemorrhage. ABCDE and escalation Orders imaging before observations or emergency help. ABCDE assessment, monitoring, oxygen if indicated, calls senior vascular/interventional team and anaesthetic help if unstable. Allocates team tasks and rechecks perfusion and observations during resuscitation. Haemorrhage control Massages lump or tries unplanned blind puncture. Maintains supine position and appropriate directed manual pressure for external access-site bleeding while urgently escalating. Coordinates compression with vascular team; recognises pressure may not control retroperitoneal bleeding. Circulatory support No IV access or blood preparation despite shock. Obtains large-bore IV access, sends FBC, coagulation, group and crossmatch and renal function; gives monitored resuscitation. Early activation of local major haemorrhage process when ongoing severe bleeding suspected;
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-critical actio: Fails to recognise haemodynamic instability and delays resuscitation or senior emergency escalation. Discharges a patient with an expanding painful access-site swelling and hypotension. Attempts blind aspiration/puncture of a possible femoral pseudoaneurysm. Ignores a newly ischaemic limb or ongoing major bleeding while awaiting routine imaging.
sections.6. Curveball and actor prompt: At minute 5 the patient becomes pale and confused, BP 78/42 mmHg. Examiner asks: “Would you wait for a formal duplex?” Expected: no; call major haemorrhage/vascular/interventional and anaesthetic teams urgently, resuscitate and arrange immediate haemostasis.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If first reassured it was a haematoma: explicitly revise the assessment once the hypotension, tachycardia and expanding swelling are disclosed; begin ABCDE and call emergency support. If initially requested outpatient duplex: cancel non-urgent pathway and request bedside specialist review; investigate retroperitoneal bleeding without delaying resuscitation. If antiplatelets were stopped reflexively: acknowledge recent stent risk and immediately discuss a coordinated decision with the procedural/vascular team.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “It is a groin bruise; arrange a scan tomorrow.” Does not respond to hypotension and fails to assess distal circulation. Pass “This may be active femoral access-site haemorrhage or pseudoaneurysm. I need ABCDE, emergency senior vascular support, IV access, crossmatch, ongoing pressure if appropriate, and urgent definitive imaging/intervention while monitoring the leg.” High-performance “An expanding groin mass with falling BP can coexist with retroperitoneal bleeding. Activate emergency haemorrhage arrangements, coordinate immediate specialist haemostasis, monitor the limb and agree antiplatelet decisions given the new stent; imaging must not delay source control in shock.”

stations.title: Swollen Leg - Lymphoedema

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B B2-113 — Swollen Leg - Lymphoedema History / examination • 9-minute practice station • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • 12 October 2026 AMaC educational marking framework; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Draft pending clinical sign-off and live station-register check.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are in the vascular outpatient clinic. A 61-year-old woman describes gradually increasing left-leg swelling over 10 months. Take a focused history, describe your examination and explain the likely diagnosis, differential, investigations and first-line management.
sections.2. Examiner brief and setting: Patient well, afebrile, normal vital signs. Unilateral swelling extending to the foot, thickened skin, a positive Stemmer sign (cannot easily pinch a skin fold at base of second toe). Pedal pulses present; no focal erythema or calf tenderness. No obvious active malignancy signs on this simulated examination. If asked about risk factors: no heart, kidney or liver disease, no dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker; no previous DVT. If asked for investigations: diagnosis is mainly clinical, ultrasound can exclude venous disease when indicated; further imaging if unexplained, atypical or concern about recurrent nodal disease.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Her left leg feels heavy and shoes no longer fit. She underwent groin lymph node dissection for melanoma 16 months ago and had one episode of cellulitis. No acute pain or breathlessness. “Will this ever go away?” If asked, swelling involves the dorsum of the foot and has become more persistent.
sections.4. Structured marking grid: Assessed domain Fail Pass High-performance Onset and pattern No chronology or acute versus gradual distinction. Establishes onset, progression, unilateral/bilateral distribution, fluctuation and functional impact. Asks whether swelling extends to the foot, response to elevation and increasing tissue firmness. Primary versus secondary risk Fails to ask about past surgery or cancer. Asks about cancer treatment, nodal surgery, radiotherapy, infection and injury; distinguishes possible primary disease. Recognises lymph-node surgery as likely secondary lymphatic damage and checks for recurrent disease symptoms. Urgent differential Labels all swelling lymphoedema despite possible DVT. Screens for DVT symptoms and risk, infection/cellulitis, acute limb pain, PE symptoms. Explains acute swelling or PE symptoms require urgent alternative pathway rather than routine compression. Other causes No venous/systemic differential. Considers chronic venous insufficiency, DVT/post-thrombotic syndrome and systemic oedema. Asks about medicines, immobility, cardiac/renal/hepatic symptoms and pelvic obstruction. Inspection and palpation Does not examine both legs or feet. Compares both legs including toe
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-critical actio: Fails to consider urgent DVT or pulmonary embolism in an acutely symptomatic patient. Recommends compression without assessing for significant arterial insufficiency or an acute contraindication. Misses suspected cellulitis with systemic illness and delays acute treatment. Attributes unexplained rapidly progressive swelling after cancer to benign lymphoedema without considering recurrence.
sections.6. Curveball and actor prompt: At minute 6, actor adds “Since this morning it has become hot, red and painful, and I feel shivery.” Expected: suspect cellulitis, check observations and systemic illness, arrange prompt acute assessment/treatment; do not continue routine lymphoedema counselling alone.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If you focused only on previous lymph node surgery: reopen the differential with new acute painful swelling and ask about DVT, infection and cancer recurrence. If you prescribed diuretics: correct to specialist-directed compression/decongestive management after vascular and clinical assessment; diuretics are not routine lymphoedema therapy. If you promised the leg would return to normal: acknowledge the condition is often chronic and focus on symptom reduction, skin care and sustained support.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “You had lymph-node surgery, so it is harmless water retention. Take a diuretic.” Ignores acute mimics and no physical assessment. Pass “This fits secondary lymphoedema after groin node surgery. I will examine both legs and feet, check skin and pulses, consider venous causes or infection, and refer you for fitted compression and skin/exercise advice.” High-performance “The pattern and positive Stemmer sign support lymphoedema, but neither excludes venous disease or recurrence when the story changes. We can improve control through a specialist programme, monitor skin and limb size, and act urgently if you develop cellulitis, sudden swelling or PE symptoms.”

stations.title: Clot Retention After TURP

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B B2-114 — Clot Retention After TURP Procedural / emergency urology • 9-minute practice station • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • 12 October 2026 AMaC educational marking framework; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Independent clinical review and duplicate-register clearance pending.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar covering the ward. A 72-year-old man is 12 hours after TURP. The nurse reports lower abdominal pain, visible haematuria and no catheter drainage although bladder irrigation is running. Explain and demonstrate verbally how you assess and manage the problem. You are not required to perform catheterisation on a model.
sections.2. Examiner brief and setting: At presentation: alert, distressed; BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 104/min, temperature 36.8°C, SpO₂ 97% on air; suprapubic tenderness and distension. Three-way catheter in situ with dark red fluid and clots in tubing; inflow irrigation bag has continued to empty but drainage bag shows minimal return. If requested: FBC Hb 105 g/L (preoperative 131 g/L), platelets 238 ×10⁹/L, INR 1.1, creatinine 103 µmol/L. A trained clinician performs gentle washout only after checking the system; 300 mL of clot-containing effluent is recovered and free drainage resumes. If missed, patient becomes pale, BP 86/52 mmHg and HR 126/min.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient asks, “My bladder feels like it is going to burst. Is the operation bleeding again?” He takes aspirin for coronary artery disease (last dose held according to pre-op plan). If candidate explains actions, patient agrees; if they continue irrigation with no outflow, actor reports worsening pain.
sections.4. Structured marking grid: Score observed behaviours. Mark each row with a specific descriptor; serious safety omissions may trigger a critical-fail review. Domain / observable action Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and immediate review Assumes low catheter output means oliguria; does not assess the painful bladder. Recognises visible haematuria, suprapubic pain and absent drainage as likely clot retention. Explicitly considers blocked catheter, bladder overdistension and ongoing postoperative haemorrhage; requests urgent bedside assessment. ABCDE and haemodynamic status Records a single BP but fails to evaluate active blood loss. Checks consciousness, BP, pulse, perfusion, observations and blood loss; repeats observations. Identifies signs of evolving shock, triggers urgent resuscitation and haemorrhage escalation when indicated. Catheter and bladder assessment Runs more irrigation into a non-draining catheter. Checks tubing for kinks, catheter drainage, bag, bladder distension and pain; pauses irrigation if blocked. Checks catheter patency and input-output discrepancy before restarting, preventing overdistension. Blood tests and access Does not request blood count or crossmatch despite ongoing bleed
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-critical actio: Continues inflow of irrigation into a blocked, non-draining catheter with an increasingly distended bladder. Forcefully flushes against resistance or pain, risking bladder injury after TURP. Fails to respond to haemodynamic deterioration or significant postoperative haemorrhage. Delays senior urology escalation despite persistent clot retention or falling haemoglobin.
sections.6. Curveball and actor prompt: At minute 5 the nurse says, “The irrigation bag has gone in, but almost nothing has come out, and his pain is worse.” Expected: stop inflow immediately, examine the system/bladder, ensure gentle trained washout and urgent urology support; never force fluid into an obstructed bladder.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If initially labelled renal oliguria: reassess the palpable bladder and irrigation balance; identify outflow obstruction rather than prescribe a fluid challenge alone. If CBI was started prematurely: stop irrigation, arrange gentle removal of established clots, confirm free outflow, then restart CBI safely. If the candidate initially overlooked blood loss: obtain repeat observations, FBC/clotting/group-and-save and activate resuscitation with urology if haemodynamic changes appear.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “Keep the irrigation running and check his urine output in an hour.” The catheter is blocked, pain rises and no urgent assessment occurs. Pass “This is likely clot retention after TURP. Stop irrigation while outflow is blocked, check the catheter and distended bladder, assess for bleeding, call urology and arrange gentle manual washout, then restart CBI once draining.” High-performance “I need to prevent bladder overdistension while assessing bleeding severity. I will reconcile irrigation input and effluent, arrange safe clot evacuation, monitor serial haemoglobin and observations, and prepare for cystoscopic haemostasis if retention or haemorrhage persists.”

stations.title: Raised PSA - Counselling

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B B2-115 — Raised PSA - Counselling Communication / urology • 9-minute practice station • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • 12 October 2026 AMaC educational marking framework; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Independent clinical review and duplicate-register clearance pending.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are seeing a 62-year-old man whose GP has referred him after a PSA of 7.2 ng/mL. He is worried he has prostate cancer. Explain what this result means, the diagnostic pathway and shared decisions about investigation. Do not claim he has a diagnosis.
sections.2. Examiner brief and setting: Actor is a 62-year-old man, generally well, with mild nocturia; no fever, haematuria or bone pain. No previous PSA result is available. On request: DRE by GP documented “smooth enlarged prostate, no suspicious nodule”; no family history known; no recent proven UTI. If candidate requests: repeat PSA considerations and urine testing can be discussed according to history, but do not delay appropriate suspected-cancer referral solely to repeat PSA. The candidate is expected to explain the specialist pathway, not to commit to a fixed MRI or biopsy outcome. Curveball at minute 6: patient says, “I have read that biopsies cause cancer to spread. Can I just have the gland removed instead?”
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: At start: “My brother says PSA 7.2 means cancer. Am I going to die?” Follow-up questions include “Can a scan tell me?”, “What are the risks of biopsy?” and “Could I avoid treatment if a small cancer is found?” Patient values sexual function and avoiding unnecessary surgery.
sections.4. Structured marking grid: Score observed behaviours. Mark each row with a specific descriptor; serious safety omissions may trigger a critical-fail review. Domain / observable action Fail Pass High-performance Rapport and concerns Opens with a statement that the patient has cancer. Asks the patient’s understanding and primary worry; provides calm, non-alarmist explanation. Checks what the patient hopes to know and tailors information to health literacy and preference. Interpretation of PSA Says a raised PSA diagnoses prostate cancer. Explains PSA is prostate-related, not cancer-specific; can rise with benign enlargement or inflammation. Interprets in age, symptoms, trend, examination and risk context; avoids false reassurance. Relevant clinical history Asks only about urinary frequency. Asks about LUTS, infection, haematuria, bone pain, previous PSA testing and family history. Asks about recent infection/instrumentation, medicines and prior investigations that affect interpretation. Examination and referral Ignores abnormal DRE or assumes normal DRE excludes cancer. Discusses DRE, symptoms and threshold-based referral; arranges suspected-cancer referral when indicated. Separates urgent cancer concern from c
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-critical actio: Falsely tells the patient that raised PSA proves prostate cancer, causing serious misinformation. Dismisses the elevated PSA and provides no appropriate referral or follow-up plan. Promises no cancer solely because DRE is smooth or MRI might be negative. Recommends prostate surgery or biopsy as compulsory without explaining alternatives and shared decision making.
sections.6. Curveball and actor prompt: Patient: “Can you remove my prostate now rather than wait for a scan?” Expected: acknowledge anxiety, explain risk of unnecessary surgery and major side effects, and outline MRI-based assessment followed by an individualised biopsy/treatment decision.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If the candidate said “You have cancer”: explicitly correct it — PSA is not diagnostic — and apologise for the imprecise wording. If biopsy was presented as inevitable: explain MRI and clinical risk guide the need for biopsy and the patient can discuss benefits and harms. If the patient remains distressed about death: explain that an elevated PSA has several causes, summarise timely referral and agree a named follow-up route.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “A PSA over seven means prostate cancer. You need a biopsy and probably removal of your prostate.” No explanation of uncertainty or choice. Pass “PSA can rise for reasons other than cancer, but this result warrants further assessment. We will organise appropriate urology referral; MRI often guides whether a biopsy is useful. We will explain the options and risks before any decision.” High-performance “I can see why the number worries you. We cannot diagnose cancer from PSA alone. We will assess your overall risk, refer through the appropriate pathway, discuss MRI and potential biopsy, and make choices around what matters most to you, including avoiding unnecessary treatment.”
