sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | B2-116 Examination of the Scrotum DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Physical examination • 9-minute station • Internal review only Educational simulated station; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Final station ID assigned by AMaC. Live register duplicate clearance and independent clinical sign-off outstanding.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: Introduce yourself, verify identity, explain an intimate scrotal examination and obtain explicit consent. Explain chaperone availability; ask about pain and whether the patient wishes to proceed. Demonstrate a structured examination and interpret the findings. Explain investigations and the immediate plan to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Provide privacy, drape, and a model; do not require touching an actual actor. Patient is afebrile and stable. If asked: no acute onset pain, trauma, dysuria, urethral discharge or systemic symptoms. Examination: right testis contains a firm 2-cm non-tender intratesticular nodule; does not transilluminate; left testis normal; no obvious skin changes. If asked about imaging: no scan yet. Assess whether the candidate initiates appropriate urgent specialist action without implying ultrasound replaces suspected-cancer referral.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: 35-year-old; swelling discovered in shower, painless, growing slowly over three weeks. Anxious when cancer is mentioned; asks: “Could it just be a cyst?” If asked, no previous undescended testis, no fertility issues, no fever, no sudden pain.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Judge the demonstrated action, not keywords alone. Critical rows marked ★. Descriptors are row-specific; apply global critical fails separately. Domain / action Fail Pass High-performance 1. ★ Consent, privacy and chaperone Starts intimate examination without consent or privacy. Explains, obtains consent, offers chaperone, maintains draping. Checks comfort and permission at each stage; documents chaperone choice.
sections.2. Presenting symptoms: Fails to clarify pain or evolution. Asks onset, progression, pain and associated urinary/systemic symptoms. Specifically rules out sudden severe pain, fever and constitutional symptoms.
sections.3. Inspection: Omits visual scrotal inspection. Inspects standing/supine as appropriate for asymmetry, skin, scars and swelling. Assesses for erythema, scars, visible veins and groin swelling without unnecessary exposure.
sections.4. Palpate each testis: Does not identify testis separately from mass. Palpates each testis systematically for size, consistency, tenderness and mass. Correctly localises hard nodule to testis and contrasts both sides.
sections.5. Epididymis and cord: Ignores epididymis/cord. Palpates epididymis and spermatic cord separately. Uses their relationships to distinguish epididymal cyst, varicocele and intratesticular mass.

stations.title: Fournier’s Gangrene

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | B2-117 Fournier’s Gangrene DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Critical care • 9-minute station • Internal review only Educational simulated station; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Final station ID assigned by AMaC. Live register duplicate clearance and independent clinical sign-off outstanding.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: Lead the initial assessment of a severely unwell patient; state the immediate bedside actions. Identify the likely diagnosis and initiate safe treatment. Explain your definitive treatment plan and escalation, including when imaging might be appropriate. Hand over to the receiving senior surgeon.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Observations: T 39.1°C; HR 128/min; BP 88/54 mmHg; RR 28/min; SpO₂ 95% air; alert but distressed. If asked: severe pain out of proportion, rapidly progressive swelling, diabetes, no recent surgery; perineal skin oedema, dusky patches and crepitus. Bloods if requested: WCC 19 x10^9/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 175 μmol/L. Blood cultures can be taken promptly but must not delay antibiotics. Theatre team and urology/colorectal senior are available if called. CT could define extent only if it will not delay resuscitation or urgent debridement.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: severe pain, frightened; says “Can you just give me tablets?” If asked: urinary symptoms and discomfort began yesterday and deteriorated rapidly. Examiner plays nurse for urgent actions and registrar for handover.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Judge the demonstrated action, not keywords alone. Critical rows marked ★. Descriptors are row-specific; apply global critical fails separately. Domain / action Fail Pass High-performance 1. ★ Recognition Calls it uncomplicated cellulitis/abscess without considering necrotising infection. Recognises suspected Fournier’s gangrene / necrotising perineal soft-tissue infection. Links disproportionate pain, systemic toxicity, dusky skin and possible crepitus to time-critical source control. 2. ★ Call for help Plans outpatient treatment or delayed junior review. Calls senior urology/general-colorectal surgery, anaesthetics and critical care urgently. Explicitly activates emergency theatre coordination with simultaneous resuscitation.
sections.3. ABCDE: Only examines the perineum and misses shock. Performs ABCDE, observations, oxygen if needed and continuous monitoring. Repeatedly reassesses perfusion, consciousness and respiratory effort as shock evolves. 4. ★ Access and resuscitation Does not obtain IV access or address hypotension. Requests two IV cannulas, bloods including FBC/U&E/CRP/coagulation/lactate, cultures and prompt IV crystalloid resuscitation. Uses small reassessed boluses appropriate to physiology, tracks urine output and anticipates vasopressors with ICU if fluid-refractory. 5. ★ Antibiotic therapy Delays antibiotics pending CT or cultures. Starts prompt IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local necrotising infection/sepsis protocol; reviews allergies and renal function. States need for broad Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, microbiology input and subsequent culture-directed narrowing.
sections.6. Examination and extent: Does not assess perineal findings or pain. Describes careful genital, perineal and perianal examination with privacy, consent and analgesia. Recognises extent can exceed visible skin changes; documents rapid progression and likely source.
sections.7. Imaging decision: Insists on CT before referral/debridement in an unstable patient. States CT may help in stable patients if no delay to surgery. Clearly prioritises theatre if clinical suspicion is high and patient unstable; imaging must not postpone source control. 8. ★ Surgery and source control Treats with antibiotics alone or plans next-day routine debridement. Requests emergency exploration and debridement of necrotic tissue, with planned reassessment and further debridement as needed. Anticipates multidisciplinary operative assessment, repeated debridement and tissue samples without delaying initial surgery.
sections.9. Handover and aftercare: Fails to state diagnosis, shock or next action. Provides SBAR including vitals, suspected diagnosis, antibiotics, fluids and theatre request. Adds lactate, renal injury, response, analgesia, glycaemic control, ICU needs and explicit closed-loop ownership.

stations.source_heading: B2-120 Recurrent UTI in a Man

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-120 — Recurrent UTI in a Man History / applied management • 9-minute practice station • Draft: 12 October 2026 • Final MB ID pending Status: PROVISIONAL — independent clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check required. Not an official MRCS mark scheme. 1 | Candidate instructions You are the surgical/urology SHO in clinic. A 67-year-old man has had three treated episodes of dysuria over the last 9 months. Take a focused history and explain the investigations and initial management. The examiner may provide examination findings and previous urine results if requested. No intimate examination is performed in this station. 2 | Examiner brief Observations: afebrile, BP 132/76, pulse 78. Mildly enlarged non-tender prostate, no palpable bladder; no loin tenderness. Urine cultures from two attacks grew E. coli; one was resistant to trimethoprim. Current symptoms have settled after antibiotics. On questioning: weak stream, hesitancy and nocturia for two years; no visible haematuria. Creatinine within normal range. No catheter. 3 | Patient / actor instructions Friendly but frustrated: “Why does this keep coming back? Can I just take antibiotics perma
sections.1. Establish episodes and cultures: Accepts repeated “UTI” labels without dates, culture results or treatment history. Asks number/timing of episodes, documented symptoms, urine cultures, antibiotics and response. Distinguishes relapse from reinfection and reviews susceptibilities, specimen quality and previous resistance.
sections.2. Characterise urinary symptoms: Only asks about dysuria; fails to consider urinary obstruction. Elicits dysuria, urgency, frequency, haematuria, stream, hesitancy, nocturia and incomplete emptying. Quantifies LUTS, asks post-void dribbling and retention and relates episodes to voiding difficulty.
sections.3. Identify danger features: Misses fever, flank pain or acute retention. Screens for fever, rigors, loin pain, vomiting, retention and systemic illness. States fever/systemic features require assessment for pyelonephritis/prostatitis and urgent sepsis escalation if unwell.
sections.4. Probe alternative and underlying caus: Attributes all symptoms to simple cystitis. Asks about stones, instrumentation/catheters, diabetes, prostate symptoms and sexual health/STI exposure. Explores perineal pain/ejaculatory pain suggesting prostatitis, prior urological surgery and immunosuppression without assuming STI.
sections.5. Examination plan: No observations, abdomen or genital assessment. Proposes observations, abdomen/loin, bladder distension, genital examination and indicated prostate assessment. Prioritises haemodynamic assessment if ill; contextualises DRE and avoids prostatic massage in suspected acute prostatitis.
sections.6. Urine testing: Treats empirically without requesting urine culture. Obtains mid-stream urine for culture/susceptibility before antibiotics where feasible. Reviews previous cultures and adjusts treatment to susceptibilities; avoids interpreting asymptomatic bacteriuria as recurrent symptomatic infection.
sections.7. Further investigations: Orders CT and cystoscopy for all without rationale or overlooks obstruction. Checks renal function; considers post-void residual and renal tract imaging based on obstruction, stones or red flags. Explains that specialist-directed imaging/cystoscopy are selective, not automatic; considers haematuria cancer pathway separately.
sections.8. Treatment and stewardship: Offers indefinite prophylaxis without work-up or treats a positive culture with no symptoms. Manages active infection per local sensitivities, reviews response and advises hydration/voiding measures. Reviews recurrent triggers and medicines, avoids automatic long-term antibiotics, and uses culture-led reassessment for relapse.

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-121 — Paraphimosis Procedural / urgent management • 9-minute practice station • Draft: 12 October 2026 • Final MB ID pending Status: PROVISIONAL — independent clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check required. Not an official MRCS mark scheme. 1 | Candidate instructions You are the on-call surgical SHO. A 52-year-old uncircumcised man has painful penile swelling after a catheter was inserted earlier today. Explain your diagnosis and demonstrate verbally how you would manage it on a model. Use the anatomical model provided; do not perform the manoeuvre on an actor. The examiner will provide a response to your first attempt. 2 | Examiner brief Glans swollen and erythematous, with a tight ring of retracted foreskin proximal to the corona. Symptoms began 3 hours ago. The glans is still pink and sensate; he can pass urine. The catheter was inserted then removed after a trial without catheter; the foreskin was not replaced. If candidate describes appropriate analgesia and compression/reduction: swelling reduces but the first manual attempt fails; senior urologist available urgently. 3 | Patient / actor instructions Embarrassed and in pain; asks
sections.1. Recognise emergency: Describes paraphimosis as harmless phimosis and arranges routine review. Identifies a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans as an urgent urological emergency. Explains venous/lymphatic obstruction progressing to impaired arterial perfusion and possible tissue necrosis.
sections.2. Urgency and initial assessment: Leaves patient in waiting room without pain or circulation assessment. Assesses onset, pain, ability to pass urine, glans colour and systemic observations. Asks about catheter/instrumentation and immediately identifies duskiness, inability to void or marked ischaemia as urgent senior triggers.
sections.3. Consent, dignity and analgesia: Manipulates without consent, chaperone offer or analgesia. Explains manoeuvre, obtains consent, offers chaperone and gives suitable analgesia/local anaesthesia. Uses calm language, offers privacy and anticipates discomfort, checking understanding throughout.
sections.4. Identify constricting ring: Attempts unrelated scrotal procedure or fails to inspect the glans. Describes oedematous glans with a tight preputial ring behind corona. Checks skin viability and distinguishes phimosis (cannot retract) from paraphimosis (cannot replace).
sections.5. Gentle reduction technique: Forcefully pulls swollen foreskin without compression or stops without plan. Describes gentle sustained compression of oedematous glans/foreskin followed by pushing glans back while bringing foreskin forward. Coordinates pain control, controlled compression and gentle sustained technique; stops traumatic repeated attempts.
sections.6. Escalation if unsuccessful: Repeatedly tries for prolonged time despite worsening ischaemia. Calls urgent urology senior if manual reduction fails. States senior may perform urgent dorsal slit or other definitive release; does not let preparations delay restoring perfusion.
sections.7. Following successful reduction: Leaves foreskin retracted or does not re-examine. Confirms foreskin covers glans and reassesses colour, perfusion, pain and passing urine. Documents procedure, reassesses swelling and explains recurrence prevention after complete resolution.
sections.8. Counselling and prevention: Tells patient to retract and leave foreskin behind the glans. Advises returning foreskin to natural position after washing, sex or catheter care; discusses follow-up. Explains possible elective circumcision for recurrence/scarring, using shared decision-making rather than implying it is mandatory after first episode.

stations.title: Ureteric Stone Treatment Options

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B — B2-122 Ureteric Stone: Treatment Options Group 12 · Data interpretation / applied urology · 9 minutes · Development draft — not an official MRCS mark scheme Station purpose: Interpret a written CT report and choose observation, medical expulsive therapy or intervention; identify when immediate decompression is necessary.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee asked to discuss a CT urinary tract report and make an initial treatment plan for a 42-year-old with flank pain. You have 9 minutes. Explain your interpretation and management to the examiner; you may request further observations and tests.
sections.2. Examiner case and written data: 42-year-old, colicky left flank pain for 8 hours, now improved after analgesia. CT KUB: 6 mm calculus in distal left ureter, mild upstream hydroureteronephrosis, no other stones. sections.1. Introduction, consent and pain [SC]: Starts touching knee without introduction or consent; forces movement despite pain. sections.1. Candidate brief: A 24-year-old right-handed patient fell onto an outstretched left hand playing football 6 hours ago. They have persistent pain on the thumb side of the wrist. sections.2. Examiner brief and station setup: Provide the written imaging report only: “Left wrist PA, lateral and dedicated scaphoid views: normal alignment; no visible fracture or dislocation.” No actual image needed. sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Reports fall onto extended left wrist; persistent 6/10 radial wrist pain; difficulty gripping and lifting. Anxious about work absence; asks why treatment is necessary if film normal. No fever or other injuries. Will accept splint if rationale explained.

Arrange MRI as first-line imaging consideration and timely fracture/hand pathway with named follow-up responsibility; give warnings.

sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in an emergency department. Explain your assessment and demonstrate with a forearm model your preparation, reduction principles, immobilisation, checks and disposition. You may ask for equipment and X-ray findings.
sections.2. Examiner brief / setup: 62-year-old right-handed woman fell on an outstretched hand. sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The simulated patient says the wrist is very painful; asks whether she will need an operation. If analgesia is discussed, she is willing to consent. She reports new tingling in thumb/index finger only if specifically asked in the curveball.

Explains red
sections.6. Critical fails (unsafe actions): Missing evolving median nerve compression or vascular compromise before/after reduction.
