sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar in the emergency department. A 7-year-old child has fallen on an outstretched arm. The distal humeral fracture is displaced. The radial pulse is not palpable. Explain your immediate assessment, management and communication with the parent and orthopaedic consultant. You may request further examination findings and a written X-ray report from the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: On request: HR 118, BP 105/65; severe elbow pain; intact skin, moderate swelling, no skin puckering. Written X-ray: displaced extension-type supracondylar humeral fracture. Initial hand: pink and warm; capillary refill 2 seconds; radial pulse not palpable. Doppler signal may be detectable. Median/anterior interosseous motor (OK sign), radial nerve (thumb extension), ulnar nerve (finger abduction) should be tested and documented along with sensation. If the candidate asks specifically about deteriorating perfusion: the hand becomes cool and pale with refill 5 seconds. This constitutes a threatened limb requiring immediate senior action. After reduction and fixation, pulse remains absent but hand is pink and well perfused; examiner tests whether the candidate automatically demands vascular exploration.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Parent: “His hand looks fine to me, so can we just get a plaster and go home?” You are anxious but cooperative. If asked, child has no previous health problems or allergies. Do not volunteer neurological findings unless examiner provides them.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Domain / weight Fail Pass High-performance ★ Perfusion triage (critical) Treats absent pulse as harmless or labels pink hand as definitely ischaemic. Checks colour, warmth, refill and radial pulse; identifies pink pulseless versus pale ischaemic hand. Repeats and records serial perfusion and distinguishes change in vascular status from absent palpable pulse alone. ★ Immediate escalation (critical) Discharges child or defers senior review. Calls urgent paediatric orthopaedic consultant and prepares urgent reduction/fixation. Coordinates theatre/anaesthesia promptly; communicates potential vascular compromise and need for transfer if capability absent. Neurovascular examination Documents “NV intact” without testing. Tests median/AIN, ulnar and radial nerve motor/sensory function and documents perfusion. Records reproducible baseline findings before and after manipulation with comparison and timed serial checks. Imaging and diagnosis Misreads findings or delays necessary action awaiting extra imaging. Identifies displaced supracondylar fracture on written report and relevant urgency. Highlights displacement and soft-tissue risk without requesting angiography to delay threatened-limb t
sections.5. Critical fails: Discharging or delaying management solely because the pulseless hand looks pink. Failing to act on a pale, cold, poorly perfused hand after reduction. Omitting documented nerve and perfusion examination before and after reduction. Using Doppler/capillary refill alone to exclude arterial injury while perfusion worsens.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: After reduction, the radial pulse remains absent but the fingers are warm, pink and have normal refill. Does the child automatically need brachial artery exploration? Expected: no, not solely for an absent pulse if the limb is well perfused; ongoing close observations and consultant-directed management are essential.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If initial examination was incomplete: “Before moving forward I need to record finger perfusion and median/AIN, ulnar and radial nerve function now.” If a deteriorating hand is disclosed: “The limb is now ischaemic; urgent consultant-led reduction and vascular-capable exploration are required—do not wait for angiography.” If they incorrectly requested universal exploration: “A pulseless but warm, pink hand after reduction may be observed closely; perfusion, not pulse alone, guides exploration.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “There is no pulse but his hand looks okay, so we can put him in plaster and review tomorrow.” No nerve assessment or senior involvement. Pass “This is a displaced supracondylar fracture with an absent radial pulse. I will document circulation and nerve function, give analgesia, keep him nil by mouth and urgently involve paediatric orthopaedics for reduction and fixation. I will check circulation again and monitor carefully.” High-performance “I distinguish a perfused pulseless hand from a cold ischaemic hand; both demand prompt senior assessment and stabilisation. Persistent ischaemia after reduction needs immediate vascular-capable exploration, whereas a warm perfused hand need not undergo routine arterial exploration solely for absent pulse. Document serial checks and escalation thresholds.”

stations.title: Back Pain in a Patient with Cancer
stations.source_heading: B2-131 Back Pain in a Patient with Cancer

sections.preamble: AMaC • MRCS PART B • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT B2-131 — Back Pain in a Patient with Cancer Suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) | 9-minute emergency referral station. Station duration: 9 minutes | Format: Clinical assessment and emergency management Status: PROVISIONAL — independent clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate clearance required. Educational simulation; not an official examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar assessing a 66-year-old patient with metastatic prostate cancer, new severe thoracic back pain and worsening walking difficulty. Take a focused history from the patient, explain your immediate assessment and management and communicate the emergency plan. You can ask the examiner for examination findings and the written imaging report.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: On request: 10-day progressive nocturnal thoracic pain, 24-hour bilateral leg weakness and tingling; new difficulty initiating urine. No fever or trauma. Examination: lower-limb power 3–4/5, brisk knee reflexes, extensor plantar responses; reduced pinprick below the umbilicus; bladder scan shows 520 mL residual. Haemodynamically stable. No scan yet. If candidate requests MRI, radiologist can arrange urgent whole-spine MRI and MSCC coordinator is available. If candidate asks about stability: severe mechanical pain on movement—treat as potentially unstable pending expert assessment. Curveball: patient asks whether a plain X-ray first would be quicker.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You are concerned about becoming paralysed and ask “Do I have to lie still?” If asked about pain, it becomes worse when sitting up. If asked about continence, difficulty initiating urine began today. Request clear explanation and involvement in decisions.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Domain / weight Fail Pass High-performance ★ Recognition and urgency (critical) Labels weakness as ordinary cancer pain; plans routine outpatient follow-up. Recognises suspected MSCC as emergency based on cancer, pain, progressive weakness and bladder symptoms. Names spinal cord compression and irreversible neurological risk; initiates pathway immediately without waiting for MRI result. Focused symptoms Asks only about pain score. Elicits pain pattern, mobility change, weakness, sensory and bladder/bowel symptoms. Establishes onset and rate of deterioration, gait/falls, radicular pain and functional baseline. Neurological examination Does not assess legs or bladder. Documents lower-limb power, reflexes, sensory level, gait safety and sphincter/retention concerns. Records serial motor/sensory findings and objective bladder assessment without delaying referral. ★ Specialist escalation (critical) Does not contact MSCC coordinator or spinal service. Immediately alerts MSCC coordinator and relevant oncology/spinal team. Gives concise SBAR including cancer, deterioration, neurological findings, pain and need for urgent MRI and definitive plan. ★ Imaging (critical) Orders plain X-ray or d
sections.5. Critical fails: Failing to recognise acute neurological deficits in a cancer patient as suspected MSCC. Leaving MRI as routine outpatient imaging or using normal plain radiographs to exclude MSCC. Not escalating immediately to the MSCC pathway / specialist team. Mobilising a patient with suspected unstable spinal disease and worsening neurology without specialist assessment.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: The patient asks: “Can we just do an X-ray tonight and my MRI next week?” Expected: plain X-ray cannot rule out MSCC; urgent whole-spine MRI as soon as possible and within 24 hours, with specialist contact now.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If initially called ordinary pain: “New progressive weakness and retention change this into suspected MSCC; I am activating the emergency pathway now.” If only lumbar imaging requested: “Compression may be at more than one level. The MRI must assess the whole spine.” If patient has been mobilised: “We will help you into a safe, comfortable position and obtain urgent spinal-stability advice; do not walk unassisted.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “It may be muscular pain; I’ll arrange an X-ray and see how you are next week.” Does not identify neurological emergency. Pass “Your cancer, new back pain, leg weakness and bladder symptoms may mean pressure on the spinal cord. I am contacting the MSCC team now, organising urgent whole-spine MRI within 24 hours and starting appropriate steroid treatment.” High-performance “I will document the neurological level and changes, activate the MSCC coordinator and oncology/spinal service immediately, arrange the earliest whole-spine MRI, start dexamethasone 16 mg, assess potential instability before movement and plan supportive care. I will explain that urgent surgery or radiotherapy depends on specialist review.”

stations.title: After a Fragility Fracture

near_match.title: Fragility Fracture After a Simple Fall / The Wrist Is the Warning, the Hip Is the Risk

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | STATION DRAFT B2-132 — After a Fragility Fracture Type: Communication / secondary prevention | Time: 9 minutes | Status: PROVISIONAL · 12 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 74-year-old woman is attending fracture clinic six weeks after a distal radius fracture following a fall from standing height. The fracture was treated in a cast. She asks whether her bone is now fragile and what can prevent another fracture.Your task: Explain the significance of the fracture, assess future fracture and falls risk, and agree an evidence-based prevention and follow-up plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Observations stable; wrist healing as expected. No new neurological deficit. No known fracture-risk assessment or DXA. Local fracture liaison service is available.Provide only findings requested by the candidate. Assess applied judgement, patient-centred communication and safe completion, not recital of facts.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You are 74, independent, and worried about a hip fracture. You have fallen twice in a year while rushing to the toilet. No osteoporosis treatment. You take intermittent oral prednisolone for inflammatory arthritis; your mother fractured her hip. You ask if a normal bone density scan would mean no risk. If asked, you have not had a falls or medication review.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Fracture significance Calls it only an accident; gives no bone-health explanation. Explains that a low-trauma fracture is a warning of increased future fragility-fracture risk. Uses plain language to explain imminent re-fracture risk and invites concerns about independence. Risk history Omits steroid exposure, prior falls and parental hip fracture. Asks about previous fractures, falls, glucocorticoids, smoking, alcohol and parental hip fracture. Also asks about height loss/back pain, menopause, mobility, nutrition and other secondary causes. Falls and physical assessment Does not enquire into mechanism or falls risk. Assesses gait/balance, vision, postural symptoms, home hazards and medication-related falls risk. Targets her rushing-to-toilet falls with toileting plan and strength/balance referral. Formal fracture risk Assures on basis of a healed wrist. Proposes FRAX-based risk stratification and FLS assessment. Explains that an existing fragility fracture itself can warrant prompt treatment assessment. BMD imaging States DXA mandatory before any treatment. Explains DXA can refine risk and aid monitoring where appropriate. Clarifies that normal or
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe actions: 1. Fails to recognise a low-trauma fracture as a sentinel event and makes no secondary-prevention plan. 2. Dismisses repeated falls without any falls risk or safety response. 3. Reassures that normal DXA excludes clinically important fracture risk despite her fragility fracture. 4. Recommends medication without accounting for major contraindications or necessary clinical review.
sections.6. Curveball and response: She says: “My friend had a normal DXA. If mine is normal, can I forget about osteoporosis?”Safe response: “A scan helps us understand risk, but your wrist fracture and falls already tell us prevention matters. We should assess you properly and not use one scan result as the whole answer.”
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: • If steroid exposure was missed: revisit medication history and ask dose/duration of prednisolone, then flag glucocorticoid-related fracture risk. • If DXA was described as compulsory: correct explicitly that treatment can be considered after a fragility fracture even if DXA is delayed or impractical. • If falls were underexplored: address her two falls and toileting urgency, arrange balance assessment and a practical falls-prevention plan.
sections.8. Model performance bands: Fail: “Your wrist is healing. Take calcium and ask your GP if you need a scan.” [Misses the sentinel fracture, falls risk and definitive referral.] Pass: “This wrist fracture from a standing-height fall suggests fragility risk. I will arrange FLS assessment, review falls and medicines, use FRAX and consider DXA and appropriate bone protection.” [Pass.] High-performance: “I’m glad your wrist is recovering, but this tells us you may be at risk of another fracture. We will assess your falls and steroid exposure now, arrange coordinated bone and falls assessment, discuss treatment without unnecessary delay and agree what matters most to keeping you independent.” [High-performance.]

stations.title: Consent for Total Hip Replacement
stations.source_heading: B2-133 Consent for Total Hip Replacement

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | STATION DRAFT B2-133 — Consent for Total Hip Replacement Type: Communication / consent | Time: 9 minutes | Status: PROVISIONAL · 12 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 68-year-old patient with painful left hip osteoarthritis is considering elective primary total hip replacement. Walking to the shops is difficult despite physiotherapy, activity modification and analgesics. They ask for a balanced explanation before making a decision.Your task: Conduct a shared decision-making and consent discussion for primary total hip replacement, including benefits, alternatives, material risks and recovery.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: X-ray description: advanced left hip osteoarthritis with severe joint-space narrowing. Normal observations. No prior hip surgery; no listed medication allergies. Final implant choice, anaesthetic risk and personalised risk estimates require surgical and anaesthetic assessment.Provide only findings requested by the candidate. Assess applied judgement, patient-centred communication and safe completion, not recital of facts.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You are 68 and value independent walking and gardening. You are anxious because a relative developed an infection after surgery. You want to know whether the operated leg can be longer, whether the artificial hip lasts forever and when you can drive. No known cognitive impairment. You have hypertension and mild obesity. If rushed, say you are not ready to sign today.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Patient goals Begins with a standard script and ignores concerns. Asks what pain and disability matter most and patient goals. Uses walking, gardening and infection worries to personalise the discussion. Indication and benefits Guarantees complete pain relief or perfect movement. Explains realistic pain/function improvement, limitations and uncertainty. Sets expectations against preoperative function and rehabilitation. Procedure overview Does not explain what is replaced. Describes replacing the damaged ball and socket with prosthetic components in accessible terms. Explains implant/fixation choices are discussed with surgeon, without implying one suits everyone. Alternatives Implies surgery is mandatory. Discusses continued non-operative care and option to delay or decline. Explains why options may be less effective now, reflecting impact on quality of life. Material surgical risks Omits infection or dislocation. Covers infection, dislocation, VTE, bleeding, fracture and neurovascular injury. Frames individual relevance and acknowledges rare but serious complications and death. Long-term and function risks Promises implant lifetime or equal leg l
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe actions: 1. Pressures the patient to sign despite explicitly asking for time to decide. 2. Conceals or dismisses the patient’s expressed concern about major infection risk. 3. Guarantees complete pain relief or promises there is no chance of complications. 4. Omits reasonable alternatives and the option not to undergo surgery.
sections.6. Curveball and response: “My neighbour says her leg became longer. Can you guarantee my legs will be equal, and that I can drive after four weeks?”Safe response: “A difference in leg length can happen, and we work to minimise it, but cannot promise an exact match. Driving depends on safe control of the car, medication, recovery and your team’s advice—not simply a fixed number of weeks.”
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: • If risks were presented as a rote list: return to infection specifically, elicit personal concerns and check understanding. • If a definitive driving date was promised: correct the statement and give functional/clinical criteria for return. • If the patient felt pushed to sign: acknowledge this, explicitly offer time and a later decision with the surgical team.
sections.8. Model performance bands: Fail: “The operation is routine, it will stop pain and you can sign today.” [Fails informed consent and misrepresents certainty.] Pass: “Replacement may improve pain and mobility, but there are alternatives and risks including infection, dislocation, clots, leg-length difference and later revision. You can take time to decide.” [Pass.] High-performance: “You’ve said getting back to gardening matters most, while infection is your major worry. Let’s compare continued non-surgical care with replacement, discuss the risks that matter to you, and agree time for questions and a decision you’re comfortable with.” [High-performance.]

stations.title: Bleeding After Tonsillectomy

sections.preamble: B2-135 | Bleeding After Tonsillectomy AMaC MRCS Part B • ENT / critical care • 9-minute station • Editorial draft: 12 October 2026 PROVISIONAL — independent clinical review, local protocol confirmation and live-register duplicate check required. Educational station; not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical trainee called to the emergency department. A 19-year-old arrives eight days after tonsillectomy with fresh bleeding from the mouth and repeated swallowing.Task: Prioritise initial assessment and resuscitation, explain emergency escalation and definitive haemostasis, and decide on safe disposition.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings: Observations: HR 124/min, BP 98/60, RR 24, SpO₂ 96% room air, pale and anxious. Blood-stained saliva and a small clot in the left tonsillar fossa. They describe two episodes of bright red bleeding and nausea, swallowed blood likely. An airway-trained anaesthetist and ENT consultant can attend immediately. Do not require examination that risks disturbing the clot. Blood count, coagulation, group and crossmatch are available but must not delay resuscitation. Secondary bleeding is after 24 hours; sentinel bleeding can precede significant haemorrhage.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: “It was just a little blood earlier but it keeps coming back. I feel faint.” If prompted: last ate 4 hours ago, no known bleeding disorder or anticoagulants. Later spits out a large amount of fresh blood. If the candidate says go home, ask, “Are you sure it is safe?”
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Judge the candidate against observable actions; no compensating for a serious safety failure by polished presentation. Performance bands: Fail / Pass / High-performance. Domain Fail Pass High-performance 01 Recognises emergency [critical] Labels bleeding as normal postoperative spotting and reassures home. Identifies secondary post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage as a potentially life-threatening emergency. Recognises recurrent small bleeds and repeated swallowing as possible concealed haemorrhage. 02 Airway first [critical] Lays patient flat, forces examination or ignores aspiration risk. Assesses airway, calls ENT and anaesthetics urgently, positions sitting forward if tolerated, provides suction and oxygen as indicated. Prepares senior-led difficult-airway plan and avoids disrupting clot while supporting effective suction. 03 Circulation and shock [critical] Ignores tachycardia or waits for hypotension to become profound. Assesses shock, establishes large-bore IV access, monitors and starts indicated resuscitation. Requests help with haemorrhage protocol when severe, assesses perfusion and trends repeated observations. 04 Bloods and blood products Does not order blood group / crossmat
sections.5. Critical fails: Discharges a patient with active or recurrent post-tonsillectomy bleeding without emergency ENT review. Fails to call experienced airway/ENT assistance during brisk haemorrhage or airway compromise. Attempts traumatic blind clot removal or provokes bleeding with inappropriate throat manipulation. Fails to resuscitate a haemodynamically compromised patient or delays intervention pending laboratory results.
sections.6. Curveball: The patient suddenly spits a large volume of bright red blood and becomes drowsy. Expected: activate resuscitation/emergency ENT and anaesthetics, protect airway with senior expertise, suction, IV access, haemorrhage response and urgent haemostasis in theatre.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If you dismissed a small bleed: “Any fresh post-tonsillectomy bleeding may be a sentinel event; I would involve ENT now even if it appears to stop.” If you focused only on blood tests: “I will resuscitate and call ENT/anaesthetics immediately; blood results must not delay treatment.” If you planned throat manipulation: “I would not dislodge the clot or attempt uncontrolled instrumentation; airway and definitive control take priority.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “The tonsil bed looks as expected; I will check a haemoglobin and discharge if it stops.” Does not secure airway support or recognise shock. Pass “This is a secondary post-tonsillectomy bleed. I am calling ENT and anaesthetics, moving to resus, assessing airway and circulation, placing IV access and crossmatching blood. Persistent or severe bleeding needs theatre.” High-performance “Despite a small visible clot there may be major swallowed blood loss. Keep forward with suction if tolerated, continuous monitoring, rapid haemorrhage support, senior airway plan and urgent ENT haemostasis; prevent aspiration and document repeat bleeding.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Any fresh post-tonsillectomy bleed may herald major haemorrhage. SAY: “This can become serious quickly; we are calling ENT and anaesthetics now.” DO: Airway/suction, resuscitation, IV access, bloods/crossmatch, ENT and anaesthesia. FINISH: Continuous observation, named handover and theatre if ongoing or significant bleed. TRAP: Never discharge after an apparent sentinel bleed or disturb a tonsillar clot. NUMBERS: Secondary haemorrhage: more than 24 hours after surgery.

stations.title: Facial Weakness

sections.preamble: B2-136 — Facial Weakness AMaC Medical Education | MRCS Part B | Draft for clinical review | 12 October 2026 9-minute practice station • Educational simulation; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Final MB- ID assigned only after publication review.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to assess a 42-year-old adult with a new one-sided facial weakness noticed yesterday. Perform a focused facial and neurological examination on the simulated patient, explain your differential and outline immediate management.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Provide normal observations. Examination: right forehead cannot wrinkle; weak right eye closure, flattened right nasolabial fold, asymmetric smile; no limb weakness, aphasia or ataxia. Ear canal clear and no parotid mass. If candidate asks, eye feels gritty. Ask candidate specifically how to keep the eye safe. Never reveal absent stroke features unless examined/asked.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: right side of face droops from yesterday morning; cannot fully close right eyelid, no arm weakness or speech change. No trauma, ear vesicles or hearing loss. Worried about stroke. If asked, onset was gradual over 3 hours, and there is mild altered taste.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Mark each row against the described behaviours; safety-critical rows are marked ★. Descriptors are behavioural anchors, not a mechanical score. Domain Fail Pass High-performance ★ Immediate triage Dismisses new facial weakness as Bell’s without asking onset or associated deficits. Establishes time of onset and screens for speech, limb and visual symptoms. States that sudden facial weakness with other focal signs warrants immediate stroke assessment, checking glucose. History Asks only whether the face is weak. Asks onset, progression, ear pain, vesicles, hearing symptoms, trauma and preceding illness. Adds tick exposure, parotid symptoms, previous episodes and risk factors while remaining concise. Facial nerve exam Does not compare sides or check eye closure. Tests eyebrow elevation, eye closure, smile, cheek inflation and documents asymmetry. Differentiates complete ipsilateral upper/lower facial weakness from forehead-sparing pattern without claiming it alone excludes stroke. Other neurology Omits neurological screen. Screens limb power, speech, gait and other cranial nerves. Actively interprets additional findings as atypical and changes referral urgency. Ear and parotid Ignores
sections.5. Critical fails (significant safety br: Fails to activate emergency stroke assessment when new limb weakness or aphasia is disclosed. Discharges a patient with inability to close eye without corneal protection or suitable referral. Explains an atypical progressive or recurrent facial palsy as definitely benign without assessing other causes. Ignores marked ear vesicles and painful facial weakness with possible Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
sections.6. Curveball: At minute 6, examiner adds: “The patient now says the right eye is painful and vision is blurred.” Candidate should stop routine reassurance, assess corneal risk and arrange urgent ophthalmology evaluation.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If candidate initially calls it stroke solely due to facial droop, they should re-examine forehead and eye closure and state that an isolated peripheral pattern supports Bell’s palsy but does not overrule other neurological signs. If eye care was missed, state lubrication, protected closure and urgent eye referral for pain or blurred vision.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “It is just Bell’s palsy. You will get better. Go home.” Does not examine other neurological functions or protect the eye. Pass “I’ll check your face and the rest of your nervous system. Your forehead and eye closure are affected, which fits a peripheral facial palsy. We must protect the eye, and can consider early steroids after checking suitability. I will explain when to return.” High-performance “I have checked for stroke features, examined the ear and parotid, documented the complete peripheral pattern and assessed corneal exposure. I will discuss early steroids, protect the eye today, and escalate immediately for visual symptoms or any new focal neurological sign.”

stations.title: Orbital Floor Fracture

sections.preamble: B2-137 — Orbital Floor Fracture AMaC Medical Education | MRCS Part B | Draft for clinical review | 12 October 2026 9-minute practice station • Educational simulation; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Final MB- ID assigned only after publication review.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are in the emergency surgical assessment area. A 24-year-old was struck around the left eye during sport. Examine the eye and surrounding structures using a simulated patient (no pressure on the globe); the examiner will supply findings. Explain the likely diagnosis, imaging and escalation.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Observations initially stable. Acuity 6/6 right, 6/9 left; equal reactive pupils, no RAPD. Bruising around left orbit; left infraorbital numbness; painful restricted upgaze with vertical diplopia. Written CT if ordered: left orbital-floor defect with orbital fat herniation and possible inferior rectus tethering; globes intact. A CT description does not by itself prove muscle entrapment; correlate with exam. Do not simulate forced duction.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: left orbital swelling after elbow strike 3 hours ago. Double vision on looking up; numb upper cheek. No previous eye condition. Ask, “Can I blow my nose?” When prompted by curveball, nausea develops during eye movements.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Mark each row against the described behaviours; safety-critical rows are marked ★. Descriptors are behavioural anchors, not a mechanical score. Domain Fail Pass High-performance ★ Initial trauma safety Starts orbital manipulation without trauma/airway assessment. Confirms initial trauma survey and checks observations, conscious state and associated head injury. Links vomiting/bradycardia during examination to possible oculocardiac reflex and calls urgent help. Mechanism and symptoms Asks only about pain. Asks about blunt mechanism, diplopia, vision loss, pain on eye movement and infraorbital numbness. Also checks flashes/floaters, nausea, vomiting and symptoms suggesting associated globe damage. ★ Visual function Does not check visual acuity. Documents visual acuity in both eyes and pupil responses, including RAPD assessment. Explains that reduced acuity or abnormal pupil responses require immediate ophthalmology involvement. Orbital inspection Overlooks swelling, position and wounds. Inspects symmetry, bruising, globe position and subconjunctival changes without pressure. Recognises proptosis or tense orbit with deteriorating vision as threatened orbital compartment syndrome. Eye
sections.5. Critical fails (significant safety br: Fails to recognise or escalate sudden vision deterioration, abnormal pupil or orbital compartment signs. Ignores bradycardia/vomiting with restricted gaze and delays suspected entrapment review. Applies external pressure or attempts forced manipulation to a potentially injured globe. Discharges a patient with significant ocular restriction/diplopia without specialist assessment.
sections.6. Curveball: At minute 6, while looking up the patient feels faint and vomits; pulse falls from 78 to 45/min. Candidate should cease eye movement testing, assess ABC, seek emergency ophthalmology/maxillofacial review for possible entrapment with oculocardiac reflex.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If visual acuity was overlooked, stop and document each eye, pupils and red flags before imaging discussion. If entrapment was treated as routine swelling, explicitly recognise vertical movement restriction plus nausea/bradycardia and request urgent specialist evaluation. If the patient asks about blowing the nose, advise avoiding it.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “This is just a black eye. Take analgesia, blow your nose normally, and return if it hurts.” No acuity or eye-movement assessment. Pass “I will check the vision in each eye, pupils, movement and feeling under the eye. Your diplopia and upgaze restriction suggest an orbital floor injury. We need CT and specialist eye and facial surgery review; do not blow your nose.” High-performance “I have documented acuity and pupillary examination, identified restricted upgaze and infraorbital sensory change, and correlated them with CT. Bradycardia and vomiting raise concern for entrapped tissue causing an oculocardiac reflex, requiring immediate multidisciplinary review.”

stations.title: Swelling Under the Jaw at Mealtimes
stations.source_heading: B2-139 Swelling Under the Jaw at Mealtimes

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | B2-139 Swelling Under the Jaw at Mealtimes DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute station • History / assessment • Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible in ex: A 43-year-old patient presents with episodic painful swelling under the left jaw, especially during meals. Take a focused history, describe the relevant examination and explain the probable diagnosis and management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief and information on req: Patient has had three episodes over six weeks, worse at meals, resolving over about an hour. Afebrile, well, no airway symptoms or weight loss. A mildly tender left submandibular gland is palpable; small firm focus along the floor of mouth; no purulence, no cervical lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound, if requested, demonstrates a 5 mm stone in the distal left submandibular duct with mild duct dilatation. No deep-neck infection. Examiner provides findings when the candidate states how they would examine.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: “It swells when I start eating and then gradually settles.” If asked, no fever, dental infection, difficulty swallowing, breathing problems, persistent lump or unexplained weight loss. Ask whether tablets alone will stop it recurring and whether surgery means losing the gland.
sections.4. Marking grid: Domain / action Fail Pass High-performance Focused symptom chronology Does not ask whether swelling is meal-related. Asks about recurrent swelling and pain during meals, duration and resolution. Links obstructed salivary flow with symptom pattern and asks if episodes are becoming persistent. Infection and airway red flags Ignores fever, trismus or swallowing difficulty. Asks about fever, redness, discharge, severe pain, dysphagia and breathing difficulty. Differentiates uncomplicated obstruction from acute suppurative infection or deep-neck spread. Relevant history Asks no medication or systemic history. Asks hydration, prior stones/infections, dental symptoms, dry mouth and medications. Asks about recurrent episodes, salivary dryness, autoimmune symptoms and previous ENT treatment. Extraoral examination Examines only the overlying skin. Inspects/palpates submandibular region and compares sides, tenderness and gland size. Assesses cervical nodes and seeks discrete persistent mass or facial/lingual nerve symptoms. Intraoral examination Does not inspect the mouth. Examines floor of mouth and Wharton duct opening, looking for stone, swelling or pus. Describes bimanual palpation and ge
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-critical: Fails to recognise rapidly progressive floor-of-mouth swelling with airway symptoms as an emergency. Recommends traumatic duct probing or self-removal with a sharp instrument. Treats overt suppurative infection with sepsis features as uncomplicated stone without escalation. Reassures and discharges a persistent hard mass with malignant features without investigation.
sections.6. Curveball (examiner-triggered): Examiner: “The patient returns with fever, marked tenderness and pus at the duct opening.” Candidate must assess severity and airway, suspect acute bacterial sialadenitis, involve ENT/OMFS as indicated, and give appropriate antimicrobial treatment according to local protocol, with drainage if abscess develops.
sections.7. Recovery after a missed step: If the candidate initially suggests only antibiotics for recurrent meal-related swelling without infection, prompt: “What is causing the swelling?” Recovery requires explaining obstruction, examining Wharton duct, arranging ultrasound/specialist removal if persistent, and reserving antibiotics for infection.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail Takes a generic neck-lump history, overlooks meal-triggering and gives antibiotics without examination or safety-netting. Pass Elicits meal-related swelling, screens for infection and airway issues, examines gland and duct, identifies likely stone, explains conservative measures and ENT follow-up. High-performance Distinguishes intermittent obstruction from infection and malignancy, offers ultrasound and minimally invasive gland-preserving options, addresses concerns and provides explicit urgent-return advice.

stations.title: Hand Laceration Flexor Tendon Examination
stations.source_heading: B2-140 Hand Laceration  Flexor Tendon Examination

near_match.title: Hip examination

sections.preamble: B2-140 — Hand Laceration: Flexor Tendon Examination AMaC | MRCS Part B | Round 2 · Draft for clinical review · 12 October 2026 Format: Examination / applied decision-making | Suggested station time: 9 minutes | Not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical trainee in the emergency assessment area. A 29-year-old chef has a 2-cm palmar laceration over the left index finger after cutting it on a kitchen knife four hours ago. Examine the hand on the simulated patient, explain your findings, and state immediate management. Do not probe the wound or perform invasive procedures.
sections.2. Examiner brief and controlled disclos: No actual open wound or blood: a marked palmar cut over the proximal phalanx of the index finger is simulated. Patient is haemodynamically stable. If tested: isolated DIP flexion is absent; PIP flexion is present but painful. Radial side of index fingertip feels reduced light touch; ulnar side intact. Capillary refill 2 seconds, warm digit; active extension intact. A composite fist appears weak but is not diagnostic by itself. No gross contamination, no fracture or foreign body on the written X-ray report, if requested. Expected synthesis: suspected FDP disruption with possible radial digital nerve injury; urgent hand-service assessment, initial wound care and protection.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You cut your left index finger while cooking; it hurts to bend the fingertip. You are worried about returning to work as a chef. Answer only when asked: no prior hand injuries, no anticoagulants, last tetanus booster unknown; fingertip feels slightly numb on the thumb side. If told “it is just a skin cut”, ask: “Why can’t I bend the tip of my finger?”
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Assess each row using the exact observed action. “Pass” is the expected safe performance; High-performance adds precision, not extra rote detail. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial safety and consent Examines the bleeding wound without analgesia, permission or safety check. Checks haemorrhage, hand perfusion and patient stability; explains examination and obtains consent. Controls bleeding safely, documents baseline function before local anaesthetic, and adapts to pain. Mechanism and history Does not ask how, when or with what the hand was cut. Asks time, mechanism, glass/foreign body, contamination, dominance and occupation. Also considers bite/crush mechanism, tetanus history and hand-function priorities. Inspection and posture Fails to expose the hand or assess resting finger posture. Inspects site, orientation, depth, swelling, finger cascade and resting flexion. Recognises a straighter resting digit as a clue to flexor disruption and identifies relevant tendon zone. FDP isolation Tests a composite fist only; misses isolated FDP loss. Stabilises the PIP joint in extension and asks for isolated DIP flexion. Compares with other side and interprets loss of DIP flexion as li
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe actions: Fails to identify and refer suspected flexor tendon injury despite absent active isolated DIP flexion. Fails to assess/document fingertip perfusion when a deep digital injury is suspected. Performs blind deep wound exploration or forceful painful manipulation in an unsuited environment. Closes and discharges without considering a concurrent digital-nerve deficit.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: Actor says: “I can make a fist if I force it; can I just go back to the kitchen tomorrow?” Examiner expects isolated tendon testing, not false reassurance from composite motion.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If missed FDP injury: “I need to isolate the distal joint; please keep the middle joint straight while trying to bend the fingertip.” If missed nerve injury: “Before anaesthetic, I should check sensation on both sides of the fingertip and record the map.” If moving to discharge: “Loss of DIP flexion needs urgent hand-surgery assessment; I would protect the finger and discuss timing with the hand service.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “The skin cut is small, so tendon injury is unlikely.” Tests a fist only, skips sensation and proposes simple closure and discharge. Pass “Your fingertip does not bend when tested alone, suggesting a damaged deep flexor tendon. Sensation is reduced on one side. I will dress/protect the hand and arrange urgent hand-team assessment.” High-performance “I have documented isolated FDP loss, preserved but painful PIP flexion, reduced radial digital sensation and intact perfusion. I will discuss prompt specialist assessment, potential repair and hand therapy; I will not explore the tendon blindly here.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Palmar cut plus loss of isolated DIP movement = FDP injury until assessed. SAY: “A small wound can still injure a tendon or a digital nerve.” DO: Check FDP, FDS, both fingertip sensory borders, perfusion and active extension. FINISH: Dress, protect, document and arrange prompt hand-team assessment. TRAP: A partial fist does not exclude a tendon injury. NUMBERS: BSSH flexor repair standard: ideally seen within 24 h; repair timing target within 4 days where operative repair indicated.

stations.title: Explaining Skin Grafts and Flaps
stations.source_heading: B2-141 Explaining Skin Grafts and Flaps

sections.preamble: B2-141 — Explaining Skin Grafts and Flaps AMaC | MRCS Part B | Round 2 · Draft for clinical review · 12 October 2026 Format: Communication / reconstructive options | Suggested station time: 9 minutes | Not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical trainee speaking to a 54-year-old patient due for removal of a skin cancer from the lower leg. The surgeon expects a defect that may require reconstruction. Explain the differences between a skin graft and skin flap, reasonable alternatives, material risks and aftercare. Do not promise a particular reconstruction until the surgeon has assessed the final defect.
sections.2. Examiner brief and controlled disclos: Patient is clinically well. Planned wide excision of a lower-leg lesion with a possible defect of 4 × 3 cm, depth not yet known. The reconstructive plan will be decided by the operating team after excision; do not tell candidate what choice is mandatory. Expected content: graft transferred without its original blood supply, dependent on recipient bed; flap transferred with an ongoing/reconnected vascular supply; cover, aesthetics and function affect planning. The candidate should personalise the discussion (patient smokes; lives alone), explain donor-site impact, no guarantee of take, protective dressings and follow-up. No image required; verbal explanation only. Do not expect a detailed flap dissection or microsurgical technique.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are worried about how the leg will look, how long you will need off work as a delivery driver and whether skin is taken from another part of your body. If asked: you smoke ten cigarettes daily, no diabetes, live alone. You would prefer a smaller donor-site scar if safe. Curveball: “My neighbour’s graft fell off. Can you promise mine will take?” Ask this once the doctor has described reconstruction.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Assess each row using the exact observed action. “Pass” is the expected safe performance; High-performance adds precision, not extra rote detail. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction and preferences Begins with technical jargon without establishing patient concern. Confirms planned excision/wound and asks what matters most: function, appearance, healing or donor-site concerns. Uses accessible language and checks baseline understanding before comparing options. Graft versus flap Claims grafts and flaps are identical. Explains a graft is skin moved without its original blood supply; a flap brings tissue with an attached or reconnected blood supply. Links choice to wound bed, depth, exposed vital structures and reconstruction requirements. Reconstructive options Claims a graft is the only available treatment. Outlines healing by secondary intention, direct closure, graft or flap depending on defect. Explains a reconstructive ladder is a decision aid, not an inflexible rule; specialist plan may change. Graft type and sites Does not mention where skin comes from. Explains split- versus full-thickness grafts and likely donor-site scar/dressing. Clarifies thinner grafts may be u
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe actions: Promises a graft/flap will certainly survive or gives misleading guarantee of cosmetic result. Fails to explain donor-site morbidity and materially relevant risk of tissue loss or further surgery. Proceeds as though consent is valid after patient expresses uncertainty or refusal, without discussion. Ignores concerning postoperative signs of flap ischaemia or infection when specifically raised.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: Patient asks: “If a flap keeps its blood supply, why not always use a flap instead of a graft?” Examiner expects balanced explanation of defect suitability and donor-site consequences.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If overclaiming survival: “I should correct that: any graft can fail to take, and a flap can suffer circulation problems; the risk depends on the wound and your health.” If donor site omitted: “You will also have a separate site where tissue is taken, which can be painful and scar.” If jumping to consent: “We need to review alternatives and your preferences before you choose; the specialist will confirm the plan after examining the defect.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “A graft and a flap are both just skin transfers, and either one will heal perfectly.” Neglects risks, donor sites and consent. Pass “A graft takes skin completely free of its original blood supply; a flap carries its own supply. The best choice depends on the wound. Both may scar or need further treatment, and we will look after the donor site too.” High-performance “The final depth, exposed tissues and blood supply affect reconstruction. We will balance function, contour, donor-site effects, your smoking and recovery needs; I can explain options, but the operating surgeon will confirm the plan and your consent.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Choose coverage for tissue needs, function and patient preference. SAY: “A graft must establish blood supply from the wound; a flap brings blood supply with it.” DO: Compare options, donor sites, material risks and practical aftercare. FINISH: Invite questions, check understanding and document the shared plan. TRAP: Do not promise perfect graft take or a scar-free result. NUMBERS: No universal healing time: site, depth and patient factors determine recovery.

stations.title: Dog Bite to the Hand
stations.source_heading: B2-142 Dog Bite to the Hand

near_match.title: Dog bite to the forearm: wound care, antibiotics and tetanus

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | Round 2 B2-142 — Dog Bite to the Hand DRAFT • For educational use, not an official MRCS marking scheme • 12 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical doctor in ED. A 34-year-old was bitten on the dominant right hand by a neighbour’s dog four hours ago. Assess the injury, describe initial treatment, and explain what requires specialist involvement. Station time: 9 minutes. State actions clearly; any invasive procedure is simulated, not performed on an actor.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Observations: T 36.8°C, HR 84, BP 126/78, SpO₂ 98%; no systemic illness. Two punctures over dorsal MCP joint of index finger, one deep; blood was drawn. Pain on passive movement, mild swelling; no gross tendon deficit. Sensation and finger perfusion preserved. No radiograph yet. Patient is unsure of last tetanus vaccination. Dog bite occurred in England, domestic dog reportedly healthy. No overseas exposure. If candidate asks: local hand-surgery team available; diabetic status negative; penicillin allergy none; patient can make decisions.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Concerned that the dog was unprovoked; wants stitches immediately and asks whether the wound is safe. If asked, confirms the index MCP location, last tetanus unknown and a dog kept locally in England. Curveball prompt at examiner direction: “It is a tiny hole — why can’t you just close it and send me home?”
sections.4. Marking grid: Assess each domain separately. Safety-critical rows marked ★. Fail / Pass / High-performance are descriptive performance levels, not numerical cut-offs. Domain Fail Pass High-performance 1. ★ Immediate risk and priorities Discharges without checking hand function or deep injury. Recognises hand puncture near a joint as high-risk; checks systemic stability. Prioritises possible joint/tendon breach and communicates urgent hand review.
sections.2. History and host risk: Does not ask animal, time or infection risk. Asks timing, species, location, mechanism, comorbidity, allergy and medication. Adds animal health/travel history and immunisation status without delaying treatment.
sections.3. Tendon, nerve and vascular exam: Omits perfusion or sensation and claims no deep injury. Tests active flexion/extension by digit, distal sensation and capillary refill. Documents individual joint movement, digital nerve territories and compares hands.
sections.4. Wound assessment: Probes wound blindly or overlooks MCP-joint puncture. Assesses site, depth, tissue damage, contamination, foreign body and movement pain. Recognises subtle joint penetration signs and avoids traumatic probing. 5. ★ Irrigation and wound disposition Closes contaminated puncture primarily without assessment. Analgesia, copious irrigation, dressing; considers debridement; avoids routine primary closure. Plans hand surgical exploration or washout when joint involvement is suspected.
sections.6. Antibiotics: Omits prophylaxis despite deep puncture into a high-risk hand structure. Prescribes prophylactic antibiotic per NICE for deep puncture with bleeding; checks allergy. Names co-amoxiclav first line when appropriate and adapts to allergy/local policy.

stations.title: Basal Cell Carcinoma Treatment Options
stations.source_heading: B2-143 Basal Cell Carcinoma Treatment Options

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | Round 2 B2-143 — Basal Cell Carcinoma: Treatment Options DRAFT • For educational use, not an official MRCS marking scheme • 12 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are in a skin surgery clinic. Explain a biopsy-confirmed basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on a patient’s cheek, the treatment options and shared decision-making. No actual procedure is required. Station time: 9 minutes. State actions clearly; any invasive procedure is simulated, not performed on an actor.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: A 72-year-old with an 8 mm biopsy-confirmed nodular BCC on the right cheek, a cosmetically sensitive area. No perineural symptoms, no previous treatment; edge appears clinically well defined. Histology: nodular BCC, no infiltrative/morphoeic features in sampling. Final risk classification and treatment depend on anatomical risk zone, size and tumour characteristics. Actor is worried about facial scarring and believes this cancer will spread rapidly throughout the body. If asked, patient is medically fit and prefers a reliable cure with reasonable cosmetic outcome.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: “They said it was cancer. Does this mean it has spread?” “Can you freeze it or use a cream so I do not have a scar?” Curveball: “My friend had Mohs surgery — surely everyone needs that?”
sections.4. Marking grid: Assess each domain separately. Safety-critical rows marked ★. Fail / Pass / High-performance are descriptive performance levels, not numerical cut-offs. Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Diagnosis and empathy: Calls BCC harmless or implies inevitable metastasis. Explains BCC is a common skin cancer that typically grows locally and rarely metastasises. Balances reassurance with seriousness of destructive local growth if untreated.
sections.2. Risk assessment: Assumes biopsy alone guarantees low risk. Checks site, size, border, histologic subtype, recurrence and immune status. Recognises cheek anatomy and need for risk classification, MDT input for high-risk factors. 3. ★ Treatment selection Offers cream as equivalent to surgery for all BCCs. Explains surgical excision as standard first-line for suitable lesions. Individualises margin control, preservation of function and cosmetic priorities.
sections.4. Mohs and reconstruction: Says Mohs is always needed or is never useful. Describes Mohs as staged margin assessment for selected high-risk or recurrent tumours. Explains tissue conservation, specialist suitability and reconstruction timing.
sections.5. Non-surgical treatments: Offers topical treatment for high-risk infiltrative disease without caveat. Mentions topical treatments/PDT for selected low-risk superficial disease when appropriate. Explains suitability limits, recurrence trade-offs and radiotherapy in selected cases.

stations.title: Undescended Testis

near_match.title: Inguinal hernia and undescended testis in an infant

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — Round 2 B2-144 — Undescended Testis Group 15 • Paediatric surgery • 9-minute practice station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED Independent AMaC educational material; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Check against live station register before publication.
sections.1. Station purpose: Assess a child with an empty hemiscrotum, distinguish a genuinely retractile testis from undescended/ascending testis, and communicate safe timing and implications of paediatric urology referral.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are an MRCS candidate in a paediatric surgical clinic. A parent brings a 10-month-old boy because the right testis has not been felt in the scrotum. Take a focused history, describe your examination to the examiner, explain the likely diagnosis and management to the parent. No genital examination of a real child is required; examination findings are supplied.
sections.3. Examiner brief / case facts: Child age 10 months; well, born at term. Right hemiscrotum underdeveloped, left testis in scrotum. Right testis palpable in distal inguinal canal and cannot be maintained in scrotum without tension. No pain, red or swollen scrotum; no urinary complaint. No hypospadias; left testis normal. Expected: examination in a warm room with parental consent, assess both testes and penis, avoid repeated painful traction; identify right palpable undescended testis rather than retractile testis. No scan is needed to establish the diagnosis of a palpable undescended testis. Refer promptly for paediatric surgical/urology assessment and timely orchidopexy.
sections.4. Actor / parent brief: You are worried surgery might damage fertility. Ask: “Will he grow out of it?” and “Is this cancer?” Only volunteer information if asked: it has not been seen in the scrotum since birth. No family history of genital problems. Child thriving. If candidate says “just wait until school age”, express concern about whether this misses a treatment window.
sections.5. Examiner prompts and disclosures: If asked to examine: right testis palpable in groin and cannot rest in scrotum; left normal; no acute tenderness. If candidate asks for ultrasound: ask how the result would change management. Curveball: “Our GP said it might be retractile. What is the difference?”
sections.6. Critical-weighted marking grid: Grade each element from observed actions, not inferred knowledge. “Critical” flags a safety-relevant domain; automatic station fail requires a separately defined critical-fail action below. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Weight Introduces and seeks permission Begins genital assessment without consent or privacy. Explains focused assessment to parent and seeks consent, ensures chaperone. Uses parent-friendly language and checks comfort before sensitive examination. Standard Focused history Ignores onset, previous scrotal position and acute symptoms. Clarifies never descended versus acquired ascent; asks pain and swelling. Also asks prematurity, prior examinations, surgery and associated genital concerns. Standard Examination plan Examines only the empty hemiscrotum; forcefully pulls the testis. Examines both sides in a warm environment, groins, scrotum and penile anatomy gently. Explains positioning, assesses whether testis can remain scrotal without tension and notes size/asymmetry. Standard Classification Calls palpable inguinal undescended testis a harmless retractile testis. Correctly identifies a palpable undescended testis. Distinguishes congenital, acquired ascending, ecto
sections.7. Critical fails — unacceptable safety: Dismisses an acutely painful or swollen scrotum as undescended testis without urgent torsion assessment. Reassures a 10-month-old with persistent palpable undescended testis that intervention can safely wait until school age. Fails to escalate bilateral nonpalpable testes with atypical genitalia/associated red flags for urgent specialist evaluation. Performs or proposes forceful repeated traction likely to injure the child.
sections.8. Must-not-miss actions: Differentiate testis that remains scrotal without tension (retractile) from one that cannot (undescended). Explain paediatric surgery referral now and orchidopexy target by 12 months, at latest 18 months. Mention persisting cancer risk even after surgery; no promise of elimination. State urgent review if sudden scrotal pain, redness, swelling or vomiting.

stations.title: Umbilical Hernia in an Infant
stations.source_heading: B2-145 Umbilical Hernia in an Infant

near_match.title: Umbilical and epigastric hernia in an adult: examination and management principles

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — Round 2 B2-145 — Umbilical Hernia in an Infant Group 15 • Paediatric surgery • 9-minute practice station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED Independent AMaC educational material; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Check against live station register before publication.
sections.1. Station purpose: Explain the benign natural history of an uncomplicated infant umbilical hernia, identify rare red flags for incarceration/strangulation, and discuss when specialist review or elective repair is warranted.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are in paediatric surgery outpatient clinic. A parent of an otherwise healthy 8-month-old asks whether a soft swelling at the umbilicus needs an operation. Take a focused history, describe the examination you would perform and explain an appropriate management plan.
sections.3. Examiner brief / case facts: Eight-month-old thriving infant; soft 1.5 cm reducible umbilical bulge, more visible when crying, normal overlying skin, non-tender. Passing stool normally, no vomiting or abdominal distension. No signs of incarceration, obstruction or strangulation. No known syndromic features. Expected: reassuring counselling, observation with age-appropriate review; do not recommend taping/coins or routine surgery in infancy.
sections.4. Actor / parent brief: You are worried the lump will burst. Ask “Can we tape a coin over it?” and “What if it gets bigger when crying?” If asked: reduces when infant settles, no pain, no vomiting, feeding and growth normal. Curveball: “Yesterday it seemed bigger while he was straining—should I take him to A&E?”
sections.5. Examiner prompts and disclosures: If candidate asks to inspect: soft round swelling through umbilical ring, normal skin. If candidate assesses reducibility: easily reduced without discomfort. If sudden severe persistent pain, vomiting, discolouration or irreducibility appears: expect immediate emergency assessment rather than routine reassurance.
sections.6. Critical-weighted marking grid: Grade each element from observed actions, not inferred knowledge. “Critical” flags a safety-relevant domain; automatic station fail requires a separately defined critical-fail action below. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Weight Introduction and consent Examines infant without consent or fails to address worried parent. Introduces self, seeks parental permission and uses calm, plain explanation. Invites concerns and gives child-appropriate, minimally distressing assessment. Standard History of swelling Ignores changes, pain or feeding pattern. Asks onset, variability, reducibility, pain, vomiting and bowel function. Checks growth, previous incarceration, skin changes and impact on family. Standard Focused examination Relies on appearance alone and does not assess tenderness/skin. Describes abdomen, umbilical defect, reducibility and surrounding skin. Assesses general wellbeing, distension and signs of obstruction without forceful reduction. Standard Diagnosis Labels soft reducible congenital bulge as urgent strangulated hernia. Identifies uncomplicated infant umbilical hernia. Explains ring defect and distinguishes associated lesions when relevant. Standard Natural history Claims
sections.7. Critical fails — unacceptable safety: Reassures a child with a newly tender irreducible/discoloured umbilical bulge and vomiting without emergency referral. Recommends taping a coin or tight abdominal binder over the infant hernia. Uses forceful reduction despite signs of painful incarceration or compromised bowel. States that obstruction symptoms can be safely watched at home without assessment.
sections.8. Must-not-miss actions: Demonstrate that the current hernia is soft, painless and reducible. Most umbilical hernias in young children resolve spontaneously by about five years; observation is usually safe. Warn about persistent pain, vomiting, skin colour change and irreducibility: urgent emergency assessment. Avoid unproven taping and binding; make review/referral plan if persistent, large or symptomatic.

stations.title: Circumcision Request for a Child
stations.source_heading: B2-146 Circumcision Request for a Child

near_match.title: Phimosis and the request for circumcision

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | GROUP 15 B2-146 — Circumcision Request for a Child Communication / professionalism • 9-minute practice station • Draft 12 October 2026 • UK practice context Educational rehearsal only; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme. Provisional: requires independent clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a surgical registrar meeting the parents of a healthy 4-year-old boy. They request circumcision for non-medical reasons. Explore the request, explain options and risks, and establish a safe consent plan. Do not obtain a signature during this consultation.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Child is four years old, healthy, no penile symptoms and no recurrent balanitis or urinary infections; foreskin has never been forcibly retracted. One parent is keen to proceed; the other has not attended and their view is initially unknown. No examination is required in this communication station; candidate may offer appropriate examination in a separate appointment with consent. The correct outcome is an informed, child-centred discussion and deferred decision until parental responsibility, agreement and best interests are established.
sections.3. Actor / parent brief: Parent: “We would like him circumcised like other boys in our community.” You are courteous but anxious about delaying the decision. If asked why: cultural or faith reasons, not a medical problem. If asked about the other parent: “We haven’t really discussed it properly.” Ask: “Is it safe? Won’t it prevent infections?” If candidate is dismissive, become upset: “Are you judging our beliefs?” If child’s views are discussed, say the boy is nervous about hospitals and has not expressed a wish for surgery.
sections.4. Marking grid — use best-fit descripto: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Rapport and respect Criticises the family’s beliefs or dismisses the request. Thanks parent, uses neutral language and establishes the reason for the request. Affirms respect without promising surgery and frames the consultation around this particular child’s welfare. Medical history / indication Assumes phimosis or infection without history. Asks about urinary symptoms, balanitis, foreskin issues, bleeding problems and general health. Separates physiological non-retractability from pathological disease and checks previous attempts at retraction. Child and best interests Considers parents’ preference alone sufficient. Explains best interests and age-appropriate child involvement. Explores child’s feelings, future autonomy, potential benefits and burdens without assuming a universal answer. Parental responsibility and agreement Proceeds on the attending parent’s request despite known disagreement or uncertain authority. Checks who has parental responsibility and whether the other parent agrees. Identifies dispute as reason to pause, seek senior/legal advice and never force an elective decision. Procedure and benefits Says surgery is harmless or medi
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe behaviours: Arranges elective non-therapeutic circumcision despite active parental dispute without resolving consent and best interests. Uses force, coercion or ignores material objection expressed by the child in a way that makes proceeding unsafe. Claims the procedure has no material risks or is medically necessary in a healthy child. Proposes surgery in an unsafe/non-qualified setting or without an appropriate anaesthetic and safeguarding framework.
sections.6. Curveball: Parent says: “His other parent thinks we should wait. Can we book anyway and I will persuade them?” Candidate should explicitly decline to book before disagreement is resolved, explain why, and offer appropriate discussion and advice.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If you promised immediate surgery: stop, clarify no decision can be made until both the child’s best interests and valid parental consent are addressed. If you made an insensitive comment about faith: apologise, state respect for their reasons and return to a non-judgemental discussion. If you overlooked the child: ask how he feels and whether there is a clinically urgent reason (none here); consider deferral.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “There are no significant risks and you can sign today.” Does not establish both parents’ position, child’s interests or alternatives. Pass “I understand why this matters to you. There is no medical need from what you have told me. It is permanent, with bleeding, infection and anaesthetic risks. We should check both parents’ agreement, consider your son’s welfare and arrange a planned review.” High-performance Explores family motivation without judgement, distinguishes therapeutic and non-therapeutic circumcision, involves the child appropriately, elicits disagreement, explains why elective surgery must pause, offers written information and documented specialist review. 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Elective, permanent intervention on a healthy child: best interests first. SAY: “I respect the reason for your request; my duty is also to your child.” DO: Check indication, child’s wishes, parental responsibility, agreement, risks and alternatives. FINISH: Document, provide written information and arrange senior review—not immediate booking. TRAP: One parent’s enthusiasm does not resolve a known dispute. NUMBERS: No numeric risk estimate without procedure- and service-specific d

stations.title: Swallowed Button Battery

near_match.title: Parent Rings After a Toddler Swallowed a Small Round Battery / Do Not Wait for Symptoms

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | GROUP 15 B2-147 — Swallowed Button Battery Paediatric critical care / applied management • 9-minute practice station • Draft 12 October 2026 • UK practice context Educational rehearsal only; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme. Provisional: requires independent clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A 2-year-old boy has possibly swallowed a button battery about 45 minutes ago. He is currently talking and breathing comfortably. Explain your immediate assessment, investigations, escalation and management to the examiner. A written imaging report is supplied on request.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Observations: RR 24/min, HR 112/min, SpO₂ 99% air, afebrile, no drooling or stridor. Caregiver noticed a missing 20 mm lithium coin-cell battery from a remote control. Ingestion was not witnessed. Urgent frontal and lateral radiographs including neck, chest and abdomen show a 20 mm circular object at the upper thoracic oesophagus with double-rim/halo and step-off appearances, consistent with an impacted button battery. The correct plan is immediate paediatric ENT/upper-GI surgical and anaesthetic coordination for endoscopic extraction; ideally removal within two hours of ingestion. Do not delay definitive treatment for medications or routine tests. If asked about oral honey: this is not an automatic prescription. Consult up-to-date specialist/local poison pathway; consider only in eligible children over 12 months with ingestion within 12 hours and no contraindications, and never delay removal.
sections.3. Actor / parent brief: Parent: “He seems absolutely fine. Could we just watch him?” Say he may have swallowed a round battery from a remote control. If asked: ingestion was ~45 minutes ago; child has eaten nothing since. No known oesophageal disease. If candidate waits for symptoms, ask: “But he is running around — why would he need an operation?” If candidate explains urgency well: “Will he be fine once it is out?” Candidate should discuss delayed injury surveillance and uncertainty.
sections.4. Marking grid — use best-fit descripto: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and urgency Treats asymptomatic ingestion as low risk or schedules routine review. Calls possible button-battery ingestion a time-critical emergency. Explains rapid caustic oesophageal injury despite no symptoms and acts while localising object. Immediate assessment Ignores airway and vital signs. Assesses ABCDE, swallowing, drooling, stridor, pain, bleeding and observations. Prepares resuscitation resources and flags signs of perforation or airway involvement. Exposure history Does not identify battery type, timing or possible source. Asks time, device, battery size, witnessed event and symptoms. Seeks packaging/device information without allowing this to postpone imaging. Imaging Suggests only an abdominal film or assumes coin. Requests urgent AP and lateral radiographs to localise neck, chest and abdominal battery. Recognises double-ring and lateral step-off signs and communicates radiology findings immediately. Team escalation Waits for routine outpatient endoscopy. Calls paediatric ENT/upper GI team, anaesthetist and paediatric services immediately. Allocates responsibility for theatre/endoscopy transfer and ongoing airway risk. De
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe behaviours: Delays urgent referral/removal of an oesophageal button battery because the child has no symptoms. Mistakes radiographic features for a harmless coin and sends the child home. Recommends oral intake or honey in a contraindicated child, or lets mitigation delay endoscopy. Fails to act on airway compromise, haematemesis or shock if these emerge.
sections.6. Curveball: Parent asks whether to give honey now. Candidate says: “This should never delay theatre. Because he is two and presentation is early, I would discuss the local battery pathway immediately with the paediatric specialist/poisons team; I would not substitute honey for extraction.”
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If you described observation: correct to emergency endoscopic removal because the radiograph shows oesophageal impaction. If you asked only for chest X-ray: extend imaging to include neck and abdomen, in AP and lateral projections, and urgently review with radiology. If you offered immediate discharge after removal: acknowledge potential delayed serious injury; follow specialist surveillance instructions and safety-net.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “He looks well, so repeat an X-ray tomorrow.” Misses the oesophageal battery emergency and gives false reassurance. Pass “I will assess airway and observations, obtain immediate AP/lateral imaging, contact paediatric ENT/GI and anaesthetics now, and organise urgent removal—ideally within two hours. He may be badly injured despite looking well.” High-performance Acts in parallel: ABCDE, exact timings, prompt imaging and recognition, early theatre and airway coordination, no treatment delays, and explicit post-extraction injury and delayed haemorrhage surveillance in specialist care. 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Button battery lodged in oesophagus = emergency even if asymptomatic. SAY: “The battery can cause severe internal injury before symptoms appear.” DO: ABCDE, localise on AP/lateral X-rays, alert paediatric endoscopy/ENT and anaesthesia. FINISH: Urgent extraction, assess mucosal injury and agree specialist follow-up. TRAP: Never treat a halo-sign battery as an ordinary coin or let honey delay removal. NUMBERS: Aim for oesophageal removal within 2 hours; eligible mitigation only if ≤12 hours since ingestion.
