stations.title: The Limping Child

near_match.title: The limping child: irritable hip at age 6

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-150 The Limping Child Group 15 · Paediatric Surgery | 9-minute station | Draft: 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in the children’s emergency assessment unit. A parent brings a 5-year-old boy who has been limping since yesterday. Take a focused history, explain your assessment and immediate plan to the parent. You may request observations, examination findings and investigations from the examiner. Do not physically examine a child actor.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Scenario: previously well 5-year-old, 24 hours of left hip pain and reduced weight bearing; febrile to 38.6°C, HR 130/min. No known trauma. This is a possible septic hip, not a reassurance station. Provide observations and investigations only when asked. Responses: temperature 38.6°C; heart rate 130; blood pressure 96/60; alert but uncomfortable. Painful restriction of left hip internal rotation; refuses to walk. Knee looks normal. CRP 46 mg/L, WCC 14.5 ×10⁹/L; blood cultures pending. Hip ultrasound: effusion. The candidate must distinguish urgent septic arthritis from transient synovitis and discuss Perthes disease, referred knee pain, trauma, osteomyelitis and malignancy if indicated. Kocher criteria are aids, not a rule-out test.
sections.3. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “He was running about two days ago. Now he will not put weight on his leg and has a temperature.” If asked: no fall, no prior episodes, recent mild cold, no weight loss or night sweats; child is eating less; no regular medicines or allergies. If reassured without a plan, ask: “Could there be an infection inside his hip?” If appropriately informed, ask: “Will he need an operation?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: On focused examination: child looks uncomfortable; left hip held flexed; painful passive internal rotation and limited movement. No joint redness. Neurological and distal vascular function intact. Ultrasound confirms effusion but does not determine whether it is sterile or infected. Plain pelvis radiographs are initially unremarkable. Curveball: parent reports he has taken ibuprofen and now has no fever. Explain why antipyretics do not exclude septic arthritis.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score each row at one performance level. A critical fail is considered separately; no arbitrary pass score is implied. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening / sick child Starts detailed hip differential without triage or observations. Asks about fever, systemic illness, pain severity and ability to bear weight; checks observations. Immediately identifies a febrile non-weight-bearing child as a potential time-critical infection and assesses circulation/sepsis features. History Misses onset or functional loss; asks only about trauma. Elicits onset, site, trauma, weight bearing, fever, recent infection, joint and systemic symptoms. Adds night pain, weight loss, previous episodes, sickle-cell/immunosuppression and referred pain without derailing prioritisation. Focused examination Moves painful hip forcefully or omits hip assessment. Describes gait if safe, inspection, gentle hip range, knee, spine and distal neurovascular examination. Examines both hips for symmetry and identifies pain on passive movement as concerning; avoids forced manoeuvres. Differentials Labels all limps as transient synovitis. Includes septic arthritis, transient synovitis, osteomyelitis, trauma and Perthes.
sections.6. Critical fails (unsafe actions): Discharges a febrile, non-weight-bearing child without urgent investigation or senior review. Declares septic arthritis excluded by a normal X-ray or falling temperature after ibuprofen. Delays urgent orthopaedic assessment despite suspected infected hip. Forcefully manipulates an acutely painful hip or fails to assess a deteriorating child.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner: “He seems better after ibuprofen; his temperature is 37.2°C. Can you send him home?” Expected response: “No. His earlier fever, inability to bear weight and painful limited hip movement remain red flags. I would continue urgent paediatric and orthopaedic assessment.”
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: If initially suggesting transient synovitis: “I need to correct that. A febrile child unable to bear weight may have septic arthritis; I would not discharge.” If the examination omitted the knee: “Hip pathology can present as knee pain. I would assess the ipsilateral knee and both hips carefully.” If antibiotics were described as routinely delayed: “In a systemically unwell child, I would follow urgent sepsis management and not delay treatment for aspiration.”

stations.title: Newborn Hip Check

near_match.title: Newborn Check on a Baby Who Was Breech — Normal Hips Still Need a Scan

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-151 Newborn Hip Check Group 15 · Paediatric Surgery | 9-minute station | Draft: 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are performing the hip component of a newborn infant physical examination (NIPE) on a stable term baby, 36 hours after delivery. Explain the examination to the parent, describe and demonstrate the examination using the mannequin, interpret the examiner’s finding, and explain follow-up. Use gentle, age-appropriate technique.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Term female newborn, breech at 36 weeks, now well. Mother is present. NIPE screening consent is sought. The candidate should undertake gentle Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres and assess symmetry and abduction. On request: no family history of DDH, no other health concerns. Hip examination: palpable clunk on left Ortolani; right normal. No pain. This is screen positive and requires the NIPE pathway. If candidate asks for ultrasound: for a baby born ≥34 weeks, schedule hip ultrasound at 4–6 weeks with outcome decision/specialist review by six weeks under the NIPE pathway. Earlier expert assessment may be indicated locally for clinically unstable or dislocated hips; never reassure or defer without referral.
sections.3. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “She looks fine. Why do you need to check her hips?” If asked: baby was breech, feeds normally and was born without complications. After a palpable clunk is described, ask “Will she walk normally? Do we need a scan? Can I swaddle her tightly?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prepare warm, comfortable baby; explain consent and keep infant supported throughout. Observe resting leg alignment, movement, length, knee heights and hip abduction. Ortolani: gently abduct flexed hip while elevating greater trochanter to identify reduction clunk. Barlow: gentle adduction with posterior pressure to assess dislocatability. Do not repeat aggressively. Abnormality: distinct left Ortolani clunk, not a harmless click; left hip screen positive.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score each row at one performance level. A critical fail is considered separately; no arbitrary pass score is implied. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Consent / comfort Handles infant without explaining or supporting head. Explains purpose, obtains permission, warms hands and supports baby safely. Checks parent understanding and positioning, limits distress and avoids repeated provocative testing. Risk factors Ignores breech presentation. Asks about breech position and family history. Explains an otherwise normal examination cannot erase a relevant screening risk factor. Inspection Starts forceful manoeuvre without looking. Inspects spontaneous leg movement, leg lengths, skin folds and symmetry. Assesses Galeazzi knee-height difference and knows skin-crease asymmetry alone is non-specific. Abduction Fails to assess hip movement. Checks bilateral hip abduction with hips flexed, comparing sides gently. Identifies restricted unilateral or substantial bilateral abduction as screen-positive evidence even without a clunk. Barlow manoeuvre Describes rotation or traction instead of the test. Demonstrates gentle adduction with posterior directed pressure and explains dislocatability. Uses
sections.6. Critical fails (unsafe actions): Dismisses a definite Ortolani clunk as a normal click without referral. Uses forceful, repeated manoeuvres risking discomfort or injury. States that breech risk or a positive screen requires no follow-up because the baby looks comfortable. Fails to arrange and document the screen-positive NIPE referral pathway.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner: “The baby is feeding well and there is no pain. Can we simply recheck at 6–8 weeks?” Expected response: “No. An Ortolani clunk is a positive newborn hip screen; I will follow the NIPE referral pathway now and arrange timely ultrasound and specialist outcome assessment.”
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: If the candidate equates click and clunk: “I should distinguish a soft click from a definite reduction clunk. The latter is abnormal and requires referral.” If ultrasound was suggested at birth as the routine pathway: “For a term baby with a positive screen, the NIPE timing is typically 4–6 weeks, with an outcome decision by six weeks; urgent specialist input may alter timing.” If parent worries about disability: “This is a screening finding, not a confirmed lifelong problem. Prompt specialist evaluation and early treatment can improve the outcome.”

stations.title: Inhaled Foreign Body in a Toddler
stations.source_heading: B2-152 Inhaled Foreign Body in a Toddler

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-152 Inhaled Foreign Body in a Toddler Group 15 · Paediatric Surgery | 9-minute station | Draft: 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee asked to assess a previously well 2-year-old who had a choking episode while eating peanuts. The parent reports that he coughed violently, then seemed better, but now has persistent cough and wheeze. Assess the situation verbally, identify immediate dangers and explain the management plan to the parent. No actual choking manoeuvres on the actor.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Nine-minute paediatric acute-assessment communication/clinical reasoning station. If asked: child is alert, RR 34/min, SpO₂ 95% on air, HR 128/min, intermittent cough, no current stridor; unilateral reduced air entry on the right with focal wheeze. Parent witnessed a sudden choking fit while eating peanuts 40 minutes ago. The child can now cry and speak. An X-ray reported in words shows no definite radio-opaque foreign body. The examiner should switch to an airway-emergency question only at the curveball, not assume the child has current complete obstruction.
sections.3. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “He was eating peanuts and suddenly started coughing. He went red in the face, then got better. Is it safe to take him home?” If asked: no preceding cold, no asthma, no fever, no trauma, no blue episode; cough has continued and breathing sometimes sounds whistly. If told the normal X-ray rules it out, ask: “But I saw him choke—could the peanut still be there?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Examination if requested: right-sided focal wheeze and mildly reduced breath sounds; normal alertness and perfusion; no cyanosis or increased work of breathing at baseline. Written radiology report: “No radiopaque object seen. Mild right-sided air-trapping cannot be excluded.” The child remains at risk of an aspirated radiolucent nut. Curveball: the child abruptly stops coughing effectively and cannot cry, develops cyanosis and struggles for breath. Ask the candidate for the immediate sequence, rather than actual manoeuvres on an actor.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score every row against the described behaviour. Critical fails are assessed separately; no automatic overall pass mark is implied. Assessment domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate airway triage Treats choking as a routine cough; does not assess whether the child can vocalise or cough. Asks if cough is effective; assesses breathing, colour, consciousness and oxygenation. Explicitly separates complete/ineffective choking from stable suspected bronchial aspiration and anticipates deterioration. Focused history Does not elicit choking event or timing. Asks about witnessed peanut aspiration, abrupt cough, persistent wheeze and interval recovery. Asks about food/object, aspiration timing, biphasic symptoms and previous respiratory disease without delaying airway care. Initial assessment Omits observations or airway examination. Obtains respiratory rate, saturation, work of breathing, air entry and auscultation. Reassesses continuously; seeks asymmetrical findings, stridor, silent chest, cyanosis and fatigue. Active choking response Attempts a blind sweep or imaging in an obstructed child. For ineffective cough in conscious toddler, calls for help and gives up to five back blows th
sections.6. Critical fails (unsafe actions): Discharges the child because chest radiograph is normal despite clear witnessed aspiration and focal signs. Fails to initiate immediate choking management when the child becomes unable to cough or cry effectively. Attempts a blind finger sweep or delays emergency response for imaging. Continues to treat as a routine wheeze without urgently involving the paediatric airway team.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner: “He can no longer cry or cough and his lips are turning blue. What now?” Expected: call resuscitation team, give up to five back blows; if ineffective in this 2-year-old give up to five abdominal thrusts, repeating and reassessing; if unresponsive start paediatric BLS (five initial rescue breaths), no blind sweeps.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: If initially calling this viral wheeze: “The sudden choking onset and focal findings change my assessment to suspected foreign-body aspiration; I would not discharge him.” If mistakenly relying on chest X-ray: “A peanut may be radiolucent and a normal film cannot exclude it. He needs urgent specialist airway assessment.” If omitting transition to emergency response: “Now his cough is ineffective, the immediate priority is paediatric choking manoeuvres and the resuscitation call, not bronchoscopy paperwork.”

stations.title: Pain Relief After Paediatric Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-153 Pain Relief After Paediatric Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-153 Pain Relief After Paediatric Surgery Group 15 · Paediatric Surgery | 9-minute station | Draft: 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee reviewing a 6-year-old child four hours after uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy. The child has abdominal pain rated 7/10 on a faces scale and is reluctant to move. Discuss a safe postoperative analgesia plan with the parent and the examiner. Prescriptions are described rather than written; use locally approved paediatric weight-based regimens.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Case: 6-year-old, 22 kg; stable and alert, HR 108/min, BP 100/60, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 98% air, temperature 37.2°C; port-site dressings dry, abdomen mildly tender near incisions without peritonism. Already received IV paracetamol at 15:00 and intraoperative local anaesthetic; time now 17:00. He tolerates sips, is not vomiting; no known drug allergies; normal renal function; no NSAID contraindication. Pain score 7/10 on an age-appropriate faces scale. If asked whether another paracetamol dose can be given immediately, direct the candidate to the administration record and local interval limits.
sections.3. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “He keeps crying when he moves. Could he have morphine? Will it make him stop breathing?” If asked: pain is at port sites, not rapidly worsening; he has passed urine, no dizziness or breathing difficulty; no history of kidney problems or bleeding. If told to use codeine, ask: “I heard codeine is unsafe for children. Is he old enough?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Expected evaluation: assess physiological observations, site of pain, wound and abdomen; consider postoperative complications if pain is disproportionate or deteriorating. Discuss age-appropriate validated assessment (FLACC for younger or non-verbal children; faces/numeric self-report where developmentally suitable). Do not require an exact opioid dose without a local protocol. Curveball: after prescribed rescue opioid, child becomes unusually sleepy and respiratory rate drops to 8/min. The candidate must stop further opioid, call urgent anaesthetic/resuscitation support and begin airway/breathing assessment and supportive management.
sections.5. Marking grid: Score every row against the described behaviour. Critical fails are assessed separately; no automatic overall pass mark is implied. Assessment domain Fail Pass High-performance Age and pain assessment Uses only a generic “Are you in pain?” without estimating severity. Assesses age, weight, procedure, self-report and FLACC or appropriate faces scale. Repeats scores after treatment, checks child-specific behavioural cues and function including breathing, drinking and mobilisation. Identify reversible complications Assumes all severe pain is expected surgical pain. Checks observations, wound, bleeding, urinary retention, distension and fever. Escalates disproportionate, worsening or new pain with abnormal observations for surgical reassessment before analgesic escalation. Safe prescription checks Omits allergies or recent recovery-room doses. Checks recorded weight, allergy, medicines already given and correct route. Prevents duplicate paracetamol/NSAID dosing, checks renal, hepatic, hydration and bleeding contraindications and charts reassessment. First-line multimodal plan Offers an opioid alone as first choice for mild pain. Uses weight-appropriate paracetamol ± ibuprofen where not
sections.6. Critical fails (unsafe actions): Gives codeine to this 6-year-old despite age restriction. Administers a repeat paracetamol dose without checking the previous dose/time and appropriate interval. Ignores marked sedation and respiratory depression after opioid treatment. Dismisses severe or worsening postoperative pain with abnormal findings without surgical reassessment.
sections.7. Curveball and examiner response: Examiner: “Following a rescue opioid, he is difficult to rouse and breathing eight times a minute. What would you do?” Expected: stop opioid, immediate ABC/oxygen as needed, call anaesthetic/resuscitation team, support ventilation and monitor closely; consider naloxone according to local paediatric protocol and senior direction.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: If first suggestion was more paracetamol: “I must check his 15:00 dose and minimum interval; I will not duplicate it. I can use another appropriate class if safe and assess again.” If opioid was suggested without monitoring: “Any opioid rescue requires verified weight-based dosing, sedation and respiratory monitoring and a clear escalation plan.” If treating persistent severe pain as routine: “I should repeat observations and examine for bleeding, peritonitis, urinary retention or another complication rather than simply increase analgesia.”

stations.title: Phaeochromocytoma Before Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-154 — Phaeochromocytoma Before Surgery AMaC • MRCS Part B • Group 16 • Development draft • 12 October 2026 Station format: Applied surgical knowledge | Time: 9 minutes | Editorial status: PROVISIONAL — independent clinical review and duplicate clearance required
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible in ex: You are the surgical registrar seeing a 42-year-old referred for removal of a 4.2 cm adrenal mass. He reports episodic headache, sweating and palpitations. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly elevated. Explain the diagnosis, the essential preparation before surgery and major perioperative concerns to the examiner. You are not required to prescribe doses.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: BP 164/96 mmHg, pulse 104 regular; no chest pain, currently stable. Adrenal-protocol CT describes a unilateral enhancing right adrenal lesion. No evidence of distant spread on supplied staging information. If asked: ECG shows sinus tachycardia; no clinical heart failure. Endocrinology has confirmed biochemical findings. The intended operation is elective adrenalectomy after appropriate medical preparation.
sections.3. Patient / examiner role and prompts: Patient asks: “Can we just remove it next week?” Expected: explain delay for monitored preparation. If asked what medicines are being taken: amlodipine only; no alpha blockade yet. At minute 6 ask: “Could you just give me a beta-blocker for the racing heart?” Examiner should provide findings on request, not volunteer the diagnosis.
sections.4. Marking grid — use performance-specif: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognises syndrome Labels symptoms as anxiety and ignores catecholamine excess. Identifies episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with hypertension as concerning for phaeochromocytoma. Links biochemical catecholamine excess to unpredictable induction and tumour-manipulation crises. Confirms diagnosis Proposes biopsy or relies on a single unverified random catecholamine result. Requests plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines; reviews correct sampling and imaging findings. Explains false positives and endocrine-supervised repeat testing where equivocal. Specialist planning Books adrenalectomy without endocrine or anaesthetic assessment. Involves adrenal MDT/endocrinology, experienced surgeon and anaesthetist before operative scheduling. Assigns a coordinated preparation and postoperative high-dependency plan. Alpha blockade Gives no preoperative blockade plan to a symptomatic catecholamine-secreting tumour. Describes specialist-led alpha blockade (e.g. doxazosin/phenoxybenzamine) prior to surgery, usually 7–14 days. Mentions monitored supine/standing BP and gradual titration while preventing symptomatic hypotension. Beta-blocker seq
sections.5. Critical fails (unsafe omissions/acti: Proceeding to elective adrenalectomy of a symptomatic functional tumour without specialist haemodynamic preparation. Initiating beta blockade before alpha blockade for catecholamine-mediated tachycardia. Adrenal biopsy without first excluding phaeochromocytoma. Failing to recognise/call for urgent help in a simulated hypertensive emergency during induction.
sections.6. Curveball: As the patient waits for surgery, they report faintness when standing after alpha blocker titration. Candidate should arrange lying/standing BP, review volume status and coordinate safe adjustment with endocrinology rather than simply insisting on a fixed dose.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If initially rushed to surgery: stop the booking process, explain elevated perioperative risk and request endocrine–anaesthetic preparation. If beta blockade was suggested first: explicitly withdraw it, explain the unopposed alpha risk and correct the sequence. If the patient develops orthostatic symptoms: review BP/volume status and escalate medication adjustment to the specialist team.
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail “This is an adrenal tumour. We should remove it; I would give a beta-blocker for the fast pulse.” No mention of endocrine preparation or haemodynamic risk. Pass “This is a catecholamine-producing tumour. Before elective surgery I will involve endocrine and anaesthesia specialists, establish alpha blockade, then add beta blockade only if needed. We will optimise BP and volume, and monitor closely during and after surgery.” High-performance Adds metanephrine interpretation, safe titration and postural checks, the risk of induction/manipulation crises and post-resection hypotension/hypoglycaemia, and a clear follow-up plan without burdening the patient with doses. 9. 60-second recall card — written afresh THINK: Catecholamine excess turns an elective operation into an anaesthetic risk. SAY: “We must stabilise your circulation before removal.” DO: Confirm metanephrines, MDT plan, alpha blockade, volume/BP optimisation. FINISH: Agree postoperative monitoring and long-term endocrine follow-up. TRAP: Never start beta blockade before effective alpha blockade. NUMBERS: Typically 7–14 days of specialist-led preparation; individualise to response.

sections.preamble: B2-155 — Adrenal Incidentaloma AMaC • MRCS Part B • Group 16 • Development draft • 12 October 2026 Station format: Data interpretation / applied knowledge | Time: 9 minutes | Editorial status: PROVISIONAL — independent clinical review and duplicate clearance required
sections.1. Candidate instructions (visible in ex: A 56-year-old woman has an incidental 2.8 cm left adrenal mass on a CT performed for renal colic. The report describes a homogeneous lesion measuring 6 Hounsfield units on an unenhanced scan. BP is 128/78 mmHg and serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. Interpret the finding, identify appropriate hormonal assessment and advise on management according to current guidance.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: No known malignancy; no features of Cushing syndrome, episodic catecholamine symptoms or virilisation. Unenhanced CT is diagnostic-quality and reports a homogeneous, smooth, 6 HU adrenal lesion. If asked: woman has no hypertension, no unexplained low potassium and no relevant adrenal history. A follow-up prompt replaces the finding with a 5.1 cm heterogeneous lesion measuring 28 HU.
sections.3. Patient / examiner role and prompts: Patient asks: “Does a lump mean cancer?” Candidate must not equate incidentaloma with malignancy. Patient asks whether surveillance CT is necessary every year. At minute 6 examiner introduces the alternate CT report (5.1 cm / 28 HU). No image is required: CT findings are supplied in words.
sections.4. Marking grid — use performance-specif: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Frames incidentaloma Assumes every adrenal mass is malignant or requires removal. Defines incidentaloma and organises assessment into imaging malignancy risk and hormonal activity. Adds clinical context, prior malignancy and adrenal MDT role. Reads CT correctly Treats a 2.8 cm homogeneous 6 HU lesion as an automatic surgical referral. Explains homogeneous unenhanced attenuation ≤10 HU strongly indicates benign adenoma with no further imaging in typical cases. Notes 2023 ESE benign imaging rule does not require a <4 cm cutoff. Recognises mild autonomous cortisol secretion and reviews metabolic comorbidities. Phaeochromocytoma screen Orders metanephrines universally without considering imaging or overlooks atypical lesions. Understands 2023 ESE recommends metanephrines when imaging is not typical of benign adenoma. Clarifies that indeterminate imaging or symptoms mandates biochemical exclusion prior to intervention. Aldosterone assessment Measures aldosterone/renin in every normotensive patien
sections.5. Critical fails (unsafe omissions/acti: Recommend routine adrenal biopsy without excluding catecholamine excess. Dismiss heterogeneous 5.1 cm / 28 HU adrenal lesion without timely specialist MDT evaluation. Recommend surgery solely for the original 2.8 cm / 6 HU homogeneous lesion without hormonal or clinical assessment. Fail to assess potential hormone excess prior to an invasive procedure on an indeterminate adrenal lesion.
sections.6. Curveball: An updated radiologist report reads “5.1 cm heterogeneous mass, unenhanced attenuation 28 HU.” Candidate should switch from reassurance/no further imaging to expedited adrenal MDT consideration of malignancy, functional assessment and staging; not merely schedule an arbitrary repeat scan.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If biopsy suggested: stop and explain endocrine assessment and why biopsy can precipitate a catecholamine crisis. If annual CT suggested for original lesion: correct to no further imaging after benign unenhanced CT characteristics (assuming appropriate work-up). If atypical scan appears: explicitly withdraw benign pathway and request MDT evaluation and appropriate staging.
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail “It is an adrenal lump, so we should biopsy it or operate because it could be cancer.” No imaging stratification or hormone screen. Metanephrines are generally reserved for lesions not typical of benign adenoma. sections.preamble: B2-156 — Neck Swelling After Thyroidectomy Draft for independent clinical review • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute station • Critical care / postoperative emergency
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar called to the recovery unit 3 hours after total thyroidectomy. A 52-year-old patient is anxious, has progressive neck tightness and difficulty swallowing. Explain your immediate assessment and actions to the examiner. You are not required to perform a procedure on a real person.
sections.2. Examiner brief and information disclo: Patient is seated, awake and distressed. HR 118/min, BP 156/90 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 96% on air. Tight, expanding anterior neck swelling under the dressing. Voice becoming muffled. If candidate acts: senior anaesthesia and thyroid surgeon can attend; bedside post-thyroid emergency box is available. If candidate waits: audible stridor and oxygen desaturation occur. No laboratory result is needed to trigger action.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Say: “My neck feels tight and I cannot swallow properly.” If asked, the swelling began 20 minutes ago, is enlarging, and breathing is becoming uncomfortable. Become more breathless if candidate delays. Do not volunteer a reassuring normal oxygen saturation as excluding airway risk.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific performa: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Labels swelling as routine postoperative oedema and misses evolving airway threat Identifies expanding post-thyroidectomy haematoma as an airway emergency, even with SpO₂ 96% Immediately anticipates rapid airway compromise; verbalises DESATS triggers and simultaneous team actions Call for help Reassures or requests routine review later Activates emergency help; calls senior anaesthetist and thyroid/ENT surgeon now Specifies parallel task allocation, difficult-airway support and crash trolley Immediate positioning and oxygen Leaves patient flat or omits oxygen Sits patient up, administers supplemental oxygen, continuous pulse oximetry and frequent observations Keeps patient in monitored resuscitation area and avoids unnecessary transfer Airway assessment Waits for stridor or desaturation to act Assesses speech, breathing, respiratory effort, swallowing, swelling and voice concurrently Recognises stridor is late and plans oxygenation with senior anaesthesia Evacuation decision Requests CT or ultrasound before wound opening despite compromise States airway compromise from suspected haematoma requires immediate bedside wound opening using S
sections.5. Critical fails — safety override: Fails to recognise potentially obstructing post-thyroidectomy haematoma and leaves patient without urgent review. Delays emergency wound opening for imaging or transfer once airway compromise is evident. Does not summon expert anaesthetic and surgical support despite progressive airway symptoms. Treats currently normal SpO₂ as proof airway obstruction cannot develop.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At minute 5 the actor develops stridor and SpO₂ falls to 90% despite oxygen. Expected response: emergency bedside SCOOP evacuation at once with senior airway team preparing intubation/rescue, not a CT request.
sections.7. Recovery opportunities: After initially saying “I will ask for an ultrasound”, candidate retracts: “The expanding swelling and airway symptoms make that unsafe; I am calling anaesthesia and opening the wound now if compromised.” After noting normal SpO₂, candidate corrects: “Oxygen saturation can remain normal until late; dysphagia, anxiety and progressive tightness require immediate action.”
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail: “The oxygen is normal, so I will book a scan and watch overnight.” Pass: “This is a suspected postoperative neck haematoma. I will call senior anaesthesia and thyroid surgery, sit the patient up, give oxygen and monitor. If breathing is compromised I will open the wound immediately using SCOOP.” High-performance: “We have an evolving thyroidectomy haematoma: call emergency anaesthesia and the surgeon, bring the thyroid box, provide oxygen and monitoring. Progressive airway compromise needs immediate bedside release through superficial and strap-muscle layers, then airway rescue if needed, followed by definitive theatre haemostasis.”

sections.preamble: B2-157 — Tingling After Thyroidectomy Draft for independent clinical review • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute station • Data interpretation / postoperative management
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 43-year-old patient the morning after total thyroidectomy. They report tingling around the mouth and fingertips. You are given an adjusted calcium of 1.78 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (local normal 0.7–1.0), and an ECG with QT prolongation. Interpret the results and manage the patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief and information disclo: Patient alert, HR 98/min, BP 126/76 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO₂ 98%. Perioral and fingertip paraesthesia with intermittent hand cramps. Adjusted calcium 1.78 mmol/L; Mg 0.62 mmol/L; phosphate 1.65 mmol/L; PTH low (below local postoperative reference). ECG: prolonged QT, no arrhythmia yet. If candidate asks: no stridor or neck swelling. Patient has IV access. If candidate postpones treatment, carpopedal spasm occurs.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Say: “My lips and fingers are tingling, and my hands sometimes cramp.” Ask: “Could this be because of the operation? Will it be permanent?” If candidate dismisses symptoms, say cramps are worsening. Do not volunteer the laboratory diagnosis.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific performa: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognise cause Dismisses tingling as anxiety without biochemical interpretation Identifies symptomatic post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia likely from transient parathyroid dysfunction Connects low PTH, low calcium, raised phosphate and concomitant low magnesium without assuming permanent hypoparathyroidism Severity assessment Treats as harmless despite calcium 1.78 and QT prolongation States symptomatic severe hypocalcaemia is a medical emergency Explicitly checks tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, rhythm disturbance and clinical stability Initial safety No ECG or timely senior input Commences ECG monitoring, checks ABC and contacts senior surgical/endocrine team Checks IV access and arranges monitored bed with repeat clinical assessments Calcium replacement Gives oral calcium alone and leaves symptomatic patient Initiates IV calcium gluconate using emergency protocol with ECG monitoring Specifies 10–20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate diluted and given over 10 minutes, repeated if needed according to response and local protocol Further replacement Gives a single bolus and omits further plan Plans ongoing replacement/infusion as indicated and serial calcium
sections.5. Critical fails — safety override: Fails to treat symptomatic calcium 1.78 mmol/L with QT prolongation as a medical emergency. Gives oral supplements only despite significant symptomatic hypocalcaemia. Administers IV calcium without ECG monitoring or without checking response. Discharges despite continuing symptoms, ECG abnormality or no reliable calcium follow-up.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At minute 5 the patient develops painful carpopedal spasm. Expected response: urgent monitored IV calcium gluconate, senior involvement and reassessment; do not wait for a repeat PTH result.
sections.7. Recovery opportunities: After proposing oral calcium alone, candidate corrects: “Because this is symptomatic, the level is 1.78 and QT is prolonged, IV calcium with ECG monitoring is needed now.” After focusing only on calcium, candidate adds: “Magnesium is low and must be corrected as well to avoid persistent hypocalcaemia.”
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail: “Tingling is usual after thyroid surgery; I will give calcium tablets and discharge.” Pass: “This is symptomatic severe postoperative hypocalcaemia, likely hypoparathyroidism. I will check ABC and ECG monitoring, seek senior advice, give IV calcium gluconate per the emergency protocol and replace magnesium, then recheck calcium and ECG.” High-performance: “Symptoms, calcium 1.78, low PTH and prolonged QT demand monitored emergency IV calcium. I will correct low magnesium, plan further infusion or oral calcium/active vitamin D according to response and protocol, and provide a safe biochemical follow-up plan.”

sections.preamble: B2-158 — Sudden Severe Headache — Suspected Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Draft for independent clinical review • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute station • Emergency / applied knowledge
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar asked to assess a 47-year-old with abrupt severe headache in the emergency department. Take a focused history, interpret the written CT findings when supplied and outline immediate investigation and management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief and information disclo: Patient alert, GCS 15; sudden maximal-intensity headache 9 hours ago during exercise; vomiting and photophobia; no fever, no trauma. BP 164/92, HR 94, SpO₂ 98%, T 36.8°C. Initial non-contrast CT head report (disclose when requested): “No acute intracranial haemorrhage identified.” CT was performed 9 hours after onset. If candidate requests lumbar puncture: appropriate after at least 12 hours from symptom onset; spectrophotometric xanthochromia is positive. Subsequent CT angiogram shows a 5-mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm with a compatible subarachnoid bleeding pattern. A second examiner branch: if initial CT performed within 6 hours and formally reported negative by an appropriately experienced radiologist, lumbar puncture is not routinely offered; seek specialist advice if concern persists.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Say: “It felt like someone hit me on the back of the head. It was instantly the worst headache I have had.” If asked: vomiting twice, neck discomfort, no preceding fever or head injury, no weakness. If offered discharge because CT is clear: “But why did this happen so suddenly?”
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific performa: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and stabilisation Treats headache as uncomplicated migraine; no observations or neurological assessment. Assesses ABCDE, observations, GCS and analgesia; recognises possible intracranial emergency. Prioritises monitoring, IV access, senior emergency/neurosurgical advice and repeated neurological observations. Onset and red flags Does not establish timing or thunderclap onset. Establishes exact time to peak, exertional onset, vomiting, neck stiffness, collapse and focal symptoms. Elicits anticoagulants, prior sentinel headache and personal/family aneurysm history without delaying work-up. Focused examination Omits GCS, pupils or focal neurology. Checks GCS, pupils, cranial nerves, limbs and meningism as tolerated. Repeats exam for deterioration; avoids falsely relying on absent meningism. CT first Requests no urgent CT or substitutes MRI/LP first. Requests urgent non-contrast CT head and interprets reported negative CT. Explains that diagnostic confidence depends on scan timing and expert radiology reporting. CT/LP timing States a negative 9-hour CT excludes SAH or orders immediate LP. Recognises CT after 6 hours may miss SAH; considers LP a
sections.5. Critical fails — safety override: Discharges a patient after a negative CT obtained 9 hours after thunderclap onset without further assessment. Fails to arrange urgent CT/neurosurgical escalation despite clinical deterioration or confirmed SAH. Performs or advocates LP before 12 hours solely to exclude SAH after a negative delayed CT. Neglects a suddenly falling GCS or new focal deficit while continuing routine history-taking.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At minute 6 the patient becomes drowsier (GCS 12). Expected: immediately stop routine interview, summon resuscitation and senior anaesthesia/neurosurgery, repeat ABCDE, protect airway as indicated and expedite imaging/transfer.
sections.7. Recovery opportunities: After saying “CT is normal,” candidate corrects: “It was nine hours after onset; I cannot use this scan alone to rule out SAH. I will discuss LP after 12 hours and urgently obtain specialist advice.” After initially considering LP immediately, candidate clarifies the need for at least 12 hours from symptom onset for bilirubin detection. After proposing routine neurology follow-up, candidate explicitly contacts the neurosurgical centre once SAH is confirmed and arranges CTA.
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail: “The CT is clear. This was probably a migraine; go home.” Pass: “This is thunderclap headache. Obtain urgent CT; because this negative scan was nine hours after onset, consider LP at least twelve hours after onset. If SAH is confirmed, arrange CTA and urgent neurosurgical consultation.” High-performance: “I will reassess GCS and focal neurology, monitor, treat symptoms and discuss imaging urgently. Timing is central: a negative CT after six hours does not reliably exclude SAH; CSF bilirubin after twelve hours may confirm it. Confirmed SAH requires CTA, early neurosurgical transfer and specialist consideration of nimodipine and aneurysm occlusion.”

stations.title: Confusion on Warfarin

sections.preamble: B2-159 — Confusion in an Older Patient on Warfarin — Chronic Subdural Haematoma Draft for independent clinical review • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute station • Emergency / history and data interpretation
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar on call assessing a 79-year-old taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation, brought by family with three weeks of progressive confusion and gait unsteadiness. Take a focused history, interpret the written head CT and describe urgent management.
sections.2. Examiner brief and information disclo: Older adult mildly confused, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), HR 82, BP 148/78, T 36.7°C. Minor unwitnessed fall 4 weeks ago; no clear recent head injury. Warfarin 4 mg daily, last INR unknown. Left-sided mild weakness (4/5). FBC Hb 118 g/L, platelets 215 ×10⁹/L, INR 3.4, creatinine 91 µmol/L. CT head report when requested: “Right frontoparietal crescentic mixed-density extra-axial collection up to 17 mm with approximately 6 mm midline shift, in keeping with acute-on-chronic subdural haematoma.” This is an imaging-confirmed intracranial haemorrhage, not an anticoagulated minor head-injury-only imaging scenario.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Daughter: “He has been slower and forgetful for weeks, but yesterday he almost fell again. Could it just be dementia?” If asked: takes warfarin, has had headache and mild left arm clumsiness, no fever. Patient becomes sleepier if escalation delayed.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific performa: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognise emergency Attributes presentation to dementia or delirium without considering structural brain disease. Recognises evolving focal neurological symptoms on warfarin as possible intracranial bleeding. Explicitly identifies subdural haematoma even after minor or forgotten trauma. Stabilisation Does not assess GCS, vitals or capacity to protect airway. Performs ABCDE, baseline GCS, pupils, limb examination and frequent neurological observations. Plans urgent airway support if GCS declines; protects against falls and avoids delays. History and drugs Fails to ask about warfarin or falls. Asks about timing, falls, headache, focal symptoms, seizures, warfarin indication and last dose. Checks interacting medicines, antiplatelets and INR history; asks about baseline function. Urgent tests Requests only routine bloods or cognitive clinic referral. Requests urgent CT head, FBC, U&E, coagulation/INR and group-and-save. Coordinates blood sampling with immediate imaging; repeat investigations as condition changes. CT interpretation Calls the crescentic collection an infarct or ignores midline shift. Identifies subdural blood, mixed density and mass effe
sections.5. Critical fails — safety override: Fails to obtain urgent CT and neurological assessment for evolving confusion plus weakness on warfarin. Continues warfarin or fails to initiate urgent reversal after confirmed intracranial haemorrhage. Fails to contact neurosurgery despite 17-mm subdural collection, midline shift and focal deficit. Ignores falling GCS or treats acute neurological decline as uncomplicated delirium.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At minute 6 the patient drops to GCS 10 and develops a larger left arm deficit. Expected: immediate ABCDE/anaesthetic support, urgent neurosurgical update, continue emergency anticoagulant reversal and expedite definitive care.
sections.7. Recovery opportunities: After saying “likely dementia,” candidate identifies the asymmetric weakness and anticoagulant use and switches to urgent CT and neurological observations. After saying “withhold warfarin and monitor,” candidate corrects: “This is confirmed intracranial bleeding; he needs immediate PCC and IV vitamin K under the emergency protocol.” After initially suggesting outpatient imaging, candidate recognises midline shift, telephones neurosurgery and arranges monitored transfer.
sections.8. Model performance examples: Fail: “This sounds like dementia. We can arrange a memory-clinic appointment and repeat the INR next week.” Pass: “He may have a subdural bleed. I will assess GCS and focal signs, organise urgent CT and coagulation tests. The scan confirms a significant subdural with shift; stop warfarin, give emergency PCC with IV vitamin K and refer to neurosurgery immediately.” High-performance: “This is symptomatic acute-on-chronic subdural haemorrhage with mass effect and warfarin-associated coagulopathy. Start serial GCS/pupil checks, avoid delay to CT, initiate four-factor PCC and IV vitamin K per major-bleeding protocol with repeat INR, and discuss urgent evacuation and monitored transfer with neurosurgery while updating the family.”

stations.title: Organ Donation Conversation

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-162 Organ Donation Conversation DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Communication / Applied Knowledge • 9-minute station • Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar supporting an ICU team. A 56-year-old adult has suffered a devastating intracranial haemorrhage. The ICU consultant has explained to the family that recovery is not possible and life-sustaining treatment is being reviewed. The patient may be a potential organ donor. The specialist nurse for organ donation (SN-OD) has been contacted and will join shortly. Speak with the patient’s sister, who is distressed and asks what organ donation would mean. Do not seek consent yourself or announce that death has been confirmed.
sections.2. Examiner brief and room setup: Communication station, 9 minutes. Actor plays the sister; no physical examination. Assess compassionate understanding of end-of-life context, correct SN-OD involvement, patient wishes and legal nuances, and separation of treatment decisions from donation. Candidate should not be required to give a definitive donation suitability decision.
sections.3. Actor brief — sister: You are Ms Patel, 52. Your brother has been in intensive care since a catastrophic bleed. You understand doctors have said he will not recover, but you are unsure whether he is dead. You say: “Are you asking us to give up on him so you can take his organs?” You do not know if he registered a decision, but recall he once said he liked helping others. Ask whether your faith will be respected. You want time with your brother.
sections.4. Opening and relationship: Introduce name and role; check sister’s identity and what she understands; offer a private space and support person. Begin with the existing clinical discussion, not a sales pitch for donation.
sections.5. Main communication tasks: Ask what the sister has understood about prognosis and the treatment plan; acknowledge grief and correct misunderstandings without implying that donation determines care. Explain that decisions about treatment and determination of death follow separate clinical processes; do not falsely state the patient is dead when death has not been established. Explain that specialist nurses discuss donation eligibility, register decisions and the legal/consent framework; arrange their involvement rather than independently securing a signature. Explore known wishes, beliefs, prior conversations and who else should be involved. Explain that England has an opt-out framework for many adults but exceptions apply; family is consulted. Avoid coercion, promises of organs being suitable or specific transplant outcomes; offer time, questions and bereavement/faith support. Arrange clear documentation and handover to ICU and SN-OD; maintain privacy.
sections.6. Examiner disclosures (only when asked: Patient age 56; residence in England >20 years; no known registered opt-out. SN-OD has not yet checked register; death has not been formally established. Family has not agreed to discuss donation in depth. ICU consultant remains responsible for treatment plan.
sections.7. Expected clinical framing: Possible organ donation should be considered in appropriate ICU end-of-life pathways with early SN-OD involvement. Explain that consent/deemed consent and family support are assessed by specialists; do not pressure relatives. Any potential donation decision must not distort best-interest treatment or death determination.
sections.8. Closing and handover: Summarise that clinical care remains the priority, invite questions and offer a specific next contact with ICU and SN-OD. Document questions and any expressed patient wishes without writing “family consented” when they have not. Marking grid — station-specific performance anchors Area Fail Pass High-performance Opening and privacy Begins discussing organs in corridor without checking who the relative is. Introduces self, checks relation and moves to private setting. Asks permission to talk, offers support person and checks immediate emotional needs. Understanding of prognosis Assumes the patient is already dead or repeats jargon. Elicits understanding of prognosis and acknowledges uncertainty around the current process. Uses teach-back to distinguish irreversible prognosis, treatment withdrawal and formal death determination. Empathy Dismisses distress or says “you need to be strong”. Acknowledges shock and gives the sister time to respond. Names the concern about losing her brother, tolerates silence and addresses guilt. Treatment–donation separation Suggests treatment is being stopped to obtain organs. States treatment decisions are independent of donation. Clarifies the ICU team

stations.title: Fever in a Kidney Transplant Recipient
stations.source_heading: B2-163 Fever in a Kidney Transplant Recipient

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-163 Fever in a Kidney Transplant Recipient DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Communication / Applied Knowledge • 9-minute station • Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to review a 48-year-old kidney transplant recipient on the acute assessment unit. The patient has fever, rigors and reduced urine output. Interpret the observations and laboratory data supplied by the examiner, explain your immediate plan and deliver an SBAR referral to the transplant team. No physical procedure is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and room setup: 9-minute applied knowledge / critical care station. Candidate must recognise sepsis/AKI risk in an immunosuppressed patient, obtain cultures without delaying time-critical antibiotics, check transplant-specific medicines, consider urinary/graft and other infectious sources, and involve transplant nephrology, microbiology and critical care appropriately.
sections.3. Actor brief — patient: You received a deceased-donor kidney 8 months ago. You take tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisolone, plus other routine medicines. Since yesterday you have fever and shivering, burning urine and passing less urine. You are frightened of losing the graft. You ask, “Should I stop my anti-rejection tablets?” You have no known drug allergies.
sections.4. Examiner observations / results: T 39.1°C; HR 122/min; BP 92/56 mmHg; RR 25/min; SpO₂ 96% air; new confusion absent. Creatinine 235 µmol/L versus usual 115; lactate 3.1 mmol/L; WBC 15.8 ×10⁹/L; urinalysis positive for nitrite/leucocytes. Transplant is in right iliac fossa and mildly tender. NEWS2 is high-risk in this scenario; ask for repeated observations and senior assessment.
sections.5. Immediate assessment and treatment: ABCDE, oxygen only if indicated, IV access, repeat full observations/NEWS2, assess perfusion, fluid balance and urine output; call senior help promptly. Send blood cultures and urine culture (plus source-specific specimens), FBC, renal profile, lactate, CRP, glucose, coagulation; do not delay antibiotics in a high-risk patient to await sampling or imaging. Treat as suspected high-risk sepsis per current NICE NG253 with prompt locally guided IV antibiotics, checking allergies, renal adjustment and interactions. Give reassessed crystalloid fluid boluses if hypoperfused, with attention to fluid overload and graft function; monitor lactate and haemodynamics. Urgently discuss with transplant nephrology / transplant surgeon, microbiology and senior acute-care team; assess need for critical care. Request transplant kidney ultrasound if obstruction or vascular compromise suspected, and consider graft pyelonephritis, UTI, bacteraemia, chest infection and opportunistic infection based on context. Confirm immunosuppressant doses and recent changes, measure tacrolimus level where indicated, and do not unilaterally stop maintenance immunosuppression; seek transplant-team advice on adjustments.
sections.6. Examiner disclosures (if requested): No recent rejection treatment; no central line. Last tacrolimus trough unavailable; last dose taken this morning. Chest is clear. No focal abdominal peritonism. Urine output 15 mL/h. Lab cannot give culture result during station.
sections.7. Differential and graft considerations: Infection is the leading concern; urinary infection involving graft is plausible. Consider obstruction, rejection, drug toxicity and BK virus when relevant, but none justify delaying stabilisation and infection management. Rejection is not diagnosed simply from fever and creatinine rise.
sections.8. SBAR and close: Situation: febrile transplant recipient with hypotension and AKI. Background: kidney transplant 8 months ago, tacrolimus/mycophenolate/prednisolone. Assessment: likely urinary sepsis with graft dysfunction. Recommendation: urgent bedside transplant/nephrology advice, antibiotics, fluid-guided resuscitation, ultrasound and critical-care assessment if not improving; agree immunosuppression plan. Explain escalation to patient and document. Marking grid — station-specific performance anchors Area Fail Pass High-performance Recognises emergency Labels as uncomplicated cystitis and suggests discharge. Identifies suspected sepsis with graft dysfunction and need for admission. Identifies shock physiology, AKI and immunosuppression as compounding risks. ABCDE and escalation Fails to check circulation or call for urgent help. Performs structured assessment and alerts senior. Names repeat NEWS2, monitored bed and critical-care triggers. Cultures and blood tests Orders urine dip only and ignores creatinine change. Requests cultures, bloods, lactate and renal function. Adds appropriate site sampling, cultures before antibiotics if no delay, tacrolimus-level assessment. Antimicrobials Waits for

stations.title: Types of Shock

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-164 — Types of Shock Group 17 • Data interpretation / critical care • 9-minute practice station • 12 October 2026 • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT Educational simulation only; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Final live-register duplicate check and independent clinical sign-off outstanding.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar asked to assess a 67-year-old patient two hours after emergency laparotomy. The patient looks unwell, BP 82/48 mmHg, HR 128/min, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO₂ 94% on air, temperature 36.1°C. An arterial gas reveals pH 7.29, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. Your task: Interpret the physiological information; classify possible shock mechanisms; request discriminating bedside information; and state your immediate management and escalation.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosed findings: At outset: pale, cool, clammy; capillary refill 5 seconds; conscious but restless; urine output 10 mL over the last hour. If asked: abdomen distended; drain has 350 mL fresh blood over 30 minutes; wound dressing bloodstained. Hb 112 g/L immediately after surgery and 109 g/L now. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Focused bedside echo: no major LV impairment, no pericardial effusion. Lung assessment: equal air entry without signs of tension pneumothorax. If the candidate asks for an alternative mechanism, provide: septic/distributive — warm peripheries and suspected infection; cardiogenic — pulmonary oedema and reduced cardiac function; obstructive — tension pneumothorax, tamponade or major PE signs.
sections.3. Patient / examiner prompts: The examiner asks: “Can a blood pressure above 100 exclude shock?” Answer: no, compensated shock is possible. At 4 minutes: “The early haemoglobin is nearly normal. Are you reassured?” Expected: no; acute bleeding may precede Hb decline. At 6 minutes: “Would you give repeated large fluid boluses without reassessment?” Expected: no; use cause-directed resuscitation and early blood where haemorrhage is likely.
sections.4. Marking grid — observable actions: Score each domain on the behaviour actually demonstrated. Safety-critical rows are marked ★. Bands: Fail / Pass / High-performance. Domain Fail Pass High-performance ★ Recognition of shock Calls this anxiety or routine postoperative pain despite hypotension, poor perfusion and lactate 5.2. Identifies circulatory shock with tissue hypoperfusion from BP, pulse, CRT, oliguria and lactate. Identifies shock early and notes a normal blood pressure or early Hb cannot exclude evolving hypoperfusion. ABCDE and monitoring Discusses blood tests before bedside assessment and omits reassessment. Calls for ABCDE, oxygen if indicated, monitors, repeated BP/ECG/SpO₂, glucose and urine output. Delegates monitoring and frequent reassessment while pursuing immediate reversible causes. Shock classification Lists shock labels without mechanisms or links to the presentation. Classifies hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic and obstructive shock with a defining mechanism for each. Explains why cold, blood-loss-associated shock is most likely here, while actively screening competing causes. ★ Haemorrhage assessment Accepts normal early Hb and overlooks surgical drain bleeding. Requests drain losses, ope
sections.6. Curveball: After the first fluid intervention, BP remains 78/42 and the drain fills with another 200 mL blood. Ask candidate to prioritise: activate major haemorrhage response, call the operating surgeon/anaesthetist, start blood-directed resuscitation and prepare urgent source control; do not wait for repeat Hb.
sections.7. Specific recovery lines: “I previously concentrated on the lactate; the new rapidly filling drain changes my priority to postoperative bleeding. I am calling the operating surgeon and anaesthetist now.” “The early Hb cannot exclude blood loss. I will group and crossmatch, activate the major haemorrhage pathway as required, and reassess perfusion continuously.” “I will check for other immediate obstructive and cardiac causes, but not let this delay surgical haemostasis.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail: “Lactate is high, so this is sepsis. I will give fluids and monitor. Hb is acceptable.” Misses active blood loss, no urgent surgical action (grid 1, 4, 7, 9).
sections.9. Model performance — Pass: “This patient is shocked. I will assess ABCDE, give monitored resuscitation, obtain IV access and crossmatch, and urgently inform the operating team; active bleeding is likely.” (grid 1, 2, 4, 7, 9).

stations.title: Falling Platelets After Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-165 — Falling Platelets After Surgery Group 17 • Data interpretation / applied surgical science • 9-minute practice station • 12 October 2026 • DEVELOPMENT DRAFT Educational simulation only; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Final live-register duplicate check and independent clinical sign-off outstanding.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 62-year-old patient on day 7 after colorectal surgery. Platelets were 280 × 10⁹/L before operation, 230 on day 2 and are now 95. The patient has received daily prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin since surgery and has a new painful swollen left calf. There is no major active bleeding. Your task: Interpret the platelet trend, calculate the 4Ts score using supplied data, investigate suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), and outline safe initial management.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosed findings: Platelet fall: 280 to 95 × 10⁹/L, a 66% fall with nadir above 20: thrombocytopenia component 2 points. Timing: day 7 following first heparin exposure: timing component 2 points. If requested: urgent duplex confirms new proximal DVT: thrombosis component 2 points. No sepsis, DIC, massive transfusion, new marrow-suppressive medication or other apparent explanation: other causes component 2 points. Total 4Ts = 8/8 (high probability). Renal function eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m², Hb 110 g/L, normal coagulation profile. Requires specialist choice of alternative anticoagulant.
sections.3. Patient / examiner prompts: Examiner asks: “Does the platelet count have to be below 150 to diagnose HIT?” Expected: percent fall and timing matter, count may remain above 150. Examiner asks: “Would you give platelets just because the count is 95?” Expected: not routinely in HIT without major bleeding or another indication. The anaesthetist asks whether IV heparin for the confirmed DVT is safe: candidate must reject heparin and arrange suitable non-heparin anticoagulation.
sections.4. Marking grid — observable actions: Score each domain on the behaviour actually demonstrated. Safety-critical rows are marked ★. Bands: Fail / Pass / High-performance. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Platelet trend Notes only 95 without comparing baseline or percentage fall. Calculates an approximate 66% fall from baseline 280 to 95 and highlights day 7 timing. Explains the delayed immune thrombocytopenia pattern rather than treating it as expected immediate postoperative dilution. 4Ts thrombocytopenia Awards zero points because platelets are above 20, or miscalculates the fall. Correctly awards 2 points for >50% fall with nadir ≥20. Explains why the relative fall matters more than an absolute platelet threshold. 4Ts timing Calls day 7 impossible for HIT. Awards 2 for clear onset 5–10 days following heparin exposure. Checks for earlier heparin exposure that could alter onset and interpretation. 4Ts thrombosis / other causes Omits DVT or assumes sepsis is present without evidence. Awards 2 for confirmed DVT and 2 for no apparent other cause; total 8, high likelihood. Separates observed data from uncertainty and recalculates if an alternative thrombocytopenia cause emerges. ★ Heparin cessation Continues LMWH after hi
sections.6. Curveball: The examiner announces a request for a heparin infusion to treat the proximal DVT. Candidate must stop that order and immediately organise appropriate non-heparin anticoagulation with haematology, noting renal function and bleeding risk.
sections.7. Specific recovery lines: “I underestimated the platelet trend. The fall is 66%, starting day 7, with DVT; this gives a high 4Ts score.” “I need to stop LMWH and any heparin flushes now and seek haematology advice for an alternative anticoagulant while sending HIT testing.” “I will document suspected HIT visibly, review thrombotic complications and reassess the plan once laboratory results return.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail: “Platelets are 95, so stop all anticoagulation and wait for the HIT antibody result.” Creates thrombotic risk (grid 5–7).
sections.9. Model performance — Pass: “This is a marked platelet fall in the usual HIT window, with new DVT. The 4Ts score is high. I will stop all heparin, send the immunoassay and contact haematology urgently for non-heparin anticoagulation.” (grid 1–7, 9).
