sections.preamble: B2-166 — Positive Blood Culture on the Ward Draft • 12 October 2026 • MRCS Part B practice • 9 minutes • NOT an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the on-call surgical registrar. The laboratory telephones: “Blood cultures taken yesterday from a day-4 postoperative patient are positive.” You have nine minutes to interpret further information, prioritise actions and give a structured management plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and scenario: Recognise clinically significant S. aureus bacteraemia with possible sepsis, stabilise the patient, involve microbiology and look for the source without premature conclusions.A 67-year-old patient underwent right hemicolectomy four days ago. They had rigors overnight. Blood cultures: both peripheral sets signal positive at 13 and 15 hours; Gram-positive cocci in clusters, subsequently identified as Staphylococcus aureus. Observations: T 38.6°C, HR 118/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 25/min, SpO₂ 95% on air, new confusion. Wound mildly erythematous; one peripheral cannula, no central line. Creatinine 150 µmol/L (baseline 85).
sections.3. Actor / nurse disclosure: Laboratory microbiologist (telephone) / nurse. Answer only questions asked. If asked: blood cultures were from two separate peripheral sites, before antibiotics; no antimicrobial allergy recorded; no heart murmur documented, and source is not yet identified. If candidate asks about susceptibility, it is pending.
sections.4. Examiner disclosure and prompts: Give the observations, investigations or history details only when requested. Candidate is expected to prioritise safe immediate actions; do not volunteer the answer. If an action is described but not actually performed, score on the stated action only where the station is verbal/data-based.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Mark each domain from demonstrated actions. Fail / Pass / High-performance are domain descriptors, not a numerical summation formula. Safety-critical items take precedence. Domain
sections.1. Immediate recognition: Fail Labels this an insignificant contaminant and gives no review. Pass Recognises S. aureus in two sets as significant and attends urgently. High-performance Explicitly states bacteraemia may indicate invasive infection and that early growth and separate sets strengthen significance. Domain
sections.2. Physiological assessment: Fail Ignores hypotension, confusion or tachypnoea. Pass Performs ABCDE, reviews observations and NEWS2, arranges close monitoring. High-performance Names perfusion, mental status, urine output, oxygen need and serial reassessment. Domain
sections.3. Sepsis actions: Fail Orders antibiotics without clinical assessment or delays resuscitation. Pass Calls senior/critical care as needed, gains IV access, takes blood gas/lactate, FBC, U&E and appropriate cultures, and starts risk-based resuscitation. High-performance States urgent antibiotics for high-risk suspected sepsis and checks response with documented reassessment. Domain

stations.title: Nutrition After Major Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-167 — Nutrition After Major Surgery Draft • 12 October 2026 • MRCS Part B practice • 9 minutes • NOT an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a patient after major abdominal surgery. In nine minutes, assess nutritional risk, interpret provided information, select a safe route for nutrition support and explain your monitoring plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and scenario: Identify malnutrition and high refeeding risk, avoid starvation and inappropriate forced enteral feeding, and involve the nutrition team for a safe supervised plan.A 71-year-old has undergone emergency small-bowel resection for adhesive obstruction, with primary anastomosis. Day 6: persistent ileus, vomiting with oral trials and large nasogastric aspirates; currently unsafe oral intake. BMI 18.2 kg/m²; 12% unintentional weight loss over 3 months; negligible intake for 8 days. Electrolytes: phosphate 0.55 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.57 mmol/L; glucose 5.7 mmol/L; creatinine 112 µmol/L. Haemodynamically stable. No current evidence of anastomotic leak.
sections.3. Actor / nurse disclosure: Dietitian / ward nurse. If asked: eating poorly for weeks before admission; no existing feeding tube; ileus prevents sufficient enteral feeding currently. Patient is alert and concerned that “drips are not real food”.
sections.4. Examiner disclosure and prompts: Give the observations, investigations or history details only when requested. Candidate is expected to prioritise safe immediate actions; do not volunteer the answer. If an action is described but not actually performed, score on the stated action only where the station is verbal/data-based.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Mark each domain from demonstrated actions. Fail / Pass / High-performance are domain descriptors, not a numerical summation formula. Safety-critical items take precedence. Domain
sections.1. Nutrition risk: Fail Calls patient adequately nourished based on single current weight. Pass Identifies weight loss, low BMI and prolonged limited intake; screens with a validated tool. High-performance States multiple high-risk refeeding features and records baseline intake and weight trajectory. Domain
sections.2. Clinical assessment: Fail Ignores ongoing vomiting and losses. Pass Assesses ileus, obstruction/leak features, hydration, stool/flatus, NG output and fluid balance. High-performance Integrates abdominal recovery and realistic timing of gut function return before selecting route. Domain
sections.3. Baseline investigations: Fail Starts nutrition without electrolytes. Pass Checks phosphate, magnesium, potassium, U&E, glucose, LFT and clinical fluid balance. High-performance Highlights concurrent hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia as safety risks. Domain

stations.title: Is This Test Any Good
stations.source_heading: B2-168 Is This Test Any Good

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-168 — Is This Test Any Good Applied science / data interpretation • 9-minute practice station • 12 October 2026 • PROVISIONAL DRAFT Educational simulation; not an official MRCS Part B mark scheme. AMaC assigns final live MB identifier after register review.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar. A screening test is proposed for a condition affecting 10% of this sample. Review the 2×2 table provided and explain sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and clinical implications to the examiner. You may use a calculator. You have nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Provide the table below. Ask the candidate to calculate four test characteristics, then ask whether a positive test establishes the diagnosis and how prevalence affects interpretation. Mark mathematical accuracy and clinical judgement separately. No external image is required.
sections.3. Examiner disclosure / scenario data: Reference-standard disease PRESENT: test positive 80, test negative 20 (total 100). Reference-standard disease ABSENT: test positive 90, test negative 810 (total 900). Total sample 1,000; test positive 170; test negative 830. Correct results: sensitivity 80%; specificity 90%; PPV 47.1%; NPV 97.6%; prevalence 10%; overall accuracy 89%.
sections.4. Actor / interlocutor brief: Examiner acts as a colleague asking “Does a positive mean this patient definitely has disease?” If prompted about clinical use, say the test is intended for an asymptomatic lower-risk population and a confirmatory investigation is available.
sections.5. Marking grid — observable descriptors: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Table orientation Reverses disease/test axes and cannot identify TP/FP/FN/TN. Labels rows by disease status and columns by test result; identifies all four cells. Explicitly checks reference-standard status and denominator orientation before calculating. Sensitivity Divides positive tests by all tested patients. 80/(80+20) = 80%; measures positivity among truly diseased. Explains that high sensitivity supports ruling out when a negative result is obtained in a suitable context. Specificity Uses 80/100 or counts false positives as correct negatives. 810/(810+90) = 90%; measures negativity among truly disease-free. Links high specificity to the usefulness of a positive result for ruling in, subject to clinical context. Positive predictive value Calls a positive result 80% likely to be disease. 80/(80+90) = 47.1%; proportion of test-positive people truly diseased. Explains low prevalence creates many false positives even when specificity is 90%. Negative predictive value Uses 810/900, excluding false negatives. 810/(810+20) = 97.6%; proportion of negatives truly disease-free. Qualifies reassurance by population and pre-test probability. Accuracy and p
sections.6. Critical fail criteria (unsafe action: Recommends that a positive screening test establishes disease and authorises invasive treatment without confirmation. States that a negative screening result absolutely excludes disease in a patient with strong red flags. Misidentifies false negatives as true negatives and uses this to advise against necessary review. Uses a predictive value from a low-prevalence sample as an invariant estimate for a high-risk population.
sections.7. Examiner curveball: “The same test is offered to a specialist clinic where disease is much more common. What happens to the positive predictive value, assuming sensitivity and specificity remain similar?” Expected: PPV increases; calculate only if new prevalence is supplied.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery: After arithmetic error, redraw the four cells and write the denominators explicitly (diseased / non-diseased / all positive / all negative). If a positive was overinterpreted, state that 90 of 170 positive tests in this sample are false positives and arrange confirmation. If a negative was overinterpreted, point to 20 false negatives and retain a safety-net for persisting clinical suspicion.

stations.title: Diathermy Safety

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-170 — Diathermy Safety Applied surgical science / theatre safety • 9-minute practice station • 12 October 2026 • PROVISIONAL DRAFT — requires clinical sign-off and register duplicate check Educational simulation; not an official MRCS Part B mark scheme. Final station ID allocated by AMaC after live-register clearance.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are assisting during a laparoscopic operation. Explain how you would safely use monopolar and bipolar electrosurgery. The examiner may introduce an equipment problem. State your actions and who you would involve.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Set the scene before skin incision: alcohol-based chlorhexidine has just been applied, a monopolar unit and bipolar forceps are present, and the patient has an implanted pacemaker. No hands-on activation. Mark spoken checks/actions only.
sections.3. Examiner disclosure / scenario data: Monopolar: current goes from active electrode through patient to a return electrode; bipolar: current concentrated between forceps tips. Patient: implanted pacemaker, type/dependence not yet confirmed; anaesthetist available. Antiseptic appears visibly wet at edge of drape. During use, return-electrode contact-quality alarm sounds. There is no need to give fixed wattages: energy settings follow device instructions and task.
sections.4. Actor / interlocutor brief: Examiner plays scrub practitioner. If asked, report the prep is still wet; if asked about pacemaker, say no written plan has yet been confirmed. Offer a contact alarm if candidate proceeds to device activation.
sections.5. Marking grid — observable descriptors: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety Purpose & device selection Calls monopolar and bipolar identical; offers no choice. Explains monopolar current passes through patient to return electrode; bipolar current between instrument tips. Selects modality for haemostasis/tissue and explains why bipolar may reduce unintended current paths. — Pre-use equipment check Activates device without checking lead, electrode or generator. Checks compatible generator, leads, insulation, footswitch and activation controls. Performs verbal team confirmation of equipment integrity and safe inactive holster. SC Return electrode Places pad over scar/poor contact or ignores pad alarm. Selects sound perfused skin, correct pad size/contact and manufacturer-approved positioning. Verifies return-current path, contact monitoring, documentation and reassesses following repositioning. SC Fire triangle Uses diathermy while wet alcohol preparation remains. Checks prep has fully dried by evaporation, no pooled solution or soaked drapes. Coordinates oxygen delivery, draping and ignition sources in a shared fire-risk briefing. SC Implanted device Ignores pacemaker in history. Identifies implanted cardiac device an
sections.6. Critical fail criteria (unsafe action: Activates diathermy while alcohol-based antiseptic is still wet or pooled, creating avoidable fire risk. Ignores an active return-electrode alarm and continues monopolar activation. Continues monopolar electrosurgery despite known pacemaker without suitable team/device plan. Fails to stop activation when an electrosurgical burn or operating-room fire is suspected.
sections.7. Examiner curveball: “The return electrode alarm sounds after the patient is repositioned; the surgeon asks you to continue. What do you do?” Expected: stop energy delivery, state the concern, inspect/reapply electrode and reassess circuit per manufacturer and theatre policy before resuming.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery: If the alcohol risk was overlooked, explicitly halt activation, uncover any pooled/soaked material and allow full evaporation before use. If pacemaker precautions were missed, stop and involve anaesthesia plus the device-management service for a tailored plan. If the alarm was ignored, immediately cease use, check skin/electrode contact and inspect for burn before any restart.

stations.title: Preventing Surgical Site Infection

near_match.title: Surgical site infection prevention

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-171 — Preventing Surgical Site Infection Applied surgical science / perioperative safety • 9-minute practice station • 12 October 2026 • PROVISIONAL DRAFT — requires clinical sign-off and register duplicate check Educational simulation; not an official MRCS Part B mark scheme. Final station ID allocated by AMaC after live-register clearance.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are reviewing the infection-prevention plan for an adult scheduled for elective colorectal resection. Describe evidence-based steps before, during and after surgery. The examiner will provide a safety challenge.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Ask for a structured perioperative prevention plan. Candidate need not recite an antibiotic drug/dose without local protocol. Reward explicit appropriate prophylaxis and allergy checks, rather than blanket long-course antibiotics.
sections.3. Examiner disclosure / scenario data: Patient aged 64, type 2 diabetes with variable glycaemia and current smoking. No recorded allergy at briefing; the drug chart lists a historical chlorhexidine reaction, revealed if checked. Hair at the incision site is minimal and does not impair access. Nurse reports chlorhexidine-alcohol prep remains wet and diathermy is ready. Wound will be closed with a standard postoperative dressing.
sections.4. Actor / interlocutor brief: Examiner plays operating department practitioner. If asked about preparation, report a chlorhexidine reaction on prior admission. If challenged after surgery, say the patient has worsening wound pain and fever on day 4.
sections.5. Marking grid — observable descriptors: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety SSI risk evaluation Does not identify modifiable risks. Names diabetes control, smoking, nutrition, colonisation history and procedure factors. Prioritises practical changes with patient and team without claiming all risks eliminate infection. — Pre-op hygiene/hair Recommends routine razor shaving at home. Advises showering with soap and no routine hair removal; if essential, use clippers on day of surgery. Explains microabrasion risk of razors and checks site-specific local preparation. SC Prophylactic antibiotic Says give antibiotics to every patient or after closure. Selects prophylaxis based on procedure/local protocol; verifies allergy and timing before incision. Accounts for dose/weight, re-dosing if prolonged surgery and avoidance of unnecessary courses. SC Skin antisepsis Chooses inappropriate antiseptic or uses wet prep under diathermy. Chooses alcohol-based chlorhexidine first-line unless contraindicated/special site; allows full drying. Identifies mucosal-site and chlorhexidine allergy alternatives and fire hazard of pooling. SC Aseptic technique Does not discuss hand preparation or sterile precautions. Covers appropriate hand dec
sections.6. Critical fail criteria (unsafe action: Proceeds with chlorhexidine despite a confirmed serious chlorhexidine reaction. Uses diathermy before alcohol-based antiseptic has evaporated or with pooling beneath drapes. Neglects essential prophylactic antibiotic when indicated, without justifiable rationale, or overlooks a serious antibiotic allergy. Dismisses postoperative systemic illness with a potentially infected wound and offers no urgent assessment.
sections.7. Examiner curveball: “The theatre nurse says the patient previously developed widespread hives after chlorhexidine. The surgeon is ready to start.” Expected: stop, clarify reaction, choose an appropriate alternative antiseptic and follow theatre allergy policy, then ensure the field is dry before diathermy.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery: After advocating shaving, correct to no hair removal unless necessary and use electric clippers rather than a razor. After missing antiseptic allergy, stop preparation and replace with an appropriate allergy-safe product after confirmation with team. If postoperative fever was dismissed, organise immediate wound and systemic assessment, cultures if appropriate, and surgical review for deep infection/source control.

stations.title: Tourniquet Use in Limb Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-172 Tourniquet Use in Limb Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-172 Tourniquet Use in Limb Surgery Applied surgical science / operating-theatre safety • 9-minute station • Draft for clinical review • 12 October 2026 Educational simulation only; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar briefing the team before a knee procedure. The surgeon plans a pneumatic thigh tourniquet. Explain your safety checks, pressure and duration principles, risk controls and documentation. You may ask the examiner for observations. No equipment demonstration is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Adult aged 57, elective knee surgery. Baseline systolic BP 125 mmHg; thigh cuff available; anticipated operating time 95 minutes. No acute infection or suspected DVT. If asked: significant peripheral arterial disease not known; skin intact; no contraindication to cuff identified. If candidate discusses hypotensive episodes, ask how pressure should be reviewed. Expect reference to operating surgeon and anaesthetist rather than independent unilateral decisions.
sections.3. Actor / simulated-team brief: Examiner plays operating-department practitioner: “Shall we set the tourniquet to 300 for everyone?” On probing, “Skin prep has run beneath the padding.” Remain neutral and disclose these only when candidate asks/at curveball.
sections.4. Marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Indication and contraindications Uses tourniquet reflexively; ignores limb vascular disease, infection, DVT concern or specific operation. Explains benefit for bloodless field and weighs patient/limb factors with surgeon and anaesthetist. Justifies use against duration, vascular/neurological risk and available alternatives; tailors plan. Equipment and site Omits equipment check or places cuff over uneven skin/poor padding. Checks device, selects suitable cuff/limb site and thin even padding; protects skin. Checks cuff width > half limb diameter or suitable contour and accessibility for surveillance. Exsanguination Uses compressive exsanguination despite current infection, malignancy or suspected DVT. States compressive exsanguination must be avoided in these risk settings; follows team plan. Differentiates exsanguination method from simply elevating and identifies clot/embolism concern. Safe pressure Uses fixed 300 mmHg for everyone, with no BP or occlusion assessment. For adult lower limb uses systolic BP +70–130 mmHg or validated limb occlusion pressure per protocol. Chooses the lowest effective individually validated pressure and rechecks when h
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-related: Continuing with tourniquet inflation despite antiseptic pooling under cuff without correcting it (preventable chemical burn risk). Using compressive exsanguination with suspected DVT/infection/malignancy despite identifying the risk. Ignoring prolonged tourniquet time without alerting the operating surgeon, reassessing and documenting extension. Failing to react to new postoperative limb ischaemia or neurovascular compromise.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At 118 minutes the operator says, “Another 35 minutes, no need to say anything.” Candidate should alert surgeon that the ideal 120-minute threshold is approaching, seek documented risk-benefit decision, start 10-minute reminders if extended and recognise >150 minutes is rarely justified.
sections.7. Recovery after a lapse: If the wrong pressure is suggested, state adult lower-limb BOAST systolic +70–130 mmHg / limb occlusion method and request confirmation before inflation. If cuff preparation was missed, pause before inflation, correct padding and prep-fluid isolation and communicate the change. If time warning missed, notify the surgeon immediately, document elapsed inflation time and agree risk-based continuation/deflation plan. If postoperative paresthesia appears, promptly assess/document motor, sensory, perfusion and cuff-site findings and escalate.
sections.8. Model performance: three levels: Fail “Set it at 300; it is routine. We can leave it for as long as needed.” No checks of prep pooling, time or limb state. Pass “Check cuff width and padding, exclude pooled prep, set adult lower-limb pressure from BP or measured occlusion pressure, start a timer and warn the surgeon before 120 minutes.” Documents pressure, time, skin and limb checks. High-performance Clearly allocates the safety check to team members, ensures pressure selection remains lowest effective, notes restricted exsanguination situations and anticipates a formally agreed extension and recovery neurovascular checks.

stations.title: Breathlessness After Surgery — Pulmonary Embolism
stations.source_heading: B2-173 Breathlessness After Surgery — Pulmonary Embolism

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-173 Breathlessness After Surgery — Pulmonary Embolism Critical care / data interpretation • 9-minute station • Draft for clinical review • 12 October 2026 Educational simulation only; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A patient develops sudden breathlessness 4 days after a major abdominal operation. Interpret the information provided, estimate PE probability, and outline immediate investigation, treatment and escalation. Explain how the recent operation changes anticoagulation and thrombolysis decisions.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: 62-year-old following colectomy day 4, new pleuritic pain, SpO₂ 88% room air, respiratory rate 30/min, heart rate 122/min, BP 112/72, alert, no ongoing active bleeding reported. Right calf tenderness is absent; no prior VTE, haemoptysis or cancer active. PE judged more likely than alternatives after assessment. Two-level PE Wells: PE more likely 3; HR >100 =1.5; surgery in past 4 weeks 1.5; total 6 = PE likely (>4). CTPA available. Curveball: BP falls to 78/48 and operative drain becomes bloodstained; ask about reperfusion strategy. Results if sought: CTPA shows bilateral pulmonary emboli with right ventricular strain. Do not presume every unstable patient can undergo CT transport.
sections.3. Actor / simulated-team brief: Examiner plays ward nurse: “Could this just be atelectasis? Shall I order a D-dimer?” If candidate calls surgeon, reply “We can assess bleeding risk immediately.” Give no clotting result unless requested.
sections.4. Marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and triage Attributes new hypoxia/tachycardia to pain without review. Recognises PE as important postoperative cause while considering bleeding, pneumonia, atelectasis and ACS. Prioritises PE and life-threatening alternatives using case-specific findings and instability. Immediate ABCDE Does not reassess BP, saturation or consciousness. Starts ABCDE, oxygen for hypoxaemia, monitor, IV access, urgent senior help. Coordinates resuscitation, early critical care input and serial reassessment. Wells calculation Misstates Wells score or relies on D-dimer alone. Calculates two-level Wells: signs DVT 3, PE more likely 3, HR>100 1.5, surgery/immobilisation 1.5 (this case 6 if PE more likely + tachycardia + surgery). Explains which specific variables justify score and avoids D-dimer to gate imaging in PE-likely pathway. Imaging / alternatives Requests plain radiograph alone to exclude PE. Requests immediate CTPA if suitable and stable enough; assesses iodinated contrast issues. Uses V/Q alternative when appropriate; does not delay resuscitation or unstable-team discussion for scanner. Anticoagulation and bleeding Automatically gives full anticoag
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-related: Failing to recognise shock or deteriorating oxygenation and continuing routine investigation without resuscitation. Excluding PE solely because a D-dimer is negative/positive postoperative, without applying appropriate probability and imaging pathway. Giving systemic thrombolysis automatically in a recently operated patient without considering major bleeding contraindication and expert decision-making. Ignoring active surgical bleeding before initiating or continuing therapeutic anticoagulation; or omitting urgent expert discussion when anticoagulation is contraindicated.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: The patient becomes hypotensive at 78/48 mmHg and fresh blood appears in the abdominal drain. Candidate immediately revisits ABCDE, calls anaesthesia/ICU, surgical consultant and PE team, assesses active bleeding and recognises that systemic thrombolysis may be unsafe after recent surgery; discuss catheter or surgical embolectomy with the specialist team.
sections.7. Recovery after a lapse: If a D-dimer is suggested as the next test, correct the likely-PE Wells classification and request CTPA promptly. If anticoagulation is proposed reflexively, pause to evaluate surgical haemostasis, active bleeding and consultant decision. If the patient deteriorates, stop plans for unmonitored transfer, initiate resuscitation and coordinate bedside assessment and reperfusion advice. If thrombolysis is suggested, explicitly flag recent major surgery and identify urgent expert-led alternatives.
sections.8. Model performance: three levels: Fail “It is probably atelectasis; send a D-dimer and observe.” Gives no immediate escalation; recommends routine lysis despite fresh postoperative bleeding. Pass “Assess ABCDE, oxygen and monitoring; Wells 6 means PE likely: urgent CTPA if stable, senior review and anticoagulation after checking bleeding. Shock triggers critical-care and PE-team escalation.” High-performance Adds right ventricular assessment and explicit postoperative haemostasis review, coordinates treatment before delayed imaging when safe, distinguishes high-risk rescue options and delegates time-critical tasks.

stations.title: Disclosing a Medication Error

sections.preamble: B2-174 — Disclosing a Medication Error Nine-minute station | 12 October 2026 | Provisional | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A postoperative patient received a second dose of IV antibiotic in error. The patient is currently clinically well and has asked why the nurse has taken extra observations. Speak to the patient, explain what is known, address concerns and outline the next steps. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Mrs Helen James, 62, day 2 following uncomplicated laparoscopic colectomy. Cefuroxime was prescribed as a single postoperative dose under the local protocol, but an additional dose was given approximately 90 minutes later due to an administration-chart misunderstanding. Exact timing and dose have been verified against chart; a pharmacist has been contacted. Currently BP 128/76, pulse 82, oxygen 97% on room air, no rash, wheeze, hypotension or new symptoms. No known beta-lactam allergy. No established harm at present; clinical and renal review are planned. The team is investigating the chart error. Patient must not be told an unverified cause is established.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Open: “Why am I having so many checks? Has someone made a mistake?” If told clearly, respond: “Am I going to be harmed? Who made the mistake?” If candidate minimises, ask: “Can you guarantee I will be okay?” If candidate becomes defensive, say: “Are you trying to cover this up?” If offered support, ask whether your daughter may attend the follow-up conversation. You are worried but not aggressive.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Open with the actor’s stated first line. Reveal additional facts only if asked. Test both what the candidate says and the response to uncertainty. Curveball is introduced around minute 6. Score performed communication, not merely a plan to communicate.
sections.5. Marking grid — critical-weighted: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Focuses on reputation; does not establish patient condition. Checks for current reaction, confirms clinical review and monitoring. Names evolving allergic reaction, haemodynamic change and renal considerations, with prompt escalation if symptoms emerge. Opening and setting Introduces incident abruptly in corridor, without privacy. Introduces self, confirms identity, uses private setting and checks how patient wishes to discuss. Offers a support person and allocates time for questions without delaying disclosure. Plain explanation Uses jargon or obscures that a second dose was given. Clearly explains an additional antibiotic dose was administered unintentionally. Distinguishes verified dose/timing from why the chart error occurred, still under review. Apology and candour Avoids apology or blames nursing staff. Offers unambiguous apology and accepts organisational responsibility to investigate. Acknowledges distress and explicitly explains that apology does not depend on proven harm. Risk and uncertainty Claims there can be no side effects, or exaggerates severe harm as certain. Describes current reassuring state and the need to moni
sections.6. Four critical fails: Conceals the known error or deliberately misleads the patient. Does not assess or provide a plan for possible immediate medication-related harm. Attributes blame as established fact despite an unresolved investigation. Leaves the erroneous medication order active with risk of further unintended doses.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient asks: “So was it the nurse’s fault? Can you promise this will not damage my kidneys?” Candidate should avoid personal blame, explain verified facts and uncertainty, apologise, and arrange appropriate observation/renal review according to the clinical situation.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: “I was too vague. An extra dose of antibiotic was given by mistake, and I am sorry.” “I should not have guaranteed there is no risk. You look well now, but we will monitor and explain any change.” “I should not have blamed an individual before the review; the priority is your care, a full explanation and preventing recurrence.”

stations.title: A Patient Who Wants to Self-Discharge
stations.source_heading: B2-175 A Patient Who Wants to Self-Discharge

sections.preamble: B2-175 — A Patient Who Wants to Self-Discharge Nine-minute station | 12 October 2026 | Provisional | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar on the ward. Mr Khan, 46, wants to leave hospital immediately on postoperative day 3 despite continued monitoring for a suspected intra-abdominal collection. Explore his decision, assess capacity for this decision, explain choices and create a safe plan. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Mr Khan had laparoscopic appendicectomy for perforated appendicitis three days ago. Today T 38.1 C, HR 104, BP 117/70; has localised abdominal discomfort but is alert, orientated and speaking normally. CT is booked within hours owing to possible intra-abdominal collection; IV antibiotics and observation are in progress. He urgently needs to collect his dependent child because his partner is unwell. No intoxication, delirium or known cognitive impairment. Has not yet heard a clear explanation of the CT purpose. If candidate performs a structured capacity assessment, patient can understand, retain, weigh and communicate the risks, and repeats the consequences back.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Open: “I need to go. You cannot keep me here.” If approached respectfully, explain: “My child has nobody else to pick him up.” Ask: “Will I die if I leave?” If told he has “no capacity because he is making an unsafe choice”, become upset. If alternative childcare is offered, say you are open to calling your sister but still want the risks explained. You will consider staying if the candidate works constructively with you.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Open with the actor’s stated first line. Reveal additional facts only if asked. Test both what the candidate says and the response to uncertainty. Curveball is introduced around minute 6. Score performed communication, not merely a plan to communicate.
sections.5. Marking grid — critical-weighted: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate clinical risk Allows exit without reviewing possible postoperative infection. Checks current observations, pain and signs of deterioration; states concern for collection/sepsis. Explains timing of planned CT and the consequences of delayed antibiotics/source control with proportionality. Explore reasons Assumes noncompliance and lectures patient. Asks why leaving is urgent and elicits childcare problem. Works collaboratively on realistic solutions with the patient and ward team. Respect and rights States every patient must remain until doctor approves. Acknowledges that an adult with capacity can refuse continued treatment. Explains that disagreement alone does not demonstrate lack of capacity. Capacity: understanding / retention Presumes capacity from alertness or incapacity from refusal. Checks understanding and retention of relevant risks and options. Uses clear patient-specific information and repeats assessment after supporting communication. Capacity: weighing / communication Uses a one-question “do you understand?” test. Assesses ability to use/weigh information and communicate a choice. Checks reasoning with teach-back, identifies
sections.6. Four critical fails: Detains or physically restrains a capacitated adult solely because the clinician disagrees with refusal. Declares incapacity solely because the patient wants to leave, without decision-specific assessment. Provides no meaningful warning about potential serious infection or deterioration before departure. Fails to offer any safety-netting or plan after an informed, capacitated refusal.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Mr Khan says: “If the scan is so important, tell me exactly what might happen if I go and come back tomorrow.” Candidate must explain that infection or an abscess could worsen, potentially leading to sepsis and urgent treatment; cannot quantify risk without more information; offers childcare help, continuing investigation and a plan if he still refuses.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: “I was wrong to say you are not allowed to leave. Let me explain the risks and make sure the decision is informed.” “Your decision is not proof of incapacity. I will assess your ability to understand, retain, weigh and communicate this specific choice.” “I missed the childcare issue. Could we explore a safe arrangement so the CT and antibiotic treatment can continue?”

stations.title: Teaching a Student to Tie a Surgical Knot
stations.source_heading: B2-176 Teaching a Student to Tie a Surgical Knot

sections.preamble: B2-176 — Teaching a Student to Tie a Surgical Knot Nine-minute station | 12 October 2026 | Provisional | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a CT2 surgical trainee in the skills room. A third-year medical student has never tied a surgical knot independently. You have a knot-tying board, two lengths of practice suture and a needle holder (no patient or sharps). Teach the student to tie a secure instrument-tied square knot, invite practice and give useful feedback. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: The student is keen but nervous and has watched one online video. On request, a training pad and instrument are available. Demonstration can be simulated verbally while showing actual hand movements. A correct square knot requires successive flat, opposing throws; this is a basic teaching exercise, not a validated assessment of surgical competency. The student at first makes two same-direction throws and creates a slip/granny configuration; on coaching, corrects it. At minute 6 student asks whether the knot is safe to tie around a patient’s artery now. Examiner assesses active teaching with demonstrated action, not a lecture or just a checklist.
sections.3. Learner / patient actor brief: Open: “I have seen people do it but my hands get mixed up.” If teacher asks goals say, “I want to make a knot that stays flat and does not slip.” On first practice, repeat the same throw direction twice and pull up unevenly. Ask, “Why must the second throw go the opposite way?” If criticised harshly withdraw. If corrected specifically, try again and achieve a flat knot. At minute 6 ask, “Can I now tie off a vessel in theatre?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Start with actor opening. Reveal relevant facts only on request. Introduce the listed curveball at around minute 6. Score what the candidate actually demonstrates or communicates, not claims of intent. Set / dialogue / demonstrate / practise / feedback applies to the teaching scenario.
sections.5. Marking grid — critical-weighted: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction and rapport Begins an unexplained demonstration; ignores learner anxiety. Introduces purpose, invites learner to state experience and makes environment supportive. Confirms exact achievable objective and adapts explanation to learner’s first attempt. Set and safety Starts with needles or a patient; gives no safety boundaries. Uses a practice board, checks equipment, establishes this is supervised simulation. Positions instruments and practice strands visibly, checks safe handling and keeps clinical use outside scope. Explanation of goal Says “just copy me” with no success criterion. States the aim: a secure, flat square knot made with opposing throws. Contrasts a stable flat knot with a twisted or slipping granny knot using the model. Demonstration Speeds through movements without showing instrument pathway. Demonstrates grasping the free end, forming the first throw and reversing direction on the next. Pauses at each step, keeps ends visible, names the reversal and shows controlled apposition without excessive tension. Chunking and communication Uses confusing jargon and continuous monologue. Explains in brief steps at a learner-appro
sections.6. Four critical fails: Allows or encourages an unsupervised patient procedure on the basis of a first simulation attempt. Fails to recognise or correct a repeated same-direction unstable knot demonstrated in the scenario. Handles sharps or clinical equipment in an unsafe manner despite an available no-sharps training setup. Humiliates the learner or refuses them a meaningful opportunity to practise the task.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Student: “I can do it now — could I ligate an artery in theatre alone?” Expected: praise progress with a simulation knot but clarify this is not proof of independent clinical competence; requires training, appropriate selection of material, direct supervision and local authorisation. Invite another practice attempt.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: “I spoke too quickly. Watch the first throw and the reversed second throw slowly, then tell me what changes.” “I missed your two same-direction throws. That may leave a knot that slips; let me show the reversal and have you retry.” “I should not have said you were ready to operate independently. Today we achieved a practice knot on a model, not clinical sign-off.”

stations.title: Discharge Advice After Day-Case Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-177 Discharge Advice After Day-Case Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-177 — Discharge Advice After Day-Case Surgery Nine-minute station | 12 October 2026 | Provisional | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in the day-surgery unit. Ms Patel, 39, underwent uncomplicated excision of a benign upper-back cyst under general anaesthesia today. She is comfortable, awake and eager to go home. Give clear, tailored discharge advice and check that arrangements are safe. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief / disclosure: Procedure completed at 11:00; current time 16:00. Uncomplicated general anaesthetic; stable observations, oral fluids tolerated, mobilising comfortably; incision closed with non-absorbable sutures and dry dressing. Paracetamol prescribed according to local chart; no opioids prescribed. Wound review and suture removal are planned by local pathway; booking details are on written sheet to verify. No antibiotics required. She had arranged a taxi but says she intends to be alone tonight and drive tomorrow morning for the school run. Her 8-year-old daughter may need care. Her sister lives 15 minutes away and could stay if asked. At minute 6 she reports her dressing is rapidly soaking with blood at home. Scenario applies UK day-surgery discharge planning, not a universal fixed timetable for resuming every activity.
sections.3. Learner / patient actor brief: Open: “The wound feels fine. Am I okay to leave, and when can I shower or drive?” If asked about support: “I am on my own with my daughter tonight, but my sister might come.” If asked about medicines: “I will take whatever the leaflet says, but how often?” If too much jargon say, “Can you explain that simply?” Curveball: “What if the dressing is soaked with blood tonight?” If examiner asks teach-back: “No driving for 24 hours from the anaesthetic, arrange an adult, follow the wound sheet and call for serious problems.”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Start with actor opening. Reveal relevant facts only on request. Introduce the listed curveball at around minute 6. Score what the candidate actually demonstrates or communicates, not claims of intent. Set / dialogue / demonstrate / practise / feedback applies to the teaching scenario.
sections.5. Marking grid — critical-weighted: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Readiness and suitability Gives permission to leave without verifying discharge checks. Confirms clinical stability, nausea, mobility, pain control and written discharge plan with nursing team. Checks actual support and any unresolved anaesthetic or surgical concern before authorising departure. Explanation of operation Says “minor surgery, no risks” or introduces unverified complications. Explains benign cyst removal, closure and expected soreness using plain terms. Checks patient understanding and distinguishes expected mild symptoms from warning signs. Anaesthetic precautions Allows immediate driving or sole childcare after GA. Advises no driving, machinery, alcohol or major decisions for the first 24 hours after GA. Explains judgement and coordination may be impaired despite feeling alert; arranges responsible adult support. Transport and home support Does not ask who will escort or stay. Checks adult escort/home support and revises unsafe plan before discharge. Contacts sister with patient permission and discusses child-care contingency before departure. Pain relief and medicines Gives no dosing guidance or suggests extra drugs without chart r
sections.6. Four critical fails: Discharges patient to provide sole dependent-child care immediately after general anaesthesia despite knowing no responsible adult is available. Tells patient to drive within 24 hours of general anaesthesia. Reassures that rapidly saturating dressings or significant ongoing bleeding require no urgent help. Offers no written safety-net advice or contact route for postoperative complications.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Ms Patel asks, “What if my dressing suddenly becomes soaked with blood and I feel dizzy?” Candidate should advise immediate help rather than routine wound review; direct pressure may be applied if safe, emergency services for severe ongoing haemorrhage or collapse, and urgent surgical assessment. Also reconsider suitability for discharge if symptoms already present.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: “I missed that you would be the only adult caring for your daughter tonight. We need a responsible adult with you before discharge.” “I was wrong to say driving tomorrow morning is automatically fine. You must not drive for at least 24 hours after the anaesthetic and only later when safe to control the car.” “I should have specified the bleeding warning signs: rapidly soaking dressings, persistent bleeding or faintness need urgent assessment, not a routine appointment.”

stations.title: A Colleagues Social Media Post
stations.source_heading: B2-178 A Colleagues Social Media Post

sections.preamble: B2-178 — A Colleague's Social Media Post Group 18 · Communication and Professionalism | 9-minute station | Draft 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar. A junior doctor asks for advice after seeing a colleague post a photograph from theatre on an ostensibly private social-media account. Explain how you would respond professionally, protect the patient and escalate proportionately. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Acknowledge a credible potentially identifiable disclosure, seek swift containment and patient protection without unsafe reposting or premature assertions about consent, and use appropriate local information-governance/senior routes.The post says “Unbelievable trauma case tonight — survived against the odds!” It contains a photograph showing part of the patient’s face, distinctive tattoo and a theatre whiteboard with date and hospital. It was uploaded 40 minutes ago; colleagues have shared it. No documented patient consent for this post. The patient is alive, stable in recovery and has not been informed.
sections.3. Actor brief and responses: Junior doctor, concerned but reluctant to “get someone into trouble”. If asked: you saw the post yourself and have the link; the account has about 500 followers; the poster is a surgical registrar who says “it’s only visible to friends”; you do not know whether any prior photograph consent was for a different educational use. Respond anxiously to public confrontation suggestions.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Disclose details only in response to relevant questions. Invite the candidate to explain the immediate first action, how they will communicate, and what they will document. Use the curveball if time permits; assess actual statements, not vague intentions.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Nine domains. Give a judgement per domain; safety-critical omissions may override otherwise strong performance. Each band describes a distinct observable performance. Domain
sections.1. Identifies concern: Fail Says a restricted account makes disclosure acceptable. Pass Identifies patient recognition risk from face, tattoo, date and location. High-performance Explains cumulative clues can identify someone even without a name and distinguishes consent for photography from consent for online posting. Domain
sections.2. Immediate containment: Fail Ignores the post until next week. Pass Promptly asks poster privately to stop sharing and remove post; alerts appropriate senior. High-performance Coordinates prompt containment through senior/information-governance routes and seeks help with third-party reposts without amplifying the image. Domain
sections.3. Preserving evidence: Fail Forwards the patient image widely to prove the breach. Pass Records URL, time, platform and factual observations by an approved secure route. High-performance Seeks information-governance advice on proportionate evidence preservation and avoids new unnecessary copies. Domain

stations.title: Optimising an Obese Smoker Before Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-179 Optimising an Obese Smoker Before Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-179 — Optimising an Obese Smoker Before Surgery Group 18 · Communication and Professionalism | 9-minute station | Draft 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar in preoperative clinic. Discuss risk and optimisation with an adult awaiting elective incisional hernia repair. Agree a practical plan and address concerns about delay without blaming the patient. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Individualise modifiable perioperative risks, offer evidence-based help and shared decisions; avoid stigmatisation and blanket refusal of surgery. Recognise incarceration/strangulation red flags.A 54-year-old with a symptomatic but reducible incisional hernia is booked for elective repair in seven weeks. BMI 37 kg/m²; smokes 15 cigarettes/day; type 2 diabetes with latest HbA1c 80 mmol/mol; BP 146/88 mmHg; no resting dyspnoea. The patient wants surgery quickly because the hernia limits work and has not received formal stop-smoking support. No episodes of irreducibility or obstruction.
sections.3. Actor brief and responses: Patient: “Are you refusing to operate because I am fat?” and “I have tried quitting and it never works.” If asked: open to medication and support; fears lost wages if delayed; does not understand what an HbA1c is. If asked about red flags: no vomiting, severe persistent pain, skin changes or inability to reduce. Wants a specific follow-up date.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Disclose details only in response to relevant questions. Invite the candidate to explain the immediate first action, how they will communicate, and what they will document. Use the curveball if time permits; assess actual statements, not vague intentions.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Nine domains. Give a judgement per domain; safety-critical omissions may override otherwise strong performance. Each band describes a distinct observable performance. Domain
sections.1. Agenda and empathy: Fail Starts by scolding about weight or smoking. Pass Asks what matters to patient and acknowledges work and anxiety. High-performance Negotiates a practical agenda and explores previous attempts and barriers without stigma. Domain
sections.2. Surgical urgency: Fail Treats symptomatic reducible hernia as an automatic emergency. Pass Asks about acute pain, irreducibility, vomiting and obstructive symptoms. High-performance Gives specific emergency return advice for irreducible painful lump, vomiting or skin change. Domain
sections.3. Risk communication: Fail Promises no complications if they lose weight. Pass Explains smoking, BMI and high glucose can increase wound and chest problems. High-performance Relates potential infection, healing, anaesthetic and recurrence issues to the proposed repair without invented absolute risk numbers. Domain

stations.title: A Gift From a Grateful Patient
stations.source_heading: B2-181 A Gift From a Grateful Patient

near_match.title: Gifts from a Patient

sections.preamble: B2-181 — A Gift From a Grateful Patient Group 18 · Communication and Professionalism | 9-minute station | Draft 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a surgical registrar at a follow-up appointment. A patient who recovered well after major surgery offers you a personal gift as thanks. Respond in a way that preserves trust and professional boundaries. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Thank patient without encouraging gift or shaming; decline the substantial personal benefit, clarify conflict-of-interest and declaration requirements and preserve ongoing equal care.A 63-year-old patient has recovered well from a laparoscopic colectomy. At the end of clinic, the patient gives you a sealed envelope containing a £250 department-store voucher, saying “Please keep this for yourself; you deserve it.” Their next surveillance review will be with your team. No gift was previously requested or discussed.
sections.3. Actor brief and responses: Warm but insistent patient: “It would offend me if you refused. Just keep it between us.” If asked, says gift is voluntary, no expectation of special treatment and no financial difficulty disclosed. They suggest giving the voucher to your children if you cannot use it. When declined respectfully, they seem initially embarrassed and ask whether they can thank the team another way.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Reveal details only when asked, rather than coaching the candidate. Ask for the immediate response, exact words used with the patient and how the matter will be recorded and followed up. Introduce the curveball after the candidate has outlined an approach. Score concrete actions rather than “I would act professionally”.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Nine domains. Assign a separate judgement to each; safety-critical failings can override otherwise strong performance. Domain
sections.1. Opening and gratitude: Fail Accepts without discussion or treats patient as dishonest. Pass Thanks the patient warmly and recognises the kindness behind the gesture. High-performance Uses appreciative, nonjudgemental language and reassures that gratitude is valued regardless of a material gift. Domain
sections.2. Identify nature of gift: Fail Assumes a £250 voucher is merely a card or minimal token. Pass Recognises the substantial personal financial benefit and potential appearance of influence. High-performance Distinguishes unsolicited minimal-value token from significant cash-equivalent personal gift and checks scope and context. Domain
sections.3. Professional decision: Fail Accepts voucher in return for follow-up priority. Pass Politely declines the voucher as inconsistent with professional guidance. High-performance Explains personal financial benefit and perceived conflict, while avoiding claims that all small gifts are always banned. Domain

stations.title: Inviting a Patient Into a Clinical Trial
stations.source_heading: B2-182 Inviting a Patient Into a Clinical Trial

sections.preamble: B2-182 — Inviting a Patient Into a Clinical Trial Group 18 · Communication and Professionalism | 9-minute station | Draft 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the colorectal surgical registrar. A 62-year-old patient has resectable colon cancer and has been offered standard surgery. Your unit is recruiting to an approved randomised study comparing two accepted postoperative follow-up schedules. Explain the study, check understanding and discuss whether the patient wishes to consider participation. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Explain research versus usual care without therapeutic misconception or pressure; randomisation, uncertainty, reasonable risks and burden, voluntariness, withdrawal and research consent pathway.The patient has no metastases, has been counselled for elective curative-intent colectomy and remains eligible for standard care regardless of study participation. The REC-approved research team supplied a current patient information sheet. Randomisation is 1:1 to standard five-year follow-up schedule A versus schedule B involving additional remote symptom check-ins; exact tests, visit frequency, privacy and data retention are specified in the study information sheet, which the examiner can supply rather than improvising. No evidence of superiority of either arm is established. Patient has decision-making capacity. No enrolment or consent form should be finalised in this simulated encounter without appropriate approved processes and study-specific information.
sections.3. Actor brief and responses: Patient: “I thought the experimental option would be better. Does my surgeon want me to join? If I say no will it affect my operation?” You are anxious about cancer recurrence, have limited time today and wish to ask your daughter. When asked, you prefer plain English and would like to read the leaflet at home. Curveball: “Can I quit if the tests make me anxious, and can I have my data erased?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Reveal scenario facts and documents when requested. Ask the candidate to explain the governing principle in plain English, demonstrate exact patient-centred wording and specify documentation and safe next steps. Introduce the curveball after the core explanation. Score what was actually said and done, not vague intentions.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Nine domains; mark each separately. Safety-critical failings can override other domains. Domain
sections.1. Opening and agenda: Fail Starts with a signature request without checking understanding of diagnosis or concerns. Pass Explains this is an optional research discussion and asks what patient already knows. High-performance Elicits hope and fear of recurrence; separates today’s invitation from a decision to consent. Domain
sections.2. Purpose of trial: Fail Claims new schedule is proven to improve survival. Pass Explains the study compares accepted follow-up approaches because relative outcomes are uncertain. High-performance Explains the research question, routine-care comparison, and that participation is not individualised treatment optimisation. Domain
sections.3. Randomisation and allocation: Fail Promises assignment to preferred arm. Pass Explains allocation by chance, approximately equal chance of either schedule. High-performance Checks patient can restate randomisation and addresses the misleading term “experimental equals better”. Domain

stations.title: Lasting Power of Attorney Before Major Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-183 Lasting Power of Attorney Before Major Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-183 — Lasting Power of Attorney Before Major Surgery Group 18 · Communication and Professionalism | 9-minute station | Draft 12 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the upper-GI surgical registrar. A 71-year-old patient is considering a major elective gastric operation. They have decision-making capacity but worry that complications might leave them unable to speak for themselves. Their daughter attends and says she has power of attorney. Explain who makes decisions now, what documents matter if capacity is later lost, and agree safe next steps. Nine minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure: Protect capacitous patient autonomy; distinguish property/finance LPA from registered health-and-welfare LPA, decision-specific capacity, advance decisions to refuse treatment, best-interests decision-making and lawful proxy authority if capacity is lost.The patient understands the proposed operation and wishes to plan ahead. Daughter has brought a document titled “Property and Financial Affairs Lasting Power of Attorney”; it contains no health-and-welfare appointment. The patient recalls completing an advance decision refusing blood transfusion but cannot locate the signed document. No current refusal has yet been clearly established for this operation. This is England and Wales. No emergency surgery is needed today. The surgeon must confirm the patient’s actual wishes about treatment now and coordinate documentation and perioperative planning rather than relying on assumption.
sections.3. Actor brief and responses: Patient: “I want my daughter to decide if anything goes wrong. Does she take over as soon as I’m asleep?” Daughter says, “I have power of attorney, so I should sign the consent today.” If respectfully asked, patient can explain goals, values and what they would want if a serious complication occurred. Curveball: “The old form says no blood even if I might die, but I don’t remember whether I signed it.”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Reveal scenario facts and documents when requested. Ask the candidate to explain the governing principle in plain English, demonstrate exact patient-centred wording and specify documentation and safe next steps. Introduce the curveball after the core explanation. Score what was actually said and done, not vague intentions.
sections.5. Critical-weighted marking grid: Nine domains; mark each separately. Safety-critical failings can override other domains. Domain
sections.1. Open and identify concerns: Fail Directs all questions to daughter without asking patient. Pass Asks patient about fears, understanding and future planning wishes. High-performance Normalises advance care planning, explores blood-transfusion concerns and distinguishes planning from today’s operative consent. Domain
sections.2. Current capacity and consent: Fail Assumes age or planned anaesthesia removes decision-making capacity. Pass Presumes capacity and confirms patient makes their own current surgical decisions. High-performance Explains capacity is decision- and time-specific; supports patient participation and informed consent for operation today. Domain
sections.3. Recognise LPA types: Fail Treats financial LPA as authority for medical consent. Pass Identifies daughter’s property-and-financial-affairs LPA is not health-and-welfare authority. High-performance Asks to review registered document, scope, restrictions and any multiple-attorney arrangements, rather than relying on title alone. Domain

stations.title: Early postoperative haemorrhage

near_match.title: Acute postoperative haemorrhage

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-61 — Early postoperative haemorrhage DRAFT FOR SPECIALIST REVIEW | 9-minute practice station | Critical care / applied management Authoring status: original expanded draft built from supplied gap list; not live, not an official MRCS mark scheme. Final MB- ID assigned only after approval.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar called to the recovery ward 2 hours after a laparotomy. A 68-year-old patient is pale and dizzy. Heart rate 128/min, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 27/min, SpO₂ 95% on air. The drain contains 350 mL fresh blood in the last 20 minutes. Explain and prioritise your actions to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner / actor instructions: If asked: the patient is increasingly drowsy; peripheral perfusion is poor. Initial postoperative haemoglobin is 111 g/L (preoperative 119 g/L). They have received 500 mL crystalloid and remain hypotensive. The operating consultant is contactable and theatre is available. The drain was previously dry. Disclose additional facts only when appropriately asked. Do not rescue missed actions. Mark explicit observed behaviours.
sections.3. Frame: essential performance: Recognise major postoperative bleeding with shock; do not be reassured by a near-normal early Hb. Call for immediate help: consultant surgeon, anaesthetist, senior nurse, critical care; activate the local major haemorrhage protocol as indicated. Perform and repeat ABCDE, obtain high-flow oxygen if indicated, continuous monitoring, two large-bore IV cannulae, blood sampling including FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, blood gas/lactate and urgent group and crossmatch. Start warmed, appropriately matched blood products guided by haemorrhage protocol and senior/anaesthetic team; avoid delaying definitive control with repeated crystalloid boluses. Review surgical site and drains while arranging urgent return to theatre for haemostasis; do not send an unstable patient for nonessential imaging. Communicate deterioration and decisions to the team, document timings and ensure direct transfer with resuscitation ongoing.
sections.4. Marking grid — Fail / Borderline / Pa: Domain Fail Borderline Pass High-performance Recognises shock Calls this postoperative discomfort and does not consider bleeding Suspects bleeding but initially relies on the haemoglobin or fails to identify shock States likely postoperative haemorrhage causing shock, and prioritises immediate intervention Explains that early Hb may remain deceptively reassuring and anticipates ongoing hidden loss Immediate escalation Does not call for assistance despite hypotension Calls the ward senior but delays surgeon/anaesthetist involvement Immediately calls senior surgeon and anaesthetist and seeks critical-care help Allocates explicit team roles and requests theatre readiness in parallel ABCDE and reassessment Does not check airway, breathing or circulation Performs a partial examination without repeat observations Runs structured ABCDE, monitors ECG, SpO₂, BP, consciousness and perfusion Reassesses response continuously and communicates deterioration to the team Access and blood samples Uses one small cannula or omits blood bank samples Obtains access and FBC but delays crossmatch/coagulation Requests two large-bore lines, FBC, coagulation/fibrinogen, gas/lactate and urgent group/crossmat
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe omissions or: Fails to recognise shock with ongoing bleeding and leaves patient unmonitored. Delays senior/anaesthetic escalation despite persistent hypotension. Uses early near-normal haemoglobin to exclude bleeding and withholds treatment. Sends unstable patient for nonurgent imaging instead of resuscitation and surgical control. These are safety flags for examiner review; do not automatically infer exam-board scoring rules.
sections.6. Curveball: The nurse says: “The haemoglobin is only 111; perhaps it is not bleeding.” Candidate should explain that early Hb cannot exclude acute blood loss and continue resuscitation and urgent surgical review.
sections.7. Model performance — concise action fl: Recognise major postoperative bleeding with shock; do not be reassured by a near-normal early Hb. → Call for immediate help: consultant surgeon, anaesthetist, senior nurse, critical care; activate the local major haemorrhage protocol as indicated. → Perform and repeat ABCDE, obtain high-flow oxygen if indicated, continuous monitoring, two large-bore IV cannulae, blood sampling including FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, blood gas/lactate and urgent group and crossmatch. → Start warmed, appropriately matched blood products guided by haemorrhage protocol and senior/anaesthetic team; avoid delaying definitive control with repeated crystalloid boluses. → Review surgical site and drains while arranging urgent return to theatre for haemostasis; do not send an unstable patient for nonessential imaging. → Communicate deterioration and decisions to the team, document timings and ensure direct transfer with resuscitation ongoing.
sections.8. Recovery line: “The physiology and drain output indicate potentially life-threatening haemorrhage. I will call the consultant and anaesthetist now, activate the major-haemorrhage pathway, continue ABCDE resuscitation and arrange urgent operative control.”

stations.title: Consent for blood transfusion

near_match.title: Consent for a First Transfusion in Heart Failure — One Unit, Honest Risks and the Lifelong Donor

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-62 — Consent for blood transfusion DRAFT FOR SPECIALIST REVIEW | 9-minute practice station | Communication Authoring status: original expanded draft built from supplied gap list; not live, not an official MRCS mark scheme. Final MB- ID assigned only after approval.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar. A 64-year-old patient with symptomatic postoperative anaemia has been advised to have a red-cell transfusion. They ask: “Do I really need someone else’s blood? Is it safe?” Explain the proposal, discuss alternatives, and obtain an informed decision. The patient is alert and has capacity.
sections.2. Examiner / actor instructions: Patient is stable, Hb 73 g/L, breathless walking to the bathroom and dizzy on standing. The consultant considers one unit with reassessment appropriate. No active bleeding. If asked: there is no known previous transfusion reaction; the patient is worried about infections and fluid overload. Disclose additional facts only when appropriately asked. Do not rescue missed actions. Mark explicit observed behaviours.
sections.3. Frame: essential performance: Introduce the reason for transfusion and discuss symptoms, clinical context and expected benefit, without presenting the Hb threshold as an automatic command. Explain the blood component, process, checks, observation during transfusion and the intention to reassess before further units. Discuss material risks in understandable terms: reactions, circulatory overload (TACO), very low but nonzero infection risk, and other relevant hazards; explain that monitoring reduces risk. Compare suitable alternatives in context, such as treating iron deficiency, correcting causes of anaemia and observation where clinically reasonable; explain limits if symptoms require more immediate correction. Explore beliefs, previous reactions, personal risk concerns, information preferences, and assess understanding and voluntariness. Explain the right to decline or withdraw consent, consequences of refusing, and individual component/product choices; document the decision and make it visible to the transfusion team.
sections.4. Marking grid — Fail / Borderline / Pa: Domain Fail Borderline Pass High-performance Indication Says transfusion is compulsory because of Hb alone Names low Hb but does not relate it to symptoms Explains symptomatic anaemia and expected immediate benefit Distinguishes symptom-driven need from longer-term treatment of the cause Transfusion process Cannot explain what will happen States blood goes through a drip without checks Explains red cells, bedside identity checks and monitoring Describes reassessment after each unit and opportunities to pause Benefits Claims there are no drawbacks States only that Hb will increase Explains potential improvement in oxygen delivery and symptoms Balances likely benefit with uncertainty and clinical context Material risks Says it is risk-free Mentions allergy only, omitting overload Explains reactions, TACO and residual infection risk in plain language Tailors risks to comorbidity and invites the patient’s priorities Alternatives Says no alternative exists Names oral iron without relevance to immediate symptoms Discusses cause-specific treatment and watchful waiting where appropriate Explains when alternatives may be too slow for the current clinical need Patient concerns Dismisses fear
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe omissions or: Pressures a capacitous patient into transfusion or ignores a clear refusal. States that transfusion is risk-free or hides material risks. Proceeds despite unresolved concerns or absent valid consent outside an applicable emergency exception. Fails to communicate a documented refusal or restrictions on accepted components to the administering team. These are safety flags for examiner review; do not automatically infer exam-board scoring rules.
sections.6. Curveball: The patient asks: “I am afraid I will get an infection or fluid on my lungs. What happens if I say no?” Explain both concerns, offer the risks in balanced language, explore alternatives, and respect refusal.
sections.7. Model performance — concise action fl: Introduce the reason for transfusion and discuss symptoms, clinical context and expected benefit, without presenting the Hb threshold as an automatic command. → Explain the blood component, process, checks, observation during transfusion and the intention to reassess before further units. → Discuss material risks in understandable terms: reactions, circulatory overload (TACO), very low but nonzero infection risk, and other relevant hazards; explain that monitoring reduces risk. → Compare suitable alternatives in context, such as treating iron deficiency, correcting causes of anaemia and observation where clinically reasonable; explain limits if symptoms require more immediate correction. → Explore beliefs, previous reactions, personal risk concerns, information preferences, and assess understanding and voluntariness. → Explain the right to decline or withdraw consent, consequences of refusing, and individual component/product choices; document the decision and make it visible to the transfusion team.
sections.8. Recovery line: “You have the right to decline this transfusion. Let me explain what we hope it will achieve, the important risks including reactions and fluid overload, and the alternatives, so we can agree on a plan that fits your preferences.”

stations.title: Renal colic with fever

near_match.title: Sudden Severe Back Pain in a Smoker With Hypertension / 'Renal Colic' at 71 Is a Suspected Ruptured Aneurysm

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — B2-65 Renal colic with fever DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • 9-minute simulated station • not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Station header and aim: Format: Critical care / management. Assessment focus: Renal colic with fever. Candidate is assessed on prompt clinical decisions, communication and safe escalation.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical SHO in the acute admissions unit. Interpret the findings and explain immediate treatment and definitive management to the examiner.
