sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-66 — Painless Visible Haematuria Round 2 • Draft for clinical review • 12 October 2026 • History / investigation Educational simulation — not an official examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief (exam mode): You are the surgical trainee in an urgent urology assessment clinic. A 62-year-old man has noticed red urine twice in the past week. He feels well and has no pain. Take a focused history, explain your concerns and outline the investigation and referral pathway.
sections.2. Examiner / actor brief (exam mode): Mr Taylor, 62. Two episodes of uniformly red urine without clots, dysuria, fever or loin pain. Smoked 20 cigarettes daily for 35 years; stopped 5 years ago. No stone history, trauma, recent instrumentation or anticoagulant use. No weight loss. Worried that it might be cancer; asks whether lack of pain means it is harmless. Nine-minute communication and focused history station. The actor supplies negative findings only if asked. At minute 6: “My GP said the urine test was normal today. Can we leave it?” Assess explanation and referral, not rote lists.
sections.3. Marking grid: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Opening and agenda Does not introduce self or obtain account Introduces self, verifies identity, asks what happened and patient concerns Elicits patient’s expectations and checks understanding without prematurely reassuring Haematuria characteristics Fails to establish visible blood or timing Asks onset, episodes, colour, clots, relation to micturition and recurrence Distinguishes true urinary bleeding from pigmentation, asks about urinary retention Associated symptoms Omits infection or obstruction assessment Asks dysuria, urgency, fever, loin pain, colic and voiding difficulty Screens for clot retention, systemic illness and red flags warranting same-day care Cancer risk and systemic history Omits age/smoking and constitutional symptoms Asks smoking, occupational exposures, weight loss, appetite and relevant history Explains risk without assuming that cancer is present Alternative causes and medications Attributes bleeding to benign cause without evidence Asks stones, trauma, recent procedures, infections and anticoagulants Notes anticoagulant use never removes need to assess unexplained haematuria Examination and baseline tests Declares no ex
sections.4. Critical fails — safety override: • Fails to arrange urgent suspected-cancer assessment for this 62-year-old with unexplained visible haematuria. • Reassures that painless haematuria or a normal dip today excludes serious disease and closes follow-up. • Ignores clot retention or cardiovascular compromise if described in the curveball.
sections.5. Model performance (Pass standard): “Because you have seen blood in your urine, we should investigate even though it does not hurt and it is clear today. There are several possible causes, including infection, stones and changes in the bladder or kidney. Cancer is one possibility we must exclude; I am not saying you have it. I will arrange an urgent urology referral. The specialist team commonly examines the bladder with a camera and images the kidneys and urinary tract, choosing the scan based on your kidney function and pathway. If you cannot pass urine, pass heavy clots, become faint or feverish, seek urgent help. What worries you most?”
sections.6. Distinguishing performance bands: Fail: misses one or more safety priorities, gives false reassurance, or delays time-critical action. Pass: performs all key decisions and explains a practical, safe referral and treatment plan. High-performance: delivers Pass actions plus accurate risk framing, purposeful checking and closed-loop coordination without unnecessary detail.
sections.7. Curveball: Actor: “Today’s urine test is normal. Does that mean I am clear?” Expected: intermittent visible bleeding still meets referral criteria; a normal test between episodes does not cancel evaluation.
sections.8. Recovery opportunity: If the candidate initially proposes routine follow-up, the examiner asks, “Does the patient’s age and visible haematuria alter the urgency?” Strong recovery: explicitly correct to urgent suspected-cancer referral, apologise for the earlier reassurance, and outline follow-up ownership.

stations.title: TIA and Carotid Stenosis

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-67 — TIA and Carotid Stenosis Round 2 • Draft for clinical review • 12 October 2026 • Applied knowledge / vascular Educational simulation — not an official examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief (exam mode): You are the vascular surgical registrar discussing an urgent referral. A 71-year-old man had 15 minutes of right arm weakness and speech difficulty earlier today; all symptoms resolved. His GP sent him to the stroke service. Explain the immediate TIA pathway, interpretation of a written carotid duplex report and management.
sections.2. Examiner / actor brief (exam mode): Examiner-led case; there is no patient actor. At 3 minutes give report: “Left internal carotid artery stenosis 75% using NASCET criteria, right 25%; no occlusion.” At 6 minutes: “Would you book routine vascular outpatient review in six weeks?” Nine-minute applied-knowledge discussion. If symptoms are still present or recur, candidate must switch to acute stroke assessment. Clarify left symptomatic territory, urgency and intervention criteria. Do not ask to interpret an image.
sections.3. Marking grid: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and acute screen [SAFETY] Dismisses episode because signs resolved Identifies suspected left-hemisphere TIA and checks symptoms resolved; rapid neurological/FAST review Checks onset/last known well and redirects persistent or new deficits to emergency stroke pathway Exclude mimics and factors Fails to check blood glucose or mimic history Checks glucose, seizure/migraine differential, blood pressure and AF history Keeps differential open while not delaying TIA pathway Immediate therapy [SAFETY] Omits prompt antiplatelet or suggests no treatment until scans For suspected TIA, starts aspirin 300 mg daily immediately unless contraindicated per NICE and arranges review Checks allergy, bleeding risk and other antithrombotics; delegates subsequent regimen to stroke team Referral timing [SAFETY] Plans assessment next week or relies on ABCD2 score Requests immediate specialist TIA review, to be seen within 24 hours of symptoms Explicitly avoids ABCD2 as a referral gate and verifies handover Imaging pathway Orders routine CT brain for all uncomplicated TIAs States routine CT is not indicated for suspected TIA without an alternative diagnosis;
sections.4. Critical fails — safety override: • Treats transient symptoms as benign and fails immediate suspected-TIA referral. • Leaves suspected TIA without appropriate immediate aspirin (unless contraindicated) or specialist plan. • Delays urgent vascular referral despite stable symptomatic 75% NASCET carotid stenosis and potential CEA candidacy. • Ignores persistent or recurrent neurological deficits instead of activating acute stroke pathway.
sections.5. Model performance (Pass standard): “These transient right-arm and speech symptoms suggest a left hemispheric TIA. I would check for ongoing deficit and glucose immediately. With fully resolved symptoms, NICE advises aspirin 300 mg daily straight away unless contraindicated and immediate specialist assessment within 24 hours; ABCD2 should not decide urgency. A routine CT head is not necessary for every TIA. The specialist team will determine brain MRI and urgently image the carotids if surgery is possible. The duplex shows 75% left internal carotid stenosis by NASCET, corresponding to the symptomatic side. I would discuss urgently with the vascular service for carotid endarterectomy assessment and best medical therapy, rather than book a routine review. Recurrent or persisting neurological symptoms demand emergency stroke assessment.”
sections.6. Distinguishing performance bands: Fail: misses one or more safety priorities, gives false reassurance, or delays time-critical action. Pass: performs all key decisions and explains a practical, safe referral and treatment plan. High-performance: delivers Pass actions plus accurate risk framing, purposeful checking and closed-loop coordination without unnecessary detail.
sections.7. Curveball: Examiner: “He develops new right facial droop as you are talking.” Expected: immediately stop elective counselling and activate emergency stroke assessment, document time and arrange acute imaging/treatment pathway.
sections.8. Recovery opportunity: If the candidate first says “ABCD2 is low so he can be seen in a week,” ask, “Would that change under NICE NG128?” Strong recovery: withdraw ABCD2 triage, request immediate specialist assessment within 24 hours and urgent carotid/vascular pathway.

sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a surgical trainee in vascular clinic. Examine the lower limbs of an adult with prominent veins and present findings, likely diagnosis and next investigation. State any manoeuvre you would perform rather than simulating a dangerous one.
sections.2. Examiner setup / release: Provide a standing mannequin/volunteer or written simulated findings above. sections.3. Actor or patient brief: Patient is 48, reports right-leg heaviness at the end of shifts and ankle itching. sections.4. sections.5. Critical fails (safety-sensitive): Fails to identify or escalate active bleeding from a varicose vein when specifically disclosed. Ignores acute painful unilateral swelling/redness suggesting DVT, instead offers elective treatment. Recommends firm compression for a limb with suspected significant arterial insufficiency without assessment.
sections.6. Curveball: After presentation, examiner says: “Last week one of these veins started bleeding when I knocked my ankle.” Expected: clarify current bleeding, immediate first aid if bleeding (elevation and direct pressure), prompt vascular assessment/referral; do not minimise risk.
sections.7. Specific recovery lines: If initially seated: “To assess their full extent, I would examine both legs standing if safe.” If skin changes missed: “I should check the gaiter areas for pigmentation, eczema and ulceration.” If bedside tests overemphasised: “The reflux anatomy must be confirmed with duplex ultrasound.” If bleeding history emerges: “A bleeding varicose vein warrants immediate referral to a vascular service.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail / Pass / Hig: Fail “The vein is enlarged. I would prescribe support stockings.” Does not inspect skin or seek duplex; misses bleeding escalation. Pass “I would inspect both legs standing for varices and venous skin changes, palpate carefully, check arterial pulses and request duplex; symptomatic disease merits vascular referral.” High-performance “The distribution suggests superficial venous reflux with early chronic venous skin change. I would document symptom burden and previous thrombosis, screen for ulceration and bleeding, refer for duplex mapping and discuss NICE treatment hierarchy.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Symptomatic superficial venous reflux; look for complications. SAY: “I will examine both legs, ideally standing, and check the skin and circulation.” DO: Inspect distribution and gaiter skin; palpate gently; check pulses. FINISH: Venous duplex and vascular referral when symptomatic or complicated. TRAP: Bedside valve tests are not a substitute for duplex; bleeding changes urgency. sections.preamble: AMaC MEDICAL EDUCATION | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-69 — Epistaxis in an Anticoagulated Patient Format: Critical care / procedural • 9-minute practice station • Status: DRAFT / NOT CLINICALLY SIGNED OFF AMaC teaching material; not an official MRCS marking scheme. sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical trainee covering emergency care. A 72-year-old patient taking warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve has been bleeding from the nose for 25 minutes. Explain and demonstrate your immediate management and outline next steps to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner setup / release: Provide simulation equipment. If pressure is applied correctly for 10–15 minutes, say flow slows but continues from a small right anterior septal point. If candidate asks INR: 3.1 (the valve-specific therapeutic range must be checked rather than assumed). If they omit anticoagulant history, do not volunteer indication. At 6 minutes, offer curveball.
sections.3. Actor or patient brief: Patient is alert, worried and repeatedly dabs the nose. BP 132/78, pulse 96, oxygen saturation 98%. Bright-red flow from right nostril; breathing normally. Warfarin for mechanical mitral valve; last dose last night. No trauma. No earlier attempt at uninterrupted pressure. If asked, no haematemesis but has swallowed some blood.
sections.4. Station marking grid: Assessable action Fail Pass High-performance Initial safety and haemodynamics Fails to assess airway or circulation in profuse bleeding Calls for help as needed, assesses ABC, vitals and active loss Recognises posterior/brisk bleed risk, aspiration and shock; prioritises resuscitation Immediate first aid Tilts head back or applies pressure to nasal bridge Sits upright leaning forward; continuous firm pressure to soft nostrils for 10–15 minutes Coaches breathing through mouth and spitting blood; times uninterrupted pressure Focused history Ignores anticoagulant indication or duration of bleeding Asks onset, trauma, prior episodes, swallowed blood, anticoagulant name/dose/last dose and indication Screens other bleeding, liver disease, missed/double dosing, concurrent antiplatelets Investigation strategy Orders no bloods in significant ongoing anticoagulated bleed For persistent/heavy bleed requests FBC, U&E, coagulation including INR if warfarin, group and save Interprets INR in warfarin context; understands routine INR is not a DOAC activity measure Nasal examination and source Blindly cauterises without seeing site After initial control examines anterior nose with good light and su
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-sensitive): Fails to manage airway or summon urgent support when haemodynamic collapse or airway compromise is introduced. Instructs the patient to lie flat/head back and continues despite substantial blood going into pharynx. Indiscriminately reverses anticoagulation for a stable anterior bleed without assessing severity or the mechanical-valve thrombosis risk. Discharges a patient with persistent significant bleeding without haemostasis, reassessment or escalation.
sections.6. Curveball: Examiner says: “Now the patient is pale, pulse 128, BP 84/50 and blood is running into the throat.” Expected: call resuscitation team/ENT and anaesthetics, airway positioning and suction, IV access, bloods including crossmatch, activate major haemorrhage pathway as appropriate, urgent haemostasis and specialist-led anticoagulation reversal.
sections.7. Specific recovery lines: If pressure was applied to bone: “I will move my fingers to compress the soft lower part of the nose continuously.” If posture wrong: “Lean forward and spit out blood; do not tilt backwards.” If focusing only on INR: “My priority is control of haemorrhage and clinical severity, not the numerical INR alone.” If considering warfarin reversal: “This patient has a mechanical mitral valve, so reversal needs coordinated senior assessment of bleeding and thrombotic risks.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail / Pass / Hig: Fail “Stop warfarin and reverse it, then send home after packing.” Does not apply compression correctly or evaluate major bleed. Pass “Sit forward, pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes; assess observations and anticoagulants. For persistent bleed I will identify the source, consider cautery/packing and involve ENT; check INR and blood count as indicated.” High-performance “I will stabilise and control bleeding first, recheck after uninterrupted pressure, use local haemostasis if possible, and distinguish minor bleeding from major haemorrhage. The mechanical valve makes indiscriminate reversal dangerous; I will coordinate with ENT/haematology and document a clear plan.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK: Airway and blood loss first; anticoagulation adds complexity. SAY: “Lean forwards; I am going to pinch the soft part continuously.” DO: Assess ABC/vitals, compress, identify source and treat persistent bleeding. FINISH: Reassess, agree anticoagulation plan, document and safety-net. TRAP: Do not tilt head back or reflexively reverse for minor controlled bleeding. NUMBERS: Firm pressure for at least 10–15 minutes without release.

sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are assessing a 42-year-old patient in the emergency department with severe low back pain radiating to the legs and new urinary symptoms. sections.2. Examiner setup / release: Patient reports 24 hours of difficulty initiating urination and reduced sensation of urinary flow following four days of worsening back pain. sections.3. Actor or patient brief: Patient: 42 years old, anxious that you might be overreacting. sections.4. Station marking grid: Markable action Fail Pass High-performance Immediate recognition Treats new urinary disturbance as uncomplicated back strain. Leg and sexual neurological symptoms Asks only pain score. Assesses unilateral/bilateral radicular symptoms, weakness, gait and new sexual dysfunction. Explores progression and severe bilateral deficits; avoids assuming unilateral symptoms exclude CES. Focused examination Uses a normal straight-leg raise to rule out CES. Checks lower-limb power, reflexes, sensation, gait if safe and perineal sensation with consent/chaperone. Documents
sections.5. Critical fails (safety-sensitive): Dismisses recent urinary difficulty with back/leg pain and discharges without emergency MRI assessment. sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are an MRCS candidate in an outpatient hand clinic. A 46-year-old office worker reports intermittent right-hand tingling and reduced dexterity. Examine both hands focusing on median nerve function, explain your findings and next steps. There is no need to examine the entire upper limb unless indicated.
sections.2. Examiner brief and data disclosure: Simulated patient: right-handed; numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers for 4 months; worse at night; sometimes drops a mug. No acute injury or severe pain. Findings provided on request: mild right thenar wasting; reduced light touch over right index pulp; diminished thumb palmar abduction; positive Phalen reproducing typical tingling; no objective ulnar deficit. Do not give the diagnosis unless candidate interprets findings.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Cooperative, concerned about ability to work. Say: “I wake up and shake my hand to relieve it.” Asked about neck: no radiating neck pain. Asked about little finger: not affected. Asked about functional decline: reports difficulty with buttons recently. Only volunteer examination findings when specifically tested.
sections.4. Clinical frame, traps and flow: Frame: localise the sensory distribution, demonstrate specific thenar function, then interpret overall pattern. Trap: grip is not a median-specific test; provocative tests are imperfect. Flow: consent → compare both hands → look/feel → median sensory/motor → provocative tests → alternative nerve/root screen → summary and plan.
sections.5. Marking grid — specific descriptors: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Preparation and focused history Does not ask hand preference or symptom pattern; launches into isolated tests. Asks dominant hand, intermittent paraesthesia, nocturnal symptoms, dropping objects and functional impact. Also asks neck pain, trauma, diabetes/pregnancy and symptom progression without derailing examination. Consent and exposure Examines without permission or fails to expose both hands. Explains sensory/motor examination, obtains consent and exposes hands and forearms bilaterally. Checks comfort, compares sides and positions forearms for clear inspection. Inspection Misses obvious unilateral thenar wasting. Inspects palms/dorsa, thenar bulk, scars and deformity, comparing both hands. Names abductor pollicis brevis wasting and differentiates other patterns such as ulnar intrinsic wasting. Median sensory assessment Tests only a nonspecific finger area or omits sensation. Compares light touch over palmar index fingertip with other digits and opposite hand. Maps thumb/index/middle and radial ring finger and explains palmar cutaneous sparing in isolated carpal tunnel syndrome. Median motor assessment Tests grip alone and calls it median mo
sections.6. Critical fails (safety-critical omiss: • Does not recognise or escalate progressive objective thenar weakness with functional deterioration. • Performs a painful or forceful provocative test despite request to stop. • Confidently excludes a major alternative neurological cause despite discordant history or signs.
sections.7. Curveball: Patient adds: “My thumb feels weaker every month. Can I simply wait six months?” Candidate should recognise progressive motor change and arrange timely hand specialist evaluation, not reassure solely from provocative tests.
sections.8. Recovery lines: • If testing sensation in the wrong distribution: “I need to compare the index fingertip with the little finger and the other hand to localise the deficit.” • If missing severity: “The thenar wasting and loss of thumb abduction suggest motor involvement; this changes urgency.” • If wrongly claiming a negative test excludes disease: “Phalen and Tinel are supportive, not definitive; I will integrate the full pattern.”

stations.title: Ankle Injury After a Fall
stations.source_heading: B2-73 Ankle Injury After a Fall

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — B2-73 Ankle Injury After a Fall DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Data interpretation / management • 9 minutes • Independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical SHO in the emergency department. A 34-year-old patient twisted the left ankle stepping off a kerb and cannot take four steps. Discuss assessment, decide whether X-ray is indicated, interpret a written radiology report and outline immediate management. No image is supplied.
sections.2. Examiner brief and data disclosure: Vitals stable; closed ankle with moderate lateral swelling and medial tenderness; no deformity, skin tenting or neurovascular compromise. Unable to weight-bear immediately and in ED. On request, read: “AP/mortise/lateral views: oblique distal fibular fracture at the level of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. Medial clear space increased compared with superior joint space; no other fracture seen.” If asked, ankle is neurovascularly intact, foot warm with intact capillary refill. Candidate should interpret as Weber B pattern with concern for instability, not definitive stable fracture.
sections.3. Actor / simulated patient brief: Painful but cooperative. Says “Can I just walk home in a boot?” No altered sensation. Reports no head injury or other significant trauma. If asked where tender: lateral malleolus and medially. If asked four steps: impossible both at scene and now.
sections.4. Clinical frame, traps and flow: Frame: identify threatened limb before applying decision rules. Trap: Weber category is not equivalent to stability. Flow: triage/analgesia → assess open injury and NV → Ottawa rules → written AP/mortise/lateral report → stability/medial injury → immobilisation and orthopaedic review → safety-net.
sections.5. Marking grid — specific descriptors: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety assessment Misses threatened skin, open injury or neurovascular compromise. Asks about deformity/open wound, checks perfusion, sensation, movement and skin before imaging interpretation. Recognises urgent reduction/escalation needs with deformity, skin tenting or perfusion deficit. Mechanism and symptoms Assumes a simple sprain despite inability to walk. Asks inversion/eversion mechanism, time, weight-bearing ability and site of pain. Adds proximal fibula pain, prior injury and comorbidities affecting management. Ottawa ankle rules Orders radiographs solely for swelling or omits four-step criterion. States malleolar pain plus posterior edge/tip malleolar bony tenderness OR inability to take four steps immediately and in assessment as indication. Distinguishes ankle versus foot criteria and applies to eligible patient without substituting for emergency assessment. Examining injuries Ignores medial tenderness, proximal fibula or syndesmosis. Examines both malleoli, medial tenderness, ankle alignment and neurovascular status. Checks proximal fibula and midfoot where mechanism suggests Maisonneuve or associated injury. Reading writt
sections.6. Critical fails (safety-critical omiss: • Fails to recognise a neurovascularly threatened or open ankle injury when presented. • Discharges a fracture with mortise widening as a definite stable sprain without orthopaedic input. • Fails to immobilise/protect a potentially unstable ankle and instructs unrestricted weight-bearing.
sections.7. Curveball: The patient asks “My friend had a Weber B fracture and walked on it. Why can’t I?” Explain that Weber level alone does not determine stability and the widened medial clear space may indicate ligament injury.
sections.8. Recovery lines: • After overlooking Ottawa criteria: “The inability to take four steps both immediately and in ED is a qualifying imaging feature with malleolar pain.” • After labelling a Weber B stable: “I need to look for mortise widening and medial injury, not rely on fibular fracture level alone.” • After initial splinting: “I must repeat and document distal neurovascular findings.”

stations.title: Painful Perianal Swelling

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-74 — Painful Perianal Swelling Draft | History / management | 9 minutes | 12 October 2026 | Provisional—clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check required Station purpose Identify perianal abscess, assess sepsis and deep infection, arrange timely drainage, and consider fistula and underlying disease.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar in the emergency surgical assessment unit. A 38-year-old patient has attended with a painful swelling beside the anus for 3 days. Take a focused history from the patient, explain your likely diagnosis and immediate management, and answer questions. You may describe an examination but do not perform an intimate examination. You have 9 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess safe prioritisation, task-specific clinical reasoning and clear communication. Disclose findings only when requested or appropriate. Performance levels: Fail / Pass / High-performance. The candidate may verbalise management; no procedure is performed.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You are Sam, 38. Increasing severe constant pain near the anus for 3 days, worse sitting; a tender lump; fever overnight. No significant bleeding. First episode. No known Crohn’s disease, diabetes or immunosuppression. You are worried this is cancer and ask whether antibiotics alone will work. If asked about urinary retention, say no. If asked about spreading redness, say you cannot see clearly. Respond anxiously but cooperatively.
sections.4. Findings available on request: Observations if requested: temperature 38.2°C, pulse 108/min, BP 117/74 mmHg, RR 18/min. Examination (offer only if appropriately explained, consent obtained and chaperone offered): tender fluctuant 3-cm left perianal swelling with erythema; no obvious necrosis or crepitus. DRE is too painful and is not required to establish the diagnosis. No image is supplied.
sections.5. Examiner frame — key steps: OPEN: Introduce self, ensure privacy, obtain consent for focused history; identify immediate deterioration symptoms. HISTORY: Clarify onset, location, fever, drainage, bowel habit, urinary symptoms, prior abscess/fistula, Crohn’s symptoms, diabetes, steroids or immunosuppression. SAFETY: Check observations and screen for systemic illness, spreading infection, severe pain out of proportion, perineal skin changes or necrotising infection. EXAM: Explain perianal inspection with chaperone; avoid forcing a painful DRE; consider deeper abscess if disproportionate pain/no external findings. DECIDE: Explain likely anorectal abscess; call senior/colorectal team and arrange prompt surgical drainage, often under anaesthesia if appropriate. TREAT: Analgesia, fasting if operative, IV access and bloods if unwell, fluids and sepsis management when indicated; antibiotics for systemic illness, cellulitis, immunocompromise or other clinical indication, not sole treatment of uncomplicated drainable abscess. FINISH: Explain follow-up for recurrence or persistent discharge indicating fistula, and safety-net for fever, worsening pain or spreading redness.
sections.6. Marking grid (nine task-specific rows: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Communication and consent Fails to introduce self or clarify concern. Introduces self and obtains consent for history. Establishes rapport, checks cancer worry and explains sensitive examination. Pain and time course Does not establish location, progression or severity. Identifies progressive painful perianal swelling. Elicits constant pain, sitting intolerance, possible spontaneous discharge. Systemic infection [SC] Omits fever and observations despite illness. Asks fever and requests vital signs. Interprets tachycardia/fever and promptly assesses for sepsis. Relevant background No prior episodes or comorbidity questions. Asks about recurrent abscess, Crohn’s and diabetes. Also checks immunosuppression, prior fistula and bowel symptoms. Examination and dignity Insists on painful DRE or no examination plan. Offers chaperoned inspection and avoids forced DRE. Mentions deep abscess if severe pain without a visible lesion. Diagnosis and alternatives Calls it haemorrhoids without considering infection. Identifies likely perianal abscess. Differentiates fissure, thrombosed external haemorrhoid and deeper abscess. Drainage [SC] Sends home on oral anti
sections.7. Critical fails — serious unsafe omiss: Discharges this febrile tachycardic patient with no urgent surgical assessment or drainage plan. Treats a drainable anorectal abscess with antibiotics alone and asserts drainage is unnecessary. Fails to react to findings suggesting necrotising perineal infection if the curveball is disclosed. Safety-critical rows are marked [SC] in the grid. Examiners should apply critical fails with clinical judgement, not an automatic numerical scoring rule.
sections.8. Curveball: Curveball: the patient reports rapidly spreading perineal pain and dark skin patches. Expected response: treat as possible Fournier’s gangrene; immediate senior/anaesthetic involvement, resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency debridement pathway, not delayed outpatient drainage.

stations.title: Rectal Bleeding in a 60 Year Old
stations.source_heading: B2-75 Rectal Bleeding in a 60 Year Old

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-75 — Rectal Bleeding in a 60-Year-Old Draft | History | 9 minutes | 12 October 2026 | Provisional—clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate check required Station purpose Distinguish important causes of rectal bleeding, identify cancer red flags, use current FIT referral guidance and safety-net despite potentially benign anorectal findings.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a surgical registrar assessing a 60-year-old patient referred by a GP for intermittent rectal bleeding. Take a focused history, explain the next steps and respond to concerns. An examination may be described, not performed. You have 9 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess safe prioritisation, task-specific clinical reasoning and clear communication. Disclose findings only when requested or appropriate. Performance levels: Fail / Pass / High-performance. The candidate may verbalise management; no procedure is performed.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: You are Alex, 60. Bright red blood mixed with stool on 4 occasions in 6 weeks. New tendency to looser bowel motions, no severe pain. Unintentional 3 kg weight loss over 2 months. No previous bowel investigations. No first-degree family history of colorectal cancer. You suspect haemorrhoids and are worried about cancer. If asked about dizziness, fainting or large-volume bleeding, say no. You have not had a FIT test.
sections.4. Findings available on request: Observations on request: haemodynamically stable. No palpable abdominal mass. Rectal examination may be offered with consent and chaperone; if requested: no palpable rectal mass, small non-bleeding external haemorrhoid. FBC pending. No imaging.
sections.5. Examiner frame — key steps: OPEN: Introduce self, check amount of bleeding and haemodynamic red flags, then establish patient concern. HISTORY: Characterise colour, timing, mixing with stool, frequency, pain, mucus and tenesmus. CANCER: Ask change in bowel habit, weight loss, fatigue/anaemia symptoms, abdominal pain, family history and previous screening. OTHER: Ask anticoagulants/NSAIDs, IBD history, bowel infection or anorectal symptoms; consider fissure, haemorrhoids, diverticular disease, inflammation and cancer. EXAM: Offer abdominal examination and appropriate consensual chaperoned rectal examination; findings do not exclude proximal pathology. TEST: Arrange FBC and quantitative FIT (symptomatic pathway). Explain FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g triggers suspected colorectal cancer pathway; a low FIT does not exclude cancer if concerning ongoing symptoms. REFER: Document symptoms and arrange urgent appropriate specialist assessment if FIT threshold met or strong concern persists; endoscopic investigation/CT colonography follows specialist triage. FINISH: Explain uncertainty and safety-net for heavy bleeding, syncope, worsening symptoms or delayed investigations; check understanding.
sections.6. Marking grid (nine task-specific rows: Criterion Fail Pass High-performance Rapport and immediate safety Starts with reassurance without checking bleeding severity. Checks significant bleeding and establishes rapport. Actively excludes shock, syncope and severe associated symptoms. Bleeding character Does not ask timing, colour or relation to stool. Characterises visible blood and duration. Clarifies mixed blood, mucus, change over time and rectal pain. Cancer symptoms [SC] Fails to ask about weight loss or bowel change. Asks weight loss, new bowel habit and anaemia symptoms. Integrates age, mixed blood, bowel change and weight loss into risk assessment. Background and differentials Assumes haemorrhoids without questioning. Checks family history, medicines and benign causes. Also clarifies previous FIT/screening, IBD and relevant comorbidity. Examination States no examination is useful. Offers abdominal and chaperoned anorectal assessment. Explains a small haemorrhoid does not account for or exclude serious disease. FIT pathway [SC] Says age alone requires direct referral irrespective of FIT or says FIT diagnoses cancer. Offers quantitative FIT for unexplained bleeding at age 60. Explains role and limitations of FIT and
sections.7. Critical fails — serious unsafe omiss: Reassures that haemorrhoids explain bleeding and makes no cancer assessment or investigation plan. Claims that a negative FIT definitively rules out colorectal cancer and offers no review of persistent symptoms. Fails to act on a disclosed positive FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g or a palpable rectal mass. Safety-critical rows are marked [SC] in the grid. Examiners should apply critical fails with clinical judgement, not an automatic numerical scoring rule.
sections.8. Curveball: Curveball: The patient later mentions a FIT result of 6 µg Hb/g but ongoing rectal bleeding, bowel change and weight loss. Expected response: do not discharge or reassure solely because below threshold; arrange appropriate specialist assessment based on continuing strong clinical concern and safety net.

stations.title: Raised Calcium on Routine Bloods
stations.source_heading: B2-77 Raised Calcium on Routine Bloods

near_match.title: A Raised Calcium on a Routine Blood Test — Proportionate, Honest, and the PTH Comes Next

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-77 — Raised Calcium on Routine Bloods Station type: Data interpretation / applied knowledge | Time: 9 minutes | Status: DRAFT — clinical and duplicate review required AMaC educational station; not an official MRCS mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman referred after repeat blood tests show albumin-adjusted calcium 2.93 mmol/L (reference 2.2–2.6), PTH 9.2 pmol/L (laboratory upper limit 6.9), creatinine normal and phosphate slightly low. Interpret the result, outline the differential, investigations, and indications for specialist referral.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Candidate should identify PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia, likely primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) pending proper confirmation and alternative causes, assess severity, and know NICE NG132 referral indications. Do not demand localisation imaging to establish diagnosis.
sections.3. Actor / patient instructions: Examiner supplies these results verbally or on paper. Patient has constipation, thirst and previous renal colic. No acute confusion. Takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. No known cancer. On questioning, has had two prior kidney stones.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific descript: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Pattern recognition Reads calcium alone; ignores PTH Identifies hypercalcaemia with inappropriately raised PTH Explains PTH should be suppressed when calcium is high Verify abnormality Assumes one abnormal result proves diagnosis Checks repeat albumin-adjusted calcium, PTH paired with calcium and lab context Reviews trends, assay limitations and albumin / renal status Symptoms and severity Fails to ask symptoms or acute complications Asks thirst, polyuria, constipation, stones, fractures, confusion Assesses hydration, ECG and urgent action if severe/symptomatic Causes Concludes all hypercalcaemia is cancer Suggests PHPT; distinguishes suppressed-PTH malignancy causes Mentions familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia and lithium/thiazide context Further investigations Orders sestamibi to diagnose PHPT Plans renal function, vitamin D, phosphate, urinary calcium assessment and bone/renal evaluation Explains urinary calcium helps separate FHH and stones/osteoporosis matter Medication review Ignores prescribed medicines Checks thiazides, lithium, supplements and calcium/vitamin D products Proposes supervised medication review and reassessment rather than a
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-impact trigge: • Treats a calcium of 2.93 mmol/L plus elevated PTH as definitively malignancy-related with no investigation of PHPT. • Fails to recognise urgent severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia if confusion, arrhythmia or very high calcium emerges. • Declares a normal localisation scan excludes PHPT or removes surgical eligibility.
sections.6. Curveball: Examiner changes calcium to 3.65 mmol/L and says patient is confused. Candidate must switch to acute assessment, ECG, IV isotonic fluid with monitoring and urgent senior/endocrine involvement; no routine outpatient pathway.
sections.7. Recovery after an initial error: After first suggesting a sestamibi scan for diagnosis: “Correction: biochemical tests establish PHPT; neck imaging is used only to plan surgery. I would first complete the biochemical and organ-impact work-up.”
sections.8. Example candidate performances: Fail “The calcium is high; this is probably cancer. Order a sestamibi scan and review later.” Misses non-suppressed PTH, kidney stones, and referral indication. Pass “The raised PTH is inappropriate in hypercalcaemia, pointing to PHPT. I would verify paired results, check renal function and vitamin D, assess urinary calcium and renal/bone complications, review medications, and refer because she has stones and calcium above 2.85.” High-performance “Biochemistry suggests PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia, most likely PHPT, though FHH and medication effects need consideration. Renal stones and 2.93 mmol/L both support surgical referral. Localisation imaging is for surgical planning, and I will distinguish this routine assessment from any severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia needing immediate stabilisation.”

stations.title: Projectile Vomiting in a 5-Week-Old

near_match.title: Projectile Vomiting in a Five-Week-Old / Correct the Chemistry Before the Surgeon

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | ROUND 2 B2-78 — Projectile Vomiting in a 5-Week-Old Paediatric surgery | history and applied data | 9 minutes Draft | 12 October 2026 | 9-minute station | AMaC development content; not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical trainee assessing a 5-week-old infant referred with repeated vomiting. Take a focused history from the parent, request relevant findings and investigations from the examiner, explain your working diagnosis and immediate plan. You do not need to physically examine a baby.
sections.2. Examiner / actor setup: At 3 minutes, supply examination upon request: alert but mildly dehydrated; HR 166/min, CRT 3 seconds, sunken fontanelle, no fever, soft abdomen, occasional visible left-to-right peristalsis, no definite olive. At 5 minutes, supply: Na 134, K 3.0, Cl 89 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, venous pH 7.51; ultrasound reports elongated thickened pyloric muscle consistent with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. At 7 minutes ask whether the infant should proceed immediately to anaesthesia. If the candidate hears bile-stained vomiting (curveball), state this is a different hypothetical infant.Actor: You are the mother of a 5-week-old boy. He has vomited forcefully after almost every feed for 6 days. It is milky, NOT green. He remains hungry after vomiting. There have been fewer wet nappies and he seems to be losing weight. Pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated. If asked: no fever, no blood, no sick contacts; birth weight 3.4 kg, now 3.3 kg. Ask: “Does he need an operation tonight?”
sections.3. Clinical frame and examiner lens: Recognise likely infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis from progressive, non-bilious projectile vomiting in an infant aged 2–8 weeks. Focus on dehydration, weight trend and electrolyte loss; recognise bilious vomiting as a separate emergency obstruction pathway.
sections.4. Marking grid — specific behavioural d: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Focused chronology Does not establish age, progression or feed association. Asks onset, progression, forcefulness and timing after feeds. Builds pattern and distinguishes effortless reflux from escalating projectile vomiting. Vomitus and obstruction red flags Fails to ask whether vomit is green. Asks bilious versus non-bilious, blood, distension and pain. States green bilious vomiting needs immediate obstruction assessment and surgical escalation. Feeding and hydration Omits intake and urine output. Asks feeding volume, ability to retain feeds, wet nappies and weight. Quantifies fluid deficit indicators and assesses clinical deterioration. Differential and examination Assumes simple reflux; requests no examination. Names pyloric stenosis and asks for weight, hydration, abdomen and vital signs. Recognises a palpable olive is not required and considers infection or other obstruction if atypical. Tests and interpretation Ignores electrolyte abnormality or blood gas. Requests U&E, glucose, blood gas and ultrasound; identifies hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Links potassium/chloride depletion to persistent gastric losses; acknowledges early cases ca
sections.5. Critical fails — unsafe decisions: Fails to ask or respond to green bilious vomiting and dismisses possible obstruction. Proceeds to pyloromyotomy/anaesthesia with marked uncorrected alkalosis and dehydration. Discharges a dehydrated infant with ongoing forceful vomiting and poor urine output. Prescribes potassium replacement without confirming renal function/urine output and monitoring.
sections.6. Curveball: If the examiner changes the vomit to green, stop the pyloric-stenosis script: nil by mouth, resuscitation, urgent paediatric surgical evaluation for obstruction/malrotation, not routine outpatient ultrasound.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If you initially call it reflux: “The progressive projectile nature and reduced wet nappies change my assessment; I am admitting this infant for pyloric stenosis work-up.” If you forget the biochemical result: “The pH 7.51 and low chloride make immediate anaesthesia unsafe; correct and recheck before theatre.” If your initial plan omits family involvement: “I will explain why fluids and blood tests come before the procedure, and check the parent’s concerns.”
sections.8. Model performance: Fail “Probably normal reflux. Continue feeding and come back next week.” Omits green-vomit question, fluids and biochemical interpretation. Pass “This is likely pyloric stenosis. I would assess hydration, do blood tests and ultrasound, admit for IV fluids, correct alkalosis and involve paediatric surgery before pyloromyotomy.” High-performance “Progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting with persistent hunger, weight loss and hypochloraemic alkalosis is classic. I would admit, establish IV access, monitor urine output, carefully replace deficit and gastric losses, repeat electrolytes and gas, and plan surgery only once medically optimised, with clear parent communication.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK — Progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting at 5 weeks: pyloric stenosis. SAY — “His fluid and salt levels must be corrected before surgery.” DO — Assess dehydration, IV access, U&E/gas, ultrasound, admit. FINISH — Repeat biochemistry and arrange paediatric surgical/anaesthetic review. TRAP — Never rush anaesthesia with unresolved metabolic alkalosis. NUMBERS — Case: Cl 89, K 3.0, pH 7.51; correction is needed.

stations.title: Abnormal Clotting Before Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-80 — Abnormal Clotting Before Surgery Station format: Data interpretation / applied perioperative management | Duration: 9 minutes | Draft: 12 October 2026 PROVISIONAL — Requires clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate review.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: A 72-year-old man is booked for elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy tomorrow. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Today’s INR is 2.6, APTT 34 seconds (laboratory 25–35), platelets 215 × 10⁹/L, Hb 126 g/L, creatinine 105 µmol/L. The operation is not immediately life-saving. The anaesthetist asks whether he can proceed.Your task: Interpret the clotting results, identify the missing risk information and give a safe plan for proceeding or postponing. Discuss how the plan differs for DOACs and when bridging may be considered.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess contextual, not automatic, interpretation. INR 2.6 reflects warfarin effect and is not acceptable without an agreed reversal/management plan for this high-bleeding-risk elective operation; the decision involves surgery, anaesthesia and anticoagulation team. APTT and platelets are not abnormal. Do not expect candidate to prescribe a universal interruption interval.
sections.3. Actor / team prompt: Anaesthetist: “The list is full, can we just go ahead?” If asked, the patient’s most recent warfarin dose was last night; no mechanical valve, stroke or VTE history. Warfarin indication is non-valvular AF. No anticoagulation plan documented.
sections.4. Marking grid — each row assessed inde: Assessed action Fail Pass High-performance Recognises risk Treats INR 2.6 as normal because it is therapeutic for AF. Explains that therapeutic anticoagulation increases operative bleeding risk and requires a plan. Differentiates therapeutic AF INR from an acceptable procedural haemostasis threshold. Classifies pattern Calls this thrombocytopenia or an isolated APTT disorder. Identifies prolonged PT/INR on warfarin with normal platelets and APTT. Lists other potential causes of abnormal PT if warfarin history were absent. Checks context Issues an unconditional proceed/cancel decision without history. Checks urgency, procedure bleeding risk, indication, last dose, renal function and prior clotting/bleeding. Explicitly checks recent stroke/VTE and prosthetic valves to stratify thrombosis risk. Immediate decision Recommends incision tomorrow with INR 2.6 and no plan. Stops automatic progression; discusses postponement and individualised INR correction/plan with senior team. Communicates a clear decision point and timing for repeat INR and rebooking. Warfarin plan Orders empiric high-dose reversal or heparin bridging for everyone. Explains elective interruption/correction guided by loc
sections.5. Critical fails: Proceeding to elective major surgery at INR 2.6 without a documented agreed haemostasis plan. Prescribing routine therapeutic heparin bridging for non-valvular AF without assessing risk. Treating a normal INR as proof that apixaban is absent or safe for surgery. Failing to escalate an unexplained severe coagulopathy before surgery.
sections.6. Curveball: The anaesthetist says: “What if the drug were apixaban and INR was 1.0?” Expected: do not infer clearance from INR; check last dose, renal function, procedural bleeding risk and local DOAC interruption advice.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If candidate initially says proceed: “I need to correct that: therapeutic INR for AF is not surgical clearance; do not proceed without the agreed perioperative plan.” If candidate initially suggests automatic bridging: “I would first establish embolic risk; routine LMWH bridging is not indicated for most non-valvular AF patients.” If candidate interprets a normal INR in a DOAC patient as safe: “INR does not reliably measure DOAC anticoagulant effect.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail: “INR is in range for his AF, so the procedure can go ahead. Bridge everyone with LMWH.” Pass: “INR 2.6 reflects warfarin anticoagulation. I would not proceed with this elective high-bleeding-risk operation without an agreed perioperative plan. I will confirm urgency, indication, last dose, bleeding and clotting risks, and discuss interruption and repeat INR with anaesthesia and the surgical team. Bridging is not automatic.” High-performance: “The lab pattern fits warfarin effect, not thrombocytopenia. Today I will stop automatic theatre progression and agree a documented plan with the operating and anaesthetic teams, considering the patient’s thromboembolic risk and timing of correction, repeat testing and restart. If the drug were a DOAC, routine INR would not establish drug clearance.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK — INR reflects drug effect, not operative clearance. SAY — Elective high-bleeding-risk surgery needs an individualised anticoagulation plan. DO — Check indication, last dose, urgency, procedure risk and thrombotic history. FINISH — Document delay/proceed decision, repeat test and restart owner. TRAP — Do not bridge every AF patient; INR does not quantify DOAC ef

stations.source_heading: B2-81 A Wrong-Site Surgery Near Miss

near_match.title: Wrong-site surgery near miss: stopping the procedure and reporting

sections.preamble: B2-81 — A Wrong-Site Surgery Near Miss Station format: Communication / professionalism / patient safety | Duration: 9 minutes | Draft: 12 October 2026 PROVISIONAL — Requires clinical sign-off and live-register duplicate review.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: During the WHO team time-out for an elective LEFT inguinal hernia repair, you notice that the booking list and theatre board say RIGHT. The patient’s signed consent form and clinic documentation say LEFT; the surgeon is about to prepare the wrong side. No incision has been made. A senior colleague tells you to “sort it out afterwards; we are late.”Your task: Explain and demonstrate what you do immediately, how you reconcile the discrepancy, whom you tell and how the near miss is recorded and reviewed.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Near miss before incision is not itself completed wrong-site surgery. The candidate must stop progression; reconcile identity, side, planned procedure with consent, records, site mark and reliable preoperative confirmation; perform a fresh team check; report the near miss. Discuss disclosure sensitively: GMC says professional judgement applies for near misses that caused no harm, and senior advice when uncertain. Do not claim statutory candour is automatic for every harmless near miss.
sections.3. Actor / team prompt: Theatre practitioner: “Everyone else is ready. Are you really stopping the list?” If prompted, there is no reliable confirmation that the original site mark was checked in the ward. The patient is under general anaesthesia.
sections.4. Marking grid — each row assessed inde: Assessed action Fail Pass High-performance Stop-the-line response Allows the team to cut while sorting paperwork afterwards. Clearly says stop; do not prep/incise until discrepancy resolved. Uses closed-loop language to direct entire team to pause and confirm acknowledgement. Names the discrepancy Dismisses list and consent mismatch as admin only. Identifies LEFT consent/clinic records versus RIGHT board/booking. States both the planned procedure and correct site must be revalidated independently. Identity and consent Checks theatre board alone. Rechecks patient identity, signed consent, intended operation and side. Explains patient’s own prior confirmation is important and cannot be replaced by assumption once anaesthetised. Site verification Changes board to LEFT based on one document then proceeds. Checks clinical documentation, site mark and preoperative verification, involving operating surgeon. Recognises unresolved conflict requires delay until reliable evidence/patient confirmation available. Repeat safety pause Assumes previous time-out is sufficient. Requires corrected documentation and renewed team time-out before starting. Requests all staff verbally confirm patient, si
sections.5. Critical fails: Permitting skin incision or operative intervention despite unresolved side discrepancy. Quietly changing documents without verifying the intended side. Obeying pressure to proceed before completing a repeated team verification. Concealing or failing to report the wrong-site near miss through local safety processes.
sections.6. Curveball: The consultant says “I examined her last month; it is definitely the right side.” Expected: maintain pause, reconcile evidence and obtain reliable verification; senior confidence cannot replace the formal process.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If candidate initially agrees to continue: “I must stop the case now; an unresolved laterality mismatch is a patient safety threat.” If candidate says any near miss automatically requires statutory duty-of-candour notification: “A harmless near miss needs professional judgement on patient disclosure, with senior advice if uncertain.” If candidate suggests editing consent: “I cannot rewrite consent to fit the board; we must establish what the patient actually agreed to.”
sections.8. Model performances: Fail: “The surgeon knows the patient, so we should continue and fix the board later.” Pass: “Stop. The consent and notes say left but the theatre board says right. We must not proceed. I will confirm identity, consent, clinical notes and site marking with the surgeon, correct the discrepancy only once properly verified, repeat the team time-out, document and report the near miss.” High-performance: “I am stopping the line and asking everyone to acknowledge the pause. There is a laterality mismatch between consent/clinic records and the theatre list. We cannot infer the correct side from any single source, especially now the patient is anaesthetised. We need reliable confirmation; if we cannot achieve it, postpone. Once reconciled, conduct a fresh team time-out. Then report and debrief the incident, and decide with a senior whether disclosure of this harmless near miss is relevant to the patient.” 9. 60-second recall card THINK — Discrepant laterality is a stop signal, not admin trivia. SAY — “Stop: consent says LEFT, theatre board says RIGHT.” DO — Reconcile identity, consent, history, mark and team confirmation. FINISH — Renew time-out, document, report, debrief and allocate follo

stations.title: Angry Relative After a Cancelled Operation
stations.source_heading: B2-82 Angry Relative After a Cancelled Operation

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — Round 2 B2-82 | Angry Relative After a Cancelled Operation Station type: Communication / professionalism • Timing: 9 minutes • Status: PROVISIONAL / clinical sign-off pending Educational practice station; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Code is commissioning reference, not final MB station ID.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar asked to speak with a distressed relative following cancellation of an elective operation. Respond to the concern, respect confidentiality and agree a safe practical next step. You have 9 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner setup and case information: Patient: 64-year-old adult booked for elective hernia repair; case cancelled this afternoon. The hospital has not yet confirmed the reason or a replacement date. Relative is angry after time off work and arranging transport. Patient is awake, has capacity and has not yet confirmed what may be disclosed. No indication of current acute deterioration.Examiners should not supply a cancellation reason: reward acknowledgment of uncertainty and verification. A safe response can listen to an unauthorised relative without disclosing confidential details. If candidate seeks patient permission, examiner confirms patient would agree to relative receiving practical scheduling information only. Grade actionable ownership, not unrealistic booking promises.
sections.3. Actor / patient briefing: Opening: “My father fasted all day. Nobody told us anything. This hospital is a disgrace.” If asked about consent: “He wants me involved, but I don’t know whether he told staff.” If asked about symptoms: “He is uncomfortable but not suddenly worse.” If candidate promises tomorrow: “Can you guarantee that?” If candidate is sympathetic: “We need a proper explanation and a date.” Do not volunteer confidential details or a verified cancellation reason.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Each row is judged against its own observable descriptors. Safety-critical rows are marked [SC]. Overall standard: Fail / Pass / High-performance; no automatic numerical pass score is implied. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance 01 Opening and emotional validation Interrupts, argues about rota pressure or tells relative to calm down. Introduces self, invites concerns, explicitly recognises distress. Uses calm non-defensive language and acknowledges disruption without minimising the experience. 02 Immediate concern and safety Never checks whether patient is currently unwell or needs urgent care. Asks if the patient has deteriorated or has unmanaged symptoms; arranges review if indicated. Separates emotional concerns from urgent clinical needs and states who will assess deterioration. 03 Confidentiality [SC] Discloses diagnosis, test results or details without establishing patient permission. Asks what patient has consented to share; confines information to authorised scope. Offers to involve patient directly or to seek consent promptly while continuing to listen. 04 Discover specific consequences Offers generic apology and ignores transport, work or fasting impact. Asks about waste
sections.5. Critical fails (unsafe actions): 1. Discloses confidential patient information to relative without appropriate basis or consent. 2. Ignores clear new or worsening patient symptoms when raised, without arranging assessment. 3. Invents a medical or operational reason as established fact and uses it to dismiss concerns. 4. Guarantees an unconfirmed operation date or clinical safety with no review or safety-net.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: At minute 6, actor says: “Tell me exactly which doctor cancelled it, and I’ll put their name online.” Candidate should avoid speculation or inappropriate personal information, offer to verify events and invite formal concerns reporting.
sections.7. Recovery after an omission or misstep: If you shared too much: stop further disclosure, acknowledge mistake without adding detail, and seek patient permission before continuing; report if confidential information was wrongly disclosed. If you promised an unconfirmed date: correct it immediately — “I cannot guarantee tomorrow; I will check with the booking and clinical teams and tell you what is confirmed.” If you dismissed the practical impact: ask specifically about transport, work, care arrangements and pain; agree a named owner and timescale.
sections.8. Model performance by band: Fail: “It was cancelled because anaesthetics made an error. You will be back tomorrow. Complaining will not help.” Gives invented reason, false commitment and discourages feedback. Pass: “I’m sorry this was cancelled and for the disruption. I can listen to your concerns now; before discussing his clinical details, I need his permission. I’ll ask the team to confirm the reason, his clinical plan and who will contact him about a new date. If he becomes more unwell, we’ll reassess him.” High-performance: “You have arranged leave and travel and your father fasted; that is upsetting. I won’t guess the reason or promise a date until I’ve checked. Let’s make sure he is clinically comfortable; then, with his consent, I’ll coordinate an update from the theatre/booking team and give you a named contact. You can also speak to PALS or complain formally if you wish.”

stations.title: Explaining a Stoma Before Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-83 Explaining a Stoma Before Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B — Round 2 B2-83 | Explaining a Stoma Before Surgery Station type: Communication / consent • Timing: 9 minutes • Status: PROVISIONAL / clinical sign-off pending Educational practice station; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Code is commissioning reference, not final MB station ID.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are a surgical registrar seeing a patient before planned colorectal surgery. Explain what a stoma is, why it may be needed, what temporary means, day-to-day effects, professional support and the consent process. This is a counselling station, not formal procedure-specific written consent.
sections.2. Examiner setup and case information: Patient: 58-year-old with rectal cancer attending preoperative discussion for possible anterior resection with temporary defunctioning loop ileostomy; final operative approach requires surgeon confirmation. Patient asks whether the stoma is permanent and fears being unable to work. No acute symptoms.Examiner must treat the proposed loop ileostomy as possible, not inevitable. No fixed reversal schedule may be promised. Candidate may say surgery-specific risk, the precise plan and possibility of permanence must be confirmed with the operating colorectal surgeon. No need to quote complication percentages unless reliable and individualised.
sections.3. Actor / patient briefing: Opening: “My surgeon said I might need a bag. Will I have it forever?” If asked lifestyle: “I work in a shop and worry about smell and leaks.” If candidate says guaranteed reversal: “So I’ll definitely be normal in three months?” If asked preferences: “I want honest answers and to meet someone who uses a stoma.” Patient is willing to meet specialist stoma nurse.
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Each row is judged against its own observable descriptors. Safety-critical rows are marked [SC]. Overall standard: Fail / Pass / High-performance; no automatic numerical pass score is implied. Criterion Fail Pass High-performance 01 Invitation and current understanding Launches into anatomy without asking worries or checking patient’s understanding. Asks what patient understands about proposed bowel surgery and stoma concern. Elicits personal priorities including body image, work, activities and sexuality. 02 Why a stoma may be needed [SC] States every bowel operation requires a stoma, or denies it is possible. Explains diversion or removal of diseased bowel may require opening bowel onto abdominal wall. Ties possible stoma to this operation while distinguishing planned from unforeseen intraoperative need. 03 What a stoma is Calls it a drain or says patient will still pass all stool normally. Explains bowel comes through abdominal wall into appliance collecting stool. Uses simple check-back and acknowledges mucus may still pass per rectum depending on operation. 04 Temporary versus permanent [SC] Guarantees reversal or says any stoma can be reversed. Explains temporary or permanent
sections.5. Critical fails (unsafe actions): 1. Guarantees temporary stoma reversal or provides a fabricated time frame as certain. 2. Denies possibility of a stoma when it forms part of the planned operation or rescue strategy. 3. Pressures the patient to consent or refuses discussion of alternatives and material risks. 4. Fails to offer specialist stoma nurse input or preoperative siting in an elective case where feasible.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: Patient asks at minute 6: “Can you promise it will be reversed by Christmas?” Candidate must distinguish intention from guarantee, explain dependence on healing, treatment and fitness, and arrange surgeon-specific advice.
sections.7. Recovery after an omission or misstep: If you overpromised reversal: correct promptly — “I should not have guaranteed that. A reversal may be intended, but it depends on healing, cancer treatment and further surgical assessment.” If you overwhelmed the patient with technical terms: use “a small opening on the tummy connected to the bowel”, show a diagram or appliance, and check understanding. If you ignored work and body-image concerns: ask what tasks they do and what they fear; offer practical teaching and stoma nurse follow-up.
sections.8. Model performance by band: Fail: “It is only temporary and you’ll definitely have it reversed in three months. You just wear a bag and there’s nothing else to know.” Pass: “A stoma is a section of bowel brought onto your tummy, with a bag to collect stool. In this operation it may protect the bowel join while it heals. The plan may be for a temporary ileostomy, but reversal cannot be guaranteed. Our stoma nurse can show you bags and help choose a suitable site.” High-performance: “What worries you most about the bag? We can address leaks, work and clothing practically. If a stoma is needed, a specialist nurse can mark a suitable position, show equipment and support you after discharge. The operating surgeon will explain your personal chance of reversal and alternatives; I want you to have time to decide with realistic expectations.”

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B B2-84 — Colorectal Cancer - Staging CT and MDT Draft • Data interpretation • 9 minutes • 12 October 2026 • NOT FOR PUBLICATION BEFORE CLINICAL SIGN-OFF Station focus Use a written CT report to interpret provisional clinical stage, identify an indeterminate lesion and form an MDT plan. No imaging needed.
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar. A 67-year-old with biopsy-confirmed sigmoid adenocarcinoma has had staging imaging. Interpret the written report, identify further information needed and outline management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Hand candidate this report: CT chest, abdomen, pelvis: 4.5 cm sigmoid tumour extending into pericolic fat, no documented peritoneal or adjacent organ invasion; two morphologically suspicious regional mesocolic lymph nodes; 12 mm indeterminate liver segment VI lesion; no pulmonary lesions. Colonoscopy could not pass the stenosing lesion. No other metastases identified. Patient stable without obstruction. If asked, baseline CEA available but not yet reviewed. Prompt: “Give a defensible cTNM and what you would do next.” Allow provisional cT3 cN+; do NOT insist on a single definitive N subclass or assert M0 with an indeterminate hepatic focus.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor required. Examiner may simulate MDT chair asking for an explicit plan. The candidate should not imply CT proves nodal metastasis.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific descript: Nine domains. Rate each domain Fail / Pass / High-performance. A critical safety failure overrides otherwise satisfactory performance. Not an official MRCS mark scheme. Assessed domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical context Treats written CT as proof of final pathological stage. States this is pretreatment clinical stage of biopsy-proven colon cancer. Distinguishes cTNM from subsequent pTNM and flags radiology limitations. Primary tumour extent Calls any extramural extension T4. Identifies invasion through muscularis propria into pericolic tissue as cT3. Explains T4 requires peritoneal surface or adjacent organ/structure involvement. Nodes Assumes size alone confirms histological nodal disease. Identifies regional mesocolic nodes described as suspicious as cN-positive, provisionally. Qualifies imaging uncertainty and requests radiologist clarification as needed. Metastatic spread Ignores the described liver lesion or labels it definitely benign. States indeterminate liver lesion means M status cannot be confidently settled. Requests liver MRI / specialist characterisation before committing to a curative plan. Staging completion Does not check chest imaging or histology. Checks
sections.5. Critical fail triggers: Labels indeterminate liver lesion definitively benign and commits to curative resection without addressing it. Claims definite metastatic disease based solely on an indeterminate 12 mm lesion and denies potentially curative review. Misses need to assess the unexamined proximal colon following incomplete colonoscopy. Provides falsely definitive prognosis or treatment without MDT and outstanding staging resolution.
sections.6. Examiner curveball: “The liver lesion has no definite malignant features. Would you call this M0?” Expected: do not classify distant spread with certainty; discuss expert radiology and liver MRI if appropriate.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery: If candidate prematurely says M0: explicitly retract and name the unresolved segment VI lesion and imaging follow-up. If candidate says N2 without evidence: revise to suspicious regional nodes / provisional N-positive and explain scan limits. If candidate overlooks incomplete colonoscopy: add documented plan for full colonic examination when safe.
sections.8. Model performances: Fail “The cancer is stage III, there is no spread, so book surgery and chemotherapy.” Omits liver lesion and colonic clearance. Pass “This is provisionally cT3 with suspicious regional nodes. The hepatic lesion is indeterminate, so we need further characterisation, completion of staging and colorectal MDT discussion. Complete assessment of the colon is needed.” High-performance “CT suggests a cT3 sigmoid primary with possible nodal involvement, not a histological N stage. Segment VI must be reviewed by specialist radiology, potentially with liver MRI, before a definitive M classification. Clarify incomplete colonoscopy, performance status and treatment preferences; present MDT pathways without overpromising.”

stations.title: Gastric Cancer — Staging and Nutrition
stations.source_heading: B2-94 Gastric Cancer — Staging and Nutrition

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-94 — Gastric Cancer — Staging and Nutrition DRAFT • 12 October 2026 • Group 10 • Data interpretation / applied knowledge • 9 minutes • Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief — reveal in Exam Mode: You are the surgical registrar in the upper-GI cancer clinic. You have a biopsy report and a written CT staging report for a patient with newly diagnosed distal gastric cancer. Your task: Interpret the report, set out the next staging and MDT steps, and explain the initial nutritional and treatment pathway to the examiner and patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief — reveal in Exam Mode: Provide written CT and histology only, no images. A strong candidate must not invent a pathological TNM category or promise resection from an apparently M0 CT. Present the patient question at minute six.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: 68 years old, endoscopic biopsy confirms distal gastric adenocarcinoma; 8 kg unintentional weight loss and early satiety. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis report: thickening of distal stomach with two small adjacent nodes, no definite liver or lung deposits and no ascites. When asked: eats half-sized meals; no current obstruction; ECOG performance status 1; independent. If questioned about treatment: “Does no spread on CT mean I can just have an operation?”
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Score each row on its own evidence. A critical fail triggers an overall safety review; do not infer competence from a total alone. Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Initial interpretation: Calls the lesion “early gastric cancer” without staging or histology. Identifies biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinoma requiring formal staging and upper-GI MDT review. States that a CT report cannot by itself establish microscopic nodal disease or exclude occult peritoneal spread.
sections.2. Clinical / nutritional assessment: Ignores weight loss, swallowing difficulty and performance status. Assesses weight trajectory, intake, functional state, symptoms, comorbidity and fitness for treatment. Requests dietitian-led nutritional screening promptly and considers sarcopenia and prehabilitation.
sections.3. Baseline staging: Offers surgery solely on the endoscopy finding. Requests contrast-enhanced CT chest, abdomen and pelvis and reviews endoscopic histology and site. Clarifies tumour location, distant disease and resectability; flags indeterminate lesions for MDT-directed clarification.
sections.4. Additional staging: Treats a negative CT as excluding peritoneal metastases. Discusses staging laparoscopy for potentially curable gastric cancer, with washings as directed by specialist team. Explains why occult peritoneal disease can change a curative surgical plan.

sections.1. Candidate brief — reveal in Exam Mode: You are the surgical registrar asked to explain planned endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for a probable common bile duct stone. Your task: Explain the purpose, steps, material risks and alternatives; establish an informed preference and identify any issues that need specialist resolution before consent is finalised.
sections.2. Examiner brief — reveal in Exam Mode: This is a shared-decision conversation, not a numerical risk memorisation exercise. The candidate should not independently prescribe anticoagulant interruption without procedural/thrombosis assessment. Give the apixaban prompt only if the candidate asks about medications.
sections.3. Actor / patient brief: Patient: 58-year-old with jaundice from a likely common bile duct stone. Stable, afebrile; ERCP is planned for duct clearance. Ultrasound report: dilated CBD and probable distal 9 mm duct stone. Bilirubin raised, no shock or cholangitis currently. Patient takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation and has been told “it is only a camera test.” Ask if addressed: “I had pancreatitis years ago. Can this procedure cause it again?”
sections.4. Critical-weighted marking grid: Score each row on its own evidence. A critical fail triggers an overall safety review; do not infer competence from a total alone. Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Capacity and purpose: Assumes a signature alone is valid consent. Confirms identity, indication, capacity, communication needs and invites patient priorities. Checks existing understanding and describes shared decision-making without coercion.
sections.2. Indication / expected benefit: Says ERCP is a routine camera test only. Explains therapeutic ERCP to relieve duct obstruction, remove a stone and/or place a stent as indicated. Links aims to the actual suspected common bile duct stone and distinguishes investigation from treatment.
sections.3. What happens: Misdescribes ERCP as abdominal surgery. Explains endoscope via mouth to duodenum, duct access using X-ray guidance, contrast and possible sphincterotomy, extraction or stenting. Describes likely sedation/anaesthetic arrangements and recovery at the appropriate patient level.
sections.4. Pancreatitis risk: Omits post-ERCP pancreatitis. Explicitly discusses pancreatitis, potentially severe, and symptoms needing urgent assessment. Explains individual risk varies and that prevention measures will be considered by the ERCP team.

sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific descript: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and alternatives Calls this reflux or gastritis; misses perforation Identifies probable spontaneous oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave) after vomiting; keeps ACS and other critical chest causes in differential Explicitly links oesophageal leak to mediastinal/pleural contamination, sepsis and need for immediate source control Initial safety response No ABCDE or leaves unstable patient unattended ABCDE, continuous monitoring, oxygen if indicated, immediate senior/anaesthetic support Reassesses response repeatedly and anticipates airway/ICU needs without delaying definitive help Resuscitation Delays access or ignores hypotension Two IV lines, blood cultures where feasible without delay, FBC/U&E/CRP/coagulation/VBG-lactate, cautious IV crystalloid with reassessment Recognises distributive/volume-loss physiology and guides further resuscitation using response and critical care input Oral intake and medicines Offers food, drink or blindly inserts NG tube Nil by mouth; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering aerobic and anaerobic organisms; IV analgesia and PPI per team plan Makes early antimicrobial and nutrition plan with antimicrobial/specialist
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-critical acti: Fails to recognise suspected oesophageal perforation despite classic vomiting-plus-sudden-chest-pain presentation and shock. Gives oral intake or attempts blind nasogastric instrumentation despite suspected acute oesophageal rupture. Does not arrange urgent specialist source-control assessment in a septic, hypotensive patient. Withholds resuscitation and broad-spectrum antimicrobials while waiting for a routine test or review.
sections.6. Curveball: The initial chest X-ray is reported “no obvious pneumomediastinum”. Expected response: do not rule out perforation; continue urgent CT and surgical escalation.
sections.7. sections.5. Critical fails — safety-critical acti: Guarantees bariatric surgery solely from BMI, bypassing full specialist MDT assessment and shared decision-making. Claims there is no need for long-term follow-up or nutritional monitoring after surgery. Promises diabetes cure or risk-free surgery without discussing major harms and uncertainty.
