sections.6. Curveball: The patient says she is from a South Asian family and her sister with BMI 34.5 has type 2 diabetes. Expected response: note NICE lower BMI thresholds by 2.5 kg/m² for specified ethnic backgrounds; individual specialist assessment rather than guaranteed eligibility.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: Having said “you need BMI 40”, candidate corrects: “With your BMI 38 and diabetes/OSA you meet the NICE criteria for referral for comprehensive specialist assessment.” After suggesting surgery cures diabetes, candidate corrects to possible remission/improvement and explains that medication and follow-up may still be needed.
sections.8. Model performance — Fail: Dismisses a BMI 38 patient as ineligible, gives no MDT referral and provides unrealistic promises about outcomes.

sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Patient underwent laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 18 months ago; lost 42 kg. Two hours of sudden severe colicky central/left upper abdominal pain, nausea, retching without much vomit. Pulse 108, BP 112/74, respiratory rate 20, temperature 37.0°C, SpO₂ 98% air. Abdomen soft with minimal tenderness. FBC, renal profile and lactate currently within local reference limits. Pregnancy test negative. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast describes possible mesenteric swirl without free air; not conclusive. Award marks for urgency despite deceptively reassuring results. If candidate asks, history of earlier self-resolving similar attacks.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are frightened by the severe pain and say: “They say my scans and blood tests are nearly normal; can I go home?” If asked about surgery, say you had gastric bypass 18 months ago and previous shorter bouts of similar pain. If asked about vomiting, say you have retched but barely vomited. If asked about pregnancy, confirm a negative test.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific descript: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognises altered anatomy Calls it uncomplicated gastritis without considering bypass complications. Names internal hernia/closed-loop small bowel obstruction as urgent possibilities after Roux-en-Y bypass. Links intermittent preceding attacks to transient herniation and possible threatened bowel ischaemia. Immediate assessment Does not assess observations, perfusion or abdominal signs. Initiates ABCDE, repeat observations, analgesia, abdominal examination and serial reassessment. Explains why pain can be disproportionate to a relatively benign early examination. Resuscitation and preparation Offers discharge or oral intake while diagnosis remains unsafe. Keeps nil by mouth, obtains IV access, gives analgesia, IV fluid if indicated, and monitors output. Prepares for possible urgent operation while avoiding indiscriminate fluid boluses. Investigations Uses normal lactate/FBC to rule out strangulation. Requests FBC, U&E, CRP, blood gas/lactate, pregnancy test where appropriate; reviews CT with radiology. Interprets serial lactate as supportive but not exclusionary and actively seeks CT signs of internal hernia. CT interpretation States negative/equi
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-critical acti: 1. Discharges the patient because early blood tests or CT are reassuring despite severe ongoing pain. 2. Fails to obtain urgent senior/bariatric surgical assessment when internal hernia is suspected. 3. Allows eating or delays action despite concern for closed-loop obstruction requiring urgent exploration. 4. Explicitly rules out bowel ischaemia solely from a normal lactate.
sections.6. Curveball: At minute 6 the pain becomes continuous, pulse rises to 125 and the patient looks pale. Ask: “The radiologist says there is no definite obstruction; what now?” Expected: repeat ABCDE, resuscitate, urgent senior/anaesthetic discussion and expedited exploration rather than observing for confirmatory CT.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If reassured by normal tests: “I must correct that: a normal lactate or non-diagnostic CT cannot rule out an internal hernia; I am contacting the bariatric surgeon now.” If initially suggested discharge: “I withdraw the discharge plan because ongoing severe pain after bypass may represent threatened bowel; admit nil by mouth for urgent assessment.” If analgesia was missed: “Give appropriate titrated analgesia now while proceeding with surgical assessment; symptom relief must not postpone diagnosis.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail: “The bloods are fine, the scan is inconclusive; it is probably indigestion. Take oral fluids and see your GP if worse.” [Misses rows 1, 4, 5, 6 and 9; unsafe discharge.]

stations.title: After Splenectomy

near_match.title: Fever After Splenectomy / No Spleen Means You Do Not Wait for the Flu Swab

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B • B2-99 After Splenectomy Type: Communication / patient safety | Station time: 9 minutes | Development draft — not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar on a discharge ward. A 42-year-old patient had an emergency splenectomy following trauma ten days ago. They ask what they need to do to stay safe once home. Explain infection prevention, vaccinations, antibiotic arrangements and how to respond to illness. An examiner is present.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosures: Patient stable, recovering after emergency splenectomy for blunt splenic injury. No history of pneumococcal or meningococcal vaccination is documented; routine childhood vaccinations were received. No known penicillin allergy. Discharge proposed once safe follow-up is organised. Vaccine schedule must follow current UKHSA Green Book and local specialist protocol; do not insist on obsolete universal adult Hib booster. Patient asks if tablets can be stopped after a few weeks and whether fever can wait overnight.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are worried about infections now that your spleen has been removed. Ask: “Will a cold kill me? Do I need injections? Do I take antibiotics forever? Can I just wait until morning if I get a fever?” If asked about travel, say you hope to travel abroad in six months. You are not allergic to antibiotics.
sections.4. Marking grid — task-specific descript: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Explains lifelong infection risk Says there are no additional risks after wound healing. Explains lifelong increased susceptibility to serious rapidly progressive infection, especially from encapsulated bacteria. Explains early post-splenectomy risk and uses calm language without claiming every infection is fatal. Recognises emergency warning signs Advises routine GP appointment for fever or systemic illness. Instructs immediate urgent medical assessment for fever, shaking chills or systemic illness; tells clinicians about asplenia. Explains time-critical assessment, treatment and escalation even if the patient initially appears well. Vaccination plan Omits vaccines or states routine childhood vaccines alone suffice. Arranges vaccination review for pneumococcal, meningococcal and annual influenza immunisation using UK schedule. Checks prior immunisations and exact current UKHSA/local schedule, arranging documentation and boosters as indicated. Timing after emergency surgery Delays vaccination indefinitely or claims the operation should have been delayed. Explains vaccines are usually planned at least 2 weeks after emergency splenectomy if feasible,
sections.5. Critical fails — safety-critical acti: 1. Tells an asplenic patient with fever to wait until morning rather than seek immediate urgent medical assessment. 2. Fails completely to address the lifelong serious infection risk and emergency response. 3. Discharges without any vaccination/prophylaxis plan or owner for follow-up. 4. Advises standby antibiotics alone as a substitute for urgent assessment of suspected sepsis.
sections.6. Curveball: At minute 6 the patient says: “I am flying to a malaria-risk region next month, and yesterday a dog bit my hand.” Expected: immediate evaluation of the bite and infection risk, careful travel/malaria prevention assessment, local antimicrobial advice, and clear safety-netting.
sections.7. Station-specific recovery lines: If fever was minimised: “I need to correct that: with no spleen, fever or severe illness warrants urgent assessment straight away, not overnight observation.” If vaccination was oversimplified: “I will check your documented vaccines and follow the current UKHSA asplenia schedule rather than assume every adult needs the same injections.” If prophylaxis duration was stated absolutely: “Duration depends on individual risk and specialist/local guidance; I will confirm your plan in writing before discharge.”
sections.8. Model performance — Fail: “Your spleen is gone but infection is only a short-term issue. Have your usual flu jab. If you get a temperature, take paracetamol and call your GP tomorrow.” [Misses rows 1, 2, 3 and 5; unsafe fever advice.]

sections.1. Title and header: Station type: Examination | Content area: Post-cardiac-surgery cardiovascular assessment | Duration: 9 minutes examination + 1 minute reading. Candidate: core surgical trainee. Simulated patient / examiner-provided findings. No real image or prop required. Guideline versions: NICE NG208 (published 17 November 2021; recommendations 1.8 and 1.9); British cardiovascular/valve/cardiothoracic societies joint statement (August 2021). Accessed 12 October 2026. Related AMaC station: B2-17 (thoracic surgical scars; distinct respiratory examination).
sections.2. Candidate brief: You are a core surgical trainee in an outpatient surgical assessment bay. A 64-year-old patient has undergone open heart-valve surgery several years ago and is attending for assessment of exercise intolerance. Please perform a focused cardiovascular examination, describe the findings and explain your differential and immediate next steps to the examiner. You have 9 minutes. The patient is stable and can sit or lie comfortably.
sections.3. Before you walk in: FRAME: Identify the operation using scars and prosthetic sounds, assess haemodynamic status and complications, and interpret anticoagulation safely. TRAP: Calling the click normal without investigating new breathlessness, or recommending a DOAC for a mechanical valve. FIRST MOVE: “I am the core surgical trainee. May I examine your heart? I will explain each step and stop if uncomfortable.”
sections.4. Flow: 0–1 min: introduction, consent, symptoms and immediate distress check. 1–3 min: hands, pulse, blood pressure (verbalised), face, neck/JVP. 3–6 min: inspect sternotomy/leg harvest; palpate apex/heaves; auscultate valve areas and carotids appropriately. 6–7.5 min: examine chest, lungs and peripheral oedema; reposition respectfully. 7.5–9 min: present findings, explain prosthetic-valve concern, anticoagulant check, investigations and escalation.
sections.5. Marking grid: Nine independent rows scored 0–2 each = 18 marks maximum. Descriptors: 0 = Fail, 1 = Borderline, 2 = Pass; High-performance describes additional quality within an already safe 2-mark response (no additional points). Overall examiner judgement remains separate. Do not present this as the official MRCS mark scheme. Row Domain Fail (0) Borderline (1) Pass (2) High-performance (within 2) R1 Introduction / consent No identity, consent or comfort check. Introduces self but minimal explanation. Core surgical trainee; permission, positioning, chaperone offer where appropriate. Sensitive pacing; anticipates discomfort and checks tolerance. R2 General / hands / pulse Fails to assess perfusion or pulse. Checks pulse only. Observes distress, hands/perfusion; measures pulse rate and rhythm; asks for BP. Connects pulse rhythm to postoperative arrhythmia risk without overdiagnosis. R3 Face / neck Omits neck/JVP entirely. Limited face/neck examination. Checks conjunctival pallor, neck/JVP and carotid pulse one side at a time if indicated. Explains significance and avoids unsafe simultaneous carotid palpation. R4 Surgical scars Misses obvious midline sternotomy and leg-harvest scar. Identifies ster
sections.6. Three performances — word-for-word: Examiner staging: each script is one alternative 9-minute attempt in the SAME simulated scenario. Examiner supplies the same examination findings only when the relevant manoeuvre is performed or requested. Stage directions are not spoken dialogue. FAIL — incomplete, unsafe assessment Candidate [R1]: Hello, I’m one of the doctors. I need to listen to your heart. Patient: All right. Candidate [R2]: Are you breathless at the moment? Patient: No, only when I walk up the hill near my home. Candidate [R2]: Let me feel your wrist. Examiner: Pulse 88 per minute, regular. BP 132/76 mmHg if requested. Candidate [R4]: I can see your chest scar, so you must have had a bypass. Patient: I had a heart valve replaced too. Candidate [R6]: I’ll listen at the front of the chest. Examiner: Metallic closing click and an ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge. Candidate [R6]: That click means the valve is fine, so I would not investigate it. Examiner: Any other examination? Candidate [R7]: No, I have finished. Examiner: The patient takes warfarin, but asks whether a newer blood thinner would save INR checks. Candidate [R9]: Yes, apixaban would be more convenient; I would change it. Exa
sections.7. Critical fails: R8: Reassures or discharges despite new exertional dyspnoea and murmur without considering echo or specialist assessment; risks missed valve deterioration. R9: Recommends a DOAC (apixaban/rivaroxaban etc.) instead of warfarin for a mechanical valve; risks prosthetic valve thrombosis. R2/R8: Ignores new syncope, chest pain or haemodynamic collapse if disclosed; risks delayed emergency care. R6/R8: States the prosthesis is definitely functioning normally solely because a click is audible; risks missed obstructive or regurgitant dysfunction.
sections.8. Recovery lines: “I must correct that: an audible prosthetic click does not rule out dysfunction. The change in symptoms warrants echo and valve-team review.” “I need to retract my suggestion of a newer anticoagulant. A mechanical valve should not be switched to a DOAC; I would confirm the anticoagulation plan with the valve service.”

stations.title: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

sections.preamble: B2-296 | Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge • Draft for specialist review • 13 October 2026 Teaching and simulated assessment only. Not an official MRCS marking scheme. Independent paediatric surgical / neonatal specialist sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to advise a neonatal team about a term baby, 3 hours old, who has repeated frothing at the mouth, cough and desaturation when feeding. A nasogastric tube could not be advanced beyond approximately 10–12 cm from the nostril. Explain your working diagnosis, interpret the supplied investigation, outline immediate management, associated anomalies and definitive treatment. You are not expected to perform a procedure.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight-minute applied knowledge station. Assess prioritisation of airway/aspiration, recognition of oesophageal atresia (OA) ± distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF), investigation, VACTERL screening, specialist transfer and surgery. Do not provide imaging: findings are narrated. Candidate may request observations and film report. Prompt neutrally after 90 seconds if silent.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor. Examiner supplies neonatal case findings on request. If the candidate asks for a parent discussion, examiner asks for a short understandable explanation and emphasises uncertainty about operative timing until specialist assessment.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Initial observations: Term baby, HR 155/min, RR 64/min, SpO2 93% in air, intermittent cough and froth; abdomen mildly distended; oral secretions pool. Recognise aspiration risk and respiratory monitoring. Tube/X-ray description: A soft NG tube stops in the upper chest. A plain chest/abdominal film described in words shows its tip curled within the upper oesophageal pouch, with gas visible in stomach and bowel. Infer OA with likely distal TOF; distal air supports a fistula, but classification needs specialist confirmation. If asked about alternative diagnoses: Consider isolated OA (typically gasless abdomen), H-type fistula (oesophagus continuous; NG passage often possible), upper airway disease and structural swallowing disorders; case strongly favours OA/TOF. If asked for antenatal clues: Polyhydramnios and a small/absent stomach bubble may raise suspicion; many cases are only detected after birth. If asked for associated anomalies: Check VACTERL: vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal, limb; also consider CHARGE and other syndromic associations; check anus and limbs, request echocardiogram and renal/other imaging in specialist pathway. Curveball at minute 5: Th
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and diagnosis Attributes frothing to reflux and misses the obstructed NG tube. Identifies OA with probable distal TOF from frothing, failed tube and abdominal gas. Explains upper pouch and distal tracheal connection, distinguishes evidence from confirmed anatomy. Immediate safety Allows oral feeds or milk trial despite coughing. Stops oral feeding, keeps nil by mouth and recognises aspiration hazard. Explicitly communicates NBM to bedside team and documents safe handling of secretions. Stabilisation Offers no monitoring or neonatal resuscitation assessment. Calls neonatal senior; assesses ABC, oxygenation, glucose, temperature and perfusion; establishes IV access and fluids. Balances oxygenation/ventilation with fistula-related gastric distension risk and escalates deterioration promptly. Pouch management Repeatedly forces NG tube or ignores pooled saliva. Requests Replogle/upper-pouch suction by neonatal team, with positioning per neonatal pathway. Emphasises gentle continuous drainage and checks suction effectiveness during transfer. Investigation interpretation Claims bowel gas excludes oesophageal atresia. Interprets coiled upper tu
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: CF1. Gives oral feeds or a contrast swallow trial despite active choking/frothing in suspected OA. CF2. Forces a feeding tube repeatedly past resistance, risking injury to the upper pouch. CF3. Fails to institute NBM and secretion drainage or fails to escalate to neonatal/surgical specialist care. CF4. Ignores deteriorating breathing or abdominal distension and neither summons immediate senior airway help nor initiates resuscitation.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: A junior proposes CPAP because SpO2 has dropped to 86% and the abdomen is becoming more distended. Expected: stop feeds, urgently call neonatology/anaesthesia and paediatric surgery, provide appropriate oxygen/resuscitation; explain that positive pressure with distal TOF can distend the stomach. Do not categorically withhold necessary ventilation; airway support must be expert-led.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. After overlooking suction: “I missed the immediate aspiration risk: keep the baby nil by mouth and start gentle upper-pouch drainage with a Replogle tube now.” 2. After calling the film non-diagnostic: “A tube curled in the upper pouch confirms obstruction; abdominal gas makes a distal fistula likely.” 3. After proposing routine CPAP: “I need senior neonatal airway support urgently, because positive pressure can inflate the stomach through a distal fistula.”

stations.title: Jaundice in a 6-week-old baby

sections.preamble: B2-297 | Jaundice in a 6-week-old baby AMaC MRCS Part B • Data interpretation • Draft for specialist review • 13 October 2026 Teaching and simulated assessment only. Not an official MRCS marking scheme. Independent paediatric surgical / neonatal specialist sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing results for a term infant aged 6 weeks, referred with persistent jaundice. The baby is feeding reasonably well but the parents report pale putty-coloured stools and dark urine. Serum total bilirubin is 132 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 88 micromol/L; INR is 1.5. Interpret the results, explain the differential, immediate investigations and referral, and how suspected biliary atresia is treated.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight-minute data interpretation station. Candidate must recognise conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia/cholestasis, treat pale stool/dark urine as red flags for biliary obstruction, urgently contact paediatric hepatology / tertiary liver service, assess synthetic function and describe time-sensitive Kasai portoenterostomy. Do not reward routine phototherapy for conjugated disease.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Parent prompt optional: “She looks well—could it just be breast milk jaundice? Can we wait until the next health-visitor check?” Parent is worried and needs an honest, non-alarming explanation. No actor necessary for the main data task.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Laboratory data: Age 42 days; total bilirubin 132 micromol/L, conjugated 88 micromol/L (~67%); ALT 95 U/L, GGT 410 U/L, INR 1.5, glucose 4.4 mmol/L. Recognise pathologic conjugated jaundice and potential vitamin K deficiency/coagulopathy. History and examination if requested: Term infant, growing, no fever. Stools reported grey-white for two weeks, urine stains nappies. Firm liver edge 3 cm below right costal margin; no obvious dehydration. Assess growth, feeding, bleeding/bruising, fever and sepsis. Referral question: Candidate should arrange same-day urgent paediatric/hepatology assessment and contact a designated specialist liver unit directly; investigations must not delay referral. Investigation prompt: Confirm fractionated bilirubin; FBC, liver panel, GGT, albumin, PT/INR, glucose, metabolic screen review; consider cultures if febrile/ill, endocrine/metabolic evaluation; ultrasound by specialist service. Ultrasound alone does not exclude biliary atresia. Diagnosis confirmation: Specialists may arrange further hepatobiliary evaluation and operative cholangiography; biliary atresia should be excluded urgently rather than awaiting serial local tests. Surgery question: Kasai port
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Bilirubin interpretation Calls bilirubin physiological without checking conjugated fraction. Identifies conjugated fraction 88/132 micromol/L as abnormal neonatal cholestasis. Calculates fraction ~67% and links it to hepatobiliary disease, not benign unconjugated jaundice. Red-flag recognition Ignores acholic stools and urine staining. Recognises pale stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly as biliary obstruction red flags. Explains why a well-looking baby can still have time-critical biliary atresia. Urgency and referral Books routine follow-up in weeks. Requests urgent same-day paediatric/hepatology and designated liver-centre discussion. Explicitly says local imaging/blood work will not delay specialist contact. Clinical assessment Asks only about jaundice colour. Assesses feeding, growth, stool/urine, fever, bleeding; examines hydration, liver, spleen and sepsis features. Adds birth/newborn screening, family/infection/drug/metabolic history and documents stool colour. Initial investigations Relies on un-fractionated bilirubin alone. Orders FBC, fractionated bilirubin, LFT/GGT, albumin, INR/PT, glucose and newborn-screen review. Plans specialist-dir
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: CF1. Dismisses predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia as physiological or breast-milk jaundice and recommends routine review only. CF2. Fails to escalate pale/acholic stools with conjugated jaundice urgently to paediatric hepatology / specialist liver service. CF3. Proposes phototherapy as definitive management for suspected biliary obstruction and sends the baby home without referral. CF4. Ignores abnormal INR or clinical bleeding and omits assessment/escalation of coagulopathy in a cholestatic infant.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The mother asks: “If it is breast-milk jaundice, can I carry on breastfeeding and come back in two weeks?” Expected: support feeding with paediatric oversight, explain benign breast-milk jaundice is predominantly unconjugated, whereas an 88 micromol/L conjugated fraction plus acholic stool requires immediate referral today; do not wait for further community monitoring.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. After initially reassuring: “I need to correct that: most of this bilirubin is conjugated, which is not normal breast-milk jaundice.” 2. After suggesting ultrasound before referral: “I will contact the specialist liver service today; imaging must not delay that conversation.” 3. After focusing only on surgery: “The INR is raised, so I will assess bleeding risk and ask paediatrics to address possible vitamin K deficiency immediately.”

stations.title: Hypospadias

sections.preamble: B2-298 — Hypospadias AMaC MRCS Part B | Original training station | 13 October 2026 | Draft for clinical editorial sign-off
sections.1. Station identity and purpose: Paediatric urology | structured genital assessment and parent counselling | 9-minute simulated encounter; no examination of a real child without appropriate safeguards.
sections.2. Candidate brief: You are the CT2 in paediatric surgical clinic. Parents of a 3-month-old boy have been told his urethral opening is not at the tip. Take a focused history, explain the examination you would perform, give your working diagnosis, and explain safe next steps to the parent. A genital model/photo is available; do not perform a procedure.
sections.3. Simulated parent / examiner briefing: Parent: concerned about future urination, fertility and whether circumcision is safe. Baby feeds and voids well, no febrile illness. Model shows subcoronal meatus, dorsal hooded foreskin, no obvious severe chordee; both testes are palpable in scrotum. Reveal the model findings only when candidate asks to inspect genitalia. If candidate asks about urinary stream: downward/splayed stream. Curveball disclosed on cue.
sections.4. Focused history — expected content: Confirm onset since birth; wet nappies, stream direction/spraying, straining or poor output, UTIs and fever. Pregnancy/birth, any antenatal anomalies, family history of hypospadias, associated anomalies or prior genital procedures. Ask specifically if circumcision is planned, and what the parent fears about future function and appearance.
sections.5. Examination — expected demonstration: Explain chaperone/parent presence, consent, warmth and gentle inspection of model; respect child’s dignity. Locate and describe ventral meatus relative to glans and shaft, calibre and shape; inspect dorsal preputial hood and ventral foreskin deficiency; assess suspected curvature without forcibly straightening. Assess glans size, shaft length, scrotal configuration and both testicular positions; do not retract a non-retractile foreskin forcibly or instrument the urethra.
sections.6. Interpretation and applied anatomy /: Embryological failure of normal ventral urethral tubularisation/closure produces a ventrally displaced meatus and often dorsal hooded prepuce. Classify distal (glanular/subcoronal), midshaft, or proximal (penoscrotal/scrotal/perineal); meatal level alone does not determine severity—curvature and urethral plate matter. Isolated distal hypospadias with both descended testes is usually a clinical diagnosis; proximal lesion or undescended testes raises the need to assess for differences of sex development (DSD).
sections.7. Differential diagnoses and discrimina: Hypospadias: ventral ectopic meatus with dorsal hood. Epispadias: dorsal meatus, different bladder-exstrophy association. Megameatus intact prepuce variant may be concealed; congenital ventral curvature can occur with normally sited meatus.
sections.8. Investigations and justification: Isolated distal hypospadias generally needs no routine renal ultrasound, blood tests or karyotype; arrange paediatric urology clinical assessment. If bilateral undescended testes, atypical genitalia or severe proximal phenotype: urgent specialist multidisciplinary endocrine/genetic evaluation for DSD; do not assign specific tests without specialist coordination. Document urinary stream and consider UTI work-up only with symptoms, not automatically.

stations.title: Abdominal Mass in a Toddler
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-299 Abdominal Mass in a Toddler

sections.preamble: B2-299 — Abdominal Mass in a Toddler AMaC MRCS Part B | Original training station | 13 October 2026 | Draft for clinical editorial sign-off
sections.1. Station identity and purpose: Paediatric surgery / oncology | recognition of possible childhood cancer and urgent referral | 9-minute parent encounter.
sections.2. Candidate brief: You are the surgical CT2 seeing a 2-year-old child whose parent noticed a painless abdominal fullness while bathing. Take a focused history and describe a safe examination. Interpret a supplied examination finding and explain your immediate plan to the parent. Do not perform repetitive deep abdominal palpation.
sections.3. Simulated parent / examiner briefing: Parent: mass first noticed yesterday; child playful, eating well, normal stools; no fever or trauma. On examiner card: well child, stable vitals, firm left-sided flank mass, no peritonism, palpable separately from liver. No haematuria noted by parent. BP not yet recorded. Parent asks whether it is constipation. Curveball on cue: repeat BP is elevated for age.
sections.4. Focused history — expected content: Onset, growth, pain, trauma, fever, night sweats, lethargy, weight/appetite change, vomiting, constipation, urinary frequency or haematuria. Ask systemic and metastatic clues: bone pain/limp, bruising or periorbital discoloration; developmental history and any congenital anomalies. Family history of malignancy / predisposition, prior imaging, and parent’s own assessment or persistent concern.
sections.5. Examination — expected demonstration: Hand hygiene; age-appropriate explanation and parent present; observe child before touching; general appearance, hydration, pallor, bruising, lymph nodes and respiratory status. Record complete paediatric observations including blood pressure; inspect distension and visible veins; auscultate as indicated and gently palpate once to localize size, site, tenderness and mobility. Check hepatosplenomegaly and possible bladder distension with gentle assessment; avoid repeated vigorous palpation of a suspected renal tumour; complete appropriate systemic examination.
sections.6. Interpretation and applied anatomy /: A painless unilateral flank mass in a toddler raises Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma), but cannot be diagnosed by palpation alone. Neuroblastoma can arise in adrenal/sympathetic tissue and may have constitutional symptoms, bone pain or periorbital bruising; both require specialist evaluation. Renal masses can cause haematuria or hypertension; normal behaviour does not exclude malignancy.
sections.7. Differential diagnoses and discrimina: Wilms tumour — young child, often painless renal/flank mass ± haematuria / hypertension. Neuroblastoma — adrenal/retroperitoneal origin, possible systemic or metastatic signs. Hydronephrosis/multicystic kidney, renal cyst, constipation/faecal loading, hepatosplenomegaly, bladder distension or other intra-abdominal pathology.
sections.8. Investigations and justification: Arrange urgent same-day paediatric assessment and paediatric abdominal ultrasound via specialist pathway; measure blood pressure and urinalysis (blood) and obtain paediatric-directed blood tests such as FBC, renal function when indicated. If a suspicious mass is confirmed, specialist team organises further cross-sectional imaging/staging and oncology investigations; possible urinary catecholamine metabolites when neuroblastoma considered. Do not biopsy, aspirate, or organise unplanned surgery in the referring setting; potential Wilms management is protocol-driven at a specialist centre.

stations.title: Painless rectal bleeding in a child
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-300 Painless rectal bleeding in a child

sections.preamble: B2-300 — Painless rectal bleeding in a child AMaC MRCS Part B | History taking | Draft for clinical sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Station purpose and tested competence: Elicit a focused history, recognise significant bleeding and prioritise Meckel diverticulum without overlooking alternatives.
sections.2. Candidate instructions (8-minute enco: You are the surgical registrar in a paediatric assessment unit. A parent brings their otherwise well 3-year-old child after two episodes of dark-red blood passed per rectum. Take a focused history, explain differentials and outline safe investigation and management. No intimate examination is required.
sections.3. Examiner brief and standardised infor: Give the candidate only the information requested. Mark clinical reasoning and safety, not rote list length. Do not disclose the diagnosis or legal resolution initially.
sections.4. Parent / actor brief: Parent: child playful between episodes; two moderate episodes of maroon blood in toilet today, no pain or constipation, no fever or diarrhoea, no weight loss; no relevant medicines; worried about cancer. If asked about new symptoms: no vomiting or lethargy. If curveball given: child becomes pale and sleepy in waiting room.
sections.2. Which features of the bleeding and st: 3. What associated history separates a fissure, polyp, intussusception and Meckel diverticulum? 4. Which examination would you request, and what would you avoid as routine? 5. Give a prioritised differential for painless bleeding. 6. Which blood tests and imaging/nuclear study would you request, and what does the scan detect? 7. How would you manage confirmed symptomatic Meckel diverticulum? 8. What would you do if the child became pale and tachycardic while awaiting tests?
sections.6. Expected clinical reasoning and actio: Checks activity, colour, vital signs, bleeding rate, hydration and red flags; requests immediate assessment if unwell. Elicits age of onset, volume, frequency, bright/dark blood, relation to stool, clots and pain. Asks constipation, painful defecation, diarrhoea, fever, abdominal pain, bilious vomiting and weight change. Reviews prior episodes, growth, surgery, family GI disorders, medication and bleeding history. Requests observations, hydration, abdomen and gentle external perianal inspection with parent/child assent. Prioritises Meckel diverticulum with juvenile polyp, fissure, infection and intussusception considered by pattern. Chooses FBC and targeted blood tests, discusses paediatric surgical review and technetium-99m pertechnetate Meckel scan. Arranges timely paediatric/surgical assessment; resuscitates and escalates if heavy bleeding; discusses surgery if symptomatic Meckel confirmed. Explains likely cause, tests, uncertainty and when parents should seek emergency care.

stations.title: Parents disagree about consent for their childs surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-301 Parents disagree about consent for their childs surgery

sections.preamble: B2-301 — Parents disagree about consent for their childs surgery AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / ethics | Draft for clinical sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Station purpose and tested competence: Demonstrate legally literate, child-centred consent when adults with parental responsibility disagree; distinguish emergency from elective treatment.
sections.2. Candidate instructions (8-minute enco: You are the surgical registrar. A 7-year-old child has symptomatic gallstones with recurrent biliary colic, but no sepsis or acute obstruction. The consultant recommends elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. One parent agrees; the other refuses. Speak with the two parents about how a safe decision will be made.
sections.3. Examiner brief and standardised infor: Give the candidate only the information requested. Mark clinical reasoning and safety, not rote list length. Do not disclose the diagnosis or legal resolution initially.
sections.4. Parent / actor brief: Parent A wants the operation and says another attack could be dangerous. Parent B fears anaesthetic death and believes diet will fix it. Both have parental responsibility. Child says they are frightened of hospital but would like the pain to stop. If asked, this is not an emergency and surgery can safely be delayed for multidisciplinary resolution. Curveball: Parent A asks you to operate tomorrow without telling Parent B.
sections.1. How would you establish whether this: 2. What are the child’s views and how do age and competence affect your discussion?
sections.3. How do you verify parental responsibi: 4. How would you explore each parent’s disagreement constructively? 5. What information about proposed surgery, alternatives and not operating is needed? 6. Can one parent’s consent usually suffice, and what changes when strong opposition is known? 7. When and how should consultants, legal colleagues or the court be involved? 8. What changes if delay will cause death or serious deterioration?
sections.6. Expected clinical reasoning and actio: Establishes diagnosis, proposed operation, urgency and consequences of delay. Asks age, understanding and wishes; considers competence/capacity appropriate to age. Confirms who has parental responsibility and documents who agrees or objects. Invites each parent’s concerns and listens without judgement. Describes diagnosis, benefit, material risks, alternatives and risks of no surgery in comprehensible language. Notes one person with parental responsibility normally suffices, but significant unresolved disagreement needs senior and legal escalation. Bases recommendations on child’s best interests; seeks consultant, MDT and trust legal advice if dispute persists. Explains emergency treatment can proceed to save life/prevent serious deterioration when consent cannot be obtained. Maintains respectful impartiality and documents discussions, capacity/competence, responsibility and agreed plan.

stations.title: Paediatric Fasting and Anaesthesia
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-302 Paediatric Fasting and Anaesthesia

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-302 Fasting and anaesthesia rules for children DRAFT — MRCS Part B training station • Not an official intercollegiate mark scheme • Clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Station identity and objectives: Type: Applied knowledge / perioperative safety Target: MRCS Part B level; clinical prioritisation, communication and surgical judgement. Time: 8 minutes; no image assets; verbal results only.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar preparing a 4-year-old child for an elective inguinal hernia repair. The parent asks why breakfast is prohibited, whether water is allowed and what happens if the child eats. Explain the fasting plan, manage new information from the parent and answer examiner questions. You do not prescribe an anaesthetic technique.
sections.3. Examiner brief and disclosures: Elective child, 4 years, otherwise well, booked for morning general anaesthesia. No history of reflux or swallowing dysfunction; assessment and anaesthetic plan pending. Judge safety, distinction between clear fluids and food, and correct escalation. Do not penalise candidate for avoiding an invented fixed theatre time.
sections.4. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “My child is thirsty. We were told nil by mouth since midnight.” Initially reports last solid meal yesterday at 19:00. If asked, says child had water this morning. At curveball, admit child ate half a biscuit at 08:15. Concerned surgery will be cancelled. Be worried, not confrontational.
sections.5. Examiner prompts — eight distinct tes: 1. State the purpose of pre-operative fasting and why unnecessarily prolonged fasting is undesirable. 2. Give the current APAGBI fasting categories for a low-risk elective child, including the clear-fluid approach. 3. Explain what counts as a clear fluid versus milk, formula and solids. 4. Identify the exclusions or risk factors requiring anaesthetic individualisation. 5. Describe what you check and record about the child’s actual last intake. 6. Manage disclosure of a biscuit after the scheduled fasting cut-off. 7. Explain how emergency surgery in a non-fasted child differs from elective surgery. 8. Give an empathetic parent explanation, safety-net and anaesthetic handover.
sections.6. Nine-domain critical-weighted marking: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial framing and priorities Calls this a starvation rule, ignoring aspiration or comfort. Explains fasting mitigates pulmonary aspiration while avoiding dehydration/thirst. Balances rare aspiration risk against thirst, distress and unnecessary delays; aligns with anaesthetic plan. Focused data gathering Never establishes last food/drink times or constituents. Asks exact time, quantity and type of all food, milk and fluids. Reconciles parent, notes and ward chart; clarifies ambiguity such as juice with pulp. Clinical interpretation Calls milk clear, or insists every child fasts from midnight. Distinguishes clear fluids from formula/milk/solids and states correct categories. Applies APAGBI November 2025 approach to actual case without treating local policies as universal. Risk and red flags Misses aspiration-risk factors or assumes elective protocol fits all. Screens reflux/motility disorder, airway concerns and urgent surgery. Also recognises neurodisability, severe obesity, GLP-1 therapy and extreme anxiety as reasons for individual review. Investigations / checks Proceeds without checking reported biscuit or dismisses its timing. Checks last in
sections.7. Four station-specific critical fails: Critical fail 1: Treats milk/formula or biscuit as clear fluid and authorises immediate routine elective induction despite incomplete fasting. Critical fail 2: Conceals or fails to convey the newly disclosed 08:15 biscuit to the anaesthetist. Critical fail 3: Delays genuinely life-saving emergency surgery purely to achieve an elective fasting interval without senior discussion. Critical fail 4: Issues a definitive proceed/cancel decision outside remit instead of referring the aspiration-risk decision to anaesthesia.
sections.8. Single realistic curveball: Parent reveals that the child ate half a biscuit at 08:15 after the ward confirmed fasting. Candidate should thank them, stop any assumption of adequate elective fasting, document details, contact anaesthetist and explain an individual plan, without blaming the family.

stations.title: Paediatric Trauma Differences
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-303 Paediatric Trauma Differences

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-303 Trauma in a child: what is different? DRAFT — MRCS Part B training station • Not an official intercollegiate mark scheme • Clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Station identity and objectives: Type: Applied knowledge / paediatric major trauma Target: MRCS Part B level; clinical prioritisation, communication and surgical judgement. Time: 8 minutes; no image assets; verbal results only.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar attending the resuscitation room after a 6-year-old child has been struck by a vehicle. The child is alert but pale and tachycardic, with abdominal tenderness. Explain the age-specific assessment, early resuscitation and definitive pathway to the examiner; the child’s observations and investigation results will be supplied verbally.
sections.3. Examiner brief and disclosures: Six-year-old; estimated/actual weight not yet available. HR 145/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 30/min, SpO₂ 97% room air, GCS 15. Bruising over left abdomen, no external bleeding; concern about splenic injury. Do not infer absence of shock from preserved systolic BP. Candidate must identify haemorrhage as priority. On request, provide venous gas lactate 4.5 mmol/L, Hb 104 g/L (single early Hb does not exclude bleeding).
sections.4. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent: “They said blood pressure is normal, so is she fine? Will you have to remove her spleen?” At curveball, disclose that injury account from accompanying adult changes significantly; child quietly says they were hit at home yesterday too.
sections.5. Examiner prompts — eight distinct tes: 1. Identify paediatric anatomical and physiological differences relevant to major trauma. 2. Lead the initial systematic trauma assessment, including early senior and paediatric trauma-team involvement. 3. Interpret the observations and explain compensated shock with preserved blood pressure. 4. Describe weight-based vascular access and haemorrhage resuscitation, distinguishing active bleeding from non-haemorrhagic shock. 5. Choose age-appropriate imaging for possible intra-abdominal injury and explain why a negative FAST does not exclude injury. 6. Explain non-operative splenic management versus indications for urgent intervention. 7. Address pain, hypothermia, reassessment and safe transfer to a paediatric major trauma service. 8. Handle safeguarding concerns, neutral documentation and child-centred family communication.
sections.6. Nine-domain critical-weighted marking: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial framing and priorities Treats child as a small adult and misses hidden haemorrhage. States paediatric physiology: preserved BP until late shock; higher surface-area heat loss. Explains flexible ribs, proportionately larger head, age-related vital signs and narrow physiological reserve. Focused data gathering Fails structured survey or senior escalation. Performs cABCDE with cervical-spine protection, seeks paediatric major trauma help. Coordinates targeted tasks and repeats primary survey whenever physiology changes. Clinical interpretation Calls 92 systolic reassuring and ignores tachycardia/skin/lactate. Recognises pallor, tachycardia and abdominal signs as possible compensated shock. Integrates perfusion, capillary refill, mental state, serial trends and lactate despite early Hb. Risk and red flags Uses adult volumes without weight or gives large unmonitored boluses. Seeks measured/estimated weight, obtains IV/IO access, activates paediatric haemorrhage protocol if active bleeding. Prioritises warmed weight-based blood components and minimises crystalloids in active haemorrhage per NICE NG39. Investigations / checks Orders indiscriminate
sections.7. Four station-specific critical fails: Critical fail 1: Reassures and discharges/defers reassessment solely because a child has a preserved blood pressure despite signs of haemorrhagic shock. Critical fail 2: Gives repeated large crystalloid boluses for suspected active internal haemorrhage instead of activating a weight-based paediatric major haemorrhage pathway. Critical fail 3: Delays urgent haemorrhage control or transfer for unnecessary imaging in an unstable child. Critical fail 4: Fails to act on credible disclosure of possible inflicted injury or leaves the child exposed to immediate safeguarding danger.
sections.8. Single realistic curveball: During the assessment, the accompanying adult changes the account and the child says quietly, “Someone hit me at home yesterday.” The candidate prioritises resuscitation, records the child’s words verbatim, avoids leading questions and raises an immediate safeguarding referral via the senior/paediatric team.

stations.title: Ovarian Torsion in a Girl
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-305 Ovarian Torsion in a Girl

near_match.title: Ovarian Torsion / A Reassuring Doppler Does Not Exclude It

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-305 Ovarian torsion in a girl DRAFT — MRCS Part B training station | Not an official intercollegiate mark scheme | Independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Station identity and objectives: Type: Critical care / paediatric surgical emergency Eight-minute candidate performance; written or verbal findings only; no images or intimate examination on an actor. Target: MRCS Part B safe prioritisation, clinical judgement, examination and family communication.
sections.2. Candidate instructions: You are the surgical registrar in paediatric emergency receiving a 13-year-old girl with sudden right lower abdominal pain and vomiting. Explain your initial assessment, differential, ultrasound interpretation and definitive management. You must discuss the operative consent approach with the parent and adolescent.
sections.3. Examiner brief and disclosures: 13-year-old; six hours of acute right iliac fossa pain and repeated vomiting. HR 112, BP 108/65, afebrile. Pelvic transabdominal ultrasound shows enlarged oedematous right ovary and peripheral follicles; Doppler reports preserved arterial flow. Pregnancy status not yet known. The key is that preserved Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion; coordinate urgent gynaecology/paediatric surgical laparoscopy.
sections.4. Parent / patient actor brief: Parent fears “surgery will mean removing the ovary and she cannot have children.” Girl is scared of intimate examination. Curveball: ultrasound sonographer phones and says normal arterial Doppler excludes torsion, and parent asks to go home.
sections.5. Eight examiner prompts: 1. Identify initial priorities, analgesia, pregnancy possibility and resuscitation needs. 2. Obtain sensitive targeted history including onset, intermittent episodes, periods and potential pregnancy. 3. Describe child-centred examination and the role of consent, assent and chaperones. 4. Formulate differential including appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy and urinary pathology. 5. Interpret ultrasound appearances and limitations of preserved Doppler flow. 6. Decide urgency and surgical pathway without delaying for unnecessary tests. 7. Describe fertility-preserving laparoscopic detorsion and consent conversation. 8. Respond to false reassurance from sonographer and arrange team escalation, documentation and follow-up.
sections.6. Nine-domain critical-weighted marking: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial framing and priorities Mislabels as simple appendicitis/gastroenteritis without torsion. Prioritises torsion as time-critical ovarian ischaemia in adolescent with unilateral pain/vomiting. Arranges early simultaneous gynae and paediatric surgical discussion rather than sequential delays. Focused data gathering Omits menstruation/pregnancy or treats child insensitively. Asks onset, episodic pain, vomiting, periods, sexual/pregnancy possibility sensitively, urinary/bowel symptoms. Offers time alone with adolescent to discuss confidentiality and pregnancy risk without assumptions. Clinical interpretation Undertakes unwanted intimate exam or ignores consent. Assesses observations, hydration, abdominal guarding; explains chaperone and no routine intimate exam without indication/consent. Uses assent, trauma-informed language and recognises examination cannot exclude torsion. Risk and red flags Overlooks ectopic pregnancy or peritonitis. Considers appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy if possible, ruptured cyst, UTI and renal colic. Separates immediate haemodynamic instability/bleeding from stable but ischaemia-threatened ovary. Investigations / checks
sections.7. Four station-specific critical fails: Critical fail 1: Discharges or delays surgery solely because the ultrasound reports preserved ovarian arterial Doppler flow. Critical fail 2: Fails to consider or urgently test pregnancy when biologically possible, missing a potential ectopic pregnancy. Critical fail 3: Fails to escalate suspected torsion for time-sensitive specialist surgical assessment despite convincing symptoms and imaging. Critical fail 4: Recommends routine removal of a dusky but structurally salvageable torsed ovary rather than attempting preservation.
sections.8. One realistic curveball: Sonographer reassures parent that preserved Doppler arterial flow excludes torsion and parent requests discharge. Candidate must explain Doppler limitations and secure urgent gynaecology/paediatric surgical consultation without blaming colleague.

stations.title: Pectus Excavatum

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | WORKING STATION B2-306 — Pectus Excavatum: Parents Asking About Surgery Communication • 8-minute structured station • 13 October 2026 • Draft for independent clinical review
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar in a specialist chest-wall clinic. Speak with the young person and their parents, assess their concerns, explain investigation and treatment choices, and agree a safe plan. Do not promise an operation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight-minute simulated conversation. Award credit for addressing the adolescent directly and separating psychological impact, symptoms and objective cardiopulmonary impairment. Reveal information only if sought.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Teenager: “I hate changing for PE; I do get breathless when I run.” Parent: “Isn’t the Nuss operation straightforward? We want a date.” No syncope or current chest pain. Family has not received formal cardiopulmonary evaluation.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Opening and autonomy: Invite the teenager’s account first; establish what they want; explore parental expectations and confidentiality within appropriate limits. 2. Symptoms: Ask exertional breathlessness, chest pain, exercise tolerance, palpitations, syncope, progression and any asthma or other causes. 3. Psychosocial impact: Explore body-image distress, bullying, avoidance of sport/swimming, mood, and impact on daily function without dismissing cosmetic concerns. 4. Examination and differential: Describe inspection of chest-wall depression/asymmetry, posture/scoliosis, respiratory and cardiac findings; consider syndromic features such as Marfan phenotype when indicated. 5. Investigations: Offer specialist assessment, echocardiography and lung-function/exercise assessment when clinically indicated; quantify anatomy with specialist imaging only if useful to planning, mindful of radiation. 6. Options: Explain observation/support for mild cases; specialist physiotherapy/posture and psychological support where suitable; discuss Nuss bar or open Ravitch reconstruction based on individual assessment. 7. Consent and risks: Explain Nuss bar insertion behind sternum, later removal, pain
sections.5. Clinical frame and decision points: A 15-year-old and both parents request surgery for a sunken chest. The teenager avoids swimming and sometimes becomes breathless running. Expected reasoning: distinguish the key clinical risks, identify the action that changes management, and apply the relevant UK guidance to this specific patient.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Person-centred opening Talks over teenager and assumes parental cosmetic preference Addresses teenager and asks their treatment goals Explores teenager–parent differences respectfully and negotiates shared agenda Focused symptoms Does not ask about exertional limitation or syncope Asks breathlessness, chest discomfort, exercise limits, syncope Explores progression and alternative contributors to breathlessness Psychosocial understanding Dismisses concern as merely cosmetic Asks body image, bullying, school/sport impact Validates emotional burden and identifies support needs without pathologising Examination and context Offers surgery without assessment Describes chest-wall, cardiorespiratory and spinal assessment Recognises syndromic clues and tailored wider evaluation Investigations Claims Haller index alone dictates surgery Outlines specialist imaging where needed and cardiopulmonary testing Explains why anatomy and functional/psychological burden jointly inform decisions Treatment choices Presents Nuss as mandatory Discusses observation/support and Nuss versus Ravitch Personalises options, age, symptom burden and specialist expertise Risk disclo
sections.7. Critical fails — four specific safety: Promises an operation or assured cure without specialist evaluation and informed consent. Fails to mention potentially serious intrathoracic injury when specifically counselling on Nuss risks. Dismisses severe exertional syncope or progressive cardiac symptoms as cosmetic without urgent assessment. Overrides the adolescent’s expressed concerns and treats parents’ preference alone as sufficient consent.
sections.8. Curveball: The teenager says privately, “I do not want surgery, but Dad booked this appointment.” Candidate should stop any assumed surgical pathway, explore concerns and capacity, offer private discussion and document the adolescent’s wishes.

stations.title: Preoperative Tests

near_match.title: Preoperative counselling for a stoma

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS PART B | WORKING STATION B2-307 — Preoperative Assessment: Which Tests? Applied knowledge • 8-minute structured station • 13 October 2026 • Draft for independent clinical review
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar at preoperative assessment. Explain how to select investigations using NICE NG45, ASA physical status and surgery grade. State which tests are or are not routinely indicated and how abnormal results change the plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight-minute oral applied-knowledge station. Require explicit recognition that NICE NG45 is for patients over 16 having elective operations and excludes cardiothoracic and neurosurgical procedures. Do not treat an ASA label as a substitute for clinical judgement.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner gives cases: A, healthy 25-year-old ASA I having minor skin lesion removal; B, adult ASA II with diabetes having intermediate inguinal hernia repair; C, 68-year-old with CKD/diabetes undergoing major colonic surgery. Ask “Should everyone have ECG, chest X-ray and coagulation screen?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Stratification: Define ASA I–IV and classify minor, intermediate and major/complex surgery; clarify NG45 population and exclusions. 2. History and function: Review comorbidities, exercise tolerance, symptoms, anaesthetic problems, bleeding history, medication and anticoagulants, CKD/AKI risk, recent test results. 3. Minor case: Healthy ASA I minor skin excision: no routine FBC, renal, coagulation, ECG or lung function tests; justify targeted exceptions. 4. Intermediate case: ASA II with diabetes, inguinal hernia: kidney tests if AKI risk; consider ECG for cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity; FBC not routinely; avoid universal coagulation screen. 5. Major case: Colonic resection: FBC for all; kidney function for ASA II–IV and consider for ASA I at AKI risk; ECG for ASA II–IV and consider if ASA I over 65 without recent ECG. 6. Special tests: Do not routinely request chest radiograph, resting echocardiogram or lung-function tests; perform directed testing if relevant findings; HbA1c if diabetes and no result in last 3 months. 7. Bleeding and medication: Coagulation not routine in healthy adults; consider with chronic liver disease for major surgery; anticoagulant changes
sections.5. Clinical frame and decision points: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy. He has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease; no new chest pain or breathlessness. The examiner then asks you to compare two lower-risk procedures. Expected reasoning: distinguish the key clinical risks, identify the action that changes management, and apply the relevant UK guidance to this specific patient.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Guideline scope Applies NG45 indiscriminately to children or cardiothoracic cases Limits NG45 to elective surgery age over 16 and states exclusions Checks exclusions and documents where specialist pathways supersede routine matrix ASA and surgery grade Ignores risk and orders one fixed panel Distinguishes ASA I–IV and minor/intermediate/major grades Maps patient-specific risk and surgery grade without treating ASA as definitive Focused preoperative assessment Does not review symptoms or medications Checks cardiovascular/respiratory symptoms, comorbidities, drugs and previous tests Identifies active disease, functional limitation and potential optimisation needs Minor surgery decisions Orders universal ECG, FBC and coagulation for healthy minor case Avoids routine FBC, coagulation, kidney tests and ECG in ASA I minor case Explains exceptions only on clinical indication and prior results Intermediate surgery decisions Orders same panel for all ASA groups For ASA II diabetes considers ECG; kidney tests if AKI risk; avoids routine FBC Accurately differentiates consider versus offer and checks comorbidity relevance Major surgery decisions Fails to order
sections.7. Critical fails — four specific safety: Declares a normal INR/APTT excludes clinically relevant DOAC anticoagulation and proceeds without a medication plan. Fails to assess new unstable cardiac or respiratory symptoms and clears patient for elective surgery solely from normal routine tests. Ignores severe abnormal renal function or symptomatic anaemia found before major surgery without informing anaesthesia or planning optimisation. Insists routine tests replace clinical assessment, and refuses to act on significant relevant symptoms or examination findings.
sections.8. Curveball: The patient reveals that he has new exertional chest pressure climbing one flight of stairs. Candidate should pause routine clearance, assess suspected cardiac disease and discuss timely evaluation with anaesthesia/appropriate specialist before elective surgery.

stations.title: Antiplatelets and Coronary Stents
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-308 Antiplatelets and Coronary Stents

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | 308 B2-308 — Antiplatelets and Coronary Stents Before Surgery Applied knowledge / perioperative decision-making | 8-minute structured station | 13 October 2026 | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 67-year-old man is booked for elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy for a non-obstructing colonic cancer in three weeks. He had a drug-eluting coronary stent inserted for an acute coronary syndrome four months ago. His drugs include aspirin 75 mg and ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily. He has no current angina. Your task: Explain the perioperative risks, assess whether surgery can safely proceed and formulate a multidisciplinary antiplatelet plan. You are not asked to prescribe an unsupervised drug change.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess safe prioritisation, decision quality and patient communication. Reveal further information only when requested. Do not reward unsupported certainty. The candidate must not independently change antiplatelets or prescribe high-risk interventions without escalation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The surgeon asks: “Can we stop both antiplatelets a week before surgery?” If challenged, they add: “The cancer cannot wait a whole year; what is your practical approach?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Immediate recommendation: Do not stop both agents automatically; flag recent ACS-related DES and urgent cardiology/anaesthetic/colorectal MDT decision. 2. Stent history: Obtain exact PCI date, indication (ACS versus chronic disease), DES details, complexity, previous thrombosis, ventricular function and any ongoing symptoms. 3. Operation risk: Establish cancer stage/urgency, alternative delay or bridging oncological plan, major operative bleeding likelihood and consequences of bleeding. 4. Time thresholds: After DES for ACS, elective surgery requiring interruption ideally deferred at least 12 months; after chronic coronary disease DES generally at least 6 months; time-sensitive surgery may be considered earlier after multidisciplinary balancing. 5. DAPT plan: Aim to continue aspirin where possible; decide with cardiology whether P2Y12 interruption is unavoidable, recognising high thrombotic risk in the first months. 6. If interruption agreed: For noncardiac surgery ESC 2022: ticagrelor 3–5 days, clopidogrel 5 days, prasugrel 7 days; drug-specific and procedural plan with prompt postoperative restart once haemostasis allows. 7. Emergency deterioration: Identify acute coronary syn
sections.5. Clinical frame and decision points: Competing harms — Stopping P2Y12 prematurely risks potentially fatal stent thrombosis/MI; continuation increases perioperative bleeding and may complicate surgery. Timing nuance — Do not confuse 12 months following ACS-DES with the 6-month chronic coronary disease DES recommendation. An oncological operation can be time-sensitive, not simply “elective”. Practical team decision — Colorectal surgeon, anaesthetist, interventional cardiologist and patient agree whether to defer, proceed with tailored antiplatelets or use alternative cancer management. Aspirin / bridging — Continue aspirin after prior PCI if surgically feasible. Intravenous antiplatelet bridging is exceptional and specialist-led; heparin is not an equivalent substitute for platelet inhibition.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Agrees both drugs can stop without review. Recognises recent DES and prevents unsupervised cessation. Explicitly frames early stent thrombosis risk, directs immediate cardiology-MDT consultation and assigns ownership. Clinical facts Does not establish when or why the stent was inserted. Elicits ACS versus stable disease, stent date and current symptoms. Adds complexity, prior thrombosis, LV function and PCI report to personalise risk. Operative assessment Treats cancer operation as invariably deferrable or urgent. Assesses haemorrhage risk and tumour urgency. Explores stage, alternative oncological pathways and acceptable delay with colorectal MDT. Guideline interpretation States all DES cases must wait the same interval. Identifies ideal 12-month interval for ACS-DES requiring interruption. Contrasts ACS-DES 12 months, chronic disease 6 months and time-sensitive 3-month consideration as context. Antiplatelet planning Unilaterally stops aspirin and ticagrelor. Seeks MDT plan aiming to continue aspirin if possible. Specifies written, individualised P2Y12 strategy and considers extreme bleeding procedures distinctly. Drug specifics G
sections.7. Critical fails — four specific safety: 1. Directs cessation of both aspirin and ticagrelor in this recent ACS-DES patient without cardiology-led assessment. 2. Labels the operation low risk and permits routine DAPT interruption despite a four-month-old ACS stent. 3. Fails to escalate new postoperative chest pain, hypotension or ECG changes suggestive of acute coronary occlusion. 4. Leaves P2Y12 therapy discontinued indefinitely after surgery without a haemostasis-based restart plan.
sections.8. Curveball: The colorectal consultant says the tumour has become partially obstructing and surgery is required within 72 hours. Expected: make surgery genuinely time-sensitive, urgent cardiology/anaesthetic/oncology MDT, assess whether DAPT continuation is viable, prepare blood/bleeding plan, document risk; do not apply a rigid 12-month ban.

stations.title: Liver Cirrhosis and Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-309 Liver Cirrhosis and Surgery

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B | 309 B2-309 — Liver Cirrhosis and Surgery Applied knowledge / perioperative risk stratification | 8-minute structured station | 13 October 2026 | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 59-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is referred for elective open incisional hernia repair. He had an admission with tense ascites six weeks ago. He is currently on spironolactone. Examination reveals mild ascites and muscle wasting; recent results: bilirubin 48 μmol/L, albumin 27 g/L, INR 1.6, creatinine 105 μmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L. He is alert and orientated. Your task: Assess the surgical risk, explain the significance of Child–Pugh and MELD, and develop a safer perioperative plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess context-based operative risk stratification and correct management of decompensation. Reveal findings when requested. This is an applied-knowledge discussion, not a demand to calculate unprovided data.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient asks: “My blood clotting test is bad: will I bleed to death?” If reassured, he asks: “Can you just give me plasma until the INR is normal?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Initial safety: Recognise recently decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and malnutrition; defer routine elective repair pending hepatology, anaesthesia and surgical discussion. 2. Focused assessment: Seek encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, infections, jaundice, renal dysfunction, alcohol use, nutritional status, ascites control and cardiopulmonary disease. 3. Child–Pugh: State five variables: bilirubin, albumin, INR/prothrombin time, ascites and encephalopathy; describe A/B/C grades; with moderate ascites and these labs likely B depending on clinical ascites severity. 4. MELD / MELD-Na: Uses bilirubin, INR, creatinine (and sodium for MELD-Na); flags mortality risk but not a stand-alone permission for surgery. 5. Procedure / prediction: Account for open abdominal repair and portal hypertension; use VOCAL-Penn where available and consider procedure/urgency, frailty and ASA status. 6. Optimisation: Treat and investigate ascites, avoid active infection, assess varices, optimise nutrition, abstinence and reversible renal/electrolyte derangement; consider specialist portal hypertension evaluation. 7. Bleeding / INR: Explain INR in cirrhosis poorly predicts procedural bleeding; do not
sections.5. Clinical frame and decision points: Core diagnosis — Decompensated cirrhosis is suggested by recent tense ascites and ongoing ascites. Operative risk depends on liver reserve, portal hypertension and type/urgency of surgery. Scores — Child–Pugh uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. MELD uses bilirubin, INR, creatinine; MELD-Na adds sodium. Neither substitutes for surgical-context risk estimation. Coagulation — “Rebalanced haemostasis” means INR alone does not measure procedural bleeding tendency reliably. Avoid reflex correction; manage actual bleeding and specific deficits with specialist advice. Elective decision — Do not promise safety or impose a blanket lifetime prohibition. Stabilise decompensation and share a documented MDT decision, including consequences of delaying hernia surgery.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety triage Books surgery without recognising recent decompensation. Identifies ascites and asks for hepatology/anaesthetic risk review. Explicitly recognises decompensated cirrhosis and pauses elective surgery pending optimisation and MDT. History / examination Asks only about alcohol consumption. Assesses encephalopathy, ascites, bleeding, infection and nutrition. Adds variceal history, renal status, frailty, medications and portal hypertension burden. Child–Pugh Confuses its five components or grades. Names bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy and A–C bands. Explains subjective grading of ascites/encephalopathy and avoids spurious exact scoring without required definitions. MELD assessment Uses albumin as a MELD component or ignores renal function. Names bilirubin, INR, creatinine and sodium for MELD-Na. Explains limitations of MELD, renal deterioration and value of validated procedure-specific models. Operation-specific risk Bases decision on INR alone. Discusses abdominal operation, urgency and liver dysfunction. Considers portal hypertension, open repair, infection/wound risks and VOCAL-Penn predicted outcomes. Optimisation Offe
sections.7. Critical fails — four specific safety: 1. Proceeds with non-urgent open hernia repair without addressing recent decompensated ascites or seeking specialist assessment. 2. Gives fresh frozen plasma routinely to normalise INR 1.6 in the absence of bleeding or a specific indicated correction. 3. Interprets a reassuring calculated score as excluding operative risk and ignores current infection, encephalopathy or renal decline. 4. Fails to recognise and urgently escalate postoperative confusion with renal dysfunction as possible encephalopathy, infection or acute kidney injury.
sections.8. Curveball: The patient develops fever, worsening ascites and creatinine rises to 185 μmol/L the day before surgery. Expected: cancel/postpone elective surgery, admit and evaluate for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis/infection and AKI, undertake appropriate ascitic fluid assessment with senior/hepatology involvement, treat promptly.

stations.title: Dialysis Patient for Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-310 — The Dialysis Patient for Surgery AMaC • MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge • 8-minute structured station • 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A 62-year-old man on Monday/Wednesday/Friday haemodialysis via a left forearm AV fistula is booked for elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy on Tuesday. Last dialysis was Monday. He has ischaemic heart disease and receives epoetin and phosphate binders. Explain your assessment, key decisions and perioperative management to the examiner. No physical intervention is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess prioritisation, safety, interpretation, escalation and communication. Use eight prompts below; disclose investigations or changes only when requested. A critical fail triggers examiner review; do not infer a regulatory pass mark.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient asks: “Can my dialysis wait until after the operation? Can nurses put a drip in my fistula arm?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Immediate assessment — Confirm indication/urgency and operation; symptoms of dyspnoea, chest pain, infection or hypotension; review dialysis prescription, dry weight, last run, residual urine and access. 2. Preoperative risks — Discuss hyperkalaemia, fluid overload or depletion, acidosis, uraemic platelet dysfunction, anaemia, vascular disease and altered medicine clearance. 3. Timing dialysis — For elective surgery coordinate with nephrology/anaesthesia for dialysis usually the day before; tailor ultrafiltration, potassium and anticoagulation to status; avoid rigid timing rule. 4. Investigations — Check recent potassium, bicarbonate, sodium, calcium, glucose, full blood count and ECG when clinically indicated; check fluid balance, weight and access function. 5. Vascular access — Identify thrill/bruit and avoid cannulation, BP cuffs and venepuncture on fistula arm; agree alternate IV access and preserve future access veins. 6. Medicines — Review renally cleared drugs and doses, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, insulin, antihypertensives and nephrotoxins with renal pharmacist; dose antibiotics appropriately. 7. Intraoperative and postoperative plan — Individualised fluid strategy, c
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Prioritisation Proceeds to elective theatre without renal/anaesthetic input. Identifies dialysis status and requests timely renal/anaesthetic review. Coordinates documented multidisciplinary go/no-go decision using urgency, volume and laboratory status. Dialysis history Fails to ask last dialysis or access type. Establishes dialysis schedule, last treatment and access. Also asks missed sessions, dry weight, ultrafiltration tolerance and residual urine. Physiology/risk Assumes dialysis normalises all surgical risk. Identifies potassium, fluid, anaemia and cardiovascular risks. Links each risk to a practical pre/intraoperative mitigation. Tests Omits potassium testing before major surgery. Checks potassium, chemistry, haemoglobin and indicated ECG. Interprets trends and arranges repeat tests after dialysis when required. Dialysis planning Insists on operating without considering urgent dialysis need. Discusses individualised pre-op dialysis often on preceding day. Tailors dialysate/UF/anticoagulation and postoperative dialysis contingency with nephrology. Access protection Uses fistula arm for blood pressure or routine cannula. Specifically prohibits
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: Proceed with elective anaesthesia despite untreated severe hyperkalaemia or ECG instability. Cannulate or apply blood pressure cuff to the functioning fistula arm despite warning. Give indiscriminate large-volume fluids to a clinically overloaded anuric patient without reassessment. Fail to involve renal/anaesthetic team when dialysis or metabolic optimisation is clearly necessary.
sections.7. Curveball: Morning-of-surgery potassium is 6.8 mmol/L with peaked T waves. Examiner asks whether to proceed because the patient dialysed yesterday.
sections.8. Recovery lines — three station-specif: 1. “I withdraw my suggestion to proceed: this is an immediate hyperkalaemia emergency and elective surgery must be deferred.” 2. “I will obtain monitored IV access away from the fistula arm, summon senior help, give membrane stabilisation and protocol-based potassium-shifting therapy.” 3. “I will urgently contact renal services for definitive potassium removal/dialysis and reassess ECG and potassium before reconsidering surgery.”

stations.title: Parkinsons Disease and NBM

sections.preamble: B2-311 — Parkinson’s Disease and Nil by Mouth AMaC • MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge • 8-minute structured station • 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A 74-year-old woman with Parkinson’s disease is admitted with a small-bowel obstruction and needs urgent surgery. She takes co-careldopa at 07:00, 11:00, 15:00 and 19:00. She is vomiting, has an NG tube on free drainage and has missed her 11:00 dose. Explain your assessment, key decisions and perioperative management to the examiner. No physical intervention is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess prioritisation, safety, interpretation, escalation and communication. Use eight prompts below; disclose investigations or changes only when requested. A critical fail triggers examiner review; do not infer a regulatory pass mark.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient’s daughter says: “Mum becomes completely rigid when her tablets are late. Can you just stop them until she is eating?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Why urgent? — Identify time-critical dopaminergic treatment; missed doses can cause rigidity, immobility, swallowing deterioration and parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. 2. Medication reconciliation — Record exact products, doses, formulation and patient-specific administration times; check last administered dose and specialist therapies. 3. Initial perioperative plan — Request anaesthetic, Parkinson’s specialist and pharmacist input; schedule priority theatre where possible and minimise NBM time. 4. Can a sip of water be used? — For routine fasting, medicines may often be given with a sip of water until induction; this obstructed, vomiting patient needs explicit aspiration-risk and GI-route review. 5. Enteral alternatives — If access and absorption suitable, consider dispersible co-beneldopa through a correctly positioned NG tube with appropriate clamping/absorption plan after specialist/pharmacy advice. 6.
