Non-enteral alternatives — If gut route unreliable, obtain specialist conversion to transdermal rotigotine; conversion is not one-for-one and may under-treat high levodopa requirements. 7. Other drugs and complications — Avoid metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol a
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Describes Parkinson tablets as optional during NBM. Recognises medication as time critical and checks last dose. Explains serious withdrawal syndrome and specific aspiration/mobility consequences. History/reconciliation Uses a vague “usual meds” prescription. Documents exact dose, formulation and schedule. Checks last administration, interactions and existing infusion/device therapies. Risk of NBM Assumes all NBM patients can swallow tablets. Distinguishes routine fasting from vomiting/obstruction. Assesses enteral absorption and aspiration risk with anaesthetist and surgical team. Urgency/list planning Accepts prolonged avoidable interruption. Requests early theatre and drug timing plan. Synchronises theatre/NG protocol with pharmacy and specialist nursing. Enteral route Crushes modified-release tablets without review. Considers dispersible levodopa via safe enteral route. Confirms formulation, tube position, drainage/clamp policy and reliable absorption. Non-oral route Makes up a rotigotine patch equivalent dose. Requests specialist-guided rotigotine conversion if needed. Recognises conversion limitations, frailty and hallucination/or
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: Deliberately withhold all dopaminergic therapy for an indefinite NBM period without an alternative plan. Prescribe metoclopramide or haloperidol despite recognising Parkinson’s disease, without compelling specialist justification. Invent a 1:1 oral-levodopa-to-rotigotine patch conversion without specialist/pharmacy review. Ignore high fever, severe rigidity and autonomic instability after missed doses.
sections.7. Curveball: In recovery the patient becomes rigid and confused, temperature rises to 39°C and blood pressure is labile; her last levodopa was 12 hours ago.
sections.8. Recovery lines — three station-specif: 1. “This is not simply routine postoperative confusion: I suspect parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome precipitated by missed levodopa.” 2. “I will perform ABCDE, seek critical care and Parkinson’s specialist input, check for other causes including infection and restore dopaminergic treatment safely.” 3. “I will revise the medication chart with explicit administration times and a verified NG or transdermal pathway so no further doses are missed.”

stations.title: Alcohol Withdrawal on Surgical Ward
stations.source_heading: B2-312 Alcohol Withdrawal on Surgical Ward

near_match.title: Alcohol Withdrawal — CIWA-Ar

sections.preamble: B2-312 — Alcohol Withdrawal on the Surgical Ward AMaC | MRCS Part B | Critical care | 8-minute station | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A 52-year-old man admitted with acute cholecystitis has tremor, sweating, tachycardia and agitation 18 hours after his last drink. He drinks approximately 20 units daily, has previously had withdrawal seizures and is eating poorly. Assess the problem and outline safe management. No actual intervention is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight examiner prompts follow. Award the observed behaviour band in each domain; four critical fails are reviewed separately. Reveal results on request. This is not an official MRCS mark scheme.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The nurse says: “His CIWA-Ar is 17 and he is seeing insects on the wall. Can we give an extra sedative and leave him on the ward?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. First response — ABCDE, vitals, NEWS2, glucose, oxygen saturation, delirium and seizure assessment; call senior medical/critical care help if severe. 2. History and differential — Last drink, baseline intake, seizures/DT, drugs, head injury, sepsis, pain, hypoglycaemia and hepatic encephalopathy. 3. Risk stratification — Recognise high-risk withdrawal with hallucinations and past seizures; CIWA-Ar supports clinical assessment but is unreliable in some delirious or non-communicating patients. 4. Investigations — Capillary glucose, FBC, electrolytes including magnesium, renal and liver tests, ECG; seek source of infection or alternate delirium cause. 5. Withdrawal drug plan — Use hospital symptom-triggered benzodiazepine regimen with repeated trained assessment and sedation/respiratory monitoring; adjust for liver disease and escalate if refractory. 6. Thiamine plan — Give prophylactic thiamine by route appropriate to nutrition/risk; suspected Wernicke requires urgent parenteral thiamine and specialist protocol. 7. Glucose nuance — Do not delay lifesaving glucose in hypoglycaemia; administer thiamine promptly before or alongside glucose where possible, rather than enforcing a dang
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Calls agitation purely behavioural and leaves patient unassessed. Starts ABCDE, observations and glucose; obtains senior review. Also plans seizure precautions and high-acuity monitoring with explicit triggers. Withdrawal history Does not ask last drink or previous seizures. Asks last drink, daily use and past DT/seizures. Elicits previous detox, co-ingestants, nutrition and safeguarding needs. Differential diagnosis Attributes all confusion to alcohol. Considers infection, glucose disturbance and head injury. Examines for hepatic encephalopathy and other perioperative delirium drivers. Risk tools Treats a CIWA score as diagnosis without judgement. Uses CIWA-Ar as adjunct and recognises severe signs. Explains score limitations in delirious patients and observation frequency. Investigations Omits bedside glucose. Checks glucose, electrolytes, FBC, renal/liver markers. Includes magnesium, ECG and targeted infection/head injury investigation. Pharmacotherapy Provides sedative without respiratory assessment or review. Uses supervised symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocol. Adjusts for liver impairment and specifies rescue/escalation
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Fail to assess or treat hypoglycaemia in an acutely confused patient. 2. Dismiss hallucinations with autonomic instability and previous withdrawal seizures without urgent senior review or monitoring. 3. Give escalating sedatives to a hypoventilating patient without airway review and observation. 4. Fail to consider and urgently treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy with parenteral thiamine.
sections.7. Curveball: Thirty minutes later the patient has a generalised seizure followed by reduced consciousness and noisy breathing.
sections.8. Recovery lines — three station-specif: 1. “This is a withdrawal seizure or another acute neurological emergency: I will call the emergency team and prioritise airway, breathing and immediate glucose.” 2. “I will protect from injury, follow seizure protocol and reassess causes including sodium, glucose and head injury.” 3. “I will escalate to anaesthesia/critical care, review the withdrawal regimen and give appropriate thiamine.”

stations.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and Surgery
stations.source_heading: B2-313 Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-313 — Obstructive Sleep Apnoea and Surgery AMaC | MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute station | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A 58-year-old man, BMI 39 kg/m², is planned for elective laparoscopic hernia repair. He snores loudly, his partner observes apnoeas, he is sleepy by day, takes treatment for hypertension and owns CPAP but uses it inconsistently. Assess the problem and outline safe management. No actual intervention is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight examiner prompts follow. Award the observed behaviour band in each domain; four critical fails are reviewed separately. Reveal results on request. This is not an official MRCS mark scheme.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient asks: “If I bring the CPAP machine, can I still go home the same day? I heard my breathing can stop after painkillers.”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Recognise risk — Recognise suspected/known OSA and associated airway obstruction, hypoxaemia, sedation/opioid susceptibility and postoperative risk. 2. Screen and clarify — Use STOP-BANG components: snoring, tiredness, observed apnoea, pressure, BMI, age, neck and sex; ask OSA severity, sleep study and CPAP adherence. 3. Preoperative decision — Inform anaesthetist; review comorbid cardiopulmonary disease and consider obesity hypoventilation, rather than cancelling all elective cases automatically. 4. Airway and anaesthesia — Plan difficult mask ventilation/intubation precautions, minimal sedatives, regional/local options when appropriate and careful neuromuscular reversal. 5. Analgesia — Prefer multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, local infiltration and cautious titration of any opioids. 6. CPAP strategy — Encourage bringing own functioning CPAP with settings and use pre-/postoperatively when appropriate, with recovery staff informed. 7. Recovery/monitoring — Monitor oxygenation, ventilation and obstruction risk; use appropriate postoperative area, observe especially during sedation/sleep and ensure safe discharge criteria. 8. Disposition — Day-case suitability is individual, ba
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance OSA recognition Ignores witnessed apnoeas as irrelevant. Identifies OSA as perioperative respiratory risk. Links hypoventilation and opioid sensitivity to realistic harms. Risk assessment Does not ask about CPAP or symptoms. Assesses STOP-BANG factors and CPAP history. Also considers hypoventilation, comorbidity and previous anaesthetic events. Pre-op planning Proceeds without anaesthesia communication. Alerts anaesthetist and documents risk. Integrates procedure, disease severity, analgesia and setting. Airway safety Assumes standard airway management without preparation. Anticipates airway difficulty and sedation hazards. Discusses positioning, rescue plan and full reversal of neuromuscular blockade. Analgesia Prescribes unrestricted opioids and sedatives. Uses multimodal opioid-sparing options. Individualises rescue analgesia with observation and avoids sedative stacking. CPAP Advises stopping established CPAP after surgery. Plans perioperative CPAP and brings equipment. Confirms device availability, tolerance and staff handover. Monitoring Discharges despite recurrent obstruction in recovery. Requires appropriate recovery monitoring and reasses
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Ignore recurrent postoperative apnoea or desaturation and discharge without assessment. 2. Administer repeated opioids/sedatives despite airway obstruction without monitoring or support. 3. Fail to inform the anaesthetic team of significant suspected or documented OSA before induction. 4. Deny an established CPAP user access to clinically needed postoperative respiratory support without alternative plan.
sections.7. Curveball: In recovery he repeatedly obstructs and desaturates to 84% when drowsy after opioid analgesia; he requests discharge.
sections.8. Recovery lines — three station-specif: 1. “Recurrent obstruction and desaturation mean he is not currently safe for discharge.” 2. “I will call the anaesthetist, position and support his airway, assess ventilation and institute CPAP as appropriate.” 3. “I will review opioid/sedative exposure, increase monitoring and arrange admission to a suitable postoperative area.”

stations.title: Day Case Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-314 Day Case Surgery

near_match.title: Explaining the enhanced recovery pathway before day-case surgery

sections.preamble: B2-314 — Day-case Surgery: Who Is Suitable? AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / perioperative selection | 8-minute structured station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: Assess suitability for a day-case pathway, explain the decision to the examiner and describe the discharge safeguards. You are not required to choose anaesthetic drugs. Clinical context: A 58-year-old woman is listed for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She has treated hypertension, BMI 34, well-controlled type 2 diabetes and lives alone. Her daughter can collect her but cannot stay overnight. The list is in three weeks.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test safe prioritisation, explicit escalation decisions, MRCS-level reasoning and patient-centred communication. Release findings only on request. Use the eight prompts in Section 4; do not lead the candidate.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient wants to avoid staying in hospital. If asked, she mobilises independently, can understand instructions and has no recent chest pain, unstable illness or previous anaesthetic problems. Daughter lives 20 minutes away but works nights.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. What makes an operation suitable? → Check procedure-specific BADS day-case rates/pathway, anticipated postoperative pain, bleeding, nausea and need for prolonged observations; lap chole is commonly day-case but individual factors decide. 2. Which medical factors matter? → Assess stability and optimisation of diabetes, BP, cardiopulmonary disease, OSA risk, frailty, obesity-related airway issues, previous anaesthetic complications and anticipated postoperative support; no rigid ASA/BMI exclusion. 3. What social factors matter? → Confirm informed consent, access to a telephone, transport, home environment, distance and reliable help; discuss alternatives where no responsible escort/support is available. 4. How do you address the daughter working nights? → A lift alone does not establish an acceptable home support plan. Ask the day unit/anaesthetist about local supervision requirements, organise alternative support or an overnight admission. 5. What is decided in preassessment? → Joint surgical/anaesthetic assessment; optimisation, medication and fasting advice, analgesia/antiemetic plan, OSA/CPAP and diabetes plans as indicated. 6. What are recovery/discharge criteria? → Stable ph
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — Fail / Pas: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Procedure suitability Lists laparoscopy as automatic day-case regardless of risk. Confirms procedure fits local day-case pathway and checks likely recovery needs. Matches BADS procedure expectations to anticipated analgesia, PONV and complication risk. Medical optimisation Disregards active comorbidity or labels stable diabetes an absolute bar. Checks stability of diabetes, BP, cardiopulmonary disease and exercise tolerance. Plans condition-specific preassessment including anaesthetic review and perioperative diabetes management. OSA/airway assessment Ignores symptoms of significant OSA or anaesthetic history. Asks about snoring, apnoea, CPAP and previous anaesthetic difficulty. Connects suspected OSA with opioid-sparing plan and appropriate monitoring/discharge requirements. Social support Approves discharge because daughter offers a lift, ignoring overnight support. Verifies escort, communication, home support and transport; identifies the gap. Arranges viable alternative support or planned overnight pathway without shaming patient. Consent/preferences Gives unilateral decision without explaining risks. Explains benefits, alternatives and uncerta
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Discharges a patient with persistent vomiting, unstable observations or suspected postoperative bleeding. 2. Approves discharge without checking whether an escort and safe post-discharge support arrangements are available. 3. Dismisses unstable cardiopulmonary symptoms or poorly controlled major illness without anaesthetic review. 4. Provides no emergency contact or red-flag safety advice before discharge.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: On the morning of surgery the patient reveals she has developed exertional chest pain during the past week. Expected response: suspend routine day-case progression, urgent clinical assessment and anaesthetic/surgical review; do not proceed purely to preserve the theatre list.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I previously treated a planned day-case label as proof of discharge suitability; I will verify actual medical and social criteria now.” 2. “The lift does not cover post-discharge support. I will discuss alternatives with the day unit and plan overnight care if necessary.” 3. “Vomiting and worsening abdominal pain change the discharge decision. I will reassess and ask the surgeon/anaesthetist to review before any discharge.”

stations.title: NEWS2 Escalation

sections.preamble: B2-315 — NEWS2 and Escalating a Deteriorating Patient AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / clinical deterioration | 8-minute structured station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: Calculate the NEWS2 using standard SpO₂ Scale 1, explain escalation thresholds and demonstrate immediate assessment, communication and documentation. No images are provided. Clinical context: You are the on-call surgical registrar asked to review a 67-year-old postoperative patient with fever and increasing oxygen requirement. Observations: RR 26/min, SpO₂ 93% on 4 L/min oxygen, systolic BP 92 mmHg, pulse 124/min, temperature 39.2°C, new confusion.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test safe prioritisation, explicit escalation decisions, MRCS-level reasoning and patient-centred communication. Release findings only on request. Use the eight prompts in Section 4; do not lead the candidate.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Bedside nurse is concerned the patient became confused over 30 minutes. The patient had a laparotomy yesterday and has abdominal pain and a new oxygen requirement. If asked: IV access is present; urine output over four hours is low.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Calculate NEWS2 precisely. → RR 26 =3; SpO₂ 93% Scale 1 =2; supplemental oxygen =2; systolic BP 92 =2; pulse 124 =2; temperature 39.2 =2; new confusion =3; total =16. 2. What does 16 trigger? → NEWS2 ≥7 is high-risk requiring emergency response with critical-care competencies including airway management, continuous monitoring and consideration of higher level of care. 3. What about 5–6 or a single 3? → Aggregate 5–6 triggers urgent response; a single parameter scored 3 (red score) also triggers urgent ward-based assessment even if the total is below 5; local escalation chart governs timing. 4. First minute action? → Call for urgent help/critical care outreach immediately, ABCDE at bedside, monitoring, oxygen titrated to appropriate target, access, bedside glucose, reassessment. 5. What causes are plausible? → Postoperative sepsis or intra-abdominal complication, haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, aspiration/pneumonia, myocardial event; evaluate without anchoring on fever alone. 6. What tests and treatment? → Venous/arterial gas including lactate, FBC, renal function, cultures when indicated, glucose, ECG, imaging targeted to source; infection management per local sepsis pathway; f
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — Fail / Pas: Domain Fail Pass High-performance NEWS2 computation Underestimates score or omits oxygen/confusion. Calculates 16 from seven weighted inputs including 2 for oxygen. States individual component scores and flags Scale 1 as appropriate unless authorised otherwise. Threshold recognition Treats NEWS2 16 as a routine ward review. Recognises ≥7 high-risk emergency and 5–6 urgent threshold. Also explains red single-parameter 3 trigger and local escalation adaptation. Early escalation Waits for investigations before calling for help. Immediately calls senior response and critical care outreach/rapid response. Specifies airway-capable team, continuous monitoring and likely critical care transfer. ABCDE/resuscitation Discusses scoring without assessing the patient. Performs structured ABCDE, oxygen assessment, IV access, glucose. Repeats ABCDE as treatment evolves and links perfusion and respiratory support to findings. Differential and sources Assumes fever equals uncomplicated infection. Considers sepsis, bleeding, PE and postoperative intra-abdominal pathology. Prioritises time-sensitive complications and organ support in parallel. Investigations Orders CT first while patient is unstable.
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Fails to summon urgent senior/critical care help for NEWS2 16. 2. Treats altered consciousness and shock as non-urgent while awaiting imaging. 3. Omits oxygen supplementation or new confusion from NEWS2 to falsely downgrade severity. 4. Does not initiate bedside ABCDE assessment/resuscitation in a visibly deteriorating patient.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: Nurse says the patient has COPD and asks to change to NEWS2 SpO₂ Scale 2 so the score is lower. Expected response: Scale 2 is only used on direction of a suitably qualified clinician for the appropriate hypercapnic respiratory failure context, not based on COPD alone; do not delay escalation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I missed the additional two points for supplementary oxygen: the NEWS2 is 16, and I am activating emergency escalation now.” 2. “I focused on infection too early. I will reassess ABCDE and actively exclude bleeding, PE and surgical complications.” 3. “I should not change saturation scale on COPD history alone; I will confirm the prescribed target and senior authorisation while continuing urgent care.”

stations.title: Cardiac Arrest Surgical Ward

sections.preamble: B2-316 — Cardiac Arrest on the Surgical Ward AMaC MRCS Part B | Critical care | 8 minutes | 13 October 2026 | Draft — independent clinical review required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar called to a 64-year-old who collapses six hours after major abdominal surgery. Demonstrate aloud the initial ALS response, discuss the rhythm and manage operative reversible causes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Run a simulated adult in-hospital arrest with no live interventions. At prompt 7 give PEA and 800 mL of bright blood in the drain over 15 minutes. Mark priorities and specific actions, not memory of an undifferentiated list.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Ward nurse: “He suddenly became unconscious; I cannot see normal breathing.” When asked, the patient had abdominal surgery today and a drain has rapidly filled with blood.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. First action on finding the patient — Assess responsiveness and normal breathing rapidly, shout for help, call hospital arrest team and start CPR immediately. 2. Initial sequence and CPR quality — 30:2 until advanced airway, compression rate 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, minimise pauses; oxygen and bag-mask ventilation with trained help. 3. Defibrillator and rhythm — Attach pads, shock VF/pVT promptly, resume CPR without pulse check after shock; do not shock PEA/asystole. 4. Drugs and timing — IV first then IO if needed; 1 mg adrenaline ASAP for PEA/asystole or after third shock for VF/pVT, repeat every 3–5 min; amiodarone 300 mg after third shock in VF/pVT. 5. Reversible causes — Identify hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia/metabolic derangement, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, coronary/pulmonary thrombosis. 6. Surgical-specific causes — Review blood loss/drains for haemorrhage, recent surgery for tamponade or tension pneumothorax, PE risk and perioperative potassium/blood gases; organise surgical control of haemorrhage. 7. Data supplied by examiner — Monitor shows PEA, BP absent, fresh drain has 800 mL blood in 15 minutes; state non-shockable pathway,
sections.5. Core clinical frame: Recognition → call for help → immediate high-quality CPR and defibrillator → rhythm-specific ALS → correct causes without interrupting compressions → treat catastrophic bleeding and transfer after ROSC.
sections.1. Recognition and call: Waits for ECG before recognising arrest. Identifies absent normal breathing and calls arrest team immediately. Delegates call, airway trolley and defibrillator while commencing CPR.
sections.2. CPR technique: Does not start compressions or performs prolonged pauses. Gives 30:2 with 100–120/min and 5–6 cm depth. Allocates compressor swaps and monitors minimal no-flow time.

stations.title: Penicillin Allergy Surgical Prophylaxis

sections.preamble: B2-317 — Penicillin Allergy and Surgical Prophylaxis AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8 minutes | 13 October 2026 | Draft — independent clinical review required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old scheduled for elective mesh hernia repair. The preoperative record states “penicillin allergy”. Explain how you assess this label and arrange appropriate surgical prophylaxis.
sections.2. Examiner brief: The candidate should not automatically omit prophylaxis or classify all beta-lactams as unsafe. Give reaction details only on request; use the SCAR curveball to probe safe escalation. Do not reward memorised antibiotic doses when local policy is decisive.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I’m allergic to penicillin — does that mean I can’t have antibiotics?” Initially reports a childhood itchy rash. For curveball, produces a discharge letter describing blistering and mouth ulcers after an antibiotic.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. Clarify the label — Ask actual drug, date, timing after dose, rash versus nausea, severity, treatment, admission and subsequent tolerated antibiotics. 2. Differentiate allergy — GI upset or isolated headache is not immune allergy; immediate wheeze, hypotension or angio-oedema suggests anaphylaxis; severe blistering/mucosal rash suggests SCAR. 3. Establish prophylaxis indication — Identify clean uncomplicated non-prosthetic versus prosthetic/implant/contaminated procedure; use local infection-prevention policy and surgical site organisms. 4. Assess time-critical surgery — Do not blindly remove allergy label or administer suspect antibiotic in theatre; check alternative with anaesthetist, infection/pharmacy team. 5. Choose antibiotic safely — Local formulary first; non-beta-lactam alternative may be necessary for true severe allergy; certain cephalosporins may be possible based on side-chain/reaction phenotype and local policy. 6. Correct timing — Give chosen IV prophylaxis with adequate time before incision; NICE suggests on starting anaesthesia and earlier for tourniquet; consider infusion time and re-dosing. 7. Curveball response — A previous course caused blistering, mucosal u
sections.5. Core clinical frame: Procedure indication → detailed allergy phenotype → patient-specific/local formulary choice → appropriate pre-incision timing → documentation and longer-term allergy review. Prior severe delayed reactions require specialist input.
sections.1. Allergy history: Accepts “penicillin allergy” without details. Asks drug, reaction, timing, severity and treatment. Also asks tolerated beta-lactams and records a structured phenotype.
sections.2. Reaction classification: Labels simple nausea as anaphylaxis or disregards collapse. Separates intolerance from immediate allergy and severe delayed reaction. Recognises SCAR indicators and differing risks for re-exposure.

stations.title: Epidural Causing Hypotension After Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-318 Epidural Causing Hypotension After Surgery

near_match.title: Hypotension Hours After Bowel Surgery / Blame the Epidural Last

sections.preamble: B2-318 — Epidural Causing Hypotension After Surgery AMaC | MRCS Part B | DRAFT for independent specialist review | 13 October 2026 Applied knowledge / acute postoperative deterioration | 8-minute station | Educational assessment, not an official MRCS examination or mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. Six hours after open colorectal surgery, a 68-year-old patient with a thoracic epidural becomes hypotensive (BP 78/44 mmHg). Explain your immediate actions, differential diagnosis and ongoing plan to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test whether the candidate responds to shock first and does not label all hypotension as an epidural side effect. Provide scenario information only when requested; assess recognition of bleeding, high block and early anaesthetic help.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse: “The epidural was running at 8 mL/hour and the blood pressure has fallen. Shall I just turn it down?” The patient feels dizzy. If asked, the patient reports new abdominal fullness but no chest pain.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and supplied informa: 1. Immediate response? — Call for senior surgical and anaesthetic/acute pain help; ABCDE, supine positioning, monitor ECG/BP/SpO2, oxygen if hypoxaemic, check consciousness and perfusion; stop/pause epidural pump while assessing. 2. What observations and access? — Repeat BP, HR, RR, SpO2, temperature, urine output, NEWS2, blood glucose, two IV cannulae and check current analgesia/epidural chart. 3. What possible causes? — Sympathetic vasodilation from epidural, postoperative haemorrhage, hypovolaemia, sepsis, MI/arrhythmia, PE and high neuraxial block; consider local anaesthetic systemic toxicity if features suggest it. 4. Examine the block? — Check sensory height to cold, lower limb motor power, respiratory effort, ability to move arms, bradycardia and level of consciousness; do not overlook high block. 5. What tests are urgent? — FBC, U&E, blood gas/lactate, coagulation and group-and-save/crossmatch if bleeding; ECG; urgent targeted imaging after initial stabilisation if clinically indicated. 6. Haemodynamic management? — Assess response to cautious isotonic crystalloid bolus if indicated, reassess often; activate major haemorrhage pathway and blood products if haemorrhagic shock
sections.5. Clinical findings / interpretation: New systolic BP 78 mmHg, HR 124/min, cool peripheries, urine output 15 mL in last hour; new abdominal distension and 250 mL fresh blood in drain. These strongly suggest haemorrhage, not uncomplicated epidural sympathectomy. If asked: sensory block T6–T12; normal arm function, no dyspnoea or increasing motor block.
sections.6. Expected safe clinical framework: Treat hypotension as possible postoperative shock: call help and perform ABCDE; prioritise haemorrhage in a tachycardic, poorly perfused patient. Stop/pause the epidural, obtain anaesthetic review, inspect block height and neurological status; avoid reflexively attributing haemodynamic collapse to neuraxial block. Obtain monitoring, vascular access, urgent bloods including crossmatch, assess blood loss, and deliver cause-directed resuscitation; urgent senior decision on return to theatre if bleeding. Once stabilised, establish safe analgesia without restarting epidural unilaterally; record and hand over cause, response and review plan.
sections.1. First response: Calls it benign epidural-related low BP; leaves patient unattended. Recognises shock, calls urgent help, performs ABCDE and reassesses BP. Coordinates anaesthetic and surgical response and prioritises time-critical perfusion.

stations.title: Hypokalaemia and Ileus After Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-319 Hypokalaemia and Ileus After Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-319 — Hypokalaemia and Ileus After Surgery AMaC | MRCS Part B | DRAFT for independent specialist review | 13 October 2026 Data interpretation / applied knowledge | 8-minute station | Educational assessment, not an official MRCS examination or mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. On day 3 after laparotomy, a 61-year-old patient has persistent vomiting, abdominal distension and reduced bowel sounds. Potassium is 2.7 mmol/L and magnesium 0.55 mmol/L. Interpret the data and outline management.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess interpretation of electrolyte depletion, reversible contributors to ileus, safe IV replacement with monitoring, and recognition of postoperative mechanical obstruction or sepsis. Do not accept unmonitored concentrated potassium bolus.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse reports the patient is nil by mouth, with a nasogastric tube draining 1.2 L in 24 hours. “Can I push potassium IV so the bowel starts working?” The patient has palpitations but no chest pain.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and supplied informa: 1. Interpret results? — K 2.7 mmol/L is moderate hypokalaemia; magnesium 0.55 mmol/L low; electrolyte losses can worsen ileus and cause dysrhythmia. 2. What history and observations? — Review onset, vomiting/NG losses, drugs including diuretics and laxatives, oral intake, flatus/stool, pain, fever, urine output and haemodynamic state. 3. Examination? — ABCDE if unwell; abdominal distension, tenderness, peritonism, bowel sounds, wounds, hernias and hydration; do not diagnose simple ileus if strangulation or anastomotic leak is possible. 4. Immediate tests? — Repeat U&E and magnesium, renal function, ECG for arrhythmia/U waves and QT changes, FBC/CRP, blood gas if unwell; imaging guided by obstruction or leak suspicion. 5. Sources of deficit? — Vomiting/NG suction, low intake, renal losses (diuretics), intracellular shifts; low magnesium may make potassium replacement ineffective. 6. Potassium replacement plan? — Because NBM and symptomatic, prescribe premixed dilute IV potassium per local protocol with pump; usually rate no more than 10 mmol/h and peripheral concentration at most 40 mmol/L; repeat levels and monitor ECG as indicated. 7. How address magnesium and fluids? — Replace ma
sections.5. Clinical findings / interpretation: Temperature 37.4 °C, BP 116/72, HR 102, NG drainage 1.2 L/24 h; ECG shows flattened T waves and prominent U waves; U&E: K 2.7 mmol/L, Mg 0.55 mmol/L, creatinine 78 µmol/L. Abdomen moderately distended without peritonism. No passage of flatus. New colicky pain or fever would trigger reassessment for mechanical obstruction or leak.
sections.6. Expected safe clinical framework: Recognise potassium and magnesium depletion as potentially important contributors to postoperative ileus and arrhythmia, but assess for competing surgical complications. Obtain ECG, check renal function and losses, use locally authorised premixed IV potassium at a controlled rate with appropriate monitoring; never administer IV potassium as an undiluted push. Correct magnesium alongside potassium, replace ongoing NG losses separately from routine fluid requirements, and serially reassess electrolytes, urine output and ECG. Provide supportive ileus care and seek imaging/senior surgical assessment for persistent or worsening symptoms, peritonism, sepsis or mechanical obstruction.
sections.1. Interpretation: Calls K 2.7 normal or ignores low Mg. Identifies moderate hypokalaemia and concomitant hypomagnesaemia. Links electrolyte depletion to motility impairment and dysrhythmia risk.

stations.title: COPD Patient Drowsy on Oxygen After Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-320 COPD Patient Drowsy on Oxygen After Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-320 — COPD Patient Drowsy on Oxygen After Surgery AMaC | MRCS Part B | Draft for independent clinical review | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A 72-year-old with COPD is drowsy six hours after emergency laparotomy. The nurse has increased oxygen to a reservoir mask because saturations were 87%. Interpret the supplied blood gas, initiate safe immediate management and explain escalation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test recognition of acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, not reflex withdrawal of lifesaving oxygen. Provide blood gas when asked. Candidate should consider other causes of postoperative drowsiness and determine suitability for NIV versus airway protection.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse: “He was 87%, so I put on 15 litres. His saturations are 99% now, but he is much harder to wake.” Patient opens eyes to voice, answers briefly, respiratory rate 9/min; recent IV morphine, no documented baseline home oxygen.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: Immediate first response: Call for urgent senior anaesthetic/critical-care assistance; ABCDE, assess airway protection, continuous monitoring and obtain repeat ABG. Interpret the ABG: Acidaemia with marked hypercapnia and raised bicarbonate suggests acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure; high PaO₂ under excess oxygen. Oxygen adjustment: Use controlled oxygen and prescribe target SpO₂ 88–92% while ensuring oxygenation; never abruptly remove oxygen from a hypoxaemic patient. Contributors: Review opioids/sedation, residual anaesthetic effect, COPD exacerbation, mucus plugging, atelectasis, pneumonia, PE and other surgical causes. Immediate supportive interventions: Sit up, check glucose, ECG and chest imaging as indicated, blood tests, bronchodilator if bronchospasm, treat trigger; consider naloxone titration if opioid-induced respiratory depression while maintaining analgesia. When is NIV indicated?: Acidosis pH <7.35 with PaCO₂ >6.5 kPa persisting after initial treatment supports NIV if awake enough to protect airway and appropriately staffed; this patient needs immediate senior airway assessment first. NIV versus intubation: Severe drowsiness/inability to protect airway, vomi
sections.5. Clinical findings / data supplied: Observations: BP 116/68, pulse 105, RR 9, temperature 37.2°C, SpO₂ 99% on reservoir mask. ABG on high-concentration oxygen: pH 7.24; PaCO₂ 10.0 kPa; PaO₂ 15.1 kPa; HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L; lactate 1.6 mmol/L. Prior bicarbonate 30 mmol/L. Chest: bilateral wheeze, reduced air entry; no unilateral absence; abdomen soft with no major drain loss.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Labels drowsiness as routine postoperative sedation despite abnormal ventilation. Identifies potentially life-threatening hypercapnic respiratory failure and summons help. Interprets acuity, recent oxygen change and contributing drug effects together. ABCDE / airway Fails to assess consciousness or airway protection. Uses ABCDE, monitors continuously and checks airway/ventilation. Explicitly anticipates aspiration/intubation risk and coordinates anaesthetic assessment. Blood gas interpretation Calls the gas simple hypoxia or metabolic acidosis. States respiratory acidosis with PaCO₂ 10.0 kPa and pH 7.24. Recognises raised HCO₃⁻ as chronic compensation with acute decompensation. Controlled oxygen Leaves saturation at 99% without re-evaluation or withdraws oxygen indiscriminately. Titrates oxygen towards 88–92% with monitoring. Prescribes range, checks device and repeats gas after controlled adjustment. Drug / differential assessment Ignores recently administered morphine and postoperative causes. Assesses opioid contribution, chest examination and alternative triggers. Plans cautious naloxone if indicated and searches for reversible caus
sections.7. Critical fails: Fails to recognise a threatened airway or to summon urgent airway/critical-care help despite marked drowsiness and acidosis. Maintains uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen despite clear hyperoxia and hypercapnia, without titration or review. Abruptly removes oxygen while hypoxaemic rather than safely titrating it. Uses NIV despite loss of airway protection or allows NIV to delay indicated intubation.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: The nurse reports the patient received morphine 10 minutes before becoming obtunded and has pinpoint pupils. Candidate reassesses breathing and airway immediately, seeks expert support, considers titrated naloxone according to local protocol, and does not attribute the whole picture to oxygen alone.

stations.title: The Metabolic Response to Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-321 The Metabolic Response to Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-321 — The Metabolic Response to Surgery AMaC | MRCS Part B | Draft for independent clinical review | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar discussing care of a 68-year-old patient on day 1 after elective colorectal resection. Explain the metabolic stress response and how enhanced recovery pathways can reduce unnecessary catabolism and complications.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess core neuroendocrine, inflammatory and metabolic changes and practical ERAS measures. Candidate must not suggest withholding necessary analgesia or feeding an unstable patient with ileus/aspiration risk.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient asks: “Why is my sugar high when I do not have diabetes, and why are you encouraging me to eat and get out of bed so soon?” They are alert and stable, with controlled pain, no nausea or signs of ileus.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: Describe immediate stress pathways: Tissue injury stimulates sympathetic nervous system and hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis; catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon, ADH, aldosterone and inflammatory mediators. Explain metabolic effects: Insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, hepatic glucose output, proteolysis, negative nitrogen balance and lipolysis; fluid and sodium retention. Describe cytokine response: IL-6 and other cytokines drive acute-phase response, CRP synthesis, fever and immune changes; inflammatory markers alone are non-specific. Why does catabolism matter?: Muscle weakness, delayed mobilisation, impaired wound healing and vulnerability to infection; degree varies with insult and complications. Preoperative ERAS interventions: Counselling and prehabilitation when appropriate, nutrition risk screening and optimisation, avoid unnecessarily prolonged fasting and individualised carbohydrate loading when indicated. Intraoperative stress reduction: Minimally invasive approach when appropriate, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, normothermia, nausea prevention and individualised euvolaemic fluid management. Postoperative strategies: Early oral/enteral intake if safe, early
sections.5. Clinical findings / data supplied: Observations stable; plasma glucose 10.8 mmol/L; mild transient neutrophilia and raised CRP expected in context, interpret with trajectory rather than exclude sepsis. Patient tolerated oral fluids; no vomiting. Epidural removed; multimodal pain plan established. No evidence of anastomotic leak.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Neuroendocrine activation Cannot name stress mediators or says insulin rises and cures stress response. Describes SNS/HPA activation, catecholamines and cortisol. Adds glucagon, ADH/aldosterone and relative reduction in insulin effectiveness. Glycaemic effects Fails to explain postoperative hyperglycaemia. Links insulin resistance to increased hepatic glucose production. Connects catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and peripheral insulin resistance to case. Protein / fat metabolism Claims stress is anabolic without qualification. Describes proteolysis and negative nitrogen balance. Relates proteolysis and lipolysis to weakness, substrate supply and healing. Inflammation States raised CRP necessarily means surgical sepsis. Names cytokine-induced acute-phase response and CRP. Distinguishes expected inflammation from concerning trends and clinical deterioration. Stress severity / consequences Treats all operations as producing identical responses. Links degree of stress to tissue injury and postoperative catabolism. Includes infection, pain, complication burden and pre-existing nutritional vulnerability. Preoperative ERAS Orders routine prolonged fasti
sections.7. Critical fails: Attributes new tachycardia, fever, peritonism or deterioration solely to normal metabolic stress and fails to assess for anastomotic leak or sepsis. Forces oral intake in a vomiting patient with suspected ileus or aspiration risk instead of reassessing. Recommends withholding appropriate analgesia or necessary resuscitation simply to “suppress” stress response. Recommends indiscriminate intravenous carbohydrate/insulin administration without glucose monitoring or an established clinical protocol.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: On day 3 the same patient develops tachycardia 122/min, increased pain, temperature 38.5°C and rising CRP. Candidate explicitly rejects a reassuring “normal stress response” explanation, repeats ABCDE and assesses for leak/sepsis with urgent senior review and imaging as indicated.

stations.title: Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-322 Abdominal Compartment Syndrome

near_match.title: Acute compartment syndrome

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B — B2-322 Abdominal Compartment Syndrome Critical care | 8-minute station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 64-year-old man is 12 hours post emergency laparotomy for perforated viscus. He has received substantial resuscitation, is ventilated on ICU, has a tense abdomen, rising airway pressures, reduced urine output and falling blood pressure. Explain your interpretation and immediate management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use the eight prompts below in sequence; release findings when asked. Award a band per grid row based on actual actions stated. Safety-critical omissions override an otherwise fluent performance.
sections.3. Patient / team actor brief: The patient or team member is concerned about deterioration. Answer only on request. Ask: “Is another operation needed?”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and data: 1. Immediate approach — ABCDE, summon senior surgeon and ICU consultant, assess perfusion, airway pressures, lactate and urine output. 2. Risk factors and differentials — Fluid overload, visceral oedema, sepsis, tight abdominal closure; consider haemorrhage, septic shock, tension pneumothorax, tube obstruction. 3. Define condition — IAH is sustained/repeated IAP ≥12 mmHg; ACS is sustained IAP >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. 4. Measure correctly — Transvesical pressure at end expiration, supine without abdominal contraction; zero at mid-axillary line; sterile saline instillation ≤25 mL. 5. Interpret data — IAP 26–27 mmHg and deteriorating renal, respiratory and circulatory function constitute ACS; do not use distension alone. 6. Immediate treatment — Oxygenation/ventilation and haemodynamic support, analgesia/sedation, gastric/colonic decompression, drain collections if suitable, stop avoidable positive fluid balance. 7. Definitive escalation — Urgent senior surgical/critical-care decision for decompressive laparotomy if overt ACS or worsening despite measures; no CT-related delay in unstable patient. 8. After decompression — Prepare temporary abdominal closure, monitor reperfu
sections.5. Case findings / interpretation: HR 124/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, urine 12 mL/h, peak airway pressure increased, lactate 4.1 mmol/L; bladder IAP 26 mmHg, repeated 27 mmHg at end expiration; new AKI. Key interpretation: Pressure >20 mmHg with newly impaired organs is abdominal compartment syndrome.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls this simple postoperative bloating and misses organ failure. Recognises suspected ACS from distension plus renal and ventilatory deterioration. Names physiology and diagnoses overt ACS from documented pressure and new organ failure. Initial safety Delays review of shock or airway compromise. Uses ABCDE and summons senior surgical/ICU help promptly. Coordinates simultaneous ventilation, haemodynamic support and urgent operative readiness. Risk assessment Omits abdominal surgery, sepsis and fluid loading. Identifies major risk factors including visceral oedema and positive fluid balance. Differentiates primary/secondary causes and competing postoperative shock causes. Pressure technique Uses palpation alone or incorrect pressure reading. Requests correctly performed bladder measurement and repeat/serial readings. Specifies supine end-expiration zeroing and instillation no more than 25 mL. Interpretation Uses pressure >12 as the diagnostic threshold for ACS. Distinguishes IAH ≥12 from ACS >20 plus organ dysfunction. Integrates 26–27 mmHg with renal, circulatory and respiratory decline. Initial management Gives unlimited fluids withou
sections.7. Four critical fails: 1. Fails to recognise severe postoperative organ dysfunction and does not escalate to ICU/senior surgeon. 2. Rules out ACS solely because abdominal examination is equivocal, without pressure assessment. 3. Defers urgent decompression in established deteriorating ACS to obtain nonessential imaging. 4. Persistently gives large unassessed fluid boluses despite clear fluid overload and worsening organ compromise.
sections.8. Curveball: The ICU registrar reports a repeat correctly measured IAP of 29 mmHg with anuria despite gastric decompression. Candidate must urgently activate consultant-led decompressive laparotomy, not wait for another scan.

stations.title: DKA Presenting as Abdominal Pain
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-323 DKA Presenting as Abdominal Pain

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B — B2-323 DKA Presenting as Abdominal Pain Critical care | 8-minute station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 24-year-old adult with type 1 diabetes is referred for suspected appendicitis after 18 hours of abdominal pain and vomiting. They missed insulin doses while unwell, are thirsty and tachypnoeic. The abdomen is diffusely tender without guarding. Explain your interpretation and immediate management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use the eight prompts below in sequence; release findings when asked. Award a band per grid row based on actual actions stated. Safety-critical omissions override an otherwise fluent performance.
sections.3. Patient / team actor brief: The patient asks: “I was told I need my appendix out. Why are you treating my diabetes first?” Do not volunteer additional results.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and data: 1. Initial approach — ABCDE; assess dehydration, mental state and haemodynamic instability; call diabetes/medical team. 2. History and examination — Insulin omission, infection, vomiting, polyuria/polydipsia; look for focal peritonism, pregnancy possibility, precipitating illness. 3. Interpret results — Hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis diagnostic of DKA; Kussmaul breathing; abdominal pain can be metabolic. 4. First investigations — Bedside capillary glucose and blood ketones, VBG pH/bicarbonate, U&Es/potassium, ECG, infection assessment and pregnancy test if relevant. 5. Initial fluids — Begin IV 0.9% sodium chloride according to adult JBDS pathway with assessment for shock, cardiac/renal comorbidity and input/output. 6. Insulin and potassium — Fixed-rate IV insulin 0.1 units/kg/h once safe with potassium assessment; continue usual long-acting basal insulin if already prescribed; follow potassium replacement algorithm. 7. Ongoing reassessment — Hourly capillary glucose and ketones; regular VBG/electrolytes and urine output; add 10% dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L while continuing insulin. 8. Surgical decision — Reassess abdomen after DKA treatment; urgent surgical
sections.5. Case findings / interpretation: HR 118/min, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 30/min with deep respirations, glucose 24 mmol/L, capillary ketones 5.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, potassium 4.7 mmol/L. Key interpretation: DKA is a metabolic cause of acute abdominal pain; the abdomen must be reassessed during correction.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Assumes appendicitis and ignores ketones and acidosis. Identifies DKA as likely explanation for abdominal pain. Uses all three biochemical features and respiratory compensation to establish DKA. Initial safety Sends to theatre without resuscitation or senior review. Assesses ABCDE, perfusion and mental state and contacts medical team. Organises concurrent high-acuity monitoring, surgical review if needed and diabetes specialist input. History Does not ask about diabetes or insulin omission. Elicits missed insulin, illness, polyuria, vomiting and pain evolution. Targets precipitant, pregnancy possibility and high-risk concurrent surgical findings. Investigations Only requests abdominal imaging. Orders capillary ketones, glucose, VBG, electrolytes, ECG and precipitant checks. Prioritises repeated ketone and potassium measures, renal function and tailored infection tests. Fluid treatment Withholds needed IV fluids or gives unmonitored excess. Starts 0.9% saline under JBDS pathway with reassessment. Adjusts pace to circulatory status and cardiorenal risk, recording urine and balance. Insulin/potassium Gives insulin without checking K or sto
sections.7. Four critical fails: 1. Proceeds to avoidable emergency abdominal surgery without recognising overt DKA. 2. Starts IV insulin despite severe hypokalaemia without correcting/escalating potassium risk. 3. Stops insulin solely because glucose normalises while ketonaemia persists. 4. Fails to escalate haemodynamic instability, reduced consciousness or worsening acidosis.
sections.8. Curveball: Two hours into treatment glucose is 13.2 mmol/L but ketones remain 3.7 mmol/L. Candidate adds 10% dextrose according to protocol and continues insulin, monitoring potassium; does not declare DKA resolved.

stations.title: Breathless After Transfusion TACO or TRALI
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-324 Breathless After Transfusion TACO or TRALI

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-324 — Breathless After Transfusion: TACO or TRALI? Critical care | 8-minute station | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are surgical registrar. A 76-year-old is breathless 30 minutes after starting red-cell transfusion after colectomy: RR 30, SpO₂ 85% on air, BP 175/95, crackles, raised JVP and fluid balance +2.5 L. Explain immediate management and differential; no actual blood product or image is supplied.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Ask all eight prompts. Reward immediate transfusion cessation and ABCDE before diagnostic debates. The case favours TACO but candidates must consider TRALI and other dangerous transfusion reactions.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse says “Shall I just turn the blood down?” If asked, temperature 37.1°C, no rash/wheeze; CXR report: bilateral pulmonary opacities; urine output reduced.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. First action? — Stop the transfusion immediately; summon help; maintain IV access with fresh line and appropriate fluid; ABCDE and oxygen. 2. What further checks? — Confirm identity/blood unit labels, examine bag, retain bag and set; contact transfusion lab urgently. 3. Clinical interpretation? — BP 175/95, raised JVP, positive 2.5 L balance and crackles favour TACO, but do not assume diagnosis before assessment. 4. How distinguish TACO/TRALI? — TACO: circulatory overload, hypertension, fluid positive, supportive echo/BNP, diuretic response. TRALI: acute hypoxaemia with non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, no primary overload; may be hypotensive. 5. Investigations? — SpO₂, ABG, CXR described verbally, ECG, FBC/U&E; fluid balance, consider BNP/NT-proBNP and echocardiography as adjuncts; additional reaction tests with lab. 6. Immediate treatment? — Sit upright if tolerated, oxygen/titrate, monitored care, consider IV loop diuretic for probable TACO after assessment; do not give routine diuretics for TRALI. 7. Other dangerous reactions? — Exclude anaphylaxis, acute haemolysis, bacterial contamination/sepsis, bleeding and cardiac causes using bedside findings. 8. Next actions? — Escala
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Misses acute transfusion reaction despite new dyspnoea. Identifies severe reaction with respiratory compromise during blood administration. Names differential early and recognises simultaneous postoperative risks. Immediate transfusion action Continues current unit while assessing. Stops unit at once and preserves access with new giving set. Coordinates stopping, line preservation and checking component identity rapidly. ABCDE Does not assess airway/oxygenation or escalate SpO₂ 85%. Calls help, examines ABCDE and gives oxygen with monitoring. Anticipates ventilatory support, repeats observations and defines ICU triggers. TACO clues Ignores fluid balance/JVP and treats all pulmonary oedema as TRALI. Identifies hypertension, JVP and positive balance as supportive of TACO. Explains why features favour but do not definitively establish TACO. TRALI clues States any transfusion dyspnoea equals volume overload. Describes TRALI as acute non-cardiogenic lung injury without primary overload. Notes mixed presentations and need for integrated imaging and haemodynamic review. Investigations Orders no relevant bedside/lab tests. Requests ABG, CXR rep
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: CF1: Allows the implicated transfusion to continue despite new severe respiratory compromise. CF2: Fails to provide urgent ABCDE/oxygen/help for SpO₂ 85%. CF3: Deliberately administers a large indiscriminate fluid bolus in this hypertensive overloaded presentation without reassessment. CF4: Discards the implicated unit and set and does not inform transfusion service, preventing reaction investigation.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: The nurse reports that the patient was given IV furosemide earlier and remains dyspnoeic. Candidate must not interpret lack of immediate response as proof of TRALI; reassess oxygenation, overload and other postoperative causes, escalate.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “Stop this transfusion now; keep access open through a new set and call the transfusion laboratory.” 2. “Hypertension and positive balance support TACO, but severe hypoxia needs ABCDE and investigation regardless of label.” 3. “I would reassess response to treatment and involve senior anaesthesia/critical care rather than automatically restart blood.”

stations.title: Surface Anatomy of the Inguinal Region
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-325 Surface Anatomy of the Inguinal Region

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-325 — Surface Anatomy of the Inguinal Region Applied surgical anatomy / viva | 8-minute station | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: On an anatomical model (not a patient), verbally surface-mark the inguinal region and demonstrate clinical relationships relevant to groin surgery. No images or real intimate examination are required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Provide an unlabelled anatomical model or ask the candidate to describe every mark verbally; test the distinct midpoints and vascular relationships. Eight prompts are separate competencies.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner acts as junior colleague asking: “Is the mid-inguinal point the same as halfway along the inguinal ligament?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. Landmarks to identify? — ASIS, pubic tubercle, pubic symphysis, femoral pulse; explain consent/exposure and compare sides. 2. Ligament surface line? — Draw ASIS to pubic tubercle: inguinal ligament; not ASIS to symphysis. 3. Deep ring? — About 1–1.5 cm above midpoint of inguinal ligament, an opening in transversalis fascia lateral to inferior epigastric vessels. 4. Superficial ring? — Above and lateral to pubic tubercle; opening in external oblique aponeurosis. 5. Mid-inguinal point? — Midway ASIS to pubic symphysis, for femoral arterial pulse; not same as ligament midpoint. 6. Canal boundaries? — Anterior external oblique aponeurosis; posterior transversalis fascia, reinforced medially; roof arching internal oblique/transversus; floor inguinal ligament. 7. Hernia relations? — Indirect lateral and direct medial to inferior epigastric vessels; femoral hernia below ligament, generally medial to femoral vein. 8. Clinical application? — Femoral NAVL lateral to medial (nerve, artery, vein, lymphatic); femoral triangle bordered by inguinal ligament, sartorius, adductor longus; avoid nerve/vascular injury.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Orientation Cannot identify ASIS/pubis accurately. Identifies ASIS, pubic tubercle and pubic symphysis correctly. Builds reproducible bilateral landmarks and explains clinical positioning. Ligament Marks ligament to pubic symphysis. Marks ASIS-to-pubic-tubercle ligament. Correlates ligament with canal floor and femoral structures below. Deep ring Places deep ring at superficial ring or medial to epigastric vessels. Marks above ligament midpoint; describes transversalis opening. Adds lateral inferior epigastric relation and individual variability. Superficial ring Misplaces at ASIS. Identifies superolateral pubic tubercle in external oblique. Explains course of canal between the rings. Femoral artery Equates ligament midpoint with mid-inguinal point. Defines femoral pulse midpoint ASIS-to-pubic symphysis. Contrasts both midpoints and their different anatomical uses. Canal walls Cannot name major wall components. Correctly names anterior/posterior/roof/floor core structures. Clarifies medial reinforcement and avoids a universal “conjoint tendon”. Vessel / nerve relationships Places femoral vein lateral to artery. Gives lateral-to-medial nerve, artery
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: CF1: Uses the pubic symphysis instead of the pubic tubercle to locate the inguinal ligament and then plans a procedure from the incorrect line. CF2: Confuses femoral artery and vein positions when proposing a vascular puncture or repair. CF3: States an indirect hernia is medial to inferior epigastric vessels and uses this wrong relationship to guide dissection. CF4: Marks the superficial ring over the femoral canal and proposes blind dissection at that site without confirming anatomy.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: The trainee points halfway between ASIS and the pubic symphysis and calls this the deep ring. Correct the mistake sensitively: that is the mid-inguinal point for the femoral pulse; locate deep ring above midpoint ASIS-to-pubic tubercle.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “These are different midpoints: symphysis for femoral pulse, pubic tubercle for the ligament.” 2. “The deep ring is above the midpoint of the ligament and lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.” 3. “Before any incision or needle, I would re-identify landmarks and confirm the expected anatomy.”

stations.title: Abdominal Incisions and the Layers Divided
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-326 Abdominal Incisions and the Layers Divided

sections.preamble: B2-326 — Abdominal Incisions and the Layers Divided AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / anatomy | 8-minute station | Draft — 13 October 2026 Educational material; not an official MRCS Part B marking scheme. Independent clinical sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar teaching a core trainee before an elective abdominal operation. Explain the layers crossed by common open abdominal incisions, contrast rectus sheath anatomy above and below the arcuate line, and identify structures at risk. You are given verbal scenarios; no diagrams or images are required.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight prompts should be asked in sequence. Require anatomical accuracy and an explanation of implications for safe access; this is an anatomy viva, not a demonstration of incision-making.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The examiner acts as a junior trainee asking how tissue layers differ between incisions. No patient actor.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. Midline laparotomy: Skin → subcutaneous tissue (Camper/Scarpa where distinguishable) → linea alba → transversalis fascia/extraperitoneal fat → parietal peritoneum. Rectus muscle is not normally divided; note controlled entry and nearby viscera. 2. Paramedian incision: Skin/subcutaneous tissues → anterior rectus sheath → rectus displaced laterally (or split, technique-dependent) → posterior sheath above arcuate line → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal fat → peritoneum; identify epigastric vessels. 3. Arcuate line: Above: anterior sheath external oblique plus anterior internal oblique; posterior sheath posterior internal oblique plus transversus abdominis aponeurosis. Below: all three aponeuroses anterior; posteriorly transversalis fascia (no substantial posterior aponeurotic sheath). 4. Right subcostal/Kocher: Describe subcostal route through skin, fat, anterior musculoaponeurotic layers and upper abdominal wall musculature as encountered, transversalis fascia and peritoneum; discuss segmental nerves/vessels and use for hepatobiliary access. Tissue division varies with medial versus lateral extension. 5. Pfannenstiel: Curved suprapubic skin/subcutaneous incision → anterior r
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Task framing Cannot describe incision options or confuses anatomy with indications. Sets out the requested comparison and uses correct surface reference points. Prioritises choice of access by exposure, anatomy and risk without wandering into operative trivia. Midline sequence Claims rectus is routinely cut or omits peritoneum. Names linea alba, deep fascia/fat and peritoneum in correct order. Separates linea alba from rectus sheath and highlights safe entry with adhesions. Paramedian technique Calls paramedian identical to midline or ignores rectus and vessels. Describes anterior sheath, rectus displacement and posterior layers when present. Explains technique variability and vulnerability of epigastric branches. Arcuate-line anatomy Incorrectly states substantial posterior rectus sheath exists below arcuate line. Accurately distinguishes aponeurotic sheath above and below. Connects anatomical transition to fascial plane identification and vascular protection. Subcostal incision Misidentifies it as lower abdominal or ignores muscle/neurovascular layers. Describes upper subcostal route, variable muscle division and biliary access. Anticipates segme
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: Advises blind entry into the peritoneal cavity in a patient with possible adhesions without protection or assessment. Recommends deliberately dividing the inferior epigastric vessels without recognition or haemostatic plan. Teaches a Pfannenstiel incision without recognising the bladder as an at-risk structure. Misidentifies the posterior rectus sheath below the arcuate line as a substantial aponeurotic layer and uses that error to advise unsafe dissection.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: The trainee says: “Below the arcuate line I can close the posterior rectus sheath because it is still there.” Correct this explicitly: no substantial posterior aponeurotic sheath exists there; describe the transversalis fascia/deep tissues and the fascial closure that matters.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: “I incorrectly described the layers below the arcuate line; the three aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus there, with transversalis fascia behind.” “For Pfannenstiel I should have named protection of the bladder and separating, rather than routinely cutting, the rectus muscles.” “Before entering the abdomen, I would re-identify the anatomical plane and protect underlying viscera rather than continuing blind.”

stations.title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-327 Brachial Plexus Injuries

sections.preamble: B2-327 — Brachial Plexus Injuries AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / trauma examination | 8-minute station | Draft — 13 October 2026 Educational material; not an official MRCS Part B marking scheme. Independent clinical sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are reviewing a 24-year-old motorcyclist after a high-energy traction injury to the right shoulder. The patient has weakness and altered sensation in the right arm. Explain the immediate assessment, localisation of plexus injury and next investigations and referral. The examiner supplies clinical findings in words.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess trauma safety, limb perfusion, root/trunk localisation and early specialist referral. Do not overstate the ability of early electrodiagnostic testing to exclude severe injury.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is distressed by arm weakness and severe burning pain. If asked, says weakness started immediately after the crash. No previous neurological symptoms.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected respons: 1. Initial priorities: ABCDE with cervical spine and associated chest/shoulder injuries; urgent examination of pulses, capillary refill, temperature, expanding haematoma, respiratory difficulty and neurological deficit; call trauma/vascular teams for threatened limb. 2. Mechanism and patterns: Traction between neck and shoulder can affect upper roots/trunk (C5–C6); overhead traction can damage lower plexus (C8–T1); differentiate a focal peripheral nerve deficit from widespread plexopathy. 3. Focused motor assessment: Document shoulder abduction/external rotation, elbow flexion/extension, wrist extension, finger flexion, finger abduction, thumb opposition, with MRC grades and side comparison. 4. Sensory/reflex examination: Map C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm; biceps and triceps reflexes; assess neck pain and cervical neurological signs. 5. Pattern localisation: Upper plexus: impaired deltoid/biceps and shoulder external rotation (Erb-type). Lower: intrinsic hand weakness and ulnar-side sensory involvement (Klumpke-type). Explain overlap and that patterns are not absolute. 6. Root avulsion clues: Severe burning/deafferentation pai
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Trauma priorities Focuses on arm weakness while ignoring life-threatening chest/neck injuries. Begins with ABCDE, spinal and associated injuries. Integrates chest, cervical spine, shoulder girdle and limb priorities coherently. Vascular assessment Does not check pulses or recognises expanding haematoma too late. Documents radial/ulnar pulses, perfusion and vascular red flags. Escalates suspected arterial injury immediately and considers urgent vascular imaging. Mechanism Calls every weakness a radial nerve palsy without mechanism. Connects traction mechanism to upper/lower plexus distribution. Recognises alternative isolated nerve or cervical root patterns and polytrauma context. Motor localisation No graded examination or skips intrinsic hand function. Tests shoulder, elbow, wrist, digits and hand intrinsics systematically. Uses MRC grading and links muscle groups to roots/trunks/terminal branches. Sensory/reflex mapping Reports vague numbness without dermatomes or reflexes. Checks key C5–T1 sensory points and biceps/triceps reflexes. Correlates motor and sensory abnormalities to refine lesion level and alternatives. Preganglionic red flags Misses
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: Fails to assess limb pulses/perfusion despite a high-energy shoulder-girdle injury and possible vascular injury. Dismisses a dense post-traumatic arm paralysis as a simple neuropraxia and arranges no urgent specialist assessment. Ignores signs of cervical spine or associated thoracic trauma while examining the arm. Treats a normal very-early EMG/NCS as proof that no major brachial plexus injury exists.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: Examination reveals ipsilateral partial ptosis and miosis with profound hand intrinsic weakness. Identify a possible lower-root preganglionic avulsion and explain urgent specialist referral, without implying Horner syndrome alone proves avulsion.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: “I must document pulses and hand perfusion now; traction injuries can coexist with axillary or subclavian arterial injury.” “I should not reassure based on an early normal nerve-conduction result; timing and specialist imaging matter.” “The new Horner syndrome changes my localisation: I would urgently discuss possible lower-root avulsion with a plexus specialist.”

stations.title: Lower Limb Nerve Injuries
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-328 Lower Limb Nerve Injuries

sections.preamble: B2-328 — Lower Limb Nerve Injuries AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / examination | 8-minute station | Draft · 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 42-year-old develops right foot drop following a fibular neck fracture fixed yesterday. He has intact distal perfusion and marked weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Explain your assessment, immediate actions, differential, definitive pathway and communication.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use the supplied scenario only; reveal additional findings in response to focused questions. Score stated actions, prioritising patient safety and localisation or anatomy. No patient-contact practical procedure required.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient asks whether the weakness means permanent nerve damage. He has no back pain, sphincter symptoms or new severe leg pain.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Immediate priorities — Reassess limb perfusion and compartments, examine wounds/splint tightness and evolving neurological deficit; urgent review of new postoperative deficit. Focused motor assessment — Test ankle dorsiflexion and great-toe extension (deep fibular), eversion (superficial fibular), inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve/L5), and plantar flexion. Sensory mapping — First dorsal web space = deep fibular; dorsum of foot = superficial fibular; sole = tibial; lateral leg can reflect common fibular distribution. Localisation — Fibular-head common fibular neuropathy causes weak dorsiflexion and eversion with relatively preserved inversion; L5 radiculopathy may also weaken inversion/hip abduction. Sciatic comparison — A proximal sciatic lesion after hip trauma/replacement may affect hamstrings plus both fibular and tibial divisions; assess plantar flexion and sole sensation. Urgent exclusion — Escalate suspected compartment syndrome, compressive haematoma, tight cast, associated vascular injury or significant new deficit; do not postpone for outpatient nerve studies. Investigations and support — Review operation/fracture and imaging, obtain appropriate imaging for compr
sections.5. Clinical frame and diagnostic reasoni: Examine and stabilise first, then localise the lesion; do not allow an anatomical label to replace exclusion of a time-critical limb threat.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Award Fail / Pass / High-performance for each domain. A critical fail overrides an otherwise strong performance; descriptors are station-specific. Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety and prioritisation Misses acute limb risk Checks perfusion and limb compartments before nerve localisation Reassesses splint pressure, serial signs and time-sensitive escalation History / mechanism Does not ask fracture/operation course Elicits timing, trauma, casts and progression Integrates pre/postoperative deficits and red flags Examination or operative anatomy Does not test ankle movements Tests dorsiflexion, eversion, inversion, plantar flexion and key sensation Links precise movement pattern to fibular versus tibial versus L5 Differential and localisation Calls every foot drop L5 radiculopathy Contrasts fibular neck lesion with root and sciatic causes Uses preserved inversion and hamstring involvement to refine localisation Investigations Orders delayed EMG as sole assessment Reviews fracture/operative records and urgent structural concern Requests targeted imaging for compressive haematoma and coordinates later neurophysiology Immediate management Provides routine reassurance despite fresh
sections.7. Critical fails — four: Critical fail 1: Attributes new foot drop to routine swelling without urgent neurovascular/compartment reassessment. Critical fail 2: Misses disproportionate escalating pain and delays emergency assessment for compartment syndrome. Critical fail 3: Fails to assess and record inversion, eversion, plantar flexion and cutaneous territories before declaring a lesion site. Critical fail 4: Discharges progressive postoperative weakness without senior review, splint/pressure assessment or follow-up plan.
sections.8. Curveball: Two hours later the patient reports increasing disproportionate leg pain and pain on passive toe stretch despite strong palpable pulses. Urgent compartment syndrome assessment and senior surgical escalation; pulses do not exclude it.

stations.title: Ureteric Injury During Pelvic Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-329 Ureteric Injury During Pelvic Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-329 — Ureteric Injury During Pelvic Surgery AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / intraoperative complication | 8-minute station | Draft · 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: During difficult sigmoid resection for diverticular disease, a tubular structure near the left pelvic brim is divided. There is concern it may be the left ureter. Explain your assessment, immediate actions, differential, definitive pathway and communication.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use the supplied scenario only; reveal additional findings in response to focused questions. Score stated actions, prioritising patient safety and localisation or anatomy. No patient-contact practical procedure required.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The simulated senior surgeon asks: “How would you identify the structure, deal with the injury and later explain this complication to the patient?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Course and danger points — Trace ureter from renal pelvis over psoas, crossing anterior to iliac vessels at pelvic brim, along lateral pelvic wall and beneath uterine artery in women; note sigmoid mesentery, ovarian vessels and bladder entry. Risk factors — Prior pelvic operations, inflammation/diverticulitis, malignancy, radiotherapy, distorted anatomy and difficult haemostasis increase risk. Immediate action — Stop dissection, protect operative field and kidneys, call consultant/urologist immediately; avoid blindly clipping or further devascularising the suspected ureter. Confirm injury — Directly inspect course and viable ends; consider intraoperative cystoscopy, retrograde pyelography/stent or appropriate dye assessment with urologist; absence of visible urine leakage does not exclude thermal/partial injury. Principles of repair — Early specialist repair when feasible; debride nonviable tissue, tension-free watertight mucosa-to-mucosa reconstruction over stent with drainage and preserved blood supply. Repair by level — Upper/mid ureter may allow ureteroureterostomy if viable and tension-free; distal injury commonly needs ureteroneocystostomy, sometimes psoas hitch or Boari flap
sections.5. Clinical frame and diagnostic reasoni: Maintain suspicion in distorted anatomy; classify mechanism, site and vascularity before deciding immediate reconstruction versus diversion.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Award Fail / Pass / High-performance for each domain. A critical fail overrides an otherwise strong performance; descriptors are station-specific.
