Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety and prioritisation Continues cutting suspicious structure Stops dissection and calls senior/urologist Protects perfusion and avoids extending damage History / mechanism Ignores altered anatomy Identifies diverticulitis, past surgery and radiation Explains why inflamed sigmoid mesentery raises risk Examination or operative anatomy Cannot identify ureter Traces pelvic brim and sidewall course Names uterine-artery crossing and bladder insertion danger points Differential and localisation Assumes no leak means no injury Considers ligature, crush, thermal and transection Distinguishes delayed devascularisation from simple division Investigations Offers no way to confirm Uses direct inspection and urological retrograde assessment Selects delayed-phase CT for suspected postoperative leak Immediate management Blindly ties suspicious structure Calls urology and protects viable ureter ends Coordinates immediate reconstruction versus diversion depending on stability Definitive treatment and referral Recommen
sections.7. Critical fails — four: Critical fail 1: Recognises probable transection but continues operating without identifying or urgently involving urology. Critical fail 2: Blindly ligates or cauterises the structure, risking further ureteric damage or devascularisation. Critical fail 3: Dismisses postoperative urine-like drain output and fever without testing for ureteric leak or arranging urinary drainage. Critical fail 4: Conceals confirmed ureteric injury from the patient or omits candour, documented disclosure and escalation.
sections.8. Curveball: On postoperative day 4 a patient develops fever and high-output clear fluid from the pelvic drain after an apparently uncomplicated colectomy. Test drain fluid creatinine, investigate urinary leak with delayed-phase CT urography, treat sepsis and request urgent urology/drainage.

stations.title: Portal Hypertension and Portosystemic Anastomoses
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-330 Portal Hypertension and Portosystemic Anastomoses

sections.preamble: B2-330 — Portal Hypertension and Portosystemic Anastomoses AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied anatomy / knowledge | 8-minute structured station | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are asked to explain the portosystemic venous anastomoses in a 56-year-old with cirrhosis, splenomegaly and previously banded oesophageal varices. Describe the anatomy, clinical relevance and the role of TIPS.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use verbal anatomy rather than images. Eight separate prompts. Reward accurate vein names and recognition of bleeding priorities; do not expect advanced interventional technical details.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient asks: “Where do these swollen veins come from, and would a shunt fix my liver?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. What produces portal hypertension? — Raised portal vascular resistance, commonly cirrhosis, with increased collateral flow. 2. How is the portal vein formed? — Splenic and superior mesenteric veins join posterior to neck of pancreas; recognise important tributaries. 3. Explain distal oesophageal varices. — Left gastric portal tributary communicates with oesophageal veins into azygos system. 4. Give two other portosystemic channels. — Superior rectal to middle/inferior rectal; paraumbilical to abdominal-wall systemic veins. 5. What would you examine and investigate? — Ascites, splenomegaly, collaterals; bloods, Doppler and endoscopy as appropriate. 6. How do you prevent and treat variceal bleeding? — Individualised non-selective beta-blockers or endoscopic banding; urgent resuscitation, vasoactive therapy, antibiotics and endoscopy if bleeding. 7. What is TIPS and when might it help? — Radiological tract from portal to hepatic vein; selected high-risk/refractory bleeding and refractory ascites. 8. What are TIPS limitations? — Hepatic encephalopathy, liver failure, cardiac decompensation; specialised MDT assessment.
sections.5. Clinical scenario and supplied findin: Stable clinic scenario: prior oesophageal banding, ascites controlled with medication, palpable spleen; haemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 95 × 10⁹/L. No image is needed.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and physiology Calls collateral veins the primary disease; misses portal pressure gradient. Connects raised portal resistance with collateral formation and splenomegaly. Explains cirrhotic sinusoidal resistance, splanchnic inflow and clinically significant portal hypertension. Portal venous anatomy Cannot describe formation of portal vein or major tributaries. Identifies SMV + splenic vein, and left gastric, short gastric and superior rectal drainage. Accurately relates inferior mesenteric drainage variability and site-specific tributaries. Oesophageal collaterals Misidentifies oesophageal varices as arterial vessels. Links left gastric portal tributary to azygos/hemiazygos systemic veins. Explains location in distal oesophageal submucosa and haemorrhage risk. Other collateral sites Does not identify rectal or paraumbilical pathways. Describes superior rectal to middle/inferior rectal veins and paraumbilical to superficial epigastric veins. Distinguishes anorectal varices from haemorrhoids and recognises retroperitoneal/stomal ectopic sites. Clinical findings Misses haematemesis as urgent; claims caput medusae is universal. Elicits vari
sections.7. Four critical fails: 1. Fails to initiate emergency resuscitation/escalation when examiner reveals active massive haematemesis. 2. Recommends an unprotected routine endoscopy or outpatient follow-up despite haemodynamic instability. 3. States all patients with varices should undergo TIPS irrespective of hepatic or cardiac reserve. 4. Assures patient that a TIPS shunt reverses cirrhosis or eliminates risk of encephalopathy.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: Halfway through, the examiner says he is vomiting fresh blood and is hypotensive: interrupt anatomy explanation, call for help, ABCDE, IV access, bloods/crossmatch, urgent variceal bleeding pathway and endoscopy.

stations.title: Gangrene Dry Wet and Gas
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-331 Gangrene Dry Wet and Gas

sections.preamble: B2-331 — Gangrene Dry Wet and Gas AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied pathology / urgent surgery | 8-minute structured station | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are reviewing a 68-year-old with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease presenting with a black toe. Distinguish dry, wet and gas gangrene and give a safe management plan for each.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Provide three successive described cases; candidate must adapt urgency. Do not make radiological gas mandatory for diagnosis. Examine ability to separate limb ischaemia from overwhelming necrotising infection.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: A worried relative asks: “Is it just dead skin, or could this spread? Will they need an amputation?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Classify the three patterns. — Dry: ischaemic desiccated demarcation; wet: infected moist necrosis; gas: fulminant myonecrosis often clostridial. 2. Which historical features matter? — PAD, diabetes, immunosuppression, trauma, rapid pain progression, fever, systemic signs. 3. What examination is essential? — Obs and ABCDE; pulses, Doppler if available, perfusion, sensory/motor status, extent, crepitus. 4. Initial investigations? — FBC, renal, glucose, lactate, cultures; vascular studies when appropriate; imaging only if safe and helpful. 5. Management of stable dry gangrene? — Protect area and obtain vascular assessment for potential revascularisation, without automatic antibiotics if uninfected. 6. Management of wet gangrene? — Admission, urgent surgical source control, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, sepsis care and vascular input. 7. Management of suspected gas gangrene? — Immediate surgical exploration and radical debridement with antibiotics; do not delay for imaging or adjunctive oxygen. 8. Counsel about treatment and outcomes. — Explain urgency, repeat operations, potential amputation, organ support and informed communication.
sections.5. Clinical scenario and supplied findin: Case A: cool, dry, well-demarcated black second toe, afebrile, poor pedal pulses. Case B: malodorous wet forefoot necrosis, fever 39 °C, tachycardia. Case C (curveball): rapidly progressive post-trauma thigh necrosis with shock.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and classification Calls every black toe an immediate clostridial infection. Differentiates dry ischaemic mummification, infected wet gangrene and rapidly progressive gas myonecrosis. Identifies grey areas: infected ischaemia can rapidly become wet gangrene; tissue gas is not pathognomonic for clostridia. History and risks Misses diabetes, peripheral arterial disease or acute deterioration. Asks pain progression, wound/trauma, fever, diabetes, PAD, smoking and systemic symptoms. Probes immunosuppression, prior vascular procedures and sudden severe pain out of proportion. Focused examination Fails to check vital signs or limb perfusion. Performs ABCDE if unwell; assesses demarcation, discharge, pulses, capillary refill, sensation and crepitus. Documents neurovascular findings and proximal spread while avoiding aggressive manipulation. Sepsis and shock Ignores hypotension and altered consciousness. Recognises systemic toxicity; oxygen if needed, IV access, bloods/lactate, cultures, careful fluids and escalation. Coordinates immediate sepsis resuscitation with urgent operative source control and critical care. Investigations Waits for CT/M
sections.7. Four critical fails: 1. Sends a septic patient with wet gangrene home with only oral antibiotics. 2. Delays emergency exploration of suspected gas gangrene to obtain CT, MRI or hyperbaric oxygen. 3. Fails to recognise shock or initiate resuscitation and urgent senior/anaesthetic help. 4. Plans revascularisation alone for rapidly spreading infected necrotic tissue without source control.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: Case changes: a different patient has excruciating thigh pain after penetrating trauma, rapidly spreading bronze discolouration, bullae and BP 82/48: treat as suspected necrotising infection/gas gangrene and activate emergency theatre pathway.

stations.title: Tuberculosis in Surgical Practice
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-332 Tuberculosis in Surgical Practice

sections.preamble: B2-332 — Tuberculosis in Surgical Practice AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute station | DRAFT — independent specialist sign-off required | 13 October 2026 Not an official MRCS marking scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only in exam mode; remaining sections are examiner material.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar assessing a 34-year-old with a slowly enlarging, painless cervical node, weight loss and recent travel to a country with high TB incidence. The examiner will also ask about a patient with suspected ileocaecal TB. Explain safe diagnostic, surgical and public-health management.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess applied clinical/surgical reasoning, explicit safety actions and realistic escalation. Award marks for actions stated, not assumed. Reveal scenario information only when asked. Eight prompts follow; no real patient examination or images required.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient has had 8 weeks of painless swelling, intermittent fever, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. No known TB treatment. Worried the lump is cancer and asks whether it can simply be removed.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: Scenario data: Neck ultrasound: 2.8 cm necrotic node. Chest X-ray: no obvious pulmonary infiltrates. In the abdominal extension: CT shows ileocaecal mural thickening with regional nodes and intermittent partial obstruction; patient is haemodynamically stable. 1. Immediate clinical assessment? — Ask about cough, haemoptysis, fever/night sweats, weight loss, exposure, prior TB, immunosuppression/HIV and obstructive symptoms; examine neck, chest, abdomen and nutritional status. 2. Differential diagnosis? — Lymphoma, metastatic head and neck malignancy, other infections and nontuberculous mycobacteria for the node; Crohn disease, malignancy and other infection for ileocaecal disease. 3. Isolation and respiratory assessment? — Ask about pulmonary symptoms, arrange chest X-ray and respiratory specimens where appropriate; apply airborne precautions according to local IPC if infectious pulmonary/laryngeal TB is suspected, not for all isolated extrapulmonary presentations. 4. Lymph-node diagnosis? — Discuss ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or biopsy; request histology/cytology, microscopy, mycobacterial culture and molecular testing as appropriate. Send fresh sterile specimen for culture
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety and triage Misses obstruction/perforation or infectious pulmonary risk. Assesses stability and symptoms of obstruction, perforation and pulmonary TB. Prioritises emergency surgical physiology and appropriate IPC in parallel. History and exposure Does not elicit TB exposure or systemic symptoms. Asks exposure, prior treatment, constitutional and respiratory symptoms. Adds immunosuppression, HIV risks, medication interactions and adherence barriers. Differential reasoning Calls every necrotic node TB and overlooks cancer. Names lymphoma/malignancy and inflammatory or infective mimics. Explains why histological and microbiological confirmation both matter. Specimen pathway Places the entire sample in formalin for culture. Separates unfixed culture material from fixed histology samples. Plans sampling with microbiology, including culture and molecular resistance testing. Investigations Uses IGRA alone to diagnose active TB. Requests appropriate imaging and tissue/respiratory testing. Chooses site-specific sampling and interprets negative rapid tests cautiously. Management Performs unnecessary immediate excision/resection. Arranges TB team-led an
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Sends the only biopsy specimen in formalin while requesting mycobacterial culture, destroying the culture opportunity. 2. Fails to assess or act on peritonitis/complete bowel obstruction in the abdominal extension. 3. Ignores suspected infectious pulmonary TB and permits unprotected exposure contrary to IPC advice. 4. Fails to arrange specialist TB management or statutory notification once active TB is suspected/established.
sections.7. Curveball: The node biopsy shows necrotising granulomas but the first molecular test is negative. Parenthetical examiner challenge: “Can we rule out TB?” — No: retain malignancy and other infections in differential; ensure culture/histology review and TB-specialist discussion.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I would correct the specimen request now: fresh sterile tissue for mycobacterial culture, separate formalin-fixed tissue for histology.” 2. “I cannot label the abdominal mass as TB alone; I will check for obstruction/peritonitis and obtain adequate tissue to exclude cancer and Crohn disease.” 3. “I will contact the TB service today for infection-control risk assessment, treatment planning and notification.”

stations.title: Decontamination and Sterilisation of Instruments
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-333 Decontamination and Sterilisation of Instruments

sections.preamble: B2-333 — Decontamination and Sterilisation of Instruments AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute station | DRAFT — independent specialist sign-off required | 13 October 2026 Not an official MRCS marking scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only in exam mode; remaining sections are examiner material.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in theatre. A reusable instrument tray arrives with visible biological debris after processing; the next patient is already anaesthetised. Explain the immediate action, the decontamination pathway and special precautions for prion risk and single-use devices.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess applied clinical/surgical reasoning, explicit safety actions and realistic escalation. Award marks for actions stated, not assumed. Reveal scenario information only when asked. Eight prompts follow; no real patient examination or images required.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Scrub practitioner reports blood-like residue on a hinged instrument from a wrapped tray labelled “sterile”. A second instrument in the same tray has a damaged hinge. The patient is stable and this is an elective laparoscopic operation.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: Scenario data: The tray has an apparently intact sterile wrap and cycle label. The theatre manager asks whether wiping the visible soil with antiseptic is enough. Later the examiner introduces a suspected CJD high-risk tissue procedure. 1. First action on contaminated tray? — Do not use the affected instruments; quarantine/reject compromised set, alert scrub practitioner, theatre coordinator and sterile services; obtain verified replacement and consider delay if safe instruments unavailable. 2. Cleaning versus disinfection versus sterilisation? — Explain cleaning removes soil, disinfection reduces viable microorganisms and validated sterilisation aims to inactivate all microbial life including spores; sterilisation cannot compensate for visible residual organic material. 3. Decontamination workflow? — Point-of-use care, safe transport, validated washer-disinfector or approved manual steps per device IFU, inspection/function testing, packaging, validated sterilisation, controlled storage and traceability. 4. Reusable device verification? — Check manufacturer instructions, device integrity, cycle records, packaging, expiry/status under local system, tracking and sterility assurance;
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate infection safety Uses visibly soiled “sterile” instrument. Rejects soiled tray/instrument and obtains verified replacement. Quarantines implicated devices and alerts sterile services for traceability. Definitions Claims a disinfectant wipe makes an instrument sterile. Distinguishes cleaning, disinfection and sterilisation accurately. Relates correct process selection to device IFU and risk classification. Cleaning process Skips soil removal before autoclaving. Describes approved cleaning followed by inspection before sterilisation. Specifies hinged joints/lumens, mechanical integrity and validated cleaning. Sterilisation assurance Accepts torn/wet pack because cycle label looks valid. Checks pack integrity, validated cycle evidence and instrument condition. Explains batch tracking, release criteria and response to failed process. Single-use governance Routinely resterilises a labelled single-use device in theatre. Identifies single-use designation and respects approved procurement pathway. Escalates ambiguous reprocessing claims to medical devices/governance leads. Prion risk States normal autoclaving reliably destroys prions. Recognises
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Uses an instrument with visible biological soil in the sterile field despite warning. 2. Permits routine wipe-clean and immediate reuse of an invasive surgical instrument as a substitute for validated reprocessing. 3. Uses suspected CJD high-risk instruments in another case without following specialist quarantine/traceability requirements. 4. Proceeding with elective surgery despite absence of a safe verified instrument set, without escalation.
sections.7. Curveball: The apparently sterile set contains one damaged instrument, but the theatre lead says the cycle passed. — Reject damaged device; a passed cycle does not guarantee physical integrity or safe use; document and replace.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. “A sterile cycle label does not overrule visible soil: I am removing and quarantining this set now.” 2. “I would not use a disinfectant wipe as a substitute for validated cleaning and sterilisation of invasive instruments.” 3. “For suspected prion exposure I will pause, identify the tissue and instrument traceability, and contact IPC and the decontamination lead.”

stations.title: Imaging and Radiation Safety in Pregnancy
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-334 Imaging and Radiation Safety in Pregnancy

sections.preamble: B2-334 — Imaging and Radiation Safety in Pregnancy AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / counselling | 8-minute structured station | DRAFT • independent review required | 13 October 2026 Not an official MRCS mark scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only; Sections 2–13 are examiner / feedback material.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar assessing a 27-year-old at 16 weeks’ gestation with fever, right iliac fossa pain and guarding. Ultrasound has not identified the appendix; she is haemodynamically stable. Explain the next investigation, assess the risks of imaging and agree a safe plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Evaluate choice of appropriate imaging, individualised risk–benefit discussion, escalation in clinical deterioration and accurate, non-alarmist consent. Provide written imaging results on request. Candidate must not be expected to memorise one fixed fetal dose for every CT protocol.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is worried: “Will a CT cause a miscarriage or cancer? Would it be safer to wait until after my baby is born?” She wants an understandable plan and an opportunity to ask questions.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Observations: T 38.4°C; HR 102; BP 118/70; focal right iliac fossa guarding. Obstetric ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy. Appendix not seen on abdominal ultrasound. MRI without gadolinium is available urgently. If candidate asks: MRI shows an enlarged, inflamed appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding but no collection. 1. Immediate assessment and differential? — ABCDE if unwell, pain pattern, obstetric and urinary symptoms, peritonism, sepsis; appendicitis, urinary infection/stone, ovarian pathology, obstetric causes. 2. Imaging selection after nondiagnostic ultrasound? — Urgent MRI abdomen/pelvis without gadolinium if available without harmful delay; communicate suspected appendicitis to radiologist and obstetric team. 3. What if MRI is unavailable or equivocal? — Discuss justified CT with radiology if clinically needed; pregnancy is not an absolute contraindication and diagnostic delay can harm mother and fetus. 4. What determines radiation risk? — Fetal absorbed dose, body region, scanning protocol, gestation; pelvic CT differs greatly from a chest radiograph; do not give a blanket numeric risk. 5. How would you counsel consent? — Explain benefit of identif
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial safety assessment Dismisses fever/guarding as normal pregnancy or omits observations. Identifies likely acute surgical pathology; checks haemodynamic state and peritonism. Adds pregnancy-specific and sepsis red flags, prioritising unstable physiology. Differential diagnosis Assumes appendicitis is proven by symptoms alone. Considers appendicitis, urinary, adnexal and obstetric causes. Explains how pregnancy changes examination and diagnostic uncertainty. First-line imaging Orders CT immediately without considering ultrasound/MRI availability. Recognises initial ultrasound was nondiagnostic and requests urgent MRI without gadolinium. Communicates focused imaging question and realistic urgency to radiologist. CT justification States CT is forbidden in pregnancy or risk-free. Uses CT if clinically necessary after weighing alternatives and delay. Individualises benefit/risk by field, protocol and gestation with radiology input. Radiation understanding Quotes invented universal fetal dose or claims all scans induce miscarriage. Differentiates ionising CT/X-ray from ultrasound/MRI and acknowledges dose dependence. Explains that deterministic harm
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Refuses all indicated CT solely due to pregnancy when MRI is unavailable and delay threatens serious harm. 2. Gives categorical reassurance that an indicated CT has zero fetal risk or guarantees miscarriage/teratogenicity. 3. Fails to resuscitate/escalate a newly shocked or peritonitic patient while awaiting imaging. 4. Administers gadolinium as routine MRI contrast without necessity assessment or specialist review.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: MRI scanner becomes unavailable for six hours; the patient develops rising lactate and spreading guarding. Explain why the choice between urgent CT and operative assessment changes.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “I was too categorical about CT: if delaying diagnosis risks maternal sepsis, I would urgently agree the most appropriate imaging with radiology.” 2. “I would first assess maternal physiology and involve senior surgery, anaesthetics and obstetrics; imaging must not delay source control if she deteriorates.” 3. “I would explain that fetal exposure depends on scan type and protocol, discuss the risk of non-diagnosis, and document a shared decision.”

stations.title: Anatomy of the Epidural Space
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-335 Anatomy of the Epidural Space

sections.preamble: B2-335 — Anatomy of the Epidural Space AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied anatomy / procedural safety | 8-minute structured station | DRAFT • independent review required | 13 October 2026 Not an official MRCS mark scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only; Sections 2–13 are examiner / feedback material.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate asked to describe the anatomical route of a midline lumbar epidural needle, define the epidural space, give the adult spinal cord termination level and explain the complications of inadvertent dural puncture. No invasive procedure is to be performed.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Ask for precise layers, relationships and clinical implications. The scenario is an adult undergoing abdominal surgery. Accept anatomical variation in conus termination; no claim that a surface landmark guarantees the spinal level.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Simulation setting: an anaesthetic trainee asks which layer signals entry into the epidural space and why an unexpectedly extensive block can be dangerous. No patient contact or consent exercise is required.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Describe a midline approach at L3–L4: skin → subcutaneous tissue → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space. Dura and arachnoid lie deeper. Epidural space contains fat, venous plexus and nerve roots; no CSF should be freely obtained through correctly placed epidural needle. 1. Define epidural space and limits. — Real space between vertebral canal/periosteal boundary and spinal dura; continuous cranio-caudally with lateral foraminal communication; not the CSF-filled subarachnoid space. 2. List needle layers in a midline lumbar approach. — Skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space; dura/arachnoid are deeper. 3. Contents and clinical importance? — Fat, connective tissue, internal vertebral venous plexus and spinal nerves; vascular puncture, systemic local anaesthetic toxicity or epidural haematoma risk. 4. Conus and dural sac termination? — Adult spinal cord typically ends near L1–L2 with individual variation; dural sac generally to S2; cauda equina extends below conus. 5. What is loss of resistance? — Reduced injection resistance when the needle enters epidural space after ligam
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Spatial definition Calls epidural space intrathecal or within spinal cord. Locates epidural outside dura and inside vertebral canal. Explains anterior, posterior and lateral relations and foraminal extension. Midline layers Places dura before ligamentum flavum or misses major ligaments. Correctly sequences skin, subcutis, supraspinous, interspinous, flavum and epidural. Explains why off-midline approach alters tissue sequence and landmarks. Contents Calls space empty and avascular. Names fat, veins and nerve roots. Relates venous plexus to vascular puncture/haematoma and local anaesthetic toxicity. Cord levels States cord routinely ends at S2 in an adult. Gives conus usually near L1–L2, dural sac roughly S2 and cauda equina below. Highlights normal variation and danger of assuming palpated surface levels are exact. Loss of resistance Assumes a pop proves safe placement or CSF return is normal. Defines transition through flavum to lower-resistance epidural space. Recognises false loss of resistance and variable ligamentum flavum anatomy. Epidural versus spinal Calls intrathecal CSF injection an epidural. Explains dura/arachnoid distinction and inten
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Describes intentional penetration of dura and arachnoid as the target for routine epidural placement. 2. Ignores apnoea or severe hypotension after an unexpectedly high neuraxial block instead of resuscitating and summoning help. 3. Dismisses progressive postoperative leg weakness and bladder dysfunction as normal epidural effect without urgent assessment. 4. Proposes proceeding with neuraxial needle placement despite an unassessed significant coagulation/anticoagulant contraindication.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: Two hours after an epidural, the patient develops worsening bilateral leg weakness and new urinary retention despite stopping local anaesthetic. Describe the concern and urgent next actions.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “I should distinguish epidural from intrathecal: the epidural space lies outside the dura, reached before any intentional dural puncture.” 2. “I should state adult conus typically lies near L1–L2 but varies, and verify level and anaesthetic safety rather than relying on one landmark.” 3. “With progressive weakness and urinary retention I would stop the infusion, contact anaesthesia and spinal services urgently, and arrange emergency MRI for possible epidural haematoma.”

stations.title: Choosing Sutures and Needles
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-336 Choosing Sutures and Needles

sections.preamble: B2-336 — Choosing Sutures and Needles AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute draft | 13 October 2026Educational draft — not an official MRCS marking scheme; independent specialist sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are assisting at elective colorectal surgery. The consultant asks you to choose sutures and needle types for midline fascia, bowel anastomosis, skin and a small vascular repair. Explain your choices and respond to a contaminated-wound variation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess defensible, tissue-specific material choices, needle geometry and safe closure; there is no requirement to recite brands or to demonstrate suturing.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner acts as consultant. Provide each tissue scenario in turn. If asked about a patient, the abdomen is elective, with no sepsis and adequate perfusion unless the curveball is introduced.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Material classes: Contrast absorbable (hydrolytic versus enzymatic degradation) and non-absorbable, with retained tensile strength versus full absorption. 2. Filament structure: Contrast mono- versus multifilament: drag, handling, knot security, tissue reaction and bacterial wicking; braided material is generally avoided in infected wounds. 3. Needles: Identify taper/round-bodied needles for delicate bowel and vessel, reverse-cutting for skin; match curvature and size to access and tissue. 4. Midline closure: Recommend continuous, slowly absorbable monofilament fascial closure with small bites in eligible elective midline laparotomy; avoid closing only fat or overtightening fascia. 5. Bowel: Choose appropriate absorbable monofilament with atraumatic taper needle; ensure perfusion, tension-free apposition, no luminal narrowing; technique depends on anastomotic method. 6. Skin: Offer interrupted monofilament non-absorbable or suitable absorbable subcuticular closure according to site and circumstances; avoid closing a heavily contaminated wound under tension. 7. Vascular repair: Select fine non-absorbable monofilament such as polypropylene on an atraumatic needle; protect intima a
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical prioritisation Selects materials by familiarity alone, disregarding tissue and contamination. Starts with tissue, loading and infection risk before choosing closure. Balances strength retention, tissue handling and contamination for all four sites. Relevant science / anatomy Confuses absorbability with tensile-strength loss or reverses monofilament properties. Distinguishes absorption, tensile-strength retention and mono/braided properties. Explains hydrolysis, capillarity, memory and knot security as clinical trade-offs. Applied decision-making Uses braided permanent suture indiscriminately for fascia, bowel and infected skin. Chooses defensible fascia, bowel, skin and vessel materials. Explains when wound contamination or poor perfusion changes closure strategy. Technical detail and accuracy Uses cutting needle for vessel or picks an excessively traumatic needle. Uses taper for bowel/vessel and reverse-cutting for skin, matched to tissue. Matches needle curvature, calibre and tissue thickness with atraumatic technique. Recognition of hazards Ignores tissue strangulation, dehiscence, leaks or needlestick hazards. Names dehiscence, bowel l
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: 1. Uses an inappropriate traumatic cutting needle for a delicate vascular repair despite explicit warning of intimal injury. 2. Continues closure after an unresolved missing-needle count without initiating the local retained-item procedure. 3. Closes a frankly infected, undrained wound as clean primary closure and disregards source control. 4. Constricts a vascular repair until distal flow is compromised and refuses to reassess.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: The surgeon now reports faecal contamination and questionable skin-edge perfusion. How does that change your closure plan? Expected: source control, irrigation/debridement where indicated, reconsider closure (possibly delayed), avoid poorly perfused tight closure; consult senior.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “I would stop the closure and reconcile the needle count before proceeding.” 2. “For this contaminated wound I would prioritise source control and reassess whether primary skin closure is safe.” 3. “I would replace that cutting needle with an atraumatic vascular needle and verify distal flow.”

stations.title: Surgical Haemostasis and Haemostatic Agents
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-337 Surgical Haemostasis and Haemostatic Agents

sections.preamble: B2-337 — Surgical Haemostasis and Haemostatic Agents AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute draft | 13 October 2026Educational draft — not an official MRCS marking scheme; independent specialist sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: During an elective colorectal procedure a diffuse oozing operative field persists despite basic haemostasis. Explain a systematic approach to mechanical, energy-based, topical and systemic haemostatic methods; the examiner will then introduce brisk arterial bleeding.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess prompt control of active bleeding, safe use of diathermy and topical adjuncts, appropriate TXA context and escalation; candidate must not mistake topical products for definitive vessel control.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner plays operating surgeon. Initial field has mild surface oozing with stable observations. In the curveball, bleeding becomes brisk, and the patient becomes hypotensive.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Immediate priorities: Ask for suction and exposure, identify bleeding point, apply direct pressure, monitor physiology, call anaesthetist and senior help as needed. 2. Mechanical techniques: Explain compression, clips, ties, transfixion or sutured ligation, vascular clamps and when direct surgical control is required. 3. Thermal methods: Compare monopolar and bipolar diathermy, adjacent thermal injury, insulation failure, airway/oxygen fire risks in suitable settings and energy use near bowel/vessels. 4. Topical agents: Describe oxidised cellulose, gelatin, collagen and fibrin sealants as adjuncts; avoid inappropriate intravascular or compressive application and follow product IFU. 5. TXA indications: Distinguish perioperative blood-loss prevention under NICE NG24 from urgent use in major traumatic bleeding per NG39; consider patient factors and indication. 6. Coagulopathy: Request FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, calcium, temperature, pH; discuss anticoagulant history and targeted replacement through major-haemorrhage protocol. 7. Bleeding complications: Recognise ongoing shock, concealed bleeding, anaemia, hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy and anastomotic/organ injury. 8. Clos
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical prioritisation Continues gentle diathermy during brisk haemorrhage without pressure or escalation. Suction/exposure, compression and rapid assessment precede definitive source control. Immediately leads coordinated bleeding control and resuscitation with anaesthesia. Relevant science / anatomy Cannot distinguish mechanical control from energy or topical adjuncts. Categorises mechanical, thermal, topical and systemic options accurately. Matches technique to vessel calibre, tissue and coagulopathy. Applied decision-making Chooses topical powder alone for spurting arterial bleeding. Uses direct control or ligation for identifiable vessel; adjunct for diffuse ooze. Switches strategy appropriately with haemodynamic instability and exposure limitations. Technical detail and accuracy Applies uncontrolled monopolar energy against bowel. Describes bipolar precision, safe clips/ties and energy awareness. Checks thermal spread, clip security and tissue viability before closure. Recognition of hazards Misses falling BP, expanding haematoma and ongoing blood loss. Recognises shock, concealed haemorrhage and dilutional coagulopathy. Anticipates temperat
sections.6. Critical fails — four specific unsafe: 1. Treats brisk arterial haemorrhage with topical haemostat alone and delays definitive vessel control. 2. Continues extensive energy application directly against vulnerable bowel despite an observed thermal injury risk. 3. Fails to summon anaesthetic/resuscitation support for hypotensive haemorrhage. 4. Conceals unresolved bleeding and closes without checking haemostasis, exposing the patient to preventable shock.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: A clipped arterial branch has slipped, with rapid blood loss and systolic BP 75 mmHg. Expected: direct pressure/clamp, announce emergency, senior/anaesthetic help, activate major haemorrhage protocol, identify and definitively secure vessel; topical product alone is inadequate.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “This is now arterial haemorrhage: I would compress it and gain definitive control rather than apply more sealant.” 2. “I would stop energy application near the bowel and assess for thermal damage.” 3. “I would inform the anaesthetist immediately, activate the major-haemorrhage pathway and request senior help.”

stations.title: Physiology of Laparoscopy
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-338 Physiology of Laparoscopy

sections.preamble: B2-338 — Physiology of Laparoscopy AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | Eight-minute station | Draft • 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are assisting at elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a 68-year-old patient with COPD and treated hypertension. Shortly after CO₂ pneumoperitoneum and head-up positioning, the peak airway pressure rises and blood pressure falls to 82/48 mmHg. Explain the physiology, interpretation and safe immediate response.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight prompts. Candidate should relate pressure, CO₂ uptake and position to cardiovascular and respiratory changes, and treat instability while excluding haemorrhage, gas embolism and tension pneumothorax.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No patient actor. Anaesthetist reports: end-tidal CO₂ 48 mmHg (was 36), oxygen saturation 95%, sinus tachycardia 112/min. On request: insufflation pressure 15 mmHg; no visible bleeding.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Why use CO₂ and what does it do? → CO₂ is non-combustible and readily absorbed; insufflation increases intra-abdominal pressure and systemic CO₂ load. 2. Explain haemodynamics. → Increased systemic vascular resistance/afterload; venous compression and head-up tilt may reduce venous return and cardiac output; response depends on pressure and volume status. 3. Explain respiratory changes. → Raised diaphragm reduces compliance and functional residual capacity, raises airway pressures, promotes basal atelectasis/V–Q mismatch. 4. Interpret the rising end-tidal CO₂. → Absorbed CO₂ and impaired elimination increase ETCO₂; communicate to anaesthetist for ventilation adjustment, assess ABG where warranted. 5. What is the effect of patient positioning? → Head-up usually further lowers preload; steep head-down worsens diaphragmatic splinting and intracranial/airway pressures. 6. What do you do now? → Alert anaesthetist; assess ABC/monitoring and operative bleeding; lower insufflation pressure or temporarily desufflate; treat haemodynamic issue collaboratively. 7. What major complications must you exclude? → Vagal bradycardia at insufflation, haemorrhage/vascular injury, CO₂ embolism, pneum
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — Fail / Pas: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Physiology of pressure Calls pneumoperitoneum haemodynamically neutral Explains rise in resistance and possible reduced preload/output Integrates IAP, position, preload, SVR and individual cardiovascular reserve Respiratory physiology Misses loss of compliance and atelectasis Links splinting to peak pressures and V/Q mismatch Explains FRC loss and differentiated causes of high airway pressure CO₂ balance Ignores ETCO₂ rise or assumes oxygen fixes it Identifies absorption and need for ventilation review Distinguishes expected hypercarbia from abrupt changes of major complication Position effects Claims head-up always improves circulation Describes head-up preload risk and head-down respiratory burden Integrates positioning with COPD, cardiac reserve and operative needs Immediate response Persists with insufflation without escalation Calls anaesthetist, reassesses, reduces pressure/desufflates if unstable Coordinates timely reversible intervention with assessment for shock causes Dangerous differential Attributes collapse exclusively to CO₂ absorption Considers bleeding, vagal effect, embolism and pneumothorax Uses ETCO₂, rhythm, airway pressure and
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Continues high-pressure insufflation despite sustained severe hypotension without informing anaesthetist. 2. Does not consider or assess major haemorrhage when cardiovascular collapse develops. 3. Ignores abrupt circulatory collapse with capnography changes suggesting gas embolism. 4. Fails to recognise or respond to clinically significant ventilation/oxygenation deterioration.
sections.7. Curveball: During insufflation ETCO₂ suddenly falls from 48 to 15 mmHg and profound hypotension develops. Candidate should immediately call for help, stop CO₂, desufflate, give 100% oxygen via anaesthetist and manage suspected gas embolism while considering other causes.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “I would stop insufflation and decompress the abdomen now while the anaesthetist resuscitates.” 2. “I would assess the operative field for bleeding and review ETCO₂ and the rhythm before attributing this to pneumoperitoneum.” 3. “I would restart only at a lower pressure after stable physiology and a joint surgeon–anaesthetist decision.”

stations.title: Blood Products and When to Use Them
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-339 Blood Products and When to Use Them

sections.preamble: B2-339 — Blood Products and When to Use Them AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | Eight-minute station | Draft • 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are surgical registrar reviewing an adult after major bowel surgery. A stable patient has Hb 68 g/L without active bleeding. During your discussion, the examiner presents further patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, low fibrinogen and sudden operative major haemorrhage. Select the correct component and escalation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Eight prompts: apply NICE NG24 thresholds to NON-major haemorrhage separately from major-bleeding protocols. Distinguish red cells, platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate and PCC; include identity checks and monitoring.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor. Data cards are spoken: patient A Hb 68 g/L, no active bleeding; B platelet 38 ×10⁹/L awaiting laparotomy; C bleeding, PT ratio 1.8; D significant bleeding with fibrinogen 0.9 g/L.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. How will you manage patient A? → Assess symptoms, cause, comorbidities and consent; restrictive red-cell threshold usually 70 g/L in those without major haemorrhage, ACS or regular transfusions; single unit then reassess. 2. When are platelet products used? → Bleeding with platelets <30 ×10⁹/L; consider >50 ×10⁹/L for invasive surgery; >100 ×10⁹/L for critical-site surgery; context-sensitive exceptions. 3. When is FFP appropriate? → Consider for clinically significant bleeding plus abnormal coagulation (e.g. PT/APTT ratio >1.5) outside major bleeding; not routine for isolated abnormal INR or vitamin-K-antagonist reversal. 4. When is cryoprecipitate appropriate? → Bleeding with fibrinogen <1.5 g/L; prophylactic consideration <1.0 g/L before procedures with significant bleeding risk; reassess fibrinogen. 5. What about warfarin-related severe bleeding? → Immediate PCC plus IV vitamin K according to reversal policy; do not substitute FFP for specific warfarin reversal where PCC indicated. 6. What changes in major haemorrhage? → Activate local major haemorrhage protocol, surgical haemostasis, group/crossmatch and rapid coordinated red cells and haemostatic components with laboratory-
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — Fail / Pas: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Red-cell indication Transfuses stable Hb 90 g/L automatically Uses 70 g/L restrictive trigger in suitable adults and checks clinical context Identifies exceptions and single-unit reassessment Platelet selection Uses one fixed count for every clinical setting Distinguishes active bleeding and operative thresholds Applies critical-site and disease-specific exclusions judiciously Plasma indication Uses FFP for isolated mildly abnormal INR Requires bleeding with significant coagulation abnormality or qualifying procedure Explains why FFP is not the default warfarin reversal product Fibrinogen correction Gives red cells to correct isolated low fibrinogen Selects cryoprecipitate with significant bleeding and fibrinogen <1.5 g/L Reassesses fibrinogen and differentiates prophylactic invasive-procedure criteria Anticoagulant reversal Treats severe warfarin bleeding with FFP alone Requests urgent PCC and IV vitamin K per protocol Coordinates haemostasis, INR monitoring and haematology advice Major haemorrhage Waits for Hb threshold despite shock Activates major haemorrhage protocol and urgent haemostasis Coordinates balanced initial delivery with iterative l
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Fails to activate major haemorrhage response in a patient with haemorrhagic shock. 2. Transfuses a component without performing essential patient-identity and compatibility checks. 3. Continues a transfusion despite suspected severe acute reaction without stopping it and resuscitating. 4. Uses fresh frozen plasma alone as the definitive urgent reversal treatment for severe warfarin bleeding instead of initiating PCC-based reversal.
sections.7. Curveball: A postoperative patient becomes hypotensive with brisk drain bleeding but Hb is 105 g/L. Candidate must not withhold emergency transfusion because Hb exceeds 70 g/L; activate haemorrhage protocol and pursue haemostasis.
sections.8. Recovery lines — station-specific: 1. “I would activate the local major haemorrhage protocol now because the patient is bleeding and shocked despite a relatively preserved Hb.” 2. “I would select the component matching the deficit—platelets, coagulation factors or fibrinogen—not give FFP for every abnormal result.” 3. “I would check bedside identity, document the indication, and reassess clinically and with targeted blood tests after transfusion.”

stations.title: Screening Programmes

sections.preamble: B2-340 — Screening Programmes AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | 8-minute station | Draft — 13 October 2026 Educational assessment only; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Independent clinical and editorial review required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 61-year-old asymptomatic patient attending a general surgery clinic asks why the NHS posts bowel screening kits and why their 65-year-old brother received an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening invitation. Explain the purpose, pathways, benefits and harms of screening.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess population-screening principles, informed choice, NHS England bowel FIT and AAA pathways, diagnostic escalation, and biases. No image is required. Disclose information only in response to relevant questions.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You feel well, have no bleeding, bowel change or pain. Ask: “If my FIT is negative, can I ignore symptoms later?” and “Does finding cancers earlier always mean people live longer?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. What distinguishes screening from diagnosis? Screening offers tests to an asymptomatic eligible population to identify those needing further assessment; symptoms require diagnostic investigation irrespective of screening. 2. What makes a screening programme appropriate? Important condition, detectable preclinical phase, suitable acceptable test, effective treatment, evidence that benefit exceeds harm, reliable quality-assured pathway and equitable access; Wilson–Jungner principles. 3. Describe England bowel screening eligibility and test. Offer FIT every two years to people aged 50–74, home stool sample; those aged 75+ can request kits; programme details are specific to England. 4. What happens after an abnormal FIT? Positive result triggers programme contact and specialist screening assessment with colonoscopy offered when appropriate; FIT alone does not diagnose cancer. 5. Describe AAA screening eligibility and next steps. Men in England invited for a one-off abdominal ultrasound in the year they turn 65; older unscreened men may self-refer; abnormal aortic diameters enter surveillance or vascular referral according to size. 6. Explain benefits and harms of screening. Earlier
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Task framing Treats screening as diagnostic testing. Defines population testing of asymptomatic people. Contrasts screening with symptom-led referral and names population-level outcomes. Selection principles Cannot describe why to screen. Gives key Wilson–Jungner conditions: test, treatment, pathway. Adds benefit–harm balance, quality assurance and equity. Bowel programme Wrong ages or substitutes colonoscopy for routine FIT. Identifies England FIT every 2 years at ages 50–74. Adds opt-in kits after 74 and explains invitation versus diagnostic care. Positive FIT pathway Calls positive FIT confirmed malignancy. Explains further assessment and appropriate colonoscopy. Explains false positives and patient support around investigation. AAA pathway Offers universal serial CT or wrong initial pathway. Describes one-off ultrasound invitation for men at 65. Notes older unscreened self-referral and surveillance/vascular referral if abnormal. Benefits and harms Calls screening harmless or obligatory. Discusses early detection plus false results and procedure harm. Explains overdiagnosis, anxiety and meaningful mortality outcomes. Bias interpretation Claims l
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Reassures a symptomatic patient that a negative screening FIT excludes bowel cancer and declines diagnostic assessment. 2. Claims a positive FIT establishes a cancer diagnosis without colonoscopy or further assessment. 3. Assures the patient screening is risk-free or compulsory and suppresses informed choice. 4. Ignores acute collapse with severe abdominal/back pain in a patient at possible AAA risk instead of emergency escalation.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: Actor reports new persistent rectal bleeding despite a negative FIT six months ago. Expected: switch from screening advice to symptomatic urgent clinical assessment and appropriate colorectal pathway; never simply repeat routine kit.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. After calling FIT a cancer diagnosis: “Correction: a positive FIT indicates blood and prompts further investigation; it is not itself a cancer diagnosis.” 2. After over-reassuring about negative FIT: “A negative screening result does not rule out disease if symptoms develop; I would arrange diagnostic assessment.” 3. After praising survival time alone: “Earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without altering death; I must assess mortality outcomes and screening harms.”

stations.title: Reading a Survival Curve
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-341 Reading a Survival Curve

sections.preamble: B2-341 — Reading a Survival Curve AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | 8-minute station | Draft — 13 October 2026 Educational assessment only; not an official MRCS mark scheme. Independent clinical and editorial review required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: At the colorectal multidisciplinary meeting, you must interpret a written Kaplan–Meier summary of a hypothetical randomised postoperative trial comparing treatment A and treatment B. Explain survival, censoring, median survival and the hazard ratio without claiming individual certainty. No figure is provided.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Present the supplied numerical Kaplan–Meier description exactly as written. Candidate must distinguish overall survival probabilities from hazards and be alert to censoring and non-proportional hazards. All numbers are fictional for educational interpretation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No patient actor. A consultant asks: “The curve for A stays higher; can we say each patient gains six months?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. What do the axes and steps of a Kaplan–Meier survival plot represent? X is elapsed time from specified time zero; Y is estimated probability of remaining event-free or alive; downward steps are observed events. 2. Interpret survival at 12 and 24 months. Written table: A 12-month survival 82%, B 75%; at 24 months A 62%, B 52%. Absolute survival difference at 24 months = 10 percentage points. 3. Define censoring. A participant last known event-free at a specified follow-up time, withdrew, or reached study end without the event; a tick means censored rather than death. 4. What are the median survival values? A reaches 50% survival at month 30; B at month 24. Medians are 30 vs 24 months for cohorts, not a guaranteed six-month extension for each patient. 5. Interpret the reported hazard ratio. A versus B HR 0.72; approximately 28% lower estimated instantaneous event hazard under model assumptions, not 28% greater 24-month survival. 6. Interpret statistical uncertainty. HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94; CI excludes 1 under the stated model. Do not equate statistical with clinical significance. 7. Why assess numbers at risk and crossing curves? Small numbers at risk make late-tail estimates u
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Axes and endpoint Calls Y-axis mortality rate regardless of label. Explains time and survival/event-free probability. Checks time zero and exact event definition. Reading survival Swaps values or treats 62% as death probability. Reports A 62% and B 52% at 24 months. Computes 10-percentage-point absolute difference. Censoring Equates tick marks with deaths. Defines last known event-free follow-up without observed event. Explains contribution to risk set and non-informative-censoring assumption. Median survival Calls 30 months the mean or individual life expectancy. Identifies A 30 months, B 24 months at 50% survival. Notes median may be unestimable if curve never reaches 0.5. Hazard ratio Says 0.72 equals 72% survival. Interprets relative hazard about 28% lower in A. Distinguishes model assumptions from fixed-time absolute probability. Confidence intervals Says CI is range for 95% of patients. Notes HR CI 0.55–0.94 excludes 1. Distinguishes statistical precision, p inference and clinical importance. Late curve interpretation Makes strong claims from tiny late tail. Checks at-risk numbers before late estimates. Flags seven at risk and crossing curves
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Interprets censoring marks as deaths and fabricates event counts. 2. States HR 0.72 means 72% of patients survive or guarantees a 28% absolute benefit. 3. Claims the 6-month difference between group medians is a guaranteed individual survival gain. 4. Declares late crossing curves conclusive superiority despite only seven at risk and no proportional-hazards assessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball: Examiner says the curves cross at month 36, and only 7 patients remain at risk in A. Expected: withdraw simple constant-treatment-effect claims, inspect proportional hazards and uncertainty, avoid overinterpreting tail.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. After saying 28% survival improvement: “Correction: 0.72 is a relative hazard estimate, not an absolute change in survival probability.” 2. After confusing censoring: “A censored participant contributed follow-up until their last known event-free time; that mark does not mean death.” 3. After promising six extra months: “Medians describe groups; they do not predict how long an individual gains.”

stations.title: Reading a Forest Plot
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-342 Reading a Forest Plot

sections.preamble: B2-342 — Reading a Forest Plot AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate asked to interpret a written forest-plot summary of a meta-analysis comparing an enhanced recovery intervention with usual care following elective colorectal surgery. Explain the pooled result, confidence intervals, heterogeneity, and clinical applicability.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Use the supplied fictional dataset; no image is required. The event is postoperative complication (lower is better). Do not award marks for declaring a definitive practice change solely because the pooled CI excludes 1.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No patient actor. Examiner provides the summary and challenges claims of certainty.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Identify the outcome and effect measure → Complication risk; ratio <1 favours intervention because events are harmful; no-effect RR=1. 2. Interpret study A and B → A CI excludes 1, compatible with a reduction; B CI spans 1, compatible with benefit and harm; avoid describing B as proof of no effect. 3. What do square sizes and whiskers represent? → Square size generally reflects study weight; horizontal lines show confidence intervals; large weight does not assure low risk of bias. 4. Interpret the pooled diamond → Pooled point estimate RR 0.76 with 95% CI 0.60–0.97; relative reduction approximately 24%; uncertainty remains. 5. Explain the null line and CI crossing it → For ratios, line at 1; confidence intervals including 1 do not exclude a null effect at the conventional 95% confidence level. 6. Interpret heterogeneity → I²=42% suggests some between-study inconsistency; explore populations, methods and outcome definitions rather than treating I² as proof of bias. 7. What is the absolute benefit and NNT? → Cannot compute from RR alone: require representative baseline risk and time horizon; NNT varies with baseline risk. 8. Would you change surgical practice? → Assess study quali
sections.5. Written examiner dataset: FICTIONAL EDUCATIONAL DATA — outcome: 30-day complications; risk ratio (RR), intervention / usual care. Trial A RR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54–0.96), weight 40%; Trial B 0.90 (0.64–1.27), weight 35%; Trial C 0.62 (0.38–1.01), weight 25%. Precalculated random-effects pooled RR 0.76 (0.60–0.97); I²=42%; total n=1,200; no absolute baseline risks supplied. These rounded trial-level values are illustrative; pooled summary is a stipulated result, not recalculated from rounded values.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Effect and outcome Calls RR an odds ratio or reverses direction of benefit. States event and RR correctly, identifies lower RR as fewer complications. Explains that effect direction depends on outcome coding and comparator. Individual-trial interpretation Asserts every trial significant or B proves equivalence. Recognises A interval excludes 1 and B spans 1. Explains imprecision and why failure to exclude 1 does not prove absence of effect. Plot components Mislabels whiskers as standard deviations or squares as sample sizes only. Identifies point estimates, CI bars, weight and pooled diamond. Connects weight with precision without equating it with study quality. Pooled estimate Mistakes 0.76 for absolute risk reduction or says 76% risk reduction. Explains pooled RR 0.76 (0.60–0.97) as approx 24% relative reduction. States denominator, CI and uncertainty in clear clinical language. Null line Says null is zero for an RR or treats crossing 1 as proof of harm. Identifies RR null at 1; distinguishes inclusion/exclusion of 1. Distinguishes statistical uncertainty from clinically important possible effects. Heterogeneity Ignores I²=42% or treats I² as per
sections.7. Critical fails — four station-specifi: CF1. Reverses the direction of the adverse-outcome comparison and recommends a potentially harmful intervention on that basis. CF2. Invents an absolute benefit or NNT from RR alone and presents it as patient-specific fact. CF3. Claims a pooled statistically significant result guarantees an intervention is safe or effective for every surgical patient. CF4. Dismisses material heterogeneity or evidence quality while making an unequivocal clinical policy recommendation.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: Examiner: “A hospital manager says an RR of 0.76 means 76 of every 100 patients avoid complications. Do you agree?” Expected response: No. RR 0.76 represents estimated 24% lower relative risk, not 76 fewer complications per 100. Actual number helped depends on baseline complication risk.

sections.preamble: B2-343 — Levels of Evidence and Study Designs AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: At a surgical journal club, a consultant asks you to choose appropriate study designs for assessing a new perioperative treatment, identifying risk factors for an uncommon postoperative complication, and estimating complication incidence. Compare study strengths, limitations and causal inference.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess RCT, cohort, case–control, cross-sectional studies, systematic reviews and evidence certainty. Avoid teaching a rigid hierarchy without considering study quality and the question.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: None; discussion with examiner.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Randomised controlled trial: Random allocation balances measured and unmeasured confounding on average; allocation concealment prevents selection bias; blinding can reduce performance/detection bias; intention-to-treat preserves randomisation. Cohort: Begin with exposure and follow to outcome; prospective or retrospective; estimates incidence and relative risk, useful for uncommon exposures; vulnerable to confounding and loss to follow-up. Case–control: Select cases with outcome and controls without, then compare prior exposure; efficient for rare outcomes or long latency; usually estimates odds ratio; selection and recall bias. Cross-sectional: Exposure and outcome at a point in time; measures prevalence and associations, limited for temporality and incidence. Systematic review: Predefined question, reproducible search, selection and risk-of-bias assessment; meta-analysis optional and cannot rescue biased primary studies. Evidence certainty: Consider risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias; well-conducted observational evidence may be more useful than flawed RCT for some questions. Apply scenarios: New intervention: RCT where ethical/feasible; r
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Question matching Uses one design for every question. Matches RCT to intervention and cohort to incidence. Justifies rare-outcome case–control efficiency. Randomisation Equates random sampling with allocation. Explains random allocation reduces confounding. Describes allocation concealment and ITT. Blinding Claims blinding always possible. Explains detection/performance bias reduction. Distinguishes blinding from concealment. Cohort Says starts by selecting cases. Starts from exposure and follows outcomes. Identifies incidence, RR and confounding. Case–control Claims directly measures incidence. Selects by outcome and estimates exposure odds. Explains odds ratio and rare-disease approximation limits. Cross-sectional Infers temporal cause. Describes prevalence snapshot. Notes reverse causation and temporality. Systematic review Assumes pooled studies automatically valid. Describes systematic search and appraisal. Distinguishes synthesis from meta-analysis. Bias Names no specific bias. Identifies selection, recall and confounding. Matches bias prevention to study design. Evidence appraisal Uses hierarchy without quality. Considers bias and applicabil
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Recommends withholding proven emergency treatment solely to randomise patients without considering ethics. States case–control sampling can directly calculate population incidence without a denominator. Claims association in a cross-sectional study proves temporal causation. Treats a meta-analysis of seriously biased studies as definitive without appraisal.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The examiner says the postoperative complication occurs in only 1 in 20,000 patients. Expected: a conventional small RCT is unlikely to answer the risk-factor question; propose a large multicentre registry-based cohort or carefully sampled case–control study, acknowledge confounding and define outcome ascertainment.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should separate random allocation from random sampling and explain concealment.” “A case–control study samples by outcome and usually provides an odds ratio, not direct incidence.” “Study design alone is not the quality grade; I must examine bias and precision.”

stations.title: Relative Risk Absolute Risk and NNT
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-344 Relative Risk Absolute Risk and NNT

sections.preamble: B2-344 — Relative Risk, Absolute Risk and NNT AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar presenting a fictional randomised trial of a postoperative infection-prevention intervention. At 30 days, 20 of 200 patients allocated standard care developed an infection, compared with 10 of 200 allocated the intervention. Calculate the risk measures and explain them in plain language to a patient. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Give the written 2×2 data only. Award marks for denominators, correctly oriented comparisons, appropriate rounding, uncertainty and communication. The counts are invented for education; no confidence intervals have been provided. Do not infer significance from event counts alone.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: A patient asks: “Does this mean I have a 50% chance of avoiding an infection?” They want benefits, harms and whether the trial applies to their situation.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Establish risks — Control event risk 20/200=0.10 (10%); treatment event risk 10/200=0.05 (5%) over 30 days. 2. Relative risk — RR=treatment risk/control risk=0.05/0.10=0.50. Relative risk reduction=1−RR=0.50 or 50%. 3. Absolute difference — ARR=control minus treatment risk=0.10−0.05=0.05: five percentage points; 50 fewer infections per 1,000 treated if effect generalises. 4. NNT calculation — NNT for benefit=1/0.05=20 patients treated for 30-day follow-up to avert one additional infection on average; always state outcome/time horizon. 5. Communicate to patient — Without intervention, around 10/100 experience infection; with it, around 5/100; approximately five additional people in 100 avoid infection; not a 50-percentage-point absolute improvement. 6. Interpret relative and absolute effects — Explain a 50% relative reduction from a 10% baseline; baseline risk matters. A RR alone cannot give ARR or NNT in another population. 7. Discuss uncertainty and interpretation — Check randomisation, losses, complications and confidence intervals; these counts alone do not justify claiming proven efficacy or statistically significant benefit. 8. Clinical application — Consider intervention h
sections.5. Written examiner dataset: FICTIONAL 30-DAY TRIAL: intervention n=200, infections=10, no infection=190; standard care n=200, infections=20, no infection=180. No confidence interval, hypothesis test, or adverse-event data supplied. For the same RR and 2% control risk, estimated treatment risk is 1%, ARR 1 percentage point and NNT 100 (assuming transportability).
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Denominator and timing Quotes 10/20 as risks or ignores 200 per arm. Calculates both 30-day event risks from denominators. States risks per 100 and per 1,000 with an explicit 30-day horizon. Risk ratio Inverts the comparator or reports RR=2 as benefit. Calculates RR=0.50, treatment divided by control. Explains interpretation depends on outcome coding and comparator. Relative risk reduction Calls 0.50 a 50-point absolute change. Explains RRR=50% of baseline risk. Contrasts RRR with the absolute reduction using the actual counts. Absolute risk reduction Subtracts counts without denominators or states ARR=50%. Calculates ARR=5 percentage points. Translates ARR to five fewer infections per 100 and 50 per 1,000. NNT Derives NNT=2 or omits the follow-up period. Calculates NNTB=20 using 1/0.05. Specifies benefit, outcome, 30-day time frame and upward rounding convention. Baseline risk transport Assumes NNT stays 20 in all populations. States absolute benefit depends on baseline risk. For 2% baseline risk, correctly derives 1% ARR and NNT 100 if RR applies. Uncertainty Claims statistical significance with no inference data. Acknowledges CI and harms are no
sections.7. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Reverses which group has the lower infection risk and recommends the higher-risk option as safer. CF2. Tells the patient the intervention prevents infection in 50 out of 100 people, despite the five-percentage-point absolute reduction. CF3. Presents NNT=2 (or any fabricated absolute NNT) as fact after being shown the original data. CF4. States the trial proves safety and mandatory use despite explicitly missing adverse-event and uncertainty data.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: Examiner: “If the standard-care infection rate were only 2%, would NNT still be 20?” Expected: no; if RR 0.50 were transportable, treatment risk ≈1%, ARR 1% and NNTB 100 over 30 days; this is a conditional illustration.

stations.title: P Values and Confidence Intervals
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-345 P Values and Confidence Intervals

sections.preamble: B2-345 — P Values and Confidence Intervals AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | Draft: 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate at colorectal morbidity-and-mortality journal club. A fictional trial reports 30-day complications: risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.62–1.03, two-sided p=0.08. A second much larger trial reports RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.95–0.99 and p=0.004. Explain statistical versus clinical significance, type I/II error and power. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Written findings only; no graph. Both numerical examples are explicitly fictional and illustrative. Test correct null values, conditional p-value meaning, CIs, sample size/power and cautious clinical application. Do not imply that one p-value is probability of benefit.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No patient actor. Consultant asks whether the larger trial should change practice immediately and whether the first trial proves no benefit.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Interpret the first estimate — RR 0.80 suggests estimated 20% relative reduction in complications; CI 0.62–1.03 includes both potentially important benefit and small harm/no benefit. 2. Meaning of p=0.08 — Under the specified null model and assumptions, a result at least as extreme has probability 8%; it is not an 8% chance the null is true. 3. Interpret the 95% CI — A frequentist interval generated by a method that covers the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under assumptions; it communicates estimate precision and compatible effects. 4. What is the null value? — For RR and OR the null is 1; for absolute differences the null is 0. The first CI includes 1; it does not establish equivalence. 5. Type I error — False-positive rejection of a true null; alpha 0.05 is a preselected long-run error rate under the test model, not an individual patient risk. 6. Type II error and power — A type II error fails to reject a false null; beta probability; power=1−beta for a prespecified effect size, alpha, variance and sample. 7. Interpret the large trial — RR 0.97 with p=0.004 is statistically inconsistent with RR=1 but estimated relative reduction is only 3%; clinical importance requ
sections.5. Written examiner dataset: FICTIONAL STUDIES: Trial A, 30-day complications RR 0.80 (95% CI 0.62–1.03); p=0.08. Trial B, same outcome RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.95–0.99); p=0.004. Numbers are stipulated educational summaries, not results of actual trials. The CI and p-value are approximately consistent but may differ by exact analytical methods and rounding.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Effect estimate Calls RR 0.80 an 80-point absolute fall. Interprets RR 0.80 as estimated 20% relative reduction. Defines harmful end point and checks what effect sizes remain compatible with the interval. P-value meaning Says p=0.08 means 8% chance null is true. Explains tail probability under specified null hypothesis. Identifies assumptions and warns p value is not posterior probability or effect magnitude. First CI Says CI including 1 proves no effect. Recognises 0.62–1.03 includes null and possible benefit. Communicates uncertainty around clinically consequential effects. Null value Uses zero as RR no-effect value. Uses RR null of 1, risk difference null of 0. Explains why crossing a null differs by measure and model. Type I error Calls type I error a missed true effect. Defines false rejection of true null; alpha. Relates threshold to long-run frequency and multiple comparisons. Type II and power Claims power is probability study hypothesis is true. Defines false-negative non-rejection and power=1−beta. Notes power depends on target effect, sample, variability and design. Trial B interpretation Claims p=0.004 proves major clinical benefit. Not
sections.7. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Recommends stopping established beneficial treatment solely because a different small trial gives p=0.08, asserting proof of no benefit. CF2. States p=0.004 means a 99.6% probability the new therapy is safe for the patient and mandates treatment. CF3. Describes a confidence interval including material benefit and harm as proof of clinical equivalence, despite no equivalence margin or appropriate design. CF4. Treats statistical significance as sufficient to override a documented serious intervention harm without evaluating effect magnitude or absolute risk.
sections.8. Realistic curveball: Examiner: “The larger trial has p=0.004. Surely it is the clinically superior intervention?” Expected: no. RR 0.97 may be a small relative effect; ask for baseline event risk, absolute difference, serious harms, cost, study quality and patient priorities.

stations.title: Clinical Governance and Risk Management
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-346 Clinical Governance and Risk Management

sections.preamble: B2-346 — Clinical Governance and Risk Management AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar after a patient received the wrong dose of prophylactic antibiotic but has no apparent harm. A junior colleague asks whether this is a reportable incident and whether to tell the patient. Explain your immediate response, governance pathway and how to learn from the event.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test immediate clinical risk assessment, truthful communication, incident reporting, PSIRF, audit versus improvement, human factors and just culture. Candidate must not substitute paperwork for patient care.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Junior colleague: “There is no harm, so can we leave this off the system? I fear blame.” If asked: drug was administered in theatre, dose was twice the intended dose; patient stable, renal function not yet checked.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. First clinical response → Check patient, drug/dose/time, allergies, observations, renal function and potential toxicity; seek pharmacy/senior advice, monitor and treat any harm. 2. Immediate communication → Inform senior and relevant teams; document factual chronology; ensure appropriate disclosure to patient and duty-of-candour assessment. 3. What to report → Record near misses and incidents through local reporting process even without evident harm; avoid concealment. 4. How PSIRF works → Proportionate systems-based learning response; not automatic “serious incident” classification or mandatory full investigation for every event. 5. Governance pillars → Clinical effectiveness/audit, patient safety/risk, education, research/evidence, patient involvement, staffing/leadership and information governance. 6.
