Audit versus QI → Audit measures against an explicit standard and re-audits; QI uses iterative change and process/outcome/balancing measures. 7. Human factors → Explore look-alike packaging, interruptions, handover, prescribing and checking processes without premature blame. 8. Closing loop → Agree safety action, named ownership, feedback to staff and patients, check effectivene
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Files a report without assessing patient. Checks stability, medicine exposure and immediate treatment need. Adds toxicity/renal review, pharmacy input and monitoring plan. Escalation Hides error from supervising team. Alerts senior clinician and appropriate teams. Clarifies roles, urgency and continuity to recovery/ward. Candour Promises secrecy because no harm obvious. Explains open discussion and relevant candour duties. Distinguishes professional openness from statutory notification threshold. Reporting Claims near misses should never be reported. Uses local incident-reporting process. Records objective facts and preserves evidence without attributing blame. PSIRF Demands old Serious Incident process for every event. Describes proportionate systems-learning response. Connects response choice to organisational policy, risk and those affected. Audit Equates audit with one-off punishment. Compares practice to a defined standard and re-audits. Specifies denominator, outcome and feedback loop. Quality improvement Offers training alone as complete solution. Proposes testable process change. Includes PDSA, balancing measures and sustai
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Deliberately conceals the dosing error from the patient and clinical team. CF2. Leaves the patient unassessed while solely completing governance forms. CF3. Alters or destroys medication/chart records to avoid reporting. CF4. Orders automatic punishment without considering immediate safety and system factors.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Examiner: A manager says there was no demonstrable harm so no report or conversation is necessary. Expected: Explain that an incident can warrant reporting and compassionate communication without confirmed harm; assess what candour obligations apply and act under local policy.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: I prioritised the incident form over the patient; I would first assess exposure, observations and toxicity risk. I called PSIRF a mandatory full investigation; it promotes proportionate system-based learning responses. I blamed the administrator alone; I must examine prescribing, storage, interruptions and checks.

sections.preamble: B2-347 — Writing an Operation Note AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a draft operation note after an emergency laparoscopic appendicectomy. The note reads: “Lap appendix. General anaesthetic. Inflamed appendix removed. No problems. Home tomorrow.” Identify omissions, produce a safe structured replacement and explain why the note matters. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess ability to critique incomplete documentation and state the Royal College of Surgeons operative record elements, including findings, procedures, specimens, complications and postoperative instructions. Do not invent patient-specific facts.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: No actor. Examiner may provide additional details only when asked: operation date 13 October 2026; surgeon Mr A and assistant Dr B; laparoscopic appendicectomy under GA; gangrenous non-perforated appendix; appendix sent for histology; minimal blood loss; no intraoperative complications reported; standard port closure; postoperative plan depends on clinical assessment and local policy.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is missing from the draft? EXPECT: Patient identifiers; date/time; operating team; anaesthetist; indication and consent; procedure and approach; detailed findings; key steps; specimens; blood loss; complications; closure; counts when relevant; postoperative orders; signature/name and designation. How would you document findings and procedure? EXPECT: State gangrenous non-perforated appendix, laparoscopic approach, key operative steps including securing appendiceal base and mesoappendix, specimen retrieval and port closure; do not add unconfirmed observations. What postoperative instructions are essential? EXPECT: Specify observations, analgesia, fluids/diet, mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis assessment, antibiotic plan with indication, wound care, review triggers, histology follow-up and discharge criteria; individualise to case. How do you record complications and blood loss? EXPECT: Use provided facts: minimal blood loss and no intraoperative complications reported; never substitute “none” if unsure; verify counts/implant details with team where relevant. What if the record was entered late? EXPECT: Use correct date/time of operation and actual entry time, mark late entry, ident
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Patient and timing Omits patient identifiers and operation date. Includes identifiers, operation date/time. Differentiates operative time from later entry time. Team and procedure Records “lap appendix” only. Names surgeon, assistant, anaesthetist, procedure and approach. Documents role changes or conversion if relevant. Indication and consent Omits diagnosis and indication. States suspected appendicitis and documented indication. Distinguishes preoperative diagnosis from operative findings. Operative findings Writes “inflamed” without important detail. Records gangrenous non-perforated appendix. Documents relevant contamination and anatomical findings only if confirmed. Key operative steps Gives no technical account. Documents access, appendiceal division, retrieval and closure. Includes important variation, haemostasis and count confirmation where verified. Specimens and implants Omits appendix histology. Records appendix sent for histology and any drains/implants. Tracks specimen label/destination and states none only if confirmed. Blood loss and complications Uses vague “no problems”. Records minimal blood loss and known complications. Makes un
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Writes a fabricated intraoperative finding or complication status without verification and presents it as witnessed fact. Omits postoperative escalation instructions despite a patient requiring continued surgical review. Backdates a late operation note or alters the existing record without preserving an audit trail. Fails to document a specimen sent for histology, creating a risk that the result is never tracked.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The examiner says: “The consultant asks you to record that the appendix was perforated, but you did not see perforation and the theatre record says non-perforated.” Expected: do not invent or silently change findings; clarify with operating surgeon, reconcile evidence and document any correction transparently with attribution and time.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I wrote a discharge date rather than criteria; I will document clinical review and safety triggers.” “I have not confirmed the specimen pathway; I will verify the histology request and record it accurately.” “I cannot backdate or add unsupported findings; I will enter a timed, attributable addendum after checking the operative team.”

sections.preamble: B2-348 — Reviewing a Drug Chart for Errors AMaC MRCS Part B | Data interpretation | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a fictional inpatient prescription chart for a 68-year-old woman, 62 kg, admitted with postoperative infection. Allergy band and admission record state immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin. eGFR is 24 mL/min/1.73 m²; creatinine is rising. The chart lists: (A) IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g every 8 hours, first dose not yet administered; (B) gentamicin 320 mg IV once daily prescribed for the next five days without levels or review; (C) enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily without renal or bleeding review; (D) oral morphine modified release 30 mg twice daily newly started, with no prior opioid use documented; (E) paracetamol 1 g orally four times daily. Identify and prioritise errors and explain a safe response. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Show the candidate the chart as written in the candidate brief; there is no physical image. Assess allergy, renal adjustment, high-risk medicines, safe prescribing, urgent communication and documentation. Do not demand a single alternative antibiotic without infection source, culture or local policy.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: No actor. Examiner can confirm: patient is haemodynamically stable, no doses have yet been given, urine output has fallen, no baseline chronic opioid prescription is documented. No additional allergy clarification is available.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Which error needs immediate action? EXPECT: Stop and prevent co-amoxiclav administration because documented immediate penicillin anaphylaxis; verify allergy history and alert nurse/prescriber; choose an appropriate non-penicillin regimen with microbiology/pharmacy and local guidelines. What is concerning about gentamicin? EXPECT: Renal impairment/acute kidney injury, repeated daily dosing without indication, weight-based review, levels or monitoring; withhold further doses pending senior/microbiology/pharmacy review, assess level/timing if already administered. What about enoxaparin? EXPECT: Renal clearance and bleeding risk require indication, weight, renal function and local dose/prophylaxis guidance; do not reflexively omit VTE prophylaxis without a safe alternative plan. What about the morphine? EXPECT: New high-dose modified-release opioid in apparently opioid-naïve patient, renal accumulation and sedation/respiratory depression risk; withhold, assess pain, opioid history and prescribe safer individualised analgesia. Is paracetamol necessarily erroneous? EXPECT: 4 g/day is usual adult maximum but check weight, liver disease, nutrition, other combination products and clinical c
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Allergy recognition Approves co-amoxiclav despite recorded anaphylaxis. Flags and prevents administration of penicillin-class drug. Escalates allergy verification and agrees safe infection-specific alternative. Immediate prioritisation Focuses on minor chart formatting before hazardous prescriptions. Prevents imminent high-risk doses and informs nurse. Ranks allergy, renal toxicity and opioid harm with immediate containment. Gentamicin safety Approves fixed repeated aminoglycoside dosing without review. Identifies AKI and need for indication, dosing and levels review. Specifies timing-dependent drug levels, renal trends and microbiology input. Anticoagulant assessment Ignores renal impairment or stops all prophylaxis without assessment. Reviews enoxaparin indication, renal function and bleeding risk. Balances VTE risk against bleeding and local renal-adjusted alternatives. Opioid review Continues new high-dose MR morphine without opioid history. Questions initiation and assesses sedation and renal clearance. Designs monitored analgesic alternative with reassessment. Paracetamol reasoning Calls all four prescriptions errors without justification. Re
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Allows imminent co-amoxiclav administration despite clearly documented immediate penicillin anaphylaxis. Continues repeated gentamicin in worsening renal function without reassessment or monitoring. Approves newly initiated high-dose modified-release morphine without assessing opioid exposure or respiratory risk. Changes high-risk prescriptions without documenting and communicating them to the administering team.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The nurse says the co-amoxiclav infusion was started five minutes ago and the patient is wheezing with facial swelling. Expected: stop infusion, call emergency help, assess ABCDE and treat suspected anaphylaxis immediately according to current resuscitation guidance, including IM adrenaline as indicated; do not wait for blood tests.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I missed the documented anaphylaxis; I would stop the prescription and notify the administering nurse now.” “I should check whether gentamicin was already administered, the dosing time and levels before any further dose.” “I should not simply stop VTE prevention; I would document renal-adjusted prophylaxis after bleeding-risk assessment.”

stations.title: Prioritising an Emergency Theatre List
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-349 Prioritising an Emergency Theatre List

sections.preamble: B2-349 — Prioritising an Emergency Theatre List AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call general surgical registrar. Three patients compete for a single staffed emergency operating theatre. Decide their NCEPOD urgency categories, sequence the work, describe stabilisation and escalation, and communicate a safe plan. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess category assignment by physiological urgency, not arrival time or diagnosis alone. Require early consultant/anaesthetic/theatre co-ordinator input; candidates should re-triage if patient condition changes. Scenario is fictional.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Theatre co-ordinator says: “The next theatre becomes free in 45 minutes, and an elective list is running. Which operation goes first?” A concerned colleague argues the longest-waiting case deserves priority.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Initial triage → Review ABCDE, shock physiology, haemorrhage/source control, organ/limb threat, resuscitation in progress and access to theatre; distinguish clinical urgency from waiting time. 2. Identify immediate case → Patient A after splenic injury: BP 72/40 despite blood and active intraperitoneal haemorrhage; NCEPOD Immediate—resuscitation concurrent with emergency operative haemorrhage control. 3. Identify urgent case → Patient B with CT-described free air, peritonitis, fever and rising lactate but haemodynamically stable after initial fluids; NCEPOD Urgent—source control within hours with continued sepsis management. 4. Identify expedited case → Patient C with stable, reducible intermittent obstructive symptoms from known tumour, no peritonism, normal lactate; senior decision may permit Expedited (days) if truly stable, while reassessing for acute obstruction; no fixed label irrespective of deterioration. 5. Coordinate immediate theatre access → Call consultant surgeon and anaesthetist, theatre co-ordinator and blood bank; trigger major haemorrhage protocol for A as indicated and request break-in or parallel theatre capacity without waiting passively. 6. Prepare urgent p
sections.5. Written examiner dataset: WRITTEN THREE-CASE LIST, 18:00: A—26-year-old following road traffic collision, free intraperitoneal blood, ongoing shock BP 72/40 after resuscitation, suspected active splenic bleed. B—59-year-old diffuse peritonitis, CT reports pneumoperitoneum; BP 118/72 post-fluid, lactate 3.2 mmol/L; receiving antibiotics. C—72-year-old planned cancer resection, intermittent pain, soft abdomen, passing flatus, vitals normal, no clinical or biochemical ischaemia. One theatre free in 45 minutes; an elective list remains occupied. Categories apply to current patient condition, not inherently to procedure name.
sections.6. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition of urgency Prioritises by booking time alone, disregarding shock. Recognises A has immediate life-threatening haemorrhage. Explains concurrent resuscitation and source control, and urgency may change minute-to-minute. NCEPOD classification Calls all non-elective operations “Immediate”. Uses Immediate, Urgent, Expedited and Elective categories appropriately. Describes minutes/hours/days context and avoids classifying by theatre session. Haemorrhage plan Leaves A waiting while considering C. Requests immediate operating access, anaesthesia and haemorrhage resuscitation. Triggers blood-bank and cross-specialty coordination, securing a second theatre if needed. Perforation/sepsis plan Treats stable BP as grounds for days-long delay of peritonitis. Classifies B as urgent and starts antibiotics, fluids and senior source-control planning. Reassesses lactate, perfusion and triggers to upgrade priority if deteriorating. Stable third case Operates C ahead of life-threatening cases merely because booked. Defers C safely with clinical monitoring and review. Tests for new obstruction, peritonitis or ischaemia before retaining expedited status. Resou
sections.7. Critical fails — four station-specifi: CF1. Prioritises a clinically stable case over continuing life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage without urgent consultant-level review. CF2. Fails to seek emergency theatre access and blood resuscitation for the actively shocked bleeding patient. CF3. Delays peritonitis with sepsis for several days solely because blood pressure has temporarily normalised. CF4. Refuses to revise prioritisation when a waiting patient develops new shock or organ ischaemia.
sections.8. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: While A is being transferred to theatre, B becomes hypotensive (75/45), confused and poorly perfused. Expected: immediate ABCDE/resuscitation and senior reassessment; escalate B to potentially immediate life-saving source control, request parallel theatre and decide priority through consultant/anaesthetic coordination based on current physiology, rather than rigid original queue.

stations.title: Taking a Referral from a GP
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-350 Taking a Referral from a GP

sections.preamble: B2-350 — Taking a Referral from a GP AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8-minute station | Draft 13 October 2026 Educational draft — not an official MRCS Part B mark scheme. Independent clinical/editorial sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call general surgical registrar. A GP telephones about a 68-year-old woman with worsening abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. Take a focused referral, decide disposition and provide a safe shared plan. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: The actor is a GP, not the patient. Assess active information gathering, triage, ownership and closed-loop communication. Only disclose findings when asked. Stable observations at the surgery do not exclude evolving obstruction or ischaemia.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: GP: Mrs Ellis, 68, has cramping abdominal pain for 24 hours, bilious vomiting, distension and has passed no flatus since yesterday. Past operations: open hysterectomy. BP 108/68, HR 108, temperature 37.7, RR 22; she looks dry. Abdomen distended and tender but no reported peritonism. She is currently in the practice, 35 minutes from hospital. GP initially asks: “Could I just arrange an urgent outpatient CT?” If specifically asked: no blood in stool, no known hernia, no anticoagulant, penicillin causes a rash (details unknown), last ate six hours ago.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Confirm caller and reason: Identify GP, callback number, patient identifiers/location, chief concern and timeline; agree urgent structured referral. 2. History of obstruction: Clarify pain onset and progression, colicky versus constant pain, vomiting character, last stool/flatus, bleeding, previous operations, hernias and malignancy. 3. Physiological severity: Request contemporaneous BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, mental state, urine output, oral intake and trend. 4. Red flags and differential: Ask about continuous severe pain, peritonism, shock, fever, sepsis and irreducible hernia; consider adhesional SBO, incarcerated hernia, volvulus and ischaemia. 5. Disposition now: Suspected bowel obstruction with tachycardia, vomiting and dehydration requires same-day hospital emergency assessment, not outpatient imaging. 6. Safe transfer: Arrange urgent ambulance transfer if deterioration or unsafe private transport; request nil by mouth, observations, IV access/fluids only if available and no transfer delay; send referral details. 7. On-arrival plan: Alert senior surgical team/ED as needed; ABCDE, analgesia/antiemetic, IV access, bloods including renal fun
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and identifiers Accepts vague call without identifiers or callback. Confirms identity, caller, contact and location. Establishes time-critical purpose and makes call-back/transfer failure plan. Targeted surgical history Fails to ask vomiting, flatus or prior surgery. Elicits obstructive symptoms and hysterectomy. Distinguishes evolving strangulation and enquires about hernia and malignancy. Physiological assessment Trusts “looks well” without observations. Asks full current observations, hydration and urine output. Requests trends and recognises tachycardia as significant despite preserved BP. Red flags Ignores peritonism or shock. Checks constant pain, peritonism, sepsis and shock. States bowel ischaemia/strangulation cannot be excluded by phone. Triage and urgency Offers routine outpatient CT review. Requests immediate hospital surgical assessment. Explains why waiting risks dehydration, perforation or ischaemia. Transfer safety Leaves dehydrated vomiting patient to drive alone. Gives NBM and safe transfer instructions without delay. Coordinates ambulance threshold, destination and deterioration actions. Initial investigations Asks for CT
sections.6. Four station-specific Critical fails: CF1. Declines urgent hospital assessment and directs this suspected obstruction for a routine outpatient scan. CF2. Dismisses shock, peritonism or relentless pain described by GP and gives no emergency escalation. CF3. Leaves a vomiting, potentially unstable patient to arrange unsupervised transport without safety advice. CF4. Fails to establish an accepting destination or handover yet tells the GP the patient is safely transferred.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: GP reveals during the call: “She has just become confused and the systolic BP is 82.” Expected: declare emergency, direct ambulance/999, GP immediate ABCDE resuscitation within capability, alert ED and senior surgical/critical care team and do not delay transport for elective investigations.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I initially suggested outpatient imaging; this is a possible obstruction with physiological compromise and needs emergency hospital assessment today.” “I missed the trend in observations: I must ask for current BP, pulse, mental state and urine output, and escalate any deterioration immediately.” “I have not confirmed ownership. I will identify the receiving team, repeat the transfer plan and document the handover before ending the call.”

stations.title: An Unexpected Finding During Surgery
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-351 An Unexpected Finding During Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-351 — An Unexpected Finding During Surgery AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8-minute station | Draft 13 October 2026 Educational draft — not an official MRCS Part B mark scheme. Independent clinical/editorial sign-off required.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar speaking to a 55-year-old patient after a planned laparoscopic cholecystectomy. At operation, the team found an unexpected 2 cm firm lesion on the anterior stomach. The planned cholecystectomy was completed safely, and no gastric biopsy or resection was performed. Explain what happened, what was and was not done, and the next steps. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess factual, compassionate postoperative disclosure and boundaries of consent. The incidental gastric lesion is of uncertain nature; no histology exists. There was no operative injury or emergency requiring immediate additional intervention. Consultant was informed intraoperatively and agreed investigation after recovery.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient Ms Patel is awake, anxious and asks: “Is it cancer? Why didn’t you remove it while you were in there?” Consent was for cholecystectomy and foreseeable necessary related procedures, not unplanned gastric surgery. No biopsy taken. She is haemodynamically stable and has expected mild postoperative pain. If asked, operative note documents the lesion location and size and the consultant has requested upper GI MDT review and appropriate endoscopic assessment. She wants a copy of the plan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected answers: 1. Set up and check understanding: Confirm identity, capacity/comfort, appropriate privacy and preferred support person; ask what she understands of her planned operation. 2. Give clear account: State gallbladder operation completed as planned; a separate unexpected 2 cm gastric lesion was seen. 3. Communicate uncertainty: Explain appearance alone cannot diagnose cancer or benign disease; no pathology result exists. Avoid falsely reassuring or labelling it malignant. 4. Explain limits of action: State no biopsy/removal was undertaken; not an immediate life-threatening finding, and additional gastric surgery was outside informed consent. 5. Explain consent principle: Non-urgent unrelated procedures need discussion and informed consent; clarify rare emergency exception if delay poses immediate serious harm. 6. Plan investigation: Consult senior/upper GI team and discuss endoscopy with possible biopsy as clinically appropriate and imaging/MDT based on subsequent findings; give expected contact route. 7. Support reaction and questions: Acknowledge anxiety, allow silence, check values/preferences, offer written summary and follow-up; avoid promising a benign diagnosis or fixed timeline
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and empathy Starts with jargon and disregards distress. Checks understanding and speaks privately and calmly. Invites supporter and tailors explanation to patient priorities. Operative facts Implies stomach was operated on or omits finding. States cholecystectomy completed and 2 cm lesion found. Precisely distinguishes observed finding from interventions performed. Diagnostic uncertainty Declares lesion cancer without evidence. Explains appearance cannot establish diagnosis. Explains why histology and specialist assessment may be required. Consent boundary Says surgeon may remove any incidental lesion without asking. Explains unrelated elective removal needs informed consent. Distinguishes unforeseen immediate threat exception from non-urgent choice. Explanation of decision Claims lesion was biopsied when it was not. Says no biopsy/resection because finding was non-urgent and unconsented. Explains risk/benefit and senior discussion without defensiveness. Follow-up planning Discharges without named follow-up. Proposes upper GI team review and appropriate endoscopy/biopsy. Explains communication of results, responsible clinician and contingen
sections.6. Four station-specific Critical fails: CF1. States the lesion is definitely cancer or definitely benign despite no tissue diagnosis and recommends treatment as certain. CF2. Tells the patient that a non-urgent additional gastric resection could lawfully be done without discussing consent. CF3. Falsely claims a biopsy or resection was performed and that histology is pending. CF4. Offers no referral or follow-up for the suspicious incidental lesion, creating foreseeable loss to care.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient asks, “If you had found a perforated stomach with uncontrolled bleeding instead, would you still have stopped?” Expected: explain the immediate serious-harm emergency exception when consent cannot reasonably be obtained; act only as necessary and proportionate, document, obtain senior help, and explain afterward.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I used the word cancer without evidence. I need to correct that: the lesion is unexplained until the appropriate investigations are completed.” “I implied we removed tissue. We did not; I will explain exactly what was observed and why an unrelated elective procedure needs separate consent.” “I gave no clear ownership of results. I will name the responsible upper GI team, explain how follow-up is arranged and document the plan.”

stations.title: A Patient Demanding a Scan That Isnt Indicated
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-352 A Patient Demanding a Scan That Isnt Indicated

sections.preamble: B2-352 — A Patient Demanding a Scan That Isn’t Indicated AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8-minute station | 13 October 2026 | DRAFT — not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in an outpatient clinic. A 34-year-old patient with 4 months of intermittent mild abdominal discomfort, normal observations, no alarm symptoms, normal examination and reassuring initial investigations insists on an urgent CT abdomen because a friend was diagnosed with cancer. Explain your assessment and agree a safe plan. No additional scan is currently clinically indicated.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess listening, recognition of new red flags, explanation of why immediate CT is not indicated, balanced discussion of harms, shared decisions, safety netting and documentation. If red flags emerge, candidate must reassess—not rigidly refuse imaging.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You say: “I pay my taxes; I demand a CT. My friend had cancer and everyone missed it.” You are anxious, not aggressive. If asked, symptoms have not progressed, weight and appetite are stable, no rectal bleeding, vomiting, fever, family history of bowel cancer or bowel habit change. Curveball: “I have started passing blood in my stool this week.”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Open and hear concern — Introduce self; invite the specific fear, acknowledge the friend’s experience and avoid dismissing anxiety. 2. Test current risk — Confirm site, duration, course, associated symptoms, previous results, personal/family cancer risk, prior imaging and alarm symptoms. 3. Explain assessment — State findings are reassuring so far but not a guarantee; explain which changes would alter urgency or justify further investigation. 4. Discuss options — Explain appropriate clinical review, symptom monitoring, targeted investigations/referral if indicated, and the option of a second opinion. 5. Address CT risks — Explain ionising radiation, possible incidental findings, downstream tests and contrast risks if relevant, without exaggerated claims. 6. Respond to demand — Respectfully explain that consent or payment does not make an unindicated test appropriate; do not promise CT merely to end dispute. 7. Agree follow-up — Offer review at a defined clinically suitable interval through GP or clinic, written clear return precautions and an accessible contact route. 8. Handle new bleeding — Clarify amount, timing, associated instability; undertake fresh assessment and arrange
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Empathy and rapport Belittles fear of cancer or argues about entitlement. Acknowledges the friend’s diagnosis and anxiety without promising a scan. Elicits what the patient most fears and checks understanding before discussing tests. History and red flags Declines imaging without asking about new alarm symptoms. Checks bleeding, weight loss, vomiting, bowel changes and family history. Links each newly found alarm symptom to a changed investigation/referral threshold. Clinical interpretation States normal tests absolutely exclude serious disease. Explains why immediate CT has low expected benefit in this supplied low-risk picture. Communicates uncertainty and an evidence-informed threshold for reassessment. Explanation of risk Says CT is harmless or inevitably causes cancer. Explains radiation and incidental findings proportionately. Distinguishes potential contrast risks and downstream testing from direct scan risks. Shared decisions Issues a bare refusal without offering alternatives. Offers symptom-based assessment, review and reasonable alternatives. Uses patient goals to agree a plan and offers a second opinion without defensive language. Profe
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Refuses to assess a newly disclosed serious red flag because a prior scan decision was made. CF2. Falsely assures the patient that cancer is impossible because initial tests were normal. CF3. Orders an unindicated CT solely under pressure without considering risks or alternatives. CF4. Discharges a patient with significant new bleeding or acute instability without urgent assessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient now discloses fresh rectal bleeding for a week. Candidate must stop relying on the earlier low-risk scenario, clarify bleeding and other features, examine/reassess, and decide appropriate urgent pathway; imaging choice follows assessment.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I was too quick to refuse. I will first ask about symptoms or risk factors that could change the need for imaging.” “I said a normal assessment rules out cancer; I should say the risk appears low now but give specific return precautions.” “The newly disclosed rectal bleeding changes the assessment. I will reassess its severity and arrange appropriate follow-up or urgent referral.”

stations.title: Consent with a Patient Who Has a Learning Disability
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-353 Consent with a Patient Who Has a Learning Disability

near_match.title: Equality and Diversity — Reasonable Adjustments for a Patient with Learning Disability

sections.preamble: B2-353 — Consent with a Patient Who Has a Learning Disability AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8-minute station | 13 October 2026 | DRAFT — not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar discussing an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent symptomatic gallstones with a 29-year-old adult with a learning disability. They communicate verbally and use easy-read information. Their mother says, “I will sign for them.” Show how you would obtain valid consent in England and Wales and adapt communication. Assume no immediate emergency.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess decision-specific capacity with support, direct dialogue, reasonable adjustments, understandable options and material risks, role of relatives and best interests only if capacity is absent. Do not equate learning disability with incapacity.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I want the pain to stop, but I am scared of being asleep.” You understand short sentences and pictures, can describe the options after time. Mother: “They cannot decide; let me sign.” If supported, patient can explain the operation’s purpose, major risks and alternatives and can express a consistent choice. Curveball: patient says “No, I do not want surgery now.”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Begin consent dialogue — Address patient directly; ask preferred communication and whether mother should stay; use accessible quiet setting and adequate time. 2. Check the proposed decision — Explain why surgery is offered, expected benefit, realistic option of no surgery or conservative management and material risks in plain language. 3. Make adjustments — Offer easy-read sheets, drawings, teach-back, breaks, speech-language help or independent advocacy when suitable. 4. Assess capacity correctly — Presume capacity; assess understanding, retention, using/weighing and communicating this specific decision after support; unwise choice alone is not incapacity. 5. Respond to mother — Hear helpful information with patient permission; clarify that family do not automatically consent for a capacitous adult and check formal legal authority if relevant. 6. Discuss risks and anaesthesia — Explain common and significant individual risks, including bile duct injury, conversion to open surgery, bleeding, infection and anaesthetic risks without excessive detail. 7. If capacity truly absent — Document assessment; use MCA best-interests process, relevant wishes/values, consultees, valid attorne
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Respectful introduction Talks only to the mother and ignores the patient. Addresses patient and checks preferences for family involvement. Facilitates direct conversation using patient-chosen support and private discussion if needed. Accessible information Uses jargon and asks for a signature immediately. Explains operation and choices in short sentences with aids. Uses teach-back and adapts pace after checking which explanation was understood. Capacity presumption Equates learning disability with legal incapacity. Presumes capacity and identifies decision-specific assessment. Assesses functional abilities after practical support; separates understanding from agreement. Functional assessment Uses diagnosis or IQ instead of capacity criteria. Checks understand, retain, use/weigh and communicate. Elicits patient’s account of benefits, risks and alternatives in their own words. Benefits and alternatives Says surgery is compulsory to treat gallstones. Explains likely relief, nonsurgical choices and possible recurrence of symptoms. Balances symptom benefit against patient’s anaesthesia concern and preference to defer. Material risks Conceals bile duct i
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Assumes the adult lacks capacity solely because of a learning disability. CF2. Obtains the mother’s signature as a substitute for a capacitous adult’s informed consent. CF3. Proceed with elective surgery despite a decision-capable patient’s explicit refusal. CF4. Labels the patient incapable without providing practicable communication support or considering the four statutory functional abilities.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient says “No, I do not want an operation.” The mother insists on proceeding. Expected: check this is an informed, uncoerced and capacitous decision; respect refusal, explain consequences and alternatives, document and offer later review.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I spoke to your mother instead of you. I should ask you directly how you would like information explained and who should help.” “I assumed incapacity from a learning disability. Capacity is decision-specific, and I must first provide practical support.” “I suggested family consent despite your refusal. If you have capacity, your decision prevails even if others disagree.”

stations.title: Bullying in Theatre
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-354 Bullying in Theatre

sections.preamble: B2-354 — Bullying in Theatre AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / professionalism | 8-minute structured station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the junior surgical registrar during an elective laparotomy. The consultant has repeatedly called an FY2 “useless” in front of the team and threatened their training report. During closure, the consultant dismisses the scrub nurse’s concern that a swab count is incorrect. Explain what you would do now and afterwards.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess immediate patient safety, professional challenge, recognition of bullying and appropriate confidential escalation. Actor may test response to power imbalance.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The examiner voices the consultant and nurse. Consultant: “Stop wasting my time. Put it down as a counting error.” Nurse: “I still cannot account for one swab.”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Opening response to a public humiliation? → Maintain calm and the sterile field; do not retaliate; ensure the scrub team can work safely. 2. What is unacceptable here? → A consultant repeatedly insults a trainee and threatens their assessment; identify bullying and power imbalance, not constructive feedback. 3. How do you protect the immediate patient? → Ask for a pause or support if distraction affects safety; use a clear graded challenge about an unsafe action. 4. What if the surgeon demands you ignore a swab-count mismatch? → Explicitly stop progression/closure, request repeat count and locate missing item using the team and local protocol. 5. What would you say after the list? → Describe specific behaviour and its effect in private if safe, seek a supportive senior/supervisor, avoid an accusatory public confrontation. 6. How do you report and document? → Make a dated factual account of words, actions, witnesses and patient-safety effects; use local speaking-up, educational supervisor, HR or Freedom to Speak Up Guardian routes. 7. What if the perpetrator is your trainer? → Seek an alternative trusted supervisor, guardian or postgraduate training route; ask for protection agai
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate composure Responds with insults or abandons sterile role. Stays professional and continues safe patient care. Recruits neutral support while preserving team function. Recognising bullying Dismisses repeated threats as normal theatre culture. Names repeated humiliation and coercion as unacceptable. Distinguishes firm case-related feedback from intimidation and retaliation. Patient safety Ignores distraction and near-miss. States patient safety takes priority and seeks pause if needed. Uses explicit graded challenge for swab discrepancy and verifies resolution. Speak-up technique Confronts abusively or stays silent on risk. Raises concern in factual, respectful terms. Names specific risk, required action and checks team acknowledgement. Evidence Writes allegations with no factual record. Records date, exact observed conduct, witnesses and impacts. Separates first-hand facts from hearsay and retains contemporaneous chronology. Escalation channels Reports only to alleged perpetrator despite power imbalance. Identifies safe senior or Freedom to Speak Up channel. Offers educational, employer and professional routes tailored to ongoing risk. Sup
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Allows closure despite an unresolved missing swab without a safety check. CF2. Threatens or humiliates the FY2 further while purporting to address bullying. CF3. Conceals or falsifies the patient-safety event to protect the consultant. CF4. Repeatedly ignores a credible continuing risk to colleagues/patients rather than raising it through a safe route.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The consultant says: “If you report this, your ARCP will be affected.” Expected: do not argue over grading; calmly insist on resolving the missing swab, record threat factually and seek an independent speaking-up or postgraduate training route.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should first ensure the swab discrepancy is resolved before the operation proceeds.” “I called this banter; repeated humiliation and threatened training retaliation warrant a factual concern.” “I would avoid gossip and raise it confidentially through a route independent of the consultant.”

stations.title: Conflict with the Nurse in Charge About a Discharge
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-355 Conflict with the Nurse in Charge About a Discharge

sections.preamble: B2-355 — Conflict with the Nurse in Charge About a Discharge AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / professionalism | 8-minute structured station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar asked to discharge a patient on postoperative day two after laparoscopic colectomy. The nurse in charge objects: the patient became dizzy when mobilising, blood pressure fell to 88/54 mmHg and there is fresh wound ooze. The bed manager says the bed is urgently needed. Explain your response.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess interdisciplinary listening, recognising acute deterioration, preventing unsafe discharge and resolving conflict without undermining nursing colleagues.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse: “You haven’t examined them since this happened. I am not comfortable with discharge.” Bed manager presses for immediate discharge.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. How will you begin? → Thank nurse in charge for raising concern, pause discharge and ascertain exact reason, without blaming. 2. What is the clinical status? → Review observations, NEWS2 trend, examination, pain, oral intake, mobility, urine output and new symptoms. 3. What has the nurse noticed? → On mobilisation, patient became dizzy with systolic BP 88 and fresh wound ooze: assess for bleeding or sepsis. 4. What is your immediate plan? → Do not discharge; ABCDE, repeat observations and clinical examination, IV access and appropriate investigations, escalate urgently. 5. What else determines discharge readiness? → Review medication reconciliation, analgesia, anticoagulation, wound care, support at home, capacity and patient preferences. 6. How do you resolve disagreement? → Discuss findings jointly, listen and agree objective criteria; involve registrar/consultant and ward leadership if unresolved. 7. What if the bed manager pressures an immediate discharge? → Explain current instability and inability to safely discharge; escalate capacity pressure independently of clinical decision. 8. What documentation and handover? → Record observations, nurse concerns, assessment, rationa
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Listening Dismisses nurse without assessment. Asks for specific concern and validates observation. Elicits timeline and new symptoms, checks what nurse witnessed. Clinical reassessment Discharges without reviewing new hypotension. Repeats observations and focused examination. Runs ABCDE and evaluates haemorrhage/sepsis with trends. Immediate safety Signs discharge despite BP 88 and dizziness. Holds discharge and escalates acute change. Coordinates IV access, bloods and prompt senior help appropriate to deterioration. Differential Calls symptoms anxiety without checking. Considers hypovolaemia, bleeding, infection and medication effect. Prioritises life-threatening haemorrhage and perioperative complications. Readiness criteria Uses bed availability as sole criterion. Checks stability, pain, mobilisation, intake and aftercare. Adds medication reconciliation, support, patient wishes and contingency plan. MDT communication Belittles nursing assessment. Discusses discrepancies respectfully and shares findings. Agrees measurable discharge conditions with nurse and team. Escalation Allows managerial pressure to override risk. Contacts responsible surgica
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Authorises discharge despite new hypotension without reassessment. CF2. Ignores possible postoperative bleeding while labelling symptoms as anxiety. CF3. Bullies the nurse into accepting a plan they believe unsafe without escalation. CF4. Falsifies or suppresses new observations to meet a bed target.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient says they want to leave immediately and the bed manager threatens an incident report. Expected: assess decision-making capacity for leaving, explain risks and alternatives, involve senior support; do not misrepresent an unsafe discharge as medically approved.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I had not heard the new BP or wound observation; I will review the patient before any discharge decision.” “The nurse has identified a potential haemorrhage signal, so I will reassess and escalate, not argue over bed availability.” “I should document the nurse’s concern, senior plan and objective criteria for future discharge.”

sections.preamble: B2-356 — A Colleague Altering a Logbook or Records AMaC MRCS Part B | Professionalism | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar. A fellow trainee tells you they have changed several electronic operative logbook entries from “assisted” to “performed” to meet training targets. They say no patient records were changed and ask you to keep quiet. Explain how you respond. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test probity, distinction between training logbook and clinical record, fact-finding without accusation, support for self-correction, timely proportionate escalation, protection of patients and evidence, and confidentiality. Examiner should challenge with colleague’s fear of ARCP failure.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Colleague says: “Everyone exaggerates their numbers. I only changed six cases and the consultant will never know.” If asked, they acknowledge entering cases without the trainer confirming operative role. They are frightened of losing training progression. Do not volunteer whether clinical records were also altered.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Clarify the facts EXPECT: Ask which cases, what was changed, when, and whether operative notes, patient records or assessments were also altered; do not presume facts. State the standard EXPECT: Explain that knowingly false training records breach professional honesty and can misrepresent competence and jeopardise patient safety. Immediate action EXPECT: Ask colleague to stop further inaccurate entries and preserve original audit trail; do not delete or quietly overwrite evidence. Correct the record EXPECT: Encourage prompt transparent correction through logbook administrator and relevant trainers, recording who performed or assisted in each case. Escalation EXPECT: Explain obligation to raise unresolved or serious concerns through educational supervisor, training programme director, clinical lead or appropriate governance channel; use an alternative if conflicted. Safety and fairness EXPECT: Assess whether claimed competence has influenced unsupervised operating; ensure appropriate supervision while facts are investigated; avoid prejudging outcome. Communication EXPECT: Be supportive without promising secrecy; maintain confidentiality and document factual conversation and actions.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition of probity Treats falsification as routine embellishment. Identifies deliberate false entries as dishonest. Links accuracy to public trust, competence and supervision. Fact finding Assumes clinical notes changed without asking. Clarifies entries and whether patient records are affected. Identifies dates, cases, trainer validation and audit trail. Immediate response Encourages further false entries. Asks colleague to stop and preserve evidence. Prevents alteration of audit trail while avoiding personal investigation. Record correction Suggests deleting entries without disclosure. Requests transparent correction through proper system. Specifies authentic operative role and trainer verification. Escalation Promises secrecy regardless of ongoing risk. Names supervisor or TPD and raises concern if unresolved. Uses independent pathway if direct supervisor is implicated. Patient safety Ignores possible unsupervised operating risk. Checks impact on competence and supervision. Escalates any immediate operating risk to clinical leadership. Support Threatens public humiliation. Offers support and encourages self-reporting. Explains fair process an
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Agrees to conceal deliberate falsification when the concern remains unresolved. Helps fabricate further logbook entries or destroys the audit trail. Allows a known immediate patient-safety risk from falsely claimed operative competence to continue without escalation. Alters a clinical or training record dishonestly to shield the colleague.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Colleague says: “I am operating independently tomorrow because the logbook says I have done these cases.” Expected: immediately escalate supervision and competency concerns to responsible consultant and training leadership, without making an unsupported allegation of harm.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I cannot agree to conceal inaccurate records; we need to correct them transparently.” “Let us establish exactly which entries were changed and preserve the audit trail.” “If the entries affect your supervision tomorrow, I must raise that patient-safety concern now.”

stations.title: A Complaint About an Intimate Examination
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-357 A Complaint About an Intimate Examination

near_match.title: Hip examination

sections.preamble: B2-357 — A Complaint About an Intimate Examination AMaC MRCS Part B | Professionalism | Eight-minute station | 13 October 2026 | Educational draft, not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to respond to a patient who complains that an intimate examination in the surgical assessment unit felt unexpected and humiliating. The patient says no chaperone was offered and they did not understand what would be examined. Respond to the patient and explain your professional next steps.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess listening without defensiveness, consent requirements, chaperone choice, dignity, contemporaneous documentation, clinical safety and objective complaint handling. Do not predetermine facts or promise an investigation outcome.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “The doctor pulled down my underwear without warning. I was too shocked to object. I want to complain.” If supported: “I am worried this has happened to other patients.”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Opening? → Introduce self, provide privacy, listen uninterrupted and acknowledge distress; do not dismiss or contest experience. 2. What apology? → Express regret for the distress and, where appropriate, apologise that their care did not meet expectations; do not speculate on fault before review. 3. Consent standard? → Explain nature, purpose, steps, likely discomfort and ability to decline or stop; obtain informed consent before intimate examination. 4. Chaperone standard? → Offer suitable impartial trained chaperone wherever possible, explain role, respect support-person request; record offer, choice and identity if present. 5. Immediate safeguarding? → Check current injury, ongoing distress and whether patient wants further examination by different clinician; assess urgent safety or wider concern and escalate appropriately. 6. Complaint process? → Explain how to access patient advice/complaints team, encourage written account if desired, preserve confidentiality and cooperate with an impartial review. 7. Records and colleague contact? → Make factual dated note of complaint and clinical response; preserve original records, do not backdate or pressure witnesses; follow employer
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Empathy and listening Interrupts or blames the patient for not objecting. Listens respectfully and acknowledges distress. Reflects specific concern and checks safety and preferred support. Apology Refuses any apology or asserts colleague guilty. Offers sincere regret without prejudging findings. Separates apology for experience from objective assessment of conduct. Consent Says intimate examination does not require explanation. States informed consent and ability to stop are required. Specifies purpose, steps, discomfort and communication accommodations. Chaperone Claims any companion automatically counts as trained chaperone. Offers trained impartial chaperone and records choice. Explains role, visibility, patient support-person preference and alternatives. Privacy and dignity Discusses case openly at nurses’ desk. Uses private setting and safeguards dignity. Offers different examiner and trauma-informed choices without pressure. Safety assessment Ignores possible physical injury or repeated complaints. Assesses present wellbeing and any immediate risk. Escalates credible ongoing risk through suitable safeguarding/governance pathway. Complaint man
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Dismisses or pressures patient into withdrawing complaint, silencing credible safety concern. CF2. Retrospectively fabricates consent or chaperone documentation, or deletes relevant records. CF3. Carries out further intimate examination without valid consent or in disregard of patient refusal. CF4. Shares complaint details indiscriminately or conspires with colleague to conceal a serious concern.
sections.7. One realistic curveball: The patient says the examination was undertaken while sedated for an unrelated procedure. Expected: establish whether examination had clinical indication and valid prior consent; distinguish care from educational examination, which requires documented written/signed consent; promptly escalate and preserve records.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should listen to the complaint without insisting the patient must have misunderstood.” “I cannot assume consent or chaperone offer merely because examination was clinically useful.” “I will document facts, preserve records and help the patient access a fair complaints pathway.”

stations.title: A Patient Who Wants to Record the Consultation
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-358 A Patient Who Wants to Record the Consultation

near_match.title: A patient asks to record her consultation on her phone — respond openly, agree with sensible limits and offer a written summary

sections.preamble: B2-358 — A Patient Who Wants to Record the Consultation AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8 minutes | DRAFT • 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar explaining elective hernia repair to a patient. Before consent discussion, they place their phone on the desk and ask to audio-record the consultation so their partner can listen later. Respond to the request and proceed safely.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess accurate distinction between patient and clinician recordings, confidentiality, accessible communication and professional conduct. Do not award marks for claiming consent to a patient’s private recording is always legally essential.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I forget what you say when I am nervous. Are you refusing to speak unless I turn it off?”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected r: 1. Initial response — Welcome the request calmly, ask whether audio or video and what the patient hopes recording will help with. 2. Patient autonomy — Explain that a personal recording to recall a consultation is generally acceptable; do not claim a blanket prohibition or demand deletion. 3. Confidentiality — Check that other patients, staff outside the consultation, computer screens or background discussions are not inadvertently captured. 4. Consent and clinician recordings — Distinguish patient-made personal audio from clinician/hospital recordings: GMC recording rules for professionals have specific consent and information-handling duties. 5. Consultation conduct — Continue to discuss risks and options honestly; summarise key decisions and offer a written plan or copy of relevant patient information. 6. Concern about online sharing — Explain respectfully that public posting can create confidentiality and context concerns; do not threaten or condition treatment upon a promise not to post. 7. When to seek advice — If recording affects another patient’s privacy, move to a private room, pause briefly and seek local policy/IG advice rather than abandon care. 8. Record keeping — Rec
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Rapport Accuses patient of mistrust. Acknowledges request and responds courteously. Elicits memory or accessibility needs without defensiveness. Recording distinction Applies clinician-recording consent requirements identically to patient audio. Distinguishes patient-held from professional recordings. Clarifies audio/video and secondary use without overclaiming legal powers. Privacy Allows other identifiable patients to be captured. Protects bystanders and consultation privacy. Offers a private location and checks monitors and background audio. Patient rights Makes recording a condition of care or orders phone seized. Does not impose blanket ban on personal audio. Handles objections proportionately and seeks policy advice when necessary. Communication quality Withholds material risks because recorded. Provides ordinary informed clinical discussion. Uses teach-back and written summary to reinforce shared decisions. Online dissemination Threatens the patient to prevent publication. Explains concerns about misleading or identifying public release. Distinguishes request for discretion from legal certainty. Conflict resolution Terminates consultation wi
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Refuses clinically necessary care solely because the patient requests a personal audio recording. CF2. Knowingly allows recording of another identifiable patient’s sensitive information without taking reasonable privacy precautions. CF3. Threatens confiscation or deletion of the patient’s recording as an automatic entitlement. CF4. Intentionally withholds material operative risks because the consultation is recorded.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient switches to video and a second patient is clearly visible through the open doorway. Expected: address privacy, close the door or move location, ask that identifiable third parties are not filmed, and continue the consultation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I conflated a patient’s personal recording with recordings made by clinicians; these are distinct situations.” “I should protect the other patient’s privacy by changing location, not by punishing this patient.” “The recording does not remove my duty to explain material risks and record the shared decision.”

stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-359 Complications After Surgery Abroad

near_match.title: Complications after bariatric surgery

sections.preamble: B2-359 — Complications After Surgery Abroad AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8 minutes | DRAFT • 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call general surgical registrar. A patient returns 10 days after a privately funded abdominal operation overseas. They have fever 38.7°C, pulse 122/min, abdominal pain and purulent wound discharge. They ask whether the NHS will treat them. Discuss assessment, management and next steps.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test acute surgical sepsis, relevant travel/operation history, antimicrobial-resistance awareness, non-judgemental communication and appropriate statements about NHS treatment.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “The surgeon abroad said this is normal. Did I make a mistake going there? Will the NHS refuse to help me?”
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected r: 1. Immediate triage — Check observations and sepsis red flags: fever, hypotension, confusion, severe pain, peritonism, organ dysfunction; ABCDE if unwell. 2. Operation history — Find country, date, procedure, implant/mesh, indication, intraoperative problems, discharge summaries and previous antibiotics. 3. Complication assessment — Examine wound and abdomen; consider abscess, leak, deep SSI, VTE, haemorrhage and implant infection rather than assume superficial cellulitis. 4. Investigations — Order tailored blood tests, cultures before antibiotics if no dangerous delay, and CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast if suspected collection/leak and appropriate. 5. Initial management — Analgesia, IV access, fluid resuscitation if indicated, appropriate empiric antibiotics for suspected significant infection, urgent senior surgical review and source control. 6. Infection control — Ask about treatment abroad and prior hospitalisation; inform infection prevention/microbiology about possible antimicrobial-resistant organisms and screening needs. 7. Communication and overseas records — Explain uncertainty without criticism; ask permission to contact overseas surgeon or obtain records, but do not de
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Respect and rapport Blames patient for choosing surgery abroad. Responds with empathy and non-judgement. Clarifies expectations and acknowledges anxiety without promises. Acute severity Treats rigors and low BP as routine wound inflammation. Screens for systemic infection and instability. Initiates ABCDE and early resuscitation/escalation with specific triggers. Operative history Does not ask what procedure occurred. Asks timing, operation, implants and drugs. Seeks operative and microbiology records with permission. Differential Assumes superficial infection with no abdominal exam. Includes wound infection, abscess, leak and thromboembolism. Prioritises time-critical source control and implant complications. Investigations Orders no tests despite septic features. Requests targeted bloods/cultures and imaging as indicated. Plans imaging matched to procedure with microbiology collaboration. Treatment Offers oral antibiotics only to unstable patient. Starts indicated stabilisation, antibiotics and surgical review. Links treatment to source-control timeline and clinical response. Infection prevention Dismisses overseas-care antimicrobial resistance ri
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Refuses or deliberately delays emergency assessment because the operation was paid for overseas. CF2. Fails to recognise possible sepsis or intra-abdominal leak in a tachycardic febrile postoperative patient. CF3. Gives reassurance and discharge without assessing possible source-control needs. CF4. Conceals relevant recent overseas hospital exposure from treating infection prevention/microbiology colleagues.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient now develops BP 82/48 and confusion while the overseas clinic has not replied. Expected: immediate ABCDE, emergency senior/critical-care escalation, resuscitation, timely antimicrobials and urgent source-control assessment; do not await overseas records.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should stabilise and assess this patient before discussing elective funding or responsibility.” “I labelled this a superficial wound infection without excluding a deep collection or leak.” “I will alert microbiology/IPC about overseas admission and coordinate appropriate investigations and treatment.”
