sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-36 • ROUND 2 DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • CLINICAL REVIEW REQUIRED
sections.1. Title and header: Sigmoid volvulus Station type: Applied knowledge / critical care | 9-minute encounter + 1-minute reading. Code: B2-36; final MB- ID unassigned. Guiding specification: AMaC MRCS Part B Station Writing Guide, 11 October 2026. Related stations: cross-reference to be confirmed against live 219-station register; this topic appears on the Round 2 gap list. AMaC educational station; not an official Intercollegiate examination mark scheme.
sections.2. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in the surgical assessment area. 83-year-old with progressive distension and constipation. The information initially available is: Imaging report describes dilated sigmoid loop. Interpret the information provided, answer the examiner’s questions, and explain safe further assessment and management. You may ask for additional clinical information; it is not volunteered unless requested.
sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: Coffee-bean sign, endoscopic decompression, when to operate. Trap: Failing to recognise this safety concern — peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery. First move: “Before proceeding, I will confirm immediate safety and specifically consider peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery.”
sections.4. Flow: 1. Confirm identity, role, consent where appropriate, and assess whether immediate intervention is needed: Peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery. 2. Characterise the central presentation: Imaging report describes dilated sigmoid loop. 3. Test your working interpretation against the key discriminators: Coffee-bean sign, endoscopic decompression, when to operate; Appropriate prioritisation and escalation. 4. Address further decision points: Clear communication and safety-netting; Defensible differential. 5. Explain and document a reasoned plan: Resuscitate, interpret imaging and discuss endoscopic decompression if uncomplicated; arrange escalation, reassessment and safety-netting.
sections.5. Marking grid: AMaC practice grid: 9 rows, descriptive Fail / Borderline / Pass / High-performance bands. Source-dependent entries require independent currency checks prior to publication. R1 — Professional opening (Clinical skill) Fail: Introduces no role or fails to engage. Borderline: Introduces self but omits purpose. Pass: Explains task and obtains appropriate permission. High-performance: Confident, person-centred signposting and early prioritisation. R2 — Immediate risk recognition (Clinical knowledge) Fail: Dismisses peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery. Borderline: Mentions risk without acting. Pass: Identifies peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery and acts appropriately. High-performance: Explicitly prioritises and anticipates deterioration from peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery. Evidence tag: source list in section 11; exact recommendation and version must be confirmed during clinical review. R3 — Focused assessment (Clinical skill) Fail: Does not establish: imaging report describes dilated sigmoid loop. Borderline: Obtains one relevant finding. Pass: Elicits and interprets: Imaging report describes d
sections.6. Three performances: Educational sample transcripts for the same default scenario. They are structured as a simulated examiner–candidate exchange; they do not reproduce confidential examination content. Fail performance Examiner: “The examiner provides the scenario and asks you to interpret the findings and demonstrate your approach.”[R1] Candidate: “This is routine; there is no need to explain much.” Examiner: “What clinical concern would change your priority?”[R2] Candidate: “Peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery can be ignored.” Examiner: “How do you interpret the key finding?”[R3] Candidate: “The finding is probably irrelevant.” Examiner: “What about coffee-bean sign, endoscopic decompression, when to operate?”[R4] Candidate: “I do not need to assess coffee-bean sign, endoscopic decompression, when to operate.” Examiner: “What about appropriate prioritisation and escalation?”[R5] Candidate: “I will ignore appropriate prioritisation and escalation.” Examiner: “What further issue matters?”[R6] Candidate: “Further assessment is unnecessary.” Examiner: “What should happen next?”[R7] Candidate: “There is no need for the next steps yet.” Examiner: “Would laxatives relieve this?
sections.7. Critical fails: 1. Grid R2: Missing or dismissing peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery. Patient consequence: Delayed recognition or treatment of a time-critical clinical problem. 2. Grid R7: Proceeding with management without assessing contraindications, readiness or the need for specialist help. Patient consequence: Avoidable iatrogenic injury or deterioration. 3. Grid R9: Failing to escalate or act on important deterioration. Patient consequence: Progression of an unsafe clinical condition. These represent educationally significant unsafe actions, not a prediction of the official examination result.
sections.8. Recovery lines: “I need to correct my priorities: the safety concern is peritonitis, ischaemia or perforation changes pathway to surgery, and I will address that before routine steps.” “I should explain the uncertainty clearly, involve the appropriate senior clinician and confirm a safe follow-up plan.”

sections.preamble: B2-360 — Explaining That Surgery Is Not Funded AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar in an NHS outpatient clinic. A 42-year-old patient has symptomatic but uncomplicated abdominal wall skin laxity following major weight loss. The consultant has concluded that elective abdominoplasty is not routinely commissioned under the local NHS policy; no functional complication requiring urgent surgery is present. Explain the decision and options. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess empathetic explanation of commissioning rather than asserting the procedure is clinically impossible; check functional symptoms and psychological effect, verify local criteria, discuss individual funding request (IFR) where genuinely exceptional, alternatives, complaints and follow-up. Do not promise approval.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Patient says: “I worked hard to lose weight. You are saying I do not deserve surgery.” Reports skin irritation, embarrassment and avoiding swimming. No recurrent cellulitis, ulceration or severe functional restriction. If asked, wants to know if they can appeal and whether mental distress counts.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Elicit impact EXPECT: Ask about skin infections, intertrigo, hygiene, mobility, pain, psychological effects and previous conservative treatments; check for features warranting reassessment. Explain clinical assessment EXPECT: Distinguish potential benefit and clinical suitability from local NHS funding eligibility; avoid calling concerns merely cosmetic. Policy and uncertainty EXPECT: Explain that the integrated care board (ICB) commissions procedures against published criteria which vary locally; confirm current policy before quoting thresholds. Shared options EXPECT: Offer skin care, treatment of intertrigo, weight-stability support and referral for psychological support where appropriate; discuss private options neutrally only if patient asks. Exceptional funding EXPECT: Describe an individual funding request for genuinely exceptional circumstances supported by clinical evidence, with no guarantee; routine dissatisfaction alone does not establish exceptionality. Review and escalation EXPECT: Arrange consultant or relevant specialist review if unrecognised functional pathology or clinical indications emerge; ensure patient knows who decides funding. Challenge and fairness EXPECT:
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Empathy Calls concern vanity and ends discussion. Acknowledges effort, distress and disappointment. Explores lived impact without promising a funded operation. Clinical needs Assumes no symptoms matter once funding refused. Asks about skin, pain and function. Identifies potentially qualifying recurrent infection or functional impairment for reassessment. Funding distinction Says the operation is unsafe solely because NHS will not fund it. Distinguishes commissioning from clinical feasibility. Explains who makes funding decisions and what is still clinically uncertain. Policy accuracy Invents a universal NHS threshold. States local ICB criteria need checking. Offers to review actual published criteria and eligibility evidence. Alternatives Offers no treatment whatsoever. Discusses skin care and symptom treatment. Tailors dermatological and psychological support to patient concerns. IFR process Guarantees an IFR will succeed. Explains exceptional-case application without guarantees. Identifies clinician evidence, decision maker and potential review route. Autonomy Pressures patient into private treatment. Discusses options without coercion. Separates
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Knowingly fabricates eligibility criteria or tells the patient funding is legally impossible without checking local policy. Promises NHS funding or books a funded operation despite knowing no authorisation exists. Dismisses significant recurrent infection or functional deterioration without assessing or arranging review. Pressures the patient to purchase private surgery from the candidate or a colleague as the only option.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient produces photographs of repeated ulceration beneath the skin fold and a GP letter documenting two treated infections. Expected: acknowledge this is new material, reassess clinical severity, treat current disease, review local eligibility criteria and seek consultant reconsideration rather than repeat the refusal automatically.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I can see this decision feels unfair, and I want to understand the symptoms affecting you.” “The question is whether local NHS commissioning criteria are met, not whether your concerns are unimportant.” “If there is evidence of recurrent infection or exceptional need, I will ask the team to reassess the case and explain the funding route.”

sections.preamble: B2-361 — Trauma Team Handover Using MIST AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar receiving a trauma pre-alert by telephone. Ambulance crew reports a 29-year-old motorcyclist struck a van at approximately 45 mph, with suspected pelvic injury and falling blood pressure. Receive a structured MIST handover, clarify immediate threats, mobilise the team and repeat back priorities. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess MIST: Mechanism, Injuries suspected/found, Signs including serial physiology, Treatment given. Test pre-alert, closed-loop communication, haemorrhage control, early major haemorrhage activation when indicated, trauma team leadership and concise documentation. Do not confuse MIST with SBAR.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Paramedic: “ETA seven minutes. He was thrown five metres. GCS 14, RR 28, SpO2 95% on oxygen, HR 132, BP 82/48, cool and clammy. Pelvic pain and an open left tibial fracture. Pelvic binder applied at greater trochanters, IV access obtained, tranexamic acid given under protocol. No obvious external torso bleeding.” If asked, blood pressure was 104 systolic 10 minutes earlier; no blood products given.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Identify mechanism EXPECT: Capture high-energy motorcycle collision, speed, ejection and time of injury; recognise multisystem trauma. Identify injuries EXPECT: Record suspected pelvic haemorrhage and open tibial fracture; avoid claiming injuries are confirmed without imaging or assessment. Interpret signs EXPECT: Repeat GCS, airway, respiratory rate, saturation, heart rate and falling BP; identify haemorrhagic shock and possible occult bleeding. Clarify treatment EXPECT: Confirm binder position over greater trochanters, external haemorrhage control, oxygen, access, analgesia and TXA time; avoid loosening binder for routine examination. Pre-alert EXPECT: State ETA, shock and pelvic injury; activate trauma team, senior trauma/surgical and anaesthetic input, and major haemorrhage protocol according to local triggers. Prepare receiving bay EXPECT: Arrange monitored resuscitation, warmed blood products per protocol, rapid infuser where available, blood sampling and access to CT/interventional radiology/theatre depending on stability. Closed loop EXPECT: Repeat back MIST and immediate plan to ambulance crew, name team lead and allocate tasks; communicate changed ETA or physiology. Arriv
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance M — mechanism Omits mechanism and injury time. States collision and high-energy transfer. Captures speed, ejection and injury time relevant to occult injury. I — injuries Assumes pelvic fracture proven. Lists suspected pelvis and open tibia. Separates suspected injuries from confirmed findings and flags haemorrhage. S — physiology Ignores hypotension and tachycardia. Recognises shock from BP 82/48 and HR 132. Highlights deteriorating BP trend, GCS and respiratory status. T — treatment Fails to ask what was done. Confirms binder, IV access, oxygen and TXA. Checks binder position, timing and ongoing bleeding control. Pre-alert urgency Waits until ambulance arrives before alerting anyone. Calls trauma team and senior clinicians. Activates major haemorrhage support and specifies ETA and instability. Resource preparation Plans routine clinic bed for shocked trauma patient. Prepares resus bay, monitoring and blood access. Assigns roles and readies blood products, warming and definitive haemorrhage pathways. Closed-loop handover Hangs up without read-back. Repeats key MIST details and plan. Confirms sender agreement, contact and update trigger. Prioritisa
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Fails to recognise life-threatening shock despite HR 132 and BP 82/48 and arranges no urgent trauma response. Directs removal of an appropriately positioned pelvic binder before haemorrhage control or specialist assessment. Directs the unstable patient to unmonitored CT as a substitute for immediate resuscitation. Does not communicate the critical hypotension to the receiving trauma team, causing unsafe under-triage.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: During the call the paramedic says BP has fallen to 68 systolic and the patient is becoming drowsy. Expected: explicitly escalate pre-alert to imminent peri-arrest/major haemorrhage, mobilise immediate blood and senior trauma/anaesthetic resources, request continued haemorrhage control and rapid transport with update; do not wait for imaging.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I am receiving MIST: high-energy mechanism, suspected pelvic and leg injuries, worsening shock, binder and IV treatment given.” “This is a major haemorrhage risk; activate the trauma and blood-product response now.” “Please confirm the binder is correctly positioned and tell us immediately if airway, GCS or blood pressure worsens.”

stations.title: Explaining That a Stoma Will Be Permanent
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-362 Explaining That a Stoma Will Be Permanent

sections.preamble: B2-362 — Explaining That a Stoma Will Be Permanent AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8 minutes | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a colorectal surgical registrar meeting a 58-year-old patient six weeks after an emergency abdominoperineal excision for a very low rectal cancer. The operation removed the anus and rectum. At discharge the patient had hoped the colostomy could be reversed. Explain sensitively why it will be permanent, address concerns and agree ongoing support. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Actor-led consultation. The operative record confirms an end colostomy and removal of the rectum and anal sphincter complex. There is no reconstructible distal bowel outlet. Assess candour, factual explanation, empathy, practical rehabilitation and checks of understanding. Do not imply a routine reversal is possible.
sections.3. Actor brief: Patient initially says: “I thought the bag was temporary. Can another surgeon put me back together?” Be upset, concerned about intimacy and returning to work. If invited, mention leaks twice a week and reluctance to leave home. Curveball only when requested.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected r: 1. How do you begin this difficult discussion? → Check understanding and preferences; sit at eye level, warn of difficult news, allow time, and ask permission to explain. 2. Why is the stoma permanent? → Following abdominoperineal excision the rectum, anal canal and sphincter complex were removed; there is no safe distal outlet for reconnection. Confirm from operative details rather than guess. 3. Is reversal or an alternative operation possible? → Explain that routine reversal is not anatomically feasible in this case; offer review of operative records and senior colorectal discussion if uncertainty or a second opinion is requested. 4. What emotions and concerns should be addressed? → Acknowledge loss, grief, altered body image, fear of odour/leakage, relationships, sexual function, work, and practical burden without dismissing concerns. 5. How would you address leakage and skin problems? → Examine stoma and peristomal skin with consent, assess appliance fit and output, involve specialist stoma nurse promptly for fitting, skin protection and education. 6. What support can you offer? → Stoma nurse follow-up, peer support and Colostomy UK or appropriate local group, psychosocial/sex
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and rapport Announces permanence without checking prior understanding. Asks patient what was understood and seeks permission to explain. Warns gently, uses pauses and monitors emotion before continuing. Anatomical explanation Promises reconnection without rectum or sphincter. States APR removed rectum and anus; routine reversal not possible. Uses simple anatomy, distinguishes this case from temporary diversion. Honesty and uncertainty Invents future surgery or refuses reasonable clarification. Checks record and offers consultant discussion if requested. Acknowledges limits of personal certainty without undermining established facts. Emotional response Minimises distress or says patient should be grateful. Acknowledges grief, body-image concerns and disappointment. Responds to cues, leaves silence and offers personalised support. Stoma symptoms Ignores leakage and damaged skin. Asks about appliance fit, skin and output and refers to stoma nurse. Arranges timely appliance review and tailored troubleshooting. Daily living Never asks about relationship, work or diet impact. Elicits concerns about diet, intimacy and work. Links each problem to s
sections.6. Four critical fails: CF1. Promises reversal after removal of anus and sphincters without any anatomical basis, leading to serious false reassurance. CF2. Dismisses stated food restriction without checking immediate nutrition, hydration and psychological safety. CF3. Identifies recurrent leakage and skin injury but refuses stoma-nurse or clinical review, leaving preventable harm unaddressed. CF4. Offers a fabricated cancer prognosis or contradicts the established operative findings while discouraging clarification.
sections.7. One realistic curveball: The patient tearfully says: “If I stop eating, could I go without the bag? I would rather not eat than have accidents at work.” Expected: assess immediate nutritional and psychological safety, explain that food restriction is unsafe and will not make the stoma reversible, arrange urgent stoma fitting and dietetic/psychological support; ask sensitively about self-harm if indicated.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I implied that reversal might routinely be possible. Here, the anal sphincter and rectum have been removed; I should clarify the anatomy and offer review by the operating colorectal team.” “I focused on the surgery and overlooked the effect on daily life. I want to hear about leakage, intimacy, work and how you are coping.” “I should not simply hand over a leaflet. I will arrange a named stoma nurse review and make sure you know who to call if the appliance fails.”

stations.title: Cosmetic Surgery Request and Body Dysmorphic Disorder
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-363 Cosmetic Surgery Request and Body Dysmorphic Disorder

sections.preamble: B2-363 — Cosmetic Surgery Request and Body Dysmorphic Disorder AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8 minutes | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar in a cosmetic-surgery assessment clinic. A 25-year-old requests urgent rhinoplasty because they believe a small nasal asymmetry is “disgusting”. They have attended several clinics and ask you to book surgery immediately. Explain your assessment, whether surgery is appropriate and next steps. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: A fictional consultation with features raising possible body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), not an established diagnosis. Assess non-stigmatising exploration of motivations, impact and risk, realistic consent, psychological assessment and a safe decision not to offer immediate surgery. Avoid diagnosing solely from appearance.
sections.3. Actor brief: Patient: “I spend three hours checking my nose in mirrors, cannot go to university, and I know surgery will fix my whole life.” Become frustrated if the candidate says no. If sensitively asked, report no current self-harm plan, but persistent hopelessness; answer risk questions honestly.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected r: 1. How do you explore the request? → Ask in open language what bothers them, what change is sought and why now; assess internal or external pressures and previous procedures/consultations. 2. Which features raise concern for BDD? → Persistent preoccupation with a perceived defect, repetitive checking or camouflaging, marked distress, avoidance and functional impairment; do not equate dissatisfaction alone with BDD. 3. What specific screening questions matter? → Ask time spent thinking about appearance, impact on work/social life, repetitive checking, reassurance seeking and degree of conviction, consistent with NICE CG31. 4. Which mental-health risks do you assess? → Ask about mood, anxiety, eating/other psychiatric symptoms and directly assess self-harm/suicide risk when clinically relevant; safety-plan or urgently escalate if indicated. 5. How do you explain a decision not to operate now? → Say a procedure may not solve their distress and may cause physical/psychological harm; withhold non-urgent surgery until suitable specialist assessment and shared review. 6. What are the consent safeguards? → The operating clinician must personally discuss benefits, realistic limitations, com
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Rapport Belittles concern or uses “vain” label. Acknowledges distress respectfully and uses open questions. Validates emotion without validating unproven defect or diagnosis. Motivation Does not ask why surgery is wanted. Explores goals, expectations and prior opinions. Checks social pressure, repeat procedures and desired life changes. BDD recognition Equates all appearance concern with psychiatric disease or ignores major warning signs. Recognises preoccupation, repetitive checking and impaired function. Relates specific NICE screening domains to history and differential. Risk assessment Ignores suicide or self-harm cue. Asks about mood, hopelessness and safety. Assesses current intent, plans, protective factors and escalates according to risk. Clinical decision Offers immediate booking despite major red flags. Explains rationale for deferring surgery. Gives a firm non-stigmatising refusal where no expected net benefit. Consent quality Promises a perfect nose or delegates all consent to sales staff. Explains limitations, harms, alternatives and reflection. Clarifies operating clinician’s responsibility and voluntary decision. Psychological pathwa
sections.6. Four critical fails: CF1. Books elective rhinoplasty immediately despite marked BDD indicators without psychological evaluation or appropriate assessment. CF2. Ignores an expressed possibility of self-harm and makes no immediate risk assessment or escalation. CF3. Promises surgery will cure the patient’s distress or guarantee a specific appearance. CF4. Pressures the patient into paying or consenting immediately, without reflection or an independent decision.
sections.7. One realistic curveball: Patient says: “Unless you operate next week, I might do something stupid.” Expected: stop elective booking discussion, ask plainly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plan and immediate safety; arrange urgent mental-health/crisis assessment proportionate to risk, with consent and safeguarding as needed. Do not assume this is manipulation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I described the concern as vanity. I should ask how much time the thoughts take and how daily life has been affected, without judging you.” “I suggested surgery might fix everything. No cosmetic intervention can guarantee improvement in psychological distress; we should assess those needs first.” “I heard a possible self-harm warning and need to ask directly about your safety before discussing elective treatment.”

stations.title: A Relative Asking for Information by Telephone
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-364 A Relative Asking for Information by Telephone

sections.preamble: B2-364 — A Relative Asking for Information by Telephone AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8 minutes | Draft 13 October 2026 Independent educational material — not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A woman telephones the ward saying she is the daughter of a 72-year-old man admitted with bowel obstruction. She demands the CT result, whether he has cancer, and the operation plan. The patient is awake and has capacity. Explain what you would say and do in an eight-minute telephone consultation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess protection of identity and patient confidentiality while remaining empathic. The ward record confirms no documented permission for disclosure. If asked, the patient is alert and available; on direct enquiry he authorises a limited update to his daughter, but not discussion of an unrelated previous diagnosis.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Caller (impatient, distressed): “I am his daughter. Tell me whether the scan shows cancer. He never keeps anything from me.” If denied: “I know his date of birth—so you must tell me.” Curveball later: “He is asleep now—just tell me the CT result.” 4. Examiner prompts and expected responses — eight distinct tasks 1. Opening and verification. Introduce role and listen to concern; use an approved hospital callback or verification process to establish caller identity, but explain that identifying the caller does not itself give authority to disclose. 2. Consent and patient preference. Check record for agreed family contacts and scope of consent; as he has capacity, seek his current permission and ascertain precisely what he wants shared. 3. What may be said before consent?. Avoid confirming admission, diagnosis, CT results or proposed surgery to an unverified/unauthorised caller. Offer the ward contact process and facilitate a conversation with the patient. 4. What if the caller insists kinship suffices?. Explain kindly that being a daughter or next of kin does not automatically confer a right to clinical information; offer a safe route to obtain the patient’s consent. 5. How to disclo
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — specific b: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Telephone opening Provides clinical results immediately on greeting. Introduces self, acknowledges worry and asks who is calling. Sets empathetic boundaries without confirming confidential attendance or diagnosis. Identity verification Treats knowledge of DOB as proof of entitlement. Uses approved identity/callback checks before any contemplated disclosure. Separates reliable identity checks from the distinct test of permission/authority. Patient consent Assumes next of kin automatically has consent. Checks records and obtains capable patient’s current permission. Checks scope, exceptions and patient preferences for how and when updates occur. Unauthorised disclosure Confirms CT result or operation without permission. Withholds identifiable clinical facts pending authority. Offers facilitated patient contact while disclosing no unnecessary identifying detail. Explanation to caller Rebuffs caller rudely or makes false legal assertions. Explains privacy rule calmly and acknowledges concern. Offers a specific safe next step and checks caller understanding. Authorised update Shares entire history after limited consent. Relays only the consented clinica
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Discloses the patient’s CT result or suspected malignancy to the caller without verifying appropriate authority or patient consent. CF2. Explicitly overrides a capable patient’s refusal of disclosure because the caller is “next of kin”. CF3. Reveals an unrelated confidential diagnosis beyond the scope the patient specifically authorised. CF4. Falsely records consent or conceals an unauthorised information disclosure.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Caller says: “He has capacity but he told you not to mention his previous HIV diagnosis. I know he has it. Confirm it!” Expected: do not confirm or deny the diagnosis; respect the patient’s explicit restriction; offer a consensual update about the current surgical admission only.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I have checked who you are, but that does not mean I can release medical results; I need to check his wishes first.” “I mentioned a diagnosis outside his stated consent. I withdraw that disclosure approach and would report and document any actual confidentiality breach.” “I can take important information from you without sharing his private information; I will arrange a consented update if he agrees.”
sections.9. Model performance — Fail: Reveals suspected cancer on the telephone, treats next of kin as permission and fails to document the call.

stations.title: Medical Students in Clinic Patient Consent
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-365 Medical Students in Clinic Patient Consent

sections.preamble: B2-365 — Medical Students in Clinic: Patient Consent AMaC MRCS Part B | Professionalism | 8 minutes | Draft 13 October 2026 Independent educational material — not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar in colorectal clinic with two medical students. A 46-year-old patient has an appointment about rectal bleeding. The students wish to observe history-taking and the subsequent rectal examination. The patient seems uncomfortable but does not volunteer an objection. Explain how you would manage consent and student participation.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess voluntary, specific and continuing consent for education. The patient needs clinical assessment regardless of their decision about teaching. Separate permission for observing the consultation from permission for a supervised student-performed intimate examination. Do not ask for an intimate examination to be physically performed.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I thought students had to be there for you to treat me. I’d prefer not to have anyone watching the rectal examination.” Later: “Can one student do it instead, if you are there?” The student privately asks whether the patient’s earlier nod means consent. 4. Examiner prompts and expected responses — eight distinct tasks 1. Opening and identification. Introduce students by name and role, explain their educational status and supervision, and ask permission before they remain in the consultation. 2. Voluntary choice. Tell patient declining students will not affect their care, wait time or relationship with clinician; recognise silence or discomfort as insufficient consent. 3. Scope of observation. Seek separate permission for students hearing history or watching a general examination; allow selective participation and ask students to leave promptly when requested. 4. Intimate examination consent. Explain why a rectal examination is clinically indicated, the procedure, alternatives and chaperone option; request clinical consent separately from consent for any student to observe. 5. Student-performed examination. If the patient proactively agrees, check student competence and re
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid — specific b: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introductions Leaves students unidentified in room. Introduces student status and supervised role. Checks patient readiness before admitting learners and offers privacy. Voluntariness Suggests care depends on teaching agreement. States refusal will not prejudice care. Checks for nonverbal discomfort and offers choice without authority pressure. Specific permission Treats clinic attendance as blanket consent. Asks consent for students to observe consultation. Separately seeks consent for history, observation and any direct participation. Intimate-exam safeguards Permits student rectal exam without specific permission. Explains clinical intimate exam and offers chaperone. Distinguishes clinical necessity from student observation/examination and asks explicit permission for each. Student competence Asks an unsupervised novice to undertake procedure. Confirms competent student and registered-supervisor presence. Adjusts teaching to patient wishes, student skill and agreed direct supervision. Right to withdraw Continues exam after patient objects. Stops participation immediately on withdrawal. Restores privacy, checks comfort and continues necessary car
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Performs or allows a student to perform an intimate examination without the patient’s specific informed consent. CF2. Continues student presence or examination after the patient explicitly asks the student to leave or asks to stop. CF3. Threatens delayed or inferior treatment if the patient refuses student involvement. CF4. Allows an unsupervised student intimate examination without appropriate competence or supervision despite patient consent.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Patient agreed to the student observing the consultation, but before the rectal examination says: “I do not want the student to see this.” The student says the consultant has already approved it. Expected: ask student to leave without argument; obtain separate clinical consent and discuss a suitable chaperone; no educational or senior preference can override refusal.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I interpreted their silence as agreement. I should identify the students and ask explicitly whether they may stay.” “Consent to observe the history did not include the rectal examination. I will ask the students to leave and obtain separate consent for the examination.” “Even when a patient agrees to a student examination, I must check the student’s competence and supervision and stop if consent is withdrawn.”
sections.9. Model performance — Fail: Uses silence as consent, lets a student perform a rectal examination and dismisses the patient’s discomfort.

stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-366 HIV Partner Confidentiality

near_match.title: STI — Confidentiality and Partner Notification

sections.preamble: B2-366 — A Patient with HIV Who Has Not Told Their Partner AMaC MRCS Part B | Professionalism / communication | 8-minute station | Draft 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar seeing a 38-year-old man with well-controlled HIV during postoperative follow-up. He says his current partner does not know his diagnosis and asks you to keep it secret. Explore the situation, address risk, and describe any justified information-sharing. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assesses patient-centred communication, transmission-risk assessment, confidentiality and the exceptional public-interest disclosure threshold. Reveal that the patient takes antiretroviral treatment, states a recent undetectable viral load but cannot show its date, and is anxious about violence if he tells his partner. Do not equate HIV diagnosis with inevitable transmission.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I am doing well on treatment. My partner must never find out; she may hurt me or leave me. Will you tell her?” If asked, he reports condomless sexual contact but is unsure of the last viral-load date.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected f: 1. Immediate response → Reassure confidentiality is the starting position, avoid promising absolute secrecy, ask open questions and establish a safe private environment. 2. Assess specific transmission risk → Clarify treatment adherence, documented viral load and duration of suppression, type/timing of exposures, protection and partner testing; involve HIV specialist to establish actual risk. Sustained documented viral suppression prevents sexual transmission (U=U). 3. Explore non-disclosure → Ask what the patient fears, including domestic abuse, stigma, coercion and safety; offer psychosocial and safeguarding support without judgement. 4. Counsel on disclosure → Explain benefits of partner testing, voluntary disclosure and partner-notification support through the sexual-health/HIV team; offer assisted or anonymous notification where feasible. 5. What is the confidentiality rule? → Seek explicit patient consent before identifying them; disclosure without consent is an exceptional, proportionate action only when failure to disclose exposes an identifiable person to risk of death or serious harm. 6. Who should decide about exceptional disclosure? → Seek urgent advice from HIV/sexual-
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Rapport and non-judgement Threatens to expose the patient or stigmatizes HIV. Acknowledges distress and explains starting confidentiality. Builds trust while transparently discussing limited exceptions. Specific risk assessment Assumes HIV status alone means ongoing sexual transmission. Asks about ART, viral load, exposure and partners. Seeks documented sustained suppression and specialist risk analysis including U=U. Safeguarding Ignores stated fear of partner violence. Asks about coercion or violence and offers support. Plans a safe, individualised disclosure pathway with safeguarding input. Consent to share Automatically calls the partner without consent. Seeks consent to share necessary information. Offers supported partner notification and respects reasons for refusal. Legal/professional balance Claims absolute secrecy even with serious identifiable risk, or always discloses. Recognises exceptional serious-harm disclosure threshold. Tests necessity, proportionality and less intrusive options case by case. Specialist escalation Acts alone on uncertain virological facts. Consults HIV team and senior confidentiality advice. Coordinates urgent exp
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Contacts the partner and reveals identifiable HIV status solely because of diagnosis, without consent or a justified serious-harm assessment. CF2. Promises never to disclose under any circumstances despite credible, serious and preventable risk to an identifiable partner. CF3. Ignores a disclosed threat of partner violence and coerces immediate disclosure without safety planning. CF4. Ignores credible recent high-risk exposure and fails to arrange prompt specialist assessment when intervention could be time-critical.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: The HIV team confirms the patient has maintained a documented undetectable viral load for two years on ART. The examiner asks whether you will still tell the partner. Expected: sexual transmission risk with sustained viral suppression is effectively zero (U=U); status alone does not justify breaking confidentiality. Offer voluntary disclosure and partner services; document advice. If new evidence suggests unsuppressed virus and serious risk, reassess with specialists.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I spoke as though HIV automatically means transmission; I need the documented viral-load history and specialist assessment.” “I promised unconditional secrecy; confidentiality is strong, but the serious-harm exception needs careful individual review.” “I overlooked possible violence following disclosure; I should assess safety and offer supported notification.”

sections.preamble: B2-367 — Uncomplicated Appendicitis: Antibiotics First or Operate? AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / shared surgical decision | 8-minute station | Revised pilot 15 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme | Making the difficult easy
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the core surgical trainee working under senior supervision. A 29-year-old adult with CT-confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis is stable, has no peritonitis or perforation, and asks whether antibiotics could avoid surgery. The report describes a 7-mm appendix with periappendiceal inflammatory fat stranding and no appendicolith. Discuss reasonable treatment options, their trade-offs and the safe plan. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess genuine option discussion, recognition of suitable antibiotic-first candidates, limitations of trial data and patient preference. The patient is not pregnant, is immunocompetent and has access to follow-up. The data provided should be discussed as cohort-specific estimates, not guaranteed patient outcomes.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I want to avoid an operation and get back to work. Is antibiotics treatment a cure? What if the scan shows a stone?” May become febrile with new guarding if curveball is requested.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected f: 1. Confirm uncomplicated and stable disease → Review CT for perforation, abscess, generalised peritonitis and appendicolith; evaluate observations, pain and sepsis status and suitability for follow-up. 2. State treatment options fairly → Explain laparoscopic appendicectomy as established definitive treatment and supervised antibiotics-first as a reasonable option for selected stable adults, in line with local pathway and shared decision-making. 3. Describe expected antibiotic course → Initial observation, appropriate IV/oral antibiotics per local antimicrobial guidance, repeat clinical review and transition/discharge only with improvement and reliable return precautions; avoid a universal regimen or dosing. 4. Describe operation and complications → Explain anaesthesia, bleeding, infection, injury to nearby structures, postoperative recovery and the low but non-zero chance of complications; do not promise zero recurrence after surgery. 5. Explain short-term failure and later surgery → CODA antibiotics arm: appendectomy in about 29% by 90 days overall; 41% with appendicolith versus 25% without. Distinguish conversion to surgery from all true recurrence. 6. Explain long-term uncertain
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical eligibility Offers antibiotics without confirming uncomplicated stability. Checks CT, peritonitis and sepsis status. Identifies appendicolith and ability to return as key modifiers. Option neutrality Declares one treatment compulsory for all stable cases. Explains antibiotics and appendicectomy choices. Aligns benefits, uncertainty and patient goals without coercion. Antibiotic pathway Discharges untreated with no observation or plan. Describes monitored antibiotics per local protocol. Defines review and explicit trigger for rescue surgery. Surgical risks Promises risk-free surgery or conceals complications. Explains general anaesthetic and operative risks. Balances definitive source control with recovery and adverse-event profile. Trial interpretation Claims antibiotics guarantee permanent cure. States CODA 29% appendectomy by 90 days. Explains 41% vs 25% appendicolith effect with trial population context. Long-term outcomes Confuses ten-year appendectomy with infection recurrence. Recognises later surgery may be needed. Interprets APPAC 44.3% at ten years with selected population caveats. Escalating disease Continues elective discussion
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Offers outpatient antibiotics for unstable or peritonitic suspected complicated appendicitis without resuscitation or urgent senior surgical review. CF2. Claims antibiotics always cure appendicitis and hides the significant risk of later appendicectomy. CF3. Ignores an appendicolith while presenting antibiotics-first as carrying the same early failure risk as no appendicolith. CF4. Discharges a deteriorating patient or fails to provide any urgent return/escalation instructions after choosing nonoperative management.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: On repeat review the patient has fever 39°C, escalating pain and guarding after initial antibiotic therapy. Expected: abandon routine outpatient planning, perform ABCDE/sepsis assessment, IV access and treatment according to local protocol, prompt senior surgical assessment and reassessment for urgent appendicectomy/source control; explain change in the risk-benefit balance.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I implied no appendicolith was irrelevant; trial data show more early appendectomy in that subgroup.” “I called 29% a recurrence figure; it is the proportion of antibiotics-assigned CODA patients who underwent appendectomy within 90 days.” “I gave no contingency plan; I must specify reassessment, warning symptoms and ready access to emergency care.”

sections.preamble: B2-368 — Uncomplicated Diverticulitis: Managing Without Admission AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / outpatient management | 8 minutes | Revised pilot 15 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme | Making the difficult easy
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a core surgical trainee working under senior supervision reviewing a 52-year-old patient in the emergency surgical assessment unit. She has 24 hours of left iliac fossa pain. CT describes sigmoid diverticular inflammation with no collection, free gas or obstruction. She is afebrile, pulse 84/min, BP 124/76 mmHg and can drink. Explain whether discharge is appropriate, including treatment and safety-netting.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess patient selection rather than reflex antibiotic prescribing. The candidate may ask for laboratory results (WBC 10.8 × 10⁹/L, CRP 46 mg/L, creatinine normal), examination (localized left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding), and social history (lives with adult partner, telephone and transport available). All data are fictional. Introduce immunosuppression as a curveball.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I thought diverticulitis always needed admission and antibiotics. Can I go home without either?” She is concerned about cancer and asks if she needs a colonoscopy.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. How do you establish uncomplicated disease? → Review haemodynamic stability, sepsis signs, peritonism, hydration, comorbidity and CT for abscess, perforation/free air, obstruction or fistula; check alternative diagnoses. 2. What in this case permits outpatient consideration? → Systemically well, tolerating oral fluid and analgesia, no peritoneal signs or CT complication, reasonable support and reliable reattendance. 3. Who should NOT be discharged routinely? → Unstable or septic patient; generalized guarding, uncontrolled pain/vomiting, dehydration, complicated CT findings, significant frailty, immunosuppression or unreliable follow-up; individualise threshold. 4. Must everyone receive antibiotics? → No. NICE NG147 advises considering no antibiotic prescription if systemically well; prescribe according to NICE/local policy when systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or significantly comorbid. 5. What outpatient management do you recommend? → Explain self-limited course, offer simple analgesia such as paracetamol, oral fluids and diet as tolerated; avoid unnecessary opioids; provide an agreed review pathway. 6. What explicit safety net is required? → Urgent reassessment for worsen
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Risk stratification Ignores instability or peritonism. Checks observations, hydration and abdominal signs. Integrates trends, comorbidities and ability to reattend. CT interpretation Calls an abscess “uncomplicated”. Identifies inflammation without collection/free gas/obstruction. Checks report for uncertainty and alternative pathology. Outpatient suitability Discharges despite intractable vomiting or absent safety support. Confirms oral tolerance, symptom control and home support. Defines explicit return capacity and escalates borderline cases. Antibiotic choice Insists antibiotics are mandatory for every well patient. Considers no antibiotics in systemically well patient. Distinguishes immunosuppression, systemic illness and comorbidity indications. Symptom control Gives no analgesia or hydration plan. Offers simple analgesia and oral intake guidance. Anticipates analgesic adverse effects and individual tolerance. Complication recognition Misses worsening sepsis or peritoneal signs. Recognises perforation, abscess and obstruction red flags. Explains how red flags change disposition immediately. Cancer assessment Promises no colorectal cancer risk
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Discharges a patient with hypotension, sepsis or generalized peritonitis without urgent surgical assessment. CF2. Labels CT evidence of abscess, perforation or bowel obstruction as uncomplicated and sends the patient home without assessment. CF3. Fails to act on severe dehydration or inability to tolerate oral fluids while recommending outpatient management. CF4. Provides no meaningful safety-net advice to a patient whose condition may progress after discharge.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The examiner adds: “She takes long-term prednisolone and methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.” Expected: reconsider discharge and the no-antibiotic strategy; immunosuppression raises risk of complications and NICE recommends an antibiotic prescribing strategy. Assess illness severity, discuss with senior and use a lower threshold for admission.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I called this uncomplicated without checking the CT for an abscess or free air; I will review the report and exam before deciding discharge.” “I said antibiotics were obligatory. In a systemically well, low-risk patient NICE permits a no-antibiotic strategy; I should individualise.” “My discharge plan lacked specific danger symptoms; I will explain when to return immediately and record the agreed review route.”

sections.preamble: AMaC | MRCS Part B B2-40 • ROUND 2 DEVELOPMENT DRAFT • CLINICAL REVIEW REQUIRED
sections.1. Title and header: Haemorrhagic shock: classes and response to fluid Station type: Applied knowledge / critical care | 9-minute encounter + 1-minute reading. Code: B2-40; final MB- ID unassigned. Guiding specification: AMaC MRCS Part B Station Writing Guide, 11 October 2026. Related stations: cross-reference to be confirmed against live 219-station register; this topic appears on the Round 2 gap list. AMaC educational station; not an official Intercollegiate examination mark scheme.
sections.2. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in the surgical assessment area. 29-year-old after high-energy trauma with ongoing bleeding. The information initially available is: Tachycardia and cool peripheries despite initial resuscitation. Interpret the information provided, answer the examiner’s questions, and explain safe further assessment and management. You may ask for additional clinical information; it is not volunteered unless requested.
sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: Physiology, permissive hypotension, transient vs non-responder. Trap: Failing to recognise this safety concern — uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy. First move: “Before proceeding, I will confirm immediate safety and specifically consider uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy.”
sections.4. Flow: 1. Confirm identity, role, consent where appropriate, and assess whether immediate intervention is needed: Uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy. 2. Characterise the central presentation: Tachycardia and cool peripheries despite initial resuscitation. 3. Test your working interpretation against the key discriminators: Physiology, permissive hypotension, transient vs non-responder; Appropriate prioritisation and escalation. 4. Address further decision points: Clear communication and safety-netting; Defensible differential. 5. Explain and document a reasoned plan: Activate major haemorrhage response, haemostatic resuscitation and source control; arrange escalation, reassessment and safety-netting.
sections.5. Marking grid: AMaC practice grid: 9 rows, descriptive Fail / Borderline / Pass / High-performance bands. Source-dependent entries require independent currency checks prior to publication. R1 — Professional opening (Clinical skill) Fail: Introduces no role or fails to engage. Borderline: Introduces self but omits purpose. Pass: Explains task and obtains appropriate permission. High-performance: Confident, person-centred signposting and early prioritisation. R2 — Immediate risk recognition (Clinical knowledge) Fail: Dismisses uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy. Borderline: Mentions risk without acting. Pass: Identifies uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy and acts appropriately. High-performance: Explicitly prioritises and anticipates deterioration from uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy. Evidence tag: source list in section 11; exact recommendation and version must be confirmed during clinical review. R3 — Focused assessment (Clinical skill) Fail: Does not establish: tachycardia and cool peripheries despite initial resuscitation. Borderline: Obtains one relevant finding. Pass: Elicits and interprets: Tachycardia and cool peripheries despite initial resuscitation. High-performan
sections.6. Three performances: Educational sample transcripts for the same default scenario. They are structured as a simulated examiner–candidate exchange; they do not reproduce confidential examination content. Fail performance Examiner: “The examiner provides the scenario and asks you to interpret the findings and demonstrate your approach.”[R1] Candidate: “This is routine; there is no need to explain much.” Examiner: “What clinical concern would change your priority?”[R2] Candidate: “Uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy can be ignored.” Examiner: “How do you interpret the key finding?”[R3] Candidate: “The finding is probably irrelevant.” Examiner: “What about physiology, permissive hypotension, transient vs non-responder?”[R4] Candidate: “I do not need to assess physiology, permissive hypotension, transient vs non-responder.” Examiner: “What about appropriate prioritisation and escalation?”[R5] Candidate: “I will ignore appropriate prioritisation and escalation.” Examiner: “What further issue matters?”[R6] Candidate: “Further assessment is unnecessary.” Examiner: “What should happen next?”[R7] Candidate: “There is no need for the next steps yet.” Examiner: “Will repeated crystalloid boluses fix it?”[R8]
sections.7. Critical fails: 1. Grid R2: Missing or dismissing uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy. Patient consequence: Delayed recognition or treatment of a time-critical clinical problem. 2. Grid R7: Proceeding with management without assessing contraindications, readiness or the need for specialist help. Patient consequence: Avoidable iatrogenic injury or deterioration. 3. Grid R9: Failing to escalate or act on important deterioration. Patient consequence: Progression of an unsafe clinical condition. These represent educationally significant unsafe actions, not a prediction of the official examination result.
sections.8. Recovery lines: “I need to correct my priorities: the safety concern is uncontrolled haemorrhage and coagulopathy, and I will address that before routine steps.” “I should explain the uncertainty clearly, involve the appropriate senior clinician and confirm a safe follow-up plan.”

sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: Breslow thickness, ulceration, staging, excision margins, sentinel node. sections.4. Flow: 1. Confirm identity, role, consent where appropriate, and assess whether immediate intervention is needed: Incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion. 2. Characterise the central presentation: Breslow 1.4 mm and ulceration status given. 3. Test your working interpretation against the key discriminators: Breslow thickness, ulceration, staging, excision margins, sentinel node; Appropriate prioritisation and escalation. 4.
