sections.5. Marking grid: AMaC practice grid: 9 rows, descriptive Fail / Borderline / Pass / High-performance bands. Source-dependent entries require independent currency checks prior to publication. R1 — Professional opening (Clinical skill) Fail: Introduces no role or fails to engage. Borderline: Introduces self but omits purpose. Pass: Explains task and obtains appropriate permission. High-performance: Confident, person-centred signposting and early prioritisation. R2 — Immediate risk recognition (Clinical knowledge) Fail: Dismisses incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion. Borderline: Mentions risk without acting. Pass: Identifies incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion and acts appropriately. High-performance: Explicitly prioritises and anticipates deterioration from incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion. Evidence tag: source list in section 11; exact recommendation and version must be confirmed during clinical review. R3 — Focused assessment (Clinical skill) Fail: Does not establish: breslow 1.4 mm and ulceration status given. Borderline: Obtains one relevant finding. Pass: Elicits and interprets: Breslow 1.4 mm and ulceration status given. High-p
sections.6. Three performances: Educational sample transcripts for the same default scenario. They are structured as a simulated examiner–candidate exchange; they do not reproduce confidential examination content. Fail performance Examiner: “The examiner provides the scenario and asks you to interpret the findings and demonstrate your approach.”[R1] Candidate: “This is routine; there is no need to explain much.” Examiner: “What clinical concern would change your priority?”[R2] Candidate: “Incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion can be ignored.” Examiner: “How do you interpret the key finding?”[R3] Candidate: “The finding is probably irrelevant.” Examiner: “What about breslow thickness, ulceration, staging, excision margins, sentinel node?”[R4] Candidate: “I do not need to assess breslow thickness, ulceration, staging, excision margins, sentinel node.” Examiner: “What about appropriate prioritisation and escalation?”[R5] Candidate: “I will ignore appropriate prioritisation and escalation.” Examiner: “What further issue matters?”[R6] Candidate: “Further assessment is unnecessary.” Examiner: “What should happen next?”[R7] Candidate: “There is no need for the next steps yet.” Examiner: “Does the dep
sections.7. Critical fails: 1. Grid R2: Missing or dismissing incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion. Patient consequence: Delayed recognition or treatment of a time-critical clinical problem. 2. Grid R7: Proceeding with management without assessing contraindications, readiness or the need for specialist help. Patient consequence: Avoidable iatrogenic injury or deterioration. 3. Grid R9: Failing to escalate or act on important deterioration. Patient consequence: Progression of an unsafe clinical condition. These represent educationally significant unsafe actions, not a prediction of the official examination result.
sections.8. Recovery lines: “I need to correct my priorities: the safety concern is incorrect margin or omitted specialist staging discussion, and I will address that before routine steps.” “I should explain the uncertainty clearly, involve the appropriate senior clinician and confirm a safe follow-up plan.”

sections.preamble: B2-420 — Frostbite AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in a UK emergency department. A 38-year-old climber was stranded overnight in sub-zero conditions and now has numb, pale, swollen toes after rescue. They are alert, normothermic and have no other injury. Explain assessment, immediate management, specialist options and follow-up.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess systemic safety and hypothermia, frostbite severity, avoidance of refreezing, appropriate rewarming, wound care, urgent specialist discussion for deep injury, and avoidance of premature amputation.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The patient walked for an hour to reach help. Both forefeet were frozen; toes are numb and painful as they warm. They ask if blackening means immediate amputation. Rescue team confirms no further cold exposure is expected.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Initial survey EXPECT: ABCDE; check core temperature and treat hypothermia, trauma and dehydration first; provide analgesia, remove wet clothing and constricting jewellery. Focused history EXPECT: Document duration and intensity of cold exposure, thaw/refreeze episodes, footwear, smoking, vascular disease, medications and timing of injury. Examination EXPECT: Assess extent, colour, sensation, capillary refill, skin integrity, clear versus haemorrhagic blisters, distal perfusion and neurovascular status; photograph and document. Rewarming decision EXPECT: Only actively rewarm when refreezing is no longer possible; use circulating water about 37–39°C until tissue is pliable and erythematous, with adequate analgesia; avoid rubbing or dry direct heat. Aftercare EXPECT: Protect from trauma, elevate, use non-adherent dressings and separate digits; address tetanus, hydration and pain; avoid unnecessary prophylactic antibiotics unless infection or another indication. Assess deep frostbite EXPECT: Identify persistent hard, insensate or poorly perfused digits, haemorrhagic blisters and evolving necrosis; request urgent specialist assessment rather than declaring viability on day one. Special
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Systemic assessment Ignores hypothermia or trauma. Assesses ABCDE and core temperature. Prioritises systemic threats before local tissue care. Cold history Does not ask about refreezing. Records exposure and thaw/refreeze history. Identifies time-sensitive factors for specialist treatment. Tissue assessment Calls every blister superficial. Documents colour, blisters, sensation and perfusion. Recognises deep ischaemia and serial assessment need. Rewarming Uses hot dry heat or rubs skin. Uses controlled warm-water bath when safe. Explains analgesia, target temperature and no refreezing. Local care Leaves wet constriction or applies pressure. Protects, dresses, elevates and treats pain. Tailors blister decisions to specialist local protocol. Medication and infection Gives routine antibiotics without reason. Checks tetanus and treats infection if present. Balances pain control, contraindications and antimicrobial stewardship. Escalation Discharges deep injury without advice. Contacts burns/plastics service urgently for severe injury. Flags possible specialist perfusion imaging and early therapies. Surgery decisions Amputates before demarcation without
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Attempts rapid rewarming despite a credible risk that the tissue will refreeze before definitive shelter. Uses a direct heater or dangerously hot water on insensate tissue, causing preventable burns. Fails to identify and treat significant hypothermia or another immediate systemic threat. Recommends immediate elective amputation of a stable frostbitten digit before demarcation and specialist review.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After rewarming, the great toe remains pale, numb and poorly perfused with haemorrhagic blisters. Expected: treat as potentially deep frostbite; document neurovascular findings and urgently contact the specialist burns/vascular service about perfusion assessment and time-dependent therapies.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I will check core temperature and other injuries before focusing on the toes.” “I will rewarm only once we can prevent refreezing, with controlled water temperature and analgesia.” “Deep injury needs early specialist review; tissue viability cannot be judged reliably today.”

stations.title: Pretibial Laceration in an Older Patient
stations.source_heading: AMaC MRCS B2-421 Pretibial Laceration in an Older Patient

sections.preamble: B2-421 — Pretibial Laceration in an Older Patient AMaC MRCS Part B | Procedural | 8 minutes | 13 October 2026 | DRAFT — not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the emergency surgery trainee assessing an 83-year-old on apixaban after striking the shin on furniture. A 9-cm flap wound lies over fragile pretibial skin. Explain and demonstrate verbally the wound-management sequence.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Test fragile skin, perfusion and anticoagulant review, skin-preserving flap realignment, minimal tension, dressing choice, referral for nonviable flap and structured follow-up.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is frail with a thin U-shaped skin flap, oozing but no arterial bleeding; distal pulses present, no gross contamination or exposed bone.
sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Assess patient/wound? — Control bleeding with pressure, assess vitals, fall mechanism, apixaban timing, tetanus, pain, perfusion, sensation, contamination and extent of flap loss. 2. Prepare wound? — Analgesia or local anaesthetic as needed; irrigate gently with saline or clean water, remove obvious debris, avoid aggressive scrubbing of fragile skin. 3. Preserve flap? — Reposition viable flap gently without tension, align edges; use nontraumatic closure strips when appropriate, with skin-safe adhesive/contact dressings. 4. When not to suture? — Avoid high-tension sutures that cheese-wire fragile skin; if selected reinforcement/sutures used, apply with specialist technique and minimal tension. 5. Dress wound? — Non-adherent silicone contact layer and absorbent secondary dressing, padding/compression only if vascular assessment permits. 6. Bleeding and anticoagulant? — Control local bleeding first; assess clinically significant bleeding and individual thrombosis risk before altering anticoagulation with senior input. 7. When refer? — Large/devascularised flap, exposed structures, haematoma, infection, difficult haemostasis or need for skin graft/plastics review. 8. Discharge/follo
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Assess patient/wound Ignores apixaban use and does not assess distal blood supply. Control bleeding with pressure, assess vitals, fall mechanism, apixaban timing, tetanus, pain, perfusion, sensation, contamination and extent of flap loss. Records bleeding, anticoagulant timing, flap viability and neurovascular findings. Prepare wound Scrubs fragile flap aggressively and worsens skin separation. Analgesia or local anaesthetic as needed. Uses gentle saline irrigation and preserves remaining dermal attachments. Preserve flap Places high-tension sutures that tear through fragile skin. Reposition viable flap gently without tension, align edges. Repositions viable flap with low-tension strips/nontraumatic supports. When not to suture Applies adhesive plaster directly to friable wound bed. Avoid high-tension sutures that cheese-wire fragile skin. Uses a silicone contact layer, absorption and fragile-skin protection. Dress wound Applies constrictive compression without checking perfusion. Non-adherent silicone contact layer and absorbent secondary dressing, padding/compression only if vascular assessment permits. Checks compression suitability and reassess
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1. Places multiple tight interrupted sutures through thin skin causing flap tearing/ischaemia. CF2. Discards an otherwise viable flap without assessing viability or seeking specialist input. CF3. Sends home a rapidly expanding haematoma or uncontrolled bleeding without reassessment. CF4. Ignores poor distal perfusion, devascularisation or infection requiring specialist escalation.
sections.7. One realistic curveball: After a tight dressing, toes become cool and painful: immediately loosen/remove constriction, reassess pulses/capillary refill and escalate vascular compromise.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “This shin skin is fragile; we should preserve the viable flap rather than pull it tight with stitches.” “I will irrigate gently, approximate without tension and use an atraumatic dressing.” “We will arrange early wound review and check for bleeding or skin breakdown.”

sections.preamble: B2-422 — Swallowed Magnets AMaC MRCS Part B | Critical care | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call paediatric surgical registrar. A 4-year-old is brought to ED after swallowing several small high-powered magnetic beads approximately three hours ago. The child is currently comfortable with normal observations. Explain your assessment, imaging, management and discussion with the parent.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Recognise multiple magnets as a time-critical gastrointestinal injury even in a well child; assess for co-ingested metal, arrange prompt radiography, nil by mouth and urgent paediatric surgical/gastroenterology discussion; do not discharge solely because asymptomatic.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The parent saw the child playing with a set of magnetic beads and noticed at least three missing. They ask whether laxatives or waiting for the beads to pass is safer than an operation. Child has no current pain or vomiting.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Immediate assessment EXPECT: ABCDE, observations, abdominal examination for tenderness, distension, guarding, peritonism; check vomiting, bleeding, fever, oral intake and signs of obstruction. Exposure history EXPECT: Ask exact timing, number and type of magnets, whether any metal object was swallowed, uncertainty about count, previous surgery and symptom progression; request packaging/photo if available. Why multiple magnets matter EXPECT: Explain magnets can attract across separate bowel loops causing pressure necrosis, fistula, perforation, obstruction and sepsis; serious injury may precede symptoms. Imaging EXPECT: Obtain urgent plain radiographs of abdomen, with views sufficient to locate/count objects and identify free air or obstruction; apparent single cluster may conceal multiple magnets; do not let a normal exam overrule concern. Initial management EXPECT: Keep nil by mouth, provide analgesia and IV access as indicated, inform senior paediatric surgeon and paediatric gastroenterologist/endoscopist promptly; avoid routine laxatives or MRI. Removal decision EXPECT: Urgent specialist-led removal planning: accessible gastric/duodenal magnets may be removed endoscopically; bey
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Triage Assumes normal observations exclude harm. Assesses stability and abdomen promptly. Explicitly anticipates occult pressure injury despite no symptoms. Ingestion history Does not establish magnet count. Asks count, timing and possible metal objects. Identifies uncertain count and requests product details. Mechanism Calls magnets ordinary foreign bodies. Explains interloop attraction and perforation risk. Links pressure necrosis to fistula and delayed presentation. Imaging No imaging because child feels well. Arranges urgent appropriate radiographs. Notes overlapping magnets can mimic a single object. Immediate precautions Gives laxatives and sends child home. Keeps nil by mouth and arranges senior review. Coordinates resuscitation access and imaging without delay. Specialist escalation Leaves decision to routine outpatient clinic. Calls paediatric surgery and endoscopy teams urgently. Discusses location-dependent endoscopic versus surgical strategy. Ongoing monitoring Fails to reassess after initial image. Plans specialist-directed serial exams and imaging. Uses failure to progress or evolving findings to trigger intervention. Complication res
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Discharges a child with confirmed multiple magnet ingestion solely because they are asymptomatic. Recommends home laxatives or expectant passage without urgent specialist assessment. Fails to act on peritonitis, haemodynamic compromise or suspected perforation. Treats a radiographic cluster as proof of a single magnet despite credible history of several magnets.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The X-ray appears to show one circular density in the stomach, but the parent is certain three beads are missing. Expected: explain superimposition, obtain further appropriate views/specialist interpretation and manage as suspected multiple magnets pending clarification.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “A comfortable child can still develop bowel injury from multiple magnets.” “I will keep them nil by mouth and obtain urgent radiographs while calling paediatric surgery.” “The magnets may overlap on X-ray, so I will not assume one density means one magnet.”

sections.preamble: B2-423 — Head Injury in a Child: When to Scan AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in a paediatric emergency department. A 7-year-old fell from playground equipment about two hours ago, briefly appeared dazed, and vomited twice. GCS is 15 and there is no focal deficit. Talk through assessment, the NICE-based CT decision, observation, safeguarding and discharge advice.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Apply age-specific NICE NG232 head-injury criteria accurately; distinguish one versus multiple risk factors, appropriate observation and deterioration triggers; recognise non-accidental injury and safe discharge requirements.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The child is awake, interactive and remembers parts of the fall. Parent says the fall was around 1.2 m, with two episodes of vomiting; no witnessed seizure, no known bleeding disorder, no loss of consciousness longer than five minutes. The parent asks for an immediate scan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Primary survey EXPECT: ABCDE with cervical-spine consideration, GCS components, pupils, vital signs, glucose when appropriate and examination for associated injuries. Mechanism and history EXPECT: Clarify fall height, loss of consciousness duration, amnesia, vomiting episodes, seizure, headache, behaviour change, anticoagulants/bleeding disorder and previous neurological disease. Immediate CT indications EXPECT: Recognise high-risk paediatric NICE features such as suspected non-accidental injury, post-traumatic seizure without epilepsy, GCS <14 initially or <15 at 2 hours, suspected open/depressed or basal skull fracture, focal deficit, or infant scalp bruise/swelling/laceration >5 cm. Intermediate-risk count EXPECT: For under-16s, two or more of: loss of consciousness >5 min, abnormal drowsiness, three or more discrete vomiting episodes, dangerous mechanism, amnesia >5 min (where assessable), or bleeding/clotting disorder indicates CT within one hour. Single intermediate feature EXPECT: If exactly one intermediate feature, observe for at least four hours from injury; scan within one hour if GCS falls below 15, further vomiting occurs or abnormal drowsiness develops during observat
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial stabilisation Skips ABCDE or neurological baseline. Assesses ABCDE, GCS, pupils and spine. Documents serial neurological observations and other injuries. History Fails to quantify vomiting or mechanism. Establishes fall height, vomiting and LOC. Adds amnesia, coagulopathy and behavioural changes. High-risk CT criteria Misses seizure or focal deficit. Identifies major immediate CT indications. Includes GCS timing, skull signs and infant scalp criterion. Risk-factor thresholds Scans automatically for any single vomit. Distinguishes ≥2 intermediate criteria from one. Uses precise NICE age-specific thresholds. Observation Discharges with an eligible risk factor without plan. Observes ≥4 h from injury for one criterion. States deterioration triggers and time-critical CT. Case application Calls two vomits an automatic CT indication. Explains no automatic CT on stated features. Clarifies clinical judgement and re-evaluates evolving symptoms. Safeguarding Never considers inflicted injury. Checks mechanism consistency and safety. Escalates specific concerning findings appropriately. Communication Dismisses parent concerns without explanation. Explai
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Fails to arrange urgent CT for a child with a new focal neurological deficit or persistently reduced GCS meeting NICE criteria. Discharges a deteriorating child with increasing drowsiness or new vomiting during indicated observation without reassessment. Ignores a credible concern of non-accidental injury and discharges without safeguarding escalation. Sends home a child with impaired consciousness or no safe supervision without appropriate assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: During observation the child vomits again and becomes unusually sleepy. Expected: immediate reassessment of GCS and vital signs; apply NICE observation deterioration criteria, arrange CT within one hour and seek senior paediatric review.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I will count discrete vomiting episodes and check the exact fall height before applying NICE thresholds.” “One intermediate risk factor means four hours of observation from injury, with clear CT triggers.” “I must consider safeguarding and confirm safe adult supervision before discharge.”

sections.preamble: B2-424 — Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar called to the neonatal unit. A term newborn with antenatally diagnosed left congenital diaphragmatic hernia has severe respiratory distress immediately after delivery. Explain initial stabilisation, investigations, specialist management and timing of repair.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Prioritise gentle endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression rather than bag-mask ventilation; recognise pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension; stabilise before repair in a specialist centre.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The neonatal consultant describes a newborn with severe recession, cyanosis, reduced left air entry, a scaphoid abdomen and rightward cardiac impulse. The parents ask whether surgery must happen immediately.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Recognise the condition EXPECT: Antenatal ultrasound may show bowel or stomach in the thorax; left-sided posterolateral Bochdalek defect is common; pulmonary hypoplasia and hypertension drive early risk. Immediate resuscitation EXPECT: Call experienced neonatal airway team; avoid routine face-mask positive-pressure ventilation because gastric insufflation worsens thoracic compression; prompt controlled endotracheal intubation when respiratory support is required. Gastric decompression EXPECT: Insert wide-bore oro/nasogastric tube for continuous or intermittent suction to decompress intrathoracic stomach and bowel; avoid delaying airway stabilisation. Ventilation and monitoring EXPECT: Use gentle lung-protective ventilation with limited inspiratory pressures, pre/post-ductal saturations, blood gases, haemodynamic monitoring and early neonatal intensive care. Investigations EXPECT: Chest radiograph after stabilisation: bowel gas in hemithorax, mediastinal shift and paucity of abdominal gas; echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac defects. Circulatory support EXPECT: Manage hypoxia, acidosis, hypotension and pulmonary hypertension with neonatal intensi
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Diagnosis Does not recognise CDH from clinical clues. Identifies CDH and pulmonary hypoplasia. Links prenatal findings to pulmonary hypertension risk. Airway Uses prolonged bag-mask ventilation. Calls neonatal expert and intubates appropriately. Explains avoidance of gastric insufflation and gentle airway strategy. Decompression Omits gastric drainage. Arranges gastric tube and suction. Explains relief of thoracic bowel distension. Ventilation Recommends high-pressure ventilation indiscriminately. Uses gentle ventilation and blood-gas monitoring. Discusses pre/post-ductal oxygenation and barotrauma avoidance. Assessment No imaging or cardiac assessment. Requests chest radiograph and echocardiogram. Describes expected imaging in words and associated lesions. Haemodynamics Ignores pulmonary hypertension and shock. Coordinates NICU circulatory support. Tailors pulmonary hypertension management to physiology. Surgical plan Insists on immediate repair while unstable. Plans repair after physiological stabilisation. Explains reduction, closure and potential patch. Escalation Attempts management without neonatal specialists. Calls NICU and paediatric surgi
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Continues bag-mask positive-pressure ventilation in known CDH despite access to appropriate neonatal airway support, without recognising harm. Fails to establish a safe airway in a deteriorating newborn. Omits gastric decompression and does not recognise its role in respiratory compromise. Advocates immediate operative repair before treating severe cardiorespiratory instability.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After intubation, the baby remains hypoxaemic with a marked pre/post-ductal saturation difference. Expected: recognise pulmonary hypertension, reassess tube/ventilation, obtain blood gas and echo, and escalate immediately to neonatal intensive care for tailored support.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The main immediate threat is underdeveloped lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not the diaphragmatic hole alone.” “I will avoid mask insufflation, arrange expert intubation and decompress the stomach.” “We repair the diaphragm after physiological stabilisation, in partnership with neonatal specialists.”

sections.preamble: B2-425 — Anorectal Malformation in a Newborn AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the paediatric surgical registrar reviewing a newborn 12 hours after birth who has not passed meconium. The midwife cannot identify a normal anal opening. Describe your examination, immediate management, investigation for associated anomalies and options for repair.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Identify imperforate anus and fistula patterns, avoid unsafe blind probing, assess associated VACTERL anomalies, decompress and refer; choose primary anoplasty versus staged colostomy according to anatomy and stability.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The baby is term, stable, mildly distended, and has not passed meconium. The parent asks whether a small hole can simply be opened at the bedside. No antenatal diagnosis was made.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: First assessment EXPECT: Check ABCDE, hydration, vomiting (especially bilious), abdominal distension, urine output, passage of meconium and sepsis signs; keep nil by mouth if obstruction suspected. Perineal examination EXPECT: Inspect carefully for anal opening, perineal fistula, meconium at urethra/vagina or vestibule; assess genitalia and sacrum; do not blindly probe or incise perineum. Fistula and obstruction EXPECT: Ask about meconium in urine, vaginal/vestibular passage, urinary obstruction; recognise rectourethral/rectovesical or vestibular fistula and possible cloaca in girls. Initial management EXPECT: Contact neonatal and paediatric surgical teams, establish IV fluids as indicated, gastric decompression for distension/vomiting, monitor abdominal signs and avoid feeding when obstructed. Imaging and anatomy EXPECT: Abdominal radiograph for obstruction; targeted perineal ultrasound or cross-table lateral imaging when specialist team considers appropriate; pelvic imaging defines anatomy and fistula before repair. Associated anomalies EXPECT: Evaluate VACTERL: vertebral/sacral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb anomalies; echocardiogram, renal ultrasound,
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial assessment Ignores obstruction and vomiting. Checks stability, distension and meconium passage. Recognises bilious emesis or peritonitis as urgent deterioration. Perineal examination Attempts blind digital probing or incision. Inspects anal opening and possible fistula. Includes genital, sacral and meconium-route examination. Anatomical classification Assumes all defects are simple anal membranes. Distinguishes low and complex/high anomalies. Identifies cloaca and urinary fistula implications. Immediate care Feeds despite obstructive vomiting. Uses NBM, fluids and decompression when indicated. Plans ongoing abdominal and urine-output monitoring. Imaging Makes repair decision without defining anatomy. Requests appropriate initial imaging and specialist assessment. Chooses investigations based on perineal findings and stability. Associated anomalies Never screens beyond anus. Assesses VACTERL-associated defects. Specifies echo, renal ultrasound and spine/sacral review. Surgical options Promises bedside opening for every newborn. Explains primary repair versus staged colostomy. Matches pathway to fistula, level, physiology and complexity. Team
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Attempts blind probing or bedside incision of an unidentified anal opening. Misses bilious vomiting or progressive abdominal distension without urgent escalation. Fails to seek paediatric surgical input for suspected anorectal malformation. Ignores meconium in urine or a single perineal opening suggesting complex urinary/genital fistula.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The nurse reports green vomit and increasing abdominal distension, and meconium appears in the urine. Expected: resuscitate and decompress, urgent paediatric surgical review, recognise possible rectourinary fistula and avoid blind perineal intervention.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I must inspect the perineum carefully rather than attempt to open a presumed membrane.” “I will check for fistulae and VACTERL-associated abnormalities.” “The need for a primary repair or temporary stoma depends on the anatomy and the baby’s condition.”

sections.preamble: B2-426 — UTI in a Child and Vesicoureteric Reflux AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar discussing a 20-month-old child admitted with a second febrile urinary tract infection. Ultrasound shows mild renal pelvic dilatation. Explain immediate management, imaging decisions, vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), and follow-up to a junior colleague.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess acute illness, distinguish atypical/recurrent UTI, apply age-dependent NICE NG224 imaging principles without scanning everyone, explain VUR and selective prophylaxis/surgery.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The child is now afebrile after antibiotics, drinking well. The parent is worried about kidney damage and asks for a scan to detect reflux. The urine culture grew E. coli.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Initial severity EXPECT: Assess fever, hydration, perfusion, urine output, vomiting, sepsis and obstruction; a toxic child needs urgent paediatric resuscitation and admission. Confirm and treat UTI EXPECT: Obtain an appropriate urine specimen before antibiotics if this does not delay treatment; interpret culture and sensitivities; select age/severity-appropriate antibiotics using local guidance. Define recurrence and atypical features EXPECT: Ask about prior upper/lower UTIs, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection, failure to respond within 48 hours, raised creatinine, abdominal/bladder mass or sepsis; these alter imaging. Ultrasound decision EXPECT: For a child aged 6 months to under 3 years with recurrent UTI, NICE NG224 recommends ultrasound within 6 weeks; ultrasound during acute illness when atypical UTI is present. DMSA and MCUG EXPECT: At this age recurrent UTI warrants DMSA 4–6 months after acute infection to look for renal parenchymal defects; MCUG is not routine but considered with ultrasound dilatation, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or family history of VUR. VUR mechanism and grades EXPECT: Reflux permits retrograde urine flow from bladder to ureter/kidney; grad
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Severity Overlooks sepsis or obstruction. Checks illness severity and urine output. Distinguishes need for urgent resuscitation from stable follow-up. Microbiology Treats without obtaining urine when feasible. Requests urine culture and sensitivity-guided therapy. Describes specimen quality and avoids delaying antibiotics in sepsis. UTI classification Calls every febrile episode uncomplicated. Identifies recurrent and atypical UTI criteria. Uses 48-hour response and non-E. coli results to refine pathway. Ultrasound Orders no imaging after recurrent febrile UTI. Plans ultrasound within 6 weeks at this age. Brings ultrasound forward if atypical illness. DMSA Assumes ultrasound excludes scarring. Plans DMSA at 4–6 months for recurrence. Explains timing and what a cortical defect means. MCUG Performs MCUG routinely for every first UTI. Explains selective MCUG use. Notes dilatation and poor flow as triggers to consider it. Reflux knowledge Cannot define VUR. Explains reflux and graded severity. Relates reflux, recurrent pyelonephritis and scar risk without inevitability. Prevention Offers indefinite antibiotics automatically. Discusses bowel/bladder mea
sections.6. Four specific Critical fails: Fails to recognise septic shock or an obstructed infected urinary tract requiring emergency escalation. Discharges a clinically unwell child without treatment or safety-net advice. Misses the need to investigate recurrent febrile UTI in this age group. States that all children with a first UTI require routine MCUG or long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, exposing the child to unnecessary interventions.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The ultrasound report now states bilateral dilated collecting systems and the parent reports a weak urinary stream. Expected: consider obstruction and VUR; prompt specialist review and consider MCUG, rather than applying a blanket no-MCUG rule.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “First I will establish whether this is a septic or obstructed child.” “At 20 months with recurrent UTI, ultrasound and delayed DMSA are indicated; MCUG is selective.” “We will address bladder-bowel habits and involve paediatrics before discussing prophylaxis or surgery.”

sections.preamble: B2-427 — Duodenal Atresia AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge | DRAFT | 13 October 2026 | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the paediatric surgical registrar asked to review a newborn with persistent green vomiting and upper abdominal distension within hours of birth. A plain abdominal radiograph is described as showing two rounded gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen with no distal bowel gas. Explain diagnosis, initial management, associations and definitive treatment.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Recognise neonatal bilious vomiting as obstruction until proven otherwise; explain double-bubble sign, differentiate malrotation/volvulus, resuscitate, decompress and plan operative repair.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The baby is 18 hours old, born at 38 weeks, has green aspirates and minimal meconium. Antenatal ultrasound showed polyhydramnios. The parent asks whether this is simply reflux.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Recognise the emergency EXPECT: Green bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise; rapidly assess ABCDE, hydration, perfusion, temperature and abdominal signs. Radiograph in words EXPECT: A dilated stomach and proximal duodenum form a double bubble; absence of distal bowel gas supports complete duodenal obstruction, although findings do not remove need for expert assessment. Key differential EXPECT: Malrotation with midgut volvulus can cause bilious vomiting and bowel ischaemia; also consider annular pancreas, duodenal web, jejunal atresia and meconium ileus. Initial stabilisation EXPECT: Nil by mouth, large-bore oro/nasogastric tube to free drainage or low suction, IV access, isotonic fluid resuscitation when needed, maintenance fluids, glucose/electrolyte checks and monitoring. Urgency and referral EXPECT: Call neonatal and paediatric surgical teams urgently; a compromised baby or suspected volvulus requires immediate senior operative decision, not delay for exhaustive investigations. Further investigation EXPECT: Ultrasound or upper GI contrast study may be needed if malrotation/volvulus cannot be excluded; echocardiography and evaluation of as
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Urgent recognition Dismisses green vomit as reflux. Identifies neonatal obstruction. States volvulus must be excluded promptly. A 67-year-old patient has yellow eyes and dark urine for 10 days, pale stools, generalised itch and 4 kg unintentional weight loss. Observations: 36.8°C, HR 84, BP 132/76 mmHg. sections.4. Eight examiner prompts and expected a: 1. Cardiac output definition? — CO = heart rate × stroke volume; clinically dependent on preload, afterload, contractility and rhythm. 2. Preload? — End-diastolic myocardial stretch relates to ventricular filling; not identical to CVP. 3. Frank–Starling principle? — Within physiological limits, increased end-diastolic fibre length augments stroke volume. 4. Afterload? — Resistance/pressure against which ventricle ejects; increased afterload can lower stroke volume. 5. Contractility? — Intrinsic myocardial inotropic state independent of preload and afterload. 6. Clinical patterns? — Hypovolaemic shock lowers preload; distributive shock lowers vascular tone; cardiogenic shock impairs pump function. 7. Fluid responsiveness? — Uses dynamic assessments such as passive leg raise and stroke-volume change when applicable; checks fluid tolerance. 8. Therapy and reassessment? — Treats cause, gives cautious fluid if responsive, uses vasopressor for vasoplegia and inotrope for low-output pump failure under senior care.
sections.5. Nine-domain critical-weighted marking: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Cardiac output definition Defines cardiac output as blood pressure alone. CO = heart rate × stroke volume; clinically dependent on preload, afterload, contractility and rhythm. Distinguishes flow from pressure and perfusion. Preload Equates one CVP number with fluid responsiveness. End-diastolic myocardial stretch relates to ventricular filling; not identical to CVP. sections.2. Candidate brief: Setting and briefing: Postoperative day 5 after elective anterior resection for sigmoid cancer. The patient is alert and has capacity. Overnight, heart rate increased to 122/min, temperature to 38.6°C and abdominal pain worsened. CT with IV contrast shows perianastomotic gas and fluid, concerning for an anastomotic leak. The consultant recommends urgent reoperation after resuscitation, antibiotics and anaesthetic assessment. A stoma may be necessary; its type and permanence cannot be promised. The candidate is a core surgical trainee speaking to the patient before the consultant returns. Your task: Explain the findings, why urgent return to theatre is recommended, possible stoma and risks; respond to emotions and questions; confirm understanding and escalate consent to the operating surgeon.
sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: Explain a serious postoperative complication without hiding uncertainty or making promises; urgent treatment and the operating consultant remain central. Trap: Either blame the original operation or minimise the leak; claim a stoma will definitely be temporary. First move: “I’m concerned that there may be a leak where the bowel was joined. I’m sorry this has happened; can we talk through what that means and what we need to do next?”
sections.4. Flow: 1. Introduce role, check privacy and the patient’s readiness. 2. Explain fever, pain and CT, and give a clear warning statement. 3. Explain sepsis risk, urgent antibiotics/resuscitation and rationale for return to theatre. 4. Discuss uncertain operative findings, possible stoma and anaesthetic/operative risks, respond to fears. 5. Summarise, check understanding, arrange consultant discussion and document accurately.

Mentions abnormal scan but cannot explain what a leak means. Explains fluid and gas near join raise concern for leakage, not an absolute diagnosis. Explains the potential bowel-content contamination without jargon and checks understanding. R3 Recognition of deterioration Dismisses tachycardia and fever as routine recovery. Mentions infection but not the urgency of deterioration. Links fever, rapid pulse and pain with possible intra-abdominal sepsis and urgency. Explains the need for continuous

sections.1. Title and header: Topic: Explaining a Non-curative Colorectal Cancer MDT Outcome; format: simulated-patient communication. Sources and version details are in section 11. sections.2. Candidate brief: Setting and briefing: A 63-year-old person had staging scans following a biopsy-confirmed colorectal adenocarcinoma. The colorectal and liver MDTs have reviewed CT and liver MRI: multiple bilobar liver metastases and several pulmonary nodules; no potentially curative local treatment is currently suitable. The patient is physically stable, with intermittent pain and reduced appetite. Medical oncology has not yet assessed fitness or treatment options. The candidate is the core surgical trainee asked to explain the MDT outcome and arrange onward support, not to prescribe systemic therapy or predict individual survival. Your task: Explain the non-curative MDT recommendation with empathy and accuracy, address prognosis and treatment options without making unsupported promises, and establish a clear multidisciplinary follow-up and support plan.
sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: Acknowledge that cure is not currently achievable by surgery or local treatment while emphasising there remain meaningful treatment, symptom-control and support options. Trap: Equating “not curable” with “nothing can be done”, or offering a precise life-expectancy figure without oncology assessment. First move: “I’m afraid the team has difficult news from your scans. Before I explain it, could I check what you understand about the investigations so far?”
sections.4. Flow: 1. Prepare confidential discussion, elicit understanding and information preferences. 2. Give warning shot then explain metastatic disease and what MDT has concluded. 3. Allow silence and respond to emotions without false reassurance. 4. Discuss oncology assessment, symptom support and uncertainty around outcomes. 5. Agree follow-up, support people, written information and teach-back.

Sits down but omits what the patient already understands. Confirms privacy, patient readiness and preferred detail/support person. Checks understanding, language and whether patient wants all details now. R2 Explain scan results Falsely states scans are clear or uses unexplained jargon. Says cancer has spread but fails to name sites or significance. Explains bowel primary with deposits in both liver lobes and possible lung spread in plain language. Separates biopsy-confirmed cancer from radiological metastatic findings and checks comprehension. R3 Meaning of MDT outcome Promises curative surgery despite stated unresectability. Uses “incurable” without explaining current treatment context. States surgery/local treatments are not expected to cure disease based on current MDT assessment. Explains that options can be reassessed after oncology

We have the MDT discussion results. Is
sections.7. Critical fails: Critical fail — R2/R3: Says there is nothing to offer, concealing available oncology/supportive assessment Consequence: Destroys informed choice and delays care. Critical fail — R6: States an exact survival period without evidence Consequence: Can cause severe distress and distort decisions. Critical fail — R8: Informs daughter against expressed wishes Consequence: Confidentiality breach. Critical fail — R7/R9: Leaves uncontrolled symptoms with no review or follow-up Consequence: Preventable suffering and loss to follow-up.

sections.2. Candidate brief: You are a core surgical trainee in the colorectal outpatient clinic. Examine a simulated patient with a right-sided abdominal stoma who reports difficulty keeping the appliance sealed. Explain your findings, identify the type of stoma and possible complications, and outline a safe next step. The examiner may supply findings not demonstrable on the model. You have 9 minutes after 1 minute of reading. Ask permission before exposing the abdomen; a stoma appliance may be lifted by the examiner on request.
sections.3. Before you walk in: Frame: A safe, structured stoma examination and differentiation of anatomy, appliance problems and urgent pathology. Trap: Calling a right-sided stoma an ileostomy from location alone; treating absent output or a dusky stoma as a routine appliance problem. First move: Introduce yourself; confirm identity, consent, privacy and whether the stoma is functioning before touching it.
sections.4. Flow: 0–1 minute: explain, consent, expose only abdomen, offer chaperone, hygiene and assess immediate symptoms 1–3 minutes: inspect bag and output; scars, siting, spout, mucosa and peristomal skin 3–5 minutes: gentle examination for tenderness, retraction, prolapse and parastomal hernia (standing/cough if appropriate) 5–7 minutes: distinguish ileostomy, colostomy and urostomy using output and history; explore dehydration and obstruction 7–9 minutes: summarise findings, address appliance problem, identify emergency features and discuss stoma nurse/surgical follow-up
sections.5. Marking grid: 20 marks overall. Four band descriptors are developmental, not an official intercollegiate mark scheme. Tags [R1]–[R9] in transcripts refer to rows below. Row / domain Criterion Fail Borderline Pass High-performance R1 Professionalism Consent/privacy Touches stoma without consent Introduces but insufficient explanation Consent, dignity, hand hygiene and permission for appliance inspection Anticipates embarrassment and explains each exposure and step R2 Clinical skill Systematic inspection Does not inspect stoma or output Describes stoma colour alone Inspects site, spout, colour, lumen, output, scar and appliance Integrates skin, appliance fit and patient-reported function R3 Clinical knowledge Stoma type Names type from side alone Recognises likely intestinal stoma Distinguishes ileostomy, colostomy and urostomy by operative context and effluent Explains loop/end and acknowledges location is not definitive R4 Clinical skill Peristomal assessment Ignores leakage and sore skin Mentions skin irritation Identifies maceration, appliance seal and skin damage Links leakage to stoma retraction and prompt stoma nurse review R5 Clinical skill Complication examination Forceful palpation or no
sections.6. Three performances: Fail — continuous performance Candidate [R1]: Let me look at your bag. Pull up your top. Patient: Could you explain what you are doing? This is embarrassing. Candidate [R1]: It is a routine check; it will only take a moment. Candidate [R3]: It is on the right, so this is definitely an ileostomy. Patient: The bag leaks and my skin stings. Candidate [R4]: That happens; you can buy a stronger adhesive. Examiner: On inspection the mucosa is moist and pink, with a recessed lower edge and red excoriated skin. Candidate [R2]: It is a red stoma, so it is normal. Patient: Is it coming loose? I am scared the bowel is falling apart. Candidate [R8]: No. I am sure it is fine. I do not need to examine it further. Examiner: Would you check for a hernia or ask about output? Candidate [R5]: A hernia would be obvious from looking, and the bag looks full enough. Patient: What if I stop having output and start vomiting? Candidate [R7]: Try changing the bag and see your GP if it is still a problem next week. Examiner: The patient develops pain, absent stoma output and increasing distension the next day. What does this change? Candidate [R7]: Probably constipation; a laxative should solve it. Patient: I
sections.7. Critical fails: R1: Lifts appliance without consent; breaches dignity and may harm trust. R7: Dismisses a dusky or black painful stoma without urgent surgical escalation, risking missed ischaemia. R7: Sends a patient with absent output, vomiting and progressive distension home with routine supplies, risking delayed treatment of obstruction. R5: Forcefully attempts to reduce a painful irreducible parastomal swelling, risking injury and delayed emergency assessment.
sections.8. Recovery lines: “I have focused on the appliance; I should first ask about output, vomiting and pain and examine for obstruction.” “I cannot safely exclude a stoma complication here; I will ask the senior surgical team to review and explain that plan to you.”
sections.9. Key knowledge: A healthy intestinal stoma is generally moist, pink-to-red and soft; mild contact bleeding can occur. [NHS-I] Ileostomy effluent is typically liquid-to-pasty; site and spout contribute clues but operative history and effluent matter. [NHS-I][GATES] Loop ileostomies often have two adjacent lumens, active and distal; not every pair is visually obvious. [NHS-L] Leakage, retraction, prolapse, peristomal skin damage and parastomal hernia are recognised complications. [NHS-C] Reduced or absent output with cramps, vomiting or distension suggests obstruction requiring urgent assessment. [NHS-IC] High ileostomy output can cause dehydration, requiring clinical review and fluid/electrolyte assessment. [NHS-IC]

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-184 Haemorrhoids: banding or surgery? Format: Communication • Suggested time: 9 minutes • Editorial status: Draft — independent specialist clinical sign-off required Original AMaC teaching/assessment station; not an official MRCS station or examiner mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS trainee in a colorectal outpatient clinic. A 48-year-old office worker has intermittent bright-red bleeding after defaecation and a lump that comes out when opening the bowels but goes back by itself. They have tried an over-the-counter cream. Explain your assessment, likely diagnosis and management options, including whether rubber band ligation or an operation is appropriate. No physical examination is required; ask the examiner for findings.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Patient is well, pulse 76/min, BP 128/78 mmHg. No fever or acute severe pain. Bleeding is small-volume, on paper or in pan, not mixed with stool. Symptoms for six months. Constipation and prolonged straining; low-fibre diet. No weight loss, altered bowel habit, iron-deficiency symptoms or relevant family history; no anticoagulants. No previous procedures. When asked: inspection is normal, digital rectal examination reveals no mass; proctoscopy shows enlarged internal cushions at 3, 7 and 11 o’clock with contact bleeding, and no fissure or suspicious lesion. One cushion prolapses on straining and reduces spontaneously: grade II internal haemorrhoids. Do not volunteer grade unless candidate elicits prolapse reduction. The patient asks: “Why can’t you just operate and get rid of them for good?” Offer the curveball only after a treatment plan.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: You are worried that bleeding might be cancer. You use the toilet for 15 minutes and often strain. Your main goals are stopping bleeding and limiting time off work. Open with: “I want this fixed, but I have heard banding can make the bleeding worse.” If asked about red flags, give the negative history above. If candidate explains examination, say: “You can examine me if needed.” Clinical examination is simulated via examiner disclosure.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “How do you grade internal haemorrhoids?” Expected: I no prolapse, II spontaneous reduction, III manual reduction, IV irreducible. Prompt: “What must be checked before calling this haemorrhoidal bleeding?” Expected: history and appropriate anorectal assessment; assess colorectal cancer red flags and relevant screening/referral needs; haemorrhoids do not automatically exclude another bleeding source. Prompt: “Banding or surgery here?” Expected: optimise stool habits and offer office rubber band ligation if persistent bothersome grade II symptoms; excisional surgery not first-line. Prompt: “How does banding work and what are its risks?” Expected: band placed above dentate line to fix cushion; temporary discomfort, delayed bleeding, recurrence/repeat treatment and rare pelvic sepsis; escalating pain, fever or urinary retention require urgent review. Prompt: “What if mixed external and irreducible internal disease?” Expected: specialist surgical assessment for excisional haemorrhoidectomy; discuss post-operative pain and bleeding, urinary retention, rare stenosis or continence effects; alternatives vary by anatomy and local expertise.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and agenda Declares haemorrhoids before asking what worries the patient. Introduces self, checks identity, elicits chief symptom and main concern. Elicits preference about recovery time and explains the decision will match symptom burden and examination. Bleeding history Fails to distinguish minor wiping blood from heavy or mixed bleeding. Asks colour, amount, duration, relation to stool and associated pain. Adds anaemia symptoms and impact, and differentiates intermittent prolapse from persistent external swelling. Red flags and exclusions Reassures bleeding is benign without asking about cancer warning features. Checks altered bowel habit, weight loss, family history and suspicious masses. Explains need for further bowel investigation according to clinical risk and pathway even if piles coexist. Risk and bowel habits Offers cream alone without addressing constipation or medication. Asks about straining, fibre, fluid, time on toilet and anticoagulants. Links specific bowel habits to a practical stool-softening and toileting plan. Examination and grading Calls grade II “grade III” or skips anorectal examination. Requests inspection, DRE and
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Attributes all rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids and explicitly rules out malignancy without any red-flag assessment or indicated investigation. 2. Recommends immediate haemorrhoidectomy as mandatory first-line for the described uncomplicated grade II disease, ignoring feasible conservative/office care. 3. States significant delayed bleeding or fever with severe pain after banding can safely be ignored at home. 4. Proposes placing a rubber band below the dentate line despite severe pain, rather than stopping and repositioning.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient says: “My father had bowel cancer. So these definitely are not cancer, right?” Expected: acknowledge new first-degree family history, clarify diagnosis/age and colorectal referral considerations; do not attribute bleeding exclusively to piles; communicate that banding can be deferred while additional assessment is arranged.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “Before choosing treatment, I need to check whether this bleeding has warning features that need bowel investigation.” “Because it goes back by itself, this is grade II; banding is a sensible next option if bowel measures fail.” “A little discomfort can occur after banding, but severe increasing pain, fever, heavy bleeding or difficulty passing urine needs urgent assessment.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-185 Fistula-in-ano: classification and setons Format: Applied knowledge • Suggested time: 9 minutes • Editorial status: Draft — independent specialist clinical sign-off required Original AMaC teaching/assessment station; not an official MRCS station or examiner mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are seeing a 36-year-old man referred with recurrent discharge from a small opening next to the anus after a previously drained perianal abscess. Describe how you would assess, classify and manage a suspected fistula-in-ano. The examiner can disclose examination and pelvic MRI findings. The key decision is whether to lay open the tract or use a draining seton.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Eight months of intermittent purulent discharge; occasional swelling, currently no fever. No diabetes or immunosuppression. No prior pelvic radiation. No incontinence, no previous sphincter surgery; no inflammatory bowel symptoms or family history. Inspection: right posterior external opening 3 cm from anal verge with scant discharge, no fluctuant abscess, erythema or crepitus. DRE: normal tone, no palpable mass. Proctoscopy: no obvious proctitis; internal opening not identified in clinic. Pelvic MRI on request: single right posterior transsphincteric tract crossing approximately 60% of external anal sphincter, entering posterior midline anal canal, without secondary horseshoe extension or collection. Treat as anatomically complex/high transsphincteric disease. If candidate proposes fistulotomy ask: “You would divide more than half the external sphincter. Is that acceptable?” Expected: no routine lay-open; sphincter-preserving strategy.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Your discharge is irritating, and you want a single definitive operation. You fear a permanent bag and losing bowel control. Ask: “Can’t you just cut the tunnel out now?” If candidate raises seton, ask whether it cures the problem and how long it may stay. Accept clear explanation that drainage control may be followed by a separate definitive operation; ask about follow-up.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “Give Parks classification.” Expected: intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric; distinguish low/simple versus high/complex by sphincter involvement and patient factors. Prompt: “What does Goodsall’s rule tell you?” Expected: a rough anatomical prediction of internal opening (posterior openings often curve to posterior midline; anterior usually radial, with exceptions); do not use it in place of MRI/EUA. Prompt: “MRI says 60% external sphincter crossed. Management?” Expected: colorectal EUA, control any sepsis, consider loose draining seton without dividing substantial sphincter; later discuss LIFT or advancement flap in suitable anatomy and assess continence risk. Prompt: “Does a loose seton cure this?” Expected: usually facilitates drainage and protects against recurrent abscess, but does not reliably close fistula alone. Cutting setons carry continence risk and should not be portrayed as routine first-line. Prompt: “What changes if Crohn’s is suspected?” Expected: assess gastrointestinal symptoms and proctitis, MRI/EUA as appropriate, joint colorectal/IBD team care; drainage of sepsis, loose seton and medical treatment for symptomatic fistul
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial assessment Labels discharge “simple” without asking about abscess symptoms. Elicits course, previous abscess drainage, pain, discharge and fever. Asks about cyclical swelling, previous intervention and active sepsis requiring urgent source control. Aetiology and comorbidity Assumes every fistula is cryptoglandular. Checks Crohn’s symptoms, diabetes, immunosuppression and prior surgery. Adds radiation, trauma, malignancy concern, previous repairs and proctitis risk. Continence baseline Does not ask about bowel control before proposing sphincter division. Documents baseline leakage, urgency and previous sphincter damage. Explores quality of life and risk modifiers that change surgery selection. Examination plan Forces a probe blindly through the external opening. Requests inspection, gentle DRE, proctoscopy and EUA as needed. Maps opening and scarring, assesses active abscess and avoids creating a false tract. Anatomical classification Confuses a transsphincteric tract with an intersphincteric tract. Names Parks classes and recognises this 60% crossing as complex. Explains sphincter anatomy and why same classification may carry different func
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Performs or advises routine full fistulotomy through the MRI-demonstrated ~60% external sphincter without recognising likely continence injury. 2. Fails to drain a clinically evident perianal abscess associated with systemic sepsis, proposing elective definitive closure instead. 3. States a loose draining seton provides guaranteed definitive cure and discharges the patient without staged follow-up. 4. Blindly probes a tract forcefully and proposes division despite uncertain anatomy, risking a false passage and sphincter injury.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: On the day of planned surgery, the patient reports fever and a new throbbing perianal swelling. Expected: same-day clinical reassessment, sepsis observations, urgent examination and drainage of an abscess if present, with appropriate antibiotics only when indicated; defer planned definitive closure.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “Before dividing any tract, I must know how much sphincter is involved and the patient’s baseline continence.” “MRI shows a high transsphincteric fistula, so I would not routinely lay it open; a loose seton can maintain drainage while planning further treatment.” “If there is fever or a new painful swelling, I would urgently reassess for an abscess and arrange drainage rather than wait for elective closure.”

stations.title: Faecal Incontinence After Childbirth

sections.preamble: B2-186 | Faecal Incontinence After Childbirth AMaC · MRCS Part B · History and focused assessment · Draft for clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 34-year-old woman presents to colorectal clinic 10 months after a forceps delivery. She describes unexpected bowel leakage and is embarrassed to leave home. Take a focused history, explain the next assessment steps, and outline initial management. No examination is to be performed on the actor.
sections.2. Examiner brief: The candidate should distinguish urgency, passive leakage and flatus incontinence; assess stool consistency, obstetric injury, neurological and colorectal red flags; offer respectful examination and tailored testing; and propose stepwise management. Give findings only if requested. Findings disclosed on request: Delivery: forceps-assisted first vaginal birth, prolonged second stage, repaired third-degree perineal tear; no documented specialist follow-up. Leakage: weekly urgency with loose stool and occasional passive staining; sometimes cannot control flatus. No blood, unexplained weight loss or persistent nocturnal diarrhoea. Bowel habit: Bristol type 6 on several days weekly; no laxatives; no rectal prolapse symptoms. Impact: avoids travelling, uses pads; distress and reduced intimacy; no suicidal ideation. Background: no previous bowel surgery, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes or spinal symptoms; no family colorectal cancer history. Focused exam findings if sought: healed perineal scar, reduced resting tone and weak voluntary squeeze on simulated report; no palpable rectal mass or faecal loading. Initial investigations: stool tests only if clinically indicated by diarrhoea h
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are worried the tear was repaired incorrectly and that you will inevitably need a permanent stoma. Answer questions only when asked. If treated dismissively, say “I have stopped going out because of it.” Ask about future pregnancies near the end.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: How do you distinguish types? Urge: cannot defer the need to defecate; passive: leakage without awareness; flatus: inability to control wind; identify coexisting diarrhoea. What do you examine? With explanation, consent and chaperone: abdomen, perineal inspection for scars/prolapse, anal tone and squeeze by digital rectal examination, sacral neurology when indicated. Which specialist tests? Endoanal ultrasound to identify structural sphincter defects; anorectal manometry/physiology where specialist assessment changes management. What initial management? Optimise stool consistency, review diet and medicines, tailored bowel habits, pelvic floor physiotherapy and specialist biofeedback; refer to pelvic-floor/colorectal service. Does she need sphincter repair? Not automatically: specialist assessment and shared choice after non-surgical treatment; options depend on anatomical defect, function and individual circumstances.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction and rapport Starts intimate questioning without consent or privacy. Introduces self, checks identity, obtains permission for sensitive questions. Normalises the subject without minimising distress, offers a pause and sensitive wording. Symptom characterisation Calls all accidents diarrhoea without distinguishing control. Separately elicits urge, passive stool leakage, flatus, frequency and severity. Explores stool form, warning time, pads, episode diary and situations triggering leakage. Obstetric risk history Does not ask about childbirth or perineal injury. Asks mode of delivery, tears, repair, forceps and onset after delivery. Checks prior births, degree of tear, postnatal follow-up, later continence and future birth concerns. Differential and red flags Misses bleeding, weight loss or acute neurology. Checks bleeding, weight loss, persistent altered habit, constipation/overflow and neurological symptoms. Relates loose stool, sphincter injury, prolapse and possible bowel pathology to targeted next tests. Impact and patient priorities Treats symptoms as a minor inconvenience. Asks about activity, relationships, confidence and desired
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Dismisses persistent post-obstetric incontinence without assessment or follow-up. 2. Performs or insists on an intimate examination without consent and appropriate chaperone offer. 3. Fails to act on disclosed rectal bleeding with weight loss or new major neurological symptoms. 4. Assures patient that permanent stoma is inevitable or that a previous repair was negligent without evidence.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Actor: “I want another baby. Will I have to have a caesarean?” Expected: explain that mode of birth is individualised after specialist assessment of symptoms and sphincter function; arrange obstetric/pelvic-floor counselling rather than promise one mode.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I have focused on the accidents, but I should ask about your forceps delivery and the exact degree of perineal tear.” 2. “I said an operation might be needed too early; we should first improve stool consistency and offer specialist pelvic-floor treatment.” 3. “Before proposing internal examination, I should explain what it involves, seek consent and offer a chaperone.”

stations.title: Appendix Mass or Abscess: Source Control and Follow-up

sections.preamble: B2-187 | Appendix Mass or Abscess: Source Control and Follow-up AMaC · MRCS Part B · Applied knowledge and decision-making · Draft for clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to review a stable 42-year-old patient with five days of right iliac fossa pain and fever. CT shows perforated appendicitis with a 5-cm periappendiceal fluid collection surrounded by inflamed ileocaecal tissue. There is no free intraperitoneal gas, diffuse peritonitis or obstruction. Explain your priorities, treatment choices and follow-up.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Tests recognition of localised complicated appendicitis; resuscitation, sepsis assessment, antibiotics and source control; image-guided drainage versus operative management; and updated cancer-exclusion/interval-appendicectomy discussion. Do not score one universally mandated approach to a stable abscess. Findings disclosed on request: Vitals on request: T 38.1°C, HR 102, BP 121/74, RR 18, SpO2 97% air; alert; urine output maintained. Examination: localised right iliac fossa tenderness and guarding; no generalised rigidity. Bloods: WCC 15.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 190 mg/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, creatinine normal. CT: 5-cm well-defined abscess; radiologist believes a safe percutaneous drainage route exists; no suspicious caecal mass is definitively seen. Patient history: no previous episodes, no family colorectal malignancy; occasional recent altered bowel habit when pressed. If 24-hour progress requested: persistently febrile and rising inflammatory markers despite antibiotics; requires urgent reassessment of source control.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor is needed. The examiner may portray the senior colleague asking why the candidate has not operated and a patient concerned about malignancy.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the diagnosis? Contained perforated appendicitis with periappendiceal abscess; do not conflate localised mass/phlegmon with diffuse peritonitis. Initial priorities? A–E, sepsis assessment, IV access, bloods/cultures when indicated, analgesia, antiemetic, IV fluid according to physiology, nil by mouth pending plan, timely local-policy IV antibiotics and senior review. Source control choices? Interventional radiology review for image-guided drainage plus antibiotics if feasible; early laparoscopy in experienced hands is an alternative; immediate operation if unstable or generalised peritonitis. When to reassess? Monitor observations, examination, fluid balance, inflammatory markers and response; worsening/persistent sepsis warrants urgent senior review, repeat imaging or drainage/operation. What follow-up if he improves? Arrange deliberate appendiceal neoplasm exclusion and discuss interval appendicectomy based on contemporary WSES 2025 guidance, age and local colorectal/surgical policy; do not treat older >40-only pathways as current. What is the antibiotic duration? Individualise to adequate source control and clinical response under local antimicrobial policy; updated WSES
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Problem representation Labels CT as uncomplicated appendicitis. Diagnoses localised perforated appendicitis with drainable abscess. Explains difference between phlegmon, defined abscess and diffuse contamination. Severity assessment Ignores vital signs, lactate and organ dysfunction. Performs A–E and assesses sepsis, peritonism and haemodynamics. States how shock or evolving diffuse peritonitis changes source-control urgency. Immediate care Withholds analgesia and antimicrobials while awaiting operation. Requests IV access, bloods, fluids as indicated, analgesia, antiemetic and prompt IV antibiotics. Aligns cultures and antibiotic choice to sepsis severity, allergies and local policy without delaying treatment. CT interpretation Assumes any collection is safely drainable without review. Identifies a localised 5-cm collection and asks IR about safe access. Checks bowel involvement, obstruction, free gas and any atypical mass before choosing access. Non-operative option Sends patient home on oral antibiotics despite fever and collection. Describes admission, IV antibiotics, IR drainage when technically suitable and observation. Sets explicit response
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to initiate urgent escalation and resuscitation for new hypotension, organ dysfunction or generalised peritonitis. 2. Omits timely antibiotics and source-control assessment in a febrile patient with confirmed abscess. 3. Continues ineffective medical treatment despite documented persistent sepsis without reassessment. 4. Discharges the 42-year-old after apparent resolution without a defined plan to assess for underlying neoplasm.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: At 24 hours the patient becomes tachycardic at 132/min with BP 88/54 and diffuse guarding. Expected: call for urgent senior, anaesthetic and theatre review; A–E/resuscitate, sepsis treatment and emergency source control, rather than wait for elective IR drainage.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I treated this as an appendix mass in general; the CT actually identifies a drainable abscess, so I must involve interventional radiology.” 2. “I initially gave one definitive surgical answer; stable localised disease also allows antibiotic/drainage or experienced laparoscopic pathways.” 3. “I omitted follow-up for neoplasm; given this complicated presentation and age, a documented post-resolution investigation/interval-surgery plan is required.”

stations.title: Malignant Large Bowel Obstruction

sections.preamble: B2-188 | Malignant Large Bowel Obstruction AMaC · MRCS Part B · Applied knowledge / emergency colorectal decision-making · Draft for clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 72-year-old man attends with 3 days of distension, absolute constipation and vomiting. CT identifies an obstructing sigmoid lesion suspicious for carcinoma, proximal colonic dilation and a markedly enlarged caecum. Explain immediate assessment and choose a safe decompression/definitive pathway. The examiner will provide further CT and physiological details if requested.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Assess acute resuscitation, interpretation of the ileocaecal valve and caecal threat, staging and operative versus endoscopic options. This is not a test of committing every stable patient to a Hartmann procedure. Prompt the candidate to request contrast CT details and features of perforation. Findings disclosed on request: Initial observations: HR 108/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 20, T 37.5°C; uncomfortable but alert; dry mucous membranes. Abdomen distended, tympanitic, mildly tender; no generalised rigidity; empty rectum. Bloods: Hb 112 g/L, WCC 12.1 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 126 µmol/L (baseline 90); venous lactate 1.8 mmol/L. Contrast CT: circumferential obstructing sigmoid tumour, colon dilated upstream with caecum 11 cm; small bowel not significantly dilated; no free air, pneumatosis or portal venous gas; no distant metastasis identified on available study. If asked about valve: small bowel decompression is limited, suggesting a competent ileocaecal valve and high-pressure closed-loop physiology. If the curveball is triggered: now HR 132, BP 86/50, rising lactate 4.1 mmol/L and new generalised tenderness; CT review raises concern for caecal ischaemia.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No full actor required; examiner plays senior colorectal consultant. If asked about preferences, patient wishes to avoid a permanent stoma and understands that immediate safety may override that wish.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the immediate management? ABCDE, NBM, two large-bore IV lines, bloods including FBC/U&E/CRP/coagulation/group and save, venous gas/lactate, appropriate crystalloid resuscitation, analgesia, antiemetic, urinary catheter and fluid balance, NG decompression if vomiting/distended, VTE assessment and urgent senior colorectal/anaesthetic review. Why does the caecum matter? A competent ileocaecal valve with distal obstruction can create a closed loop; progressive caecal tension threatens ischaemia/perforation. Do not use a single diameter as an absolute determinant independent of physiology and CT. What investigations? Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis to locate level, mechanism, viability and perforation, with staging of cancer once safe; serial examination and lactate. Choices if stable without perforation? For a potentially curable left-sided lesion: discuss experienced-operator self-expanding metal stent as bridge to elective resection versus urgent oncological resection; consider decompressing stoma if stenting unsuitable or unavailable. Consider risks of stent perforation, failure and oncological consequences. Choices if unwell/peritonitic? Emergency operative source contr
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Syndrome recognition Calls this simple constipation despite vomiting and CT transition. Identifies malignant sigmoid large-bowel obstruction. Names impending proximal closed-loop threat and outlines reversible dehydration/AKI. Resuscitation Offers immediate bowel preparation or oral intake. Orders NBM, IV access, fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, bloods and monitoring. Tailors resuscitation to perfusion, urine output, lactate and comorbidities without delaying source control. Examination and danger signs Does not assess for peritonism or physiological deterioration. Checks vital signs, abdominal tenderness, peritonism and hydration. Reassesses dynamically for sepsis, ischaemia and perforation; summons senior help early. CT interpretation Ignores the valve and caecum on CT. Identifies sigmoid transition, upstream dilation and lack of free gas. Connects non-dilated small bowel/competent valve to high caecal pressure and threatened ischaemia. Investigations and monitoring Requests immediate unprepared colonoscopy as routine diagnostic first step. Requests contrast CT, blood count, renal profile, lactate and group/save. Specifies serial physiology, urine
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Attempts colonic stent despite clinical/CT evidence of perforation or peritonitis. 2. Fails to escalate new shock or suspected caecal ischaemia to urgent emergency surgery assessment. 3. Orders bowel preparation or delays decompression in established complete obstruction. 4. Promises avoidance of stoma and omits discussion of emergency resection/diversion when indicated.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient develops generalised guarding, BP 86/50 and lactate 4.1 mmol/L; radiology is concerned about caecal ischaemia. Expected: immediate ABCDE/resuscitation, urgent colorectal and anaesthetic/critical-care review, broad-spectrum antibiotics according to local sepsis/intra-abdominal infection policy, and emergency operative source control—not SEMS as an elective bridge.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I called it a simple distal obstruction; I should assess caecal size and whether a competent valve creates a threatened closed loop.” 2. “I offered a stent too readily; I must first exclude perforation and ischaemia and confirm an experienced stenting service.” 3. “I named Hartmann as mandatory; the operation depends on physiology, bowel viability and contamination, and I should explain alternatives.”

stations.title: Acute Lower GI Bleeding with Instability

sections.preamble: B2-189 | Acute Lower GI Bleeding with Instability AMaC · MRCS Part B · Critical care / investigation sequencing · Draft for clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 77-year-old woman passes a large volume of fresh and maroon blood per rectum on the acute surgical ward. She looks pale and dizzy. Explain and prioritise your immediate actions, first-line investigation and haemostasis pathway.
sections.2.
