Examiner brief: Mark actual haemorrhage resuscitation and sequential decision-making: shock index; CT angiography in ongoing unstable bleeding after initial resuscitation; urgent mesenteric angiography/embolisation if positive; consider upper GI bleeding if CTA negative. Do not reward routine unprepared emergency colonoscopy. Findings disclosed on request: Observations: HR 126/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, RR 24, SpO₂ 96% air, GCS 15; ongoing passage of blood. Shock index = 126/92 ≈ 1.37. Background: atrial fibrillation, apixaban last taken this morning; hypertension; no known liver disease. Examination on request: cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 s, non-peritonitic abdomen, frank dark red blood on rectal examination with consent/chaperone. Initial labs: Hb 91 g/L (was 119 yesterday), platelets 208 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 140 µmol/L, lactate 3.3 mmol/L; note early haemoglobin may underestimate acute loss. CTA after initial stabilisation shows active contrast extravasation in ascending colon. IR service reachable by emergency transfer if unavailable locally. Curveball: subsequent repeat CTA reports no active extravasation but persistent hypotension and melaena; urea disproportionately high relative to creatin
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor essential. Examiner acts as resuscitation nurse and asks whether waiting for haemoglobin below 70 g/L is safe in this shocked patient.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: How unstable? ABCDE, shock index HR/SBP = 1.37: haemodynamic instability. Activate major haemorrhage response according to local protocol, senior gastroenterology/colorectal, anaesthetics/critical care, transfusion laboratory. What resuscitation? Oxygen if indicated, monitored environment, two wide-bore cannulas, FBC/U&E/coagulation/fibrinogen/group and crossmatch/gas/lactate, warm the patient, blood component resuscitation guided by haemorrhage severity and protocol, monitor urine output; consider anticoagulant reversal per local major bleed protocol with haematology. What is first-line investigation after initial stabilisation? Urgent CT angiography for unstable ongoing suspected LGIB to localise bleeding. Do not send an actively shocked patient for routine bowel-prepped colonoscopy. What if CTA shows extravasation? Discuss immediately with interventional radiologist for selective mesenteric angiography and embolisation; organise urgent transfer if IR not onsite. What if CTA is negative yet instability persists? Consider brisk upper GI haemorrhage: urgent upper endoscopy after resuscitation and senior gastroenterology input; reassess other causes and need for repeat imaging. When
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and severity Calls this minor rectal bleeding because the patient is conscious. Recognises haemorrhagic shock and calculates shock index >1. Interprets cool peripheries, lactate and active loss as major haemorrhage irrespective of first Hb. Initial A–E and help Leaves patient in unmonitored ward bed. Performs ABCDE, calls senior clinicians and moves to monitored resuscitation. Calls transfusion service, anaesthetics/critical care and GI/colorectal/IR with explicit task allocation. Access and testing Orders only a repeat haemoglobin in several hours. Obtains two wide-bore IVs, FBC, coagulation, U&E, group/crossmatch and lactate. Adds fibrinogen, serial point-of-care assessment, temperature and urine-output monitoring. Blood and shock management Waits until Hb <70 g/L despite persistent shock. Activates appropriate major-bleeding transfusion pathway, using clinical shock and ongoing loss. Explains restrictive Hb trigger is for haemodynamically stable patients and adjusts blood components to protocol. Medication and coagulopathy Misses the morning apixaban dose. Checks anticoagulants/antiplatelets and withholds apixaban while arranging urg
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Does not recognise haemodynamic instability or summon emergency resuscitation help. 2. Withholds blood resuscitation while waiting for the haemoglobin to fall below a stable-patient threshold despite shock. 3. Fails to arrange urgent CTA and subsequent IR discussion for active unstable bleeding with positive extravasation. 4. Rules out a brisk upper GI bleeding source solely from haematochezia when unstable and CTA-negative.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: CTA shows no bleeding focus, but hypotension persists and the stool becomes black; urea is relatively elevated. Expected: continue haemorrhage resuscitation, urgent GI/anaesthetic support and prompt OGD for possible brisk upper GI source; do not interpret negative CTA as bleeding cessation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I focused on haemoglobin 91; the vital signs give a shock index of 1.37, so I must manage this as active major haemorrhage.” 2. “I suggested colonoscopy first; with ongoing shock, urgent CT angiography is the recommended localisation test after initial resuscitation.” 3. “I assumed haematochezia means a lower source; if CTA is negative with instability I should pursue urgent upper GI endoscopy.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-190 Ischaemic Colitis — Recognise, Investigate, Escalate Format: Applied knowledge / emergency colorectal surgery | Time: 8 minutes | Status: DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar receiving a referral for a 74-year-old woman with abrupt left-sided abdominal cramping and two episodes of bloody diarrhoea after a period of dehydration. BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 96/min, temperature 37.5°C. She has atrial fibrillation and hypertension. Explain your differential, assessment, interpretation of the supplied investigations and management plan to the examiner. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Provide only requested findings. The candidate should distinguish usually reversible left-sided colonic ischaemia from fulminant ischaemia and acute mesenteric ischaemia. No actual endoscopic image is needed. History: Pain began 8 hours ago, followed by urgency and small-volume maroon stool. Recent diarrhoeal illness, poor oral intake and a diuretic. No previous similar episodes. Examination: Alert, cool hands; tenderness over left iliac fossa without rigidity, guarding or rebound. Capillary refill 3 seconds. Rectal examination: maroon stool; no mass. Tests: Hb 122 g/L, WCC 15.0 × 10⁹/L, CRP 42 mg/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, creatinine 135 µmol/L (baseline 90). Stool tests pending. Contrast-enhanced CT report: Segmental circumferential wall thickening and oedema of descending/sigmoid colon with pericolic stranding. Mesenteric vessels patent. No free intraperitoneal gas, portal venous gas or pneumatosis. On request: flexible sigmoidoscopy if stabilised: Patchy erythema, oedema and superficial ulceration with a sharply demarcated segment; biopsies can be taken if safe. Do not insufflate forcefully or traverse severe disease. Change during station: After 4 hours HR 124, BP 88/54, lactate 4
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Not an actor station. If examiner role-plays patient: concerned about bleeding and cancer; asks whether colonoscopy is safe. Give an understandable explanation of restricted blood supply and why deterioration changes the plan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What makes ischaemic colitis likely? Acute cramping then haematochezia, vascular/low-flow risk, segmental left-colon CT abnormalities; recognise infective colitis, IBD, diverticulitis and mesenteric ischaemia as alternatives. Which regions are vulnerable? Splenic flexure (Griffith’s point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck’s point) are classic watershed regions; right-sided disease may signal more severe illness. What investigations? ABCDE and repeated observations; FBC, U&Es, CRP, coagulation, venous/arterial blood gas with lactate, group-and-save/crossmatch if bleeding; stool infection testing; IV-contrast CT. CTA if isolated right-sided disease or acute mesenteric ischaemia cannot be excluded. Should you scope now? If stable and no peritonitis, cautious unprepared flexible sigmoidoscopy/limited lower endoscopy within 48 hours, minimal insufflation and biopsies where safe; never scope a suspected perforation, peritonitis or gangrene. Immediate treatment? IV access, carefully titrated crystalloid resuscitation, stop contributing hypotensive drugs where appropriate, nil by mouth initially, analgesia, correct precipitating causes; broad-spectrum antibiotics for moderate/severe illne
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls it uncomplicated infective diarrhoea despite characteristic bloody pain. Identifies probable ischaemic colitis and names at least two relevant mimics. Links low-flow history, segmental imaging and bleeding while explicitly distinguishing acute mesenteric ischaemia. Initial physiology Ignores hypotension and ongoing fluid deficit. Performs ABCDE, repeats vital signs, assesses perfusion and urine output. Uses serial examinations, fluid balance and lactate trends to identify evolving hypoperfusion. Focused history Omits recent dehydration and vasoactive medications. Elicits onset, bleeding, vascular disease, medications and recent low-flow event. Adds recent surgery, arrhythmia, infection exposure and anticoagulant use to refine differential. Examination Fails to check for guarding or peritonism. Assesses abdomen for distension, tenderness and peritonism; performs appropriate rectal exam. Highlights disproportionate pain, diffuse tenderness and worsening signs as urgent red flags. Investigations Orders plain film alone and omits cross-sectional imaging. Requests blood count, renal profile, lactate, stool studies and contrast CT. Spec
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to recognise or urgently escalate new shock plus rebound tenderness. 2. Performs or advocates colonoscopy in established peritonitis/suspected gangrene or perforation. 3. Delays resuscitation and senior surgical review in a clearly unstable patient. 4. Rules out acute mesenteric ischaemia solely because lactate is initially normal.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: At the 4-hour review, she develops shock and generalised rebound tenderness, lactate 4.3 mmol/L. Expected response: Abandon planned endoscopy; ABCDE resuscitation, urgent senior surgeon and anaesthesia/ICU, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and immediate evaluation for emergency laparotomy/source control; imaging only if stable enough and does not delay surgery.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: I missed her new peritonism: I would stop the endoscopy plan, repeat ABCDE and contact the on-call consultant and anaesthetist immediately. The early lactate did not exclude bowel ischaemia; I would reconsider mesenteric vascular disease and request CTA if she is stable enough. I initially labelled this infective colitis; the abrupt pain-then-bleeding pattern and segmental CT changes make ischaemia the leading diagnosis.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-191 Rectal Cancer — Interpret the Staging MRI Report Format: Data interpretation / colorectal oncology | Time: 8 minutes | Status: DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a colorectal surgical registrar at the cancer MDT. A 63-year-old man has biopsy-proven rectal adenocarcinoma, 7 cm from the anal verge on endoscopy. Interpret the written pelvic MRI report provided by the examiner, explain implications for staging and next investigations, and propose an MDT treatment pathway. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Provide MRI narrative verbatim on request. Ask candidate not to assume distant-metastasis status from pelvic MRI alone. The 2026 ESGAR consensus uses “mesorectal fascia (MRF) involvement” and advises against the old 1–2 mm “threatened MRF” reporting label. Endoscopy / pathology: Circumferential lesion with biopsy confirming moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. MMR immunohistochemistry has been requested; no obstruction. MRI report: Mid-rectal tumour; lower edge 7 cm from anal verge. Tumour extends 6 mm beyond muscularis propria into mesorectal fat (cT3c by common MRI subclassification). An irregular tumour deposit lies 0.8 mm from mesorectal fascia. EMVI positive. Suspicious mesorectal nodes: cN+. No definitive sphincter/levator invasion. No adjacent organ invasion. Examination: ECOG performance status 1. On DRE lesion is palpable but not fixed. No clinical obstructive symptoms. Other staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis has not yet been performed; CEA baseline not yet documented. On request after staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis shows no distant metastasis. No liver lesions. Patient asks whether chemotherapy/radiotherapy could avoid an operation. Curveball report addendum: Radiol
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: If patient role-play is used: “Does this MRI mean it has spread everywhere? Can I skip surgery if treatment shrinks it?” Expect balanced language, explaining uncertainty and structured surveillance if deferring surgery after complete response.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Interpret the T stage. cT3 means extension beyond muscularis propria into mesorectal fat; 6 mm beyond commonly corresponds to mrT3c subclassification (5–15 mm), not T4. What is the margin issue? Irregular tumour deposit within 0.8 mm of mesorectal fascia fulfils 2026 ESGAR definition of MRF involvement (≤1 mm); do not label it simply “threatened CRM.” Does the smooth-bordered node change MRF status? Not in itself under the 2026 ESGAR definition: smooth-bordered node ≤1 mm does not establish MRF involvement. Distinguish it from irregular deposits, EMVI and primary tumour. Why mention EMVI and nodes? EMVI positivity and suspicious nodes are adverse MRI features informing local recurrence/systemic relapse risk and neoadjuvant planning; MRI nodal assessment is imperfect. What staging is still needed? Complete CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for metastases, baseline CEA, pathology review including MMR status, performance status, fitness, bowel function, preferences, and MDT review. Treatment and follow-up? Discuss preoperative radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy and systemic treatment strategy according to expert MDT risk assessment, followed by re-staging and appropriate resection/TME when indic
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Report orientation Does not identify tumour height or its relationship to the mesorectum. States mid-rectal tumour and locates lower edge 7 cm from anal verge. Links exact height to surgical planning and asks for relation to anterior peritoneal reflection and sphincter complex. T category Mistakes mesorectal fat extension for T4 organ invasion. Identifies cT3 and 6 mm extramural depth (commonly mrT3c). Distinguishes T3 extramural depth from peritoneal or adjacent-organ invasion and their implications. Mesorectal fascia Calls a 0.8 mm irregular deposit a clear margin. Recognises MRF involvement because irregular deposit lies ≤1 mm from fascia. Explains 2026 ESGAR definition and does not mechanically apply old “1–2 mm threatened” label. Nodal staging Assumes every small mesorectal node is malignant based on diameter alone. Identifies reported cN+ and acknowledges MRI nodal uncertainty. Distinguishes smooth nodes from irregular tumour deposits and requests patient-level confidence in cN category. EMVI Ignores explicitly reported EMVI positivity. Names EMVI positive as an adverse risk feature. Integrates EMVI with cT stage, MRF status and nodal finding
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Incorrectly declares M0 using only pelvic MRI, omitting systemic staging. 2. Misses the irregular deposit 0.8 mm from MRF and calls the surgical plane safely clear. 3. Offers local excision alone or guaranteed immediate resection as definitive treatment without MDT consideration of high-risk findings. 4. Describes watch-and-wait as routine treatment for partial response without explaining regrowth risk and surveillance.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: A report addendum shows a smooth-bordered mesorectal node 0.7 mm from the fascia, separate from the irregular 0.8-mm deposit. Expected response: Explain that smooth-bordered nodes close to fascia do not by themselves establish MRF involvement under ESGAR 2026; the irregular tumour deposit at 0.8 mm already makes MRF involved. Request radiology consensus at MDT.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: I described this as T4; it is cT3 with 6 mm spread beyond muscularis propria, without adjacent-organ invasion. I called the margin “threatened”; the updated MRI terminology is MRF involved because an irregular deposit is 0.8 mm away. I suggested watch-and-wait before assessing response; I would first complete staging and MDT-led treatment, then consider it only if complete response and rigorous surveillance are feasible.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-192 — Colorectal Liver Metastases Applied knowledge | Suggested station time: 8 minutes | Examiner-led role play STATUS: DRAFT. Not an official intercollegiate MRCS mark scheme. Local specialist review required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in a colorectal MDT teaching meeting. A 61-year-old patient has a sigmoid adenocarcinoma and two liver lesions on staging CT. Explain the staging, what makes liver metastases potentially resectable, and how you would plan treatment. You may request investigation results; no images are available.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only when r: Patient is fit, ECOG 0; no obstructive symptoms. Colonoscopy biopsy: moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: sigmoid tumour, two right-lobe liver lesions (2.1 and 2.8 cm), no evident extrahepatic metastases. If requested: liver MRI confirms two metastases, no additional lesions; portal vein and hepatic veins patent; left lobe looks adequate but formal volumetry not yet performed. CEA 24 micrograms/L. If asked: histology MMR-proficient; RAS/BRAF results pending. Liver function, albumin and INR normal. No previous hepatic disease. Do not give a definitive operative decision: this requires HPB MDT review, imaging review, and adequate future liver remnant assessment.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: No actor required. If an examiner plays the patient: ask “Does spread to the liver mean nothing can be done?” and “Would you operate on the bowel and liver together?” Accept a clear explanation that some liver-limited disease is potentially treatable with curative intent, with treatment sequencing personalised by the specialist MDT.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What imaging would you review?” Expected: contrast CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and dedicated liver MRI; staging for extrahepatic disease; review with hepatobiliary radiologist. Prompt: “What defines resectability?” Expected: ability to clear all macroscopic disease while retaining perfused, drained liver with adequate volume and function; not simply number/size of lesions. Prompt: “What would alter sequencing?” Expected: symptoms/obstruction of primary; synchronous versus metachronous presentation; distribution and extent of hepatic disease; patient fitness; perioperative systemic therapy and staged versus combined resection decided at MDT. Prompt: “What if not currently resectable?” Expected: systemic therapy with reassessment for conversion; consider local ablation where appropriate; specialist palliative options if not amenable to local treatment.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Problem representation Calls two hepatic lesions benign without staging. Identifies synchronous liver metastases from sigmoid cancer. States key uncertainty: full metastatic distribution and technical/functional resectability. Disease staging Looks only at the liver CT slice. Requests review of CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and liver MRI. Checks extrahepatic disease, local primary complications and imaging concordance. Biology and investigations Uses CEA alone to determine prognosis or treatment. Checks CEA baseline, histology and MMR/RAS/BRAF status where relevant. Explains biomarkers guide systemic therapy, not a substitute for anatomical operability. Resectability States two lesions are always operable. Requires complete disease clearance and an adequate functioning remnant. Checks inflow, outflow, biliary drainage and remnant volumetry/function with HPB. Multidisciplinary process Books elective colectomy without HPB input. Refers to specialist colorectal/HPB MDT before selecting sequencing. Includes HPB surgeon, radiology, oncology and patient fitness/preferences. Treatment sequencing Insists all synchronous disease requires simultaneous surgery. Dis
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Declares liver metastases universally incurable and excludes the patient from HPB MDT assessment. Commits to a major hepatectomy without assessing adequate future liver remnant and vascular/biliary inflow/outflow. Proposes immediate elective combined bowel/liver resection without completing metastatic staging or multidisciplinary review. Overlooks a clinically obstructed/perforated primary and proposes routine delayed outpatient work-up without urgent management.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The examiner now reports that interval CT shows small-volume suspicious peritoneal nodules. Candidate must stop declaring the liver disease isolated, request specialist radiology/MDT review and further staging as appropriate, then revisit curative-intent feasibility; extrahepatic disease is not an automatic universal prohibition, but disease distribution and control matter.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should clarify that the count of metastases does not by itself decide resectability; the remaining functioning liver matters.” “Before suggesting an operation, I would ask the HPB MDT to confirm extrahepatic staging, lesion distribution and future liver remnant.” “Because the bowel primary is asymptomatic, I would not assume it must be removed first; the sequencing is an MDT choice.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-193 — Lynch Syndrome and Familial Adenomatous Polyposis Applied knowledge | Suggested station time: 8 minutes | Examiner-led role play STATUS: DRAFT. Not an official intercollegiate MRCS mark scheme. Local specialist review required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are asked to interpret a hereditary colorectal cancer clinic referral. A 34-year-old woman has recently been diagnosed with right-sided colorectal cancer; immunohistochemistry shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6. Her mother developed endometrial cancer at 48. Contrast this suspected syndrome with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), outline confirmation and surveillance, and explain when surgery is considered.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only when r: Patient has no history of numerous adenomas. IHC: retained MLH1/PMS2, absent MSH2/MSH6. Germline test not yet performed. She has one child aged 8. If asked: tumour testing screens for Lynch syndrome but is not itself a germline diagnosis; refer to genetics and appropriate molecular pathway. Comparison card if requested: an unrelated 16-year-old with a parent known to carry an APC pathogenic variant, now found to have hundreds of colonic adenomas. UK surveillance reference: Lynch MLH1/MSH2 colonoscopy from 25, MSH6/PMS2 from 35, at 2-year intervals; APC/FAP colonoscopy from 12–14 at 1–3-year phenotype-adjusted intervals; duodenoscopy from around age 25, interval risk-stratified.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Actor plays the woman: “Does this prove I inherited cancer?”, “Will my child get it?”, “Should I have my whole bowel removed?” Candidate must distinguish a screening result from a confirmed germline result, avoid deterministic language, and outline specialist genetics and tailored surgical decisions.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “Why MSH2/MSH6 loss?” — Raises suspicion for MSH2-related Lynch (also EPCAM-associated mechanisms possible), not a definitive genotype. “What is the inheritance?” — Lynch and classical APC-associated FAP are typically autosomal dominant; each child of a confirmed carrier has 50% chance of inheriting the familial variant. “Do Amsterdam criteria replace testing?” — No; historical family-history criteria can identify risk but miss cases. Use universal tumour MMR/MSI testing for colorectal cancer. “How does surgical planning differ?” — Lynch: segmental versus extended colectomy balances metachronous risk, gene, age, function and wishes; FAP: colectomy/proctocolectomy timing and configuration driven by polyp burden, rectal disease and cancer risk. “What else is at risk?” — Lynch-associated endometrial/ovarian cancers; FAP duodenal and desmoid disease; specialist counselling.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Syndrome identification Calls loss of MSH2/MSH6 typical sporadic FAP. Recognises deficient MMR suggestive of Lynch syndrome. Interprets IHC as tumour-level screening and considers MSH2/EPCAM pathway. Pedigree Does not ask which relatives had which cancers. Elicits three-generation history, ages and endometrial cancer. Explains why family-history criteria cannot replace universal tumour testing. Molecular pathway Equates tumour stain with confirmed germline mutation. Refers to genetics for germline assessment and appropriate work-up. Addresses unresolved dMMR after negative germline and somatic alternatives. Inheritance/cascade Says all children will inherit the condition. Explains autosomal dominant inheritance and 50% variant risk per child of a carrier. Separates inheritance risk from cancer penetrance and age-appropriate testing. Lynch surveillance Recommends starting everyone at 20 with annual scopes. States UK biennial scope from 25 (MLH1/MSH2), 35 (MSH6/PMS2). Checks specialist adjustments after cancer/resection and counselling on extracolonic risks. FAP recognition Claims hundreds of adenomas are a normal Lynch pattern. Recognises APC-associ
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Tells the patient loss of tumour MSH2/MSH6 establishes a hereditary mutation without germline assessment. Reassures first-degree relatives there is no cancer risk and omits genetics/cascade-test discussion. States FAP can be safely managed indefinitely with colonoscopy despite hundreds of increasingly unmanageable adenomas. Uses a single mandatory colectomy approach for all Lynch patients without assessing gene, cancer site, age, function or preference.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Genetic testing finds no germline pathogenic variant despite abnormal tumour MMR staining. Candidate must not declare Lynch syndrome proven; request expert genetics/MDT assessment of somatic explanations and further work-up as appropriate; tailor family risk management to the resolved diagnosis and pedigree.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I need to correct myself: this abnormal tumour stain is a screen, not proof of a germline mutation.” “For Lynch surveillance, I should give the UK gene-specific starting ages, not a single age for every carrier.” “In FAP, the rectal polyp burden helps determine whether ileorectal anastomosis or pouch surgery is appropriate.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-194 — A Positive FIT Screening Result Communication | Suggested time: 8 minutes | AMaC MRCS Part B DRAFT • Not an official MRCS marking scheme • Independent colorectal specialist sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the colorectal surgical trainee in an NHS bowel cancer screening clinic. A 58-year-old woman has attended following a positive home faecal immunochemical test (FIT). She is frightened and asks whether she has cancer. Explain the result, discuss further investigation and obtain agreement for an appropriate next step. You are not asked to consent for operative treatment.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose findings on: Patient: 58, no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no weight loss, no iron-deficiency anaemia known. Screening programme FIT was above the programme referral threshold; numerical value need not be disclosed. No previous colonoscopy. If asked: no known inflammatory bowel disease, significant cardiac/respiratory disease, prior bowel surgery or family history of colorectal cancer. Not anticoagulated; no recorded drug allergies. She can consent and would like an explanation before deciding. If queried: a positive FIT identifies haemoglobin in a stool sample; it is not a diagnosis or stage of cancer. Most people referred for colonoscopy through screening do not have bowel cancer. If asked about alternative investigation: CT colonography may be considered following specialist assessment if colonoscopy is unsuitable or declined; it cannot remove polyps or take biopsies, and abnormal findings may still require colonoscopy.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Opening: “The letter says blood was found. Does that mean I have bowel cancer?” Anxious, alert, understands simple explanations. At 3 minutes: “I have piles. Can we just put the result down to that?” If candidate explains colonoscopy: “Will it hurt, and can it cause any damage?” If offered a decision: initially hesitant because her sister had a difficult bowel preparation; with balanced information agrees to speak to the screening specialist practitioner.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is FIT? — Detects human haemoglobin in faeces as a marker of possible lower gastrointestinal bleeding; cannot establish the source. Does a positive result mean cancer? — No. Benign causes including polyps and haemorrhoids are possible; assessment is needed to rule out significant pathology. What happens next? — Bowel cancer screening specialist practitioner fitness review, explanation, then colonoscopy where suitable; bowel preparation, inspection of colon, biopsies and polypectomy as indicated. Risks and alternatives? — Preparation-related inconvenience/dehydration risk; sedation-related risks if used, bleeding and perforation (particularly with polypectomy), incomplete test or missed lesion; CT colonography if colonoscopy unsuitable. If colonoscopy finds something? — Normal: return to advice tailored by the programme; polyp: remove/sample and histology/surveillance advice; cancer: staging and colorectal MDT referral. What if she refuses? — Respect informed refusal after exploring concerns, assess understanding, document discussion, arrange appropriate follow-up and safety net; do not dismiss positive FIT.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and rapport Says the result is “bad” without checking distress or introducing role. Introduces self, acknowledges anxiety and asks what the letter has led her to fear. Uses an open opening question, checks baseline understanding and agrees an agenda centred on her cancer worry. Meaning of FIT States FIT confirms cancer or equates the value with stage. Explains blood was detected in the stool and that FIT alone cannot diagnose cancer. Explains sensitivity/referral purpose and that benign and precancerous causes are possible without giving false reassurance. Risk communication Promises she does not have cancer or claims most positive tests mean cancer. Says cancer is possible but by no means certain; assessment is needed. Uses neutral, non-technical language and checks that the patient can distinguish test result from diagnosis. Investigations Offers repeat FIT as the routine definitive next step. Offers screening practitioner assessment and colonoscopy with biopsy/polypectomy where appropriate. Clarifies fitness, alternatives including CT colonography when appropriate, and the implications of inability to biopsy or remove polyps. Colonoscopy
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: 1. Falsely tells patient a positive screening FIT is a confirmed diagnosis of colorectal cancer. 2. Dismisses the positive FIT as haemorrhoids and advises no further investigation. 3. States a second negative FIT rules out pathology and cancels investigation without specialist review. 4. Pressures a patient who has not consented into colonoscopy or fails to respect a capacitous refusal.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: “My piles bleed sometimes, so surely that explains the test?” Expected: Acknowledge a possible benign source, but explain it does not safely exclude a polyp or malignancy; recommend the screening assessment and appropriate colonic investigation.
sections.8. Three recovery lines: 1. After saying “the test suggests cancer”: “I need to correct that: it shows blood in the sample, not cancer. We need an examination to find out why.” 2. After presenting colonoscopy as mandatory: “You have a choice. I should explain benefits, burdens and alternatives so you can decide.” 3. After minimising procedural risk: “Colonoscopy is usually safe but bleeding or perforation can occur, particularly when removing polyps; let me explain and provide written figures.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-195 — Consent: Laparoscopic Right Hemicolectomy Communication | Suggested time: 8 minutes | AMaC MRCS Part B DRAFT • Not an official MRCS marking scheme • Independent colorectal specialist sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the colorectal surgical trainee in elective clinic. A 67-year-old man has a biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis shows no distant metastases and the colorectal MDT recommends elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy with curative intent. Explain the proposed operation, options, significant risks, recovery and possible need for a stoma; establish informed consent. The consultant will confirm the definitive consent.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose findings on: Patient fit for elective surgery after anaesthetic review; hypertension controlled, independent activities; no previous laparotomy. CEA obtained as part of staging, but not relevant to this consent discussion. Diagnosis: ascending colon adenocarcinoma on colonoscopy biopsy. CT shows no distant disease; cancer stage and node involvement cannot be finalised before histopathology of the resection specimen. Proposed procedure: remove right colon including tumour, relevant blood supply and lymphatic drainage, then usually join terminal ileum to remaining colon (ileocolic anastomosis); laparoscopic ports and extraction incision. If asked: ileostomy is not routine in an uncomplicated elective right hemicolectomy but may be required if joining the bowel is unsafe or complications demand reoperation. Conversion to open surgery is possible if visibility, adhesions, bleeding or other safety issues arise. If asked: no severe frailty or anticoagulation, no prior VTE; anaesthetic risks and individual numeric risks to be established through the treating team rather than quoted as universal figures.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Opening: “They told me I have a tumour. Will you remove all of my bowel?” Concerned but able to engage. At 2–3 minutes: “A neighbour had a bag afterwards. Will I wake up with a stoma?” At 4 minutes: “If this is keyhole surgery, it cannot be dangerous, can it?” At 6 minutes: “If you open me up instead, would that mean something has gone wrong?” If asked what matters most: wants independence and to understand leak and stoma risks; spouse can help post-discharge.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Describe the operation. — Oncological right colectomy with vascular/lymph node clearance; ileocolic anastomosis if safe; laparoscopic approach with potential conversion. How can you know the stage? — Biopsy establishes cancer; imaging excludes demonstrable distant metastasis; definitive pathologic depth and nodal status from resection histology. Major procedure-specific risks? — Anastomotic leak causing peritonitis/sepsis/reoperation/stoma, haemorrhage, injury to adjacent organs/vessels, ileus/obstruction, wound/intra-abdominal infection. General major risks? — DVT/PE, pneumonia, cardiac/anaesthetic events, urinary infection, death; patient-specific quantification rather than borrowed hospital-wide rate. Stoma and conversion? — Not planned routinely for this scenario, but possible if unsafe join or serious complication; conversion to open is a safety decision not automatically an error. Alternatives and recovery? — Discuss non-operative/no-curative treatment and consequences; specialist discussion of other treatments as relevant, ERAS mobilisation, feeding and analgesia, pathology/MDT follow-up. The patient wants to sign immediately. — Check understanding, capacity, material concer
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical indication Does not name the tumour or describes surgery as palliative despite the scenario. Explains biopsy-proven right colon cancer and rationale for curative-intent resection. Separates imaging stage from pathological stage and explains the MDT recommendation without promising cure. Procedure anatomy Claims the whole colon and rectum will be removed. Explains right colon removal and joining small bowel to remaining colon. Adds regional lymph node/vascular clearance and expected laparoscopic incisions using accessible language. Approach and conversion Guarantees keyhole completion and no abdominal incision. Explains laparoscopic ports, specimen extraction and possible open conversion. Describes bleeding/adhesions/poor visibility as reasons to convert for safety, without equating conversion with failure. Anastomosis and leak Omits the bowel join and leak altogether. Explains anastomotic leak, intra-abdominal infection, possible drainage or emergency reoperation. Clearly links a severe leak to sepsis, prolonged stay and possible stoma or intensive care. Stoma discussion Guarantees no stoma or says everyone requires a permanent bag. States
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: 1. Guarantees that a laparoscopic right hemicolectomy cannot require conversion to open surgery. 2. Guarantees that a stoma will never be necessary, despite the material possibility with intraoperative findings or complications. 3. Omits anastomotic leak entirely from informed-consent discussion. 4. Obtains a signature despite evident misunderstanding and without addressing the patient’s material concerns.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: “If you need to switch to an open operation, do I have to wake up and consent again?” Expected: Explain that foreseeable conversion should be discussed and included in consent beforehand; it can be necessary for safety. Unexpected procedures beyond what is consented for should not be assumed permissible absent an emergency or other lawful basis.
sections.8. Three recovery lines: 1. After saying “there is no chance of a bag”: “That was too definite. A stoma is unlikely to be planned here, but we may need one if a safe join is not possible or a complication develops.” 2. After saying “keyhole is risk-free”: “The smaller incisions may aid recovery, but this remains major surgery with risks including bleeding, leak, clots and serious infection.” 3. After omitting alternatives: “You also need to know the choice not to have surgery and its implications, and whether other treatments may be appropriate for your case.”

stations.title: Consent: Hartmann’s Procedure and Later Reversal

sections.preamble: B2-196 | Consent: Hartmann’s Procedure and Later Reversal AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Communication • 8-minute simulated station DRAFT — independent consultant clinical/editorial sign-off required; educational simulation, not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. Explain the proposed emergency Hartmann’s procedure to a 68-year-old with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis and generalised peritonitis after initial resuscitation. The consultant has recommended resection with end colostomy; the patient is alert, has decision-making capacity and asks if the bag will definitely be temporary. Explore concerns, benefits, material risks, alternatives and next steps; do not simply recite a form.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Observations after resuscitation: pulse 104/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, temperature 38.2°C; CT: free air/fluid, inflamed perforated sigmoid, no distant mass. Anaesthetist and consultant agree urgent source control is needed. When asked: type 2 diabetes, BMI 31, lives independently, no previous stoma, anxious about intimacy and caring for spouse. No documented drug allergy; on antihypertensives; no anticoagulant. Procedure: laparotomy or laparoscopy as feasible, resect diseased sigmoid, close rectal stump, bring proximal colon out as end colostomy; no immediate colorectal anastomosis. Accept balanced discussion of resection with primary anastomosis ± diverting ileostomy in selected patients, but consultant-selected Hartmann is reasonable for this septic, contaminated scenario. Do not mark alternative as routinely suitable.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: You fear a permanent bag: ‘Can you guarantee you will put everything back in six months?’ You need time for a question, but accept urgency when explained. Ask: ‘What happens if I refuse tonight?’ and ‘Will I still have bowel movements from the back passage?’ If treated respectfully, state you understand and can decide. No scripted loss of capacity.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: At 2 min, if missing procedure: ‘Precisely what will you do inside my abdomen?’ Expect resection, rectal stump closure and end colostomy. At 4 min: ‘Will the stoma definitely be reversed?’ Expect no guarantee; future fitness, healing, anatomy, preference and risks determine eligibility. At 6 min: ‘What are the main things that could go wrong?’ Expect bleeding, infection/abscess, sepsis, injury to ureter/bowel, thromboembolism, cardiorespiratory risks, death, wound and stoma complications. If the candidate says reversal is simple: ‘Is a second operation risk-free?’ Expect adhesions, injury, leak, infection, conversion, temporary/permanent stoma possibilities.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and consent Launches into operation without checking identity, understanding or permission. Introduces self, confirms identity, asks current understanding and permission to explain. Checks immediate priorities and patient’s desired detail while acknowledging emergency pressure. Indication and urgency Treats septic perforation as elective or delays required source control. Explains perforation, contamination and why urgent surgery is recommended. Connects sepsis and uncontrolled abdominal contamination to deterioration despite antibiotics alone. Procedure explanation Confuses Hartmann’s with a loop ileostomy or says bowel will be joined now. Describes diseased-colon resection, closed rectal stump and end colostomy. Uses a simple abdomen/stoma sketch and checks comprehension of stool diversion. Benefits and alternatives Promises cure or omits an alternative to surgery. Explains source control and mentions nonoperative treatment is unsuitable for this diffuse peritonitis. Explains primary anastomosis ± diversion may suit selected patients but not automatically this case. Immediate operative risks Omits serious injury, septic or mortality risks
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Promises that the end colostomy will definitely be reversed or guarantees a specific reversal date. Describes primary anastomosis as the operation planned, concealing that the patient will have an end colostomy. Withholds the material possibility of death/major sepsis complications when discussing this emergency laparotomy. States that a capacitated patient cannot refuse treatment or seeks coercive consent despite expressed refusal.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Actor: ‘My neighbour had a colostomy reversed after three months. You can guarantee mine, can't you?’ Expected: empathise; explain reversal is considered only after recovery, assessment of fitness and anatomy, with no fixed timetable or guarantee; discuss life with a permanent stoma as a genuine possibility.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: If you omit the rectal stump: ‘I need to correct my description: we close the downstream rectal end and bring the upstream colon to the skin as a colostomy.’ If you promise reversal: ‘I spoke too definitely. Reversal is not certain and, if offered, is a separate major operation with its own risks.’ If risks are underplayed: ‘Because this is emergency surgery for sepsis, there is a real risk of serious illness or death, even with appropriate treatment.’

stations.title: Anal Cancer — Recognition, Staging and Initial Management

near_match.title: ACS / Acute Chest Pain — Recognition and Initial Management

sections.preamble: B2-197 | Anal Cancer — Recognition, Staging and Initial Management AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • History / applied knowledge • 8-minute simulated station DRAFT — independent consultant clinical/editorial sign-off required; educational simulation, not an official MRCS marking scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: In a colorectal clinic, assess a 54-year-old with three months of anal pain, small-volume bleeding and a persistent lump, previously treated as haemorrhoids. Take a focused history, explain your differential and describe the appropriate diagnostic and treatment pathway to the examiner. No intimate examination is to be performed on an actor. State what examination you would offer with consent and a chaperone, and request findings. The case concerns suspected anal squamous cell carcinoma, not rectal adenocarcinoma.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: History if asked: bleeding on wiping, increasing anal pain, sensation of lump, occasional mucus, mild urgency, no major weight loss; no fever. Past genital HPV treatment; smokes 10/day. HIV status unknown and should be sensitively offered testing according to pathway, not assumed. Examination requested: external inspection shows firm irregular 2.5-cm ulcerated lesion at anal canal margin extending into canal; DRE detects firmness; bilateral groin nodes not clearly enlarged. No acute perianal sepsis. Biopsy performed via appropriate specialist assessment: invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Pelvic MRI: 2.5-cm anal canal mass, no adjacent organ invasion, no suspicious regional nodes. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis: no metastases. Histology and staging supplied only on request after candidate proposes investigation. Assess differential of fissure, haemorrhoids, fistula, infection and anal malignancy, but persistent atypical ulcer/mass requires biopsy. HPV risk and immunosuppression belong in history, never used to imply blame.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: You are embarrassed, anxious and ask whether this could just be piles. If questioned, disclose previous HPV-related treatment but dislike moralising language. Ask whether you will need your anus removed or a permanent stoma; you wish to understand treatment and fertility/sexual consequences when relevant.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: ‘What features make you worry about cancer?’ Expect persistent ulcerated firm anal mass, pain/bleeding and failure to improve; consider suspected-cancer pathway. ‘What examination and biopsy?’ Expect perianal inspection, DRE, proctoscopy/anoscopy, inguinal nodes, chaperone, tissue diagnosis; EUA if examination poorly tolerated. ‘How do you stage this?’ Expect pelvic MRI for local/regional extent, cross-sectional systemic staging, specialist MDT; assess groins and consider HIV testing with consent. ‘What is standard curative therapy?’ Expect concurrent radiotherapy plus mitomycin and fluoropyrimidine (5-FU or capecitabine), normally organ-preserving; not routine upfront APR. ‘The lesion remains visible soon after radiotherapy — operate?’ Expect specialist MDT and appropriately timed response reassessment; avoid premature declaration of failure. Biopsy/restaging if suspected persistent/recurrent disease.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and sensitivity Uses judgemental language about sexual practices or fails to invite patient concerns. Introduces purpose, asks permission for intimate questions and reassures about confidentiality. Normalises sensitive symptoms, offers chaperone and explores impact on relationships. Symptom chronology Attributes bleeding solely to piles without examining persistent lesion. Elicits duration, bleeding, pain, lump, discharge, bowel habit and progression. Asks about continence change, tenesmus, systemic symptoms and earlier failed treatment. Risk and background Assumes HIV infection or ignores medication/immune history. Asks about HPV, smoking, immunosuppression, previous dysplasia and medical comorbidity. Offers neutral sexual-health and HIV-test discussion linked to care, without stigma. Examination plan Performs or proposes unconsented intimate examination, misses inguinal nodes. States inspection, DRE, proctoscopy and bilateral groin-node examination with consent/chaperone. Recognises pain may require specialist EUA and avoids traumatic examination. Differential and referral Reassures as haemorrhoids despite firm persistent ulcer. Identifie
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Dismisses a persistent ulcerated anal mass as haemorrhoids and does not request biopsy or urgent assessment. Recommends immediate routine abdominoperineal excision as first-line treatment for this localised anal canal SCC. Fails to assess inguinal nodes or consider pelvic/systemic staging before discussing definitive treatment. States that lack of complete regression immediately after chemoradiotherapy mandates urgent salvage surgery without MDT-led timed response assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Patient asks: ‘If it is cancer, will you take out my back passage and give me a bag?’ Expected: acknowledge fear; most localised anal SCC is treated with chemoradiotherapy intending to preserve sphincter; surgery may be considered for carefully selected early anal-margin disease or confirmed persistent/recurrent disease; explain treatment can still affect bowel and sexual function.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: If labelled piles: ‘The lesion is persistent and irregular; I cannot safely call it haemorrhoids without an urgent specialist biopsy.’ If APR offered first: ‘For anal squamous carcinoma, the usual initial curative approach is chemoradiotherapy after specialist MDT staging, not routine excision of the anus.’ If groins missed: ‘I would also examine both groins and ensure regional lymph nodes are assessed in staging.’

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-198 Crohn’s Disease: Stricture and When to Operate Format: Applied knowledge • Suggested time: 9 minutes • Editorial status: Draft — independent specialist clinical sign-off required Original AMaC teaching/assessment station; not an official MRCS station or examiner mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in an IBD clinic. A 32-year-old with eight years of ileal Crohn’s disease reports recurrent postprandial cramping and vomiting despite escalating medical treatment. Interpret requested investigations, identify the type of stricture and explain options including dilatation, resection and strictureplasty. No examination is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Symptoms: 4 months of episodic colicky central pain, bloating, reduced oral intake and occasional bilious vomiting; passes flatus and stools between attacks. No fever, peritonism or current haemodynamic instability. Prior 35-cm ileal resection five years ago. On adalimumab, no current steroid; nonsmoker. Weight loss 5 kg. On request: afebrile, pulse 88, BP 122/74, mild abdominal distension, no guarding. Hb 111 g/L, CRP 7 mg/L, albumin 31 g/L, electrolytes stable. MR enterography: 6-cm fixed distal ileal narrowed segment with prestenotic dilatation to 4 cm, minimal mural oedema, no abscess, fistula or suspicious mass; 180 cm small bowel estimated remaining before proposed surgery. An earlier colonoscopy was incomplete at the stenosis; biopsies showed no dysplasia in reachable mucosa. Symptoms and MRE suggest predominantly fibrotic obstruction; imaging cannot establish pure fibrosis with certainty.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: You are tired of attacks and afraid surgery will make you need permanent intravenous feeding. Ask “Can you just give me stronger anti-inflammatory drugs?” and “Can you stretch the narrowing instead?” You would prefer to preserve bowel but want durable relief.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What immediate features require admission? Persistent vomiting/complete obstruction, fever, peritonitis, severe pain, dehydration, sepsis or perforation; undertake ABCDE, IV access, fluids/electrolytes, nil by mouth and NG decompression where indicated; urgent senior/IBD review. How assess the stricture? MRE or intestinal US; review inflammation, length, number, angulation, upstream dilatation, penetrating disease, malignancy concern and previous resections; endoscopy/biopsy if safe. Does medication cure this? Active inflammatory components may respond to medical therapy; established symptomatic fibrosis frequently needs mechanical treatment. Do not escalate biologics as guaranteed relief of fixed obstruction. Dilatation? Consider expert endoscopic balloon dilatation for technically accessible short non-penetrating strictures, especially <4 cm anastomotic according to BSG 2025; 6-cm fixed stricture here is less suitable and may recur or perforate. ECCO supports selected <5 cm small-bowel lesions. Surgery? Joint IBD MDT and nutritional optimisation; limited resection or selected strictureplasty to conserve bowel. Strictureplasty for suitable shorter-than-10-cm small-bowel strictures
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Problem definition Treats episodic vomiting as harmless dyspepsia. Identifies partial small-bowel obstruction from Crohn’s stenosis. Differentiates intermittent from complete obstruction and identifies red flags prompting admission. Targeted history Never asks prior resection or IBD treatment. Elicits vomiting, flatus/stool passage, previous surgery and drug history. Adds weight loss, nutrition, smoking, previous penetrating disease and patient priorities. Physiology and examination Does not assess dehydration or peritonism. Requests observations, hydration, distension and abdominal tenderness. Checks for systemic sepsis and nutritional deficit, linking to urgency and preparation. Investigations Assumes low CRP excludes significant stenosis. Requests blood counts, CRP, albumin, U&E and MRE findings. Interprets fixed narrowing plus upstream dilatation with little oedema as predominantly fibrotic, not proven purely so. Inflammatory versus fibrotic Promises biologics will reverse a fixed fibrotic obstruction. Explains drugs address active inflammation but mechanical treatments are often needed for fibrosis. Relates imaging uncertainty and treatment to
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Discharges a patient with complete obstruction, peritonitis or septic physiology without urgent resuscitation and surgical review. 2. Insists established symptomatic fixed stenosis must respond to further biological therapy and refuses mechanical assessment. 3. Proposes balloon dilatation without checking for adjacent abscess, penetrating disease or suspected malignancy. 4. Plans unnecessarily extensive repeat small-bowel excision without addressing prior resections or risk of intestinal failure.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient attends emergency care 24 hours later with continuous pain, repeated vomiting, fever 38.8°C, pulse 125 and guarding. Expected: urgent ABCDE resuscitation, nil by mouth, IV fluids, bloods/cultures where indicated, antibiotics for suspected sepsis, NG decompression as indicated, immediate surgical and critical-care escalation, urgent CT and source control; do not book elective dilatation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “This may be a partial obstruction; if vomiting becomes persistent or you stop passing wind, I need to reassess you urgently.” “A fixed scar responds differently from active inflammation; imaging and the IBD team help decide which predominates.” “Because bowel length matters after your previous operation, I would discuss limited resection against strictureplasty rather than removing a long segment by default.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-199 Small-Bowel Neuroendocrine Tumour Format: Applied knowledge • Suggested time: 9 minutes • Editorial status: Draft — independent specialist clinical sign-off required Original AMaC teaching/assessment station; not an official MRCS station or examiner mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: At the gastrointestinal surgical MDT you are asked to interpret a case of suspected ileal neuroendocrine tumour in a 61-year-old with intermittent abdominal pain, flushing and watery diarrhoea. Explain diagnostic staging and management, including when surgery is indicated and how liver metastases alter planning.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Symptoms: 7 months intermittent abdominal pain, episodic flushing and 4–5 watery stools/day. No acute obstruction. No previous small-bowel surgery. Examination: stable, mild central tenderness, no palpable mass; prominent systolic murmur on request. Contrast-enhanced multiphasic CT: 2-cm hyperenhancing terminal ileal mass, spiculated 3-cm mesenteric nodal mass with radiating strands and partial tethering of adjacent bowel, and two indeterminate enhancing liver lesions. No free air, ascites or intestinal ischaemia. Biopsy of safely accessible liver lesion confirms well-differentiated NET, Ki-67 4% (grade 2 under commonly used WHO grading). Further tests on request: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA elevated; somatostatin receptor PET-CT shows avid ileal, mesenteric and both liver sites; echocardiography: moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Tumour is functional with metastatic burden and possible carcinoid heart disease.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: You are frightened “carcinoid” means a fast cancer. Ask whether removing the bowel tumour alone will cure diarrhoea and whether medicines can help. Your priority is continued work and safe surgery.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the diagnosis? Small-bowel (midgut) well-differentiated NET with mesenteric nodal disease, somatostatin receptor-positive liver metastases and carcinoid syndrome. Grade and stage are distinct; Ki-67 4% is G2 for a well-differentiated tumour. What further assessments? Histology with differentiation/Ki-67, multiphasic liver imaging as needed, receptor imaging, symptom history, 5-HIAA for syndrome, nutritional status, echo/NT-proBNP if carcinoid heart disease suspected and specialist NET MDT. Chromogranin A may be confounded and is not a stand-alone diagnostic test. Why mesenteric mass important? Nodal spread and desmoplastic fibrosis may cause bowel tethering/ischaemia; review relationship to mesenteric vessels before attempting dissection. Multifocal ileal primaries can occur; palpation of bowel is important if resecting. Management? Consider resection of local primary with regional mesenteric lymphatic disease when safe and appropriate, even in selected metastatic cases after NET MDT discussion; avoid sacrificing SMA supply for heroic dissection. Somatostatin analogues, such as octreotide LAR or lanreotide, treat functional symptoms and may control tumour growth; liver-dire
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Syndrome recognition Calls flushing and watery diarrhoea simple IBS without assessing tumour syndrome. Recognises functional midgut NET with carcinoid syndrome. Connects serotonin excess with liver metastases and possible right-sided valve disease. History and red flags Omits obstruction and cardiac symptom enquiry. Elicits pain, diarrhoea, flushing, weight loss and obstruction symptoms. Asks about wheeze, syncope, oedema and episodic hypotension with quality-of-life impact. Imaging interpretation Ignores the mesenteric mass and liver lesions. Identifies ileal primary, mesenteric nodal involvement and possible hepatic spread. Explains fibrosis/tethering and need to assess mesenteric arterial branches before resection. Pathology and grading Confuses Ki-67 grade with TNM stage. Names well-differentiated G2 NET from Ki-67 4%. Separates grade, metastatic stage and receptor status when explaining prognosis and choices. Biochemical and cardiac work-up Uses chromogranin alone as definitive proof. Requests 5-HIAA and echocardiography with suspected carcinoid heart disease. Interprets tricuspid regurgitation as clinically relevant and arranges cardiology/an
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Proceeds to major operation without acknowledging carcinoid syndrome, possible heart disease or perioperative haemodynamic crisis. 2. Proposes stripping mesenteric tumour from vital arterial branches without assessing bowel blood supply. 3. Calls confirmed liver metastatic disease completely cured by primary ileal excision alone. 4. Disregards symptomatic obstruction or mesenteric ischaemia and offers routine delayed outpatient review despite deterioration.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: At the anaesthetic preassessment the patient reports new ankle swelling and worsening breathlessness. Expected: defer non-urgent surgery, urgent review of functional status and right-sided valve disease with NET, cardiology and anaesthesia teams; establish a perioperative haemodynamic and carcinoid-crisis management plan.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The mesenteric lump can pull on the bowel and its vessels; I must check the arterial anatomy before planning resection.” “Your symptoms can improve with a somatostatin analogue even when all metastatic disease cannot be removed.” “Before anaesthesia I need a specialist plan for the heart valve finding and for possible carcinoid crisis.”

stations.title: Hidradenitis Suppurativa

sections.preamble: B2-200 | Hidradenitis Suppurativa AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Examine against the presented scenario, not inferred clinical details.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical registrar in a colorectal outpatient clinic. A 29-year-old patient has recurrent painful lumps and draining lesions in both axillae and the groin for four years. They have been referred for “incision and drainage of boils”. Explain your assessment, likely diagnosis, staging and a practical management plan. You are not required to physically examine the patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Observations normal; no fever or acute systemic illness. On asking: painful lesions recur at the same sites; malodorous drainage and scarring; significant distress and missed work; smokes 10 cigarettes daily; BMI 33; no current medication. No perianal fistula symptoms, inflammatory bowel disease or immunosuppression. If candidate asks for a description of examination: bilateral axillary inflammatory nodules, two draining interconnected tunnels and bridging scars on the right; smaller separate nodules in left axilla; groin has multiple scars. No rapidly spreading erythema, fluctuant acute collection or crepitus. Right axilla fits Hurley II; assess other sites separately. If asked: prior short antibiotic courses helped transiently; no structured dermatology management. No pregnancy; no recorded drug allergies.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Embarrassed by smell; concerned “I am dirty” and asks for repeated lancing or total removal today. Give information only if asked. If candidate is dismissive, become withdrawn. Ask whether disease is contagious and whether surgery cures it forever.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What is your working diagnosis and what distinguishes it from ordinary recurrent abscesses?” Expected: HS, chronic follicular inflammatory disease in intertriginous sites, recurrent nodules/tunnels/scars; not poor hygiene or contagious. Prompt: “How would you stage it?” Expected: Hurley I = abscesses without tunnels/scars; II = separated recurrent lesions with tunnels/scars; III = diffuse involvement with interconnected tunnels; stage each area, not just patient globally. Prompt: “What is the treatment hierarchy?” Expected: analgesia, dressings, smoking cessation/weight support without blame; dermatology-led topical/systemic treatments and escalation (including biologics where eligible); local deroofing for persistent tunnels or planned excision for extensive scarred disease; distinguish acute abscess drainage from definitive HS surgery.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction and rapport Calls disease “dirty boils”, without addressing embarrassment. Introduces role, acknowledges pain, asks what worries the patient. Explicitly removes blame, normalises sensitive symptoms and negotiates agenda. Focused history Does not ask recurrence or involved locations. Asks frequency, sites, pain, drainage, previous treatments. Also elicits functional/sexual impact, work, smoking, weight, comorbidities and flare pattern. Safety assessment Dismisses fever or spreading infection. Checks fever, spreading erythema and immunosuppression. Explains features suggesting secondary infection, urgent assessment and rarely necrotising infection. Diagnosis Labels condition isolated bacterial furunculosis. Identifies hidradenitis suppurativa from recurrent typical lesions/sites. Differentiates HS from an acute abscess, Crohn-related perianal disease and infected epidermoid cyst. Staging Calls any draining tunnel Hurley III. Correctly assigns right axilla Hurley II using tunnels and separated disease. Explains three Hurley stages and separate area-by-area grading; inflammatory activity also matters. Initial treatment Offers serial lancin
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to assess systemic toxicity or spreading severe secondary infection in a patient presenting with possible acute abscess. 2. Claims repeated simple incision and drainage provides durable definitive treatment for chronic HS tunnels. 3. Proposes extensive excision without discussing wound morbidity, recurrence and shared specialist planning. 4. Offers no meaningful plan for persistent draining tunnels and major functional impact, discharging the patient without follow-up.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Actor: “Can you just lance every lump today? Last time they came back.” Expected: explain that drainage may relieve a genuinely tense acute abscess but does not treat underlying HS tunnels; propose dermatology-directed inflammatory control and targeted surgical assessment of persistent tunnels, while assessing acute infection.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should correct my earlier wording: this is a chronic inflammatory condition, not a hygiene problem or simply repeated infection.” 2. “Although drainage can ease a tense collection, recurrent tunnels need staged HS treatment, possibly deroofing or planned excision.” 3. “Before we agree to surgery I need to document extent at each site, discuss healing and recurrence, and arrange combined dermatology–surgical review.”

stations.title: Short Bowel Syndrome After Massive Resection

sections.preamble: B2-201 | Short Bowel Syndrome After Massive Resection AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / critical care • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Examine against the presented scenario, not inferred clinical details.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar covering a patient on postoperative day 7 after emergency resection of infarcted small bowel for mesenteric ischaemia. A 54-year-old has 85 cm jejunum remaining ending in a jejunostomy, with no colon in continuity. Stoma output is 2.8 L in 24 hours, urine output 450 mL, and the patient feels dizzy. Explain your assessment and immediate and longer-term management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: BP 92/60, pulse 112, afebrile, dry mucosa; stoma pink, abdomen soft without focal peritonism. Bloods: Na 130, K 3.3, Mg 0.48 mmol/L, creatinine 185 µmol/L (baseline 80), CRP 24. No vomiting or abdominal sepsis signs. Operation note confirms 85 cm proximal jejunum ending as a jejunostomy; colon is defunctioned and not currently in continuity; reconstruction potential needs specialist review. Receiving plain water, fruit juice and unrestricted tea; no scheduled antimotility agent. If asked: weight loss 5 kg in one week; no central venous access or established parenteral plan. Refeeding and PN decisions require nutrition assessment and local protocols.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief where appropriate: No separate actor is necessary. If the examiner plays the patient, they ask “Why does drinking more water make my bag fill faster?” and “Will I be on a drip forever?” Candidate should explain carefully and avoid promises.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “Define and classify the anatomy.” Expected: short bowel syndrome with an end jejunostomy (ESPEN type 1); clinical SBS commonly with residual small bowel <200 cm; colon continuity influences absorptive prognosis. Prompt: “What must happen in the next hour?” Expected: ABCDE, sepsis/obstruction screen, senior review, IV isotonic fluid resuscitation with response monitoring, catheter/strict balance, ECG and repeated U&Es/Mg/renal function, correct sodium/water and magnesium/potassium deficits. Prompt: “Why not advise unlimited plain water?” Expected: high-output jejunostomy loses sodium; hypotonic drinks can aggravate sodium depletion and output. Specialist-prescribed glucose–saline oral rehydration and restricted hypotonic drinks once resuscitated; no blanket ban on oral intake. Prompt: “What happens beyond this admission?” Expected: intestinal failure/nutrition team, dietitian and stoma specialist; tailored diet, loperamide (and possibly acid suppression), parenteral fluids/nutrition when needed, micronutrients, renal/line monitoring, reassess anatomy and adaptation.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Labels 2.8 L/day as routine ileostomy output. Identifies high-output jejunostomy with dehydration and AKI. Relates output to short jejunal remnant and absent colon continuity. Resuscitation Suggests oral water only despite hypotension. ABCDE, IV isotonic resuscitation and urgent senior review. Plans serial haemodynamic, urine and biochemical endpoints and rules out sepsis. Fluid balance Records bag output but not urine. Strict stoma/urine intake–output, daily weight and urinary catheter as indicated. Sets a monitored fluid/sodium replacement plan and reviews output drivers daily. Electrolytes and kidney Misses magnesium and renal impairment. Requests repeated Na, K, Mg, creatinine and replaces deficits safely. Notes magnesium and sodium depletion can perpetuate hypokalaemia; checks ECG and response. Anatomical interpretation States bowel length alone predicts exact PN duration. Names type 1 SBS and importance of colon continuity. Explains how remnant length, colon, ileocaecal valve and adaptation influence prognosis. Oral fluid strategy Recommends unlimited water or fruit juice. Avoids excess hypotonic/hypertonic drinks and introduces h
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Does not recognise hypotension, oliguria and acute kidney injury as requiring immediate IV resuscitation and escalation. 2. Recommends unrestricted plain water or juice to replace high-output jejunostomy losses without sodium-replacement planning. 3. Fails to investigate or correct marked hypomagnesaemia and associated electrolyte/renal abnormalities. 4. Plans discharge or purely oral management for persistently unstable patient without intestinal failure or nutrition specialist input.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Examiner: “The patient insists more water is healthy, but output rises every time they drink.” Expected: non-judgementally explain sodium-rich jejunostomy loss and movement of fluid into the gut; first resuscitate IV, then use prescribed high-sodium glucose–saline oral rehydration and limit excess low-sodium beverages under specialist supervision.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I need to treat this as hypovolaemia with AKI now: IV isotonic fluid, close urine monitoring and urgent senior review.” 2. “I retract my advice to drink unlimited water; with a jejunostomy it can increase net sodium and water losses.” 3. “I should involve the intestinal failure and nutrition team immediately to establish fluid, electrolyte and parenteral requirements.”

stations.title: Achalasia: Manometry Results and Treatment

sections.preamble: B2-202 | Achalasia: Manometry Results and Treatment AMaC MRCS Part B • Data interpretation • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Clinical judgments must use the scenario information provided.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the upper-GI surgical trainee in an oesophageal MDT. A 46-year-old with progressive dysphagia to solids AND liquids, regurgitation and 7 kg weight loss has a high-resolution manometry report. Interpret it, define the likely diagnosis, explain additional investigations and advise on treatment options for the MDT.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: Observations stable; no previous foregut surgery. Dysphagia for 18 months; occasional nocturnal cough. Endoscopy shows a mildly dilated oesophagus with retained fluid and resistance at the gastro-oesophageal junction, without visible mucosal lesion. Biopsies if clinically indicated; cancer has not been demonstrated. High-resolution manometry: elevated integrated relaxation pressure (IRP) relative to the system’s validated normal range; 100% absent normal peristalsis; panesophageal pressurisation in 7/10 test swallows; no premature spastic contractions. The report labels conclusive type II achalasia after protocol-appropriate testing. Timed barium swallow: retained barium column with smoothly tapered distal oesophagus (bird-beak pattern), no focal shouldered lesion. Nutrition screening identifies risk of undernutrition. If asked about red flags: weight loss developed with worsening dysphagia but rapid onset, older age and marked disproportionate weight loss should prompt renewed evaluation for malignancy/pseudoachalasia.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief where appropriate: Not a role-play station. If examiner speaks as patient: “Can this be cured with tablets?” and “Which procedure causes the least reflux?” Candidate should answer without promising a permanent cure.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. Interpret this manometry in one sentence. Expected: Impaired EGJ relaxation plus absent normal peristalsis and ≥20% panesophageal pressurisation are consistent with type II achalasia on a conclusive, technically adequate study. 2. Describe the three achalasia patterns. Expected: Type I: absent contractility with no meaningful panesophageal pressurisation; type II: ≥20% panesophageal pressurisation; type III: no normal peristalsis with qualifying premature/spastic contractions. Integrate IRP, protocol, symptoms and supportive testing. 3. What must be excluded? Expected: Mechanical obstruction and pseudoachalasia: review upper GI endoscopy and biopsies as needed; re-evaluate suspicious features and consider cross-sectional imaging/EUS where clinically indicated. Assess nutrition and aspiration. 4. What treatment would you offer in this case? Expected: Discuss pneumatic balloon dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication, or POEM in an expert service. Type II generally responds well to definitive LES-disrupting therapies; select with shared decision-making and local expertise. 5. What changes if the manometry instead shows type III? Expected: Prefer consider
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and data framing Labels any dysphagia with raised IRP as reflux disease; does not read the motor pattern. Summarises elevated IRP, absent peristalsis and panesophageal pressurisation as a coherent motility disorder. States type II achalasia immediately and checks test validity and clinical–manometric concordance. Classification Confuses type II pressurisation with type III spasm. Distinguishes I, II and III by absent contractility, pressurisation and premature contractions. Explains subtype significance for treatment and limitations of IRP interpreted in isolation. Malignancy exclusion Proceeds to myotomy without checking an obstructing tumour. Reviews endoscopy and considers pseudoachalasia where red flags are present. Specifies repeat expert endoscopic evaluation/targeted EUS or CT for disproportionate suspicious features. Adjunct investigations Orders CT as the sole diagnostic test and omits endoscopy. Uses endoscopy and timed barium swallow alongside high-resolution manometry. Describes how timed barium emptying assists post-treatment evaluation and recurrent symptoms. Treatment selection Offers long-term antacids or botulinum injection
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Proceeds to an irreversible LES-disrupting procedure without having addressed possible malignant mechanical obstruction/pseudoachalasia. 2. Misreads panesophageal pressurisation as type III spasm and recommends a treatment plan on that false subtype without correction. 3. Recommends botulinum toxin as definitive first-line management for an otherwise fit patient without discussing effective alternatives. 4. Consents to pneumatic dilation or POEM while omitting major procedure-specific risks (perforation for dilation; reflux for POEM) after explicit examiner prompt.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The examiner substitutes a new report: absent normal peristalsis, elevated IRP and 30% premature spastic distal contractions (type III). Expected: revise the subtype; state a longer tailored myotomy in an expert centre, usually POEM or tailored Heller, and discuss reflux after POEM.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: • “I called this type I initially; the panesophageal pressurisation makes the presented study type II, so I will correct my interpretation.” • “Before definitive treatment I must check endoscopy has excluded a structural cancer; if the clinical picture is suspicious I would request targeted further assessment.” • “I should add that POEM can give effective dysphagia relief but is associated with more reflux; I would discuss that alongside Heller with fundoplication and dilation.”

stations.title: Gallstone Ileus
