sections.preamble: B2-203 | Gallstone Ileus AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / emergency surgery • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Clinical judgments must use the scenario information provided.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A frail 82-year-old woman with recurrent biliary symptoms presents with 3 days of colicky pain, bilious vomiting, distension and obstipation. Interpret the written CT report, describe immediate management and choose an operative strategy, explaining why you may or may not repair the biliary fistula at the same operation.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: BP 102/64, HR 108, RR 22, T 37.5 °C, SpO2 96% room air. Dry mucosa; distended abdomen with tinkling bowel sounds; diffuse tenderness but no guarding. Frailty score high; atrial fibrillation on apixaban. Lactate 2.1 mmol/L; creatinine 143 µmol/L (baseline 92), K 3.1 mmol/L; WCC 13.8. Urine output not yet recorded. Contrast-enhanced CT: dilated small-bowel loops with transition at a 3.5 cm ectopic calcified gallstone in distal ileum; air within biliary tree (pneumobilia); probable cholecystoduodenal fistula. Small volume free fluid; no free gas, no pneumatosis or definite reduced bowel enhancement. Gallbladder contains further stones. If requested: no haemodynamic collapse, no reported generalised peritonitis. Patient has capacity; anticoagulant last taken this morning. Anaesthetics advise raised operative risk. Surgical senior is available.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief where appropriate: If asked, examiner plays patient: “Do I need my gallbladder removed today?” and “Will you take out my bowel?” Respond with uncertainty and explain risk-based selection.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. What does the CT show? Expected: Gallstone ileus causing mechanical small-bowel obstruction: Rigler triad of bowel obstruction, ectopic gallstone and pneumobilia, from a biliary-enteric fistula, usually cholecystoduodenal. 2. What are immediate priorities? stations.title: Pyogenic Liver Abscess

sections.preamble: B2-204 | Pyogenic Liver Abscess AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / emergency HPB • 8-minute station • Educational assessment draft
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 64-year-old man admitted with 5 days of fever, right upper-quadrant pain and rigors. CT has identified a 6.5-cm right-lobe liver collection. Explain your interpretation, immediate management, source-control plan and subsequent investigation to the examiner. You have access to a written observation chart and CT report on request. You are not required to prescribe exact antimicrobial doses.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Observations: T 39.1°C, HR 118/min, BP 98/62 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 96% on air; drowsy but responsive; urine output decreased. RUQ tenderness without generalised peritonitis. Bloods: WCC 18.2 ×10⁹/L, CRP 245 mg/L, bilirubin 32 µmol/L, ALP 330 U/L, creatinine 161 µmol/L (baseline 88), lactate 3.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures not yet taken. CT: 6.5-cm multiloculated segment VII/VIII rim-enhancing fluid collection, adjacent inflammatory change; intrahepatic duct dilation and common bile duct stone; no free air. No portal venous thrombosis. History on request: type 2 diabetes; gallstones; no overseas travel; no recent intra-abdominal surgery. Allergies: no known drug allergies. Not taking anticoagulation.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Not required: examiner-led applied-knowledge station. If examiner acts as patient, the patient asks whether 'tablets alone' can treat the abscess; candidate should explain the need for antibiotics plus likely image-guided drainage in this case.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt A: 'What is the diagnosis and why is the patient high risk?' — Pyogenic liver abscess with sepsis, AKI and possible biliary obstruction; assess and resuscitate urgently. Prompt C: 'How do you obtain source control?' — Same-day HPB, radiology and microbiology discussion; US/CT-guided aspiration/catheter drainage, send pus for Gram stain/cultures; evaluate bile duct obstruction and arrange biliary drainage/ERCP if cholangitis/obstructed system, timed according to clinical condition. Prompt D: 'When is surgery needed?' — Rupture/peritonitis, inaccessible or failed percutaneous drainage, or concurrent surgical pathology; do not make laparotomy routine for uncomplicated drainable collection. Prompt E: 'What are the causes and follow-up?' — Biliary infection, portal seeding, haematogenous spread, post-operative infection; culture-directed a
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls this hepatitis or uncomplicated cholecystitis and ignores hepatic collection. Identifies pyogenic liver abscess on CT and fever/RUQ pain. Identifies multiloculation, size, biliary obstruction and potential rupture as factors affecting strategy. Severity Labels tachycardia, hypotension and AKI as stable. Recognises sepsis and acute organ dysfunction. Links lactate, renal injury and poor perfusion to urgent reassessment and escalation. Resuscitation Proposes oral analgesia and routine ward observations only. Starts ABCDE, IV access, fluids and close observations. Reassesses fluid responsiveness, perfusion and urine output; requests critical-care review if persistent shock. Microbiology Starts delayed narrow oral antibiotics without cultures. Obtains blood cultures promptly and initiates IV broad-spectrum coverage according to policy. Requests aspirate culture; adapts antimicrobials with microbiology and renal function. Imaging Requests plain radiograph as definitive abscess characterisation. Uses contrast CT/ultrasound to assess size and location. Actively reviews ductal obstruction, collections and percutaneous access with radiolog
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Fails to identify sepsis with organ dysfunction and withholds urgent resuscitation/escalation. 2. Delays IV antimicrobials until after planned drainage despite systemic sepsis. 3. States that a 6.5-cm drainable abscess needs only oral antibiotics, with no drainage assessment. 4. Ignores an obstructed infected biliary system and does not seek urgent biliary decompression advice.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After 2 hours of fluids and antibiotics, BP falls to 82/48, lactate rises to 4.4 and urine output remains minimal. Expected: repeat ABCDE, call critical care and HPB immediately, pursue resuscitation and vasopressor-capable care as appropriate, and expedite source control of both abscess and obstructed biliary tree; do not await routine morning review.

stations.title: Chronic Pancreatitis: Pain, Malabsorption and Operative Decisions

near_match.title: Acute Pancreatitis

sections.preamble: B2-205 | Chronic Pancreatitis: Pain, Malabsorption and Operative Decisions AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / elective HPB • 8-minute station • Educational assessment draft
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 46-year-old woman has recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back, progressive weight loss and greasy stools. CT demonstrates pancreatic calcification, a dilated main pancreatic duct and an intraductal stone. Explain the diagnosis, important causes, investigations and the management options, including when you would refer for surgery. The examiner will supply additional test results and clinical details on request.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: History: pain for 3 years; 9-kg unintentional weight loss in 12 months; six greasy stools daily; drinks 30 UK units/week, smokes 10 cigarettes/day. No documented gallstones. No family history of pancreatic disease. Examination: thin, stable, mild epigastric tenderness without jaundice. BMI 19.0 kg/m²; afebrile. Bloods: glucose 11.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 69 mmol/mol; albumin 31 g/L; normal bilirubin; lipase not elevated. Faecal elastase 75 µg/g on formed stool (supports severe exocrine insufficiency, interpret in clinical context). Imaging: CT coarse pancreatic head/body calcification, main duct 8 mm with dominant 9-mm intraductal stone; no discrete mass. MRCP confirms duct obstruction and no biliary dilatation. A suspicious new mass on subsequent imaging must trigger cancer-pathway assessment.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Not required: examiner-led applied-knowledge station. If played by an actor, patient asks whether pancreatic enzyme tablets will remove the pain and whether the condition can become cancer; answer with appropriate uncertainty and a specialist follow-up plan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt A: 'What are the diagnosis and main causes?' — Calcific chronic pancreatitis with obstructed main pancreatic duct, exocrine insufficiency and pancreatogenic diabetes; alcohol, smoking, recurrent injury, genetic, autoimmune and obstructive causes. Prompt B: 'How do you investigate?' — CT for calcification/complications, MRCP for duct anatomy, EUS if diagnosis uncertain or suspicious focal change; faecal elastase when indicated, nutritional deficiencies, bone health and HbA1c/glucose; actively assess for malignancy rather than assuming all new changes are benign. Prompt C: 'Describe nonoperative care.' — Alcohol and tobacco cessation, dietitian, pancreatic enzyme replacement with food for malabsorption, nutritional supplementation, diabetes team, stepwise pain assessment and analgesia; enzymes are for exocrine failure, not reliable analgesia. Prompt D: 'When should surgery be considered?' — Early specialist HPB MDT for painful main-duct obstruction; discuss duct-drainage procedures where anatomically appropriate (e.g. lateral pancreaticojejunostomy for an adequately dilated duct), head-preserving procedures for inflammatory head disease, and resection for selected focal diseas
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Diagnosis Calls raised glucose and steatorrhoea simple dyspepsia. Recognises calcific chronic pancreatitis with pancreatic duct obstruction. Unites ductal obstruction, exocrine failure and endocrine failure into one disease explanation. Aetiology Assumes alcohol is the only possible cause and takes no relevant history. Asks about alcohol, tobacco and past acute pancreatitis. Adds hereditary, autoimmune and obstructive causes when clinically indicated. Imaging Uses serum lipase as definitive chronic-disease test. Interprets CT calcification and MRCP duct dilatation/stone. Suggests EUS or cancer-pathway imaging for uncertain disease or a new focal lesion. Exocrine care Prescribes enzymes solely as painkillers while ignoring greasy stools. Recognises steatorrhoea and commences enzyme replacement with meals and dietetic support. Reassesses weight, symptom response, nutritional markers and dose adequacy with specialist support. Endocrine care Does not mention hyperglycaemia despite high HbA1c. Identifies pancreatogenic diabetes and seeks diabetes assessment. Notes nutritional instability and hypoglycaemia vulnerability in treatment planning. Pain Offers
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Misinterprets a new pancreatic mass or progressive painless jaundice as automatically benign and omits malignancy assessment. 2. Fails to recognise severe malabsorption with weight loss, offering no pancreatic enzyme or nutritional plan. 3. Recommends an irreversible major pancreatic resection without appropriate specialist assessment of duct and head anatomy. 4. Declares that an obstructed, painful dilated main duct has no procedural treatment and omits HPB referral.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient develops progressively painless jaundice and CT now shows a new 2.5-cm pancreatic head mass. Expected: do not attribute this to benign chronic inflammation; urgently refer to specialist pancreatic cancer pathway/MDT for pancreas-protocol imaging and EUS sampling where indicated; evaluate biliary drainage need.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The low faecal elastase and steatorrhoea mean she needs enzyme replacement with food and nutritional assessment.” 2. “An 8-mm obstructed main duct creates a treatable pain mechanism; I will involve the HPB MDT early.” 3. “New jaundice or a focal mass changes the question: I must investigate malignancy urgently.”

stations.title: Walled-off Necrosis After Pancreatitis

near_match.title: Acute Pancreatitis

sections.preamble: B2-206 | Walled-off Necrosis After Pancreatitis AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Data interpretation / applied knowledge • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT — specialist clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 56-year-old patient five weeks after severe acute pancreatitis. They have fever, persistent pain and poor oral intake. A written CT report is available from the examiner. Explain the diagnosis, investigations and management plan to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including findings di: Clinical setting: HR 112/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, T 38.5 °C, RR 22/min, oxygen saturation 96% on air. Localised epigastric tenderness, no generalised peritonitis. Urine output has fallen. On request: WBC 17 × 10⁹/L, CRP 218 mg/L; lactate 2.3 mmol/L, creatinine 145 µmol/L (previous 85), bilirubin normal. Two blood cultures pending. CT at week 5: 11 cm encapsulated heterogeneous peripancreatic collection containing fluid and non-liquid debris, with small gas locules; collection abuts posterior gastric wall. No free air, bowel infarction or active arterial bleeding. History on request: no prophylactic antibiotic course; patient has not tolerated normal meals; no biliary obstruction. ICU bed and advanced endoscopy/IR available through regional pancreatic centre.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Not required: examiner-led applied knowledge/data interpretation station. If examiner plays patient, they are frightened of needing a large operation and ask whether antibiotics alone will suffice.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “Name the collection and distinguish the earlier collection.” Expected: walled-off necrosis (WON), a mature encapsulated collection of pancreatic/peripancreatic necrotic material, typically after about four weeks; acute necrotic collection is earlier and not fully encapsulated. Distinguish pseudocyst (largely fluid, minimal solid necrosis). Prompt: “Is it infected?” Expected: fever, inflammatory response, deterioration and gas raise strong suspicion of infected necrosis; do not rely on routine FNA or gas being present in every infection. Prompt: “What now?” Expected: ABCDE, senior/critical-care assessment, sepsis management, cultures, IV fluids titrated to physiology, antibiotics for suspected infected necrosis, organ support, enteral nutrition and HPB/advanced endoscopy/IR MDT. Prompt: “What procedure?” Expected: given mature, accessible WON and infection, endoscopic transmural drainage is reasonable with specialist expertise; percutaneous drainage if endoscopic access unsuitable or lateral extension. Escalate to endoscopic necrosectomy or minimally invasive debridement only if drainage fails; avoid reflex open necrosectomy.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Definition Calls debris-filled collection a pseudocyst Identifies encapsulated WON at five weeks Explains early acute necrotic collection versus later WON and fluid-only pseudocyst Severity Ignores oliguria and tachycardia Recognises systemic infection with AKI risk Links evolving organ dysfunction to need for monitored/critical care Imaging Misses gas and location Describes gas, mixed debris and gastric adjacency Uses access route and absence of haemorrhage/perforation to guide intervention Infection Gives prophylactic antibiotics for all sterile collections or none for this patient Starts IV treatment for strongly suspected infected necrosis Obtains cultures and narrows treatment to microbiology and source control Resuscitation Leaves hypotensive patient untreated ABCDE, IV access, bloods, fluid/urine monitoring Repeated perfusion assessment and ICU escalation with shock Nutrition Keeps patient without nutrition indefinitely Supports oral/enteral feeding if tolerated Uses tube enteral feeding if oral intake inadequate; PN only if enteral infeasible Procedure choice Suggests mandatory immediate open necrosectomy Selects endoscopic or percutaneous
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Calls this a simple sterile pseudocyst and discharges a septic, oliguric patient without resuscitation or escalation. 2. Prescribes no antimicrobial treatment despite convincing infected necrosis and evolving organ dysfunction. 3. Advocates immediate open pancreatic necrosectomy as routine first-line therapy without considering drainage/step-up management. 4. Delays urgent resuscitation of haemodynamic deterioration solely to reach an arbitrary four-week threshold.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: After admission the BP falls to 82/50 mmHg and lactate rises to 4.1 mmol/L. Response: urgent ABCDE, sepsis treatment, cultures without delaying antibiotics, balanced resuscitation and early vasopressor/ICU support as indicated, urgent HPB/IR/endoscopy discussion for source control; do not delay life-saving intervention because of collection age.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The collection contains solid debris and has a wall at week five: I would call it walled-off necrosis, not a pseudocyst.” “Gas plus fever and worsening organ function makes infected necrosis likely; I will resuscitate, treat infection and seek source control.” “I would begin with drainage via a suitable endoscopic or percutaneous route, then escalate only if necessary.”

stations.title: Caustic Ingestion

sections.preamble: B2-207 | Caustic Ingestion AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Critical care / applied knowledge • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT — specialist clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical registrar. A 34-year-old adult swallowed an unknown quantity of industrial drain cleaner approximately two hours ago. They have drooling, throat pain, vomiting and a hoarse voice. Describe your immediate management, investigations and definitive treatment priorities.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including findings di: On request: HR 118/min, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 95% on air, T 37.4 °C. Patient is distressed and cannot swallow saliva; voice is worsening. Mild suprasternal stridor develops. History: deliberate ingestion after a relationship crisis; bottle suggests concentrated alkali, exact concentration unknown. One small haematemesis episode, no abdominal rigidity initially. No co-ingested tablets confirmed. Bloods on request: WBC 18 × 10⁹/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L; venous blood gas mild metabolic acidosis. CT result once airway secure: contrast-enhanced CT neck/chest/abdomen shows segmental absent mural enhancement of mid-oesophagus with adjacent mediastinal inflammatory change; no established free perforation on current scan.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Adult patient speaks with increasing difficulty and is frightened. Prompt: “What should not be done?” Expected: do not induce vomiting, neutralise with acid/alkali, give activated charcoal routinely, insert blind NG tube, or force oral fluids. Assess for other ingestions and engage toxicology/poisons advice. Prompt: “Which investigation establishes severity?” Expected: in a severely symptomatic adult, after stabilisation contrast-enhanced CT assesses full-thickness necrosis/perforation; WSES adopts CT-led adult assessment. Endoscopy may be selective when CT unavailable/contraindicated/inconclusive or per specialist pathway, not done before airway stabilisation. Prompt: “Interpret absent mural enhancement.” Expected: suggests transmural necrosis requiring immediate senior oesophagogastric/HPB-capable surgical review and likely emergency operative exploration/resection; no reliance on apparent absence of free gas to exclude serious injury. Prompt: “What happens la
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Airway recognition Dismisses drooling and hoarseness Recognises upper airway risk and summons anaesthetics Escalates evolving stridor to controlled difficult airway with ENT backup Primary survey Proceeds straight to endoscopy Performs ABCDE with vital monitoring Repeatedly assesses perfusion, breathing and developing shock Exposure history Does not ask what/when was swallowed Elicits product, timing and associated symptoms Checks deliberate intent, quantity uncertainty and co-ingestants without delaying resuscitation Harm prevention Induces vomiting or neutralises chemical Avoids emesis, neutralisation and oral challenges Also explicitly avoids blind NG placement and unprotected transfer Investigations Uses plain radiograph alone to exclude necrosis Requests appropriate blood tests and contrast CT after airway security Uses CT mural enhancement to assess transmural damage and imaging limitations Endoscopy Insists on urgent EGD before airway protection States selective expert endoscopic role Explains CT-led adult severe-injury pathway and when endoscopy clarifies equivocal findings Operative decision Reassures despite absent enhancement Flags suspe
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Sends patient for unsupervised CT or endoscopy despite progressive stridor and inability to handle secretions, without protecting airway. 2. Induces vomiting or attempts chemical neutralisation, risking repeat chemical exposure and further injury. 3. Performs blind nasogastric intubation in an acutely injured oesophagus without specialist assessment. 4. Ignores absent CT mural enhancement and discharges or observes without urgent senior surgical evaluation for transmural necrosis.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: While preparing for CT, the patient develops inspiratory stridor and SpO₂ drops to 89%. Response: stop transfer, call anaesthetic emergency help, administer oxygen as appropriate, prepare difficult-airway equipment, undertake controlled airway protection with senior anaesthetic/ENT backup; continue resuscitation once secured.

stations.title: Acute Gastric Volvulus and Paraoesophageal Hernia

sections.preamble: B2-208 | Acute Gastric Volvulus and Paraoesophageal Hernia AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Critical care / applied knowledge • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in the emergency department. A 76-year-old woman with a known large hiatus hernia has sudden severe epigastric and lower chest pain, repeated retching without productive vomiting and abdominal distension. Explain your immediate assessment, interpretation of investigations and definitive management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief (findings on request): On request: HR 124/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 94% on air, temperature 37.8°C; distressed, dehydrated, epigastric tenderness without generalised peritonism. Previous imaging documented a large paraoesophageal hernia. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Initial bloods: Hb 124 g/L, WBC 16.2 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 148 µmol/L (baseline 82), lactate 3.7 mmol/L; crossmatch requested. After resuscitation, contrast CT chest/abdomen: markedly distended, rotated stomach partly intrathoracic; pylorus displaced superiorly relative to gastro-oesophageal junction, transition points at both ends, gastric wall oedema and small perigastric fluid; no definite free intraperitoneal air. Findings support organoaxial gastric volvulus with closed-loop obstruction; viability is uncertain. If asked about NG tube: experienced clinician makes a cautious attempt if appropriate, without repeated force; inability to pass does not delay senior surgical/anaesthetic review. Endoscopic decompression may be considered by experienced team
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient is pale, nauseated and anxious; says “I keep trying to be sick but nothing comes out.” If asked about treatment, she wants to know whether the stomach can die and whether surgery is urgent. sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: PROMPT: What diagnosis and mechanism? PROMPT: What does Borchardt’s triad contain? EXPECTED: Severe epigastric pain/distension, unproductive retching, and inability to pass an NG tube; it is a classic teaching triad, not a mandatory diagnostic rule. PROMPT: What will you do in the first minutes? EXPECTED: ABCDE, NBM, two IV lines, isotonic crystalloid titrated to response, analgesia/antiemetic, blood gas/lactate, FBC/U&E/coagulation, group-and-save/crossmatch, urine output, urgent consultant UGI surgeon and anaesthetist. PROMPT: Which imaging and interpretation? EXPECTED: Contrast-enhanced CT chest/abdomen after immediate stabilisation; demonstrate abnormal rotation, intrathoracic stomach, obstruction and possible ischaemia/perforation. PROMPT: What if NG decompression fails? EXPECTED: Do not repeatedly force the tube or delay definitive treatment; early senior endoscopic versus operative decompression decision. PROMPT: When does this need an operation? EXPECTED: Urgent operation for acute obstructing volvulus with

Diagnoses acute gastric volvulus with paraoesophageal hernia and closed-loop obstruction. Explains strangulation risk and interprets the displaced pylorus and intrathoracic stomach. Coordinates simultaneous resuscitation, theatre-readiness and anaesthetic involvement. Resuscitation Leaves patient eating and drinking or omits intravenous access. sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: 1. Sends the hypotensive patient home or delays senior surgical assessment despite suspected closed-loop obstruction. 2. Fails to recognise or act on suspected gastric ischaemia/perforation (shock, peritonitis or deteriorating lactate). 3. Repeatedly forces an NG tube despite resistance or delays essential treatment solely to achieve tube placement. 4. sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: After 30 minutes the patient becomes more tender and hypotensive (BP 78/45 mmHg), lactate 6.2 mmol/L and develops guarding. Expected: activate emergency theatre pathway immediately with consultant UGI surgeon, anaesthesia/critical care; continue ABC resuscitation, NBM, blood products as indicated, antibiotics for suspected ischaemic/perforated stomach, urgent source control rather than waiting for further imaging.
sections.8. stations.title: Consent for Diagnostic Upper GI Endoscopy

sections.preamble: B2-209 | Consent for Diagnostic Upper GI Endoscopy AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Communication • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in an elective endoscopy clinic. A 59-year-old man with persistent dyspepsia despite initial treatment has been referred for diagnostic oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD), potentially with biopsies. Explain the procedure, benefits, alternatives, material risks, sedation choices and obtain an informed decision. Do not perform the procedure.
sections.2. Examiner brief (findings on request): Patient is alert, has capacity and prefers plain language. He is concerned about choking and “being put to sleep”. He has no dysphagia, active bleeding or acute abdominal symptoms. Medical information available on request: obstructive sleep apnoea treated with CPAP; BMI 36 kg/m²; on apixaban for a previous DVT (precise indication and last dose must be clarified); no known drug allergy; no prior endoscopy. The planned procedure is diagnostic OGD with possible routine mucosal biopsies; no planned dilatation, EMR or other high-risk therapy. The team must confirm antithrombotic instructions according to procedure and individual thrombosis risk rather than advising arbitrary interruption. If asked about results: initial macroscopic findings may be explained that day; biopsy histology follows later, and follow-up arrangements need to be explicit. No promise of a completely normal result or of detecting every lesion. This is an assessment of patient-centred consent, not recall of unverified single numerical rates. Accept a locally verified risk leaflet if personalised and correctly explained.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Initially asks, “Will I be unconscious? Could I choke on the camera?” If offered options asks about throat spray versus sedation. If asked what matters, says he must drive his wife home later and worries about missing cancer. When told of sleep apnoea, asks whether sedation is dangerous. May decide to defer to arrange transport.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: PROMPT: What is an OGD and why is it proposed? EXPECTED: Flexible camera through mouth, inspecting oesophagus, stomach and duodenum for inflammation, ulceration or suspicious lesions; biopsies may be taken, with histology later. PROMPT: What should you discuss before consent? EXPECTED: Indication, expected benefits and limitations, alternatives including management without immediate endoscopy where appropriate, and individual preferences. PROMPT: Which risks are material? EXPECTED: Discomfort/retching, sore throat, aspiration, sedation-related respiratory/cardiovascular events, bleeding (especially after biopsy/intervention), perforation, infection rarely and missed lesions/incomplete examination. PROMPT: What options for comfort? EXPECTED: Topical throat spray, unsedated OGD and IV conscious sedation according to service; sedation is not necessarily general anaesthesia. Explain the monitoring and recovery requirements. PROMPT: What changes with sleep apnoea and BMI 36? EXPECTED: Enhanced pre-assessment and monitoring; consider sedation adjustments/anaesthetic input under local policy; discuss airway risk and CPAP details. PROMPT: What about apixaban? EXPECTED: Clarify indication,
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction / indication Calls the procedure “just a camera” without explaining why it is offered. Explains a diagnostic examination for persistent dyspepsia and possible biopsy. Asks the patient’s main concern and links investigation to decision-making. Procedure explanation Says camera goes into the windpipe or omits the examined organs. Describes mouth-to-oesophagus, stomach, duodenum and biopsy process. Explains positioning, bite guard, expected sensations and that breathing is maintained. Benefits / limitations Guarantees a diagnosis and complete exclusion of cancer. Explains direct visual assessment and that histology can take longer. Acknowledges incomplete examinations and missed lesions, with safety-netting for persistent symptoms. Alternatives Claims endoscopy is compulsory and offers no choice. Explains reasonable alternatives and consequences of deferral for this indication. Explores preference-sensitive tradeoffs and documents a patient-led decision. Material risks Omits perforation or meaningful sedation risks. Discusses bleeding, perforation, aspiration, discomfort, missed lesion and sedative complications. Tailors risk discussion t
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: 1. Obtains a signature without explaining material harms and reasonable alternatives or without checking whether consent is voluntary. 2. Assures an OSA patient that IV sedation has no airway or respiratory risk and proposes no tailored assessment or monitoring. 3. Directs unsupervised apixaban cessation without checking its indication, planned intervention and local anticoagulant pathway. 4. Tells a patient who receives IV sedation that driving home himself immediately is acceptable.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient says, “I only have today available and I will drive home, so please sedate me anyway.” Expected: explain sedation-associated transport and driving restrictions; do not proceed on the assumption he can self-drive. Explore throat spray/unsedated OGD if suitable and acceptable, arranging an escort or rescheduling if he chooses sedation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should explain the alternatives and the risks you might personally find important before asking for your decision.” 2. “Your sleep apnoea changes sedation planning; I’ll check the monitoring and anaesthetic pathway with the endoscopy team.” 3. “I cannot safely advise you to stop apixaban from this conversation alone; we must verify the procedure and thrombosis plan.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-210 Gallbladder Polyp on Ultrasound Data interpretation / applied knowledge • 8-minute station • Independent educational assessment, not an official MRCS mark scheme. Draft for clinical sign-off.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 63-year-old patient with no biliary symptoms is referred after an ultrasound reports a solitary 8 mm sessile gallbladder polyp. Explain its significance, further questions and your management plan. The examiner will provide requested investigation details.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings on reques: Scenario: incidental lesion; do not disclose further ultrasound details unless asked. Candidate should identify a 6–9 mm lesion plus age >60 years and sessile morphology as guideline risk factors, and discuss elective cholecystectomy in a fit consenting patient. Requested ultrasound: 8 mm non-mobile non-shadowing sessile polyp; focal wall thickness 5 mm; no gallstones; bile ducts normal; no suspicious liver lesion. A prior scan two years ago did not report a polyp. History on request: no jaundice, fever, weight loss, biliary colic or PSC; age 63; normal LFTs; fit for elective operation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is anxious that “polyp means cancer”. Ask how likely this is and whether the gallbladder must come out. If candidate says all polyps are cancer, challenge that. If informed options and risks are explained, accept a shared plan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What report details influence management? → exact size, morphology/sessile features, wall thickening, growth/comparison, certainty this is a true polyp. Name the four European guideline risk factors for 6–9 mm polyps. → age >60, PSC, Asian ethnicity, sessile lesion including focal wall thickening >4 mm. What if the same patient had a 4 mm polyp and no risk factors? → no routine follow-up on the European pathway. What if 7 mm but no risk factors? → ultrasound at 6 months, 1 year and 2 years, stopping if no growth. What if measured at 10 mm? → cholecystectomy advised for appropriate patients. What if growth of 2 mm over 2 years? → assess present size and risk factors; MDT discussion may be appropriate, not automatic cancer diagnosis.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance History and symptoms Asserts polyp is symptomatic without eliciting symptoms. Checks pain, jaundice, fever, weight loss and preceding scans. Separates biliary symptoms from incidental finding and screens for alarm features. Report interpretation Misreads non-mobile lesion as a stone or omits size. Interprets 8 mm non-shadowing sessile lesion and wall thickening. Queries imaging certainty, morphology and interval growth with radiology. Risk stratification Uses 10 mm alone and disregards high-risk 8 mm findings. Identifies age >60 and sessile form as risk factors. Also identifies PSC, Asian ethnicity and focal thickening >4 mm. Guideline thresholds Claims every polyp requires resection. States ≥10 mm usually prompts cholecystectomy in fit patients. Applies 6–9 mm + risk-factor rule and distinguishes surveillance groups. Investigations Orders CT and tumour markers automatically for an uncomplicated 8 mm polyp. Reviews ultrasound quality, LFTs and clinical history. Plans selective expert ultrasound/MDT for equivocal or concerning features. Management choice Offers reassurance alone for this high-risk 8 mm scenario. Discusses elective laparoscopic chole
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Misses the 6–9 mm plus malignancy-risk-factor pathway and discharges this 63-year-old without review. 2. Labels this small incidental polyp as proven gallbladder cancer and proposes oncological resection without diagnostic assessment. 3. Offers repeated ultrasound instead of urgent assessment when new obstructive jaundice or mass-like suspicious imaging is disclosed. 4. Promotes cholecystectomy as risk-free and proceeds without discussing common bile duct injury or patient fitness.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: The patient has primary sclerosing cholangitis and asks whether waiting two years is safe. Expected: recognise PSC as a high-risk factor; with an 8 mm lesion recommend specialist HPB discussion and cholecystectomy if appropriate, rather than standard low-risk surveillance.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The lesion is 8 mm, but your age and its sessile appearance change how we approach it.” 2. “This ultrasound does not diagnose cancer; let me explain why removing the gallbladder may be advised.” 3. “We should review operative risks and arrange an elective surgical discussion rather than leave this without a plan.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-211 Asymptomatic Gallstones Found on a Scan Communication • 8-minute station • Independent educational assessment, not an official MRCS mark scheme. Draft for clinical sign-off.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 48-year-old patient requests urgent gallbladder removal because an abdominal ultrasound done for an unrelated reason showed two gallstones. Take a focused history, explain the result and agree a plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings on reques: Ultrasound (on request): two mobile shadowing gallbladder calculi, thin wall, no pericholecystic fluid, no biliary dilatation, common bile duct 4 mm. Normal LFTs and inflammatory markers. On focused enquiry: no previous postprandial right upper-quadrant or epigastric attacks, fever, jaundice, pancreatitis or hospital admissions. The ultrasound was requested during assessment of a renal cyst. No abnormal gallbladder morphology. Expected: reassure that uncomplicated asymptomatic gallbladder stones in a normal gallbladder and biliary tree do not require intervention under NICE CG188; contrast with bile duct stones and symptoms.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “If the stones are there, surely they will cause trouble; why not operate now?” You are worried about leaving a problem untreated. If alternatives are explained, ask what pain would make you seek help.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What symptoms imply biliary colic? → discrete episodes of sustained right upper-quadrant/epigastric pain, often with nausea, sometimes radiating to back, not just nonspecific bloating. What indicates possible acute cholecystitis/cholangitis? → prolonged severe pain with fever; jaundice plus fever/rigors is urgent. What changes if the report says common bile duct stone? → different pathway; arrange specialist evaluation and duct clearance even if no typical symptoms. Would incidental gallbladder calculi require serial ultrasound? → not routinely when asymptomatic with normal gallbladder/biliary tree. When would you discuss surgery? → symptomatic gallbladder stones and complications or individual complex risk context.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and rapport Dismisses patient fear without acknowledging it. Elicits concerns and explains why the scan was performed. Invites patient’s decision goals and offers balanced discussion. Symptom discrimination Treats indigestion alone as proven biliary colic. Asks about episodic upper abdominal pain, nausea and duration. Distinguishes biliary colic from dyspepsia and alternative diagnoses. Complication screen Fails to ask about fever or jaundice. Asks about fever, jaundice, pancreatitis and prior admissions. Identifies urgent cholangitis/pancreatitis clues and prior attacks. Imaging interpretation Confuses gallbladder stones with ductal stones. States mobile gallbladder calculi with normal ducts and wall. Explains why duct dilation and cholecystitis signs change care. Evidence-based choice Insists on prophylactic cholecystectomy for all stones. Reassures and does not offer routine surgery now. Anchors decision to NICE definition: asymptomatic + normal gallbladder/tree. Alternative scenarios Says no stone ever needs treatment while asymptomatic. Acknowledges new biliary symptoms would alter management. Recognises common bile duct stones need di
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Offers prophylactic laparoscopic cholecystectomy solely for uncomplicated asymptomatic gallbladder stones without discussing why it is unnecessary. 2. Reassures a patient reporting jaundice, fever and rigors without urgent investigation or escalation. 3. Treats suspected common bile duct stones as equivalent to incidental gallbladder stones and dismisses follow-up. 4. Promises there is zero future complication risk and gives no safety net for new severe pain or jaundice.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: Before leaving, the patient reports a previous six-hour attack of severe right upper-quadrant pain with vomiting after a meal. Expected: clarify whether this represents biliary colic; patient may be symptomatic, so offer surgical assessment and shared decision about cholecystectomy rather than routine reassurance.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should check whether you have ever had a typical gallstone pain episode before calling this asymptomatic.” 2. “Your scan shows stones in the gallbladder, not a blockage of the main bile duct.” 3. “If fever, jaundice or persistent severe pain develops, you should seek urgent medical review.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-212 Blunt Liver Injury Applied knowledge / trauma • 8-minute station • Independent educational assessment, not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in a major trauma unit. A 29-year-old motorcyclist has a blunt abdominal injury. After initial resuscitation, BP 116/72 mmHg, pulse 94/min, GCS 15. Contrast CT shows a grade IV right hepatic laceration with a small arterial contrast blush and moderate haemoperitoneum. There is no free intraperitoneal gas. Explain your immediate assessment and management, and how this would change if the patient deteriorated.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Examiner: do not volunteer details unless requested; expect an explicit management decision and safety escalation. Primary survey: Airway patent with cervical spine precautions; respiratory rate 20/min, SpO₂ 98% on oxygen; no tension pneumothorax; no obvious other major bleeding. Resuscitation: Two wide-bore IV lines, FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, LFT, group and crossmatch; initial Hb 112 g/L (not a reliable single measure of acute blood loss). CT details: Deep >25% right-lobe laceration consistent with AAST IV, focal arterial blush; no definite bowel injury, no major hepatic venous injury, no splenic injury. Clinical examination: Right upper-quadrant tenderness without generalized peritonitis. FAST demonstrates fluid but cannot grade injury or identify active arterial haemorrhage. Resources: 24-hour interventional radiology, emergency theatre, blood bank and critical-care monitoring available. After deterioration prompt: At 30 minutes, BP 78/48 despite blood-product resuscitation, worsening mental state and abdominal distension; non-responder to resuscitation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Not required: this is an applied-knowledge discussion with the examiner. If asked, the patient can report right-sided abdominal pain but no previous bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: How do you choose CT rather than theatre? → Decision primarily by haemodynamic response and peritonitis, not AAST grade alone; stable patients undergo IV contrast CT. What now in this stable patient with blush? → Continue monitored non-operative management with early trauma/HPB and IR consultation for angiography/possible embolisation, provided immediate rescue resources exist. What are the elements of NOM? → Close vital-sign review, serial abdominal examinations and Hb/coagulation checks, blood availability, repeat imaging for deterioration or suspected complication, clear escalation criteria. When is laparotomy essential? → Persistent instability/non-response or peritonitis/associated operative abdominal injury: damage-control resuscitation and urgent haemorrhage control. What is the operation? → Pack/compress liver, use direct haemostatic techniques and temporary abdominal closure if required; avoid heroic major hepatectomy; planned re-look and post-operative embolisation where appropriate. What delayed complications might arise? → Delayed bleeding/pseudoaneurysm, bile leak or symptomatic biloma, abscess; consider IR embolisation, drainage and/or ERCP according to problem.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Haemodynamic prioritisation Calls grade IV injury an automatic laparotomy and does not assess response to resuscitation. Uses BP, pulse, perfusion and response to resuscitation to choose initial pathway. Explicitly differentiates stable, transient responder and non-responder and states resource requirements for borderline cases. Primary trauma assessment Starts interpreting the scan without an ABCDE approach or checking for other bleeding. Conducts ABCDE, reassesses oxygenation, circulation and associated trauma. Coordinates senior trauma and anaesthetic input while actively excluding thoracic, pelvic and limb haemorrhage. Resuscitation and investigations Waits for serial Hb results before securing access or blood availability. Requests two large-bore lines, FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, gas/lactate and crossmatch; prepares blood. Triggers major haemorrhage protocol when indicated and reassesses perfusion, temperature, calcium and coagulopathy. Imaging interpretation Claims FAST grades lacerations or interprets haemoperitoneum alone as proof of surgical indication. Recognises grade IV laceration and arterial blush on contrast CT. Distinguishes acti
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Operates solely because the liver is AAST grade IV despite haemodynamic stability, with no other surgical injury or peritonitis. 2. Misses or fails to act on persistent haemodynamic instability, delaying urgent operative haemorrhage control. 3. Chooses unmonitored ward observation despite arterial blush and risk of secondary haemorrhage. 4. Performs or proposes CT in an unresponsive, persistently unstable patient instead of resuscitation and immediate haemorrhage-control pathway.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: During monitored non-operative treatment, the patient develops tachycardia, falling Hb and new right upper-quadrant pain, but maintains BP after resuscitation. Expected: re-assess ABCDE, repeat bloods/crossmatch and urgent contrast CT or direct angiography per trauma/IR team; embolise an identified arterial source if stable enough, convert to operative control if instability persists.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should correct that: haemodynamic response, not the CT injury grade by itself, determines whether immediate laparotomy is needed.” “This arterial blush deserves active IR discussion and monitored rescue capability rather than routine ward observation.” “If blood-product resuscitation fails to restore perfusion, I will call the trauma consultant and anaesthetist and move straight to damage-control haemorrhage control.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-213 Oesophageal Perforation After Endoscopic Dilatation Critical care / upper GI • 8-minute station • Independent educational assessment, not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are called to recovery 45 minutes after balloon dilatation of a benign oesophageal stricture. A 67-year-old patient has severe retrosternal pain, tachycardia and increasing breathlessness. BP 100/62 mmHg, pulse 122/min, respiratory rate 28/min, temperature 37.9 °C, SpO₂ 92% on air. Explain your immediate actions, investigations, treatment options and communication with the patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Examiner: do not volunteer details unless requested; expect an explicit management decision and safety escalation. Procedural details: Dilatation of a distal oesophageal stricture; the endoscopist noticed a deep mucosal split but no definite full-thickness defect. Procedure report and images available. Assessment: Acute chest pain radiating to back, crepitus in left supraclavicular fossa, reduced left basal air entry; abdominal examination soft. Bloods: Lactate 3.2 mmol/L; WCC 16 × 10⁹/L; CRP may still be normal shortly after injury; group and crossmatch pending. Imaging requested: Urgent CT chest and upper abdomen with IV contrast and, where appropriate, water-soluble oral contrast: paraoesophageal air/fluid, left pleural effusion and contrast extravasation from distal oesophagus. Specialist availability: Upper GI/oesophagogastric surgery, therapeutic endoscopy, anaesthesia and interventional radiology can be contacted immediately. Progression prompt: Despite fluids, IV antibiotics and analgesia, patient develops increasing oxygen needs, BP 82/50, severe pleural contamination and rising lactate.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is frightened, conscious and in pain. Ask: “Was the procedure responsible? Am I going to need another operation? Why did nobody tell me?” Examiner may play the patient if discussion is tested.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is your presumptive diagnosis? → Iatrogenic oesophageal perforation with mediastinal/pleural contamination until excluded. What do you do in first minutes? → ABCDE; senior surgical and anaesthetic help; oxygen as indicated, IV access, fluids guided by perfusion, bloods/lactate/cultures if septic, analgesia, nil by mouth, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics according to local policy; avoid oral intake. Which imaging confirms/defines injury? → Urgent CT chest/upper abdomen with IV contrast and selective oral water-soluble contrast; assess extravasation, collections, pleural disease and alternative causes. Can it be closed endoscopically? → Early small contained defects may be suitable for clips, suturing, covered stent or other expert approaches; need adequate drainage and clinical surveillance; decision depends on size, timing, site and contamination. When does surgery become necessary? → Uncontained leak, ongoing sepsis/shock, extensive contamination, necrotic tissue, or failure of endoscopic/conservative treatment; surgical drainage, repair or diversion as anatomically appropriate. What else must occur? → Document endoscopy details and imaging, open discussion and apology under dut
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls it routine post-dilatation discomfort despite tachycardia and hypoxia. Identifies possible perforation from severe pain plus systemic and respiratory findings. Links crepitus and pleural signs to mediastinal/pleural leakage and mobilises the emergency pathway immediately. ABCDE and resuscitation Focuses on diagnostic endoscopy while neglecting airway, oxygenation and perfusion. Uses ABCDE, oxygen as required, monitoring, IV access, fluids and analgesia. Involves anaesthesia/critical care early, trends lactate and reassesses response after each intervention. Sepsis / contamination Allows oral fluids or delays antibiotics until microbiology results. Makes patient nil by mouth and starts prompt IV antibiotics according to local policy. Recognises urgent source control, obtains cultures where appropriate without delaying therapy and anticipates pleural drainage. Imaging Relies on normal chest X-ray to exclude a leak. Orders urgent contrast CT to locate perforation and assess contamination. Specifies IV contrast with selective water-soluble oral contrast and uses findings to plan drainage/repair. Procedure details Makes no attempt to i
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Dismisses severe chest pain after dilation as normal and leaves the patient without urgent investigation or escalation. 2. Permits oral fluids or repeat blind instrumentation in a suspected perforation without a controlled specialist plan. 3. Delays IV antibiotics and nil-by-mouth management in a contaminated mediastinal/pleural leak. 4. Continues conservative care despite refractory shock or uncontrolled pleural/mediastinal contamination, without urgent source-control consultation.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: CT confirms a distal defect with left pleural contamination; during preparation for possible stenting, BP falls to 82/50 with rising lactate. Expected: resume ABCDE, activate sepsis/critical-care response, urgent anaesthetic and oesophagogastric consultant review, fluid/blood support as indicated, immediate pleural/mediastinal source-control plan; stenting alone is not a substitute for drainage or control in an unstable patient.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I was wrong to call this ordinary post-dilatation pain: severe chest pain with tachycardia requires urgent assessment for perforation.” “I will stop oral intake, obtain IV access, give prompt IV antibiotics and order urgent contrast CT while calling the senior upper GI team.” “Because this patient is deteriorating with pleural contamination, I must move from observation to urgent source control and critical-care support.”

stations.title: Dumping Syndrome After Gastric Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-214 | Dumping Syndrome After Gastric Surgery AMaC MRCS Part B · Applied knowledge / postoperative · 8-minute teaching/assessment station · Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 53-year-old underwent distal gastrectomy 7 months ago. He reports palpitations, abdominal cramping and diarrhoea shortly after meals; sometimes he becomes shaky and confused two hours later. Explain the likely diagnosis, investigate appropriately and plan management.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient haemodynamically stable, no fever. BMI fell from 27 to 24. The early episode begins 20 minutes after sweet tea and toast. Later episodes occur 2 hours after meals; capillary glucose was 2.7 mmol/L on one symptomatic occasion. No recurrent cancer symptoms; examination without focal abnormality. Reveal these only if requested.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Worried he is “allergic to food” and wants a scan. If asked, he often drinks large glasses of juice with meals, has missed work twice, and drives for work. Respond thoughtfully to dietary/working advice.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What is the most useful extra history?” → When symptoms start relative to meals, their nature, food triggers, syncope, low glucose and weight change. “Would a gastric emptying scan diagnose dumping?” → No; it has no established diagnostic value for this syndrome. “What if diet fails?” → Specialist review: acarbose particularly for late dumping; consider somatostatin analogue if persistent. “What about a glucose of 2.4 mmol/L with confusion?” → Recognise and immediately treat clinically significant hypoglycaemia; reassess and escalate.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and timing Calls post-meal collapse ordinary indigestion; never differentiates timings. Identifies early vasomotor/GI symptoms within 60 minutes and late neuroglycopenia 1–3 hours after eating. Relates early rapid osmotic fluid shift and late exaggerated insulin response to the two distinct histories. History and severity Omits relation to food or loss-of-consciousness episodes. Asks operation type, time from eating, palpitations, diarrhoea, sweating, syncope, weight loss and driving safety. Elicits carbohydrate triggers, specific hypoglycaemia signs, dietary restriction and nutritional impact. Differential diagnosis Assumes any postoperative dizziness is dumping without exclusion. Considers anastomotic stricture, recurrence/obstruction, dehydration, medication effects and other hypoglycaemia causes. Prioritises cancer recurrence red flags and distinguishes postoperative reactive hypoglycaemia from fasting hypoglycaemia. Initial bedside assessment Ignores a confused patient with low glucose. Checks observations, hydration, nutritional state and capillary glucose during symptomatic episodes. Rechecks glucose after correction and evaluate
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to recognise or treat acute symptomatic hypoglycaemia when the examiner supplies glucose 2.4 mmol/L with confusion. 2. Recommends high-sugar drinks with every meal as long-term therapy despite recurrent dumping. 3. Attributes persistent vomiting, weight loss with obstructive symptoms or other alarm features automatically to dumping and refuses further assessment. 4. Offers immediate revisional surgery as routine first-line management without trying diet or specialist review.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner adds: “He became confused in the waiting area; fingerprick glucose is 2.4 mmol/L.” Expected: immediate ABC assessment, hypoglycaemia treatment per local protocol, repeat glucose and observation; do not defer to routine outpatient diet discussion.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. I need to separate what happens in the first hour from what happens one to three hours after eating. 2. His documented low glucose requires treatment and a safety assessment now, not only dietary advice. 3. I would involve the upper-GI dietitian first, then consider acarbose for persistent late symptoms with specialist input.

stations.title: Consent for Oesophagectomy

sections.preamble: B2-215 | Consent for Oesophagectomy AMaC MRCS Part B · Communication / consent · 8-minute teaching/assessment station · Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in the upper-GI clinic. A 66-year-old patient with resectable distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma, after specialist MDT review, is considering minimally invasive transthoracic oesophagectomy following planned systemic therapy. Explain the operation, material risks, alternatives and long-term life changes; support an informed decision.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Staging confirms nonmetastatic potentially resectable disease; fitness assessment acceptable. MDT recommends neoadjuvant treatment and then reassessment for oesophagectomy. No fixed operation date; proposed Ivor Lewis-type oesophagectomy with gastric conduit and intrathoracic anastomosis. Exact individual mortality/complication figures are NOT supplied; candidate must seek audited unit and personalised estimates rather than invent them.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient asks: “Will I definitely be cured? Will I be able to eat with my family? What is my risk of dying?” Main concern is being independent. If candidates use jargon ask for simpler explanation. No agreed decision yet.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “Will the surgery definitely cure me?” → No. It offers a chance of cure but recurrence remains possible; discuss individual stage and MDT estimate. “What happens if the join leaks?” → Recognise potentially serious infection/sepsis; drainage, antibiotics, endoscopic or surgical treatment may be required. “Can I still eat?” → Yes, usually with permanent adjustments: small frequent meals, slower eating and nutritional monitoring. “How likely am I to die?” → Discuss meaningful individual risk using local audited data and personal fitness; do not invent a universal percentage.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction and capacity Begins a consent monologue without confirming identity or willingness. Confirms patient/operation, capacity, support needs and asks what matters to patient. Elicits priority (cure, swallowing, independence) and tailors conversation accordingly. Indication and MDT Calls operation guaranteed cure without discussing staging. Explains staged lower oesophageal adenocarcinoma, curative intent and specialist MDT recommendation. Distinguishes intent from certainty, explains reassessment after neoadjuvant treatment. Operation anatomy Describes only removal of tumour without reconstruction. Describes removing diseased oesophagus with lymph nodes, gastric conduit and new join in chest, usually chest/abdominal access. Explains that an alternative conduit/approach may be necessary depending on anatomy and operative findings. Alternative options Claims there is no alternative and consent is compulsory. Explains planned systemic therapy, definitive chemoradiotherapy in selected scenarios, supportive/palliative options and declining surgery. Links alternatives to stage, histology and fitness, offers MDT/oncolology discussion. Major early
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to mention the recognised risk of anastomotic leak or dismisses it as trivial. 2. Claims surgery guarantees cancer cure and withholds reasonable alternative radical/non-operative options. 3. Omits death or serious pulmonary complications despite the patient explicitly asking for major risks. 4. Pressures a hesitant patient to sign consent without exploring concerns, capacity or the option to defer a decision.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Patient says: “My sister died after a chest infection following an operation. I am now too frightened to sign.” Expected: acknowledge fear, quantify individually only with verified data, explain prevention/ICU care, offer discussion with consultant, CNS and anaesthetist; do not coerce.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. I have not explained clearly enough that the operation aims to cure, but cannot guarantee cure. 2. A leak at the new join, chest infection and even death are risks we must discuss before you decide. 3. If it helps, we can review the audited figures specific to you and speak again with your family or specialist nurse present.

stations.title: Peritoneal Dialysis Peritonitis

sections.preamble: B2-216 | Peritoneal Dialysis Peritonitis AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / emergency nephrology • 8-minute station DRAFT — independent specialist clinical sign-off required. Educational assessment resource; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 61-year-old patient using automated peritoneal dialysis for end-stage kidney disease develops cloudy drainage and abdominal pain over 12 hours. Temperature 38.1°C, pulse 106/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg. The PD nurse calls the surgical assessment unit because the pain is abdominal. Explain the immediate assessment and investigation of suspected PD-associated peritonitis. Interpret the results supplied and start a safe management plan. Explain when an underlying surgical cause or PD catheter removal should be considered.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: If asked about stability: alert, passing urine minimally at baseline, no rigid abdomen; lactate 1.5 mmol/L. If asked about the effluent: cloudy; after a 3-hour dwell WBC 860/µL, 83% neutrophils; Gram stain negative initially, culture pending. If asked about exit site: no erythema, discharge or tunnel tenderness. If asked about background: no recent bowel surgery, constipation for three days; no known antibiotic allergy. If asked about repeat review: persistent diffuse pain and falling blood pressure after 12 hours despite initial therapy would trigger sepsis and surgical-source reassessment.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient says: “The fluid is cloudy and my tummy aches. Do I need my dialysis tube taken out?” If asked: had two uncomplicated peritonitis-free years on PD; wants to preserve home dialysis. If the candidate says a laparotomy or immediate catheter removal is mandatory, asks why.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What makes this PD peritonitis? Cloudy effluent/abdominal pain plus WBC >100/µL with >50% PMNs after ≥2-hour dwell; two of the three diagnostic criteria are satisfied without awaiting culture. What specimens do you take? Aseptically drain and send PD effluent for cell count/differential, Gram stain and culture (prefer inoculation into blood-culture bottles according to PD unit protocol); blood cultures if septic. How do you treat initially? Escalate to PD/nephrology team, record observations and sepsis assessment; promptly give empiric antibiotic cover for Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms after sampling, preferentially intraperitoneally if feasible, according to local resistance and PD protocols; adapt to culture. When is surgery involved? New guarding/rigidity, haemodynamic deterioration, polymicrobial enteric growth, free intra-abdominal pathology or failure to improve suggest secondary peritonitis; urgent surgical assessment and CT as appropriate. When remove the catheter? Discuss fungal peritonitis, refractory disease and associated catheter/tunnel infection with nephrology; refractory peritonitis usually means effluent fails to clear after five days of appropriate the
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and prioritisation Dismisses cloudy dialysate as routine and postpones review. Identifies presumptive PD peritonitis and undertakes prompt face-to-face assessment. Identifies PD peritonitis promptly while explicitly screening for sepsis and secondary abdominal catastrophe. Focused history Does not ask about pain, effluent or recent PD exchanges. Asks timing of pain/cloudiness, fever, exchanges and recent peritonitis. Adds contamination/disconnection, bowel symptoms, recent procedures, prior organisms and antibiotic allergy. Examination and severity Does not record vital signs or examine abdomen. Checks observations, hydration, abdominal tenderness and catheter exit site. Assesses perfusion/lactate, peritonism and tunnel signs, and plans repeated observations. Dialysate testing Sends no effluent sample or treats a negative early Gram stain as exclusion. Requests effluent cell count, differential, Gram stain and culture before antibiotics if feasible. Specifies sterile collection, ≥2 h dwell context and APD short-dwell PMN nuance. Interpretation Mislabels 860 cells/µL with 83% PMN as non-infective. Identifies diagnostic effluent pleocytos
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Leaves a patient with new hypotension or rigid abdomen without urgent sepsis/surgical escalation. Withholds empiric antibiotics until the culture grows an organism despite diagnostic peritonitis. Fails to obtain a peritoneal fluid sample before antibiotics when safely feasible. Continues PD catheter salvage despite clear clinical deterioration and evidence of uncontrolled source, without escalation.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: On day five, the patient feels markedly better; effluent WBC has fallen from 860 to 140/µL but remains faintly cloudy. The registrar asks if the catheter must come out. Expected response: Do not apply day five mechanically. ISPD allows further close observation if WBC is steadily declining toward normal and clinical improvement is convincing; obtain nephrology-led review, repeat counts and remove if worsening or truly refractory.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I initially underestimated the cloudy effluent; this meets PD-peritonitis criteria and I will send effluent samples and start empiric treatment now.” “The new guarding changes the differential: I am calling senior surgery and nephrology immediately to exclude bowel pathology.” “I was too categorical about day-five removal; I will review the effluent trend and clinical status with the PD team rather than use the calendar alone.”

stations.title: Consent for Carotid Endarterectomy

sections.preamble: B2-217 | Consent for Carotid Endarterectomy AMaC Medical Education • MRCS Part B • Communication / vascular surgery • 8-minute station DRAFT — independent specialist clinical sign-off required. Educational assessment resource; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 72-year-old right-handed patient had a transient episode of left arm weakness and slurred speech eight days ago, fully resolved within 15 minutes. Duplex and CTA confirm 78% NASCET stenosis of the right internal carotid artery. Stroke-team assessment and vascular MDT recommend early right carotid endarterectomy; CT brain excludes haemorrhage. The patient attends with concern about having a stroke during the operation. Explain why endarterectomy is being offered and what it involves. Discuss meaningful benefits, alternatives, material risks and likely recovery without inventing personalised percentages. Check understanding, preferences and voluntary informed consent.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: The stenosis is right-sided and symptomatic; no disabling infarct or haemorrhage on imaging. The patient walks independently; mild hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia are treated. If asked for procedural detail: under general or regional anaesthesia, neck incision, carotid clamping with cerebral monitoring and selective shunting, plaque removal and arterial closure (often patch); technique varies by surgeon. If asked about timing: local vascular service plans surgery within the next few days, aiming within 14 days after the index neurological event when suitable. The unit-specific audited perioperative stroke/death risk is not given. Candidate should seek local figures rather than state a made-up individual probability.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “You say this prevents a stroke, but couldn’t the operation give me one?” If invited to ask more: “Will my voice or swallowing be affected? And what happens if I say no?” Patient wants written information and time to speak with daughter, but understands recent symptoms make timely action important.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Why now? Recently symptomatic 78% carotid stenosis has a substantial early recurrent stroke risk; CEA reduces future ipsilateral stroke risk in suitable patients, with maximum benefit when performed early, preferably within 14 days. What is the operation? Neck incision, expose common/internal/external carotid, temporarily control blood flow, remove plaque, close artery and monitor neurological and airway status after surgery. What are the material harms? Perioperative stroke/TIA, death, MI, neck bleeding/haematoma with possible airway compromise, infection, cranial nerve injury causing hoarseness, tongue or swallowing difficulty, restenosis and anaesthetic complications. Alternatives? Optimal medical treatment is essential with or without surgery; selective carotid stenting is an alternative for certain patients but has different procedural risk profiles. Choosing no operation leaves recurrent stroke risk. How to close? Elicit what matters to patient, explain local audited procedural risk and patient-specific factors with supervising surgeon; teach-back, written information, document discussion, no coercion.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and rapport Launches into a technical lecture without asking concerns. Checks identity, introduces role and invites patient’s concern about operative stroke. Acknowledges fear and elicits the patient’s functional goals and preferred detail. Indication and timing Calls the 78% stenosis an incidental finding unrelated to the TIA. Links ipsilateral recent TIA with 78% symptomatic ICA stenosis and early stroke prevention. Explains why benefit is time-sensitive, ideally CEA within 14 days if clinically appropriate. Procedure explanation Describes carotid stenting or brain surgery as the planned operation. Explains neck incision, carotid plaque removal and arterial closure in lay language. Adds temporary flow interruption, monitoring/shunt decisions and anaesthesia choices without overloading. Benefit and uncertainty Guarantees that surgery prevents all future strokes. Explains CEA reduces, but does not eliminate, future ipsilateral stroke risk. Distinguishes immediate operative risk from long-term risk reduction and seeks audited local figures. Stroke and cardiovascular risks Omits perioperative stroke or death. Names stroke/TIA, death and myoca
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Obtains apparent consent without explaining the material perioperative stroke or death risk. Promises that a 78% carotid endarterectomy prevents all future strokes or carries no neurological risk. Dismisses or delays assessment of new focal neurological symptoms reported during the consultation rather than activating emergency stroke care. Coerces the patient to sign immediately or ignores an expressed lack of consent/capacity concern.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: During the discussion the patient develops fresh left facial droop and slurred speech, witnessed by the candidate. Expected response: Stop consent immediately, record onset/last-known-well, activate the emergency stroke pathway, assess ABC and glucose, summon stroke/vascular teams and arrange urgent neuroimaging; do not continue elective counselling.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I did not explain the key operative stroke risk clearly; let me compare that immediate risk with the benefit of preventing a larger future stroke.” “I described the operation as compulsory; it is your decision, and I will explain medication alone and selected stenting options.” “The new facial weakness changes everything: I am stopping consent and activating an urgent stroke assessment now.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-218 Thoracic Outlet Syndrome History / examination / applied knowledge • 8-minute teaching/assessment station • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in a vascular clinic. Take a focused history, describe a targeted examination to the examiner, interpret further findings on request, and explain investigation and initial management. Eight minutes; no actual patient examination is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Present an otherwise well person with six months of posture-dependent symptoms. Do not volunteer test results. Ask the candidate to differentiate neurogenic, venous and arterial TOS and exclude mimics. Score actions explicitly rather than diagnostic buzzwords. Opening scenario: A 29-year-old overhead athlete reports intermittent right-hand tingling and arm fatigue when working above shoulder height. She asks whether she has a trapped nerve or a circulation problem. History — Symptoms worsen with prolonged overhead activity and carrying a heavy bag; improve with rest. No sustained hand coolness, colour change, swelling, sudden pain or weakness. Examination — Well-perfused warm hands, equal pulses and normal capillary refill at rest; mild right scalene tenderness, intact power including hand intrinsics, no wasting, no neck mass; check sensory map and cervical spine. Provocative manoeuvres — Elevated arm stress test reproduces familiar paraesthesia after 45 seconds; Adson manoeuvre produces reduced pulse but NOT diagnostic alone. Avoid claiming either test confirms TOS. Imaging — Thoracic inlet radiograph shows a small right cervical rib. Duplex at rest shows patent axillary/subclavia
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Friendly but anxious: “Will I need my rib removed?” Reports paraesthesia mainly ring/little fingers and aching with arm elevation; no swelling, discolouration or cold digits unless specifically asked. No neck trauma, hand weakness at rest or constitutional symptoms.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What are the three syndromes? EXPECT: Neurogenic brachial plexus symptoms; venous subclavian/axillary obstruction or effort thrombosis causing swollen cyanosed arm; arterial subclavian injury/embolisation with cold painful digits or ischaemia. Is a positive Adson test definitive? EXPECT: No. Reduced radial pulse with manoeuvre occurs in healthy people. Interpret against symptoms, examination and appropriate imaging. How will you treat this presentation? EXPECT: Likely neurogenic TOS: explain diagnostic uncertainty, supervised targeted physiotherapy, posture/activity modification and analgesia; refer to a specialist TOS service for persistent disabling symptoms, objective deficit or operative consideration. When does management become urgent? EXPECT: New swollen blue arm suggests venous thrombosis; cold painful pulseless hand suggests arterial ischaemia—same-day vascular assessment, urgent imaging and appropriate anticoagulation/revascularisation pathways.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and task framing Jumps to a diagnosis without setting out the focused assessment. Explains that symptoms may originate from nerve or vessel compression and obtains permission. Sets focused agenda and establishes the patient’s primary concern about surgery. Symptom discrimination Does not ask about arm swelling, colour change or hand ischaemia. Asks pain/paraesthesia distribution, overhead triggers, weakness, swelling, colour, coldness and sudden onset. Clarifies dominant neurological versus venous versus arterial phenotype and functional impact. Risk factors and alternatives Attributes all paraesthesia to a cervical rib without evaluating other causes. Asks occupational/repetitive overhead activity, trauma, neck symptoms, prior thrombosis and relevant medical history. Seeks ulnar neuropathy, cervical radiculopathy and shoulder pathology clues with discriminating questions. Focused examination Relies on provocative pulse change alone. Describes bilateral pulses, temperature, colour, capillary refill, motor/sensory hand assessment, neck and shoulder examination. Includes hand intrinsic wasting, cervical/ulnar provocation, arm oedema and check
sections.6. Four critical fails: CF1 — Misses a new cold, painful, pulseless upper limb and delays emergency vascular assessment. CF2 — Dismisses a suddenly swollen, cyanosed arm without considering axillosubclavian DVT. CF3 — Uses a positive Adson manoeuvre alone to diagnose TOS and recommend decompression. CF4 — Promises immediate cervical-rib excision for non-emergency symptoms without considering differential diagnosis or conservative therapy.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: Halfway through, the patient says that since this morning the entire arm is swollen and bluish. Expected response: Stop the routine neurogenic pathway. Reassess vital signs, arm perfusion and chest symptoms; consider acute axillosubclavian vein thrombosis (effort thrombosis), arrange urgent vascular assessment and duplex and discuss anticoagulation with the specialist team. Screen for PE symptoms.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. After prematurely diagnosing TOS from Adson: “I need to correct that: this manoeuvre alone is unreliable.
