I would revisit the symptom pattern and exclude cervical and peripheral nerve causes.” 2. After overlooking vascular symptoms: “I have not yet asked about sudden swelling, colour change or a cold painful hand; those findings would change the urgency of my assessment.” 3. After offering early surgery: “The initial approach for likely neurogenic TOS is targeted physiotherapy and specialist evaluation; surgery is reserved for selected cases after confirmation.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-219 Popliteal Artery Aneurysm Applied knowledge / data interpretation • 8-minute teaching/assessment station • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the vascular registrar reviewing an incidentally detected popliteal aneurysm. Interpret the written imaging, outline investigations and management, explain the operation choices and respond to an acute change. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Require clear distinction between asymptomatic elective repair and acute thromboembolic limb ischaemia. Provide the staged results only if requested. Ask why an aneurysm of this diameter is not simply discharged. Opening scenario: A 72-year-old man is referred after duplex ultrasound identifies a 26-mm right popliteal artery aneurysm with mural thrombus. He has no rest pain and walks 400 metres without claudication. Both feet are warm with palpable pedal pulses. Duplex — Right popliteal arterial maximum outer diameter 26 mm, eccentric mural thrombus, triphasic distal arterial waveforms, three patent calf runoff vessels. Left popliteal diameter 14 mm. Clinical assessment — Right leg is warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, no tissue loss, normal motor/sensory function. Associated aneurysms — Screening aortic ultrasound shows infrarenal AAA diameter 38 mm; no symptoms. Left popliteal artery is not aneurysmal. Preoperative anatomy — CTA demonstrates suitable inflow and three-vessel distal runoff. Duplex vein mapping reveals usable ipsilateral great saphenous vein; knee flexion zone relevant for stent durability. If acute symptoms
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Optional simulated patient: asks “Could it burst?” and “Is a stent less risky?” Wants an understandable explanation of loss-of-circulation risk, alternatives and follow-up. No current ischaemic symptoms unless in curveball.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the main complication? EXPECT: Thrombosis and distal embolisation causing acute limb ischaemia; rupture is comparatively uncommon. What else should be screened? EXPECT: Contralateral popliteal artery and abdominal aorta, given strong aneurysm associations. Does 26 mm require repair? EXPECT: SVS recommends elective repair for asymptomatic popliteal artery aneurysms >20 mm to lower thromboembolic and limb-loss risk; consider patient fitness, thrombus and anatomy. Carefully selected higher-risk patients may defer to >30 mm, especially without thrombus. Open versus endovascular? EXPECT: Open exclusion with bypass (preferably autologous vein where suitable) is durable; endovascular covered stent may suit selected anatomy/fitness but needs surveillance for occlusion, fracture or endoleak/persistent sac perfusion. What if sudden cold foot? EXPECT: Immediate Rutherford limb assessment, urgent vascular call, analgesia/resuscitation, IV unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, urgent imaging only if it does not delay threatened-limb treatment; thrombectomy/thrombolysis, repair or bypass chosen by limb severity.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical framing Confuses popliteal aneurysm with a DVT or assumes rupture is the chief threat. Identifies an arterial aneurysm and highlights embolisation/thrombosis risk. Explains why an asymptomatic sac can produce sudden limb-threatening distal emboli. Symptom and risk history Does not ask about rest pain or sudden limb symptoms. Asks claudication, rest pain, ulcers, acute pain, smoking, cardiovascular disease and comorbidities. Adds prior embolic episodes, functional status, operative fitness, antithrombotic drugs and patient goals. Vascular examination Documents only a popliteal lump and omits foot perfusion. Examines both femoral/popliteal/pedal pulses, foot warmth, refill, tissue loss and neurology. Describes bedside Doppler and bilateral aneurysm assessment while recognising normal resting pulses do not exclude risk. Image interpretation Treats mural thrombus as reassurance because distal flow is preserved. Reports 26-mm diameter, mural thrombus, patent runoff and current perfusion. Links thrombus burden, runoff and conduit quality to repair strategy and limb risk. Associated disease Does not assess the opposite leg or abdominal aorta. Req
sections.6. Four critical fails: CF1 — Fails to identify a newly cold, painful, pulseless foot as acute limb ischaemia. CF2 — Discharges a 26-mm popliteal aneurysm with mural thrombus without discussing repair or specialist surveillance. CF3 — Assumes palpable pedal pulses rule out mural thrombus and embolisation risk. CF4 — Delays urgent vascular treatment for a threatened limb with new motor deficit in order to arrange routine outpatient investigations.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: While discussing repair, the patient says his foot became suddenly painful and numb 30 minutes ago; it is now pale and cold, with weak toe movement. Expected response: Treat as immediately threatened acute limb ischaemia. Call senior vascular surgeon and emergency theatre pathway now; rapid ABCDE and bilateral vascular/neurovascular examination, Doppler and Rutherford classification; intravenous unfractionated heparin unless contraindicated, analgesia, urgent revascularisation planning without imaging-related delay.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. After saying “no symptoms means no repair”: “I would correct that: the aneurysm is 26 mm and contains thrombus, so elective vascular repair should be discussed even without claudication.” 2. After omitting associated aneurysms: “I should assess the opposite popliteal artery and screen the abdominal aorta, because disease can be bilateral or coexist with AAA.” 3. After under-reacting to a cold foot: “This is acute limb ischaemia, not a surveillance issue. I would call vascular surgery immediately, assess motor function and Doppler, and initiate the acute limb pathway.”

stations.title: Superficial Thrombophlebitis

sections.preamble: B2-220 | Superficial Thrombophlebitis AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / vascular • 8 minutes • Draft: independent clinical sign-off required Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Examiner uses scenario disclosures as written. Candidate sees Section 1 only.
sections.1. Candidate brief: • You are the surgical trainee in an acute assessment clinic. A 56-year-old woman has a painful red cord along the medial left thigh for four days. She is ambulant and well. Assess the condition, interpret duplex results supplied by the examiner, and plan treatment and follow-up. • You have eight minutes. You may ask for history, examination findings, and duplex details. No patient examination is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: • History: varicose veins; no previous VTE; no cancer, pregnancy or recent surgery; no breathlessness, chest pain or haemoptysis. Medications: no anticoagulants. No bleeding history; renal function normal; weight 74 kg. • Examination: afebrile, pulse 82, BP 128/76; tender palpable inflamed track medial distal thigh; no whole-leg swelling or neurovascular deficit. No cellulitis spreading beyond cord. • Duplex on request: thrombosis of great saphenous vein, 8 cm long; proximal thrombus end 6 cm from the saphenofemoral junction; deep venous system patent and compressible. Examiner must give BOTH length and junction distance.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: • A worried patient asks whether the clot will travel to her lungs and whether she can continue walking. • If asked: no chest pain or breathlessness; worried about injections and missing work; wants an understandable plan.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • ‘What further imaging do you need?’ — Whole-leg duplex mapping of SVT and exclusion of DVT; establish proximal distance and thrombus length. • ‘What is your treatment for the supplied scan?’ — Fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously daily for 45 days if no contraindication, with individual bleeding/renal assessment and local prescribing review. • ‘What if the proximal thrombus is 1 cm from the SFJ?’ — Treat as high-risk junctional SVT needing therapeutic anticoagulation and urgent vascular/haematology pathway; not the 45-day prophylactic-dose regimen. • ‘What if it is an isolated 3 cm distal tributary SVT?’ — Assess clinical risk; symptomatic treatment and follow-up often appropriate if no DVT or high-risk features; do not automatically anticoagulate every SVT.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls it simple cellulitis despite palpable cord. Identifies superficial vein thrombosis on varicose-vein background. Identifies saphenous-trunk SVT and explains variable VTE risk by anatomy. Urgent screen Does not ask about dyspnoea or chest pain. Asks about PE symptoms and unilateral deep-leg swelling. Also reviews haemodynamic symptoms and escalation threshold for suspected PE. Risk history Ignores previous VTE and bleeding history. Asks about VTE, malignancy, pregnancy, surgery and anticoagulants. Checks renal impairment, weight and medication interactions before prophylaxis. Focused examination Fails to examine either limb. Assesses cord extent, swelling, erythema and distal perfusion. Distinguishes spreading infection and signs suggesting concomitant DVT. Ultrasound interpretation Uses length alone to choose anticoagulation. States 8 cm SVT, 6 cm from SFJ, no DVT. Applies both ≥5 cm length and junction-distance thresholds correctly. Anticoagulation Only advises topical gel for 8 cm axial SVT. Offers fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily for 45 days, subject to safety checks. Explains alternatives require local licence/formulary review and
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to recognise suspected PE symptoms or arrange emergency assessment if present. 2. Does not exclude DVT or define SFJ proximity before declaring low-risk SVT. 3. Treats SVT ≤3 cm from SFJ with only symptomatic measures/low-dose regimen despite junctional risk. 4. Omits indicated anticoagulation for 8 cm saphenous trunk SVT 6 cm from SFJ without documenting a contraindication.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: Duplex addendum states the thrombus extends to 1 cm from the SFJ. Expected: Reclassify as junctional high-risk SVT; seek urgent vascular/thrombosis guidance, institute therapeutic anticoagulation if appropriate after bleeding/renal assessment, and ensure DVT/PE surveillance. Avoid continuing fondaparinux 2.5 mg as sole therapy.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I need the distance to the deep-vein junction before I can safely choose the anticoagulant dose.” 2. “This is 8 cm in the great saphenous vein, so pain relief alone is insufficient unless there is a contraindication.” 3. “If the scan reaches within 3 cm of the junction, I will urgently change to the therapeutic-anticoagulation pathway.”

stations.title: Bleeding Varicose Vein

sections.preamble: B2-221 | Bleeding Varicose Vein AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / vascular • 8 minutes • Draft: independent clinical sign-off required Educational examiner resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Examiner uses scenario disclosures as written. Candidate sees Section 1 only.
sections.1. Candidate brief: • You are the surgical registrar called to the emergency department. A 79-year-old woman is bleeding briskly from a small varicose vein at her medial ankle after taking off her sock. State and demonstrate verbally your immediate management, then plan definitive prevention and discharge advice. • You have eight minutes. The examiner will provide observations and wound findings as requested.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: • Patient initially seated with dependent leg; towel soaked with blood; a 3-mm skin defect overlies a superficial ankle varix. No arterial pulsatility; no trauma apart from scratching the skin. • Initial observations: pulse 112, BP 98/62, RR 20, alert; on apixaban for AF. With firm direct pressure and leg elevation bleeding stops; repeat BP 118/70, pulse 86 after observation and resuscitative measures. • Skin: thin, fragile, with venous eczema and pigmentation. No other bleeding site; distal pulses palpable. After haemostasis, consider FBC, renal profile, coagulation context/medication history and appropriate observation. • If candidate requests it: after dressings, visible varicosities suggest superficial venous reflux; duplex has not yet been done.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: • The patient is frightened: ‘There was so much blood. Will I die if it happens again?’ She lives alone and takes an anticoagulant. • If reassured without instructions, ask: ‘What exactly should I do if it starts when I’m at home?’
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • ‘What are your first two moves?’ — Lay flat, raise affected leg above heart level if feasible, immediate firm direct pressure over puncture, secure pressure dressing once bleeding controlled; summon help and assess ABC/vitals. • ‘Would you use a tourniquet above the wound?’ — No: proximal venous obstruction can increase distal venous bleeding; never substitute tourniquet for direct pressure. • ‘The patient becomes faint and systolic BP falls to 80.’ — Emergency call, ABCDE, continued haemostasis, IV access, blood tests/group-and-crossmatch and haemorrhage resuscitation; reassess anticoagulation and specialist reversal strategy in life-threatening bleeding. • ‘Can you discharge now the wound is dry?’ — Not without haemodynamic reassessment, recurrence plan and immediate vascular-service referral per NICE; individualise observation due to initial instability/anticoagulant.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Emergency recognition Treats bleed as cosmetic minor ooze. Recognises potentially severe external venous haemorrhage. Calls for help early when tachycardic/hypotensive and prioritises haemostasis. Posture & compression Leaves leg dependent while applying loose gauze. Lies patient down, elevates limb and applies firm direct pressure to source. Maintains focal pressure while an assistant obtains dressing and equipment. Avoiding harm Applies proximal tourniquet over thigh. Explicitly avoids proximal tourniquet and pressure above bleed. Explains venous-pressure mechanism and teaches safe compression technique. Resuscitation Ignores BP 98/62 and tachycardia. Performs ABCDE, repeats observations and assesses blood loss. Establishes IV access, FBC, group-and-save/crossmatch as clinically indicated. Medication assessment Does not check anticoagulant. Identifies apixaban use and checks last dose, renal function and bleeding severity. Plans specialist review of interruption/reversal only if clinically indicated. Local evaluation Manipulates friable vein repeatedly. Examines puncture, surrounding skin and pulses after haemostasis. Recognises atrophic skin/ven
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to apply direct pressure to the bleeding point while visible haemorrhage continues. 2. Uses a proximal tourniquet as the preferred treatment for a bleeding ankle varix. 3. Ignores signs of circulatory compromise, delaying resuscitation in an unstable patient. 4. Discharges after a significant variceal bleed without emergency safety advice or immediate vascular referral.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: While the dressing is being prepared, the patient becomes pale, confused and hypotensive at 80/45 mmHg. Expected: Keep firm pressure and limb elevation; activate emergency response, perform ABCDE, obtain two IV lines as appropriate, group-and-crossmatch, monitor continuously, manage major haemorrhage, and review apixaban with senior/haematology advice on reversal if life-threatening bleeding persists.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I will stop the bleeding first: lie her down, leg up and firm pressure directly over the hole.” 2. “Her tachycardia and low blood pressure mean I must assess and resuscitate rather than call this minor blood loss.” 3. “Even after the wound dries, the recurrence risk means immediate vascular referral and written first aid.”

stations.title: Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia

near_match.title: Acute mesenteric ischaemia: recognition, imaging and revascularisation

sections.preamble: B2-222 | Chronic Mesenteric Ischaemia AMaC MRCS Part B • History / vascular applied knowledge • 8 minutes • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required Educational assessment resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only until the assessment is complete.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the vascular surgical trainee assessing a 72-year-old woman referred because she has lost 9 kg in four months and developed abdominal pain after eating. Take a focused history, interpret requested investigations and explain your management plan. Eight-minute station; no physical examination is required. Ask the examiner for findings as needed.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Symptoms: severe cramping epigastric/periumbilical pain beginning 20–40 minutes after meals and lasting 1–2 hours; she now deliberately avoids food. Six months of worsening symptoms; no acute continuous pain, haematemesis or fever. History: smoker, peripheral arterial disease, hypertension, dyslipidaemia; no previous intestinal surgery. She takes a statin but smokes ten cigarettes daily. Examination: BMI 18, BP 142/78, HR 82; thin, soft non-tender abdomen without peritonism; palpable peripheral pulses diminished. Investigations available if requested: Hb 112 g/L, normal lactate, eGFR 63; CT angiogram shows heavily calcified high-grade proximal superior mesenteric artery stenosis and coeliac artery stenosis, patent distal vessels, no bowel wall pneumatosis or free air. Colonoscopy previously normal. The service has a multidisciplinary mesenteric vascular team and endovascular capability.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Patient is anxious because the pain is causing food avoidance and wants a test “that will prove it is not cancer”. If asked, she reports no blood in stool; she is keen to eat normally, worries about invasive treatment and accepts advice about smoking cessation.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the likely diagnosis and why? Chronic mesenteric ischaemia from atherosclerotic mesenteric artery disease, with postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss and compatible CTA; rule out other gastrointestinal and malignant causes. What would you ask about urgently? New persistent severe pain, vomiting, bloody stool, collapse or peritonism, which raise concern for acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia and require emergency escalation. How would you investigate? CTA is first-line anatomical imaging; coordinate appropriate GI workup, assess nutritional state and vascular risk; normal lactate does not exclude chronic disease. How should it be treated? Urgent specialist mesenteric MDT; anatomical revascularisation, usually endovascular stenting when suitable; consider open reconstruction if anatomy or prior treatment makes endovascular approach unsuitable. Optimise nutrition and cardiovascular risk. Would you prescribe meals or weight gain before revascularisation? Do not defer necessary revascularisation simply to improve nutrition; the patient cannot reliably eat, and aggressive feeding may aggravate ischaemia. Coordinate nutritional support. Which vessel is most important? The S
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical problem identification Calls the pattern functional pain without considering vascular aetiology. Names chronic mesenteric ischaemia and associates it with meal-induced demand. Integrates progressive food fear, weight loss and multi-vessel disease while retaining important differentials. Focused history Omits pain–meal relationship and weight loss. Elicits onset after meals, duration, food avoidance and weight change. Quantifies progression, diet reduction, vascular risks and functional impact. Emergency discrimination Offers routine follow-up despite sudden continuous pain or peritonism. Asks about severe unremitting pain, bloody stool, vomiting and collapse. Explicitly separates chronic syndrome from acute-on-chronic infarction and triggers emergency vascular/surgical review. Relevant examination Does not assess stability or abdominal tenderness. Requests observations, abdominal examination and peripheral vascular assessment. Explains that a benign abdomen does not exclude mesenteric vascular disease and checks malnutrition. Investigation interpretation Dismisses arterial lesions as incidental without correlating symptoms. Interprets SMA/
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Discharges a patient with new continuous severe pain or peritonism as uncomplicated chronic mesenteric ischaemia. 2. Interprets a normal lactate as excluding intestinal ischaemia and abandons assessment. 3. Recommends only dietary restriction despite disabling symptoms and critical SMA stenosis. 4. Delays needed revascularisation for prolonged nutritional optimisation despite worsening food fear and weight loss.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient develops sudden severe continuous abdominal pain while awaiting clinic review. Expected: treat as acute-on-chronic mesenteric ischaemia; ABCDE, IV access/bloods including lactate and renal function, urgent senior vascular and general surgical review, emergency CTA if stable enough without delay, resuscitation and immediate revascularisation/operative pathway as required.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should not let a reassuring lactate override this classic symptom pattern or the CTA findings.” 2. “If her pain becomes continuous, I will escalate immediately as possible acute-on-chronic ischaemia.” 3. “I would bring this to the mesenteric MDT promptly rather than trying to make her gain weight before assessing revascularisation.”

stations.title: EVAR or Open Repair: The Consent Discussion

sections.preamble: B2-223 | EVAR or Open Repair: The Consent Discussion AMaC MRCS Part B • Communication / vascular consent • 8 minutes • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required Educational assessment resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Candidate sees Section 1 only until the assessment is complete.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a vascular surgical registrar in clinic. A 70-year-old man with a 5.8 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm wants to know whether to have endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) or open repair. Explain the options and support an informed decision. Eight-minute consultation. The examiner will give the assessment and CT details if requested. Do not quote unsupported personalised mortality percentages.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient: independent 70-year-old, reasonably active, well-controlled hypertension; former smoker. No abdominal or back pain or features of rupture. Aneurysm measured 5.8 cm maximal diameter on CTA. CTA: standard infrarenal anatomy suitable for conventional EVAR; adequate proximal neck, access vessels suitable, no need for complex fenestrated graft; anatomy also technically suitable for elective open repair. Pre-operative: creatinine 95 µmol/L, eGFR 72; no known coronary disease; reasonable exercise tolerance. Final fitness and individualised mortality estimates not yet formally determined. The patient values long-term durability but also hopes for a quicker return home. Ask candidates to explain uncertainty and the importance of individual risk assessment.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The patient begins: “Keyhole surgery has to be safer. Can I just choose that and forget about the aneurysm?” If prompted he asks about stent leakage, renal injury, stroke/heart attack, major bleeding, bowel problems, impotence, ongoing scans and whether a second operation may be needed. His priority is avoiding repeat procedures, even at the cost of longer initial recovery; he wants his partner involved before deciding.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Why discuss repair at all? The aneurysm is above the usual elective threshold for men and rupture risk rises with size, but individual anatomy, health and wishes guide the repair decision. Explain EVAR in ordinary language. A fabric-covered stent graft is inserted through groin arteries to exclude the aneurysm sac; less invasive, usually shorter initial admission and recovery; late endoleak, migration, sac enlargement and reintervention can occur. Explain open repair. Abdominal incision and aortic clamping followed by surgical graft replacement; greater immediate physiological insult, more painful and slower recovery; often stronger long-term durability with a different follow-up burden. What changes the choice? CTA neck/access and aortic anatomy, frailty and cardiopulmonary risk, life expectancy, patient preference, centre experience and capacity for surveillance. What if he rejects lifelong checks? Explain EVAR requires long-term imaging surveillance because late complications can be silent; lack of ability or willingness to attend surveillance strongly affects suitability and shared choice. What serious complications must be discussed? Death, MI, stroke, bleeding/transfusion, ki
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Indication and context Cannot explain why a 5.8 cm AAA merits discussion of elective repair. Explains elective repair rationale and confirms symptom status. Frames rupture risk against operative risk and introduces surveillance as an alternative where appropriate. Patient priorities Gives a predetermined recommendation without asking what matters to the patient. Elicits priorities for recovery, durability and follow-up. Uses the stated preference for fewer repeat procedures to personalise the comparison. EVAR procedure Calls EVAR a cure without explaining a stent graft. Explains femoral access, endograft exclusion and shorter early recovery. Explains anatomy dependence, endoleak, migration and sac monitoring in plain language. Open procedure Describes open repair inaccurately as keyhole or minor surgery. Explains abdominal exposure, aortic clamp and surgical graft with longer recovery. Balances greater initial physiological burden against durability and long-term outcomes. Perioperative risk Omits death, MI, bleeding or renal complications entirely. Discusses major mortality, cardiovascular, bleeding and organ injury risks in both approaches. Adds
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Promises EVAR is risk-free or eliminates the need for further imaging. 2. Fails to mention material risk of death or major cardiovascular complications of elective AAA repair. 3. Recommends EVAR without considering anatomic eligibility or long-term surveillance capability. 4. Pressures the patient into consent without discussing the open alternative or eliciting their preferences.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The patient says he plans to emigrate soon and will not attend any follow-up scans. Expected: acknowledge preference; explain silent late EVAR complications and the necessity of organised lifelong imaging; discuss how this shifts relative suitability toward open repair if fitness and anatomy allow, coordinate records/arrangements with destination care and avoid forcing a choice.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should correct my wording: EVAR offers faster early recovery, but the graft requires long-term checks.” 2. “I cannot give you an honest personal risk figure until our team completes your risk assessment.” 3. “You said avoiding repeat treatment matters most; we should discuss how that changes the balance between EVAR and open repair.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-224 Endoleak After EVAR Data interpretation / vascular | 8-minute simulated station | Examiner educational draft | Clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man after elective infrarenal EVAR 18 months ago. A surveillance CT angiogram report shows contrast in the aneurysm sac and the sac has enlarged. Interpret the report, classify the endoleak and outline safe management. No images are supplied.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including findings on: Patient clinically well, BP 132/78, pulse 76. EVAR performed for 62-mm AAA. CT report: patent bifurcated endograft; contrast track adjacent to the proximal graft attachment entering sac on arterial phase; no lumbar or inferior mesenteric artery feeder; sac 65 mm, previously 58 mm six months earlier; no retroperitoneal haemorrhage. This is type Ia endoleak with sac expansion. If asked: creatinine 105 μmol/L; no fever, abdominal/back pain or leg ischaemia. Previous scan showed satisfactory proximal seal. The examiner must not assume this is a benign type II endoleak.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor essential. If a communication segment is used, patient asks: “I feel fine. Why do I need another procedure?” Response should explain pressurisation/rupture risk in plain language without predicting imminent rupture.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: “Classify endoleaks.” Type I (attachment-zone seal failure: Ia proximal/Ib distal), II (retrograde branch flow), III (component separation or graft fabric defect), IV (graft porosity, usually early), V/endotension (sac expansion without demonstrable leak). Prompt 2: “What does this CT show?” Correctly names proximal type Ia rather than type II; highlights 7-mm sac growth over six months. Prompt 3: “What next?” Same-day senior aortic/vascular review, assessment of symptoms and imaging, urgent planning for correction of high-pressure leak; options depend on neck anatomy and available expertise (proximal cuff, endoanchors/complex endovascular revision or open conversion). Prompt 4: “What about type II?” Observe selected cases if sac stable; evaluate and consider targeted treatment when there is meaningful sac expansion and type I/III have been excluded. Prompt 5: “How monitor?” Review prior CTs, endograft integrity, renal function, CTA/duplex/contrast-enhanced ultrasound per specialist surveillance plan; ongoing lifelong imaging after EVAR.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial triage Treats scan as routine without asking about pain, collapse or vitals. Checks stability, abdominal/back pain, haemodynamics. Explicitly distinguishes stable surveillance finding from symptomatic leak or suspected rupture and prioritises accordingly. Report reading Misses proximal contrast tracking or calls leak type II. Localises leak at proximal sealing zone. Links arterial-phase proximal track and absent branch feeder to type Ia mechanism. Classification Cannot distinguish type I, II and III. Correctly describes types I–V in basic terms. Explains Ia/Ib, component/fabric defects and limits of type V diagnosis. Risk interpretation Ignores 58-to-65-mm sac change. Recognises 7-mm expansion as clinically significant. Explains persistent systemic sac pressurisation and risk without making unjustified imminence claims. Further assessment Omits prior imaging, renal function and graft details. Requests previous imaging, anatomy and renal function. Checks attachment zones, migration, overlap, neck anatomy and alternative leak sources with imaging team. Management choice Prescribes observation alone for confirmed Ia. Seeks urgent specialist pl
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1 — Labels the described proximal attachment leak as harmless type II and discharges without vascular review. CF2 — Reassures that an expanding aneurysm sac needs no further imaging or intervention. CF3 — Ignores new abdominal/back pain or hypotension and fails to assess for rupture urgently. CF4 — Recommends embolising presumed lumbar feeders without recognising/excluding the type I attachment defect.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: During discussion he develops sudden severe back pain and BP falls to 88/54. Expected: immediately activate emergency vascular/major haemorrhage response, ABCDE, blood access and crossmatch, resuscitate appropriately while arranging immediate aortic imaging only if stability permits, and expedite definitive haemorrhage control; do not persist with routine surveillance planning.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I misidentified the site: contrast tracks along the proximal seal, so this is type Ia, not type II.” “The important change is sac growth: I would seek urgent aortic-team review rather than simply book routine annual surveillance.” “If symptoms or haemodynamics deteriorate, I will switch at once to a suspected rupture pathway and call the vascular consultant and anaesthetist.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS PART B | B2-225 Groin Abscess in a Person Who Injects Drugs Critical care / vascular | 8-minute simulated station | Examiner educational draft | Clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the general surgical registrar in the emergency department. A 36-year-old man who injects drugs presents with a hot, painful, swollen right groin. ED requests incision and drainage of a presumed abscess. Explain your immediate assessment, investigations and management.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including findings on: On request: temperature 38.6°C, pulse 118, BP 102/64, respiratory rate 23; 6-cm tender erythematous groin swelling with overlying puncture marks, mild fluctuance and a small ooze; no unequivocal pulsation. Foot warm, dorsalis pedis palpable but weaker than contralateral side; capillary refill 3 seconds. Haemoglobin 105 g/L, WCC 17, CRP 185, lactate 2.9. Ultrasound Doppler if requested: turbulent bidirectional flow in a sac continuous with the common femoral artery, surrounding heterogeneous collection. CTA if stable: 3.5-cm infected common femoral pseudoaneurysm with perivascular inflammatory change. No prior operative vascular graft. Blood cultures not yet taken. No airway compromise. A non-pulsatile swelling does NOT exclude arterial involvement.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: An actor is optional; worried and defensive, asks for “just a quick cut to let pus out”. The candidate should use non-stigmatising language, explain that opening the swelling might cause catastrophic bleeding, obtain consent for urgent imaging and vascular input.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: “What could be hidden here?” An infected femoral pseudoaneurysm, potentially with adjacent abscess, DVT, cellulitis, necrotising infection; look for bleeding/sepsis/limb ischaemia. Prompt 2: “Can you drain it?” No incision/needle aspiration into the groin lesion before excluding arterial pathology and securing a vascular plan. Prompt 3: “Immediate measures?” ABCDE, monitor, senior ED/vascular and anaesthetic support, two IV lines, FBC/U&E/coagulation/crossmatch/lactate, blood cultures if not delaying treatment, prompt IV antibiotics according to local severe infection policy, analgesia, resuscitation and sepsis reassessment. Prompt 4: “Imaging?” Immediate Doppler duplex where available; CTA defines extent and operative anatomy in stable patients. If haemodynamically unstable, do not delay haemorrhage control for CT. Prompt 5: “Definitive care?” Urgent vascular theatre planning, proximal/distal control, infected tissue debridement and arterial management (ligation with or without revascularisation according to perfusion, infection and anatomy). Obtain tissue cultures; monitor limb perfusion and infection markers.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Agrees to bedside drainage on referral alone. Pauses procedure and flags arterial pseudoaneurysm risk. Makes a clear no-incision/no-aspiration instruction and summons vascular support. ABCDE/sepsis Ignores tachycardia, fever and borderline pressure. Assesses observations, perfusion, lactate and organ dysfunction. Repeatedly reassesses shock, haemorrhage and sepsis and escalates early to senior/critical care. Focused history Asks only when swelling began. Asks about injection, bleeding, fever, previous vascular procedures and leg symptoms. Elicits arterial puncture history, preceding sentinel bleeds, antibiotic history and blood-borne infection considerations sensitively. Vascular examination Omits distal perfusion and misuses absence of pulsation to exclude pseudoaneurysm. Assesses groin without manipulation, feet, pulses and neurological status. Documents side-to-side pulses, capillary refill and evolving threatened-limb findings. Differential Names uncomplicated abscess only. Includes infected femoral pseudoaneurysm and adjacent infection. Adds DVT, necrotising infection and other vascular complications while prioritising arteria
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: CF1 — Cuts into or aspirates the mass before excluding an arterial pseudoaneurysm. CF2 — Sends the septic patient home with oral antibiotics and no vascular assessment. CF3 — Treats loss of distal pulses or active haemorrhage as routine cellulitis rather than immediate vascular emergency. CF4 — Insists upon CTA during haemodynamic collapse, delaying immediate haemorrhage control and senior vascular help.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: While the patient waits for a scan the groin starts briskly bleeding and SBP falls to 78 mmHg. Expected: activate major haemorrhage and emergency vascular response, apply firm direct local pressure with trained assistance, initiate resuscitation and blood products per protocol, and urgently transfer for proximal vascular control/definitive operation; no blind instrument probing or incision.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I need to stop: this could be an infected false aneurysm and must not be incised as a simple abscess.” “Even without obvious pulsation, Doppler evidence of arterial communication demands immediate vascular involvement.” “The patient is deteriorating: I will initiate the major haemorrhage pathway and expedite operative vascular control now.”

stations.title: Varicose Veins in Pregnancy and Venous Symptoms

sections.preamble: B2-226 | Varicose Veins in Pregnancy and Venous Symptoms AMaC MRCS PART B • Communication / vascular • 8-minute station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate in a vascular clinic. A 30-year-old woman at 27 weeks of an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy attends with increasingly prominent right-leg varicose veins, aching and evening ankle swelling. Explain your assessment and management to the patient. You have 8 minutes. No physical examination is required; tell the examiner what you would look for.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient is haemodynamically stable; no breathlessness, chest pain, fever, trauma, previous DVT or bleeding. No personal VTE history, thrombophilia or current anticoagulation. Right medial-calf varicosities and mild dependent ankle oedema; no erythema, palpable tender cord, ulcers, skin pigmentation or focal calf tenderness. Distal pulses and capillary refill normal. Baby moving normally. No obstetric concerns; routine antenatal visits are up to date. No imaging is available at station opening. If asked about unilateral acute deterioration: no current sudden increase in swelling; an urgent pregnancy DVT pathway is needed if it develops.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are worried that the veins will burst, harm the baby or require an operation while pregnant. Ask: “Can I have laser treatment now?” and “Will stockings prevent a clot?” If reassured too quickly, ask: “My friend had a blood clot when pregnant; how would I know?” You would prefer symptom control and a clear plan after delivery.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What history?” Expected: onset/trend, aching, swelling, skin changes, bleeding, tender cord, prior VTE, family history, mobility, obstetric risk factors; screen DVT/PE symptoms. Prompt: “What would you examine?” Expected: inspect standing when feasible, distribution/skin changes, oedema and tenderness, peripheral pulses; check for features suggesting DVT. Prompt: “Need duplex today?” Expected: no routine urgent duplex for uncomplicated varices, but obtain venous duplex for suspicion of thrombosis, atypical findings, or later treatment planning. Prompt: “Treatment in pregnancy?” Expected: explain pregnancy-related venous pressure/hormonal changes, leg elevation, activity/calf-pump, avoid prolonged standing, properly fitted compression hosiery for swelling symptoms; no routine intervention. Prompt: “After delivery?” Expected: reassess persistent symptomatic disease and consider vascular duplex and intervention according to reflux anatomy; no promise of complete spontaneous resolution.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Opening and agenda: Ignores pregnancy concerns and begins offering a procedure. Introduces role, checks gestation and explores the main symptom and worry. Acknowledges both quality-of-life and fetal-safety concerns and agrees a focused plan.
sections.2. Venous symptom history: Asks only whether veins look unsightly. Elicits pain, swelling, pattern, bleeding and skin changes. Also separates chronic dependence-related symptoms from abrupt or atypical change.
sections.3. Thromboembolic safety: Does not ask about unilateral painful swelling or chest symptoms. Screens for DVT and pulmonary embolism red flags. Links red flags to immediate obstetric/acute investigation and escalation.

stations.title: Planning Vascular Access for Dialysis

sections.preamble: B2-227 | Planning Vascular Access for Dialysis AMaC MRCS PART B • Communication / vascular access • 8-minute station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are seeing a 58-year-old right-handed man with progressive chronic kidney disease. Renal replacement therapy with haemodialysis is expected within the coming months. Explain the assessment and planning of vascular access. You have 8 minutes. Address the patient’s questions and describe the key examination and investigations to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m² with downward trend; dialysis timing to be decided by renal team based on clinical indications. No immediate urgent dialysis indication today. Type 2 diabetes and hypertension; independent, reasonable anticipated duration of HD. Renal team has discussed transplantation and home therapies. Right-hand dominant; past peripheral IV cannulation in both arms, no PICC or subclavian catheter, no previous central venous thrombosis or pacemaker. Bilateral radial/ulnar pulses present, warm hands, no arm oedema, no infection, no gross venous abnormality. Vein mapping not yet performed.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are a right-handed mechanic who wants to keep working and asks: “Can’t you just use a line in my neck? I dislike needles.” Ask whether a fistula works immediately, whether it will change your hand strength and what happens if it fails. You agree to assessment if options and trade-offs are explained without being pressured.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What access choices?” Expected: native AV fistula, prosthetic AV graft, tunnelled dialysis catheter; sometimes PD or transplantation may change access needs. Avoid a universally rigid hierarchy. Prompt: “What assessment?” Expected: dialysis life-plan, preferred arm/hand dominance, vascular access history, pulse and Allen/perfusion assessment as relevant, limb veins, central venous disease signs, bilateral duplex mapping where appropriate. Prompt: “Which arm?” Expected: non-dominant arm often preferred if anatomy suitable, but not at expense of reliable access; choose distal site where feasible, individualise with duplex and goals. Prompt: “When ready?” Expected: native fistula requires maturation over weeks to months and may never mature; graft use and timing vary by graft type; catheter may be needed as a bridge if dialysis begins before durable access is usable. Prompt: “Complications?” Expected: nonmaturation, stenosis, thrombosis, infection, bleeding, steal-related hand ischaemia, high-flow heart strain; catheter infection and central venous stenosis.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Opening and preferences: Tells the patient an access type without discussing work or fears. Checks patient understanding, dominant arm, needle concerns and life goals. Explores transplant plans, dialysis modality and priorities before choosing access.
sections.2. Renal and access planning: Assumes eGFR alone mandates dialysis or an immediate central line. Reviews anticipated dialysis timing, trajectory and renal team plan. Establishes an access plan with contingency if clinical dialysis need changes.
sections.3. Prior access history: Does not ask about previous central lines or devices. Asks about past cannulation, PICCs, CVCs, pacemaker and arm swelling. Uses historical venous injury to guide central outflow assessment and site selection.

stations.title: Rectus Sheath Haematoma on Anticoagulants

sections.preamble: B2-228 | Rectus Sheath Haematoma on Anticoagulants AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / acute surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman with new severe left lower abdominal pain after a coughing episode. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Explain your assessment, investigations and management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings on request: Initial observations: BP 104/68 mmHg, HR 108/min, RR 20/min, SpO₂ 97%, temperature 36.7°C. Repeat after 20 minutes: BP 88/54, HR 122. Examination if requested: localised tender left lower abdominal-wall swelling, faint bruising, no clear generalised peritonism; possible positive Carnett sign. Bloods: Hb 108 g/L (previous 133), platelets 212 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 110 µmol/L. Anticoagulant taken this morning. Contrast CT: 10 cm left rectus sheath haematoma below arcuate line, arterial contrast blush arising near inferior epigastric territory. If resuscitated: IR team available for angiography and embolisation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor is anxious about sudden pain and asks whether this is “internal bleeding” and whether stopping apixaban could cause a stroke. If asked about medical background: hypertension, AF, chronic cough, no recent surgery or trauma.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is your differential? EXPECT: Rectus sheath haematoma; also exclude intra-abdominal haemorrhage, diverticulitis and other acute abdomen causes. What investigation establishes extent? EXPECT: Contrast CT, with angiographic protocol if ongoing active haemorrhage is suspected. What changes when BP falls? EXPECT: Call senior, ABCDE, IV access, blood group and crossmatch, haemorrhage resuscitation, discuss anticoagulant reversal and urgent IR. What if no active blush and stable Hb? EXPECT: Conservative management with analgesia, observation and serial haemoglobin. Would you operate first? EXPECT: Usually not; embolisation is generally preferred for persistent arterial bleeding when feasible.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Attributes painful mass to appendicitis without considering abdominal-wall bleeding. Identifies rectus sheath haematoma in anticoagulated patient with focal pain. Localises swelling to abdominal wall and relates onset after cough to epigastric-vessel injury. Initial assessment Does not check blood pressure or signs of shock. Requests ABCDE, observations, perfusion and repeated abdominal assessment. Recognises occult haemorrhage despite initially modest pulse change; trends shock index and urine output. Targeted history Omits anticoagulant identity and last dose. Asks anticoagulant, indication, last dose, trauma/cough and preceding abdominal surgery. Also checks concurrent antiplatelets, renal function, bleeding history and thrombotic risk of interruption. Examination Does not assess tenderness or abdominal-wall location. Examines mass, bruising, peritonism and Carnett sign when safe. Distinguishes abdominal-wall mass from intra-abdominal signs; avoids relying on Carnett sign to exclude other emergencies. Investigations Relies on ultrasound despite deterioration. Orders FBC/serial Hb, coagulation profile, renal function, group and crossm
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fails to recognise hypotension and falling haemoglobin as significant haemorrhage. Continues apixaban despite active major bleeding. Delays resuscitation while arranging non-urgent imaging in unstable patient. Does not escalate active contrast extravasation with deterioration for urgent haemostatic intervention.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: after CT, BP drops to 76/42 and the patient becomes confused. Expected: declare major haemorrhage, senior/anaesthetic/IR escalation, activate local massive transfusion pathway, initiate supportive resuscitation, stop anticoagulant and seek urgent reversal advice, proceed to haemostasis without avoidable delay.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I initially underestimated the swelling; the falling blood pressure and haemoglobin make active haemorrhage my immediate priority.” “The arterial blush requires urgent interventional radiology discussion while I continue haemorrhage resuscitation.” “I will stop apixaban now and request the local reversal protocol and haematology support; restart will be reconsidered after bleeding control.”

stations.title: Urethral and Bladder Injury with a Pelvic Fracture

sections.preamble: B2-229 | Urethral and Bladder Injury with a Pelvic Fracture AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / trauma urology • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 32-year-old man has a pelvic ring fracture after a motorcycle collision. The trauma nurse notices blood at the urethral meatus and asks you to insert a catheter for output monitoring. Explain your immediate actions, diagnostic pathway and management of possible urethral and bladder injury.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings on request: Airway patent, GCS 15; BP 96/60, HR 116/min; pelvic binder in situ. Pelvic fracture is known from initial imaging. On inspection: meatal blood, perineal bruising, suprapubic tenderness and inability to void. After stabilisation: retrograde urethrogram shows contrast extravasation at membranous urethra with no proximal bladder filling, suspicious for major posterior urethral disruption. After urology-supervised urinary diversion: gross haematuria is noted. Active retrograde CT cystogram shows extraperitoneal leak around bladder base without intraperitoneal contrast. Further CT shows no bladder neck breach or intraluminal bone fragment. The pelvic fracture requires fixation planning.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No live patient actor is needed; trauma nurse asks: “We need urine output. Can I pass a Foley now?” If discussing with patient: explain that a urinary drainage tube may need insertion above the pubic bone under specialist direction and that follow-up is essential.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What do you tell the nurse? EXPECT: Do not pass a blind urethral catheter with meatal blood and suspected urethral injury. What is first in a shocked trauma patient? EXPECT: ABCDE and haemorrhage control, pelvic binder and senior trauma escalation; defer definitive urethral imaging until stable. How do you assess the urethra? EXPECT: Retrograde urethrography or urology-directed urethroscopy. How is bladder injury excluded? EXPECT: Retrograde CT cystography with active filling; passive IV contrast CT is inadequate. How does leak location alter treatment? EXPECT: Blunt intraperitoneal rupture needs repair; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture usually drainage; complicated extraperitoneal rupture requires surgical assessment and often repair.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Trauma priorities Prioritises catheterising over control of pelvic haemorrhage. Uses ATLS/ABCDE, pelvic binder as indicated and trauma-team escalation. Coordinates haemorrhage control, transfusion and urology while protecting spine and pelvis. Recognition Ignores blood at urethral meatus. Suspects posterior urethral injury in pelvic fracture with meatal blood. Distinguishes associated bladder injury when visible haematuria and suprapubic pain are present. Focused examination Repeatedly performs painful pelvic springing or aggressive rectal exam. Inspects meatus, perineum, scrotum, abdomen and notes urinary retention. Documents external genital and associated rectal injury concerns without delaying resuscitation. Safe catheter policy Passes Foley blindly despite meatal bleeding. Avoids blind urethral catheterisation pending injury assessment. Requests urology-led drainage strategy, considering specialist-guided catheter or suprapubic diversion. Urethral imaging Asks for routine CT abdomen to exclude urethral injury. Requests retrograde urethrogram once haemodynamically stable. Explains that retrograde urethrogram distinguishes partial and complete d
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Inserts a blind transurethral catheter despite blood at the meatus and suspicion of disruption. Delays haemorrhage resuscitation and pelvic fracture stabilisation to undertake urinary imaging. Accepts a routine IV-contrast CT as excluding bladder rupture despite pelvic fracture and gross haematuria. Fails to refer confirmed intraperitoneal bladder rupture for operative repair.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: orthopaedics plans open pelvic fixation and the CT cystogram shows an extraperitoneal leak adjacent to a fragment penetrating the bladder. Expected: urgent joint urology–orthopaedics discussion; complicated extraperitoneal injury warrants repair rather than simple prolonged drainage, coordinated with fixation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The meatal blood changes the catheter plan: I will not make a blind attempt, and I am calling urology.” “The ordinary trauma CT does not adequately test the bladder; he needs retrograde contrast cystography once safe.” “This is no longer a simple extraperitoneal injury because of the penetrating bone fragment; operative repair should be planned with the pelvic team.”

stations.title: Consent for Vasectomy

sections.preamble: B2-230 | Consent for Vasectomy AMaC MRCS Part B • Communication • 8-minute station • Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical SHO in a urology clinic. Mr Lewis, 35, requests vasectomy. He and his partner have two children. Explain the operation, alternatives, material risks, and aftercare and obtain an informed decision. Do not perform the procedure.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including requested f: Assess consent, rather than a memorised complication list. The patient is well, has no previous scrotal operations or relevant medication, and is able to give informed consent. If asked, both testes are descended; the vasa are palpable. He asks whether he can stop contraception immediately. If the candidate asks about future children: he says he is certain today but asks if reversal is always successful. If asked about previous surgery: none.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Mr Lewis: calm, understands that this is intended to be permanent. At minute 3 ask: “Will I still ejaculate and have normal sex?” At minute 5 ask: “Can we stop using condoms tonight?” If uncertainty is explored, admit you worry about changing your mind if family circumstances change.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: “What exactly is divided?” Expected: both vasa deferentia isolated and interrupted, usually using local anaesthetic; sperm continues to be produced but is not present in the ejaculate after clearance. Prompt 2: “What if he later requests another child?” Expected: reversal or sperm retrieval/assisted reproduction may be possible but cannot be guaranteed; counsel as permanent; sperm storage can be discussed before treatment. Prompt 3: “What makes the operation a success?” Expected: post-vasectomy semen analysis and explicit clinician clearance, not passage of time alone.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Purpose and choice Calls vasectomy temporary or does not ask why now. Checks desire for permanent contraception and current understanding. Elicits future-family uncertainty, voluntariness and factors warranting deferral. Procedure Says testes are removed or hormonal production stops. Describes bilateral vas interruption under local anaesthetic. Explains no-scalpel access can be used and occlusion technique varies. Permanence Guarantees fertility restoration after reversal. Counsels permanent; reversal may fail. Discusses future regret and fertility preservation options without pressuring. Alternatives Fails to mention another contraceptive option. Mentions condoms and reversible partner options. Checks suitability and preference for ongoing reversible methods. Immediate risks Denies infection or bleeding risk. Discusses bruising, haematoma, infection and short-term pain. Explains warning signs of expanding swelling, fever, discharge. Long-term risks Assures chronic pain or late failure never occurs. Explains uncommon persistent pain and rare recanalisation/pregnancy. Distinguishes sperm granuloma from important persistent pain; avoids misleading pr
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Promises immediate sterility or tells him to stop other contraception before formal semen-test clearance. 2. States reversal is reliably successful or that vasectomy is readily reversible, without correcting the assertion. 3. Omits any discussion of failure/recanalisation and possibility of unintended pregnancy when obtaining consent. 4. Proceeds despite the patient explicitly expressing unresolved doubt about permanency rather than pausing the consent process.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient says: “My partner is pregnant—should I book it for next week in case something changes?” Expected: explore whether the decision is freely made and settled; avoid coercion; discuss deferring a permanent intervention while there is meaningful uncertainty. There is no universal categorical ban on vasectomy during pregnancy.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I was unclear: the operation does not make you sterile immediately; please use contraception until your semen test is checked and you receive clearance.” “I should correct that: reversal is not guaranteed, so we should plan on vasectomy being permanent.” “Your hesitation matters; we can pause today rather than asking you to consent under pressure.”

stations.title: Varicocele

sections.preamble: B2-231 | Varicocele AMaC MRCS Part B • Examination / applied knowledge • 8-minute station • Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in an outpatient examination station. A 28-year-old man has a painless left-sided scrotal swelling and has recently started fertility investigations. Demonstrate and describe a focused examination of a suspected varicocele, give differentials, investigations and management. A simulated patient is available; do not perform intimate examination without explicit permission.
sections.2. Examiner brief (including requested f: On request: afebrile, no acute pain. Exam performed with consent, chaperone offered, privacy and warm room. Standing: soft compressible “bag of worms” above left testis, more evident with Valsalva. Lying supine: swelling largely reduces. Left testis slightly smaller than right; both testes smooth, with no hard intratesticular mass. No right varicocele. Abdomen unremarkable. If asked: 18 months of attempting conception, partner being investigated; preliminary semen analysis shows reduced concentration, repeat pending.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor: anxious that the lump might be cancer. If asked, no sudden pain, urinary symptoms, haematuria, fever or previous surgery. At 5 minutes ask “Does this mean I need an operation to have children?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: “Grade and describe.” Expected: clinical varicocele felt standing/with Valsalva; grades I palpated only on Valsalva, II palpable without Valsalva, III visible; this scenario is grade II. Prompt 2: “When is ultrasound appropriate?” Expected: atypical, uncertain examination, testicular volume assessment, suspected mass or infertility work-up; Doppler can document venous reflux but is not mandatory for every clear clinical varicocele. Prompt 3: “What if the lump appears suddenly on the right and does not reduce lying down?” Expected: evaluate for secondary causes/abdominal or retroperitoneal pathology rather than simply labelling benign disease; isolated right-sided varicocele alone does not automatically establish a renal tumour.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Preparation / dignity Begins exposure with no consent or privacy. Explains sensitive examination, seeks consent and offers chaperone. Checks comfort, uses minimal exposure and names each step in advance. Standing inspection Examines only supine; misses dynamic swelling. Inspects scrotum and groins with patient standing. Documents visible asymmetry and visible versus palpable venous dilation. Palpation / Valsalva Never palpates spermatic cord or asks for strain. Palpates pampiniform plexus above testis with and without Valsalva. Distinguishes compressible cord veins from a discrete solid lesion. Supine comparison Fails to check whether lesion reduces lying down. Re-examines supine and documents decompression. Flags a non-reducing or sudden atypical swelling for reassessment. Testis / differentials Fails to palpate testes and misses intratesticular mass. Palpates both testes and distinguishes hydrocele, hernia, epididymal lesion. Assesses relative testicular volume, excludes suspicious mass and notes alternative diagnoses. Classification Calls all scrotal swelling varicocele grade III. Describes grade I, II and III clinical varicoceles correctly. Lab
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Ignores sudden severe scrotal pain and delays assessment for testicular torsion in a changed scenario. 2. Detects a hard intratesticular mass but reassures it is just a varicocele, with no urgent ultrasound/referral. 3. Recommends routine varicocelectomy for a subclinical varicocele or normal semen parameters without individualised indication. 4. Gives categorical reassurance that an acute non-reducing new right-sided varicocele cannot reflect secondary pathology, without assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The examiner adds: “A new swelling was seen only on the right in a 52-year-old and remains tense when supine.” Expected: re-examine testes/abdomen; assess sudden onset, systemic/renal symptoms; arrange targeted imaging and urology review based on suspicious features, avoiding an unsupported blanket claim of renal cancer.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “A varicocele is a likely cause of the swelling, but I will examine both testes and exclude a separate testicular mass.” “Fertility treatment is not automatic: I need repeat semen testing and the couple’s full assessment before recommending repair.” “Because this is new, atypical and does not decompress on lying down, I would investigate a secondary cause rather than dismiss it.”

stations.title: A Catheter That Is Not Draining

near_match.title: The Post-operative Catheter That Is Not Draining / System, Bladder, Then Patient

sections.preamble: B2-232 | A Catheter That Is Not Draining AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / acute urology • 8-minute simulated station • Draft requiring specialist clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical SHO reviewing a 76-year-old man after colorectal surgery. His urethral Foley catheter has drained no urine for four hours. The nurse reports increasing suprapubic discomfort. Explain and demonstrate verbally your immediate assessment and management to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief: Simulated ward consultation; examine observations, inspect drainage circuit, assess bladder volume and renal function. Candidate must differentiate catheter obstruction from genuine oliguria or anuria. No physical catheter manipulation is required.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Anxious and uncomfortable; asks whether his kidneys have stopped working. If asked, he has no flank pain or fever and has not seen blood in the bag.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Vital signs: HR 96/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 17/min, temperature 37.0°C; no overt shock. Output and context: 400 mL over prior eight hours, none during last four; 70 kg; receiving maintenance IV fluids; no diuretics. Circuit inspection: Drainage bag is below bladder but tubing has a tight kink under the bed rail; bag is not full. After unkinking: Still no output after several minutes and lower abdominal discomfort persists. Bladder scan: Approximately 650 mL retained; verify scan in context if ascites or technical uncertainty. Catheter details: Inserted two days ago without difficulty; no traumatic insertion history; no visible haematuria. After safe replacement by trained clinician: 650 mL clear urine drains, discomfort resolves; monitor ongoing output and reassess cause. Curveball: If instead scan reveals an empty bladder (~25 mL), think true oliguria/AKI, not a blocked catheter.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical priority Dismisses absent output or waits for the next shift. Reviews patient promptly, assesses pain, vital signs and urine-output timeline. Identifies retention and acute renal compromise as alternative urgent pathways and identifies red flags. Focused history Does not ask about baseline drainage or timing. Elicits catheter insertion, prior output, pain, haematuria and fluid intake. Asks about surgery, medicines, fluid losses, baseline renal function and previous catheter difficulty. System assessment Assumes catheter failure without checking circulation. Checks perfusion, volume status, bladder distension and possible sepsis. Integrates examination with fluid balance and identifies hypotension or peritonism needing immediate escalation. Mechanical inspection Immediately replaces catheter without inspecting tubing. Checks clamps, kinks, bag height, fullness and external dislodgement. Corrects mechanical issues while preserving closed system and reassesses drainage response. Investigations Neither scans bladder nor requests renal tests when indicated. Uses bladder scan to distinguish retention from low urine production; reviews U&E/creati
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Forces irrigation or catheter insertion against pain/resistance or inflates a balloon without confirmed safe placement. 2. Ignores signs of haemodynamic instability, sepsis or evolving AKI while focusing only on the bag. 3. Treats a near-empty bladder scan as catheter blockage and neglects genuine oliguria. 4. Leaves a painful, distended bladder with no drainage or urgent escalation plan.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: The bladder scan is repeated and reads 25 mL, yet there is still no urine output. Expected response: Abandon the assumption of mechanical retention; assess haemodynamics and volume, check bloods including creatinine/potassium, evaluate sepsis and urinary obstruction where indicated, monitor, and urgently escalate persistent oliguria.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I have checked the tube but no urine is draining; I will scan the bladder now to distinguish retention from poor urine production.” 2. “There is retained urine and the catheter may be blocked; I will arrange a sterile replacement by a competent practitioner, not force a flush.” 3. “The bladder is empty, so I am changing course: this is possible AKI or systemic hypoperfusion and needs urgent review.”

stations.title: Nocturia in an Older Man

sections.preamble: B2-234 | Nocturia in an Older Man AMaC MRCS Part B • History / applied knowledge • 8-minute simulation • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 72-year-old man attends the urology clinic because he wakes four times nightly to pass urine. He assumes he needs prostate surgery. Take a focused history and explain your assessment and initial management to the examiner. You are not required to examine a real patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Give history only when elicited. Candidate must distinguish nocturnal polyuria, small bladder capacity, global polyuria and disturbed sleep, rather than presume bladder outlet obstruction. • Four voids/night for eight months; large-volume voids; daytime frequency six times, no weak stream or hesitancy. • Drinks two mugs of tea after 8 pm; takes furosemide at 6 pm; dependent ankle oedema by evening. • No dysuria, visible haematuria, retention, recurrent UTI or fever. No weight loss or neurological symptoms. • Known heart failure, treated hypertension; spouse reports snoring and witnessed apnoeas. • Urine dip negative for blood, glucose and infection; renal function currently stable; no palpable bladder. • Three-day chart: 24-hour urine 1900 mL; urine passed from sleep onset to final awakening plus first morning void 850 mL: nocturnal fraction 45%; functional void volumes typically 250–350 mL.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Concerned that prostate enlargement means an operation. If asked: disturbed sleep from frequent urination; wants fewer nighttime trips and to avoid medication harm.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What should you ask? — Quantify nocturia, volumes, urgency, weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying; enquire fluid/caffeine/alcohol timing, diuretics, ankle swelling, diabetes, sleep apnoea, sleep disturbance and red flags. What investigation changes management most? — A three-day frequency–volume chart including first morning void, total output, nocturnal output and void volumes; use a symptom score and urinalysis alongside it. Interpret the diary. — 850/1900 = 45% nocturnal urine, supporting nocturnal polyuria in this 72-year-old (conventional >33% for older adults); volumes do not suggest markedly reduced bladder capacity. First-line plan? — Discuss evening fluids and caffeine, sleep/OSA and heart-failure optimisation with the responsible clinician, review late diuretic timing safely, manage oedema, falls risk and any concurrent LUTS. Would you prescribe desmopressin now? — No automatic prescription: older age and heart failure raise hyponatraemia/fluid-retention risks; specialist-selected use requires checking contraindications and sodium monitoring.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Focused nocturia characterisation Does not establish night void frequency or duration Asks nocturnal frequency, duration, sleep interruption and bother Clarifies first-morning void, sleep-related awakenings and functional impact Lower urinary tract history Assumes obstruction without asking voiding symptoms Elicits storage and voiding symptoms and incomplete emptying Relates voided volume, urgency and obstructive symptoms to possible mixed mechanisms Systemic/sleep history Misses oedema, diuretics and snoring Asks oedema, heart failure, diabetes, sleep apnoea and diuretic timing Connects recumbent fluid redistribution and sleep apnoea with nocturnal diuresis Safety/red flags Omits blood in urine and retention history Screens haematuria, dysuria, retention, fever and systemic concerns Defines urgency of referral for visible haematuria or acute retention Diary interpretation Labels all nighttime voiding as prostate enlargement Requests three-day frequency–volume diary and differentiates causes Calculates 45% nocturnal fraction and explains large versus small void patterns Physical assessment Omits examination entirely States abdominal/bladder, extern
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Recommends prostate surgery purely on the basis of nocturia without identifying its cause. 2. Prescribes desmopressin uncritically despite heart failure without assessing contraindications or sodium risk. 3. Ignores visible haematuria or acute urinary retention when disclosed. 4. Stops or alters heart-failure diuretic treatment independently without assessing clinical risk or coordinating care.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: The patient insists his prostate must be blocking the urine. Expected response: Explain that nocturia can arise from excess nighttime production, reduced storage, global excess urine or sleep disturbance; use the measured diary to show why obstruction is not established.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I made an assumption about prostate enlargement; I need the volumes and timing from a bladder diary first.” 2. “The chart shows 850 of 1900 mL is produced at night, which points me to nocturnal polyuria.” 3. “Given his heart failure, I will not start desmopressin before specialist risk assessment.”

stations.title: Neuropathic Bladder After Spinal Injury

sections.preamble: B2-235 | Neuropathic Bladder After Spinal Injury AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / neuro-urology • 8-minute simulation • DRAFT — independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 34-year-old man with a complete T4 spinal cord injury 18 months ago develops leakage between catheterisations and recurrent episodes of headache and sweating when his bladder is full. Explain how you will investigate and manage his neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, preserve renal function and respond to a sudden hypertensive episode.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: This is a long-term neuro-urology assessment with an acute autonomic dysreflexia curveball. Do not expect operative detail beyond MRCS Part B level. • T4 injury; wheelchair user, established clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC) four times daily. • Recently drained volumes often 650–800 mL, with leakage before catheterisation and occasional difficulty passing catheter. • Over six months two symptomatic culture-confirmed UTIs; no fever today. • Ultrasound: mild bilateral hydronephrosis; creatinine rising from his personal baseline. • Video-urodynamics: reduced compliance and elevated storage pressures with detrusor overactivity; no vesicoureteric reflux shown. • During the station blood pressure rises from usual 105/65 to 185/105 mmHg with severe pounding headache, facial flushing and sweating above the lesion; catheter not draining.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: The patient is worried about losing kidney function and would prefer intermittent catheterisation over a permanent catheter. If simulated acute event occurs, report headache and sweating urgently.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Why is this bladder dangerous? — High-pressure, poorly compliant storage can threaten upper urinary tracts even when the main complaint is leakage; hydronephrosis and worsening renal function require prompt specialist review. What is your baseline work-up? — Review neurological level, bladder/bowel/sexual symptoms, catheter volumes and technique; bladder diary, urinalysis/culture if symptomatic, renal function, upper-tract ultrasound, and specialist (video-)urodynamics. Choose a drainage strategy. — Optimise regular clean intermittent catheterisation if feasible (frequency, volume, technique), train the patient; avoid routine long-term indwelling urethral catheters where possible. How do you address unsafe storage pressure? — Specialist-directed antimuscarinic therapy or other suitable medication, consider intradetrusor botulinum toxin if refractory with a safe emptying plan; follow pressures, continence and renal health. What is autonomic dysreflexia? — Potentially life-threatening exaggerated sympathetic response in susceptible SCI at or above T6, often triggered by bladder distension or catheter blockage. Immediate response to BP 185/105 and headache? — Call emergency help; sit
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Neurological assessment Ignores level or chronicity of SCI Establishes T4 injury and urinary/bowel symptoms Explains why lesions above T6 create dysreflexia risk Bladder history and volumes Does not ask how bladder is emptied Checks CISC method, frequency, leakage and recorded volumes Identifies 650–800 mL drains as a cue to reassess intervals and storage safety Upper tract risk Calls leakage merely a quality-of-life issue Identifies hydronephrosis and rising creatinine as high-risk findings Connects poor compliance/high storage pressure to renal damage Diagnostic strategy Relies on symptoms alone without renal surveillance Requests urine testing when appropriate, ultrasound, renal tests and urodynamics Explains video-urodynamic value for pressure, compliance and reflux Bladder emptying choice Immediately mandates a long-term urethral catheter Supports feasible clean intermittent catheterisation and teaching Tailors schedule to output/pressures and patient hand function/preferences Storage-pressure treatment Suggests treating only leakage with pads Discusses specialist antimuscarinic therapy and escalation Mentions refractory botulinum toxin with s
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Fails to recognise severe hypertension with headache in a T4 spinal cord injury as possible autonomic dysreflexia. 2. Does not urgently assess and relieve a distended bladder or blocked catheter during suspected dysreflexia. 3. Dismisses hydronephrosis and deteriorating renal function without urgent specialist investigation. 4. Proposes symptom-only management while ignoring documented high-pressure, poor-compliance bladder storage.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Curveball: During review the patient becomes flushed and sweaty with headache; BP 185/105 mmHg and catheter drainage has stopped. Expected response: Recognise autonomic dysreflexia immediately: summon urgent help, sit upright, loosen constraints, monitor BP frequently, assess urinary tubing/catheter and relieve bladder distension promptly using trained assistance; follow emergency BP protocol if persistent and investigate other triggers.
sections.8.
