Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The ultrasound and rising creatinine change this from a leakage problem to an upper-tract protection priority.” 2. “His T4 injury makes the sudden headache and hypertension a possible autonomic dysreflexia emergency.” 3. “I need to restore safe bladder drainage and coordinate pressure-lowering treatment and specialist follow-up.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-236 Stone Prevention After a First Renal Stone Communication / applied urology | 8-minute simulated station | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an ST3 surgical trainee in a stone clinic. A 36-year-old man has passed his first 5-mm ureteric stone. He is pain-free and asks how to prevent another. Counsel him, assess recurrence risk and outline investigations. No acute stone treatment is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure on requ: Assessor: judge explanation and shared planning, not specialist drug memorisation. The patient is asymptomatic and follow-up imaging confirms no obstruction. Offer on request: first episode; stone was saved in a container but not yet analysed; normal eGFR and creatinine; normal urine dip today; serum calcium has not yet been measured; father had kidney stones twice. Diet: drinks about 1 L/day, adds salt to meals, takes vitamin C supplements, avoids dairy because he thinks calcium causes stones. No diabetes, gout, bowel surgery or recurrent UTI. Expected outcome: stone analysis, basic metabolic screen and recurrence-risk assessment; personalised fluid and diet advice; consider further metabolic assessment if deemed high risk.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is worried the stone will recur and questions whether he should stop calcium. Ask: “Does this mean I need to drink four litres every day?” Expect sensible adjustment for sweat, heart/renal restrictions and urine output. Ask: “Could you give me a medication today so it never happens again?” Expect no unselected prophylaxis without stone composition / appropriate risk assessment.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Risk and history — Family history? — Father had recurrent stones; first stone aged 36. Ask gout, diarrhoea/bowel disease, recurrent UTI, medications/supplements and occupations with heat exposure. Investigations — What do you request? — Stone composition analysis; blood calcium and renal function; urinalysis +/- culture if infection suspected; baseline metabolic assessment. Consider 24-hour urine for high-risk formers. Diet and fluid — What do you recommend? — Aim water intake 2.5–3 L/day if medically appropriate; normal dietary calcium; limit salt and excessive animal protein; avoid excess vitamin C supplements. Follow-up — How will you verify the plan? — Review stone type, baseline results and recurrence-risk classification; offer dietetic/urology review if high risk.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical framing Treats first stone as inevitably requiring surgery or lifelong medication. Explains recurrence can occur and prevention starts with risk assessment and changes in habits. Links family history, stone type, metabolic risk and practical prevention targets without promising zero recurrence. Focused stone history Ignores prior episodes and familial or infection clues. Asks previous stone events, family history and UTIs. Also elicits gastrointestinal disease, gout, occupational heat exposure and supplement use. Basic examination/context Does not consider clinical comorbidity before fluid advice. Checks renal/cardiac restrictions and current asymptomatic status. Explicitly adjusts advice for fluid loss, body size and potential volume overload. Stone analysis Discards retrieved stone or assumes calcium oxalate. Requests formal analysis of saved stone. Explains stone composition directs specific risk testing and treatment. Metabolic investigation Never requests calcium or basic metabolic assessment. Requests serum calcium, renal function and urinalysis; assesses recurrence risk. Discusses targeted extended testing including two 24-hour coll
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Recommends severe dietary calcium restriction as the prevention strategy despite normal dietary calcium guidance. 2. Fails to investigate or escalate fever with new renal colic, suggesting routine observation only. 3. Ignores a solitary kidney/anuria/AKI if revealed and offers only lifestyle advice. 4. Starts indefinite stone-specific preventive medication without obtaining stone analysis or risk assessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Actor adds: “I work in a hot kitchen and lose a lot of sweat.” Expected: increase drinking to replace additional losses while considering medical fluid limits, aim for appropriately dilute urine, consider accessible fluids during shifts and avoid rigid one-size-fits-all targets.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I should correct one important point: you should not stop normal dietary calcium; that can increase certain stone risks.” 2. “Before discussing any tablets I will send your stone for analysis and check the baseline blood and urine tests.” 3. “Given your family history and low current intake, I suggest a realistic hydration plan and a follow-up to assess whether more detailed metabolic testing is worthwhile.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-237 Renal Colic in Pregnancy Applied knowledge / emergency urology | 8-minute simulated station | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the general surgery registrar covering the emergency department. A 29-year-old woman at 25 weeks’ gestation has acute right loin-to-groin pain and vomiting. Assess the written findings, explain your initial plan and identify when urgent urinary drainage is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure on requ: Written findings available on request: HR 106, BP 112/70, temperature 37.2 °C, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% in air; fetal movements perceived; marked right loin tenderness. No peritonism. Urinalysis: microscopic haematuria, no nitrites; bloods: WCC 10.4 ×10⁹/L, creatinine 72 µmol/L, CRP 9 mg/L. Urine culture pending. Ultrasound: mild right collecting-system dilatation and probable 6-mm distal right ureteric calculus, with preserved bilateral renal parenchyma; sonographer notes physiological hydronephrosis can occur in pregnancy. Examination requires obstetric assessment for pregnancy-specific causes of pain and fetal wellbeing, while urology reviews stone management.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Pregnant patient distressed by pain and worried tests will harm the baby. Actor asks for a CT immediately; candidate should explain ultrasound first and consider MRI when diagnostic uncertainty persists, reserving ionising imaging for carefully justified cases. If asked: no known renal disease, no solitary kidney, no contractions, no vaginal bleeding or fluid loss.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Which investigations first? — Maternal observations, urinalysis and culture, renal function, FBC; ultrasound first; obstetric review. Does mild right hydronephrosis prove obstruction? — No. Pregnancy-related dilatation is common; correlate with symptoms, stone visualisation and any infection/renal impairment. What if temperature reaches 39 °C, BP falls and imaging indicates obstruction? — Suspect infected obstructed kidney / urosepsis; sepsis resuscitation, cultures, IV antibiotics, urgent urology drainage by stent or nephrostomy; coordinate obstetrics. If pain persists despite treatment but she is stable? — Discuss ureteroscopy at specialist centre versus temporising stent/nephrostomy after multidisciplinary review. What is contraindicated? — Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy during pregnancy.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate assessment Omits vital signs or mislabels pain benign because pregnant. Checks maternal ABCDE, vitals, sepsis markers and analgesia needs. Includes obstetric symptoms and fetal assessment by the maternity team in parallel. Differential diagnosis Assumes haematuria confirms calculus and ignores other causes. Considers stone, physiological dilatation, pyelonephritis and pregnancy-related abdominal emergencies. Uses fever, urinary symptoms, contractions, bleeding and peritoneal signs to separate urgent alternatives. Investigations Orders routine CT without considering pregnancy. Requests urine studies, FBC/U&E and renal ultrasound first. Recognises limits of ultrasound and selects multidisciplinary MRI / justified further imaging if unresolved. Image interpretation Calls all right hydronephrosis pathological. Identifies probable distal stone with mild dilatation, notes physiological dilatation. Explains test uncertainty and how changes in renal function or symptoms alter treatment threshold. Symptom management Withholds all analgesia and fluids or gives routine NSAIDs without pregnancy review. Gives pregnancy-compatible analgesia, antiemetic
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Recommends extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy during an ongoing pregnancy. 2. Fails to identify an infected obstructed system as an urgent decompression emergency. 3. Discharges a septic/haemodynamically unstable patient with antibiotics alone, without resuscitation or escalation. 4. Ignores pregnancy-specific red flags (vaginal bleeding/contractions) and refuses obstetric assessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The nurse reports temperature 39.1 °C, HR 128 and systolic BP 85 mmHg; the patient becomes confused. Expected: ABCDE/sepsis management, cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay treatment, immediate pregnancy-appropriate IV broad-spectrum therapy, IV fluids with reassessment, urgent urology decompression and simultaneous obstetric/critical-care involvement. Do not await another scan before escalation.
sections.8. Station-specific recovery lines: 1. “Ultrasound is the first imaging test in pregnancy, but I would not treat mild right-sided dilatation alone as proof of obstruction.” 2. “New fever and hypotension with suspected ureteric blockage changes this to infected obstruction; I need urgent urology drainage while resuscitation and antibiotics start.” 3. “If symptoms remain troublesome without sepsis, I will discuss ureteroscopy versus temporary stenting with urology and obstetrics, explaining the trade-offs.”

stations.title: Gout or Septic Arthritis? Joint Fluid Results

sections.preamble: B2-238 | Gout or Septic Arthritis? Joint Fluid Results AMaC MRCS Part B • Data interpretation / orthopaedics • 8-minute station • DRAFT / independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee asked to assess a 64-year-old man with a 24-hour history of severe swollen right knee. Interpret the supplied aspirate and outline immediate management. You have 8 minutes. Explain your reasoning aloud to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: BP 124/76, pulse 104/min, temperature 38.1°C; very painful right knee with effusion and severely restricted passive movement; no prosthetic joint. Synovial fluid: turbid; 78,000 leucocytes/µL (92% neutrophils); negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals; Gram stain no organisms; culture pending. FBC 14.8 ×10⁹/L, CRP 156 mg/L, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m²; urate previously raised. No antibiotics yet; haemodynamically stable.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: If role-play requested, patient says: “I have gout. Can you just give me gout tablets and let me home?” The actor is distressed by pain and fears missing work; accepts admission if risks are explained without alarmism.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What does the crystal result prove?” — Gout is present but infection is not excluded. “Does a negative Gram stain exclude septic arthritis?” — No, sensitivity is inadequate; culture and clinical assessment matter. “When would you give antibiotics?” — Obtain samples first if stable; give promptly after samples; do not delay if sepsis/shock. “When should the joint be washed out?” — Urgent orthopaedic source-control decision; lavage generally required for large joint infection.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial safety Calls it gout and proposes discharge without septic-joint assessment. Treats acute hot knee as potential septic arthritis; checks observations and sepsis. Immediately identifies time-critical joint threat, ensures analgesia, nil by mouth if likely theatre, early senior review. Focused history Does not ask about fever, onset or immunosuppression. Asks onset, fever/rigors, preceding infection, prosthesis, gout, immunosuppression and recent injection. Separates previous crystal attacks from new infective features and checks bacteraemia sources and antibiotics already taken. Examination Omits observations and does not assess ability to move joint. Examines temperature, joint erythema/effusion, range of movement, adjacent joints and neurovascular status. Also looks for cellulitis/bacteraemia focus, documents passive-movement pain and tests for systemic instability. Fluid interpretation Uses urate crystals or negative Gram stain to exclude infection. Identifies MSU crystals; recognises 78,000 cells/µL with 92% neutrophils is concerning despite negative Gram stain. Explains fluid WBC thresholds are non-definitive and infection can coexist w
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Discharges with gout medication solely because monosodium urate crystals were found. Claims negative Gram stain definitively excludes infection and stops cultures. Withholds antimicrobial/resuscitation treatment from a patient developing sepsis or shock while awaiting culture. Fails to arrange urgent orthopaedic assessment of a high-suspicion septic native knee.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The examiner adds: “His blood pressure falls to 86/50 and he becomes confused before aspiration samples are fully processed.” Expected: ABCDE, sepsis call, blood cultures if immediate, prompt IV antibiotics per local policy and resuscitation without waiting for remaining joint tests.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I need to correct my earlier statement: crystals confirm gout, but they do not rule out a simultaneous infected joint.” “This negative Gram stain is not reassuring enough to discharge; I will follow culture and ask orthopaedics to assess urgent drainage.” “He is now hypotensive, so I will start sepsis treatment immediately rather than wait for further results.”

stations.title: Acute Osteomyelitis in a Child

sections.preamble: B2-239 | Acute Osteomyelitis in a Child AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / paediatric orthopaedics • 8-minute station • DRAFT / independent clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical trainee reviewing a 5-year-old girl with 5 days of worsening left leg pain, limp and fever. Interpret the investigation findings and outline urgent management. Present the initial assessment, investigations, treatment and indications for surgery to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Temperature 38.8°C, heart rate 132, BP 102/65, alert but unable to bear weight. Localised proximal tibial tenderness, swelling and pain on movement; knee joint movement relatively preserved. WBC 17.1 ×10⁹/L, CRP 112 mg/L, ESR 65 mm/h. Initial tibial radiograph shows no obvious bony destruction. Blood cultures not yet taken. MRI requested on day of admission shows proximal tibial marrow oedema and a 2.5-cm subperiosteal collection, no definite intra-articular extension.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Mother says: “She knocked her leg at nursery; are you sure she needs to be admitted?” Mother will disclose no preceding antibiotics; mild recent skin abrasion. She is concerned about anaesthesia and long-term growth.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What is your working diagnosis?” — Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis of proximal tibia with subperiosteal abscess. “Likely pathogen?” — Staphylococcus aureus is most common overall; Kingella kingae is important in younger children, especially 6–48 months. “Is a normal X-ray reassuring?” — No; early imaging may be normal. MRI is preferred for defining extent. “Does this MRI change management?” — Yes, urgent paediatric orthopaedic assessment for abscess drainage and microbiological samples.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Urgency and assessment Reassures and sends limping febrile child home. Recognises possible acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, checks ABCDE, observations and pain. Screens for sepsis, dehydration and inability to bear weight; initiates paediatric and orthopaedic joint review. History Assumes minor injury explains 5-day progressive pain. Asks pain timeline, fever, limp, trauma, infection and previous antibiotics. Asks about sickle-cell disease, immunodeficiency and focal joint symptoms suggesting septic arthritis. Examination Does not expose limb or examine nearby joint. Localises tibial tenderness, warmth/swelling, range of knee/ankle movement and neurovascular status. Documents systemic examination, skin entry sites and any joint effusion or compartment concern. Differential Names bone tumour as sole diagnosis or ignores serious mimics. Considers osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, cellulitis, fracture and malignancy. Explains urgent exclusion of septic arthritis, bone abscess and systemic sepsis without prematurely closing differential. Laboratory and microbiology Starts treatment without cultures in a stable child and omits inflammatory markers. Req
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Discharges a febrile non-weight-bearing child because initial radiography is normal. Delays treatment in septic physiology while awaiting MRI, cultures or theatre availability. Fails to involve paediatric orthopaedics urgently after MRI demonstrates a subperiosteal abscess. Ignores the possibility of adjacent septic arthritis when a new knee effusion and worsening passive-motion pain develop.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: The examiner adds: “Before surgery, her knee becomes swollen and passive movement causes extreme pain.” Expected: recognise possible contiguous septic arthritis, repeat examination and urgent orthopaedic assessment for aspiration and drainage, while continuing antimicrobial/resuscitation management.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “A normal early X-ray cannot exclude osteomyelitis; I will pursue MRI and treat the clinical infection.” “The subperiosteal collection requires prompt specialist source-control assessment, not antibiotics alone without review.” “The new joint effusion raises concern for septic arthritis; I will escalate for urgent joint assessment and drainage.”

stations.title: Clavicle Fracture

sections.preamble: B2-240 | Clavicle Fracture AMaC MEDICAL EDUCATION • MRCS PART B • APPLIED KNOWLEDGE / TRAUMA • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF PENDING
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee asked to assess a 29-year-old right-handed cyclist after falling directly onto the left shoulder. He is comfortable after analgesia and has isolated shoulder pain. Review the radiograph description provided, explain your assessment, immediate management and when operative fixation should be discussed. State important complications.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: • Patient: haemodynamically stable; closed injury; no respiratory symptoms; pain 6/10; no other injury identified on trauma survey. • Inspection on request: swelling and bruising over middle third; skin intact, not tented; no wound; shoulder contour preserved. • Palpation on request: focal clavicular tenderness and crepitus; no sternoclavicular or acromioclavicular focal tenderness. • Neurovascular: warm hand, capillary refill <2 s, palpable radial pulse; light touch and power intact in median, ulnar, radial and axillary territories. • Imaging disclosed when requested: upright AP and angled clavicle views show displaced midshaft fracture with approximately 100% displacement, comminution and shortening estimated at 1.8 cm; no obvious pneumothorax. No validated universal shortening cut-off mandates surgery. • Occupation: manual work; wishes to return to competitive cycling. No smoking or diabetes.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Anxious about a visible lump and future shoulder strength. Ask “Must I have an operation?” and “Will a sling leave my shoulder deformed?” Accept balanced explanations, not guarantees. If questioned: denies pins-and-needles, breathlessness and previous shoulder problems.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • “What must you examine before deciding treatment?” → skin and threatened opening, chest/respiration, complete distal motor/sensory/perfusion assessment and associated trauma. • “Interpret the film.” → displaced comminuted middle-third fracture; comment on displacement, shortening and patient-specific nonunion factors. • “Initial treatment?” → oral analgesia, sling rather than routine figure-of-eight brace, ice and early elbow/hand movement; documented neurovascular exam and fracture-clinic review. • “Operate?” → urgent orthopaedic involvement if open injury, skin threatened, vascular/neural compromise or polytrauma; shared discussion of fixation for displaced adult midshaft fracture due to higher union and earlier functional improvement, balanced against similar long-term patient-reported outcomes in many cases. • “Complications?” → nonunion/malunion, stiffness, neurovascular or chest injury; surgery adds infection, implant irritation, reoperation and nerve/vessel damage.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Prioritisation: Discusses sling before checking for open injury or neurovascular compromise. Identifies stability; checks skin, perfusion and neurological status before disposition. Explicitly screens chest injury and skin tenting, and identifies scenarios needing urgent trauma review.
sections.2. History: Fails to clarify injury energy, hand dominance or functional needs. Elicits mechanism, dominant arm, work/sport and previous shoulder injury. Adds smoking/comorbidity, patient preference, return-to-work constraints and concomitant trauma.
sections.3. Examination: Only palpates clavicle, missing distal examination. Inspects skin; palpates clavicle; checks shoulder and distal pulses, sensation and movement. Separately documents axillary, radial, median and ulnar function plus respiratory/chest assessment.

stations.title: Humeral Shaft Fracture with Wrist Drop

sections.preamble: B2-241 | Humeral Shaft Fracture with Wrist Drop AMaC MEDICAL EDUCATION • MRCS PART B • EXAMINATION / APPLIED KNOWLEDGE • 8-minute simulated station • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF PENDING
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are assessing a 42-year-old patient after a road-cycling fall. Radiographs show a closed spiral fracture of the distal third of the right humeral shaft. Their wrist and fingers cannot extend. Demonstrate the focused neurological assessment to the examiner, interpret the findings and explain initial management and indications for nerve exploration.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings di: • Primary survey stable. Closed arm with swelling but intact skin; no compartment tenseness; no other injuries. Pain controlled after analgesia. • Plain radiographs (AP/lateral, shoulder and elbow included): displaced spiral fracture at junction of middle and distal thirds of humeral shaft (Holstein–Lewis pattern). • Motor: wrist extension 0/5, finger MCP extension 0/5, thumb IP extension 0/5; triceps 5/5, elbow flexion 5/5, finger flexion/abduction 5/5. No pain-limited ambiguity. • Sensation: reduced first dorsal web-space pinprick/light touch; median palmar index and ulnar little finger preserved. Radial pulse and hand perfusion normal. • Finding present immediately after injury, before splint or manipulation; no prior weakness. Patient is anxious nerve has been severed. • After initial immobilisation: repeat examination unchanged. No new deficit.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Worried that absent wrist extension means permanent paralysis. Ask “Is my nerve cut?” and “Do I need an operation tonight?” If examined: cannot extend wrist or straighten knuckles; can bend fingers and spread them. Consent to demonstration on model or verbal exam steps.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • “Demonstrate localisation.” → examine bilateral wrist extension, MCP extension, thumb extension and dorsal first web-space sensation; distinguish radial nerve from posterior interosseous motor-only lesion; assess triceps and other nerves. • “What about vessels?” → document radial/ulnar pulses, capillary refill, hand temperature; consider emergency vascular evaluation if compromised. • “What does the pattern suggest?” → radial nerve palsy associated with distal-third spiral humeral shaft fracture; may be neurapraxia, not proven transection. • “Immediate care?” → analgesia, appropriate immobilisation (initial coaptation/support followed by functional brace in selected fractures), wrist-drop splint, hand therapy and serial documented nerve exams, radiographic follow-up. • “Explore?” → not automatically for primary palsy in a closed fracture; urgent/specialist consideration if open/penetrating injury, vascular injury, suspected transection/entrapment, severe high-energy injury or new deficit after surgery; if no meaningful recovery over follow-up, specialist investigation such as ultrasound/electrodiagnostics and timed exploration decisions. • “Expected course?” → many primary closed
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Safety priorities: Focuses on wrist drop and misses threatened perfusion. Checks open injury, perfusion and pain before the nerve examination. Specifies urgent escalation for absent pulse, compartment syndrome or an open fracture.
sections.2. Examination approach: Does not compare sides or obtain consent. Explains focused exam, obtains permission and compares both upper limbs. Positions arm comfortably and documents pre- and post-immobilisation findings.
sections.3. Motor localisation: Checks wrist flexion only and misses MCP extension. Tests wrist, finger MCP and thumb extension plus triceps power. Contrasts radial motor deficit with median, ulnar, PIN and proximal root findings.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-242 Calcaneal Fracture After a Fall from Height Station type: Applied knowledge / orthopaedic trauma | Suggested duration: 8 minutes | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in the emergency department. A 37-year-old warehouse worker landed on both feet after falling 3 metres. The left heel is severely painful and swollen. Explain your immediate assessment, interpret the written imaging findings and propose management. No images are provided.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Patient alert, BP 126/78, HR 102, SpO₂ 98%, GCS 15; no immediate external bleeding. On examination request: left heel widened, ecchymosis and tense swelling. Posterior heel skin is intact but blanching poorly over a prominent bony fragment. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable; sensation initially intact. Lateral foot radiograph report: comminuted calcaneal fracture, reduced Böhler angle, fragment displaced posterosuperiorly; suspected tongue-type pattern. CT: displaced posterior facet fracture with posterior tuberosity fragment threatening overlying skin. Back examination if requested: focal lumbar tenderness; neurology of lower limbs intact. Trauma survey has not yet included spine imaging. No prior diabetes, vascular disease or regular medicines; last meal 3 hours ago.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: If role-played, the patient is distressed by heel pain and asks, “Can I walk home in a boot?” Respond only to questions asked. If asked about symptoms, report lower back pain and no paraesthesia. If told about surgery, ask why swelling matters.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What else must you examine after this mechanism? — Full trauma assessment, bilateral heels, lumbar/thoracolumbar spine, neurovascular status, skin and compartments. What does the radiology description suggest? — Displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture with a posterior tongue-type component threatening heel skin. What investigations? — Appropriate foot/heel radiographs, CT for fracture mapping, spine assessment/imaging driven by trauma findings; no routine standalone foot examination only. What would you do immediately? — Analgesia, elevate and immobilise in padded non-weight-bearing splint, document neurovascular/skin examination, keep nil by mouth if urgent procedure possible, urgent senior orthopaedic review. Which patients need urgent intervention? — Open fracture, posterior skin threatened by tongue-type fragment, neurovascular compromise or evolving compartment syndrome. When is definitive fixation considered? — Tailor to soft tissues, displacement, pattern, patient factors; delayed surgery after swelling subsides for many closed fractures, but not if skin urgently threatened.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance First assessment Focuses only on painful foot; misses height-of-fall mechanism. Undertakes ABCDE and asks for mechanism and other pain. Explicitly searches for spine injury and contralateral hindfoot injury after axial loading. Heel inspection Does not inspect posterior skin or fracture blisters. Describes swelling, bruising, skin integrity and posterior heel. Recognises non-blanching/tenting posterior skin as a threatened-skin emergency. Neurovascular check Does not examine distal perfusion or sensation. Checks pulses, capillary refill, sensation and toe movement. Documents baseline and repeat neurovascular findings following immobilisation. Compartment risk Dismisses worsening pain as expected bruising. Asks about escalating pain and assesses tense compartments and neurological change. Escalates suspected foot compartment syndrome urgently despite palpable pulses. Imaging interpretation Says a normal ankle radiograph excludes fracture. Identifies reduced Böhler angle and asks for calcaneal CT. Links tongue-type posterior fragment to immediate skin jeopardy. Associated injuries Never examines back or opposite heel. Checks spinal symptoms and perfo
sections.6. Four critical fails: Fails to identify or urgently escalate posterior heel skin threatened by a displaced tuberosity fragment. Omits a neurovascular examination and discharges the patient weight-bearing. Fails to consider spinal injury despite axial loading and reported lumbar tenderness. Ignores evolving disproportionate pain/neurological change suggesting compartment syndrome.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After the original assessment, the nurse reports increased heel pain and a dusky non-blanching patch at the posterior heel. Expected: reassess skin and neurovascular status immediately, alert senior orthopaedic surgeon, avoid direct pressure, keep nil by mouth, prepare for urgent reduction/operative protection of threatened skin.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “My foot examination was incomplete: I am checking the back, opposite heel and documenting distal perfusion now.” “That posterior skin is becoming compromised, so I am requesting urgent orthopaedic review for reduction, not waiting for routine fracture clinic.” “The increasing pain may indicate a compartment problem; I will reassess and escalate immediately.” 9–11. Model performance — Fail Calls this a simple ankle injury, misses the posterior skin threat, gives a walking boot and proposes outpatient review without a trauma survey. 9–11. Model performance — Pass Recognises calcaneal fracture after axial loading, checks for spinal and opposite heel injuries, assesses skin/perfusion, orders CT and keeps the patient non-weight-bearing pending orthopaedic review. 9–11. Model performance — High-performance Identifies the displaced tongue-type fragment as a time-sensitive threat to heel skin, separates urgent temporising treatment from later definitive management and explains soft-tissue-dependent fixation decisions.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-243 Knee Pain at Night in a Teenager Station type: History / suspected bone tumour | Suggested duration: 8 minutes | Draft for independent clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in an urgent clinic. A 16-year-old student has 8 weeks of gradually worsening pain around the left knee, waking them at night. Take a targeted history, explain your differential and outline safe initial investigations and referral. The examiner supplies imaging reports in words.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: History if requested: deep pain just above knee, progressively worse, now at rest, not relieved by simple analgesia; swelling noticed over distal thigh for 3 weeks. No injury, fever or acute knee locking. Weight bearing is painful. General: 16 years old, otherwise healthy, no previous cancer, occasional fatigue but no marked weight loss. Examination on request: firm tender distal femoral metaphyseal swelling, no erythema; knee movement mildly limited by pain; distal neurovascular status intact; no pathological fracture. X-ray report: aggressive mixed lytic/sclerotic distal femoral metaphyseal lesion with interrupted periosteal reaction and extraosseous soft-tissue component. If asked what a normal early film would mean: persisting unexplained symptoms would still merit safety-netting and reassessment/specialist advice. Do not provide tissue results: candidate must not arrange unplanned biopsy before sarcoma centre referral.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Teenager and parent are worried this could be sports injury. When asked, admit pain wakes you at night. Parent asks, “Can your clinic remove a sample today?” If candidate uses jargon, ask for an explanation. Do not assert cancer as proven.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What history? — Onset, progression, pain at rest/night, swelling, limp, trauma, systemic symptoms, neurological symptoms, functional impairment. What exam? — Site of bony swelling, tenderness, joint motion, gait, local neurovascular check, systemic examination as relevant; avoid aggressive manipulation. What differential? — Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, infection, stress injury or benign lesions; X-ray pattern and age inform but do not establish histology. What urgent first test? — Very urgent X-ray for unexplained bone pain/swelling in a child or young person under NICE NG12. What if concerning X-ray? — Very urgent specialist assessment, within 48 hours under NG12 for children and young people; contact specialist bone sarcoma pathway. Who undertakes staging/biopsy? — Specialist bone sarcoma MDT plans MRI, staging and appropriately located biopsy tract; no unplanned local biopsy or excision. How discuss possible malignancy? — Explain that abnormal bone changes need urgent expert assessment, avoid premature tissue diagnosis, support patient and family.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Pain chronology Asks only whether sport caused injury. Elicits duration, deterioration and rest/night pain. Clarifies sleep disruption and escalating analgesic need as warning signs. Swelling and function Misses new mass and limp. Asks about swelling, gait and activity limitation. Establishes the time course of swelling, inability to weight bear and fracture risk. Systemic history Declares no fever means benign disease. Screens fever, weight change, fatigue and previous malignancy. Explains constitutional symptoms are variable and absence does not exclude sarcoma. Focused examination Treats as isolated ligament strain without looking at thigh. Inspects and gently palpates distal thigh; checks knee motion and distal nerves/vessels. Avoids forceful testing and documents soft-tissue mass, limb function and fracture concern. Differential Labels osteosarcoma certain from symptoms. Raises bone malignancy alongside infection and benign causes. Identifies distal femoral metaphysis as suggestive of osteosarcoma but needs specialist histology. Initial imaging Orders physiotherapy without imaging. Requests very urgent plain X-ray of symptomatic bone. Recognis
sections.6. Four critical fails: Dismisses progressive night pain and a suspicious bone lesion as benign sports injury without urgent investigation/referral. Performs or arranges an unsupervised biopsy/excision outside the specialist sarcoma pathway. Fails to refer a child/young person with a bone-sarcoma-suggestive X-ray for very urgent specialist assessment. States the X-ray alone proves a specific histological tumour type and starts definitive treatment without specialist MDT input.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The parent says a local private clinic can biopsy the lump tomorrow. Expected: advise against unplanned biopsy, explain contamination of future surgical planes/tract planning, urgently coordinate bone sarcoma specialist centre referral and acknowledge family anxiety.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I initially focused too much on sports injury; the progressive rest pain and swelling need urgent bone imaging.” “These X-ray findings may represent a tumour; I will contact the specialist bone sarcoma service today.” “I would not arrange a biopsy outside the sarcoma centre because the approach needs specialist planning.” 9–11. Model performance — Fail Attributes progressive night pain and swelling to overuse, ignores the aggressive radiograph or arranges a local biopsy before specialist assessment. 9–11. Model performance — Pass Obtains targeted red-flag history and focused examination, interprets aggressive X-ray description, arranges very urgent sarcoma referral and communicates uncertainty appropriately. 9–11. Model performance — High-performance Distinguishes suggestive imaging from confirmed pathology, navigates the 48-hour young-person referral recommendation, prevents unplanned biopsy and addresses support and fracture risk.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-244 — Prosthetic Joint Infection Applied knowledge / orthopaedics | 8 minutes | AMaC MRCS Part B | Draft • clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the orthopaedic registrar assessing a 71-year-old woman with a painful, warm right knee, 5 weeks after total knee replacement. Explain your assessment, investigations and management to the examiner. The examiner will provide observations and test results on request. Do not examine a real patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief (disclose findings onl: Initial: increasing pain and warmth over 48 hours; mild wound discharge; no antibiotics yet. The candidate must assess immediate sepsis and prosthesis status. Requested observations: T 38.2 °C, HR 106/min, BP 119/70 mmHg, RR 19/min, SpO₂ 97%; alert; no overt shock. If asked about haemodynamic deterioration: BP falls to 86/50, new confusion and rigors. Wound: small area of persistent drainage; no visible sinus tract. Knee swollen, painful with limited movement; distal neurovascular findings normal. Bloods: WCC 14.2 ×10⁹/L, CRP 118 mg/L; renal function to check; blood cultures if febrile or systemic signs. X-ray: knee prosthesis aligned; no obvious loosening or fracture. Joint aspiration under aseptic conditions, coordinated with the arthroplasty/infection team when stable: cloudy fluid, 40,000 cells/µL, predominantly neutrophils; sample sent for culture and differential. Exact thresholds must be contextualised early after surgery. If asked for deep samples during debridement: take five separate samples with separate instruments; request appropriate culture.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Patient is anxious about losing the knee replacement. Ask: “Can you just give me antibiotics instead of another operation?” If asked, disclose no known antibiotic allergies and no prior major infection. Request explanation without jargon.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is your working diagnosis? Expected: acute postoperative prosthetic joint infection, while considering alternative causes and assessing sepsis. What happens before antibiotics? Expected: urgent blood cultures if systemic illness, infection-team discussion and diagnostic aspiration/deep samples in stable patients; do not postpone antibiotics for a septic patient. How do you decide DAIR versus revision? Expected: timing and duration of symptoms, implant fixation/function, sinus presence, organism, host factors and MDT decision. When does treatment become an emergency? Expected: sepsis/shock → resuscitation, parenteral antibiotics after urgent cultures, immediate senior discussion and time-critical operative source control.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening safety Labels pain as routine postoperative soreness and sends home. Recognises possible early PJI and seeks same-day orthopaedic review. Specifies dynamic sepsis check, compares with postoperative baseline and initiates timely MDT pathway. Focused history Omits wound discharge, fever or symptom onset. Asks timing of implant, symptom onset, drainage, fever, antibiotics and comorbidities. Separates acute postoperative, acute haematogenous and chronic patterns; asks about recent bacteraemia and preceding procedures. Examination Manipulates painful joint without checking wound or perfusion. Checks observations, wound, swelling, motion and distal neurovascular status. Checks systemic perfusion and maps drainage/sinus, skin condition and other infection foci. Investigations Relies on plain film or CRP alone to exclude infection. Requests FBC, CRP, renal function, X-rays, cultures and aseptic aspiration when appropriate. Explains limitations of early postoperative markers; requests cell differential and microbiology, avoiding low-value routine bone scan. Antibiotic timing Gives antibiotics before sampling in a stable patient or delays them in sho
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Misses sepsis or shock and fails to initiate immediate resuscitation, antibiotics and orthopaedic escalation. 2. Administers empiric antibiotics before sampling to a stable patient with suspected PJI without justification, compromising diagnostic yield. 3. Treats a loose prosthesis or draining sinus by definitive DAIR alone without addressing contraindications. 4. Discharges a febrile patient with a painful draining recent knee prosthesis without urgent senior assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: During discussion her BP falls to 86/50 and she becomes confused. Expected: announce septic shock concern; ABCDE, call emergency/orthopaedic/critical-care teams, two IV lines, blood cultures promptly, lactate and bloods, immediate locally guided IV antibiotics and fluid resuscitation with reassessment, urgent operative source control.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The new confusion changes this into possible sepsis: I am calling for resuscitation and IV antibiotics immediately after urgent cultures.” 2. “This is a recent implant and I need a joint-infection MDT decision before committing to DAIR.” 3. “Even with a normal-looking X-ray, I cannot exclude infection; I will arrange proper sampling.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-245 — Dislocated Hip Replacement Critical care / orthopaedics | 8 minutes | AMaC MRCS Part B | Draft • clinical sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are called to ED for a 76-year-old woman with sudden severe left hip pain after bending down to pick up a bag. She had a left total hip replacement 18 months ago. Describe your assessment and safe immediate management. The examiner will disclose imaging findings in words.
sections.2. Examiner brief (disclose findings onl: Patient is alert; HR 92/min, BP 148/84, no fever, no major fall or head injury. Left leg shorter, flexed, adducted and internally rotated; she cannot bear weight. Neurovascular examination if requested: dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable; capillary refill normal; ankle/toe dorsiflexion and plantarflexion intact; sensation over foot intact. AP pelvis and cross-table lateral X-ray report: femoral head prosthesis displaced posteriorly relative to acetabular component; no obvious periprosthetic fracture; components appear intact. History: first dislocation; no previous recurrent instability, no known infection; operative approach and implant type to be checked from records. Post-reduction X-ray report if requested: prosthetic femoral head centred within cup; no obvious fracture or eccentric head position. Neurovascular findings unchanged. If candidate requests reduction without appropriate personnel: no prepared anaesthesia/sedation team available; appropriate safe response is to arrange controlled reduction in theatre.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Patient is frightened and wants someone to “pull it back now”. If asked, pain score 9/10; no numbness, weakness, fever or wound discharge. Ask “Will this happen again and will I need another operation?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: First actions? Expected: analgesia, observations, trauma screen, orthopaedic senior review, document pre-reduction distal perfusion and sciatic/peroneal motor-sensory function. Investigations? Expected: AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs identifying prosthesis displacement, direction, fractures or component failure. Reduction plan? Expected: timely controlled closed reduction with adequate anaesthesia/sedation, muscle relaxation and qualified team; avoid forceful unsupported attempts. After reduction? Expected: repeat neurovascular examination and X-rays; reassess component position, stability and possible fracture; supervised mobilisation and individualised precautions. When consider revision? Expected: recurrent dislocation, component malposition, instability, constrained or dual-mobility device complications, or irreducible dislocation.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate assessment Moves the painful leg forcefully before safety assessment. Checks observations, pain and associated injuries, calls orthopaedics. Explains urgent but controlled reduction and assesses trauma, anticoagulation and frailty issues. History Does not check prosthesis or earlier dislocations. Asks implant date, mechanism, previous instability and baseline function. Asks for implant type/approach, prior revisions, infection symptoms and precipitating positions. Physical examination Fails to record pulses or distal motor function. Documents limb position, skin and pulses, foot sensation and ankle/toe power. Separately documents sciatic/peroneal nerve components before intervention. Imaging Attempts reduction without X-ray or excludes fracture on clinical inspection. Requests AP pelvis and lateral hip views; recognises posterior prosthetic displacement. Checks component integrity, periprosthetic fracture and available old films/implant notes. Reduction safety Attempts forceful bedside traction without sedation or trained support. Arranges qualified controlled closed reduction with appropriate anaesthesia and monitoring. Plans theatre/flu
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Does not check or document distal neurovascular status before and after reduction. 2. Attempts unsupported forceful reduction without appropriate sedation/anaesthesia and a competent team. 3. Attempts blind reduction without first excluding obvious periprosthetic fracture or implant failure on radiographs. 4. Fails to arrange post-reduction radiographs or senior review after failed reduction or suspected component damage.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After a reduction attempt, the post-reduction film describes an eccentrically positioned femoral head within a dual-mobility cup. Expected: suspect possible intraprosthetic dislocation/liner dissociation; stop further forceful manipulation, maintain safety and consult arthroplasty specialist; obtain appropriate further imaging and plan intervention.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “Before any reduction I need to document pulses and ankle and foot nerve function.” 2. “The X-ray excludes an obvious fracture, but this must still be a controlled reduction with proper sedation and staff.” 3. “I will not accept the audible clunk alone: I need a repeat examination and confirmatory X-ray.”

stations.title: Fat Embolism Syndrome

sections.preamble: B2-246 | Fat Embolism Syndrome AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / orthopaedic trauma • 8 minutes • DRAFT — INDEPENDENT CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 26-year-old man is 30 hours after a closed femoral shaft fracture sustained in a road collision. The fracture is splinted but not definitively fixed. He is increasingly breathless and confused. You are the on-call surgical registrar asked to assess him. Assess the patient, interpret the supplied findings, give a differential diagnosis and outline immediate management and fracture strategy. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only on req: If requested: RR 32/min, SpO₂ 86% on air, HR 122/min, BP 106/68 mmHg, T 38.3°C, GCS 14 (new confusion). Pinpoint petechiae over the upper chest and axillae. Bilateral fine crackles. The splinted limb is neurovascularly intact. No clinical evidence of major haemorrhage. Findings / investigations: Hb 106 g/L (previously 132), platelets 102 × 10⁹/L (previously 218), WCC 12.8 × 10⁹/L; ABG on oxygen: hypoxaemia; chest radiograph: bilateral patchy airspace opacities. ECG: sinus tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiography if clinically warranted to exclude thrombotic PE; it does not establish FES.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor required; examiner plays the trauma nurse and supplies observations and results only when requested.
sections.1. What is your immediate approach?: Call for senior anaesthetic/critical-care assistance; ABCDE, high-concentration oxygen initially, continuous monitoring, IV access, ABG, bloods and evaluate for invasive ventilatory support if deterioration. 2. Give the most likely diagnosis and two urgent alternatives. Fat embolism syndrome following long-bone fracture; investigate thrombotic pulmonary embolism, pulmonary contusion/ARDS, aspiration or pneumonia and intracranial injury if indicated.
sections.3. What findings make this more likely?: Typically 24–72 h after fracture, respiratory compromise and neurological change with petechiae; thrombocytopenia and anaemia are supportive, not pathognomonic.
sections.4. How does Gurd’s framework help?: Traditional clinical major/minor features support recognition; criteria are not a validated definitive test, and the patient should not be left hypoxic awaiting a score.
sections.5. What treatment is specific to fat emb: No established antidote. Deliver supportive oxygen/ventilation and haemodynamic management; do not offer routine heparin or high-dose corticosteroids solely for FES.

stations.title: Consent for Carpal Tunnel Decompression

sections.preamble: B2-247 | Consent for Carpal Tunnel Decompression AMaC MRCS Part B • Communication / informed consent • 8 minutes • DRAFT — INDEPENDENT CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 58-year-old right-handed office administrator has 12 months of nocturnal tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers of the right hand. Night splinting helped initially; a corticosteroid injection helped for eight weeks. Symptoms now interrupt sleep and there is mild thenar weakness. She is considering open carpal tunnel decompression. Explain the proposed operation, expected benefits, alternatives, material risks and recovery; support an informed decision without pressuring the patient. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only on req: If asked: typical median-distribution paraesthesia, decreased pinprick at index fingertip, mild abductor pollicis brevis weakness, no neck red flags, no infection. Nerve conduction studies support median neuropathy at the wrist. No anticoagulants. Type 2 diabetes controlled with oral medication. Findings / investigations: Patient asks whether sensation and strength will be completely normal. She types for work and cares for an elderly relative. No prior surgery to this wrist. Hand surgery team proposes day-case open division of transverse carpal ligament under local anaesthetic.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is concerned about returning to typing and the chance of permanent pain. Initially says: “I’m scared it might make my hand worse.” If offered certainty, asks: “Can you promise my numbness will completely go?” Ask about alternatives and time off work if not raised.
sections.1. What is carpal tunnel syndrome?: Compression of median nerve at wrist causing nocturnal median-digit symptoms, altered sensation and sometimes thenar weakness.
sections.2. What operation is proposed?: Day-case release of transverse carpal ligament through palmar/wrist incision, generally under local anaesthesia; explain wound closure and dressing in plain language.
sections.3. What are alternatives?: Continued splinting, activity modification and steroid injection; explain diminishing response and risk of progression with weakness.
sections.4. What benefits can be expected?: Night symptoms and tingling often improve; function may improve over time, but chronic numbness/weakness may persist from established nerve damage.

stations.title: Femoral Shaft Fracture: Thomas Splint

sections.preamble: B2-249 | Femoral Shaft Fracture: Thomas Splint AMaC MRCS PART B • Procedural / orthopaedic trauma • 8 minutes • DRAFT / CLINICAL SIGN-OFF REQUIRED
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical trainee in the trauma unit. A 32-year-old adult has a radiologically confirmed isolated midshaft right femoral fracture after a motorcycle collision. The patient is haemodynamically stable after initial assessment and analgesia. Demonstrate on a manikin how you would select, prepare and apply a Thomas splint, using a trained assistant. Talk through exclusion of associated injuries and your post-application checks. Time: 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief (disclose findings on: Provide training Thomas splint, appropriately sized padding, skin traction equipment, slings and windlass. Candidate must not apply a real traction force to a person. Assume primary survey complete but allow candidate to ask for pelvic/knee/leg examination and imaging. Stop demonstration if candidate attempts traction with an unassessed pelvis or distal limb. Observations: BP 122/76, pulse 108/min, SpO₂ 98% on air; thigh swollen and painful. Repeat observations must be monitored; do not dismiss potential blood loss. Imaging on request: Written radiograph: displaced transverse fracture in mid-diaphysis of right femur; pelvis and ipsilateral hip, knee, tibia/fibula and ankle injury excluded after appropriate clinical assessment/imaging. Pre-splint limb check: Foot warm; dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses palpable; capillary refill 2 seconds; toe motion and plantar/dorsal sensation intact. Skin: No open wound, significant pressure lesion or severe distal injury. If asked, patient has received adequate pain relief. Size measurement: Contralateral inside leg measured from groin to heel; for the cited modular Kinetec Thomas splint add approximately 20 cm for foot clearance and windla
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Manikin only. Assistant follows clear instructions for manual in-line limb support and controlled traction; does not independently choose equipment, measure or assess circulation.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt — What is your first action? Expected — Confirm ATLS primary survey and haemorrhage assessment; provide analgesia, call senior/orthopaedics and document baseline neurovascular state. Prompt — Why select a Thomas splint? Expected — Temporary immobilisation and pain control for an appropriately assessed isolated femoral shaft fracture pending definitive orthopaedic treatment. Prompt — What could contraindicate traction? Expected — Pelvic/acetabular injury, fracture near hip or distal femur, knee disruption, or distal ipsilateral limb fracture/dislocation; reassess if uncertain. Prompt — Show how you measure the splint. Expected — Use unaffected inside leg groin to heel, allow extra distal length according to manufacturer, select oblique proximal hoop circumference and pad the hoop. Prompt — Demonstrate application. Expected — Assist manually maintains alignment; prepare padded slings and correctly sized hoop; safely position limb, apply skin traction excluding popliteal fossa pressure, connect cords and tension windlass gradually, secure it. Prompt — What do you document after splintage? Expected — Pain, skin/pressure checks, alignment, foot pulses, capillary refill, motor/sen
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Primary survey and bleeding Starts splintage without checking observations or shock. Confirms prior ABCDE and reassesses pulse, blood pressure and possible thigh haemorrhage. Adds search for other bleeding sources and early senior help if shock or ongoing blood loss develops. Analgesia and explanation Applies painful traction without analgesia or consent. Explains temporary splinting, gains permission and requests analgesia before handling. Coordinates analgesia, assistant roles and reassurance, checking discomfort at each step. Contraindication screening Applies traction despite unexcluded pelvic or knee injury. Checks pelvis, hip, knee and ipsilateral distal limb for associated injury before proceeding. Correlates examination with imaging and selects static immobilisation if traction safety remains uncertain. Baseline examination Does not check distal pulses or neurological function. Documents foot warmth, pulses, capillary refill, sensation and toe/ankle motor function. Repeats baseline documentation after repositioning and recognises evolving vascular compromise. Equipment and sizing Selects wrong-side or visibly undersized hoop and splint. Mea
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Applies traction when associated pelvic, knee or ipsilateral distal-limb injury remains suspected or unassessed. 2. Fails to establish pre-application distal neurovascular status or ignores loss of pulse after application. 3. Uses uncontrolled excessive traction despite worsening pain, perfusion or neurological symptoms. 4. Focuses on splint application while overlooking haemodynamic instability or suspected significant bleeding.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Immediately after tightening the windlass, dorsalis pedis pulse becomes absent and the foot cools. Expected: stop, release/reduce traction, reassess foot perfusion and distal motor/sensory status, call senior trauma/orthopaedic and vascular teams urgently, document and avoid repeating forceful traction.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: Before choosing traction I need to exclude pelvic, knee and lower-leg injuries; I will check these now. I have not documented baseline pulses and nerves; I will complete and record that before applying the splint. I will ease the windlass and repeat the neurovascular examination now because distal perfusion may have changed.

stations.title: Applying a Pelvic Binder

sections.preamble: B2-250 | Applying a Pelvic Binder AMaC MRCS Part B • Practical procedure / major trauma • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in an emergency department trauma bay. A 34-year-old cyclist was struck by a lorry. HR 126/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, GCS 14; pelvis is painful and major pelvic haemorrhage is suspected. Demonstrate application of a purpose-made pelvic binder to a manikin and narrate immediate actions. Do not repeatedly manipulate the pelvis.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Provide a pelvic manikin, binder, trauma handover and simulated monitoring. Candidate may direct team members. State that spinal precautions are in place, one peripheral line is functioning, and the major haemorrhage protocol can be activated. If asked: no active external bleeding; abdomen non-distended; left lower limb rotated, distal perfusion maintained. No prior pelvic imaging. Blood products and tranexamic acid can be requested. Successful performance: centred across greater trochanters, correctly fastened, tightened per device instructions; document application time and obtain specialist plan for removal.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Simulated injured patient: distressed, reports pain over hips and groin. If asked whether they can move their legs, says it hurts. No actor action required during hands-on application.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “Is a binder indicated?” — suspect active pelvic bleeding after high-energy blunt trauma; apply immediately alongside resuscitation. “Show where it sits.” — around greater trochanters, not iliac crests or waist. “The BP remains 80 systolic.” — continue haemostatic resuscitation, pelvic/trauma surgeon and IR escalation; binder does not replace bleeding control. “When should it be removed?” — reassess promptly; coordinate with pelvic surgeon if unstable, and remove within 24 hours.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Indication Applies for isolated minor pelvic pain without haemorrhage assessment. Names major pelvic bleeding after high-energy blunt trauma as indication. Links binder decision to shock, mechanism and exclusion of competing bleeding sources. Immediate trauma response Delays ABCDE or resuscitation while preparing device. Directs ABCDE, oxygen as indicated, monitoring and major haemorrhage response. Allocates team roles while simultaneously preventing delay in binder use. Preparation Fails to expose needed landmarks or checks no device size. Selects suitable binder and exposes/identifies both greater trochanters. Maintains warmth and spinal precautions while checking device fit. Positioning Places binder over iliac crests or abdomen. Centres device across greater trochanters. Verbalises how high placement can fail to reduce pelvic volume. Application Rotates or repeatedly springs pelvis to apply. Uses coordinated minimal movement, straightens legs if appropriate and secures device. Uses team-assisted technique without unnecessary rolling or distraction. Tension and fit Leaves loose or overtightens with unsafe force. Tightens per manufacturer instruc
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fastens binder across iliac crests/abdomen despite available greater trochanter landmarks and fails to correct it. Repeatedly springs/manipulates the painful pelvis in a shocked patient. Withholds life-saving resuscitation or trauma escalation because the binder has been applied. Removes binder from suspected unstable fracture without an agreed pelvic-team plan.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After correct application, the systolic BP drops to 72 mmHg. Expected: immediately reassess ABCDE, activate/escalate major haemorrhage, give blood products per local protocol, examine for other bleeding sites, and urgently engage pelvic surgery/IR; do not keep tightening repeatedly.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “My binder was high: I will reposition it over the greater trochanters without springing the pelvis.” “There is persistent shock despite correctly applied compression: I am activating definitive haemorrhage control now.” “I will document the application time and agree a safe early removal plan with the pelvic service.”

stations.title: Mandible and Facial Fractures

near_match.title: Mandible and orbital floor fractures

sections.preamble: B2-251 | Mandible and Facial Fractures AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / maxillofacial trauma • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are assessing a 28-year-old who was assaulted and struck across the jaw. They complain their bite feels wrong and the lower lip is numb. Examine verbally using supplied written findings, interpret CT report and explain emergency and definitive management.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Observations: HR 105, BP 118/76, SpO₂ 97% on air, speaking normally but spitting blood. There is right mandibular angle swelling, gingival tear adjacent to lower molars, loose tooth, malocclusion and reduced right lower-lip sensation. No ocular complaints on initial history. Written CT: displaced right mandibular angle fracture involving tooth-bearing region; minimally displaced left parasymphysis fracture; no intracranial haemorrhage. Cervical spine not yet cleared. If asked: no stridor, expanding floor-of-mouth haematoma or uncontrolled bleeding initially. Extraocular movements and vision normal. Patient has not eaten for 3 hours.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor: anxious, says “My teeth do not fit together. Am I going to lose feeling in my lip?” If candidate asks about breathing, says no difficulty currently. Wants to know why they need a specialist.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What is the priority?” — airway with C-spine protection, bleeding, suction and early anaesthesia/OMFS if threatened. “What does numb lip mean?” — inferior alveolar/mental nerve distribution affected by mandibular fracture. “Is it an open fracture?” — tooth-bearing mandibular fracture communicating with oral cavity/gingival tear is considered open. “How will it be treated?” — urgent OMFS assessment, analgesia, oral hygiene, appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis based on local guidance for open fractures, operative fixation versus appropriate selected nonoperative care. “What else must you check?” — occlusion, dentition, intraoral wounds, mental and infraorbital sensation, facial nerve, eyes, cervical spine and associated injury.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Primary survey Starts detailed jaw palpation despite worsening airway or bleeding. Performs ABCDE, airway/bleeding assessment with cervical precautions. Prepares suction and early airway assistance for floor-of-mouth swelling or deterioration. History Only asks about pain and mechanism. Elicits altered bite, trismus, numbness, tooth loss and other injury. Checks timing, previous occlusion, anticoagulants and aspiration/anaesthetic considerations. External examination Omits facial asymmetry and other facial injuries. Inspects swelling, deformity, bruising, TMJ movement and facial symmetry. Examines eyes, midface and cranial nerves without dangerous manipulation. Intraoral examination Misses gingival tear or loose teeth. Inspects occlusion, mucosal breaks, teeth, sublingual haematoma and oral bleeding. Recognises open fracture, aspiration hazard of loose teeth and potential bilateral injury. Neurological assessment Ignores reported lower-lip numbness. Tests and documents mental/inferior alveolar sensory territories. Adds infraorbital and facial motor function where midface injury possible. Imaging Uses an isolated normal plain film to exclude fractur
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fails to recognise or escalate new airway obstruction, expanding floor-of-mouth swelling or uncontrolled oral bleeding. Sends the patient home despite displaced mandibular fractures, malocclusion and open oral communication. Misses the loose tooth/foreign-body aspiration hazard and provides no airway or dental safety plan. Performs aggressive fracture manipulation without cervical or airway assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: While awaiting OMFS, the actor becomes muffled in speech and develops rapidly increasing floor-of-mouth swelling. Expected: stop examination, summon senior anaesthetics/OMFS and trauma team, sit appropriately if safe, prepare suction and definitive airway strategy with cervical precautions; do not send for routine imaging first.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I have not yet checked the airway thoroughly; I will reassess it immediately with cervical precautions.” “The gingival wound makes this a potentially open fracture: I will arrange urgent OMFS and follow the local antibiotic protocol.” “I must document the altered bite and lower-lip sensation before treatment and explain uncertain recovery.”

stations.title: Knee Osteoarthritis: Is It Time for a Replacement?

sections.preamble: B2-252 | Knee Osteoarthritis: Is It Time for a Replacement? AMaC MRCS Part B • Communication • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist clinical sign-off Independent educational station. Not an official MRCS examination or marking scheme. In examination mode show only section 1 (and instructions to examiner separately).
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the orthopaedic registrar in an elective clinic. Mrs Evans, 68, asks whether she now needs a knee replacement. Explain your assessment and management choices, and reach a shared plan. You have 8 minutes. Patient details: 4 years of progressive right knee pain, difficulty shopping and climbing stairs; physiotherapy and topical NSAID have helped only slightly. No acute trauma, fever or hot joint. Do not assume radiographic severity alone determines surgery.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: If asked: 7/10 activity pain, occasional rest pain, 15-minute morning stiffness; walking tolerance 200 metres; sleep disturbed twice a week. No weight loss, fever, locking or inflammatory history. Examination on request: varus alignment, medial joint-line tenderness, crepitus, range 5–105°, stable collateral ligaments, intact distal circulation and neurology. BMI 32; diabetes reasonably controlled. Radiograph report: medial compartment joint-space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis; no destructive lesion. Previous care: supported strengthening for 4 months, activity adaptations, weight-management advice, topical NSAID and intermittent oral analgesia after comorbidity review. Patient prioritises walking with grandchildren; fears an anaesthetic and wishes to hear alternatives.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Open: ‘Am I too old or overweight for a new knee?’ Ask whether the operation guarantees pain relief. If the candidate only describes surgery, ask ‘Is there anything else to try?’ Concern: your friend developed a clot after surgery. You want realistic benefits, recovery, limitations and time to think; you do not want a forced decision.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: ‘What features support osteoarthritis and what would change your diagnosis?’ Expect typical use-related pain, short stiffness, exam findings; check acute hot joint, inflammatory disease, malignancy, referred hip pain as appropriate. Prompt 2: ‘Would you refer for replacement?’ Expect major quality-of-life impact and unsuitable/ineffective non-surgical therapy; use clinical assessment, not a numeric severity score or BMI cut-off. Prompt 3: ‘What should consent include?’ Expect possible improvement but no guarantee, infection, thromboembolism, bleeding, stiffness, persistent pain, neurovascular injury, prosthesis failure/revision, anaesthetic risks; recovery and rehabilitation. Prompt 4: ‘She declines today.’ Expect support, continued personalised non-operative care, planned reassessment and safety-net.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Diagnostic synthesis Labels any painful knee as OA without examining or excluding alternative causes. Links mechanical symptoms, short stiffness and varus/crepitus to knee OA. Recognises radiographs support but do not alone dictate treatment, and checks hip/referred pain. Functional impact Records pain score only and ignores disability. Asks about walking, stairs, daily living and sleep. Elicits patient-specific goals and how symptoms affect valued activities. Non-surgical management Claims all OA needs replacement or prescribes bed rest. Explains therapeutic exercise, weight management when appropriate and suitable analgesia. Tailors supervised strengthening, self-management and medicines to diabetes and preference. Referral threshold Uses age, BMI or X-ray grade as a mandatory barrier or trigger. Offers referral because life impact persists despite appropriate conservative care. Explains clinical referral criteria and shared choice without arbitrary exclusion. Surgical explanation Cannot describe what is replaced or promises a perfect knee. Explains removal/resurfacing of diseased joint surfaces and prosthetic components. Contrasts likely pain/fu
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Pushes immediate knee replacement solely because the X-ray looks severe without assessing symptoms or alternatives. 2. States that age or BMI alone absolutely excludes a patient from referral for joint replacement. 3. Promises pain-free full recovery or conceals major infection/thromboembolism risks when seeking consent. 4. Dismisses an acutely hot, swollen or systemically unwell knee as routine OA without urgent evaluation.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Patient: ‘I have diabetes and my BMI is 32. Am I automatically refused an operation?’ Expected: No. Explain that NICE NG226 says not to exclude referral solely by age, comorbidities or BMI; assess and optimise individual risk and preferences.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. If I have rushed towards surgery: ‘First, I need to establish how your symptoms affect daily life and what treatments you have tried.’ 2. If I have implied weight excludes referral: ‘Weight affects perioperative risk, but BMI alone must not bar a referral discussion.’ 3. If I have understated complications: ‘I should be clearer: infection, blood clots, stiffness and possible revision must be part of your decision.’

stations.title: Mechanical Low Back Pain Without Red Flags

sections.preamble: B2-253 | Mechanical Low Back Pain Without Red Flags AMaC MRCS Part B • History / communication • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist clinical sign-off Independent educational station. Not an official MRCS examination or marking scheme. In examination mode show only section 1 (and instructions to examiner separately).
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical assessment doctor seeing Mr Lewis, 39, with 5 days of low back pain after lifting boxes. Take a focused history, explain the likely diagnosis and agree initial management. You have 8 minutes. He is walking independently and has no obvious systemic illness. A focused, explicit screen for serious spinal pathology is mandatory before calling the pain mechanical.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: History if asked: central lumbar ache without radiation below the buttock, 5/10, worse bending and sitting, improves gentle movement. No leg weakness/numbness, saddle sensory change, urinary retention, new incontinence or bowel change. No fever, cancer history, unexplained weight loss, significant trauma, steroid use, injection-drug use or immunosuppression. No inflammatory pattern, night sweats, or morning stiffness persisting over 30 minutes. No prior spinal surgery. Examination on request: normal vital signs, mild paraspinal tenderness, reduced flexion due to pain, normal gait/heel and toe walking, symmetrical limb power, reflexes and sensation; straight-leg raise does not reproduce radicular pain. Patient is worried that pain means a slipped disc and asks for an urgent MRI. They have been resting in bed for two days, missing work. No drug allergy, peptic ulcer or renal disease reported, but medication history still required.
sections.3. Patient/actor brief: Open: ‘Can I get an MRI to find out what is wrong?’ Say you think exercise will damage the spine. If asked about bladder/bowel or numbness, deny each. Ask ‘What if I suddenly cannot pass urine?’ and ‘Should I stay off work until the pain is gone?’ Expect non-dismissive reassurance and explicit return precautions.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt 1: ‘What red flags would demand a different response?’ Expect progressive neurology/cauda equina symptoms, malignancy, infection, fracture and inflammatory disease based on history; escalate according to the suspected cause. Prompt 2: ‘Does he need an MRI today?’ Expect no routine imaging in a non-specialist setting when uncomplicated and no serious pathology suspected; explain imaging may reveal incidental findings and does not always help management. Prompt 3: ‘How will you treat him?’ Expect information, keeping active, return to usual activities, tailored exercise/self-management, suitable short-course NSAID at lowest effective dose for shortest possible time after risks; no routine paracetamol alone, opioids, gabapentinoids or spinal injections for nonspecific low back pain. Prompt 4: ‘At home he develops saddle numbness and retention.’ Expect emergency assessment for suspected cauda equina, not planned routine review.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Pain history Does not establish site, onset, severity or aggravating activities. Clarifies lifting trigger, course, mechanical features and effect on function. Distinguishes nonradicular pain from leg-dominant neuropathic symptoms and inflammatory pattern. Cauda equina screen Fails to ask bladder, bowel or saddle sensory symptoms. Asks retention, new incontinence, saddle anaesthesia and progressive leg weakness. Explains why new bilateral symptoms or loss of perineal sensation changes urgency. Other serious pathology Does not screen fever, cancer, trauma or systemic features. Asks about malignancy, infection, fracture and inflammatory clues. Targets risk factors such as immunosuppression, steroids or significant trauma appropriately. Focused examination Skips gait and neurological screening entirely. Checks mobility, gait, lower-limb motor, sensory and reflex findings. Uses findings to decide if urgent spinal assessment is needed, without overinterpreting straight-leg raise. Diagnosis & explanation Calls a prolapsed disc certain despite absent sciatica or alarming signs. Explains likely uncomplicated non-specific mechanical low back pain. Normalise
sections.6. Critical fails — four station-specifi: 1. Fails to recognise or urgently escalate new urinary retention and saddle sensory change suggesting cauda equina syndrome. 2. Reassures without asking any bladder/bowel, perineal sensory or neurological red-flag questions. 3. Recommends prolonged bed rest and no mobilisation as the primary management of uncomplicated low back pain. 4. Prescribes ongoing strong opioids or gabapentinoids as routine first-line therapy for non-specific low back pain without relevant indication or safety review.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After the patient leaves, the examiner says that he has telephoned because he cannot pass urine and has new saddle numbness. Expected: Immediate emergency department/spinal pathway assessment for suspected cauda equina syndrome; do not book routine MRI or offer reassurance by telephone.
