sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. If I prematurely said ‘muscle strain’: ‘I must first ask about retention, saddle sensation, weakness, infection, cancer and injury.’ 2. If I promised an MRI: ‘Routine imaging is not advised without suspected serious pathology; examination and follow-up will guide changes.’ 3. If I recommended rest: ‘Prolonged bed rest is not the plan; I would support gradual movement and an achievable return to activity.’

stations.title: Clearing the Cervical Spine After Trauma

sections.preamble: B2-254 | Clearing the Cervical Spine After Trauma AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / major trauma • 8-minute station • Draft for clinical sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 38-year-old alert patient arrives after a low-speed rear-end collision. GCS 15, stable observations, delayed neck soreness, no paraesthesia, no distracting injury. You are asked whether cervical precautions and imaging are needed.Task: Assess the case aloud, interpret findings and formulate a safe management decision. Explain key decisions to the examiner.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: The candidate must apply the Canadian C-spine rule stepwise; explain when CT is needed, how to assess active movement safely, and what to do if later neurological features appear. The task is decision-making, not manual neck manipulation.Disclose ONLY when asked: • Initial ABCDE: stable; GCS 15, no major distracting injuries. • Mechanism: simple rear-end collision at low speed, no rollover or ejection. Age 38. • Neck: muscular soreness but no midline bony tenderness; no neurological abnormality. • On request to assess movement after determining low risk: patient voluntarily turns 45 degrees to both left and right without worsening symptoms. • CT variant when prompted: a 72-year-old following a fall has normal limb power but midline neck pain; age ≥65 is a Canadian high-risk criterion and requires imaging.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Simulated patient says: “My neck started hurting 20 minutes after the crash; can you take the collar off?” If asked: walked after collision, sitting comfortably, no midline bony tenderness, no limb symptoms, no intoxication; reliably follows commands.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: 1. How do you determine whether a neck can be clinically cleared? — ABCDE and reliability; apply high-risk, low-risk and 45-degree rotation branches of Canadian C-spine rule. 2. What high-risk features stop active-rotation testing? — age ≥65, dangerous mechanism, extremity paraesthesia; consider neurological deficit and impaired assessability. 3. Which imaging? — CT cervical spine in adults when indicated; urgent reporting; CT timing guided by NICE head-injury criteria if concomitant head injury. 4. What if paraesthesia develops despite a normal CT? — keep precautions, urgent senior/spinal review and MRI for neurological signs as recommended by NICE. 5. What should be documented? — examination, rule elements, collar removal decision, explanation and return precautions.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate safety Moves neck before trauma assessment. Performs ABCDE; maintains precautions pending risk assessment. Checks haemodynamics, co-injuries and reliability before any neck movement. History / mechanism Omits mechanism and age. Asks age, collision type and paraesthesia. Distinguishes simple rear-end collision from rollover/ejection and dangerous falls. Neurological assessment Fails to ask about limb symptoms. Checks limb sensation, power and paraesthesia. Screens all limbs for evolving signs and records baseline before clearance. Rule application Calls absence of pain sufficient to clear. Uses Canadian high-risk and low-risk branches correctly. Explicitly checks all three high-risk factors before considering rotation. Neck examination Forces rotation or palpates roughly. Assesses midline tenderness; only invites active 45-degree rotation when safe. Separates paraspinal pain from midline tenderness and never forces movement. Imaging choice Orders plain films as routine definitive adult imaging when CT indicated. Requests CT in adult with indicated imaging. Identifies urgent CT and immediate trained interpretation, with associated head-inju
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Forces neck rotation before excluding high-risk features or in an unassessable patient. 2. Removes spinal precautions despite new focal neurological signs or limb paraesthesia. 3. Clinically clears an adult with a Canadian high-risk feature instead of arranging indicated CT. 4. Discharges a patient with persistent neurological symptoms after a normal CT without further assessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Immediately before planned clearance, the patient reports new tingling in both hands. Expected: stop clearance, maintain precautions, repeat documented neurological examination and obtain urgent senior/spinal assessment and appropriate imaging.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. I have not yet checked your age, mechanism and limb symptoms; I will complete those before attempting movement. 2. A normal scan does not settle persistent neurological symptoms; I would keep precautions and seek spinal assessment. 3. I will document the exact rule elements and your voluntary 45-degree movements rather than just writing “C-spine clear”.

stations.title: Stab Wound to the Abdomen

sections.preamble: B2-256 | Stab Wound to the Abdomen AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / penetrating trauma • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational simulated station; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme. No images needed. Source check: 13 October 2026. Station purpose: Distinguish immediate laparotomy indications from selective non-operative management of an anterior abdominal stab wound.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the CT2 in the emergency department of a major trauma centre. A 27-year-old has a single stab wound to the left lower abdomen. Assess the patient, request findings, and outline your immediate management and disposition to the examiner. You do not physically examine the actor. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Provide observations and investigations only when requested. Initial: alert, speaking; HR 108/min, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO₂ 98% air, T 36.7°C. Single 2-cm anterior left lower abdominal wound with controlled superficial bleeding; no visible evisceration. Mild local tenderness but no guarding or rigidity. Examination of posterior torso identifies no additional wounds. E-FAST negative (does not exclude bowel injury). Venous lactate 2.2 mmol/L; initial Hb 137 g/L (cannot exclude acute bleeding). Patient is cooperative, not intoxicated. CT with IV contrast, if requested after stabilisation: small tract reaching anterior abdominal fascia, no definite bowel injury, free air, active extravasation or intraperitoneal free fluid. Experienced local wound exploration identifies fascia penetration; no hard operative sign.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is anxious: “Do I need an operation? Can I go home if the scan is clear?” Reports being stabbed about 40 minutes ago; does not know knife depth. Tetanus history uncertain. If asked, no anticoagulants, no other injury, no vomiting.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: Initial priorities? Expected: Activate trauma team; C-ABCDE, haemorrhage control, monitoring, IV access ×2, blood group/crossmatch, analgesia, keep nil by mouth, senior trauma surgeon early. Prompt: What mandates urgent theatre? Expected: Persistent haemodynamic instability, peritonitis, impalement, bowel-content leak or concerning organ evisceration, and hard evidence of significant intra-abdominal injury; do not delay for CT. Prompt: How would you investigate a stable cooperative patient? Expected: Complete front/back examination; IV-contrast CT when indicated; experienced surgeon-led local wound exploration for appropriate anterior stab wound; eFAST alone cannot exclude injury. Prompt: Can this patient be discharged after a normal CT? Expected: No: fascia has been penetrated and subtle hollow-viscus injury can be missed. Admit under trauma surgery for repeated senior abdominal exams, observations and timely re-imaging or surgery if worsening. Prompt: Other considerations? Expected: Tetanus risk assessment; antibiotics according to local penetrating-wound or operative protocol rather than automatic prolonged prophylaxis; document circumstances and safeguarding; consider f
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Trauma recognition Treats the apparently stable wound as minor without a primary survey. Identifies penetrating abdominal trauma and completes C-ABCDE with repeated vital signs. Anticipates occult bowel/vascular injury and calls trauma surgery before any deterioration. Haemorrhage and resuscitation Waits for low haemoglobin before addressing circulatory compromise. Controls external bleeding, secures two IV lines, orders blood group/crossmatch, gives appropriate analgesia and nil by mouth. Uses trends and clinical response, activates major haemorrhage protocol and early TXA when major bleeding is suspected and within 3 hours. Focused assessment Fails to inspect back or check for peritonism and evisceration. Documents wound position, anterior/posterior injuries, peritoneal signs and repeat abdominal examination. Identifies unreliable examination factors, checks associated chest/pelvic injury, documents serial findings and timing. Imaging interpretation States negative eFAST or normal CT excludes bowel injury. Requests appropriately timed IV-contrast CT in stable patient and explains limitations. Integrates wound trajectory and subtle changes with CT
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Fails to identify persistent instability or peritonitis and delays necessary laparotomy for routine CT. CF2. Discharges a patient with documented fascial penetration solely on a normal initial CT without an appropriate observation pathway. CF3. Probes or enlarges the wound blindly without expertise, risking uncontrolled bleeding or missed injury. CF4. Treats a negative eFAST as definitive proof that penetrating abdominal injury is absent.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: Curveball: After four hours, the patient develops HR 126/min, worsening generalised pain and guarding; BP 102/66. Expected response: Repeat C-ABCDE, call senior trauma surgeon and anaesthetist urgently, resuscitate, bloods/crossmatch, broad-spectrum antibiotics when bowel contamination suspected and proceed to urgent operative assessment; do not be reassured by the earlier CT.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “My earlier impression of a superficial wound was unsafe; I am repeating a full front-and-back examination, and asking the trauma surgeon to assess the wound trajectory.” 2. “A negative FAST or first CT does not rule out bowel injury; this patient needs monitored observation with repeated examinations.” 3. “The newly developed guarding and tachycardia change my plan: I am escalating immediately for laparotomy assessment rather than another routine discharge review.”

stations.title: Seatbelt Sign and Chance Fracture

sections.preamble: B2-257 | Seatbelt Sign and Chance Fracture AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / blunt trauma • 8 minutes • Draft for independent clinical sign-off Educational simulated station; not an official MRCS examination mark scheme. No images needed. Source check: 13 October 2026. Station purpose: Recognise the paired risks of thoracolumbar flexion-distraction injury and occult mesenteric or bowel injury following restraint trauma.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the CT2 in the emergency department after a high-speed frontal collision. A 32-year-old restrained rear-seat passenger has abdominal bruising and lumbar pain. Explain assessment, interpret the written CT report, and plan management. Eight minutes; no images are shown.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Initial patient: awake, GCS 15, HR 104/min, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO₂ 98% air. Prominent transverse lower abdominal seatbelt bruise, central abdominal tenderness, no initial guarding, lumbar midline pain. Distal motor/sensation intact, normal perianal sensation if requested; no urinary retention. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and spine reconstructions: “Horizontal distraction fracture extending through the posterior elements and vertebral body of L2, with widening of posterior interspinous distance. Small volume interloop free fluid, mesenteric fat stranding adjacent to proximal jejunum, no free intraperitoneal gas, no contrast extravasation.” Patient is stable but there is concern for bowel/mesenteric injury and unstable spinal injury.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient asks, “I have only bruising and a back fracture—can I walk?” Later reports more abdominal pain if asked during curveball.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: What does the bruising suggest? Expected: Seatbelt sign: substantial risk of occult bowel, mesenteric and associated spinal injury; not a simple superficial bruise. Prompt: Interpret the spine description. Expected: L2 flexion–distraction (Chance-type) injury; posterior tension-band disruption raises concern for instability; immobilise and urgently discuss with spinal service. Prompt: How do you interpret the abdominal CT? Expected: Interloop fluid and mesenteric stranding are concerning but non-specific; absence of free gas does not exclude hollow-viscus injury. Prompt: What monitoring and investigations? Expected: Trauma senior review, full CT with IV contrast and spine reconstructions, baseline/repeated bloods as supportive trends, timed repeated abdominal/neurological examinations, consider repeat CT at about 6 h if equivocal or worsening. Prompt: Can they mobilise or leave? Expected: No; maintain spinal alignment and immobilisation strategy with spinal team pending stability decision; surgical observation for bowel injury. Prompt: When operate? Expected: Peritonitis, haemodynamic deterioration, CT hard signs or increasing suspicion of bowel injury prompt urgent operati
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Mechanism and prioritisation Calls the mark uncomplicated bruising without trauma assessment. Performs C-ABCDE and recognises restraint injury as high-risk blunt trauma. Anticipates linked lumbar and mesenteric injury despite preserved initial blood pressure. Abdominal clinical assessment Does not elicit evolving pain, guarding or nausea. Examines abdomen for seatbelt mark, tenderness and peritoneal signs; plans serial reassessment. Documents timed changes and understands delayed signs from bowel perforation or mesenteric ischaemia. Spine and neurology Encourages mobilisation with an undifferentiated L2 distraction fracture. Maintains spinal precautions and documents limb motor, sensation and bladder/bowel symptoms. Requests spinal specialist assessment of stability, ligament integrity and further imaging when indicated. CT interpretation Uses absence of pneumoperitoneum to exclude a bowel injury. Identifies L2 flexion-distraction injury plus interloop fluid and mesenteric stranding as concerning. Differentiates hard surgical CT signs from equivocal findings and checks adequate spine reconstructions. Bowel injury surveillance Allows discharge after
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1. Mobilises or clears spinal precautions before expert stability assessment of the distraction fracture. CF2. Discharges a patient with seatbelt sign, concerning CT free fluid/mesenteric stranding and no observation or senior review. CF3. Dismisses mesenteric injury solely because the first CT shows no pneumoperitoneum. CF4. Fails to escalate new peritonitis or haemodynamic deterioration urgently for possible operative bowel injury.
sections.7. One realistic curveball and expected: Curveball: Six hours after arrival the patient becomes more tachycardic (HR 130/min), febrile (38.1°C), with diffuse guarding. Expected response: Immediate repeat C-ABCDE, resuscitation, urgent general/trauma consultant and anaesthetic assessment, bloods, cultures and antibiotics if contamination/sepsis suspected; urgent operative assessment without delaying for repeat CT in clear peritonitis. Maintain spine precautions during transfer and surgery.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I overlooked the significance of the seatbelt bruise; I will obtain a full abdominal trauma assessment and request surgical observation.” 2. “The L2 distraction fracture may be unstable despite a normal limb examination, so I am stopping mobilisation and contacting the spinal team.” 3. “An initially equivocal CT is not reassuring now that guarding has appeared; I am escalating to immediate operative assessment.”

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-258 Raised Intracranial Pressure Applied knowledge / neurosurgical critical care | 8 minutes | Teaching / assessment draft | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to assess a 34-year-old after a road collision, initially GCS 12, now increasingly drowsy. Explain your assessment and immediate management to the examiner. No image is provided; ask for observations, examination and CT report.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: If asked: airway gurgling, vomit in mouth; GCS E2 V2 M4 (8), previously E3 V4 M5 (12); right pupil 5 mm sluggish, left 3 mm reactive; HR 52, BP 164/90, SpO₂ 93% room air, RR 10; glucose 6 mmol/L. Urgent CT report if patient stabilised: right acute subdural haematoma with 9 mm midline shift, effaced basal cisterns. Neurosurgical transfer and theatre are available after immediate expert airway stabilisation. Do not imply CT before stabilisation.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor required (oral applied-knowledge station). Examiner role-plays trauma team; provide findings only if requested.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What do you do in the first 60 seconds?” Expected: emergency escalation, ABCDE, protect cervical spine, expert airway, oxygenation, IV access, correct hypotension. Prompt: “Explain Monro–Kellie.” Expected: fixed cranial volume containing brain, blood and CSF; exhausted compensation raises pressure. Prompt: “What if the pupil dilates further while theatre is being arranged?” Expected: treat impending herniation with immediate neurosurgical/critical-care collaboration, optimise physiology and consider specialist-guided hyperosmolar rescue; do not delay definitive evacuation. Prompt: “What numbers would you use?” Expected: BTF treatment threshold ICP >22 mmHg and CPP 60–70 mmHg in *monitored adult severe TBI*, not universal values for every raised-ICP scenario.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Labels GCS 8 as stable; omits pupils. Recognises falling GCS, unequal pupils and possible herniation. Links deterioration to mass effect; repeats GCS components, pupils and lateralising signs. Immediate actions Continues examination without emergency call. Calls senior, anaesthetics and neurosurgery; initiates ABCDE. Coordinates time-critical actions and assigns roles while reassessing. Airway / ventilation Leaves unprotected airway in drowsy vomiting patient. Requests expert airway protection and oxygenation; avoids hypoxia. Plans controlled ventilation, capnography and brief rescue measures only if herniating. Perfusion Accepts systolic hypotension or indiscriminate fluid overload. Secures IV access, monitors BP and corrects hypotension using balanced resuscitation. Explains CPP=MAP−ICP and balances cerebral perfusion with pulmonary harm. Imaging / escalation Delays CT despite neurological decline. Arranges urgent CT head after stabilisation and neurosurgical review. Anticipates evacuable lesion / hydrocephalus and definitive intervention. Physiology Cannot explain raised intracranial pressure. Describes Monro–Kellie doctrine and cere
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to summon immediate airway and neurosurgical help despite GCS 8 and neurological deterioration. 2. Allows sustained hypoxaemia or hypotension without correcting or escalating. 3. Performs or proposes lumbar puncture in this patient with obvious mass effect. 4. Uses sustained prophylactic profound hyperventilation instead of urgent definitive assessment and treatment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: While arranging CT, the right pupil becomes fixed and the patient develops extensor posturing. Expected: declare suspected herniation, urgent consultant neurosurgeon/anaesthetist response, stabilise airway/perfusion, consider temporising hyperosmolar therapy under specialist direction, expedite emergency decompression.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I have missed the urgency: I am calling anaesthesia and neurosurgery now for a deteriorating GCS and unilateral pupil.” 2. “I will prioritise airway, oxygen and blood pressure before transport to CT.” 3. “This scan shows a mass lesion with shift; I am escalating immediately for evacuation rather than observing.”

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-259 Headache Worse in the Morning History / suspected intracranial pathology | 8 minutes | Teaching / assessment draft | Not an official MRCS mark scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: Take a focused history from a 45-year-old with a gradually worsening headache over 7 weeks, now often worse on waking. Explain your likely concerns and initial plan. You may request examination findings. Patient is alert and able to give a history; do not assume a brain tumour solely from headache timing.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Spontaneous: diffuse morning headache becoming more frequent; over-the-counter analgesics less effective. If asked: episodes of nausea, two unexplained morning vomits; brief visual blurring when coughing; occasional stumbling; no thunderclap onset, fever or recent trauma. Examination on request: GCS 15, BP 138/80, afebrile; mild left-sided dysmetria, unsteady tandem gait, optic discs suspicious for papilloedema; no meningism. Patient has no previous cancer and is not anticoagulated. The examiner may offer urgent MRI report: posterior fossa lesion with obstructive hydrocephalus.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor: anxious about a brain tumour; does not volunteer imbalance or coughing-related blur until directly asked. If candidate promises it is migraine, ask “But why am I getting worse and vomiting?” Accept uncertainty explained empathetically.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What else do you need to ask?” Expected: progression, red flags, seizures, focal and visual symptoms, systemic illness, past malignancy, medication and immunosuppression. “What examination?” Expected: full neurological examination, gait/cerebellar signs, visual fields and fundoscopy if competent. “What would you arrange?” Expected: urgent neuroimaging for progressive subacute central neurological dysfunction, same-day emergency evaluation if signs suggest hydrocephalus or deterioration. “Can you perform lumbar puncture?” Expected: not before mass effect / obstructive hydrocephalus has been assessed.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening history Asks only whether headache is severe. Elicits onset, progression, timing, duration and baseline headache pattern. Clarifies raised-pressure features without assuming morning headache proves a tumour. Red flags Omits seizure, focal weakness and altered consciousness. Asks about new seizures, weakness, visual change, vomiting and behaviour. Asks about thunderclap onset, fever, immunosuppression, malignancy and Valsalva worsening. Raised ICP symptoms Ignores positional / visual symptoms. Checks morning or lying-related symptoms, vomiting and diplopia. Explores transient visual obscurations and headache provoked by cough/strain. Risk context Ignores past cancer and drug history. Asks about cancer, previous intracranial disease and relevant medicines. Includes pregnancy where relevant, anticoagulants and systemic constitutional symptoms. Examination Declares normal without examination. Checks vitals, mental status, cranial nerves, limbs, gait and visual fields. Checks optic discs where competent and identifies subtle papilloedema / sixth-nerve palsy. Differential Claims all morning headaches indicate neoplasm. Distinguishes primary heada
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Dismisses progressive headache, vomiting, ataxia and possible papilloedema as uncomplicated migraine without urgent evaluation. 2. Performs or advises lumbar puncture with possible posterior fossa mass and obstructive hydrocephalus. 3. Fails to act on new neurological deficit or deteriorating consciousness during assessment. 4. Sends patient away without emergency assessment when MRI reveals hydrocephalus and posterior fossa mass.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The actor suddenly complains of severe headache and becomes confused (GCS falls to 13). Expected: stop routine history, call emergency help, perform ABCDE and immediate neurosurgical evaluation and imaging without outpatient delay.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The progression plus imbalance changes my assessment: I need an urgent neurological examination.” 2. “I was premature to reassure: I will arrange urgent brain imaging and appropriate specialist assessment.” 3. “Given possible obstructive hydrocephalus, I will not undertake lumbar puncture and will escalate today.”

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-260 Diagnosis of Death Using Neurological Criteria (Brainstem Testing) Applied knowledge / intensive care / professionalism • 8 minutes • DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate attending an ICU teaching ward round. A 45-year-old ventilated patient has a devastating traumatic brain injury. The consultant asks you to explain whether and how death may be diagnosed using neurological criteria in the UK. You are not expected to undertake the tests yourself. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosed findings: Test conceptual recognition of prerequisites, confounders, qualified assessors, brainstem reflexes, apnoea assessment, documentation and family communication under the AoMRC 2025 Code. Do not ask candidate to certify death independently. Intubated and ventilated; no spontaneous respiratory effort seen; catastrophic structural brain injury shown on CT, with a cause capable of permanent cessation of brainstem function. Temperature 36.5 °C, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg on stable support; serial blood gases and metabolic testing are available on request. Recent sedation was stopped; exact agents, duration and clearance MUST be sought, not assumed. No residual neuromuscular blockade after appropriate checks. Pupils appear unreactive; this observation alone is insufficient to diagnose death. The ICU consultant explains that two eligible doctors will perform two full sets of tests using the 2025 Code and record results.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor in primary scenario. In the family-communication prompt, examiner plays the patient’s sibling: “His heart is beating. How could he have died?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What must be established before testing? A sufficient known irreversible brain injury; unconsciousness and ventilator dependence; absence of reversible confounders such as sedatives, paralysis, hypothermia or relevant physiological/metabolic disturbance; consider 2025 red-flag groups. Who undertakes the formal assessment? Two suitably experienced and competent doctors, each GMC-fully-registered (or equivalent) for more than five years, with at least one consultant; two complete sets of tests. Name the clinical components. Bilateral pupillary light, corneal and vestibulo-ocular responses, motor response to appropriate cranial-nerve stimulus, gag and cough reflexes, plus formally conducted apnoea test; use the Code checklist. How is the apnoea test assessed? In controlled ICU conditions, ensure preoxygenation and baseline PaCO₂ at least 5.3 kPa; no spontaneous breathing with endpoint PaCO₂ at least 8.0 kPa, rise at least 2.7 kPa, pH below 7.3 and minimum 5 minutes, when safe. What if an essential test cannot be performed? Do not declare death on incomplete routine testing; involve consultants and follow the Code on ancillary investigations and complex cases. How does organ donation r
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognises task Calls testing “switching off life support” and ignores diagnostic criteria. States neurological criteria assess permanent loss of brainstem function under UK Code. Explains the distinction between neurological diagnosis of death and decisions about withdrawal of support. Underlying cause Offers testing for unexplained coma without evaluating the cause. Seeks clear catastrophic brain injury sufficient to account for permanent brainstem failure. Also checks mechanism, imaging, trajectory and unusual isolated posterior fossa patterns. Excludes confounders Proceeds despite possible sedative or paralytic activity. Checks sedation clearance, neuromuscular blockade, temperature and metabolic/circulatory factors. Names drug accumulation, organ dysfunction and Code red flags needing enhanced scrutiny. Professional eligibility Asks an unsupported junior to sign a death declaration alone. States two experienced eligible doctors, at least one consultant, and two test sets. Specifies registration experience and competence plus formal local documentation. Reflex examination Claims fixed pupils alone establish death. Lists bilateral brainstem refl
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1: Proposes diagnosing death despite possible residual sedative or neuromuscular-blocking effect. CF2: States that a single absent pupil response or single examiner is sufficient. CF3: Performs or recommends an unsupervised apnoea test without safe ICU monitoring and prescribed physiological criteria. CF4: Declares death despite incomplete testing without resolving confounders or following the ancillary pathway.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: A recent infusion of a long-acting sedative was stopped only hours ago in severe renal impairment. Expected: Do not test until clearance is credibly established; involve intensivist/pharmacist, consider drug levels where relevant and follow Code guidance on confounders/ancillary investigations.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should not infer drug clearance from the time the infusion stopped; I will check agent, dose, organ function and residual effect.” “I was relying too heavily on fixed pupils; the formal assessment includes the complete brainstem reflex and apnoea sequence.” “I cannot declare death if this test is unsafe or uninterpretable; I will refer to the ICU consultant and Code pathway.”

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-261 Spinal Epidural Abscess Critical care / emergency spinal surgery • 8 minutes • DRAFT — specialist sign-off required
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar receiving an emergency referral. A 56-year-old man with diabetes and recent intravenous drug use reports severe mid-back pain, fever and worsening leg weakness over 12 hours. Explain your assessment, investigation and immediate management to the examiner. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosed findings: Test recognition of time-critical spinal infection with cord compression, sepsis management, focused repeated neurological examination, urgent contrast MRI, cultures, antibiotics and immediate spine/neurosurgical liaison. Temperature 38.7 °C, HR 118/min, BP 102/65, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 96% air. Thoracic midline tenderness; no skin wound. He has subjective leg heaviness, new urinary hesitancy and progressive bilateral weakness. Power: hip flexion 4/5 bilaterally; ankle dorsiflexion 4/5; brisk knee reflexes; sensation reduced below the umbilicus. WCC 16.2 ×10⁹/L, CRP 186 mg/L; creatinine 120 µmol/L. Two blood-culture sets can be obtained promptly. Urgent MRI with contrast (if suitable) shows T6–T9 posterior epidural collection compressing the cord, with adjacent inflammatory change and possible discitis.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Simulated patient answers: “I cannot walk as normally as yesterday. I’m worried I cannot empty my bladder.” If asked, reports no trauma, fever for two days and injecting heroin in the preceding week.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is your working diagnosis? Spinal epidural abscess causing evolving thoracic cord compression, with sepsis risk. What bedside assessment matters? ABCDE, observations, sepsis, serial documented lower-limb power/sensation/reflexes, level of deficit, anal/perineal symptoms where indicated and bladder function. What investigations? Two sets of blood cultures, FBC/CRP/renal function/lactate and urgent spinal MRI (contrast where suitable); discuss scope of imaging with spinal team. When to give antibiotics? Urgent IV empiric antibiotics after rapid cultures if feasible, immediately for sepsis, instability or neurological compromise; no prolonged wait for sampling. What makes this surgical? Progressive neurological deficit and cord compression require immediate spinal/neurosurgical consultation for urgent decompression/drainage plus antimicrobial therapy. Could there be another diagnosis? Malignant cord compression, haematoma, discitis/osteomyelitis or inflammatory pathology; do not delay imaging.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Treats fever plus back pain as uncomplicated muscle strain. Suspects spinal epidural abscess with cord compression given systemic illness and weakness. Explains why bladder dysfunction and evolving bilateral deficit elevate urgency. Resuscitation Ignores tachycardia and hypotension. Initiates ABCDE, sepsis assessment, IV access, bloods and appropriate fluids/monitoring. Reassesses perfusion and organ function and escalates critical-care support if instability progresses. Risk and history Does not ask about neurological change or infection risks. Asks about symptom onset, fever, weakness, sensory disturbance, bladder/bowel issues, diabetes and injecting history. Includes recent procedures, bacteraemia, immunosuppression and previous spinal infection. Neurological assessment Documents only “legs weak” without baseline. Records bilateral motor, sensory level, reflexes, gait only if safe, and bladder symptoms. Repeats timed examinations and records precise change while awaiting definitive care. Microbiology/bloods Sends no cultures or inflammatory markers. Obtains two sets blood cultures promptly and requests FBC, CRP, renal function and la
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: CF1: Discharges the patient with analgesics without emergency MRI or specialist referral. CF2: Fails to act on progressive neurological weakness or new urinary symptoms. CF3: Withholds empiric antibiotics for prolonged diagnostic sampling in a septic or neurologically deteriorating patient. CF4: Allows delayed routine review rather than urgent spinal/neurosurgical evaluation of MRI-confirmed cord compression.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: While awaiting transport for MRI, the patient develops urinary retention and power falls to 2/5 bilaterally. Expected: Repeat and document neurology immediately, urgent consultant-to-consultant spine/neurosurgical escalation, assess/resuscitate sepsis and accelerate MRI/decompression; do not wait for next ward round.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I overlooked the new urinary hesitancy; I will assess bladder function and escalate possible cord compression immediately.” “A normal plain film cannot exclude an epidural abscess; urgent MRI is necessary.” “I should obtain cultures rapidly, but I will not delay antibiotics in this deteriorating patient.”

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-262Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax Applied knowledge / thoracic • 8-minute station • Draft, independent clinical sign-off required • 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 23-year-old previously healthy man presents with sudden right pleuritic pain. He is comfortable at rest, SpO₂ 98% on air, HR 84/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min. Chest X-ray report: right-sided pneumothorax, 3.5 cm rim at hilum, no mediastinal shift. No preceding trauma. You are the surgical trainee assessing this man in the emergency department. Interpret the supplied findings, identify red flags, choose an evidence-based initial management plan and advise him about follow-up, recurrence and activities. You are not asked to insert a chest drain.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings on: Eight-minute applied-knowledge station. Let the candidate request observations, history, examination and imaging details. Challenge automatic drainage on the basis of a 3.5 cm rim alone. Accept a safely organised conservative plan with reliable review, or appropriate ambulatory care following shared decision-making; intervention should be justified by symptoms, physiology, patient circumstances or preference. History: First episode; no cough, fever, trauma, asthma, COPD or previous contralateral episode; occasional cigarettes; no anticoagulation. Examination: Comfortable; mildly reduced right-sided breath sounds; normal perfusion; no tracheal deviation. Imaging: X-ray as brief; no consolidation, pleural fluid or suspected tension. If deterioration introduced: SpO₂ falls to 88%, HR 125/min, BP 84/48 mmHg, severe dyspnoea: treat as possible tension physiology with immediate emergency escalation/decompression, not routine discharge.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: A 23-year-old university student, anxious that a large pneumothorax must mean immediate surgery. He has never been diagnosed with lung disease, smokes occasionally and has no imminent flights. If told a chest drain is mandatory because it is >2 cm, he asks why he feels so well. Wants to know when he can fly and whether he can scuba dive.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: PROMPT — What does the image report mean?EXPECTED — Primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a physiologically stable adult; size alone is not a trigger for invasive intervention under BTS 2023. PROMPT — What are your safe options?EXPECTED — Discuss conservative management (observation/review), ambulatory one-way-valve pathway if locally available, or aspiration/intercostal drainage if symptomatic, high-risk, unsuitable for observation, or patient preference. PROMPT — What follow-up will you arrange?EXPECTED — Respiratory/pleural service follow-up and repeat CXR at 2–4 weeks if observation or aspiration; urgent return for worsening pain, breathlessness or collapse. PROMPT — What if he is a scuba diver?EXPECTED — Advise against compressed-gas diving permanently unless a highly reliable definitive recurrence-prevention strategy has been performed and diving specialists have cleared it.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and classification Calls this haemothorax or labels tension without instability. Identifies first-episode primary spontaneous pneumothorax with normal physiology. States explicitly that underlying lung disease/trauma would change classification and pathway. Immediate safety assessment Fails to check oxygenation or haemodynamics. Checks breathing, observations, pain and tension features. States instability would prompt immediate resuscitation and decompression, not imaging delay. History and risk stratification Does not ask about respiratory disease or prior pneumothorax. Asks symptoms, smoking, trauma, underlying lung disease and prior episodes. Adds occupation, flight/diving plans, home support and capacity to return rapidly. Imaging interpretation Uses the 3.5-cm rim alone to mandate a chest drain. Recognises the reported pneumothorax and absence of mediastinal shift. Explains why BTS symptom/physiology-based selection supersedes size-only rules. Initial treatment choice Refuses discharge only because X-ray looks large, or discharges without assessment. Offers safe conservative care with review to this minimally symptomatic stable adu
sections.6. Four critical fails: Discharges a hypoxic, unstable or tension-suspected patient without immediate emergency management. Makes an invasive procedure compulsory solely because pneumothorax is large despite stability and minimal symptoms, without considering BTS-supported alternatives or patient factors. Allows air travel before radiographic resolution of pneumothorax. Sends the patient home without safety-netting or a defined follow-up arrangement.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: CURVEBALL — A repeat observation shows BP 82/48 mmHg, severe respiratory distress and new tracheal deviation. EXPECTED RESPONSE — Immediately call resuscitation/experienced pleural team, give oxygen and treat suspected tension pneumothorax by emergency decompression according to local trauma/pleural pathway; do not wait for another CXR.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: If you focused on size: “His large X-ray rim alone does not mandate drainage; I will base treatment on symptoms, physiology and safe follow-up.” If you omitted options: “Because he is stable, I would discuss observation and ambulatory care as well as aspiration or drain if needed.” If you missed discharge safety: “I will provide written return advice, respiratory review, repeat imaging and restrictions on flying and diving.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-263Traumatic Haemothorax Critical care / thoracic trauma • 8-minute station • Draft, independent clinical sign-off required • 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 39-year-old man has sustained a high-speed motorcycle collision. He has left rib fractures and increasing breathlessness. BP 92/58 mmHg, pulse 126/min, RR 29/min, SpO₂ 92% on oxygen. Left breath sounds are markedly reduced. The trauma team has inserted a large-bore left intercostal drain under supervision: 1,100 mL of blood drains immediately. You are the surgical trainee assisting the trauma team. Assess and resuscitate the patient, interpret haemothorax and drain output, identify when to involve thoracic surgery and explain ongoing monitoring and definitive management.
sections.2. Examiner brief, including findings on: Eight-minute emergency applied-knowledge station. The scenario begins after initial drain insertion. Expect systematic xABCDE, haemorrhage control and early specialist escalation. Do not require a universal single “immediate output” trigger: haemodynamic status and ongoing loss are decisive. If candidate focuses only on a numeric threshold, reveal persistent hypotension. Primary survey: Airway patent; tachypnoea, cool peripheries; unilateral reduced air entry. No external haemorrhage apparent. Chest imaging: Bedside report: large left pleural collection consistent with blood and three posterolateral rib fractures; no obvious pneumothorax. Contrast CT only after response to resuscitation. Laboratory results: Initial Hb 112 g/L, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, INR 1.1; crossmatch pending. Early Hb does not exclude major blood loss. Drain trend on request: Initial 1,100 mL; subsequent output 260 mL in the first hour, 245 mL in the second and 230 mL in the third. BP remains 90/55 despite initial resuscitation. Further injury search: Potential splenic injury must be considered; trauma series/CT depending on haemodynamic response.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: No actor in acute phase. A relative may ask “Is the drain enough?” if prompted: give a concise explanation that drainage treats pleural compression but ongoing bleeding may need surgery.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: PROMPT — What is the diagnosis and immediate priority?EXPECTED — Significant traumatic haemothorax with haemorrhagic shock risk: senior trauma call, oxygen, haemorrhage resuscitation, monitoring, crossmatch and early thoracic surgery involvement. PROMPT — What does the drain achieve?EXPECTED — Relieves pleural blood burden, improves ventilation and quantifies ongoing bleeding; large tube favoured in unstable traumatic haemothorax. PROMPT — When is operation indicated?EXPECTED — Instability attributable to intrathoracic bleeding or ongoing output >1,500 mL within 24 h or >200 mL/h for three consecutive hours, without alternative explanation, should trigger urgent operative evaluation; do not wait for thresholds if unstable. PROMPT — Could he have another bleeding site?EXPECTED — Yes: reassess chest tube position, pelvis, abdomen, long bones and external sources; interpret drain output with physiology. PROMPT — What about retained clot?EXPECTED — If persistent retained haemothorax despite drainage and patient stabilises, obtain thoracic surgery input for early VATS when appropriate.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition and physiology Calls it simple pneumothorax or ignores shock. Recognises traumatic haemothorax with tachycardia and hypotension. Identifies potentially concurrent tension, pulmonary contusion and extra-thoracic haemorrhage. Primary survey Discusses CT before airway, breathing and circulation. Performs xABCDE, oxygen, monitoring and trauma activation. Coordinates simultaneous ventilation, haemorrhage control and repeated assessment. Haemorrhage resuscitation Treats 1,100 mL loss with only maintenance crystalloid. Obtains two large IV/IO accesses, group and crossmatch, serial gases/Hb and major-haemorrhage support if indicated. Coordinates blood-component resuscitation with trauma leader and avoids delay to bleeding control. Pleural drain management Clamps a freely draining bloody chest tube without expert direction. Checks drain security, patency and documents initial/hours output. Checks for tube blockage, re-expansion, signs of retained haemothorax and ongoing ventilation compromise. Imaging and associated injuries Sends unstable patient alone to CT scanner. Uses bedside imaging/eFAST; CT with contrast once sufficiently stable. Systema
sections.6. Four critical fails: Fails to call immediate trauma/senior help or initiate haemorrhage resuscitation in hypotensive traumatic haemothorax. Waits for a fixed 1,500 mL chest drain output despite persisting shock and ongoing haemorrhage. Clamps or obstructs the blood-draining chest tube without a specific specialist reason. Transfers an unstable actively bleeding patient for nonessential CT instead of controlling haemorrhage.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: CURVEBALL — After three hours, the drain has produced 260, 245 and 230 mL per hour, and systolic BP stays around 90 mmHg. EXPECTED RESPONSE — Continue massive haemorrhage and physiology-guided resuscitation; immediate thoracic/trauma surgeon decision for operative haemostasis. Output exceeds >200 mL/h for three hours and haemodynamic compromise independently demands action.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: If focused on the first 1,100 mL: “I would not wait for 1,500 mL if he remains hypotensive; I am calling thoracic surgery now.” If you missed associated injuries: “I will reassess pelvis and abdomen because the chest may not be the sole bleeding site.” If you skipped trends: “I will chart drain output hourly alongside observations, transfusion needs and lactate.”

stations.title: Incidental Lung Nodule

sections.preamble: B2-264 | Incidental Lung Nodule AMaC MRCS Part B · Data interpretation · 8-minute station · Draft for independent clinical sign-off · 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an MRCS candidate in a thoracic outpatient referral clinic. A 63-year-old former smoker has an incidental pulmonary nodule on CT performed for renal colic. Interpret the written report, assess cancer probability and explain a safe next step. No images are provided.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only if req: CT chest completed subsequently: solitary 11-mm solid, mildly spiculated right-upper-lobe nodule; no enlarged thoracic nodes; no distant lesions on reported field. No prior imaging available. Ex-smoker: 25 pack-years, quit eight years ago. No prior cancer, haemoptysis, weight loss or significant breathlessness; independent with normal activities. Ask the candidate to outline the BTS risk-based pathway, rather than demand an exact risk without a calculator.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is worried the spot means lung cancer; asks if it can be removed today. Willing to undergo further imaging but frightened of biopsy. Wants to know who contacts them with the result.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What scan features influence risk? Expected: size, morphology/spiculation, upper-lobe position, growth, solidity. What is the purpose of Brock? Expected: estimate probability for ≥8-mm nodule, using clinical and CT factors. If calculated Brock risk is 14%? Expected: consider PET-CT then reassess with Herder and MDT. If PET-CT later gives a low Herder score? Expected: structured CT surveillance rather than reflex resection; confirm local nodule pathway.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical framing Calls an incidental nodule a confirmed cancer, causing undue alarm. States that a pulmonary nodule is indeterminate and needs structured assessment. Explains baseline cancer probability, differential diagnosis and limits of an isolated CT finding without falsely reassuring. History Does not ask about prior malignancy, tobacco history or prior imaging. Elicits smoking, previous cancer, symptoms and compares earlier imaging. Also explores occupational exposures, family history, immune status and prior radiological stability. Radiology description Ignores size, solidity or upper-lobe location. Summarises an 11-mm solid spiculated right-upper-lobe nodule. Requests thin-section CT review, exact volumetry and examines growth, other nodules and benign morphology. Risk assessment Uses diameter alone to label malignancy. Recommends Brock risk estimation given age, smoking and ≥8-mm size. Explains risk estimates are aids, uses full input details and avoids applying models uncritically in known extrathoracic cancer. Imaging next step Discharges without follow-up or automatically books immediate surgery. Proposes PET-CT if Brock malignancy ris
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: Calls an 11-mm suspicious solid nodule benign and discharges without a surveillance or MDT plan. States a lung nodule is definitely cancer and recommends surgery without risk assessment or MDT. Misses critical haemoptysis or clinical decline and fails to arrange urgent evaluation. Fails to ensure ownership of results or follow-up, allowing a high-risk nodule to be lost.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Patient reveals a CT from another hospital two years ago. Expected: retrieve and compare directly before finalising surveillance; reliable long-term stability can materially reduce concern, but do not treat unverified recollection as proof.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should check previous imaging before deciding the risk pathway for this nodule.” “I should calculate Brock risk using the CT features, age and smoking history; size alone is not a diagnosis.” “I need a named respiratory nodule pathway to own the next scan, result and communication.”

stations.title: Chest Drain Problems: Bubbling, Swinging, Blocked

sections.preamble: B2-265 | Chest Drain Problems: Bubbling, Swinging, Blocked AMaC MRCS Part B · Applied knowledge / pleural emergencies · 8-minute station · Draft for independent clinical sign-off · 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar on call. A nurse calls because a patient with an intercostal drain inserted for right pneumothorax has stopped swinging and bubbling. Demonstrate your systematic assessment of the patient and drain and explain what you would do if the drain were blocked or leaking. No images.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose only if req: Patient: 48-year-old with right-sided pneumothorax drained 24 hours ago; currently RR 20, SpO2 96% on air, HR 88, BP 124/76, afebrile. Drain: underwater seal bottle below chest, initially bubbled intermittently; no bubbling or swing now. External drainage tubing is bent under the bed; once straightened, mild swinging resumes. Repeat chest radiograph after checking tubing: right lung re-expanded, drain side holes within thorax; no enlarging pneumothorax. If deterioration is introduced: RR 34, SpO2 85%, BP 88/55 and unilateral poor air entry — treat possible tension physiology as emergency, not a routine bottle issue.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Nurse concerned a blocked drain could be dangerous; asks “Should I clamp it while we wait?” Patient reports mild insertion-site discomfort but no worsening dyspnoea at baseline.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the first action? Expected: assess patient/observations and call for urgent help if unstable. Why might swinging stop? Expected: kinking/blockage, re-expansion, or system malfunction. What does bubbling mean? Expected: possible patient air leak or external-system leak; context and connections matter. Can a bubbling pneumothorax drain be clamped? Expected: avoid routine clamping because of tension risk. When to use saline flush or suction? Expected: only with clinical indication, trained personnel, local/specialist protocol; do not force through a misplaced drain.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate condition Focuses only on bottle rather than deteriorating patient. Checks ABCDE, SpO2, respiratory effort and haemodynamics first. Identifies possible tension physiology and initiates immediate emergency escalation and decompression without awaiting imaging. Drain setup Leaves bottle above chest and ignores disconnections. Checks underwater seal, fluid level, upright bottle below chest, connections and kinks. Checks for cracks/dislodgement, secures system and documents output, swinging and bubbling trends. Bubbling interpretation States all bubbling means the drain is functioning normally. Recognises bubbling may indicate air leak or system leak and assesses patient and connections. Differentiates continuous versus respiratory-associated bubbling and checks radiology and surgical/pleural context. Swinging interpretation Assumes no swing always means drain blockage. Explains loss of swinging may reflect obstruction or fully re-expanded lung. Uses observations, drain position, air leak, tubing and chest imaging to distinguish causes. Obstruction response Blindly pushes the drain inward or vigorously flushes against resistance. Checks exter
sections.6. Four station-specific critical fails: Clamps a bubbling chest drain without specialist direction, risking tension pneumothorax. Ignores respiratory collapse while troubleshooting equipment instead of emergency treatment. Reinserts a partly dislodged drain through the skin or blindly advances an externalised tube. Forcefully flushes or applies unprescribed suction without checking drain position, system and patient.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: When asked to unclamp a bubbling drain, the nurse says it was clamped an hour ago and the patient is acutely breathless. Expected: immediately assess ABCDE, release inappropriate clamp, summon emergency help, treat possible tension pneumothorax immediately according to expertise and local protocol; imaging must not delay life-saving action.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “Before touching the drain I need a fresh set of observations and a respiratory examination.” “Absence of swing may be a kink, obstruction or full re-expansion; I must examine the whole system and imaging.” “Do not clamp an air-leaking pneumothorax drain routinely; call the pleural or thoracic team.”

stations.title: Cardiac Risk Before Major Non-Cardiac Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-266 | Cardiac Risk Before Major Non-Cardiac Surgery AMaC MRCS Part B · Applied knowledge / perioperative medicine · 8-minute station · Draft 13 October 2026 Teaching and assessment resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Independent specialist clinical sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 71-year-old man is listed in three weeks for elective open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. He has diabetes treated with insulin, CKD (eGFR 44), previous myocardial infarction eight years ago and reduced exercise tolerance from claudication. No chest pain at rest. Discuss cardiac risk assessment and optimisation with the examiner. You may request examination findings, investigation results and relevant background. Explain your assessment and decisions aloud.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose on request: Do not volunteer findings before the candidate requests them. Use these findings consistently: • History: MI eight years ago; no current angina, orthopnoea, syncope or palpitations. Climbs one flight slowly because of leg pain; true exercise capacity is uncertain. • Examination: BP 142/78, pulse 76 regular; no congestion, murmur or resting hypoxia. • Investigations: Hb 115 g/L; eGFR 44; current ECG shows old Q waves without new ischaemia. No recent echo. • Clarification: No active decompensated heart failure, unstable arrhythmia, recent ACS or symptomatic severe valve disease. • Plan constraint: Elective major vascular operation; anaesthetic and vascular teams are available for shared decision-making.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner-led station; no actor required. If simulated, respond only to questions asked; the patient is worried about complications and wants a clear explanation without false reassurance.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • First step? Expected: Determine urgency and screen for active/unstable cardiac conditions before risk-scoring. • How estimate risk? Expected: Name RCRI factors: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine >177 µmol/L. His RCRI is 3 (vascular operation, IHD, insulin), unless a further qualifying factor emerges; eGFR does not substitute for serum creatinine threshold. • Functional status? Expected: Explore activity limits and Duke Activity Status Index; do not assume claudication proves cardiac limitation. • Tests? Expected: ECG appropriate. Consider BNP/NT-proBNP and baseline troponin if results change management; echocardiography for new/worsening symptoms or suspected significant disease, not as blanket routine. Stress testing only if elevated risk, poor/uncertain capacity and results would change management. • What next? Expected: Continue indicated long-term cardiovascular therapy and coordinate medication adjustments with anaesthesia/cardiology; no prophylactic coronary revascularisation solely to clear elective surgery. • How counsel? Expected: Communicate individualised cardiac and surgical trade-o
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Problem framing Proceeds as if elective surgery requires no cardiac assessment. Identifies major vascular surgery and asks about current cardiac symptoms. Explicitly separates urgency, active cardiac disease and baseline risk before testing. History Does not ask about angina, heart failure or syncope. Asks about chest pain, dyspnoea, orthopnoea, syncope and prior cardiac events. Also checks prior coronary procedures, exercise limitation, medication adherence and symptoms since last review. Examination Omits pulse, blood pressure and signs of decompensation. Requests vitals, cardiac auscultation and signs of heart failure. Links new murmur or congestion to targeted investigation and change in operative timing. Risk calculation Calls eGFR 44 an automatic RCRI creatinine point or cannot identify factors. Correctly identifies RCRI 3 from surgery, IHD and insulin treatment. States RCRI limitations, uses estimated event risk and communicates uncertainty without false precision. Functional capacity Declares functional capacity normal because there is no chest pain. Recognises capacity uncertain because of claudication and asks about usual tasks. Uses stru
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Proceeds with elective major surgery despite an unassessed active acute coronary syndrome or decompensated heart failure. 2. Orders routine stress testing and treats the result as mandatory clearance regardless of whether it changes management. 3. Inaccurately gives an RCRI renal point solely because eGFR is 44, then asserts a precise event risk from that error. 4. Starts a new high-dose beta-blocker immediately before surgery without assessment or titration. Examiner note: these are safety triggers for review of performance; use the agreed station-level judgement rather than assuming an automatic numerical penalty.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: Patient reveals new episodes of chest pressure at rest over the past 48 hours. Expected response: Treat as possible active ACS: stop elective pathway, urgent clinical assessment, ECG/troponin according to ACS pathway, senior anaesthetic/cardiology review; defer elective operation pending evaluation.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I initially treated the renal impairment as an RCRI point; the original RCRI specifies serum creatinine above 177 µmol/L, so I would correct the score.” 2. “I should first establish whether he has any active cardiac condition; the new resting chest pressure would change the decision to proceed.” 3. “The patient’s walking is limited by claudication, so I would not equate low walking distance with cardiac exercise intolerance without further assessment.”

stations.title: Postoperative Chest Pain: Myocardial Infarction After Surgery

sections.preamble: B2-267 | Postoperative Chest Pain: Myocardial Infarction After Surgery AMaC MRCS Part B · Critical care / data interpretation · 8-minute station · Draft 13 October 2026 Teaching and assessment resource; not an official MRCS marking scheme. Independent specialist clinical sign-off required before publication.
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar. A 73-year-old woman develops chest pressure and breathlessness on day 1 after major colorectal resection. BP 96/62, HR 112, SpO₂ 92% on air; dressing has fresh blood, drain output 150 mL over two hours. Explain your immediate response and interpretation of ECG and troponin results. You may request examination findings, investigation results and relevant background. Explain your assessment and decisions aloud.
sections.2. Examiner brief — disclose on request: Do not volunteer findings before the candidate requests them. Use these findings consistently: • On request: Pain lasted 20 minutes and persists; awake and speaking. No calf asymmetry. Fluid balance +1.5 L since surgery. • ECG: Sinus tachycardia with new 1 mm horizontal ST depression in V4–V6; no ST elevation. • Laboratory: hs-troponin 18 ng/L preoperatively and 126 ng/L now (laboratory 99th percentile 14); Hb 108 g/L preop to 86 now. Lactate 2.6 mmol/L. • Further investigations: Repeat troponin at three hours 205 ng/L; no documented pulmonary embolism, sepsis or renal deterioration yet. • Surgical issue: Fresh wound ooze and falling haemoglobin make immediate full antithrombotic treatment potentially hazardous.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Examiner-led station; no actor required. If simulated, respond only to questions asked; the patient is worried about complications and wants a clear explanation without false reassurance.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: • What immediately? Expected: ABCDE, senior help, monitoring, oxygen if hypoxaemic, IV access, ECG, serial troponins, FBC/U&E/coagulation, blood gas/lactate, assess bleeding and resuscitation. • Interpret results? Expected: Dynamic troponin rise plus new ischaemic ECG changes supports acute myocardial infarction in this context; distinguish myocardial injury from MI and type 1 from supply-demand type 2; assess haemorrhage. • Differential? Expected: ACS, pulmonary embolism, haemorrhagic shock / demand ischaemia, pneumonia/atelectasis, pulmonary oedema, sepsis and other non-ischaemic troponin causes. • Escalation? Expected: Early cardiology/ACS consultation, surgical and anaesthetic/critical-care teams; urgent cath-lab pathway if STEMI or ongoing high-risk ACS; coordinate any therapy with bleeding control. • Drugs? Expected: Do not give automatic heparin/DAPT while active bleeding is suspected; obtain urgent cardiology and surgical consensus. Continue indicated secondary prevention when safe. • Monitoring? Expected: Serial ECG/troponin, repeat Hb, haemodynamic and urine-output monitoring, reassess symptoms, consider echocardiography and appropriate imaging when stable.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate recognition Reassures without examining the postoperative chest pain. Identifies time-critical acute cardiac problem and asks for help. Activates coordinated surgical, cardiology and critical-care response for shock and ischaemia. ABCDE/resuscitation Fails to check oxygenation, perfusion and ongoing bleeding. Assesses airway, breathing, circulation and gives oxygen for documented hypoxaemia. Titrates oxygen, establishes monitored access, evaluates blood loss and calls for blood products if indicated. History/examination Ignores nature of pain and operative bleeding signs. Asks onset, pain features, dyspnoea and reviews bleeding signs, perfusion and chest examination. Screens for PE, sepsis, cardiac failure and drug history while reprioritising immediate threats. ECG Misreads ST depression as a normal tracing. Recognises new lateral ST depression and arranges serial 12-lead ECGs. Interprets dynamic ECG changes in clinical context and escalates persistent ischaemia promptly. Troponin interpretation Calls any elevated troponin a definite type 1 MI. Recognises rising troponin and explains myocardial injury versus infarction. Links ischaemic E
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Dismisses persistent chest pain and new ST depression without ECG/troponin evaluation or urgent escalation. 2. Starts therapeutic anticoagulation and dual antiplatelet therapy without considering the suspected active postoperative bleeding. 3. Treats elevated troponin as proof of plaque-rupture type 1 MI without considering demand ischaemia and non-ischaemic causes. 4. Fails to address hypotension and a falling haemoglobin while focusing solely on the ECG. Examiner note: these are safety triggers for review of performance; use the agreed station-level judgement rather than assuming an automatic numerical penalty.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: The blood pressure drops to 78/46, drain output rises and haemoglobin falls to 71 g/L. Expected response: Activate major haemorrhage / urgent surgical source-control pathway, call anaesthetics and cardiology, resuscitate with blood as appropriate and reassess myocardial ischaemia. Avoid uncoordinated antithrombotics while active life-threatening bleeding is occurring.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “I called this a type 1 MI too early; there is definite acute myocardial injury with ischaemic evidence, but the cause needs assessment for bleeding-related supply-demand mismatch.” 2. “I need to re-examine the wound and drain immediately because haemorrhage can both destabilise her and precipitate myocardial ischaemia.” 3. “I would not administer routine heparin or dual antiplatelets until the bleeding risk has been urgently weighed with cardiology and the operating surgeon.”

stations.title: Advice After a Minor Head Injury

sections.preamble: B2-268 | Advice After a Minor Head Injury AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication | 8-minute station | Draft for independent clinical sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical SHO in an emergency department follow-up area. A 29-year-old adult was assessed after a fall, has GCS 15, a normal neurological examination and no indication for CT under the documented NICE assessment. The senior clinician has agreed discharge. Explain safe recovery and discharge advice to the patient (played by an actor). Task: check discharge suitability, communicate written and verbal advice, verify supervision and safety-netting. Do not repeat an entire initial head-injury assessment unless prompted.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Adult, fall from standing, transient mild headache improving with paracetamol; no loss of consciousness, seizure, vomiting, amnesia, anticoagulant or non-aspirin antiplatelet therapy, intoxication, skull fracture signs or focal deficit. GCS 15 from arrival; observations stable. Normal balance and gait; no neck pain. Patient lives with partner who is available for the first 24 hours; patient had planned to drive home and play football tomorrow. Written head injury advice available. If candidate asks about worsening headache, confusion or vomiting: currently none.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are worried that “concussion” means permanent brain damage. Ask: “Can I drive home? Is it safe to sleep? Can I play football tomorrow?” If candidate mentions a responsible adult, confirm partner can stay overnight. At minute six say: “My partner has suddenly been called away for work tonight.” Expect candidate to reassess safety of discharge and find another responsible adult or arrange observation, not simply ignore this.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt at 2 minutes if advice is superficial: “What should make the patient come straight back?” Expect worsening/persistent headache, repeated vomiting, worsening drowsiness, confusion, seizure, weakness, speech/vision changes or fluid/blood from nose/ears. Prompt at 4 minutes: “Does a normal examination mean there is zero risk?” Expect reassurance with residual risk, clear instructions and emergency action. Prompt at 6 minutes: “Who will be with them at home?” Expect a responsible adult for 24 hours and confirmation of accessibility of advice.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Safety of discharge Reassures despite unresolved discharge concerns Confirms senior discharge decision, current stability and no evolving symptoms Actively identifies discharge barriers, revises plan if supervision lost Symptom assessment Does not ask about current headache or neurological change Checks headache trend, vomiting, confusion, weakness and seizure history Differentiates expected transient symptoms from new deterioration and documents baseline Supervision No question about who is home Confirms responsible adult will stay for first 24 hours Plans alternative safe observation when original carer unavailable Red flag advice No warnings or vague “come back if unwell” Names worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, seizure and focal deficits Tailors red flags to patient and tells carer to call emergency services for major neurological change Expected recovery Promises full recovery by tomorrow Explains headache, dizziness, tiredness and concentration symptoms may occur Explains variability and follow-up for persistent concussion symptoms Activity and driving Permits immediate driving and contact sport Avoids driving until fully re
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Discharges the patient knowing no responsible adult is available for the first 24 hours, without arranging an alternative safe plan. 2. Tells the patient to ignore worsening drowsiness, seizures, persistent severe headache or new weakness. 3. Advises immediate return to contact sport or driving despite continuing post-head-injury symptoms. 4. Ignores new safety information that removes the required adult supervision and proceeds to discharge without reassessment.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Actor says the partner is unexpectedly unavailable tonight. Candidate checks for another trusted responsible adult; if none, contacts the supervising clinician to arrange safe observation/alternative disposition, updates documentation and gives emergency instructions.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should have checked your arrangements first: who can stay with you for the first 24 hours?” “I was too reassuring: although serious deterioration is unlikely, worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures or weakness mean urgent emergency assessment.” “To correct my driving and sport advice: do not drive until fully recovered, and return to contact sport only after appropriate symptom recovery and graduated return guidance.”

stations.title: Sciatica from a Lumbar Disc Prolapse

sections.preamble: B2-269 | Sciatica from a Lumbar Disc Prolapse AMaC MRCS Part B | Applied knowledge / spine | 8-minute station | Draft for independent clinical sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the orthopaedic SHO in a spinal clinic. A 42-year-old warehouse worker has six weeks of right leg pain following a lifting episode. Take a focused history, explain the likely cause, outline investigation and treatment options, and identify when escalation is urgent. Examiner supplies examination and written MRI findings on request.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings disclosed: Pain radiates from right buttock down posterolateral calf into lateral foot, with pins and needles. Worse on coughing/sitting. No prior cancer, unexplained fever, immunosuppression or recent major trauma. No bladder retention, new incontinence, saddle altered sensation or bilateral progressive symptoms. Neurological findings if requested: positive right straight-leg raise at 40 degrees reproducing leg pain; reduced right ankle jerk and diminished lateral-foot sensation, plantarflexion 4+/5, normal other strength, gait with mild discomfort. Written MRI (if indicated after persistent/functionally limiting symptoms): right L5/S1 posterolateral disc protrusion contacting/compressing traversing S1 root, consistent with clinical side and distribution; no central canal compromise.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: You are anxious that “a slipped disc” means you will be paralysed, and you want an MRI immediately. You have missed work but remain ambulatory. Ask whether tablets, injections or surgery are necessary. At minute six say: “Actually, today I cannot pass urine and the area between my legs feels numb.” This is a new change requiring emergency cauda equina assessment.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “Which questions cannot be omitted?” Expect new bladder/bowel change, saddle anaesthesia, sexual dysfunction, progressive weakness, bilateral sciatica, systemic red flags. “When is MRI justified?” Expect no routine non-specialist MRI without indication; specialist imaging if it will change management, or urgent emergency MRI on suspected cauda equina. “What options exist?” Expect advice to stay active, graded exercise/physio, appropriate limited analgesia, consider epidural local anaesthetic and steroid for acute severe sciatica, decompression if persistent symptoms despite non-operative care with concordant imaging.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance History and pattern Calls calf pain nonspecific without radiation history Elicits dermatomal radiating pain, triggers, duration and function Correlates lateral-foot symptoms with S1 distribution and cough provocation Cauda equina screening Omits bladder and perineal questions Checks retention, bowel changes, saddle sensation and bilateral symptoms Recognises new retention/saddle symptoms as emergency without false reassurance Other red flags Does not ask fever, trauma or cancer risks Asks fever, cancer, trauma, weight loss and progressive deficit Adjusts investigation urgency to concerning systemic or infective features Examination No leg neurological exam described Requests power, sensation, reflexes and straight-leg raise Specifies plantarflexion, ankle jerk and lateral-foot S1 correlation Imaging decisions Orders routine MRI with no management rationale Explains MRI for specialist decisions or concerning findings Balances imaging against incidental changes, requests emergency MRI for CES suspicion Conservative options Recommends bed rest and no rehabilitation Encourages activity, graded exercise/physio and prudent pain relief Agrees occupational
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: 1. Fails to act on new retention plus saddle numbness in the curveball; sends patient home routinely. 2. Reassures that cauda equina syndrome is excluded without asking bladder, bowel and perineal symptoms. 3. Recommends routine spinal decompression without concordant clinical and imaging findings or conservative-treatment discussion in stable non-emergency case. 4. Prescribes gabapentinoids, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines routinely for sciatica despite NICE advice against their use.
sections.7. Realistic curveball and expected resp: Patient reveals new inability to pass urine and saddle numbness. Candidate interrupts ordinary consultation, performs rapid focussed neurological/CES assessment and immediate senior/spinal referral for emergency MRI and assessment. Do not rely on normal motor strength or delay until outpatient imaging.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I missed an essential safety question: have you developed urinary difficulty, saddle numbness, bowel changes or worsening leg weakness?” “An MRI is not automatically helpful for every episode of sciatica; we arrange it when it will alter specialist treatment, or urgently if red flags develop.” “Your new bladder and perineal symptoms could indicate cauda equina compression; this needs emergency hospital assessment today, not a routine follow-up.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-270 Thyrotoxic Patient Listed for Thyroidectomy Applied knowledge / endocrine surgery | 8-minute station | Draft for specialist sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 36-year-old woman with Graves disease listed for elective total thyroidectomy tomorrow. She reports palpitations and tremor. Review the data supplied by the examiner, decide if surgery should proceed, and describe a safe plan.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings on reques: Setting: elective pre-assessment clinic. Patient taking carbimazole inconsistently; has missed tablets for ten days. Today HR 122/min regular, BP 138/72 mmHg, T 37.1°C, fine tremor, no stridor or heart failure; ECG sinus tachycardia. Recent TSH <0.01 mU/L, FT4 49 pmol/L (laboratory range 12–22), FT3 13 pmol/L (range 3.5–6.5). Indication: recurrent symptomatic Graves disease despite previous medication course. No current crisis. Examiner must not invent additional findings.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Alert, worried about losing her theatre date: “I stopped the tablets because I felt better. Can I still have surgery tomorrow?” If asked: no fever, diarrhoea, chest pain, confusion, syncope or breathlessness; no pregnancy; no drug allergies.
