Respond with concern about delay but accept an explanation of safety.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Ask for clinical signs: tachycardia and tremor, no decompensation. Ask for blood tests: values in examiner brief. Ask how to proceed: defer elective surgery, communicate with anaesthesia/endocrinology and surgeon, restart/adjust antithyroid therapy under specialist advice, beta-block symptoms when suitable and re-assess FT4/FT3 and clinical status. Ask about thyroid storm: fever, marked tachycardia, CNS disturbance, gastrointestinal symptoms, heart failure and urgent supportive/ICU management. Ask about Graves-specific pre-op iodide: specialist-directed short course near surgery, not a substitute for making the patient safe.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Problem recognition Calls the patient fit despite tremor, pulse 122 and high free T4. Recognises uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis and elevated operative risk. States elective thyroidectomy must be paused pending endocrine–anaesthetic optimisation and clear biochemical/clinical reassessment. Clinical assessment Does not ask about fever, confusion, heart failure or arrhythmia. Checks pulse, temperature, BP, mental state, hydration and cardiopulmonary signs. Seeks ECG, identifies evolving storm warning signs and immediately differentiates urgent illness from elective assessment. Results interpretation Uses suppressed TSH alone as evidence of ongoing severe excess. Interprets elevated FT4/FT3 alongside symptoms and TSH. Explains TSH may remain suppressed after FT4/FT3 normalise; decisions should not rely on TSH alone. Medication review Ignores omitted carbimazole or adverse effects. Checks adherence, current antithyroid drug, beta blocker, allergies and adverse effects. Explains fever/sore throat requires urgent blood count to assess antithyroid-drug agranulocytosis and coordinates changes with endocrinology. Preoperative optimisation Proceeds without medic
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Permits elective anaesthesia tomorrow despite clear uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis without senior risk review. 2. Fails to recognise severe new fever, delirium and cardiovascular compromise as possible thyroid storm. 3. Discontinues or withholds all thyroid control therapy with no alternative plan and no escalation. 4. Fails to alert surgeon/anaesthetist to the elevated free hormones and tachycardia before planned operating.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: During discussion, actor adds: “I have a temperature of 39°C and my heart has started racing today.” Expected response: stop routine consent; rapid ABCDE and vital signs, monitor ECG, obtain emergency endocrine/anaesthetic/critical-care help, assess for thyroid storm and manage per specialist emergency protocol.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “The free hormones remain high even though TSH is not a useful short-term clearance target; this is not a safe elective list case.” 2. “I need to check for storm signs now—not just repeat bloods—and call the senior thyroid and anaesthetic teams.” 3. “I will document the reason for postponement, who is adjusting treatment, and how endocrine control will be confirmed before rebooking.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: AMaC MRCS Part B | B2-271 Medullary Thyroid Cancer and MEN Syndromes Applied knowledge / endocrine oncology | 8-minute station | Draft for specialist sign-off | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 44-year-old patient has a fine-needle aspirate reported as medullary thyroid carcinoma. Explain which inherited syndromes matter, the preoperative investigations and priorities, and how you would advise the family.
sections.2. Examiner brief and findings on reques: Clinic referral: right thyroid nodule 2.4 cm, suspicious ipsilateral central neck node; cytology supports MTC. Calcitonin 630 pg/mL, CEA 24 micrograms/L. Family history unclear. No RET result yet, no catecholamine workup; surgery discussed but not booked. Serum calcium 2.62 mmol/L (local high 2.55). BP 140/85, no acute adrenergic symptoms. Examiner reveals tests only on request.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor is worried: “Is this the same thyroid cancer my aunt had? Will my children need surgery?” If asked: aunt had thyroid surgery aged 38; no known genetic results. Patient has occasional headache and palpitations but no established adrenal diagnosis. Wants explanation without deterministic predictions about children.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is MTC? C-cell neuroendocrine malignancy; calcitonin and CEA used for assessment/follow-up. Ask what to check before surgery: germline RET testing in every MTC, biochemical exclusion of phaeochromocytoma while RET status unknown, calcium ± PTH if high, expert neck ultrasound and staging. Ask MEN variants: MEN2A MTC, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism; MEN2B MTC, phaeochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas/marfanoid habitus. If metanephrines positive: endocrine review, alpha blockade and adrenal treatment before thyroid surgery. Family: cascade RET testing and variant-based paediatric surveillance/prophylactic surgery after specialist counselling.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Diagnostic recognition Calls the calcitonin-producing tumour papillary carcinoma. Recognises medullary thyroid carcinoma arising from thyroid C cells. Links calcitonin/CEA with MTC and separates its staging/treatment from follicular-cell cancers. MEN classification Misses hereditary disease entirely. Identifies sporadic and hereditary MTC, MEN2A and MEN2B. Contrasts MEN2A (phaeochromocytoma ± hyperparathyroidism) with MEN2B (mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, phaeochromocytoma). Family and genetic history Does not ask about relatives with endocrine tumours. Asks about MTC, adrenal tumours, thyroidectomy and affected first-degree relatives. Explains autosomal-dominant inheritance and that apparent sporadic MTC still needs germline RET testing. Tumour assessment Requests no biomarkers or ultrasound. Requests baseline calcitonin, CEA, neck ultrasound and node evaluation. Plans extent-of-disease imaging according to tumour burden, symptoms and specialist MDT assessment. Phaeochromocytoma safety Sends patient to thyroidectomy without excluding an adrenal catecholamine tumour. Orders plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines before surgery where
sections.6. Four critical fails: 1. Plans thyroidectomy without ruling out phaeochromocytoma despite possible MEN2 and unknown RET status. 2. Recommends immediate neck surgery after a positive phaeochromocytoma screen without adrenal stabilisation/treatment. 3. States no genetic testing is needed because the patient lacks an established MEN family history. 4. Proposes radioactive iodine as an effective definitive treatment for medullary thyroid carcinoma.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The examiner now discloses plasma normetanephrine markedly elevated on a correctly obtained test. Expected response: stop thyroid surgery planning; urgent endocrinology/endocrine surgery assessment, confirm/localise phaeochromocytoma, medically prepare and treat adrenal disease first. Do not perform unprepared thyroidectomy.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: 1. “This is medullary, not differentiated, thyroid cancer; I need calcitonin, CEA and a germline RET result.” 2. “With unknown RET status I must exclude a phaeochromocytoma before any thyroid operation.” 3. “A positive familial variant leads to counselling and testing of relatives, with timing determined by the specific mutation.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-272 — Hoarse Voice After Thyroidectomy AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / postoperative endocrine surgery | 8-minute station | Educational assessment draft | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in postoperative clinic. A 46-year-old teacher has noticed a weak, breathy voice since hemithyroidectomy 10 days ago. Explain your assessment and management to the patient. No equipment is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient stable at clinic: BP 124/76, pulse 82, SpO₂ 98% on air, no stridor or neck swelling. Left hemithyroidectomy for benign nodule; preoperative voice reportedly normal. Operative note: recurrent laryngeal nerve identified and preserved; this does NOT prove intact function. If flexible nasendoscopy is requested: left vocal fold reduced mobility in paramedian position, right mobile. If asked, no calcium symptoms.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is anxious about returning to classroom teaching; sometimes coughs when drinking water. Says “Did the surgeon cut my nerve?” Volunteer should be worried but not hostile. If candidate asks about breathlessness: none. If asked about professional impact: cannot project voice across room.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt at minute 2: “Can you say for certain the nerve was damaged?” Expected: do not diagnose mechanism without laryngoscopy and record review. Prompt at minute 4: “What if I choke when drinking?” Expected: assess swallowing/aspiration, SLT and appropriate urgency. Curveball at minute 6 as specified below.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Initial safety and acuity: Tells patient all hoarseness is harmless; ignores breathing difficulty. Asks about stridor, dyspnoea, neck swelling and immediately assesses airway if present. Separates airway obstruction from isolated dysphonia; activates senior anaesthetic/ENT/thyroid surgical help without delaying for routine clinic tests.
sections.2. Symptom history: Does not establish timing or functional effects. Checks onset after surgery, progression, weak/breathy voice, cough, swallowing and aspiration. Asks about choking on liquids, voice fatigue, pitch and professional voice requirements; compares pre-operative voice.
sections.3. Relevant operative background: Assumes nerve was cut without reviewing records. Asks procedure type, intubation course, previous surgery and documented nerve concerns. Requests operative note, preoperative laryngoscopy and postoperative events; distinguishes possible intubation trauma or laryngeal oedema.

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-273 — Consent for Superficial Parotidectomy AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / head and neck surgery | 8-minute station | Educational assessment draft | 13 October 2026
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the ENT surgical registrar. A 52-year-old patient has a 2.6-cm mobile superficial right parotid mass with cytology favouring pleomorphic adenoma. Explain the planned superficial parotidectomy and seek informed consent.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient has normal facial movements and no neck nodes. Ultrasound shows well-defined superficial-lobe lesion; fine-needle sample favours pleomorphic adenoma but is not absolute histological proof. Planned elective superficial parotidectomy with general anaesthesia and facial nerve identification. Anticoagulation and comorbidity information disclosed only on request: no blood thinner, no significant medical disease.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is concerned about facial paralysis and scar. Asks “Can I just leave it?” At minute 5 reveals they are a school photographer and worries about appearance. If asked, understands needle test is not 100% certain.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Prompt: “What exactly are you removing?” Expected: superficial parotid tissue containing lesion with facial nerve protection, not a claim that the nerve is routinely sacrificed. Prompt: “Can you guarantee my face will be normal?” Expected: realistic temporary and permanent weakness risk without made-up rates. Prompt: “Will it affect sweating while I eat?” Expected: Frey syndrome explanation.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance
sections.1. Rapport and decision capacity: Starts by presenting a form to sign. Introduces role, establishes indication and checks patient preferences and understanding. Identifies the patient’s concerns about facial movement, appearance and work, then tailors the discussion.
sections.2. Diagnosis and uncertainty: Calls the lesion definitively benign without histology. Explains imaging/cytology suggesting a benign superficial parotid lesion and histological confirmation after excision. Clarifies limitations of needle sampling and identifies facial weakness, fixation or rapid growth as reassessment red flags.
sections.3. Operation explained: Says whole parotid is removed and no scar remains. Explains general anaesthesia, skin incision, superficial-lobe removal with facial nerve identification and wound closure. Describes drain possibility, approximate inpatient/recovery expectations without inventing exact duration.

stations.title: A Mouth Ulcer That Won’t Heal

sections.preamble: B2-274 | A Mouth Ulcer That Won’t Heal AMaC MRCS Part B • History / head and neck oncology • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are in the surgical outpatient clinic. A 56-year-old patient reports a persistent ulcer along the right lateral tongue for five weeks. Take a focused history, describe your examination, explain the concern and agree the next step.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Actor has a 12-mm irregular, firm-edged ulcer on the right lateral tongue; mild local tenderness; a 1.5-cm firm right level II cervical node. Stable observations and no airway symptoms. Provide findings only if candidate asks for systematic examination, palpation and neck nodes. No histology is yet available.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient: “I thought I had bitten it. Do you think it is cancer?” Ulcer has enlarged slightly, hurts with acidic foods. Smokes 10 cigarettes/day for 25 years; drinks about 16 units/week. No recent dental changes. Mild unintentional weight loss. Wants clear explanation without a premature cancer diagnosis.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What features worry you?” — more than three weeks, indurated irregular edge, persistent growth, lymphadenopathy. “How will you examine?” — full oral cavity including tongue edges and floor, bimanual palpation as appropriate, dentition, cervical nodes and cranial nerve XII. “Who will refer?” — prompt suspected oral cancer pathway to head-and-neck / OMFS service under local pathway. “How is diagnosis made?” — specialist biopsy for histopathology; staging after malignancy confirmed, not diagnosis by appearance alone. “Can you prescribe gel and review in a month?” — no; symptomatic treatment must not delay referral.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Opening and rapport Dismisses concern as a mouth sore. Introduces role, elicits chief concern and uses clear language. Asks what the patient fears and structures an unhurried discussion. Ulcer history Does not establish duration. Clarifies five-week persistence, size trend, pain and prior episodes. Elicits trauma, altered sensation, bleeding and focal functional change. Associated symptoms Does not enquire about swallowing or neck swelling. Checks dysphagia, odynophagia, speech change, neck lump and weight loss. Adds ear pain, trismus and systemic symptoms relevant to spread. Risk and background Omits tobacco and alcohol. Asks smoking, alcohol, oral health, prior cancer and medicines. Assesses exposure empathetically without implying culpability. Oral examination Fails to inspect the tongue lesion. Describes site, size, border, depth, induration, and other mucosal lesions. Includes floor of mouth and careful palpation of margins and adjacent structures. Neck and function Misses palpable cervical node. Examines cervical levels and checks tongue mobility. Documents nodal size/site and cranial nerve function as a baseline. Clinical reasoning Calls can
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fails to initiate prompt suspected cancer pathway referral for an unexplained oral ulcer lasting over three weeks. Falsely labels the ulcer as definitely malignant and proposes cancer treatment without biopsy. Ignores developing airway compromise or inability to manage secretions if disclosed. Loses follow-up of the suspicious neck node and provides no referral or safety-net plan.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Patient reveals that a community pharmacist supplied an ulcer gel and says, “Can I try it another month?” Expected: empathise, explain why persistence over three weeks mandates urgent specialist assessment, do not postpone the referral for a therapeutic trial.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should not reassure from appearance alone: this needs an urgent specialist assessment.” “The neck node changes my concern; I will include its findings in the referral.” “I will make the referral today and ensure you know how to contact us if symptoms worsen.”

stations.title: Midline Neck Lump in a Young Adult

sections.preamble: B2-275 | Midline Neck Lump in a Young Adult AMaC MRCS Part B • Examination / endocrine and ENT surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are in an ENT clinic. A 23-year-old patient has noticed a small painless lump at the front of the neck for six months. Take a focused history, describe examination manoeuvres and explain your differential and proposed investigation.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Examiner reveals 2-cm smooth cystic midline swelling adjacent to hyoid, moving on swallowing and with tongue protrusion; separate thyroid lobes are not clearly palpable. No inflammation or stridor. Ultrasound has not yet been performed. Do not assume this lump is harmless or that normally placed thyroid tissue is present.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor: concerned about appearance and possibility of cancer. Swelling occasionally becomes sore during colds but no prior acute infection, discharge, dysphagia or breathing difficulty. Wants it removed soon. If asked: no thyroid symptoms or irradiation, no personal cancer history.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What movement tests?” — swallowing and tongue protrusion; thyroglossal duct cyst classically rises with both. “Differentials?” — thyroglossal duct cyst, dermoid cyst, ectopic thyroid, thyroid nodule and lymph node. “First investigation?” — ultrasound of lump AND confirm normally situated thyroid tissue; consider TFTs if clinically indicated. “What if no thyroid is seen normally?” — pause surgery, seek endocrine/ENT assessment and investigate ectopic functional thyroid (potential scintigraphy). “How is a confirmed symptomatic cyst managed?” — specialist discussion of Sistrunk procedure including central hyoid segment; treat acute infection before elective excision.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Introduction / goals Begins with an unconsented examination. Explains assessment and gains permission to examine neck. Explores cosmetic concern and patient preference before planning. Lump history Asks only duration. Asks growth, pain, infection, discharge and previous episodes. Identifies febrile enlargement or sinus suggesting an infected duct remnant. Compression / red flags Omits breathing and swallowing problems. Asks dysphagia, dyspnoea, voice change, rapid growth and weight loss. Identifies acute airway symptoms as requiring urgent assessment. Background Fails to ask about thyroid history. Checks thyroid symptoms, prior radiation, surgeries and family history. Considers possible ectopic sole functioning thyroid tissue despite normal symptoms. Inspection / palpation Does not localise the lump. Describes midline site, size, skin, consistency, tenderness and mobility. Checks hyoid relation, cervical nodes and any skin punctum. Dynamic testing Omits swallowing and tongue movements. Tests elevation during swallowing and tongue protrusion. Interprets both movements as supportive, not definitive, of thyroglossal cyst. Differential States every mid
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Schedules removal without confirming normally located thyroid tissue. Ignores rapidly progressive infection with difficulty swallowing or breathing. Performs or recommends blind aspiration/excision of a potentially vascular or solid thyroid lesion without assessment. Incorrectly assures the patient that an absent thyroid in its usual location is irrelevant before surgery.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Ultrasound reports a midline lesion but “no definite thyroid tissue in usual position.” Expected: stop elective excision, involve ENT/endocrinology and clarify ectopic functioning thyroid with appropriate further imaging/functional assessment; explain risk of removing the patient’s only functioning thyroid.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I cannot confirm this is a simple cyst by movement alone; I will arrange ultrasound.” “The thyroid bed is not confirmed: elective surgery must not proceed until we identify functioning thyroid.” “If a thyroglossal cyst is confirmed, I will explain a Sistrunk operation rather than simple drainage.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-276 — Ludwig’s Angina and Deep Neck Infection AMaC MRCS Part B | Critical care / head and neck | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in the emergency department. A 42-year-old with 3 days of a painful lower molar now has swelling beneath the jaw, fever and difficulty swallowing. Explain your immediate assessment and management to the examiner. No invasive airway manoeuvre is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: Patient is upright, anxious, febrile 38.7°C, HR 118/min, BP 108/67, RR 25, SpO₂ 96% air; bilateral firm submandibular swelling and raised tender mouth floor. Muffled voice, spits saliva into tissue. No audible stridor initially. Examiner only gives further findings when elicited. The airway can deteriorate rapidly; candidate should not be rewarded for waiting for hypoxia.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Actor is breathless when speaking long sentences, frightened of lying down and says “My tongue feels too big.” Reports poor dentition and progressive swallowing difficulty. If told to lie flat, says breathing feels worse. Ask “Can I just have antibiotics and go home?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What would worry you most? → drooling, tongue elevation, muffled voice, trismus, stridor, inability to handle secretions; oxygen saturation can initially remain normal. Who do you call? → emergency senior anaesthesia and ENT/maxillofacial, critical care; airway plan with surgical rescue preparedness. Would you send for CT now? → only once airway is safe / patient adequately stable; contrast CT maps deep-space infection and abscess. What treats the cause? → IV antibiotics including oral anaerobic cover, drainage when indicated, extraction or management of dental source.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Recognition Calls this simple toothache despite floor-of-mouth swelling. Identifies likely Ludwig’s angina from bilateral submandibular induration and raised tongue. Explains rapidly spreading odontogenic cellulitis and potential sudden airway obstruction. Airway threat Ignores drooling, muffled voice or inability to lie flat. Checks speech, secretions, stridor, work of breathing and oxygenation immediately. Anticipates difficult ventilation/intubation even if saturations currently normal. Senior mobilisation Arranges outpatient dental review. Calls senior anaesthetist, ENT/maxillofacial surgeon and critical care immediately. States senior-led controlled airway plan with difficult-airway and surgical-airway backup. Safe positioning Forces patient supine for oral examination. Keeps patient upright, calm, monitored and nil by mouth. Minimises distress and avoids delaying escalation for extensive mouth examination. Resuscitation Does not assess sepsis or intravenous access. Performs ABCDE, oxygen if needed, IV access, observations, bloods and lactate. Initiates timely sepsis care while preserving airway priority and haemodynamic reassessment. Antimicr
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Reassures or discharges a patient with drooling and threatened airway. Attempts sedation, blind intubation or a difficult airway without senior expert plan and surgical-airway readiness. Transfers unstable or obstructing patient alone for CT before securing airway. Fails to start urgent specialist escalation while clinical obstruction is evolving.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: While awaiting CT the voice becomes quieter, stridor begins and SpO₂ falls to 92%. Expected: abandon imaging; declare impending airway obstruction; call emergency anaesthesia/ENT/OMFS and critical care, give oxygen, maintain upright position, prepare a controlled expert-led airway with surgical backup.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “I have underestimated the airway risk; I am treating this as an immediate airway emergency.” “CT can wait: I will not move this patient without a safe airway and appropriate senior team.” “I will start IV treatment and source-control planning in parallel with airway management, not instead of it.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-277 — Mastoiditis in a Child AMaC MRCS Part B | Critical care / paediatric ENT | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical doctor asked to assess a 5-year-old brought to the emergency department with fever, ear pain and swelling behind the right ear. Describe assessment and initial management to the examiner; explain your plan briefly to the parent.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: Child is unwell but alert, T 39.1°C, HR 132/min, RR 27, BP 97/61, SpO₂ 98% room air. Right pinna protrudes forwards/laterally; postauricular redness, tenderness and boggy swelling; recent acute otitis media. No meningism or neurological deficit at first. Examiner reveals severe headache and vomiting only during curveball. No actual imaging is supplied.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Parent says “He has been taking medicine for an ear infection but the ear has started sticking out. Is this dangerous?” They worry about a CT scan and hospital admission. If asked, child is drinking poorly and has no known drug allergy.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the leading diagnosis? → acute mastoiditis, possibly subperiosteal abscess, following middle-ear infection. What clinical findings suggest intracranial extension? → worsening headache, vomiting, altered alertness, meningism, diplopia, focal signs or facial weakness. Will every child automatically need CT? → no; urgent ENT-led assessment and imaging when complication/abscess is suspected, with CT or MRI choice based on question. What if fluctuant postauricular swelling persists? → ENT assessment for myringotomy/grommet, drainage ± mastoid surgery.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial recognition Diagnoses uncomplicated earache despite protruding pinna. Recognises acute mastoiditis with postauricular swelling and lateralised pinna. Names subperiosteal abscess and intracranial spread as critical complications. Physiological status Omits paediatric observations and hydration assessment. Performs paediatric ABCDE, assesses fever, pulse, perfusion and oral intake. Identifies sepsis or deteriorating physiology early and calls paediatric resuscitation help. Focused ear exam Does not check tympanic membrane or discharge. Checks external ear, postauricular erythema/tenderness, otoscopy and hearing symptoms. Documents severity of protrusion, fluctuation and facial nerve findings without painful delay. Intracranial red flags Never asks about headache or altered behaviour. Assesses headache, vomiting, meningism, confusion, focal deficits, diplopia and facial weakness. Links new severe headache/diplopia to meningitis, abscess or sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Specialist referral Plans community oral antibiotic review. Arranges urgent ENT and paediatric assessment with admission. Calls neurosurgery/ID promptly if suspected intracranial co
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Sends a child with likely acute mastoiditis home on routine oral treatment without urgent ENT review. Fails to initiate IV antimicrobial management in a systemically unwell child requiring admission. Dismisses new headache, vomiting, neurological changes or meningeal signs as an ordinary ear infection. Delays urgent specialist reassessment in a child becoming septic or neurologically abnormal.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After initial treatment the child develops severe headache, repeated vomiting and horizontal diplopia. Expected: urgent paediatric/ENT reassessment, neuro exam and sepsis checks, consult neurosurgery/ID, obtain appropriate urgent contrast imaging for intracranial complications without delaying IV treatment.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “The protruding ear and mastoid swelling make this more than a routine middle-ear infection.” “I need urgent ENT and paediatric input, IV treatment and repeated neurological checks.” “New headache and double vision change the risk: I am escalating for intracranial complication assessment now.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-278 — Foreign Body in the Ear or Nose AMaC MRCS Part B | Procedural / ENT | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the on-call surgical doctor in ED. A 6-year-old has a small object in one nostril; the parent is uncertain whether it is a toy bead or a button battery. Explain immediate triage, safe examination and removal/referral decisions. You do not need to perform a procedure.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: The child is well, no respiratory distress; a small metallic disc is visible in the right nostril beside blood-tinged mucus. Its identity is uncertain. Examiner should give no reassurance that it is a bead. A second variation: a smooth plastic bead is visible in the outer ear canal, TM only partly visualised. Reward differentiation by urgency and harm. No actual photograph is supplied.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Parent says: “He was playing with a remote control and beads; can you pull it out quickly?” Child is anxious and pulls away from instruments. If asked, it was inserted about 40 minutes ago; parent is not sure how many objects are missing.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What if this is a button battery? → urgent ENT assistance for immediate removal; do not postpone for routine clinic. Is a magnet dangerous? → paired magnets can damage nasal septum through pressure; urgent specialist assessment. Ear bead variation? → only a safe, controlled attempt when clearly visible, accessible and the child cooperates; no blind probing. What about water irrigation? → avoid with batteries, swelling organic material and suspected tympanic perforation.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Triage Treats a possible battery as a routine bead. Asks object, location, duration, symptoms and possibility of button battery or magnets. Separates immediate chemical/pressure injury risks from a low-risk inert object and prioritises urgency. Airway and bleeding Ignores breathing difficulty or active bleeding. Checks ABC, choking, epistaxis, pain, discharge and fever. Recognises aspiration risk with displaced nasal object and stops manipulations that increase danger. Ear examination Probes without inspecting canal or drum. Uses light/otoscope to identify location, canal trauma and likely tympanic membrane status. Documents whether the object is against the drum and whether safe visibility/grasping are possible. Nasal examination Blindly instruments the nostril. Inspects nostril with adequate light and checks contralateral side; asks about unilateral foul discharge. Avoids posterior displacement and considers occult battery when unilateral irritation or bleeding is present. Battery or magnet Plans to review tomorrow despite suspected nasal battery. Calls ENT urgently for suspected button battery, and multiple magnets in the nose. Explains time-cri
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Delays a possible nasal or aural button battery for routine outpatient removal. Pushes an uncertain metallic nasal object posteriorly using blind forceps or swab. Irrigates suspected button battery or expandable organic foreign body. Continues repeated traumatic extraction attempts despite loss of visibility or child distress.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Parent shows a photo of the remote and says the battery compartment is open. Expected: treat the metallic disc as a button battery until proven otherwise, urgently call ENT, avoid any further unsafe manipulation, maintain airway observation and arrange prompt expert removal.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “Because this could be a battery, it requires emergency removal rather than watchful waiting.” “I am stopping this attempt; repeated blind probing can push it deeper or cause injury.” “I will check the canal or nostril again after removal to ensure nothing remains and no injury is missed.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-279 — Nasal Fracture and Septal Haematoma AMaC MRCS Part B | Examination / facial trauma | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: Examine and describe the assessment of a 24-year-old who was struck on the nose while playing football yesterday. The patient reports swelling, mild epistaxis and difficulty breathing through the left nostril. Explain your findings, investigations and management to the examiner. No actual patient examination is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: Patient is stable and alert, no neurological deficit or visual complaint. External bridge swollen and mildly deviated. On internal examination, left anterior septum has soft fluctuant red-purple swelling. Examiner must disclose fluctuation if explicitly checked. No clear rhinorrhoea or major facial tenderness. No imaging is supplied.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Patient says: “It looks crooked. Can you straighten it today? My left side is blocked.” No past facial injury; nose appeared straight before. If told to return in a month says “Will that be too late?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is most time-critical? → suspected septal haematoma needs same-day ENT review and urgent drainage. Would you order nasal X-ray? → not routinely for isolated nasal fracture; consider CT for complex associated trauma. When is fracture manipulation considered? → once swelling settles, with timely ENT review and local manipulation window. What if watery rhinorrhoea or diplopia appears? → urgent evaluation for skull-base or orbital involvement.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Trauma screen Assumes isolated nasal injury without head or cervical assessment. Asks mechanism, consciousness, neck pain, visual symptoms and other facial injuries. Escalates concerning head, ocular or midface features before focusing on cosmetics. External assessment Looks only at bruising. Inspects alignment, deformity, bleeding and swelling; asks whether appearance has changed. Assesses nasal airflow and compares with preinjury appearance or photographs if helpful. Internal septum Does not look inside either nostril. Inspects both sides of septum with light/speculum for boggy red-purple swelling. Gently identifies fluctuant septal swelling versus firm septal deviation without traumatic probing. Urgent complication Dismisses blocked nose as normal after trauma. Identifies a suspected septal haematoma as same-day ENT emergency. Explains risk of cartilage necrosis, abscess, septal perforation and saddle-nose deformity. Other red flags Misses clear rhinorrhoea or diplopia. Checks persistent epistaxis, CSF-type fluid, eye movements/vision, malocclusion and facial sensory deficits. Requests emergency senior assessment and targeted imaging when associ
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Fails to inspect the nasal septum after nasal trauma. Sends a suspected fluctuant septal haematoma home to await routine fracture clinic. Attempts manipulation and delays urgent assessment of a septal collection. Dismisses possible CSF leak, visual changes or major associated facial injury.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner now reveals the swelling is bilateral and nasal blockage is rapidly worsening. Expected: state high suspicion of bilateral septal haematoma, urgent same-day ENT intervention to evacuate collection, assess infection and protect septal cartilage; do not wait for fracture clinic.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “I need to examine inside both nostrils; obstruction can be due to a septal haematoma.” “A fluctuant septal swelling requires emergency ENT assessment today.” “Once that complication is treated, we can review the deformity promptly after swelling subsides.”

stations.title: Orbital Cellulitis from Sinusitis

sections.preamble: B2-280 | Orbital Cellulitis from Sinusitis AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / ENT and ophthalmology • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee in the emergency department. A 19-year-old with a week of worsening sinus pain has fever and a swollen right eye. Assess the situation, interpret the written examination findings, and explain initial management to the examiner. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Temperature 39.1°C, pulse 124/min, BP 105/66 mmHg, SpO2 97% air. Red swollen right upper and lower lids, right-sided proptosis, pain and restriction on looking laterally, diplopia, acuity 6/18 right versus 6/6 left, sluggish right pupil; left eye normal. Tender right ethmoid region. No rash. If asked, no known antibiotic allergy, no recent orbital surgery or trauma. Initial GCS 15. WBC 17, CRP 155. Written contrast CT report on request: right ethmoid and maxillary sinus opacification, postseptal inflammatory change and a 12-mm medial subperiosteal collection; no obvious intracranial collection on this study. Team: ENT, ophthalmology, anaesthetics and radiology accessible urgently. Appropriate local broad-spectrum intravenous antimicrobial guideline is available; do not require a memorised dose.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is frightened about losing sight; reports pain moving the eye and double vision. If asked about headache, says severe increasing forehead pain. If asked about vision, says the right eye is blurrier than yesterday.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: How is this different from preseptal cellulitis? — restricted/painful eye movements, proptosis, reduced vision, diplopia and possible pupil abnormality indicate postseptal disease. What happens first? — ABCDE/sepsis assessment, senior review, prompt local-guideline IV antibiotics; urgent ophthalmology and ENT together. What imaging? — urgent contrast CT orbits and paranasal sinuses, with brain assessment when intracranial spread suspected; do not delay essential treatment. What does the collection change? — multidisciplinary assessment of urgent surgical drainage and sinus source control, especially with reduced vision. What observations repeat? — acuity separately each eye, colour vision if possible, pupils/RAPD, movements, proptosis, neurological state and systemic physiology.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial recognition Calls this uncomplicated conjunctivitis despite proptosis. Diagnoses probable orbital/postseptal cellulitis associated with sinusitis. Connects ophthalmic deficits and CT collection to threatened vision and abscess. Immediate physiology Ignores fever and tachycardia. Performs ABCDE, sepsis screen, monitoring and IV access. Coordinates early fluids when indicated with senior sepsis response while checking mental state. Vision and pupil Omits acuity and pupil examination. Requests visual acuity in each eye and pupillary responses. Documents baseline acuity, RAPD assessment and serial changes for threatened optic nerve. Eye movements Treats eyelid swelling alone as diagnostic. Assesses painful/restricted ocular movements, diplopia and proptosis. Distinguishes orbital signs from isolated preseptal disease and communicates emergency severity. Differentials Fails to consider intracranial or cavernous sinus spread. Differentiates preseptal and orbital disease and screens headache or neurological symptoms. Identifies cavernous sinus thrombosis, intracranial infection and vision loss as complications. Investigations Delays all treatment
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Sends a patient with proptosis and reduced acuity home with drops or routine review. Fails to escalate worsening vision or pupillary abnormality to urgent ophthalmology and ENT. Delays intravenous antimicrobial/sepsis treatment while awaiting CT despite systemic illness. Misses altered consciousness or new focal neurological signs and does not urgently escalate possible intracranial involvement.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: repeat right-eye acuity falls to counting fingers and a relative afferent pupillary defect appears. Expected: emergency senior ophthalmology and ENT re-escalation now, repeat ABCDE, avoid delay for routine processes, prepare urgent drainage/decompression decision and anaesthetic support.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I initially focused on eyelid swelling; the restricted gaze and reduced vision identify an orbital emergency.” “This patient is tachycardic and febrile; I will begin IV antibiotics and sepsis care now while arranging imaging.” “The new visual decline needs immediate joint ENT–ophthalmology action, not a morning ward review.”

stations.title: Sudden One-Sided Hearing Loss

sections.preamble: B2-281 | Sudden One-Sided Hearing Loss AMaC MRCS Part B • History / ENT emergency • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical trainee seeing a 52-year-old adult with sudden hearing loss in the left ear since yesterday morning. Take a focused history, interpret verbal tuning-fork and otoscopy results, and explain immediate management to the patient. You have eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient awakened 24 hours ago unable to hear clearly through the left ear, with left tinnitus and a brief sensation of imbalance but no ongoing spinning vertigo. No pain, discharge, wax use, trauma or recent diving. No fever. Otoscopy on request: both canals clear, tympanic membranes intact and normal. Rinne testing: air conduction exceeds bone conduction in both ears. Weber lateralises to right ear. Cranial nerves, gait and limb examination normal at present. If asked: no facial weakness, altered sensation, dysarthria or new severe headache. No exposure to known ototoxic medication. An urgent ENT same-day referral pathway, audiology and local steroid treatment protocol are available.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Actor is frightened and asks “Could it just be wax? Will the hearing come back? Can I wait a week?” If asked about associated symptoms, describe tinnitus and mild imbalance; no hearing change in the right ear.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What is the diagnosis? — suspected sudden sensorineural hearing loss; cannot be confidently explained by outer/middle ear disease. Interpret the tests. — Weber to better/right ear and Rinne positive bilaterally support left sensorineural loss; bedside tests do not replace urgent pure-tone audiometry. How urgent? — sudden loss over ≤3 days within the previous 30 days: immediate ENT/ED referral to be seen within 24 hours under NICE NG98. What treatment? — prompt ENT discussion of corticosteroid treatment after risks and contraindications; do not promise benefit or delay referral for diagnostic audiometry. What else? — rule out neurological/stroke signs, arrange formal audiology and consider MRI internal auditory canals through ENT after initial assessment if asymmetrical sensorineural loss needs evaluation.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Time-critical triage Plans routine audiology next month. Identifies sudden hearing loss within 24 hours and immediate referral need. Quotes NICE seen-within-24-hours threshold and acts while evaluation proceeds. Focused history Asks only whether ears are blocked. Asks onset, laterality, degree, tinnitus, vertigo, pain, discharge and trauma. Elicits fluctuations, recent infection, noise/medication exposure and prior hearing baseline. Neurological safety Does not ask about stroke symptoms. Screens for facial droop, sensory change, diplopia, dysarthria, weakness or ataxia. Activates acute stroke pathway immediately if central neurological signs are present. Otoscopy Assumes wax without visualising the ear. Requests otoscopy and describes normal canal and drum. Separates conductive causes from normal outer/middle ear assessment without false certainty. Tuning-fork interpretation Misreads Weber to right as right sensorineural loss. Recognises Weber to right with Rinne-positive ears supports left sensorineural loss. Explains limitations and need for calibrated pure-tone audiometry. Differential diagnosis States unilateral hearing loss always means vestib
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Treats recent unexplained sudden unilateral hearing loss as benign wax and delays specialist assessment for weeks. Fails to activate stroke assessment when new focal neurological deficits are disclosed. Attempts ear syringing or instrumentation despite a clearly normal canal and no conductive cause. Withholds referral while waiting for routine audiology, MRI or a trial of decongestants.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Curveball: as the consultation ends, the patient reports new slurred speech and left facial numbness. Expected: stop routine ENT pathway, immediate stroke/neurological emergency evaluation with local stroke call; airway and physiology assessment and time last-known-well.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I cannot attribute this to wax because the ear canal and drum are normal; sudden nerve-related loss is possible.” “I should not delay referral for audiometry: I will contact urgent ENT now for assessment within 24 hours.” “The new speech and facial symptoms change the pathway; this is an emergency possible stroke.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-282 — Branchial Cyst AMaC MRCS Part B | Examination / head and neck | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: Examine a 32-year-old with a painless swelling high in the left side of the neck. Give your findings, differential diagnosis and safe next steps to the examiner. Do not perform invasive procedures.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: Soft 3-cm ovoid smooth lump anterior to upper sternocleidomastoid; mobile, nontender, normal skin, no stridor. It has been present 4 months and slowly enlarged. Otoscopy unremarkable, no palpable thyroid mass. The actor has a modest smoking history. The examination is simulated: provide requested findings verbally. Crucial: an adult lateral cystic neck mass must not be assumed benign.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Patient asks “Is it just a cyst I was born with? Can you remove it this week?” No fevers, dental pain or recent sore throat. If asked reports no dysphagia, haemoptysis, weight loss or voice change. Anxiety about cancer is genuine.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Describe location and differential → possible second branchial cleft cyst near anterior SCM, but must exclude cystic metastatic node. Which history raises concern? → persistent growth, older age, tobacco, otalgia with normal ear exam, dysphagia, oral/tonsillar lesions. What tests? → head-and-neck ENT assessment, ultrasound ± ultrasound-guided FNA, further imaging/endoscopic assessment as indicated. What if fine-needle aspirate shows only cyst fluid? → do not equate nondiagnostic cyst contents with exclusion of malignancy.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Characterisation Labels all lateral neck lumps harmless without duration or growth history. Documents site, duration, growth, pain and infection-related fluctuations. Contrasts congenital intermittent swelling with new persistent enlarging mass requiring cancer exclusion. Risk review Omits smoking, alcohol, or head-and-neck symptoms. Asks dysphagia, odynophagia, voice change, otalgia, oral lesions, weight loss and smoking. Explains HPV-related oropharyngeal malignancy can present as a cystic neck node. Inspection Does not identify exact location or skin change. Inspects anterior sternomastoid region, size, skin and visible scars. Assesses breathing, voice, oral cavity and tonsillar asymmetry for associated lesions. Palpation Diagnoses by visual appearance without examining lump. Assesses tenderness, consistency, mobility, fixation, warmth and cervical nodes. Examines bilateral neck levels and distinguishes a fluctuant cyst from a suspicious fixed mass. Differentials States branchial cyst is pathognomonic. Considers branchial cleft cyst, reactive node, lymphoma and cystic nodal metastasis. Adds atypical mycobacterial infection and salivary pathology
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Labels a persistent adult lateral neck lump a definite benign branchial cyst without malignancy assessment. Proceeds straight to elective excision without appropriate head-and-neck evaluation and imaging/sampling. Dismisses airway or progressive swallowing symptoms that require emergency assessment. Fails to arrange timely suspected cancer referral for a persistent unexplained neck mass.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The initial aspirate returns only fluid and macrophages without diagnostic epithelium. Expected: explain it is nondiagnostic; arrange continued ENT assessment, appropriate repeat targeted tissue sampling and mucosal evaluation rather than discharge.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “I cannot establish a benign branchial cyst from the position alone.” “A fluid-only sample does not complete the diagnostic work-up of this persistent adult neck lump.” “I will arrange timely ENT follow-up and explain the suspected-cancer pathway without suggesting a diagnosis is proven.”

stations.title: AMaC MRCS Part B

sections.preamble: B2-283 — Tonsillectomy: Is It Indicated? AMaC MRCS Part B | Communication / ENT | 8 minutes | Draft for specialist review | Not an official MRCS marking scheme
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are an ENT surgical trainee in clinic. A 25-year-old requests tonsillectomy because of repeated sore throats. Take a targeted history, explain when tonsillectomy may be appropriate and discuss benefits, risks and alternatives. Do not assume an operation is needed.
sections.2. Examiner brief and disclosure rules: The patient reports four acute, clinician-diagnosed tonsillitis episodes in the last 12 months, three in the previous year; missed five workdays; no peritonsillar abscess or hospital admissions. They are medically fit and expect surgery to eliminate every sore throat. No OSA concern. Candidate should identify current information does not meet standard recurrent-tonsillitis commissioning frequency criteria, but apply clinical judgment if disabling disease or complications emerge.
sections.3. Actor/patient brief: Actor is 25, works shifts, frustrated by sore throats and wants “tonsils out next month.” When asked can identify antibiotic use in some episodes and occasional colds between. Fears having an episode during travel. Asks “Will it guarantee I never get a sore throat again?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: What counts? → clinically significant, adequately treated acute tonsillitis with disabling impact; not all sore throats. Usual thresholds? → 7 episodes in preceding year, 5/year in each of preceding 2 years, or 3/year for each of 3 years. Are cut-offs absolute? → EBI allows flexibility in unusually severe, uncontrolled symptoms or complications after appropriate specialist judgment. What is the key post-op warning? → fresh bleeding after tonsillectomy needs immediate emergency department assessment.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Episode diagnosis Counts viral colds as bacterial tonsillitis episodes. Checks documented attacks are acute tonsillitis rather than nonspecific sore throats. Asks objective features, treatment and whether interval symptoms suggest another diagnosis. Frequency Never establishes frequency or documentation. Elicits yearly counts, clinically significant episodes and treatment history. Tests counts against 7 in 1 year, 5/year for 2 years or 3/year for 3 years criteria. Functional impact Offers operation on number alone. Explores days away from work/school, severe symptoms and normal functioning. Discusses severity and patient burden in context of shared decision and alternative explanations. Complications Overlooks previous quinsy or admissions. Asks peritonsillar abscess, hospital visits, antibiotic complications and dehydration. Recognises recurrent quinsy or severe uncontrolled disease may merit specialist individualised judgment. Options Claims surgery is the only treatment. Explains active monitoring, analgesia and appropriate episodic medical treatment. Sets a diary and review plan and acknowledges surgery may reduce recurrent tonsillitis burden.
sections.6. Critical fails (four): Commits patient to tonsillectomy without eliciting episode severity and accurate frequency or consent. Promises tonsillectomy will prevent all future sore throats. Fails to warn that any postoperative fresh bleeding needs urgent hospital assessment. Omits discussion of significant postoperative pain and hydration needs before consent.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient says: “My friend bled a week after surgery, but she waited until morning. Is that OK?” Expected: explain any fresh bleeding after tonsillectomy warrants immediate ED assessment, not delay; risk can occur after discharge.
sections.8. Recovery lines (three): “I need to distinguish true tonsillitis from other sore throats and check how often it disables you.” “At the moment your documented episodes do not meet the usual thresholds; active monitoring is reasonable.” “You are right to ask about bleeding: fresh blood after surgery is an emergency and must be assessed immediately.”

stations.title: Lymph Node Biopsy for Suspected Lymphoma

sections.preamble: B2-284 | Lymph Node Biopsy for Suspected Lymphoma AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / surgical pathology • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the general surgical registrar asked to advise on biopsy of a persistent left cervical lymph node in a 42-year-old with drenching night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Explain which sample to obtain, how to handle it, and the next steps. No operative procedure is required.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient has a 2.5 cm firm mobile level V cervical node for six weeks, several smaller nodes, no obvious infection. Bloods: mild anaemia, raised LDH; no airway symptoms. Neck ultrasound: abnormal rounded node with loss of fatty hilum; suitable for excision under appropriate anaesthesia. The regional haemato-oncology service has been contacted but tissue logistics not yet agreed. If asked about alternatives: a deep mediastinal node is present but unsafe to excise; the cervical node is accessible. The patient is not anticoagulated.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is anxious about cancer, asks whether a needle test would be easier and whether the biopsy will spread cancer. Wants to know who will give results. If asked, agrees to tissue biopsy after balanced explanation.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What is the optimal first biopsy?” — excision of an accessible representative intact node, if feasible, to preserve architecture. “Can a core be used?” — yes when excision risk outweighs benefit, with multiple adequate cores; non-diagnostic core should generally lead to excision if feasible. “Shall I put it straight into formalin?” — first agree with haematopathology: some tissue may require fresh urgent transport for flow/molecular studies; do not place all tissue in formalin automatically. “What if the node is cervical in an older adult?” — assess head and neck primary and consider metastatic squamous carcinoma, not just lymphoma. “Next steps?” — multidisciplinary histological classification, staging and haemato-oncology follow-up; no empirical steroids unless emergency discussed with specialist.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical assessment Labels any enlarged node lymphoma without examining it. Elicits B symptoms, duration, infections, exposure and examines nodal regions. Assesses organomegaly, mucosal primaries and urgency signs such as airway or SVC compromise. Differential diagnosis Assumes malignancy proven by raised LDH. Considers lymphoma, infection and metastatic head/neck malignancy. Explains biopsy diagnoses subtype; imaging and bloods cannot reliably replace tissue. Site selection Samples an incidental tiny node while ignoring accessible abnormal node. Selects accessible representative enlarged node with clinical/imaging correlation. Confirms with haemato-oncology/pathology and avoids unnecessarily hazardous sites. Choice of technique Requests FNA alone to classify suspected lymphoma. Prefers excision of accessible node where safe; core if surgery risk outweighs benefit. Explains architecture value and adequate multi-core strategy when excision impractical. Consent Promises no bleeding or nerve injury. Discusses scar, infection, bleeding, pain, anaesthetic and local nerve risks. Individualises risk to cervical site, clarifies alternatives and records inf
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Sends an accessible suspected lymphoma node for fine-needle aspiration alone as definitive diagnosis with no plan for diagnostic tissue. Places all tissue in formalin against an explicit haematopathology request for fresh specimen without seeking advice. Fails to act on new stridor or clinical superior vena cava obstruction. Starts empirical high-dose steroids in a stable patient without specialist discussion despite need for diagnostic biopsy.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Theatre calls: “The excised node is on the trolley; we have only formalin pots.” Expected: immediately ring pathology/haematopathology; clarify transport medium and time-critical fresh specimen requirements, label correctly, and do not fix all tissue before agreement.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I have not arranged fresh tissue processing; I will phone the haematopathology laboratory before excision.” “A core may be suitable if excision is unsafe, but FNA alone is not reliable enough for classification.” “I will name the clinician responsible for pathology results and ensure haemato-oncology follow-up.”

stations.title: Electrical Injury

sections.preamble: B2-285 | Electrical Injury AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / burns and trauma • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar receiving a 29-year-old electrician after contact with an industrial high-voltage cable at a building site. He fell from a short ladder. Assess the immediate risks and outline initial treatment, investigations, monitoring and referral.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Scene declared safe before ambulance access. Awake, HR 118/min, BP 102/66 mmHg, SpO2 97% room air, RR 24/min. Small deep burn on right palm, left heel lesion, very painful swollen right forearm. Brief loss of consciousness reported by coworker. No ECG yet; urine is dark. Neck soreness after fall. If asked: forearm compartments are tense; pain worsens with passive stretch and hand paraesthesia is developing. Creatine kinase markedly elevated; potassium 5.8 mmol/L; ECG now shows peaked T waves.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient says “The burns look tiny. Can I go home?” If questioned reports deep forearm pain, tingling and that he may have blacked out. The ambulance team confirms the power supply was isolated before contact.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “First action at the scene?” — isolate electricity and protect rescuers; never touch live casualty. “How severe are two small burns?” — may conceal major muscle, nerve, vascular and internal injury along current path. “What ECG/monitoring?” — obtain immediate ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring for high-voltage exposure/LOC/abnormal ECG, senior ED/critical-care input. “Arm is tense and painful on stretch.” — suspect compartment syndrome, urgent orthopaedic/plastic/burns assessment; pulses may still be present. “What does dark urine suggest?” — rhabdomyolysis, monitor CK, renal function, electrolytes, urine output; careful IV crystalloid and treat hyperkalaemia under emergency protocols. “Other injury?” — evaluate fall-related trauma including head and cervical injury, burns depth and vascular/neuro status; specialist burns centre referral.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Scene and team safety Approaches live source without confirmation of isolation. Confirms power isolated and scene safe before patient contact. Explains prevention of secondary casualties and coordinates rescue handover. Primary survey Focuses on tiny skin burns before ABCDE. Performs ABCDE, monitoring, IV access and treats immediately life-threatening problems. Balances electrical mechanisms with concurrent fall-related spinal and head assessment. Cardiac assessment Discharges without ECG after high-voltage exposure. Requests immediate 12-lead ECG and appropriate rhythm monitoring. Links loss of consciousness or abnormal ECG to monitored admission and cardiology/critical-care discussion. Burn assessment Uses small skin area to exclude major injury. Inspects contact sites, estimates cutaneous burn extent, and assesses limb perfusion/sensation. Maps plausible current pathway and anticipates evolving deep muscle and nerve damage. Compartment syndrome Reassures because radial pulse is palpable. Recognises disproportionate pain, passive-stretch pain and paraesthesia; calls surgeons urgently. Initiates serial neurovascular assessment and avoids waiting f
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Touches a patient before confirming the electrical source is isolated. Discharges a high-voltage electrical injury with loss of consciousness without ECG, monitoring or senior review. Fails to escalate a tense forearm with pain on passive movement and progressive paraesthesia. Ignores ECG changes of hyperkalaemia in a patient with suspected rhabdomyolysis.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Four hours later, the forearm is more swollen, the patient cannot extend fingers due to pain, but the radial pulse remains palpable. Expected: urgent senior surgical assessment for evolving compartment syndrome and prompt fasciotomy decision; do not use pulse presence to exclude it.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The skin marks understate risk; I will assess deep tissue injury and get cardiac monitoring now.” “This tense, painful forearm may have compartment syndrome despite palpable pulses; call the surgical team urgently.” “The dark urine and ECG changes mean possible rhabdomyolysis with dangerous hyperkalaemia; start emergency treatment and monitoring.”

stations.title: Burns in a Child

sections.preamble: B2-286 | Burns in a Child AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / paediatric burns • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar in an emergency department. A 3-year-old (15 kg) has a hot-liquid scald involving the upper trunk and right arm, estimated initially at 15% total body surface area (TBSA). Assess the child, outline immediate care, fluid strategy, burn-centre referral and safeguarding considerations. This is an applied-knowledge station, not a procedure.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Child is distressed but alert: HR 150, RR 32, BP 92/55, SpO₂ 98% air, temperature 35.8°C. Injury 45 minutes ago; a red blistered upper trunk and arm, no soot/stridor and no circumferential limb burn. Blanching partial-thickness areas cover about 15% on age-adjusted Lund–Browder assessment; superficial red erythema elsewhere is excluded. No other injury visible. Caregiver says the child pulled hot tea from a worktop. If asked: the history changed from “happened today” to “yesterday”; there is a sharply demarcated immersion-like area on the lower thigh that the triage nurse also noticed. A specialist paediatric burn service is reachable.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Caregiver is frightened, asks whether the child will need admission and says “Please do not involve anyone else.” Child cries on examination but can be comforted; the candidate must explain calmly and not conduct a confrontational safeguarding interview.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “How do you size this burn?” — Use a paediatric Lund–Browder chart; include partial and full-thickness areas, not simple erythema; do not rely on adult rule of nines. “What do you do first?” — ABCDE, exposure and warming, assess inhalation if relevant, stop burning, analgesia, cool the wound with cool running water for 20 minutes within three hours when feasible, and prevent whole-body hypothermia. “Does a child need fluids in addition to burn resuscitation?” — Yes. Significant burns may need formula-guided resuscitation PLUS weight-based maintenance fluid, glucose surveillance and specialist titration by urine output/perfusion. “Calculate a starting estimate using a 3 mL × kg × %TBSA protocol.” — 3 × 15 × 15 = 675 mL burn-resuscitation crystalloid in 24 hours; half (337.5 mL) over first 8 h FROM INJURY, remaining half over 16 h, plus separately calculated maintenance. This is an illustrative *protocol*, not a universal national formula; specialist local pathways vary. “What about the unusual pattern/history?” — Document objectively, promptly involve the named child safeguarding clinician and paediatric team; do not postpone burn care or accuse the caregiver. “Transfer?” — Early pa
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial assessment Begins dressings while overlooking ABCDE, shock and possible inhalation injury. Performs paediatric ABCDE, monitoring, weight and temperature assessment. Prioritises resuscitation and reassessment with senior paediatric/emergency input. First aid Uses ice and neglects temperature. Removes hot source and non-adherent clothing, cools burn with cool running water and keeps child warm. Balances timely 20-minute wound cooling with hypothermia prevention in a small child. Depth and area Counts superficial erythema or uses adult head proportions. Describes depth and estimates TBSA using age-adjusted Lund–Browder. Reassesses area/depth after cleaning and documents anatomical distribution. Analgesia and comfort Leaves distressed child untreated while calculating fluids. Gives age-appropriate analgesia, explains gently and uses appropriate child comfort measures. Coordinates repeated pain scoring and procedural analgesia with nursing staff. Resuscitation fluids Gives an adult-only formula and omits maintenance or glucose considerations. Recognises need for burn-resuscitation fluid plus paediatric maintenance when indicated. States formula
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Does not assess or treat a threatened airway or haemodynamic instability while attending only to the wound. Fails to consider additional paediatric maintenance fluid and glucose monitoring while calculating substantial burn resuscitation. Ignores a suspicious burn pattern and inconsistent history without safeguarding documentation or escalation. Plans discharge without paediatric burns-service discussion for the described significant burn.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After cooling, the child becomes shivery and temperature falls to 35.1°C. Expected: stop exposing the child, dry/warm unaffected skin and surroundings, use warmed fluids as appropriate, continue monitoring and discuss with senior team; do not sacrifice core temperature for prolonged cooling.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I will estimate TBSA with Lund–Browder and exclude superficial erythema before finalising fluids.” “I have calculated a resuscitation estimate, but children also need maintenance fluid and repeated glucose checks.” “The history and burn pattern warrant a documented safeguarding discussion while we treat the child.”

stations.title: Chemical Burn

sections.preamble: B2-287 | Chemical Burn AMaC MRCS Part B • Critical care / plastics and emergency surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are called to the emergency department for a 36-year-old industrial cleaner splashed with a corrosive liquid on the forearm and near the left eye 15 minutes ago. Outline your immediate management, decontamination, special chemical risks and referral.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Patient alert, severe burning arm pain and eye irritation. BP 126/80, HR 108, SpO₂ 99% air. Wet contaminated sleeve and forearm with patchy pale skin, left conjunctival redness. Product bottle not yet available; workplace reports a hydrofluoric-acid-containing cleaning product may have been involved. No airway symptoms. If asked: skin was not washed at scene; colleague was about to neutralise with an alkaline cleaner. Eye pain and photophobia persist. Finger tingling has developed. ECG currently normal, serum calcium pending.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient says “Can you neutralise it with another chemical?” and fears blindness. If asked, has no other medical history, and a colleague can bring the product safety data sheet.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “First move?” — Ensure PPE and scene safety; prevent secondary contamination; remove contaminated clothing/jewellery; brush off DRY powder before irrigation if present; start copious water irrigation immediately. “Would you neutralise acid with alkali?” — No: chemical neutralisation may generate heat and delay decontamination. “What about eyes?” — Start immediate continuous ocular irrigation, remove contact lenses when possible, check ocular surface pH according to ophthalmic protocol, obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment; never delay irrigation for visual-acuity testing. “Hydrofluoric acid suspected?” — Alert burns/toxicology urgently; systemic fluoride absorption can cause severe hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia and arrhythmias; monitor ECG/electrolytes and use specialist-directed calcium gluconate treatment. “Do you give calcium to all acid burns?” — No, agent-specific management; identify the substance from the safety data sheet without delaying water irrigation. “Follow-up?” — Repeat assessment for evolving depth, pain, perfusion and specialist plastics/burns review, tetanus and analgesia per clinical indication.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Rescuer protection Touches contaminated patient bare-handed and spreads corrosive agent. Uses suitable PPE and isolates contaminated items safely. Coordinates decontamination area and prevents secondary staff exposure. Initial survey Focuses only on visible erythema and fails to assess airway/eyes. Runs ABCDE and identifies ocular, inhalational and systemic exposure risks. Reassesses airway and haemodynamics during ongoing irrigation. Clothing and dry agents Leaves soaked sleeve on or rubs dry powder into skin. Removes contaminated clothing/jewellery and brushes off any dry agent before irrigation. Documents exposure time, route and suspected agent while decontamination continues. Immediate irrigation Waits for blood results or neutralises with alkaline cleaner. Starts immediate copious water irrigation of affected skin. Prioritises early persistent decontamination and avoids chemical neutralisation. Eye safety Delays eye irrigation until a full visual examination is complete. Starts immediate ocular irrigation and urgent ophthalmology referral. Checks pH to guide continued irrigation and removes lenses as feasible. Chemical identification Assumes
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Delays irrigation for tests, imaging or waiting to identify the chemical. Attempts to neutralise the acid with alkali rather than irrigating and protecting rescuers. Fails to irrigate an exposed eye promptly or obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment. Treats suspected hydrofluoric acid exposure as a simple skin burn despite escalating pain and systemic toxicity risk.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The colleague arrives with a label confirming 10% hydrofluoric acid and the patient develops hand cramps. Expected: continue irrigation, urgent toxicology/burns senior discussion, ECG and electrolyte monitoring including ionised calcium and magnesium, specialist-guided calcium gluconate therapy and resuscitation if symptomatic hypocalcaemia/arrhythmia.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “We must wash this away immediately—do not try to neutralise it chemically.” “The eye has also been exposed; continue irrigation and request urgent ophthalmology help.” “This may be hydrofluoric acid: call toxicology, check calcium/magnesium and ECG, and arrange targeted treatment.”

stations.title: Consent for Excision of a Lipoma or Cyst

sections.preamble: B2-288 | Consent for Excision of a Lipoma or Cyst AMaC MRCS Part B • Communication / minor surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are a surgical trainee in the day-case clinic. A 41-year-old patient requests removal of a 2-cm mobile subcutaneous lump over the upper back, assessed clinically as a likely epidermoid cyst. Explain assessment, options and risks, and obtain informed consent if appropriate. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Clinical notes: lump present 3 years, no rapid growth, no skin ulceration, no deep fixation, no neurological change; on examination superficial, mobile, non-tender, 2 cm, central punctum visible. No active inflammation. No ultrasound performed. No known local anaesthetic allergy. If asked: anticoagulants none; diabetes none; previous raised scar after piercing; occupation involves shoulder straps. If the candidate proposes immediate removal without asking for unusual growth or diagnostic uncertainty, prompt: “Could it be cancer?” Strong candidates acknowledge uncertainty and arrange appropriate imaging/referral if growth, depth, fixation or concerning findings emerge. This is a consent consultation, not an operative demonstration. The actor will only consent after discussing scar location, recurrence, histology, alternatives and their own cosmetic concerns.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient wants lump removed because a backpack catches it; worried about a conspicuous scar and recurrence. Says “My sister had a lipoma removed and it came back.” If asked about priorities: avoiding a noticeable scar matters more than speed. Ask “Does it have to come out?” and “Will it definitely be benign?”
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What is the diagnosis?” — likely epidermoid cyst, but not certain clinically; lipoma and other lesions possible. “What if the lump were enlarging?” — review sarcoma red flags and NICE NG12 urgent ultrasound/referral pathway for unexplained enlarging mass. “What options?” — observation when benign and asymptomatic; elective local-anaesthetic excision; defer if active infection; no pressure to proceed. “What operation?” — local anaesthetic, skin incision placed appropriately, careful dissection and cyst-wall removal if cyst; closure, dressing and likely histology according to policy. “What if it becomes red and painful preoperatively?” — reassess for inflammation/abscess; elective intact excision may be postponed and infection managed appropriately.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Diagnosis and uncertainty Calls every soft-tissue lump a harmless lipoma without examination. Explains a likely superficial epidermoid cyst but notes clinical diagnostic uncertainty. Links punctum and mobility to the working diagnosis while explaining when imaging or specialist review changes the pathway. Malignancy screen Ignores rapid growth, deep fixation or recurrent atypical mass. Asks about increasing size, depth, fixation, pain, previous treatment and systemic concerns. States that unexplained growth merits urgent ultrasound and uncertain/suspicious findings cancer-pathway referral. Patient priorities Assumes cosmetic concern is trivial and offers operation immediately. Asks about snagging, discomfort, aesthetics, expectations and preference for treatment. Tailors incision and scarring discussion to the upper-back backpack-strap location and prior raised scar. Options and benefits Presents surgery as mandatory for a benign asymptomatic cyst. Explains observation and planned excision with realistic symptom-relief goals. Contrasts recurrence risk, scar trade-off and implications of delaying treatment if symptoms remain mild. Procedure Says the
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Proceeds with excision of a suspicious enlarging/deep lump without appropriate sarcoma assessment. Operates without valid, informed, voluntary consent. Falsely assures the patient that malignancy or recurrence is impossible. Disregards a stated local anaesthetic allergy or serious contraindication without assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The patient says: “I had a thick raised scar after a piercing. Will this leave no mark?” Expected: explain that a permanent scar is inevitable, hypertrophic/keloid scarring is possible, particularly on the upper back, offer time to think and revisit whether symptoms justify the cosmetic trade-off.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I called this definitely benign; I should explain it is a likely clinical diagnosis and screen for warning features.” “I omitted your previous raised scar; I need to address that individual risk before you decide.” “You have a choice not to operate now; we can review if the lump changes or becomes troublesome.”

stations.title: Ingrowing Toenail: Wedge Excision

sections.preamble: B2-289 | Ingrowing Toenail: Wedge Excision AMaC MRCS Part B • Procedural / podiatry and minor surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
