sections.1. Candidate brief: You are in a supervised minor-procedure clinic. A 25-year-old has recurrent painful lateral ingrowing of the right great toenail, despite footwear advice and conservative nail care. Demonstrate the key steps of partial lateral nail avulsion with planned chemical matrix treatment on a simulation model, and explain safety checks and aftercare. Do not administer real medicines.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Examiner provides toe model, sterile tray, simulated digital local anaesthetic, nail elevator, straight nail splitter, haemostat, disposable toe tourniquet and dressing. Phenol application is described only, not undertaken on a person. History: recurrent episodes for 10 months, mild granulation tissue, no spreading cellulitis or fever; pedal pulses palpable, capillary refill normal, sensation intact; no known diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, allergy or anticoagulants. No pregnancy. If asked, peripheral perfusion is adequate. Consent has not yet been obtained. Candidate must distinguish lateral nail avulsion plus matrix treatment from full-thickness skin wedge excision, and explain selected technique and local protocol.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Simulated patient: pain from shoe pressure, wants it to stop recurring. Asks “Will the whole nail be taken off?” and “Can I walk home?” If asked about medical history, no diabetes or circulatory problems; worried about injections.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: “What must you check?” — identity/site, informed consent, vascular status, neuropathy, infection, allergies and local anaesthetic suitability. “Why not simply pull out the edge?” — recurrence can occur without planned destruction/removal of the corresponding lateral matrix. “Show the sequence.” — prepare aseptically; give ring/digital block under approved protocol; confirm sensation lost; controlled tourniquet with timing; free lateral nail strip; divide longitudinally; remove complete strip including proximal spicule; inspect matrix, apply phenol if selected with tissue protection according to local protocol, dress and remove tourniquet. “What is the key safety check after dressing?” — confirm tourniquet removed, toe perfusion restored and no excessive bleeding. “What if there are absent pedal pulses?” — do not proceed routinely; vascular/podiatry specialist assessment first.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Clinical assessment Omits limb perfusion, neuropathy and infection assessment. Confirms recurrent ingrowing edge; checks skin, infection, pulses, sensation and capillary refill. Recognises need to defer for ischaemia or complex diabetic foot disease and examine spreading infection. Consent and selection Treats matrix destruction as compulsory and promises no regrowth. Discusses conservative alternatives, partial versus total removal, recurrence, infection and permanent narrower nail. Checks expectations about cosmetic shape, phenol healing/discharge and ability to attend dressings. Preparation and sterility Begins cutting without site check, gloves or skin preparation. Uses identity/site check, antiseptic preparation, sterile instruments and drapes. Organises sharp handling, field protection and supports anxiety during procedure. Local anaesthesia Cuts before demonstrating adequate anaesthesia. Describes local-anaesthetic digital block, aspiration/appropriate technique and confirms numbness. Checks allergy, safe agent/dose per local protocol and waits for complete block without guessing a universal dose. Tourniquet safety Leaves tourniquet in place
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Proceeds despite absent pulses or critically impaired toe perfusion without specialist review. Performs nail cutting before local anaesthesia is confirmed effective. Leaves a toe tourniquet on after the procedure or fails to check return of circulation. Applies phenol broadly to normal skin without tissue protection or protocol safeguards.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: During simulated assessment the examiner adds: “This patient has diabetes and diminished pedal pulses.” Expected: stop elective matrix procedure; assess perfusion and infection, obtain specialist podiatry/vascular review, and explain that healing risk changes the management plan.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I omitted circulation checks; I will test pulses and perfusion before any injection or cutting.” “I see a remaining proximal nail spicule; I will remove it carefully before matrix treatment.” “I must remove the tourniquet now, check capillary refill and document a dressing-review plan.”

stations.title: Fingertip Injury and Nail Bed Repair

sections.preamble: B2-290 | Fingertip Injury and Nail Bed Repair AMaC MRCS Part B • Procedural / hand surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: An adult has crushed the left index fingertip in a door. On the model demonstrate assessment and describe appropriate treatment of a displaced nail plate and nail-bed laceration. You have 8 minutes; no procedure is performed on a real patient.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Healthy 32-year-old; crush 2 hours ago, painful, nail plate lifted proximally, visible clean transverse nail-bed laceration, intact volar pulp and capillary refill, full DIP movement and intact fingertip sensation. AP/lateral radiographs, if requested: undisplaced distal phalanx tuft fracture; no other injury. Tetanus history unknown. No anticoagulants; no known allergy. State that the simulation has digital-block supplies, irrigation, instruments, fine absorbable sutures, non-adherent dressing, suitable nail-fold splint and hand surgery support. Assess competency rather than demanding a patient procedure.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient is anxious about pain and whether the nail will regrow normally. If asked: works with hands; wants to return to work rapidly. If candidate fails to discuss X-ray, ask whether a fracture matters.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Assessment? — mechanism, contamination, hand dominance, tetanus, sensation, capillary refill, tendon movement, nail-fold disruption; inspect for exposed bone or tissue loss. Imaging? — AP and lateral views for suspected distal phalanx fracture. When repair? — displaced nail with visible laceration and tuft fracture merits exploration and precise nail-bed repair with suitable supervision; intact plate and isolated haematoma may permit trephination instead. Technique? — analgesia/digital block and check effect; irrigation, inspect nail and fracture, carefully remove displaced nail if indicated; repair nail bed with fine absorbable suture or approved alternative, protect nail fold and dress, arrange review. Refer? — threatened circulation, exposed bone, large tissue loss, complex/displaced/open fracture, tendon deficit or insufficient procedural competence.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Injury definition Calls this only a bruised nail despite a displaced plate. Identifies nail-bed laceration with associated tuft fracture. Distinguishes crush, subungual haematoma and avulsion and explains the injury complex. Neurovascular/tendon examination Does not assess capillary refill, sensory status or DIP function. Checks perfusion, fingertip sensation and DIP flexion/extension before block. Documents hand dominance and contrasts injured and uninjured finger function. Imaging and fracture Does not consider distal phalanx fracture. Requests plain radiographs and describes the undisplaced tuft fracture. Recognises when displacement or joint/growth-plate involvement changes referral. Anaesthesia and safety Manipulates painful nail without anaesthesia or allergy check. Checks consent, allergy and delivers/describes effective digital block. Verifies block before exploration and provides tetanus assessment and clean procedural setup. Wound preparation Sutures through dirt or fails to visualise laceration. Irrigates thoroughly, prepares sterile field and examines tissue viability. Handles germinal matrix delicately and evaluates contamination and f
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fails to identify a pale or insensate fingertip needing urgent specialist assessment. Attempts complex nail-bed repair with inadequate anaesthesia or without suitable competence/supervision. Misses a displaced/open fracture or exposed bone and discharges without appropriate assessment. Closes visibly contaminated tissue without irrigation or infection assessment.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: The examiner says, “The nail plate is actually intact and firmly seated; only a painful subungual haematoma is visible, with no fold disruption.” Expected: reassess indication; trephination for pain is often appropriate rather than routine nail removal and repair, while assessing fracture and follow-up.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I have not checked capillary refill or sensation; I will do that before local anaesthesia.” “A tuft fracture may accompany a nail-bed tear; I will review the films before deciding repair or referral.” “I overstated cosmetic certainty; nail regrowth takes months and some deformity is possible.”

stations.title: Facial Laceration Closure

sections.preamble: B2-291 | Facial Laceration Closure AMaC MRCS Part B • Procedural / maxillofacial surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A 23-year-old has a 2.5-cm clean laceration crossing the left upper-lip vermilion border after a fall. On a model demonstrate how you would examine, prepare and close the wound, including precise landmark alignment. You have 8 minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Alert, stable, no airway or dental injury; incident 3 hours ago; laceration extends through skin and orbicularis oris into wet lip mucosa, no tissue loss. No loose teeth or intraoral foreign body, normal facial sensation and facial movement. Patient reports no anticoagulants or allergies. Tetanus history uncertain. A fine-tip skin marker, anaesthesia equipment and simulated sutures are available. Candidate may describe layered sutures on model. If competence insufficient, must request maxillofacial support.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: The patient is concerned about a permanent notch in the lip and scar. They ask whether stitching will hurt and when they can go back to work.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: First assessment? — mechanism, time, contamination, bite/foreign body, teeth, facial sensation/movement, other trauma and tetanus status. Pre-block action? — identify and mark intact vermilion–cutaneous junction on both sides before local swelling distorts it. Anaesthesia? — explain suitable regional block or careful infiltration, with consent and allergy/dose checks; preserve landmarks. Closure? — irrigation, appropriate debridement, first precise vermilion-border alignment stitch; repair orbicularis and mucosa in layers with absorbable sutures, then skin with fine material. When refer? — tissue loss, crush, parotid duct or facial nerve concern, complex eyelid/ear injury or inability to align landmarks.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Initial priorities Starts sewing without excluding other trauma or persistent bleeding. Confirms stability, bleeding control and associated dental/facial injuries. Checks injury mechanism and examines lip both externally and intraorally. Consent and cosmesis Guarantees an invisible scar without explaining options. Explains procedure, pain control, scar and infection risks and obtains consent. Elicits high priority of cosmetic alignment and discusses specialist input where needed. Facial function Omits assessment of facial nerve, sensation and oral movement. Checks facial movement and local sensation before anaesthetic. Documents lip competence, dental status and when other structures require review. Vermilion mapping Fails to identify the vermilion border before distortion. Marks both vermilion border edges before injecting local anaesthetic. Plans first key alignment suture while checking symmetry against the opposite side. Wound preparation Closes an unclean wound over debris or retained tooth fragments. Provides anaesthesia, irrigation, inspection and conservative debridement. Uses asepsis, tissue preservation and reassesses for intraoral foreig
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Closes a contaminated or retained-foreign-body facial wound without assessment/irrigation. Misaligns the vermilion border substantially and ignores the resulting cosmetic deformity. Misses a significant facial nerve, parotid duct or complex associated injury requiring specialist management. Performs closure without effective anaesthesia or valid consent.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: After local anaesthetic is drawn up, the examiner says: “The wound crosses the vermilion junction and its landmarks are now starting to swell.” Expected: stop, identify/mark border, consider a regional block preserving landmarks, and align the border as first key stitch.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “Before injecting I need to identify and mark both vermilion edges.” “This wound traverses muscle, so I must repair deeper layers, not only the skin.” “The edges are stepped; I will remove and replace the alignment stitch before proceeding.”

stations.title: Extravasation Injury

sections.preamble: B2-292 | Extravasation Injury AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / plastics and infusion safety • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar asked to assess a patient with painful swelling near a peripheral cannula during an intravenous cytotoxic infusion. Explain your immediate assessment and management to the examiner. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Woman aged 58 receiving systemic anti-cancer therapy on a surgical oncology ward. Infusion is stopped on request, anthracycline agent confirmed from chart; infusion has been running 15 minutes since last site check. Forearm: painful tense swelling 7 × 5 cm, erythema, no visible blisters; fingers warm, refill 2 seconds, sensation and finger movement intact. Haemodynamically stable. A chemotherapy extravasation kit is available; clinical pharmacy, oncology and plastics on call.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient worries she will lose the arm and asks why the cannula cannot simply be removed. If asked about baseline: right-handed, no prior arm injury, no allergies known; consent and distress should be addressed.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: First action? — Stop infusion immediately, disconnect tubing, leave cannula in situ initially and summon oncology/chemotherapy specialist. Agent classification? — Identify exact drug, concentration, likely volume, time and whether vesicant; anthracyclines are vesicants. Next steps? — Attempt gentle aspiration via cannula under protocol, avoid flushing or massaging, mark/photograph swelling, assess distal neurovascular function and pain, remove cannula after aspiration according to pathway. Treatment? — Agent-specific antidote urgently with oncology/pharmacy advice; anthracycline options include dexrazoxane for indicated significant injury, with schedule/time window governed by chemotherapy protocol; compress choice varies by agent. Escalation? — Plastics review for progressing pain, blistering, skin changes, threatened perfusion or significant vesicant extravasation; monitor, document incident, arrange serial review.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Immediate recognition Continues infusion after swelling is reported. Stops infusion promptly and states suspected extravasation. Time-stamps stop and prevents further delivery while calling trained help. Cannula safety Immediately flushes the cannula or removes it before possible aspiration. Disconnects infusion; keeps cannula initially to attempt gentle aspiration. Specifies no flush, massage or compression of injured area and protocol-guided removal. Agent assessment Assumes all IV drugs cause identical tissue effects. Identifies anthracycline vesicant and verifies prescription and delivered amount. Documents volume estimate, concentration, elapsed time and anatomical location. Limb examination Does not examine fingers or document progression. Measures swelling and checks capillary refill, pulses, sensation and movement. Repeats neurovascular examination and checks for tense compartments or tissue necrosis. First local measures Applies unverified warm compress to an anthracycline injury. Aspiration, mark/photograph, analgesia and elevate as locally advised. Clarifies drug-specific hot/cold application with chemotherapy extravasation protocol. Ant
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Flushes the cannula, spreading a suspected vesicant injury. Allows vesicant infusion to continue despite pain and swelling. Misses threatened limb perfusion/compartment syndrome and fails to escalate. Fails to access the urgent agent-specific antidote pathway for anthracycline extravasation.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: “The fingers now feel numb and pain is escalating despite analgesia.” Expected: immediate repeat perfusion, motor, sensory and compartment assessment; urgent plastics and senior surgical review, while continuing oncology-directed antidote pathway.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I must leave the cannula in place until I have attempted gentle aspiration and checked protocol.” “This is an anthracycline; I will contact oncology pharmacy immediately about time-critical antidote treatment.” “The new numbness changes urgency: I am escalating possible neurovascular compromise now.”

stations.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma on the Lower Lip

near_match.title: Pathology: basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

sections.preamble: B2-293 | Squamous Cell Carcinoma on the Lower Lip AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / skin cancer and reconstructive surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A patient with a biopsy-proven 1.8 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the cutaneous lower lip has been referred. Describe staging, investigations and management, including how the anatomical site changes risk and reconstruction planning. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Man aged 71, cumulative sunlight exposure, growing crusted 1.8-cm lesion for 4 months just inferior to the lower vermilion border on cutaneous lip; biopsy reports invasive moderately differentiated cSCC, depth and perineural status not assessable on superficial sample. No obvious palpable cervical or submental nodes; oral mucosa appears uninvolved; normal facial movement and sensation. Immunocompetent, no prior head/neck cancer. The specimen is explicitly cutaneous; examine for vermilion or mucosal involvement rather than assume same pathway.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient worries about facial disfigurement and lymph-node spread, asks about radiotherapy instead and whether a normal-feeling neck guarantees no spread.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Initial assessment? — Confirm pathology and exact cutaneous vs vermilion/mucosal site; document tumour size, rapid growth, depth, ulceration, differentiation, perineural symptoms and immunosuppression. Examine? — Full lesion, mouth, lip movement/sensation, parotid, submental/submandibular and cervical nodal basins, skin field. Risk? — Lip is a high-risk site; depth, differentiation, perineural invasion, immunosuppression and recurrent disease add risk; consider specialist skin/head-and-neck MDT. Management? — Definitive surgical clearance with an appropriately planned margin or margin-controlled surgery selected by MDT; histology and margin status direct further treatment; reconstruction to preserve oral competence and appearance. Neck and imaging? — Clinically suspicious nodes need ultrasound and needle sampling per MDT; do not claim routine CT or elective neck surgery is obligatory for every small cSCC.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Anatomical classification Calls all lip SCC oral mucosal disease without checking location. Confirms lesion is cutaneous and checks proximity to vermilion/mucosa. Explains different guideline pathways if tumour crosses vermilion border. History and risk Ignores rapid growth, immunosuppression and sensory symptoms. Asks about growth, symptoms, previous cancers and immunosuppression. Screens for altered sensation, previous irradiation, scar or chronic wound origin. Focused examination Does not examine neck nodal basins or oral surface. Documents tumour size, lip and oral examination and regional neck nodes. Checks submental, submandibular and parotid areas and facial sensation. Histology interpretation Assumes superficial biopsy excludes deep/perineural disease. Recognises biopsy confirms invasive cSCC but not full depth or margins. Requests complete risk stratification from definitive histology and MDT review. Risk stratification Labels cutaneous lower lip a routine low-risk SCC solely because under 2 cm. Identifies lip location as a high-risk feature despite size. Integrates depth, differentiation, perineural involvement and immune status. Definiti
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Treats a suspicious growing lip SCC as a harmless lesion and delays definitive cancer care. Ignores a newly disclosed hard cervical node and does not initiate nodal assessment. Plans destructive treatment without obtaining tumour histology or margin control for invasive SCC. Fails to address signs of perineural involvement or deep invasive extension needing specialist escalation.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: “The patient now reports numbness of half the lower lip, new over six weeks.” Expected: recognise possible perineural invasion; urgent specialist head-and-neck/skin MDT discussion and targeted staging rather than routine local excision alone.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “I should distinguish cutaneous lip from vermilion or mucosal disease before selecting the pathway.” “Lip location itself contributes to higher risk, even with a lesion under two centimetres.” “New lip numbness suggests nerve involvement and changes the urgency and staging plan.”

stations.title: Hand Infection: Paronychia and Felon

sections.preamble: B2-294 | Hand Infection: Paronychia and Felon AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / hand surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: You are the surgical registrar assessing a 37-year-old chef with a painful swollen fingertip. Describe assessment, diagnosis, safe drainage decision, antibiotics and hand-surgical escalation. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Three days after pulling a hangnail, the right index finger has erythema and fluctuance at the lateral nail fold, plus a separate tense, exquisitely tender swelling of the fingertip pulp. Temperature 37.8°C, pulse 96, normal capillary refill and sensibility. There is no puncture wound or bite. On request: passive extension causes no pain; no fusiform whole-finger swelling; digit rests extended; no tenderness along flexor sheath. No vesicular clusters. No diabetes, immunosuppression or antibiotic allergy.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Patient has pain preventing work; asks whether tablets alone cure an abscess, whether you can lance the entire finger at home, and whether the infection could destroy the fingertip.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Distinguish conditions — Paronychia involves the periungual fold; felon is a closed-space volar pulp abscess. Confirm fluctuation, pulp tension and potential spread. Examine — Inspect nail folds, pulp, DIP joint and entire digit; assess sensation, circulation, movement, fever, wounds and bite history; check flexor sheath for Kanavel signs. Kanavel red flags — Fusiform digit swelling, flexed posture, pain with passive extension, flexor sheath tenderness; may not all be present, and clinical suspicion warrants urgent hand-surgery input. Initial care — Elevate, analgesia, suitable dressings, treat cellulitis as indicated; a drainable abscess needs appropriate drainage by trained clinician; send pus for culture where appropriate. Escalation — Hand surgery for complex/deep infection, threatened tissue, flexor sheath suspicion, tendon/joint involvement, immunocompromise or failed initial treatment. Avoid incision over neurovascular bundles; check herpetic whitlow before drainage.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Anatomical diagnosis Labels all fingertip swelling simple cellulitis. Distinguishes nail-fold paronychia from tense pulp-space felon. Explains confined pulp septa increase pressure and tissue risk. History Omits mechanism, progression and systemic illness. Asks onset, hangnail, bites, trauma, fever and comorbidities. Checks puncture, water exposure, diabetes and prior MRSA. Focused hand examination Does not check sensation or distal perfusion. Inspects nail and pulp, and checks movement, sensation and capillary refill. Checks whole digit, tendon and joint involvement with documented baseline. Flexor sheath recognition Ignores painful passive finger extension. Screens for Kanavel signs and asks about extension pain. Recognises incomplete signs do not exclude early flexor tenosynovitis. Abscess treatment Prescribes oral antibiotics alone for a tense fluctuant felon. Recognises need for appropriate drainage of confirmed abscess. Separates simple nail-fold drainage from specialist pulp-space approach. Antibiotic strategy Gives antibiotics for every minor sterile nail-fold irritation. Selects antibiotics for spreading infection/systemic risk according t
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Fails to identify suspected flexor sheath infection and delays urgent hand-surgery assessment. Attempts incision and drainage of a suspected herpetic whitlow. Ignores neurovascular compromise or severe progressive pulp-space infection. Treats an established tense felon abscess with antibiotics alone and no drainage/escalation plan.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: “Now passive extension is very painful and the finger has become uniformly swollen.” Expected: reclassify as possible pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis, immediate hand surgeon contact, admission for IV antibiotics and urgent operative assessment.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “The pain with passive extension changes my diagnosis: this may be flexor sheath sepsis.” “A tense pulp abscess needs appropriate drainage, not tablets alone.” “I will check for herpetic vesicles before any incision.”

stations.title: Gastroschisis or Exomphalos?

sections.preamble: B2-295 | Gastroschisis or Exomphalos? AMaC MRCS Part B • Applied knowledge / paediatric surgery • 8-minute simulated station • Draft for specialist sign-off
sections.1. Candidate brief: A baby has been delivered with bowel visible outside the abdomen. Interpret the verbal examination findings, distinguish gastroschisis from exomphalos and describe immediate neonatal care and surgical planning. Eight minutes.
sections.2. Examiner brief — findings disclosed o: Term infant, 3.0 kg, delivered in a district hospital. To the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord is a small full-thickness paraumbilical defect; exposed swollen small-bowel loops have NO covering membrane. Temperature 36.1°C, HR 165, capillary refill 3 seconds, mild dehydration. Pre-delivery scan suggested abdominal-wall defect; neonatal and transfer teams available. For contrast, an exomphalos is a central umbilical defect with membrane-covered contents, frequently associated with other anomalies.
sections.3. Patient / actor brief: Parent asks whether the exposed bowel can be pushed back immediately, whether this is their fault and whether the baby will feed normally. Provide reassurance without promising a fixed length of admission.
sections.4. Examiner prompts and expected finding: Identify — Paraumbilical usually right-sided exposed bowel with no sac and separate cord insertion favours gastroschisis; central membrane-covered defect involving cord insertion favours exomphalos. Initial neonatal priorities — ABC, warmth, protect and support bowel in sterile transparent bowel bag/wrap without twisting vascular pedicle, no feeding, gastric decompression with oro/nasogastric tube, IV access, glucose and fluid/electrolyte monitoring, neonatal IV antibiotics by local protocol. Fluid safety — Expect increased evaporative losses; resuscitate according to perfusion and neonatal guidance, monitor urine output and avoid unmonitored fluid overload. Associated conditions — Gastroschisis: bowel atresia/ischaemia/short bowel possible; exomphalos: increased association with cardiac, chromosomal and syndromic abnormalities; neonatal assessment/echocardiography and genetics when indicated. Definitive surgery — Urgent tertiary neonatal and paediatric-surgical consultation/transfer; assess bowel viability; primary closure when safe or staged silo reduction to avoid respiratory or perfusion compromise. Large exomphalos can require deferred closure.
sections.5. Nine-domain marking grid: Domain Fail Pass High-performance Morphological recognition Calls exposed right-sided bowel in an uncovered defect exomphalos. Identifies gastroschisis from uncovered bowel lateral to cord. Contrasts membrane-covered central defect of exomphalos. Initial stabilization Attempts forced bedside bowel replacement before stabilization. Runs newborn ABC assessment, warming and perfusion checks. Coordinates neonatology and transfer without delays from unnecessary tests. Bowel protection Leaves exposed bowel uncovered or twisted. Uses sterile bowel bag and protects bowel from heat and fluid loss. Maintains bowel vascular orientation and observes colour/perfusion. Decompression and feeding Starts oral feeds in a baby with exteriorised bowel. Keeps nil orally and places gastric tube for decompression. Documents aspirates and monitors abdominal distension and breathing. Fluids and monitoring Gives no IV fluids despite hypovolaemia. Starts IV access, glucose, electrolytes and perfusion-guided fluid management. Tracks urine, temperature, lactate/acid-base and avoids excessive fluid boluses. Infection prevention Handles uncovered bowel without aseptic precautions. Uses sterile protection and neo
sections.6. Four specific critical fails: Forcibly reduces swollen bowel without specialist assessment, risking ischaemia/compartment syndrome. Leaves exposed bowel unprotected during assessment or transfer. Fails to recognise circulatory compromise/hypothermia and delays neonatal resuscitation. Attempts routine feeding instead of gastric decompression and urgent surgical transfer.
sections.7. Curveball and expected response: Examiner: “During preparation for transport the bowel becomes dusky and the infant becomes increasingly tachycardic.” Expected: urgent bowel perfusion and mesenteric twist assessment without manipulation, ABC resuscitation, protect bowel, immediate senior neonatal/paediatric surgical escalation and accelerate transfer.
sections.8. Three station-specific recovery lines: “No protective membrane and a defect beside the cord indicate gastroschisis.” “I must prevent heat and fluid loss and ensure the bowel is not twisted.” “Dusky bowel requires immediate senior review before attempting reduction.”

bleep_cards.text: "id": "BLEEP-34", "title": "Upper or lower GI bleed", "fpc_tags": ["Clinical assessment", "Clinical prioritisation", "Communication and care"], "scenario": "Nurse bleeps: \"Mr Price has just vomited a large amount of fresh blood, he looks pale and his BP is 95 over 55.\"", "nurse_call": [ { "lead": "Is it ongoing?", "text": "Ask whether the bleeding is ongoing right now — if it is, this is a major haemorrhage and you need to attend immediately" }, { "lead": "Full obs + NEWS2", "text": "Ask for the full set of observations including BP, heart rate, and the NEWS2 score — tachycardia and hypotension indicate significant blood loss" }, { "lead": "IV access + fluids", "text": "Ask the nurse to get two large-bore IV cannulas, start IV fluids, and send bloods including a group and save and crossmatch" }, { "lead": "Resuscitation trolley", "text": "Ask the nurse to bring the resuscitation trolley and have the major haemorrhage protocol available" }, { "lead": "Anticoagulants and NSAIDs", "text": "Ask whether the patient is on any anticoagulant or antiplatelet, and whether they have been taking NSAIDs" }, { "lead": "Previous bleeds", "text": "Ask about any previous GI bleeds, known liver disease, or previous endoscopy" } ], "first_five_minutes": [ { "lead": "ABCDE and resuscitate", "text": "Assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure — the priority is resuscitation, not diagnosis" }, { "lead": "Call for help", "text": "Call the medical registrar and the gastroenterology team urgently — and activate the major haemorrhage protocol if the patient is unstable" }, { "lead": "Assess severity with Blatchford", "text": "Use the Glasgow-Blatchford score at first assessment for all patients with acute upper GI bleeding, and consider early discharge for patients with a pre-endoscopy Blatchford score of 0 or 1 [citation:5]" }, { "lead": "Blood products", "text": "Transfuse according to local major haemorrhage protocols — do not over-transfuse, as this can be as damaging as under-transfusion [citation:5]" }, { "lead": "Review medications", "text": "Stop NSAIDs during the acute phase, and discuss the risks and benefits of continuing clopidogrel (or other antiplatelet agents) with the relevant specialist [citation:5]" }, { "lead": "Do not give acid suppression before endoscopy", "text": "Do not offer acid-suppression drugs before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding — they are offered after endoscopy if stigmata of recent haemorrhage are seen [citation:5]" }, { "lead": "Timing of endoscopy", "text": "Offer endoscopy to unstable patients immediately after resuscitation, and within 24 hours to all other patients with upper GI bleeding [citation:5]" }, { "lead": "Consider variceal bleeding", "text": "If the patient has known liver disease, give terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding at presentation unless contraindicated, and involve the hepatology team [citation:6]" } ], bleep_cards.text: "id": "BLEEP-38", "title": "Ascites and abdominal distension", "fpc_tags": ["Clinical assessment", "Clinical prioritisation", "Holistic planning"], "scenario": "Nurse bleeps: \"Mr Green's abdomen has become much more distended over the last few days, he says he feels breathless and uncomfortable.\"", "nurse_call": [ { "lead": "Full obs + NEWS2", "text": "Ask for the full set of observations including respiratory rate, saturations, and the NEWS2 score" }, { "lead": "Breathlessness", "text": "Ask whether the patient is breathless — this may be due to diaphragmatic splinting from ascites or to a pleural effusion" }, { "lead": "Weight and fluid balance", "text": "Ask for the recent weight and fluid balance — rapid weight gain suggests fluid accumulation" }, { "lead": "Liver history and medications", "text": "Ask about known liver disease, alcohol intake, and current medications including diuretics" }, { "lead": "Confusion", "text": "Ask whether the patient has been confused or drowsy — this may suggest hepatic encephalopathy" } ], "first_five_minutes": [ { "lead": "ABCDE and assess respiratory status", "text": "Assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure — if the patient is breathless, this may need urgent drainage, but the priority is stabilising the patient first" }, { "lead": "Examine the abdomen", "text": "Examine for ascites (shifting dullness, fluid thrill) and look for signs of chronic liver disease and hepatic encephalopathy [citation:7]" }, { "lead": "Bloods and urine", "text": "Send FBC, U&E, LFTs, clotting, and a diagnostic ascitic tap if appropriate — send ascitic fluid for cell count, culture, and albumin [citation:7]" }, { "lead": "Calculate the SAAG", "text": "Calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) — this helps distinguish portal hypertensive ascites from other causes" }, { "lead": "Consider SBP", "text": "Consider spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) — send ascitic fluid for neutrophil count and culture, and assess the risk based on ascitic protein and Child-Pugh or MELD scores [citation:7]" }, { "lead": "Review diuretics and sodium", "text": "Review the diuretic regimen — treatment typically starts with spironolactone and adds furosemide if needed, with close monitoring of renal function and electrolytes [citation:7]" }, { "lead": "Consider paracentesis", "text": "For tense or refractory ascites, consider large volume paracentesis — this can be done in a day case setting, with albumin infusion to prevent circulatory dysfunction [citation:7]" }, { "lead": "Escalate if tense or refractory", "text": "Escalate if the ascites is tense and causing respiratory compromise, if there is suspected SBP, or if the patient is not responding to diuretics [citation:7]" } ], "can_i_do_alone": { "alone": "Assessing the abdomen for ascites, reviewing the diuretic regimen and fluid balance, sending bloods and a diagnostic ascitic tap (if competent and bleep_cards.text: "id": "BLEEP-44", "title": "New cellulitis / wound infection", "fpc_tags": ["Clinical assessment", "Clinical prioritisation", "Understanding medicine"], "scenario": "Nurse bleeps: \"Mr Reid's leg has become red and swollen around his surgical wound, it's spreading and it feels hot.\"", "nurse_call": [ { "lead": "Full obs + NEWS2", "text": "Ask for the full set of observations and the NEWS2 score — systemic symptoms determine the urgency" }, { "lead": "Draw around the edge", "text": "Ask the nurse to consider drawing around the extent of the redness with a surgical marker pen to monitor progress — but be aware that redness may be less visible on darker skin tones [citation:18]" }, { "lead": "Wound site", "text": "Ask whether the wound is clean, discharging, or dehisced, and whether there is any discharge or fluctuance" }, { "lead": "Pain out of proportion?", "text": "Ask about pain — pain out of proportion to the visible infection is a red flag for necrotising fasciitis [citation:18]" }, { "lead": "Risk factors", "text": "Ask about diabetes, venous insufficiency, eczema, oedema, or immunosuppression — these predispose to cellulitis and affect management [citation:18]" } ], "first_five_minutes": [ { "lead": "ABCDE and NEWS2", "text": "Assess airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure — if the patient is systemically unwell, this is a more serious picture" }, { "lead": "Examine the area", "text": "Examine the wound and the surrounding skin — look for spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, discharge, and any crepitus or blistering that might suggest a deeper infection" }, { "lead": "Assess for complications", "text": "Look specifically for signs of lymphangitis, abscess, or necrotising fasciitis — severe pain out of proportion to the visible infection, crepitus, or rapid progression are red flags [citation:18]" }, { "lead": "Consider the cause", "text": "Consider whether this is simple cellulitis, a wound infection, an abscess, or a deeper infection — and whether there is an underlying condition (diabetes, oedema, venous insufficiency) that needs managing [citation:18]" }, { "lead": "Antibiotics", "text": "Give oral antibiotics first-line if the patient can take oral medicines and is not severely unwell — follow your local antimicrobial guidelines.
